en: Prosperity!
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja.
Salutations to the Supreme Brahman, Śrī Raṅganātha.
The First Chapter.
Oṃ. Salutations to the wielder of the discus, the bestower of all auspiciousness, who is the cause of deliverance for those submerged in the ocean of sense-objects. || 1 ||
In the sacred field on the peak of Mount Totā, frequented by gods and gandharvas, endowed with holy pilgrimage sites, and filled with flowers of every season. || 2 ||
It was endowed with praiseworthy hermitages, graced by sacred fields,
and inhabited by great ṛṣis devoted to austerity and established in the Vedas and Vedāntas.
[He was attended] by those versed in the tenets of Sāṃkhya, those who knew the principles of Yoga,
those conversant with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and those skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras.
It was likewise joined by celestial sages skilled in the knowledge of the Vedāṅgas,
as well as by royal sages and high-souled masters who had attained perfection through mantras.
The great ascetic Sanaka, a son of Brahmā and a seer of yoga,
performed extremely difficult penance for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the Blessed One.
Even though he meditated upon the Supreme Self within himself for a hundred years,
performing most rigorous austerities, he did not obtain his desired goal.
Then that sage was overcome by great sorrow;
he, who had conquered anger and mastered his senses, became submerged in an ocean of grief.
To him who was self-controlled, devoted to the limbs of yoga, and a devotee, the Sustainer of the World— who is affectionate toward his devotees— spoke these words for the welfare of the world.
Vāsudeva, the supreme light, the invisible Puruṣottama,
the Blessed Lord, said:
"O Lord of Yogins, you have performed most excellent penance here."
O Brahmin, you shall obtain the fruit of your great asceticism before long;
take heart, may prosperity be yours, and do not despair, O high-minded one.
In this world, the great Śāṇḍilya is renowned as one who has accomplished all that was to be done;
take refuge in him—may prosperity be yours—for the sake of attaining the dharma of the Blessed One.
Long ago, on this best of mountains,
by this high-souled one [the teaching] was received directly from the manifest Lord Acyuta, who is designated as Acyuta.
He has studied the *Trisuparṇa* and other such texts that directly express the True Brahman,
as well as all the Vedic branches (*śākhās*), the *Nigamas*, the *Saṃhitās*, and those designated as *Brāhmaṇas*.
Then, the etymologies were understood, as well as the seven categories of meaning in their proper order;
furthermore, knowledge was known to be twofold, consisting of both the various scriptures and [direct] cognition. (15)
Having thus heard this first scripture, known as the Rahasyāmnāya, which consists of thirteen types of ritual action joined with the twelvefold primordial self. (16)

Endowed with the sequence of divine mantras and characterized by liberation as its sole fruit, it was [expounded] once more by him, who desires the welfare of the world, having been further impelled. (17)
Indeed, that scripture which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation has been heard by me in its entirety;
it was proclaimed by the Blessed One himself, composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter. (18)
The Sātvata, the Pauṣkara, the Jayākhyā, and so forth—all that was fully known by the high-souled Śāṇḍilya. || 19 ||
Thus Śāṇḍilya, the supreme teacher who knew all the scriptures,
dwelt in his own hermitage— which destroys all fatigue— surrounded by his disciples.
O sage, he who always performs the supreme sacrifice of the five times (pañcakālya) and is ever self-controlled—
he, the knower of dharma, will explain to you the Bhāgavata dharma.
"Take refuge in him; may prosperity be yours for the sake of attaining the wisdom of the Blessed One.
Having spoken thus, the voice uttered by Vāsudeva vanished.
Having heard these most wonderful words, the great sage’s hair stood on end with joy; at that moment, he considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Desiring a vision of Śāṇḍilya,
he traveled toward the lord of mountains and beheld the excellent hermitage of the high-souled Śāṇḍilya.
It was strewn with various flowers, endowed with various fruits, frequented by flocks of various birds, and inhabited by various wild animals. || 25 ||
It was adorned with lotus-pools filled with various kinds of lotuses and water-lilies,
and with peaceful, free-from-envy people devoted to the desire to know the dharma of the Blessed One.
Having entered that place, which was crowded everywhere with the foremost of sages and seekers of liberation,
he beheld it being attended by the chief ascetics.
Seeing him surrounded by disciples who were peaceful, established in the self, and supremely compassionate; endowed with divine knowledge and devoted to divine rites.
Sanaka, bearing supreme devotion for Vāsudeva, the highest of the high,
reverently prostrated at his feet.
Having seen with his divine eye Sanaka, who was born of Brahmā, standing firm in the dharma of the Blessed One, Śāṇḍilya, that tiger among sages, [spoke].
He spoke these sweet words: "O great sage, you have achieved your purpose;
the Blessed One is well-pleased with you, for your supreme austerity has been well-performed. (31)
"I have been commanded by the Blessed One for your sake, O storehouse of asceticism";
having said this, he taught him the Veda named Ekāyana.
But that which is the great root of the vast tree of the Veda is the sole refuge of the supreme reality known as the True Brahman, Vāsudeva.
It is adorned with divine mantras such as the Balā-mantras which directly convey its meaning;
it is free from doubt and dispels the darkness of ignorance.
Having instructed him, Śāṇḍilya spoke of his true nature and his attainment:
"This is the dharma of the Kṛta age, known as action performed without desire for rewards. (35)
The assembly known as Yoga, known as Yogadharma, and known as Śāstra is set in motion by the Blessed One in each of the first ages.
In the ages, as well as in all other times, there is a slow movement [of time] due to the eternal Aniruddha, the supervisor of infinite activity.
The first birth of Brahmā is remembered as mental; the second is said to be from his eye; another is the third, from his speech; and the fourth arises from his ear.
There is another, the Nāsikya, as well as the Aṇḍaja and the Padmaja;
in all of these as well, [the presence] of the omnipresent Lord is manifest.
By Brahmā, the foremost sages, Suparṇa and other great ṛṣis, and likewise by others headed by the Vālakhilyas and the royal sages in due order; || 40 ||
O twice-born one, this first [creation], known as the creation of primordial nature (prakṛti-dharma), was studied;
likewise, it was attained by the Blessed One during the seventh lotus-born creation.
From him it was obtained by Vivasvat, and from him by Manu Ikṣvāku;
and having been proclaimed by Ikṣvāku, it remained pervading all the worlds.
This alone is the great, primordial, and eternal Dharma, O Brahmin;
it is difficult to understand and difficult to perform, yet it is always maintained by the Sātvatas.
[They should be] always devoted to the Cāturātmya [mantras], dedicated to the five times (pañcakāla), intent on the mantras beginning with Bala, and free from devotion to other deities. || 44 ||
Listen as I speak of this Dharma just as it was attained by me:
formerly, the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and Upaniṣads were studied by me.
Those known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas], however, are intermingled with other deities;
being joined with mixed sacrifices, they bestow the fruits of worldly activity. || 46 ||
And those meanings were fully understood by him according to the rule and according to the prescribed method;
in various places, [he beheld] the Blessed One, the Lord of the World.
For they declare that his action and knowledge are not mediated by means;
likewise, they are extremely condensed and their characteristics are unmanifest.
Even in many different locations, they proclaim the Lord of the World solely through the mediation of Agni, Indra, and others; and so too do all ritual actions. (49)
O best of sages, they explain at great length that the daily rites and other such acts, which are joined with the fruits of worldly activity, are performed through the channels of other deities.
Likewise, O Brahmin, in various places they speak only of that ritual in great detail,
excluding the deities such as Indra and others.
There, the mantras were for the most part accompanied by attachment to their fruits;
thus, because of this mixed nature, he did not find steadfastness in them.
But he who is devoted solely to Vāsudeva, having abandoned other deities, possesses that supreme dharma than which nothing is greater. (53)
Then, a powerful desire to know that [truth] arose within me;
thereafter, I performed supreme austerity here on this best of mountains.
At the end of many thousands of years of austerity,
at the conclusion of the Dvāpara Yuga and the beginning of the Kali Yuga.
Having received it directly from the manifest Saṅkarṣaṇa, this most excellent [knowledge] was obtained;
this is the Veda of the single path, renowned as the Sātvata injunction.
Difficult to understand and difficult to practice, it is cultivated by those who have awakened;
this is the path leading to liberation, and no other exists. 57.
Therefore, the wise call it "the Single Path" (Ekāyana),
which was studied of old in Śvetadvīpa by the celestial sage Nārada.
Sana, Sanatsujāta, you yourself as Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, Kapila, and Sanātana as the seventh. || 59 ||
These are the teachers and the promulgators of the religion of the single-minded devotees:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (60)
And Vasiṣṭha of great splendor— these are the Citraśikhaṇḍins—
as well as Manu Svāyambhuva, having propitiated the Lord of the Universe.
And through great austerity, having studied for a thousand divine years until their conclusion, they worshipped the Lord, the Master Nārāyaṇa.
The sages were taught the original revelation exactly as it was by them;
then those eight sages, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, [proceeded].
Having examined the root Veda consisting of hundreds of thousands of verses,
they likewise composed the divine Tantras, such as the Sātvata and others.
Furthermore, Manu and others shall likewise duly compose various other treatises known as Tantras,
as well as many Dharmaśāstras.
This shall be the source of other treatises as well;
for within it, both Dharma and Artha have been explained in great detail.
Liberation has been indicated previously and is now described here exactly as it is;
likewise, sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, concerning the Imperishable Hari, have been taught.
And just as they are performed,
so too [are they done] with the mantras of Hari that are unique to him, which begin with the twelve syllables and yield the fruit of cessation (nivṛtti).

When worshipped, all the mantras beginning with the Ṛgveda are employed in their respective rituals; this has been proclaimed in this very context. King Uparicara Vasu was consecrated by means of the Mūla-veda.
This has been stated in the manner described for the purpose of attaining authority over the heavenly world.
He performed sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha according to the prescribed rules,
as well as other sacrifices dedicated to the Blessed One, because his livelihood and authority had become exhausted.
Thus, O Brahmin, that very meaning which was previously heard by me through sacred revelation now appears clearly to me: Sumantu, Jaimini, Bhṛgu, and Aupagāyana. (72)
And Maunjayana—having been thoroughly instructed by me in all that [knowledge] by Nara and Narayana out of a desire for the welfare of the world. (73)
In this manner, the fundamental dharma is practiced at Badarikāśrama;
this is known as the natural dharma, which has Vāsudeva alone as its object.
In the Kṛta Yuga it proceeds thus; thereafter, in the Tretā Yuga and the others, the Vedas undergo modification everywhere, and their scope shifts toward different deities.
This great [Purāṇa] is the root of the vast tree of the Vedas;
O Sage, the Ṛgveda and the others are its trunk, and likewise, they are its branches.
O twice-born one, it is established that the status of being called the "Root Veda" belongs primarily to Lord Vāsudeva, the root of the universe, as its proponent. 77.
In the Kṛta Yuga, which was the primordial age, human beings were capable of constantly practicing the original dharma of the Lord.
Then, in the Tretā Yuga, all people, endowed with various desires and performing mixed sacrifices, abandon the primordial, eternal [Brahman].
All this, brought forth by Vāsudeva, disappears;
thereafter, the Blessed One himself manifests for the one who is worthy.
O great sage, just as the Veda was previously obtained by me from the God through the power of my own knowledge, so has it been revealed along with its secret mysteries.
When this had been thus correctly spoken by the high-souled Śāṇḍilya,
he then, considering himself to have achieved his purpose, joined his palms in reverence.
Sanaka spoke these humble words to the sage Śāṇḍilya:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures! (83)
Through your grace, I have attained this great and supreme Dharma known as characterized by cessation (nivṛtti),
which is practiced by those who have awakened.
How can those who are unawakened and submerged in the great ocean of existence attain the Dharma of the Blessed One, which is practiced by those who are single-mindedly devoted? (85)
O Śāṇḍilya, listen; I shall declare that which I was urged by you.
For this very purpose, I previously questioned the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa.
For those who, having abandoned the supreme dharma, have resorted to a mixed dharma, yet still desire that state and have attained faith and devotion; || 87 ||
For the sake of favoring the social classes and for bringing about their fitness, as well as for the attainment of the desired fruits by all people. || 88 ||
Having taught the divine scriptures, such as the Sātvata and others, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, immediately thereafter— (89)
O bull among sages, this is especially the essence of all the scriptures of the Supreme Lord, which establishes the meaning of the Pauṣkara.
In accordance with the root Vedas and in the Anuṣṭubh meter,
this work of one hundred thousand verses is composed for the sake of attaining knowledge of the performance of all purposes.
He spoke to me that great treatise known by the name Pārameśvara;
from that, however, I have extracted the essence which is useful for all scriptures. (92)
I shall now fully proclaim to you this scripture, known by the name Pārameśvara, consisting of sixteen thousand verses; attend to it with focused attention.
O twice-born one, Nārada also formerly heard this very thing in brief directly from the Lord who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
It is divided into two parts by way of the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) and the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa),
wherein the all-pervading Vāsudeva is perfectly glorified.
The divine nature of the Self and the eternal qualities beginning with knowledge—these six primary attributes exist both collectively and individually within the three pairs. (96)
Other qualities such as fame and the like, as well as the supreme form, are eternally one and called Vāsudeva; from Him proceeds the cause of creation and so forth.
The cosmic array beginning with the withdrawal of the world, as well as the birth and other states of the universe, exist for the purpose of worship by devoted and high-souled believers. || 98 ||

For the sake of benefiting the worlds, the fourth manifestation (turīyaka) of the all-pervading Vāsudeva, whose nature is higher than the highest, consists of the fourfold arrangement (caturvyūha). || 99 ||
The array known as deep sleep, likewise the dream array, the waking array, and other arrays that are distinct forms [of manifestation]. (100)
The forms known as the Vibhavas, as well as the various other manifestations (Prādurbhāvas), and the eternal natures of Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi, exist together with the Blessed Lord. || 101 ||
The incarnations such as Kānti and others are the embodiments of ornaments;
those beginning with the crown are eternal, while other various types are non-eternal. || 102 ||
The essential nature of the discus and other [emblems], as well as of Garuḍa and the others, and even of the various individual souls (ātman), consists of both the eternal and the non-eternal.
Of these, who are the eternal embodiments of the Lord's own respective natures and serve as His means of accomplishment, the forms are of various kinds—both eternal and non-eternal. (104)
The eternal abode of the all-pervading Vāsudeva is indeed higher than the highest;
and likewise is that of the other forms of manifestation and expansions.
There are many various kinds of stainless places,
and their extent and measure are each established according to its own nature.
The number, measurement, and characteristics of its halls and gateways;
and the true nature of the individual souls (jīvātman), which consists of both the liberated and the unliberated. || 107 ||
The specific destinies of those who have the form of mantras, O Blessed One, as well as those of others, are proclaimed in detail and in their proper sequence. (108)
Mantra-meditation, as well as mudrā and the form of yoga, are proclaimed;
all this is celebrated under the designation of the Jñānakāṇḍa. || 109 ||
Wherein all the obligatory rites, such as ritual bathing and the rest, as well as the occasional, the optional, and the expiatory rites are described in detail. (110)
Various activities such as weighing and carrying loads, as well as all tasks beginning with plowing and ending with the establishment [of the image], in their entirety; || 111 ||
And the characteristics of palaces, images, auspicious thrones, and so forth—these and other such things are for the purpose of worshiping the Lord of Gods. || 112 ||
In that [text] where the ritual section (kriyākāṇḍa) is proclaimed in detail, know that to be it; thus, understand that the scripture is of two kinds, which I shall now declare. 113.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Scripture," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ!
In the section on ritual action (Kriyākāṇḍa), the second chapter:
Śāṇḍilya says— Now, for the sake of establishing eligibility, I shall first describe the ritual bath (snāna).
By this, the devotee who has been consecrated becomes worthy of performing sacrifices and fire-offerings.
One should perform two kinds of bathing for the purification of defilements by contact with impurities:
having bathed according to the general procedure, one should then bathe according to the specific procedure.
Bathing is of two kinds: the common worldly bath and the distinguished bath consecrated by mantras.
That too should be preceded by purification; therefore, I shall first explain that to you. (3)
Having reached the Brāhma-muhūrta, even before sunrise,
one who knows the mantras and is self-restrained should perform the rite according to the procedure prescribed by rule.
Having fully awakened at dawn, he should rise and, remaining upon his bed,
diligently perform the recitation of the sixteen names.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva; salutations to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa!
May there be salutations to you, Pradyumna; salutations to you, Aniruddha. (6)
Gradually, O twice-born one, [one should worship] from Keśava up to Dāmodara:
"Salutations, salutations to Keśava; salutations to Nārāyaṇa. (7)
Salutation indeed to Mādhava, and then salutation to Govinda;
one should then offer salutation to Viṣṇu, saying, "Salutation to you, O Madhusūdana. (8)
Salutations to Trivikrama, and then salutations to Vāmana;
salutations to Śrīdhara, and then Oṃ, salutations to Hṛṣīkeśa.
Salutations to Padmanābha, and salutations to Dāmodara as well;
now follows the glorification of the ten divine incarnations.
For the Lord in the forms of Ekaśṛṅga and the others, worship is prescribed in due order:
"Salutations to You in the form of the Fish; salutations again and again to the Tortoise. (11)
Salutations be to you, the primordial Varāha; salutations to you, the Man-lion (Narasimha);
salutations to you in the form of Vāmana; and salutations to the three Rāmas.
"Obration to Kṛṣṇa, the creator, who wields the axe, the bowstring, and the plough as weapons!
O twice-born one, let there first be 'obeisance to you, O Kalki-Viṣṇu,' preceded by the Praṇava. (13)
One should pay homage to these manifestations of the omnipresent Lord Hari in their established order,
at dawn, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, and at the end of the day.
Then, with a voice raised even higher and producing great joy,
he further uttered hymns and other mantras.
Having thus praised the Lord of Śrī with these and other hymns of praise,
he made this request to Hari, the bestower of boons.
Uttering "Hari, Hari," O high-minded one, he should rise from his bed and place his left foot upon the ground, saying, "Salutation to the Supporter of the Earth."
O Sage, first one should indeed move that very vessel filled with water, which has been empowered by the Astra-mantra, for the purpose of going outside.
Not in the presence of gods, fire, mountains, or cow-pens; nor by a river, nor in a cremation ground; nor on an anthill, in a mouse-hole, at the root of a tree, or in a temple. || 19 ||
One should never collect [the earth] from within water or on a path;
it should be taken from a pleasant place, leaving a space of four finger-breadths [around the root].
That which is free from animal parts, chaff, ashes, bones, wood, and clods of earth,
and which remains after the highest purification, should always be used by men desiring their own welfare.
One should bury [the remains] in an auspicious location that is free of charcoal, free of frost, black in color, and devoid of sand, using weapons and other implements consecrated with mantras.
Then he should bring earth that is free from defects,
as well as other requisites for bathing, and branches of the Śamī tree together with their foliage.
[One should take] Arka, Nyagrodha, Khadira, Karañja, Kakubha, and so forth;
as well as Śara, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Darbha grass, and bamboo. || 24 ||
One should collect mango sprouts, apāmārga, arjuna, dhātakī, śamī, and other purifying substances that are available among them. || 25 ||
Having employed this [practice] like a king according to the occasion,
one should not perform bathing in a well when tanks and other such bodies of water are available.
One should not bathe in those holy places that have little water when there are others with abundant water;
moreover, a practitioner should not bathe even in these [latter] if a river is available.
Among all rivers as well, those that flow to the ocean are distinguished;
and among those, all those whose currents always flow toward the east are preeminent.
Of all rivers as well, the southern bank is the most excellent;
likewise, those that flow toward the east are superior where they turn to face the north.
There, on the eastern bank, is a sacred ford that destroys all sins;
a stepped well is ten times more meritorious than a well, and a river is ten times more meritorious than a stepped well.
The fruit obtained by a bather in a river that flows to the ocean is such;
however, a river flowing eastward produces ten times that fruit for him.
On the eastern bank of the river Prāksrotas, which flows toward the north, one obtains infinite fruit;
however, after first washing the bank, one should sprinkle it with water and establish [the image] separately.
O Sage, having fetched earth for the sake of purification and placed it on the bank of the water, one should take a vessel filled with water, consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Having spread grass upon the ground in a pleasant and pure place,
during the daytime or at the twilights, with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) worn over the ear, he should face the north.
If one must void urine or excrement at night, one should face the south;
however, one should not void feces or urine upon the ground where long-lived creatures might be present.
Neither in water nor on a mountain, nor at courtyards or crossroads;
neither on the royal highway nor in a street, nor anywhere in a temple of the gods. || 36 ||

O best of Brahmins, one should not perform it in a cremation ground, nor at a shrine, nor in ashes, nor in a cow-pen, nor in the middle of a village; nor should one do so otherwise than according to the prescribed rule.
One should never urinate on one's own shadow or the shadow of a tree;
nor, having covered the head, should one look at the cardinal directions while impure.
Likewise, he saw celestial lights and the abodes of the deities,
as well as excrement joined with the anus, along with wood, leaves, grass, and other such things.
Having wiped himself with his left hand, and holding his penis with that same palm,
he should rise and go to the water's edge.
With water that was pleasant to the touch, held between his two thighs, he washed the anus; and with water being poured from the outside of his right knee, [he washed] the exterior. || 41 ||
Seated in the cock-posture with the left hand [supporting] the right,
he should perform the purification for cleanliness using earth and water drawn up [from a well], without touching the bathing-place.
One should perform purification untiringly so as to remove both odor and residue;
three applications of earth should be made to the penis, and one application of earth for each subsequent part.
Five [applications of earth] should be given to the left hand, and three to both hands for the sake of purification;
this is the purification after voiding urine, and likewise immediately after voiding feces. (44)
The first clay is prescribed as being the measure of half a prasṛti;
the second and the third are proclaimed to be half of that [respectively]. || 45 ||
That [space] above is proclaimed to be the size of a cat's footprint;
there should be five applications of clay at the anus, and likewise for the intervening parts.
Ten [applications] should be given to the left hand, and seven to both hands;
purification of the feet is achieved with three, and purification of the shanks with five.
Then, O Brahmin, one should apply seven applications of clay to the waist;
these destroy the fault of bodily perspiration and serve to neutralize external filth. (48)
For devotees and for those learned in the Vedas, this has been prescribed specifically for the rainy season;
therefore, compared to what was said regarding the monsoon, there is the removal of even a single [day] of softness.
Those devoted to ritual action should always perform [the bath] during autumn, summer, and spring; even from among these, however, one should omit a single [season] at a time. 50.

O Brahmin, during the winter and the cool seasons, those learned in the Vedas who abide in self-restraint should perform the purification of the paths in accordance with the requirements of place and time.
In this way, by removing the smear of odor, the mind becomes pure through mental purification;
however, for the washing of the feet, [the amount of water] prescribed is equal to the footprint of a cat.
For the four classes of foremost twice-born, there are three, two, and one application of earth respectively;
for the castes ending with the Śūdras, it is likewise for the cleansing of the hips.
Seven times from the thighs and three times from the hands;
this is declared to be the common rule for the purification of all [the limbs].
O best of the twice-born, having placed the two arms with the hands between the knees, and having taken four portions of perfectly pure water held at the wrists; 55.
Then the Brahmin should drink [the water] free from bubbles and the like, with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
he should then reduce the quantity by one measure for each of the three castes in succession.
The wise man should rinse his mouth again with water washed by the hand itself;
having thus washed according to the rule and rinsed his mouth, he becomes restrained and pure.
Then, having sat upon a seat facing either the east or the north,
one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twigs of the Arka tree or Apāmārga.
Having eaten in the morning, he should chew a soft-tipped tooth-stick that is astringent, pungent, or bitter,
taking care not to injure the gums.
It should be exactly twelve finger-breadths in length, free from curves and knots;
together with the milk and the index finger, it corresponds to the number twelve of Brahmā.
In the absence of wood or during illness, however, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with [twigs] sixteen finger-breadths long, free from curves and knots. (61)
Or likewise with objects fashioned from gold and other precious materials, or with kuśa and darbha grass;
one should perform the licking of the tongue, gargling, and the cleansing of the mouth.
O Brahmin, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with pure water;
then, free from various [impure] contacts, one should perform the five-limbed bath (pañcāṅga-snāna).
One should perform an ablution according to the prescribed rules after being defiled by contact with women and the like, [cleansing] the face along with both hands and the feet down to the waist.
Then, O twice-born one, he should anoint from the head down to the feet with his own head;
having rubbed the limbs with the Astra-mantra, he should proceed in order down to the feet.
O Brahmin, having cleansed his body with cow dung and earth,
he should first fetch a bathing cloth used by men and gods for the purpose of the ritual bath.
Having cleansed the body with black gram flour and other substances while recollecting the armor-mantra (kavaca),
one should first bathe for the sake of purification and then perform the ritual bath with mantras.
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should bathe [the deity] with royal honors using divine perfumes previously collected,
while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra upon the palm of the left hand.
Having gradually applied clay in the measure of an āmalaka fruit, reaching up to the limit of the final joint in the middle, near the wrist; || 69 ||
Having consecrated it with the five limbs in sequence using the root weapon-mantra,
and having applied it to the waters in the directions, one should then apply it as an ointment to all the limbs in due order.
Then, by joining that mantra with the binding of the mudrā both below and above,
the obstacles situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions are removed through that bath.
They depart in a state of agitation as long as that portion of earth, which had previously been consecrated with the root mantra, has not been withdrawn. (72)
Reciting that [mantra] and taking it up, one should cast it into the midst of the water;
by that means, O tiger among the twice-born, it is produced at that very instant.
[He saw] Prayāga filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā and the auspicious Yamunā,
as well as Cakratīrtha, Prabhāsa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
By the power of this mantra, they become present;
therefore, at the end of the mantra, one should utter the word "Viṣṇutīrthāya. (75)
By that act, it becomes as if one has performed a salutation in the vicinity of Viṣṇutīrtha; whenever one performs a bath at another sacred site, one should likewise apply this [merit] there.
A wise person should not recite this name at other sacred sites, except for the root mantra consisting of the words "Viṣṇu-tīrtha. (77)
If one who has bathed at a sacred ford that is eternally present should remember the name of another [ford], that other ford shall instantly cast its curse upon him.
In the common act of bathing at waterfalls, ponds, and the like,
one should recite the names of the Ganges and other rivers, as well as sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas).
One should properly perform the mantra-bath according to the prescribed rites and offer it to Viṣṇu-tīrtha;
thereafter, one should place upon the palm of the hand that portion which has been consecrated by reciting the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra).
Having stirred it with water until it is smooth, one should heat it with the rays of the sun;
when the sky is covered by clouds, one should meditate on one's own mantra as being situated in the sky like the sun.
Having shown his two palms to him, he should touch all his limbs with those two hands;
then, removing the clay smearings from the body with water while reciting the *varma* mantra, [he should perform the ritual]. 82.
Taking a bunch of *darbha* grass with the right hand,
one should rotate it in the water while reciting that mantra once, many times, or twice.

Then, one should perform either the jar-consecration (kumbhābhiṣeka) or the consecration upon the head with the water from the interior of the hand-vessel (pāṇikumbha), which has been rotated together [with the other vessels]. 84.
Having sequentially covered the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose with the fingers of one's own hands,
and then having submerged oneself along with the limbs while reciting the mantra.
One should meditate, according to one's ability, upon Hari, who consists of light—the God residing within the lotus of the heart and between the two eyes—either once or many times. (86)
Having thus performed the Aghamarṣaṇa for the purpose of dispelling all sins,
[one should do so] with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), or two, or one, performed with self-restraint.
Having arisen, he should then perform his duties after gazing at the solar disc;
possessing great splendor, he emerges from within the water as the very embodiment of the mantra.
Having discarded the bathing garment and put on another cloth,
and having bound his topknot with his hair, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.

The base of the thumb is the Brāhma-tīrtha, the tips of the fingers are the Daivika-tīrtha, and the middle of the hand is the Paitṛka-tīrtha; these are the sacred sites originating from the right hand.

One should drink water with the Brāhmaṇa (thumb) mudrā, perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with the Paitṛka (forefinger) mudrā, and touch the limbs with the Daivika (middle finger) mudrā, whichever one desires to satisfy. 91.
O Brahmin, having wiped the mouth three or four times, and having sprinkled water again upon the palm of the left hand and the soles of the two auspicious feet; 92.
Having touched the heart with the palm, the mouth with the fingers,
and having joined the thumb and ring finger, one should touch the eyes with water.

Having made the threatening gesture with that same [hand], likewise [touching] the two nostrils, and having likewise placed the little finger [there], one should touch the ear with that very same [finger]. (94)
In the same manner, having formed the middle [mudrā], one should touch both the regions of the arms;
with that very [mudrā], one should touch the region of the navel, and with it joined by the *savas*, one should touch the head. || 95 ||

O Sage, this is declared to be the rite of sipping water (ācamana) to be performed at all times during all ritual acts: having filled the right hand with water, one should bring it to the tip of the nose. 96.
Reciting the heart-mantra, smelling [the water], maintaining the armor-mantra,
and reciting [it], he should discharge the weapon-mantra while simultaneously casting it into the water.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and the body according to the tradition;
having taken water in the left hand with the heart-mantra, that [water] should be poured out.
Sprinkling water from the *śikhā* vessel, he should gladden the gods residing in the upper regions;
then, while recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astra*), he should sprinkle it upon the ground for the pacification of the faults of the wicked.
By means of the intermediate yoga, one should first go upwards and then downwards;
then, taking a handful of water while reciting the mantra and remembering Hari, [one should offer it]. 100.

Standing with his hand holding kuśa grass pointing upwards, he should then offer libations with that water to [the deity] situated in the center of the solar disc, while reciting the mantra with eyes closed.
One should cause the sun to behold the mantra that was previously worshipped with the arghya;
then, having sat down and offered libations, preceded by the purification of the base and the seat.
Thereafter, one should [worship] the mantra together with its limbs and its retinue, in due order,
as well as Indra and the other gods preceded by Viṣṇu, and Vāsudeva and the others.
The twelve forms and the twelve Śaktis, the Supreme Self alone, the elements beginning with earth, and the sages together with the ancestors; || 104 ||
First, pronouncing the name in the accusative case followed by "I satiate" (tarpayāmi), this is the mantra prescribed for libations in their proper sequence. (105)
Having offered libations with water mixed with sesame seeds to his own fathers, grandfathers,
and those known as great-grandfathers, along with their wives, he should satisfy them.
One should satisfy all the ancestors while facing south;
for the gods and others, one should face either east or north.
Afterwards, the knower of mantras, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again, should discard the pavitraka;
in the evening and in the morning, he should worship the quarters while meditating upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa.

One should perform the purification of the hands, the binding of the directions, and the veiling, together with breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the rest, accompanied by the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). || 109 ||
Then, having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and having bound the mudrās,
one should meditate upon Hari even in the midst of water, with the enjoyments of the sacrifice, such as the seat and other requisites.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having worshipped the Lord with leaves, flowers, and fruits—
since the worship prescribed therein is performed with flowers when they are available— [should proceed].
With water-offering (audaka-upacāra) cultivated through meditative development,
one should satisfy everything with water as before, by means of the visualization of the oblation (homa-bhāvanā).
Having done this, one should perform the offering of fuel to the Lord of the World, and then offer sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth, according to one's ability. (113)
For the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess and for the completion of all rites,
one should indeed perform the water libations until the conclusion of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having offered praise, O Brahmin, one should then prostrate like a staff with the eight limbs;
[one should offer] dūrvā grass together with white mustard seeds, consecrated with the śikhā-mantra. || 115 ||
Having gathered the command into one's head with the crest-lock on the crown of the head,
it should be uttered from the water into the space of one's own heart by means of the mind, as the partless self.
Having performed his visit and fulfilled his duty, the wise man should then renounce [worldly attachments],
and afterwards he should acquire enjoyments earned through righteous means.

Alternatively, with the root mantra or the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should offer flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth—provided they are acceptable, not unobtained, and not corrupted by their inherent nature. || 118 ||

One should avoid that which is mixed, deficient, touched by impurity, sour, or licked; rather, one should utter the mantra with the intellect while employing the technique of complete inhalation. 119.
Having whirled a pair of branches of Apāmārga and Śamī over his head by moving them to the left and right, he should cast them behind him while reciting the Astra-mantra.

Having wrung out the bathing garment and then performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while remaining silent, one should do as prescribed for the water-bath; now learn from me the mantra-bath. 121.

In the absence of water, during a difficult time, or when it is cold, one may act [to depart]; or for the sake of swift success in a journey, or due to lack of independence regarding a weighty task. || 122 ||
Or, O best of Brahmins, having seen that [the time] has arrived during either the portion of the night or the day,
one should wash one's feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water drawn up from a vessel.
Having purified the site and the ten directions as before, one should then sit down;
thereafter, one should perform a series of breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) within the body.
One should perform [the rite] beginning with the root mantra together with the entire collection of mantras;
for by mere bathing in water alone, one is deprived of the purificatory consecrations.
O best of beings, whatever fruit one who is twice-born obtains at sacred fords such as Prayāga from bathing,
a hundred times that fruit is obtained from the mantra-bath.
Now I shall describe the bath of meditation, which is superior even to both [the previous baths].
One should remember the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who abides in the sky and whose form is the mantra. (127)
One should contemplate the stream born from the water of his feet falling upon one's own head, entering one's body through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*). 128.
By means of that [water], he should wash away all impurity located within the body;
at that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion (viraja) and becomes like a crystal. || 129 ||
The bath of meditation is considered a hundred times superior to the bath of mantras;
it is called the "bath of meditation. Now hear about the divine baths and others.
Immediately after the rain that falls with heat, there follows a divine bath [of purification] through kindled sacrificial fuel, cow dung, and the offering of oblations. 131.
The application of white ash on the limbs and the forehead and other parts in due order, preceded by the recitation of mantras, constitutes the making of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*. || 132 ||
Bathing with ashes is indeed considered the supreme purification;
it is [efficacious] when cows are passing by and the earth-born dust is raised by the wind. || 133 ||
Touching the body with white clay produced on a praiseworthy mountain peak or similar location is declared to be the Vāyavya bath. (134)

Having uttered the names beginning with Keśava in due order upon the limbs, one should apply the forehead-mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts according to the prescribed rule. || 135 ||
This "royal bath" (pārthivasnāna) is thus auspicious and removes all sins;
therefore, one who is devoted with faith should perform at least one of these baths.
Through bathing, sipping water for purification, and breath control, the teacher—and indeed the practitioner—becomes purified both internally and externally of the body. (137)
All ritual acts preceded by bathing are the causes for the successful attainment of results;
therefore, one should perform the bath along with the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Initiate’s Bath," in the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) of the *Pārameśvarasaṃhitā* within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
Śrīḥ.

The Third Chapter: Having offered a blade of durva grass with its stalk, or a leaf, a flower, or sesame seeds along with water upon his own head and at the site of the topknot, O best of men, [he should perform the rite].
Then, taking a vessel filled with water preceded by a water-pot,
covered with a cloth, he went toward the house of the Blessed One with his hand.
One should go to a solitary, uninhabited place that is pleasing, free from defects,
favorable, pure, skillful, self-controlled, and established in its proper time.
Meditating upon the mantra residing in the center of the heart—the Vedic Ekāyana, the Brāhmaṇa who conveys the Arghya, and the embodiment of awakened bliss—[one attains liberation]. 4.
Without looking toward any direction, remaining silent and restraining the breath,
one should release that [breath] through the tip of the nose, having reached one's own mantra-position.
Uttering the twelve-syllable mantra, one should enter and circumambulate from left to right,
then sweep and sprinkle the entire area of the temple.
The attendants must indeed perform the rites up to the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) outside the door,
according to the scriptures, using pure water.
Having washed his feet up to the ankles and his hands up to the wrists, and having sipped water according to the previously mentioned procedure with upward-pointing *uṇḍraka* marks; || 8 ||
Or with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, especially in a field of dharma,
on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, or likewise on the shore of the ocean.
O twice-born one, clay from an anthill or at the root of a Tulasī plant is highly recommended;
for one desiring subjugation, [clay] that is red is used, for one desiring prosperity, yellow, and for one desiring peace, white.

One desiring liberation should apply the mark with black [sandalwood paste], while with white [paste] one should make an upward-pointing sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) in the shape of a wick-lamp or like the leaf of a bamboo.
The lotus has the shape of a bud, and the water-lily (utpala) has the form of a bud;
likewise, there are those shaped like a fish and a tortoise, and beyond that, the conch-shaped [lotus]. 12.
O Sage, [one should worship] with the thumb for the bestowing of nourishment, with the index finger for the attainment of liberation,
or with the ring finger for the granting of desired objects.
One desiring long life should perform [the rite] with the middle finger; likewise, one may use these fingers for the deities, but one must not touch them with the fingernails.
One should place Vāsudeva on the forehead and Saṃkarṣaṇa on the heart;
Pradyumna on the right shoulder and Aniruddha on the left shoulder.
Indeed, with clay ground upon a road, one should know Keśava on the forehead as the four vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen.
One should place Mādhava in the heart and Govinda in the hollow of the throat;
in the belly and on the right side, he is designated as Viṣṇu. (17)
Beside that, in the middle of the arm, Madhusūdana is prescribed;
Trivikrama is at the hollow of the throat, and Vāmana is in the left side of the belly.
One should remember Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck, Padmanābha on the other [right] side, and Dāmodara on the hump. || 19 ||
Thus, one should place the twelve names upon Vāsudeva at the head;
[the names are] sacrifice, charity, austerity, oblation, feeding, and ancestral rites.
All that is declared to be fruitless when deprived of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra);
therefore, with every effort, one should wear it, for it bestows all perfections.
The tip, measuring four finger-breadths, always has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity;
the knot, measuring one finger-breadth, has Mahāviṣṇu as its presiding deity. || 22 ||
The ring for Viṣṇu as the presiding deity is said to be two finger-breadths wide;
one should place the purifier (pavitra) upon both hands, specifically on the ring fingers.
But that bath which is without darbha grass, that worship without an offering of food (naivedya), and that gift which is without water—all that shall be fruitless. || 24 ||
Worship, recitation, burnt offerings, giving, and the libation to the ancestors—all of this perishes if one performs them without the sacred thread (apavitra) on the hand. || 25 ||
Therefore, with every effort, the sacred thread (pavitraka) should always be worn, adorned with perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and upper garments. || 26 ||
With earrings, necklaces, and the like, as well as bracelets and rings—if these are unavailable, the practitioner should adorn [the image] with at least a ring. || 27 ||
O twice-born one, having covered the nostrils of the face with a cloth,
ensure that it is not struck by one's own breath.
Clad in white garments, well-attired, with white teeth and pure vows,
his face purified by betel and his forehead adorned with unbroken grains of rice.
Endowed with these aforementioned qualities, one should awaken the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) accompanied by the sound of conchs and the resonance of kettledrums and drums.
O Great-minded One, with the loud and various words arising from the multitude of bards, and with the repeated cries of "Victory! Victory! uttered again and again; || 31 ||
Then, having awakened [the deity] from his bed with hymns characterized by awakening,
and having reached the door, standing there, he first performs the binding of the ten directions.
Then, having veiled [the area] with the index finger while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca),
one should worship within the bali-maṇḍala, whether it remains as is or has been specially prepared there.
Having taken a flower, one should recite the names of the entire retinue, beginning with Khageśa and ending with Sācyuta, preceded by the syllable Om and accompanied by the word "namaḥ. || 34 ||
Salutations again and again to the one accompanied by his entire retinue, the imperishable one;
having worshipped Vāstupuruṣa and the others in their proper order. || 35 ||
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with either the root mantra together with its ancillaries or without them,
the preceptor should clap his hands three times while reciting the heart-mantra.
Having opened the door with the root mantra and [uncovered] the eyes with the eye-mantra,
one should then kindle the perpetual lamps and wash both hands with water.
When a palace or similar structure is not available, then, having found a pleasing location, one should construct a mantra-house; that is now being described.
First, one should meditate upon the root mantra as being all-pervading like Brahman,
blazing in the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions, and the center, like ten million suns.
Having pervaded with one's own self the heart-mantra situated within that [body], and the head-mantra in its center, which has the nature of the Brahma-nāḍī; || 40 ||
But the crest-mantra (śikhāmantra), which is the pillar of the universe, brilliant like the path of movement, stands outside everything like an outer enclosure. || 41 ||
The practitioner, whose nature is action, should pierce the armor-mantra with the supreme self;
he should also contemplate the eye-mantra as being like a window or a door.
One should visualize the external weapon-mantra (astra), which is adorned by thousands of waves of flickering sparks of fire and which pacifies all obstacles. || 43 ||
Having thus meditated upon the mantra-house, one should then mentally divide the door into three parts; then, that middle part should again be divided into two.
Then, having parted the ground with his left side and his right foot,
he slowly entered within, accompanied by that very mantra while shedding tears.
Having struck the earth and bowed to the Blessed One,
he [then] mentally [honored] the lineage of his gurus and their mental command.
Having mentally resolved upon his desired fruit, he should bear it upon his head and offer it to the deity in the center of the sacrificial hall.

Having fashioned a palace and a body, and having meditated upon the armor-mantra together with its form, as well as its vital breath and the Blessed One, one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Then, having scrubbed it with Darbha grass provided with stalks mixed with Sahadevī,
and having washed it with plenty of water, he should smear it with cow-dung.

One should take fresh cow dung produced by a cow that has stood on the ground; one should avoid that which is mixed with water, that which is loose, that which is dry, and that which is infested with insects. (50)
Then, having smeared it with the weapon-mantra and having cut it into pieces, one should discard them;
or, having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow accompanied by the weapon-mantra, [one should smear it] with sandalwood.
Having smeared [the place] all over with saffron, agallochum, and camphor,
one should scatter kusha grass, durva grass, and unbroken grains for the purification of the site.
Having purified the temple, the twice-born man, intent on silence,
should then take his place either in front of the Lord of Gods or in the southern part.
On darbha grass, a skin, a cloth, or a plank made of sacrificial wood, one should place or lay down one's seat with water consecrated by the root mantra. || 54 ||
Having sprinkled [the seat] with the *choṭikā* (finger-snap) using the Astra-mantra, one should offer it again for its purification;
then, one should meditate upon a single seat there for the sake of the fourth [state] and the others.
First is the seat named Turya, which is associated with the causal Praṇava;
it is pervaded by Suṣupti, and its location is in the unmanifest lotus. || 56 ||
The dream state consists of the seat beginning with Śeṣāhi and ending with Vahni;
the waking state consists of the seats beginning with Kṣīrārṇava and ending with Bhāvāsana. || 57 ||
In that regard, one should contemplate the state of sleep (suṣupta) or the fourth state (turya) prior to the purification of the hands;
however, one should contemplate the dream-state prior to the mental sacrifice, according to the time prescribed for the fourth state.
But in the ritual procedure for the waking state, let this distinction be grasped:
prior to the placement of mantras upon one's own body, there is the triad beginning with the ocean.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and struck it with flowers empowered by the Astra-mantra,
one should perform the worship of the Lord’s Yoga-pīṭha right there, as described previously.

One should install the seat beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and ending with the conceptual seat (bhāvapīṭha); then, having meditated upon its pervasion by means of the Praṇava and by that very [mantra] consisting of its own syllables.
Having worshipped it, and upon it [the vessel] provided with one of the lotus-faces and so forth,
he should meditate upon the Blessed One as being present within the collection of sacrificial implements.
Then, O best of beings, he should command his disciplined disciples, sons, and others who have bathed; thereafter, he should perform the purification of the vessels—listen to how that is done.
One should purify gold and copper with the paste of *amlaka* and water;
silver, moreover, with house-soot or with the smoke from extinguished embers.
One should purify objects made of iron with water mixed with ashes;
and those made of conch-shell or mother-of-pearl, one should purify with salt.
One should cleanse objects made of fruit or leaves with earth and water;
purification is achieved by removing stains and odors—one should ensure this is done.
Thus the purification of the substances occurs exactly as prescribed by the rules;
then, one should commence the ritual prior to the time of sunrise.
One should worship it at the time of worship while it is covered with a cloth;
one must not show it to the most sinful, those who have fallen from their stage of life, or atheists.
One should produce the sound of a bell there, which serves as a sign for summoning the deities, for the purpose of attracting the gods and for the purpose of repelling the rākṣasas.
Accompanied by the sounding of conchs and other instruments, and provided with singing and instrumental music,
[this should be done] during the invocation, as well as during the anointing, and at the beginning and end of the bath.

Likewise, during the offering of the sectarian mark (tilaka), the lamp, the presentation of the mother-offering (mātrā), the waving of lights (nīrājana), and the bringing of the food offering from the kitchen; || 71 ||
At the time of offering that [oblation], at the conclusion of the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti), at the time of fetching water, and during the mounting and dismounting from the vehicle; || 72 ||
O best of the twice-born, when the two door-panels are being opened or closed,
one should blow the conch shell three times during these constant occasions.
For one who has truly engaged in the worship of Viṣṇu and has observed silence,
the utterance of words by that person of undistracted mind is indeed a source of great contradiction.
Therefore, those devoted to action should avoid silence that is subject to deviation;
rather, that which is auspicious and non-deviating should be practiced in all matters. (75)
When silence is maintained through unarticulated nasal sounds consisting of bodily gestures and signs,
with the lips firmly closed, that silence causes the loss of spiritual accomplishment.
That which exists within all things by its own nature through one's own intellect, even without being taught by words— that is silence (mauna), which bestows all perfections.
Next, perform the purification of the hands; listen attentively as I describe it:
both palms, both backs of the hands, and likewise all the fingers. (78)
Having purified [the hands] with the weapon-mantra while assuming the meditation-mudrā,
and having thus performed the purification of the hands, one should carry out the purification of the place.
Having meditated upon the God of blazing form, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns,
surrounded by millions of flames, and vomiting fire from his mouth.
With that, one should fill everything up to the very end of the abode of Brahmā;
one should meditate upon the flood of directions as blazing with the splendor of the mantra.
O best of the twice-born, one should contemplate this entire circle of the earth as being baked by the fire produced from the mantra, like an earthen vessel.
In this way, the purification of the place occurs through the sprinkling of waves of nectar;
one should then meditate upon the binding of the directions and place fire in the mouth. (83)
And emitting the weapon-mantra from both arms, or from the right one,
he should scatter it everywhere throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions, outside of his seat.
The wise one should construct a rampart in the form of a dense lattice of arrows;
or else, as before, he should perform the binding of the directions with the [mantras] beginning with the Heart.
One should perform the binding of the intermediate directions with the Astra-mantra, and then the upward direction with the Netra-mantra,
which is as radiant as ten thousand suns and has the form of a blazing tunic.
One should perform the protective covering with the armor [mudrā] and the index finger;
having thus performed the binding of the directions, one should then begin the breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 87 ||

Furthermore, for the sake of achieving fitness for meditative concentration and for the conquest of the vital breaths and so forth, [one must control] the mind that is turbulent, firm, or flickering. || 88 ||

And for the purpose of dispelling darkness, one should then perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), as well as [meditate upon] the arrangement of the channels within the body and the location of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth. (89)
Having understood the true nature of prāṇāyāma, one should perform the watches (yāmas).
O best of sages, I shall now explain the system of channels (nāḍīcakra) exactly as it is.
The supreme place of origin for the channels is the bulb (kanda) at the navel;
seventy-two thousand channels are situated within [the body]. (91)
Pervading the body horizontally, upwards, and downwards, they remain established—
those of fiery nature, those of gentle form, and likewise those of both gentle and fiery natures.
The channels facing upward are called fiery (āgneya), while those facing downward are known as lunar (saumya);
those that run horizontally are described as both lunar and fiery.
Among all the channels as well, ten channels are preeminent:
namely, the Iḍā, the Piṅgalā, and the Suṣumnā which ascends upwards.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and the illustrious Pūṣā;
Alambusā, Kuhū, and Kośinī is remembered as the tenth. || 95 ||
The central channel, known as Suṣumṇā, flows upward from the kanda;
situated to the left and right of this central Suṣumṇā are [the other two channels]. (96)
The two known as Iḍā and Piṅgalā extend from the nostrils;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvikā are situated at its front and back respectively.
The two [channels] named Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī, which arise from the region of the navel, are situated respectively at the end of the left and right ears. (98)
The Alambusā nāḍī extends from the root of the bulb (kanda) down to the base of the feet;
the Kuhū extends as far as the private organ (meḍhra); and the Kośinī is located in the big toe of the foot.
Śuklā is white, Iḍā is reddish-brown, Gāndhārī is red in color,
Hastijihvā has a black form, and Pūṣā should be blackish-yellow.
Yaśasvinī was dark-complexioned, Alambuṣā was tawny,
Kuhū resembled the dawn, and Kośinī had the luster of collyrium.
Thus, the ten principal channels have been proclaimed; ten vital winds are said to reside within the channels in the body.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 103 ||
The one called Iḍā carries the prāṇa, the one called Gāndhārī carries the apāna; Alambuṣā carries the samāna, while Kuhū carries the vyāna, O best of the twice-born. (104)
The udāna is known as Suṣumṇā; Piṅgalā is designated as Nāga;
Pūṣā is Vāyu; Kūrma is called Kṛkara; and Yaśasvinī is [the channel of] Devadatta. 105.
Hastijihvā [was the wife] of Devadatta, while Kośinī was the wife of Dhanañjaya;
both Prāṇa and Nāga, who resembled coral and were like Indra’s wrath, [were their sons]. 106.

Dhananjaya [controlled] the apāna and kūrma breaths, both of which resemble space; he also controlled the samāna and kṛkara breaths, as well as the devadatta and udāna breaths, which resemble lotus filaments.
Vyāna is like the color of foam; this is the settled conclusion in all the scriptures.
Now, prāṇāyati is the movement of inhalation and exhalation.
In that context, *stambhana* (stabilization) consists of the exhalation of external air through the nostrils and the drawing in of the internal air from within the abdominal cavity. (109)
Exhalation is the outward expulsion of this [breath] preceded by consciousness;
internal retention is the state of arresting the breath, which is the filling [of the body] with air from within. || 110 ||
Externally, they know that first [type] to be the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa);
the second is internal, while the third is the state of suspension (stambha). || 111 ||
Among these, the external retention of breath is considered inferior, the internal is considered middling, and the retention characterized by the state of suspension is considered supreme. || 112 ||
The external breath, which is always in the form of exhalation, is called *recaka*;
likewise, the internal breath, which is in the form of inhalation, is called *sampūraka*.
Kumbhaka consists of the state of suspension through the cessation of inhalation and exhalation;
it is classified as mild, moderate, or intense according to whether there are one, two, or three upward thrusts (udghātas). || 114 ||
These occur here in sequence from the region of the navel;
first, there is the striking of the breath as it rises, which constitutes the second *udghāta*.
Withdrawal from the abdomen upwards is its third stage;
elsewhere, its restraint here is first mild, then moderate.
The second and then the third [method] is the intense one, which involves the causes such as sweating;
one should first perform a series of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), beginning with exhalation (recaka) using the Astra-mantra. || 117 ||

In that regard, the exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka) are each known to consist of twelve mātrās; they understand the retention (kumbhaka) to consist of twenty-four mātrās and thirty-six mātrās respectively.
Then, after the kumbhaka, the further complete expulsion of the breath is also that which is called prāṇāyāma; it is designated as recaka. || 119 ||
If the measure is deficient due to an excess [of another], it is unequal;
therefore, one who seeks to conquer the vital breath (prāṇa) must understand the specific measures. 120.
Having circumambulated the knee neither too quickly nor too slowly, one should perform the snapping of the fingers; that is proclaimed as the measure (mātrā). 121.

One should perform a series of breath controls (prāṇāyāma): first exhalation (recaka) with the Astra-mantra, then inhalation (pūraka) with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and finally retention (kumbhaka) with the Netra-mantra.
O best of the twice-born, one should again perform the exhalation (recaka) as previously described,
covering the left nostril with the fingers of the right hand.

One should meditate upon Hari, situated in the region of the navel, by means of the root mantra, along with the ten vital breaths together with their embryos, which are mixed with the defects of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 124 ||
Prāṇāyāma is considered to be of two kinds: *agarbha* (without the embryo) and *sagarbha* (with the embryo).
That which is performed without recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) is *agarbha*, while that which is joined with them is *sagarbha*. || 125 ||
Prāṇāyāma performed with the *agarbha* [mantra] joined by the *garbha* [mantra] exceeds a hundred-fold;
having drawn [the breath] out through the right nostril while reciting the *astra* [mantra]. (126)
One should withdraw the wheel of breath situated within the ten channels,
releasing the *pūṣikā* from one another here by means of each successive measure.
One should exhale through the Piṅgalā with two [fingers] and outside the navel with two;
having thus performed the exhalation, one should establish Hari for that duration and then take up the fire.
One should meditate on [the deity] situated upon the wheel of wind and cause him to enter within;
closing the door with the right thumb, one should inhale through the left nostril. || 129 ||

Uttering the *hariṃ* mantra along with the *savātacakra* and the two *mātrās* through the *iḍā*, one should cause it to enter within by means of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), and meditate upon Him stationed in the heart. || 130 ||
Then, with four measures of that wind, one fills Piṅgalā;
with two, Suṣumnā; with two each, Gāndhārī and Pūṣikā. || 131 ||
With each pair [of breaths], one should successively fill the channels Hastijihvā, Lambusā, Yaśasvinī, Kośinī, and Kuhū. || 132 ||
One should hold [the breath] like a jar with the eyes [closed], above the nostrils and so forth, for thirty-six mātrās combined with the fire of the navel. || 133 ||
By those winds circulating everywhere, the accumulations of the humors (doṣas) were meditated upon and expelled,
and the channels (nāḍīs) were gradually purified.
Or, one should exhale the mere wind-circle externally as before;
or rather, it is taught that sixteen mātrās should be used for the exhalation, with double that for the retention. || 135 ||
The inhalation (pūraka) and the retention (kumbhaka) should each consist of sixty-four measures (mātrās).
One should release the channels as before, but one should release the Piṅgalā [nāḍī] with six measures.
One should acquire ten channels by means of five measures of the strings;
this is declared to be prāṇāyāma, distinguished as superior and so forth. || 137 ||
In this threefold procedure, one should perform it as far as possible;
having performed three, five, or even seven breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas). || 138 ||
The mastery of the vital breath (prāṇa) by a person is called prāṇāyāma;
thereafter, for the sake of purifying the body, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables beginning with Bhauma. 139.
O Sage, listen to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as it truly is, in due order:
the body consists of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether. (140)
Know it to be like a magical illusion, devoid of qualities such as knowledge and the rest;
it is impure, dependent, born from semen and blood, and subject to decay. (141)
As long as it has not been thoroughly purified by continuous dhāraṇās, so long will this [body] be unfit for matters such as the placement of mantras (nyāsa). || 142 ||
One should purify the body by means of five or two dhāraṇās,
having caused Hari to exit externally through the southern door of the suṣumnā.
Resembling a thousand suns, situated in the center of a circular mandala,
he sat in the supreme station, radiant with the luster of molten gold.
Having meditated upon that [deity] as being of the nature of mantra, twelve finger-breadths above [the heart],
one should visualize a wheel of light beneath it, conjoined with the presiding principle (tattvādhiṣṭhātṛ).
Having meditated upon the partless mantra-body, one should then, in the sequence below that,
contemplate the earth as yellow, four-cornered, and marked with vajras.
It was endowed with the five objects of sense, beginning with sound; it was crowded with mountains and trees, and adorned with cities, walls, excellent rivers, islands, and oceans.
One should visualize her entering from the outside into one's own body through inhalation (pūraka),
and while reciting that mantra, one should then contemplate her as having come to rest.
Then, O best of the twice-born, she gradually pervades everything from the knees down to the soles of the feet by means of the *kumbhaka* within her own mantra-form.
When the power of smell has gradually dissolved,
the king of mantras should subsequently cast that power of smell outside by means of exhalation.
And in the great stream called Water, there is then the water of sovereign power,
together with the sixfold essence of the currents of oceans and rivers, and along with the medicinal herbs.
Whatever other beings consisting of water exist within the world,
they take the form of a half-moon and are adorned with the lotus-banner.
Having meditated upon the external manifestation of Varuṇa, one should then gradually fill the body with it by means of the practice known as *pūraka* (inhalation). || 153 ||

O twice-born one, one should meditate upon one's own physical sphere extending from the root of the thighs to the knees; by means of that [breath] held in the kumbhaka state, one should contemplate that it completely pervades everything.
Having meditated upon the Vāruṇa mantra known as dhāraṇā in the center of that,
one perceives that the entire watery manifestation has dissolved into that mantra.
Then, having cast that [essence] into the power of taste— that power being within the orb of fire— by means of the exhaling breath (recaka), she likewise [cast] the splendor of the fire.
It has the form of a triangular world, adorned with radiant lightning, the moon, the sun, the stars, and with minerals and precious gems. || 157 ||

Having thus meditated upon this great manifestation, which is marked with blazing svastikas by those who possess bodies that are self-luminous and those who are bodiless, moving through the sky; || 158 ||
O tiger among sages, one should then recollect that fiery mantra, indeed pronouncing it while [visualizing] it as situated within that very mandala. (159)

One should meditate on it as having entered [the body] as before, by means of that very same instrument; having pervaded the area from the navel down to the anus and having fixed the mind thereon. (160)
O Brahmin, one should contemplate that entire splendor as consisting of light;
within the form of that mantra, it is peaceful, and that mantra is of the nature of fire.
Having gone to dissolution within the power of form (rūpaśakti), that power consists of consciousness (saṃvinmayī);
by that [power], its own mantra-body is dissolved by its own inherent power. || 162 ||
By means of the *recaka* breath, one should cast that power (*śakti*) outside into the foundation of air;
thereafter, one should indeed contemplate the expansion of the aerial element externally. (163)
It was circular, adorned with precious stones and made of gold,
filled with various kinds of perfumes and many of their excellent qualities.
One should visualize it as pervaded by one's own mantra known as *dhāraṇā*;
likewise, having meditated upon that mantra in its true form and uttered it, one should withdraw [the breath]. || 165 ||
By means of the previously described method, one should gradually, with the tip of the nose,
contemplate that [the body] is pervaded by it from the neck down to the region of the navel.
O Great-minded one, by means of the very method previously described, one should remember that aerial element (vāyavya) as having reached dissolution into its presiding deity. || 167 ||
Within the great power known as Sparśā, he [perceives] that indestructible power, which is both eternal and non-eternal, and which is endowed with the manifestations of its own powers. || 168 ||
One should cast [the consciousness] into the great support called Sound within the sphere of space;
then, having meditated upon the entire manifestation known as Space outside of the body. (169)
It was filled with a variety of sounds, yet formless and possessing the luster of collyrium;
it was full of innumerable perfected beings (siddhas) who were bodiless and composed of sound.
In the midst of that, O twice-born one, one should contemplate the dhāraṇā-mantra known as Vyoman, which always sustains its own self by its own power. (171)
Sound alone, however, is formless, all-pervading, and present even within all things;
having discerned it with the intellect and having placed it within the body, [one should meditate]. (172)
One should meditate upon that [body] as being pervaded by that very means previously described,
from the neck up to the aperture of Brahmā, by means of the expansion called Space (vyoma).
O great sage, having retained [the breath] by means of kumbhaka for as long as possible, the yogi should subsequently meditate upon his own mantra once it has been transformed.
One should meditate upon the mantra of concentration known as Vyoma as being dissolved into Śakti;
likewise, [the senses of] smell and the genitals are in Earth, while taste and the anus are in Water. (175)

At the beginning of the dissolution, one should simultaneously recollect the two feet as being in the fire element, the skin and hands in the wind mandala, and speech and hearing in the principle of space. || 176 ||
One should contemplate that power as it proceeds through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
joined with the fourfold power consisting of smell and the other [sensory objects], and imperishable.
One should take refuge in the partless mantra, conjoined with the presiding principle of reality;
together with the mantra, one should thus gradually lead the elemental manifestation to its cessation.
That consciousness which has become the individual soul (jīva), resembling a shimmering star, should be meditated upon as resting and emerged from the cage of the elements. 179.
In this supreme mantra, which is free from conceptual proliferation and whose form is said to consist of the five powers,
the individual soul (jīva), by means of itself, [unites] with the Self through this sequential yoga.
One should behold in the space of the heart that supreme, all-pervading Lord, who is immovable, resplendent as the sun, and filled with quivering rays of light. 181.
Then, abiding in the body of mantras, one should practice the supreme samādhi, through union with the five powers beginning with the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra). || 182 ||

Having understood that this [world] is thus to be abandoned, when one is strengthened by abiding in that [state], yet remains unsatisfied and has not yet accomplished one's purpose through the service of the mantra-heart-lotus; 183.

Indeed, the six-legged one, being the very essence of the Self, should, by means of the rope of knowledge, remember his own self as emerging from the upper part of the cavity of the heart by means of his own self. (184)
Indeed, that crest of the mantra-fire flows through the path of the nāḍī called Bhārūpa;
it is Suṣumnā, resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk, and it moves upward. (185)
O best of beings, having remembered that [breath] reaching the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) through that excellent path,
one who possesses knowledge should very gradually expel his own self by means of the wind of wisdom.
One should thus abandon the non-pervasive group of six organs, including the mantra-organ;
for one shall attain that which is beyond it, from the supreme form of the Lord. || 187 ||
O tiger among the twice-born, he has arisen as an incomparable mass of splendor,
delighted by his own bliss while situated at the hub of that wheel of radiance.
Thus, for the reality of the Self that stands step by step, and for the pure conscious self whose body has been liberated from [the notion of] substantiality; || 189 ||
Great bliss arises; that is indeed the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, which, having made the individual soul (jīva)—the performer of unimpaired actions—its own, [attains its goal]. || 190 ||
O best of beings, know that where it has arisen, there it remains once again; and that is free from conceptual construction and is inexpressible.
Thus, having reached his own station and abandoned the body of the ignorant,
he who remains there should burn away the subtle body (piṇḍa), divested of the powers and the subtle elements.

And [he should burn] this essence-less body composed of the six sheaths, which is like a blade of grass devoid of punishment, by means of the fire born of mantra arising from the churning of desire. 193.
Starting from that region of the foot, one should visualize that mass as blazing;
then, at the tip of the big toe of the right foot, is the syllable of the flame (Śikhā).
Having meditated [on him] as being enveloped by hundreds of flames resembling the fire at the end of an eon,
one should then meditate upon one’s own body blazing intensely on all sides.
One should meditate on fire, endowed with a mass of flames, at the central region within the navel-knot by means of the Netra-mantra; one should reduce [the object] to ashes by that [fire].
Then, while meditating on the heart-mantra,
one should burn one's own body and contemplate the flame arising from the body as having dissolved into the Lord of Mantras.
One should meditate upon that [deity] as resembling a heap of ashes, with the fire extinguished, preceded by the all-pervading *oṃkāra* and accompanied by the very subtle *sāhalāda*. (198)
Then, endowed with meditation, one should contemplate that ash falling here and there, accompanied by the mantra ending in "namas" and using its expressive name. (199)
Then, having meditated upon that image, which is accompanied by the mantra and resembles ten thousand full moons,
[one should contemplate] the flood of nectar issuing forth from it through the sky.
One should bathe the bodily ashes and meditate upon everything as being of the nature of nectar;
having placed there, in the center, the Vaiṣṇava power consisting of the support (ādhāra).
One should meditate on that which has become the seed of everything, and the lotus arising from it—
