consisting of the six paths and the principles (tattvas), white, full of splendor, and auspicious.
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is mantra, situated in the center of that [space], pervaded by the three mandalas and radiant with shimmering rays of light. (203)

O twice-born one, he should further contemplate that [deity], which is partless, absolute, pure, and whose body consists of the five excellent mantras, as being intensified by the powers of those mantras.
One should contemplate the fivefold mantra of the Lord consisting of the five elements beginning with space, and then the pervasive manifestation (vibhava) emanating from them, beginning with space.
One should meditate upon the mass produced by conjunction as possessing the fivefold manifestations:
resembling a thousand suns and possessing the radiance of a hundred moons.
Having thus produced one's own body, which resembles stainless crystal and is free from old age and death, it is the supreme means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 207 ||
O tiger among sages, that which is the innate means of accomplishment for all embodied beings is attained through the very process characterized by the desire to create. || 208 ||
Having brought about the simultaneous arising of power from his own waveless state,
he [attains] his own bliss from great bliss, and from the support of that very own bliss.
From that [state], one perceives the Marīci-wheel of the sky and one's own form,
shining with its own radiance like the brilliance of ten million suns.
O twice-born one, having thus brought the self from its own place by means of the self— shaped like a kadamba bud and as pure as a drop of dew at night— (one should meditate upon it).
One should cause one's own mantra-body to enter through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) as before,
by way of the channel of moonlight (jyotsnā-nāḍī), into the interior of the lotus of the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka).
Meditating indeed upon his own designator by means of the partless sound (dhvani),
he [then perceives] from that partless [sound] the mantras and so forth, up to the elemental body.
Having attained the fivefold form of light along with the conceit [of identity],
one should sprinkle one's own body with a stream of nectar from one's own mantra.
Then, having drawn that image [of the deity] by means of its own mantra, one should place it within the heart;
for she is the supreme power, free from waves [of agitation], and consisting of great bliss.
From one's own bliss arises the circle of light, whose form is self-luminous;
such is the path of the Suṣumṇā, as well as the partless (niṣkala) mantra of the body. || 216 ||

The first is the flood of mantra-power beginning with Satya; then the pentad of the Lords of Retention (dhāraṇeśvara). The aggregate of their manifestations is the collective "body" (piṇḍa). || 217 ||
O best of men, one should remember everything as made into a single unity, yet existing both non-different and different,
through the threefold [nature] known as gross, subtle, and supreme.
This elemental purification has been correctly explained by means of the instruments;
it consists of the five purified elements, beginning with earth and ending with space. || 219 ||
The sense organs of smell, taste, sight, touch, and hearing, as well as those consisting of the generative organ, the anus, the feet, the hands, and speech; || 220 ||
Indeed, the five organs of action are purified;
in that regard as well, the duration for the inhalations (pūraka) and so forth is prescribed to be the same as for the breath-restraints (āyāma). || 221 ||
Thus, in the primary ritual procedure, it is proclaimed as consisting of five fixations (dhāraṇās);
now I shall describe that according to the secondary procedure—understand it from me correctly. (222)
O Mahāmati, this fivefold concentration (dhāraṇā) consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and space, as well as the pair [of methods], has been briefly prescribed.
Furthermore, for the sake of purifying one's own body through burning and nourishing,
one should meditate on the vital air located in the region of the navel while reciting the armor mantra.
O twice-born one, by means of that [wind], one should lead the essence (rasa) located within the body into a state of drying up;
then, by means of the Netra-mantra, one should lead the fire into the region between the navel and the kanda.
One should meditate upon [the deity] endowed with a mass of flames and reduce [the object] to ashes by means of that;
then, while contemplating the heart-mantra, one should burn one's own body.
One should remain supported by the sky and meditate with the head-mantra (śiromantra);
then one should recollect that water produced there, as clear as a pearl.
O best of beings, with the *śikhā* mantra, one should lead the lotus characterized by the qualities of the earth (the number eight) into the self by means of its presiding deity.

One should meditate upon that sheath arising therefrom, a body consisting of the reality of the elements, while recollecting the heart and other organs as the causal forms of the five elements. || 229 ||
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) within that city arisen from meditation;
the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is proclaimed according to the distinction between the primary and secondary methods.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Explanation of Samādhi," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
Śrīḥ!
The Fourth Chapter:

Having purified his body, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), by the mere performance of which he becomes equal to the God of gods. || 1 ||
One becomes entitled to all rites such as worship and the like,
and by this means, the manifestation of all supernatural powers (siddhis) shall indeed occur.
Having performed which, one may remain fearless even in a region crowded with the wicked;
and by that which has been prescribed, there shall be victory over untimely deaths.
For although this mental activity known as "renunciation" (nyāsa) is traditionally taught,
it does not properly establish its own state without [the support of] ritual action.
That [mantra] is again dependent on the hands, for the prior placement (prāṅnyāsa) resides in those two;
then, having placed the radiant twelve-syllable [mantra] upon both hands— || 5 ||
Then, from the wrist to the tips of the nails, like the heat of the sun,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of creation, maintenance, and dissolution according to the prescribed rule.
The movement beginning from the palm of the right hand and ending at the interior of the left is known as *sṛṣṭi* (emission);
that which begins from the right thumb and ends at the palm of the left is known as *sthiti* (maintenance). || 7 ||
In the [rite of] creation, the other [method] is taught as beginning with the palm of the left hand and ending with the right;
on the right palm, the *tāra* [is placed], followed in sequence by the thumb and the other fingers.
Having placed the ten syllables upon the ten fingers starting from the left little finger, one should place the final [syllable] on the surface of the left palm.
In the [mudrā] called Sthiti, one should place the six syllables beginning with *TĀRĀ* on the five fingers starting from the right thumb, ending at the respective palms.
One should place the subsequent group of six [syllables] from the left thumb to the tip of the palm;
having placed the final syllable on the palm of the left hand in the rite called Saṃhāra.
Following the very sequence known as *apyaya*, [he should place the letters] up to the palm of the right hand;
then he should assign the remaining group of phonemes, ending with the *praṇava*.
With the index finger upon each respective thumb, and with each respective thumb upon the branches beginning with the index finger,
[one should perform the mudrās] on the palm with each respective middle finger.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the proper method, and thereafter perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa),
O twice-born one, beginning from the right thumb across the ten fingers.
One should sequentially place the twelve radiant limbs, beginning from the right hand and ending with the left little finger on both palms, starting from the heart and so forth.
In the middle of the right [hand], one should place a lotus blazing with shimmering rays;
on the left palm, one should place a mace glowing with its own splendor.
One should place a wheel of great luster on the right [hand] and a conch on the surface of the left;
a crown on the right hand and the Śrīvatsa mark in the middle of the left.
One should place the Kaustubha gem on the right side and the forest garland (vanamālā) on the other;
one should place Śrī on the right hand and Puṣṭi on the left side.
First, one should place the Gāruḍa mantra sequentially upon the ten fingers, starting from the right thumb at the base and ending with the left [thumb].
By this procedure, one should first perform the placement of the hands (hastanyāsa).
That supreme power of the Lord which resides within the cavity of the heart-lotus— || 20 ||
Assuming a wind-like form, she is established in ten ways;
by her own will and through her own flow, she has emerged via the path of the hands.
Relying upon the ten channels, those very [channels] are considered to be the fingers;
for this very reason, O best of the twice-born, they are within the form of the Lord known as Śakti.
Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of the collection of mantras, one should then perform the placement upon the body composed of the elements;
listen now to how that assembly of mantras is to be applied to the physical form.
One should place the twelve syllables upon the body from the top of the head down to the feet;
having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa), one should again place them from the feet up to the head.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The placement beginning from the head down to the feet is proclaimed as the "placement of creation" (sṛṣṭinyāsa). || 25 ||
The placement starting from the feet and ending at the head is called the *saṃhṛti-nyāsa*;
one may perform it as desired, in every way according to the will of the practitioner.
On the head, the face, the pair of shoulders, then successively on the right and left [arms], the heart, the back, the navel, as well as the hips, the two knees, and then the two feet; || 27 ||
One should perform the placement of the twelve syllables in sequence, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the letter Ya;
this is truly declared to be the placement known as Sṛṣṭi (Creation). || 28 ||
One should assign the syllables beginning with the Praṇava to the locations starting from the heart;
this is proclaimed as the Sthiti-nyāsa, performed according to the method prescribed for the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga). || 29 ||

One should place [the mantras] on the two feet, the two knees, the waist, the navel, the back, the interior of the heart, on the left and the other (right) sides, on the pair of arms, on the face, and on the root and the head.
The sequence of letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) is known as the "reabsorption" (*saṃhāra*).
Then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs and sub-limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga*) upon the locations starting with the heart.
One should place knowledge in the heart, because it is there that it is manifested;
one should place sovereignty in the region of the head, because it stands above.
O best of sages, whether it be the ordinary or the ultimate, everywhere the king of mantras,
Śakti, resides in the crest of the upward-moving flame of the heart-fire.
The strength residing in all the limbs, together with the skin and the vital air (vāyu),
which has become concentrated throughout the entire body— that is what one should place in the hands as vigor (vīrya).
That which is the nature of internal consciousness, which brings peace to the darkness of material nature— that light is merged into the Taijasa state at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa).
This very procedure shall now be explained according to the aforementioned rule;
thereafter, one should place the lotus, mace, discus, and conch as before.
Having placed upon his head a crown possessing the brilliance of ten thousand fires and suns, and the Śrīvatsa mark on his left chest, which has a luster like the full moon; || 37 ||

Having placed upon his chest the Kaustubha gem, which bears the likeness of the fierce-rayed sun, and having placed around his neck a forest garland produced from various lotus groves and flowers; (38)
Having placed Śrī on the right side from the ankle, likewise Puṣṭi on the left;
and having placed Garuḍa at the base of the thighs and at the ends of the ankles.
His limbs possess radiant forms and are the sole manifestation of consciousness;
so too are his other ornaments, such as the crown and all the rest.

Having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) in this manner according to the prescribed sequence, [one should visualize them] as having their well-known forms and each possessing its own radiance. || 41 ||
One should perform the binding of all the mudrās from the root mantra onwards, each pronouncing its own respective mantra like the Supreme Lord. || 42 ||
O Mahāmati, having intentionally visualized one's own form along with the sense of self-conceit (abhimāna),
and having consecrated a flower with the root mantra,
one should place it upon the crown of the head— one's own body— having first saturated it with scented water.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Placement of Mantras," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Pārameśvarasaṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ.
Fifth Chapter:
Having performed [the external rites] in this manner, one should thereafter commence the mental sacrifice (mānasayajña).
Assuming the lotus posture (padmāsana) or others, one should firmly join the palms in the Brahma-mudrā at the navel.
One should bring the group of senses situated externally to rest within the mind;
having cast the mind into the intellect, one should place that intellect within the sphere of pure knowledge.
One should indeed perform the ultimate rite through the cultivation of knowledge within this city of the body,
a divine abode with four wheels and nine gates.
One should meditate upon the heart-lotus, which is mounted on the throat-well and faces downward, by taking one's station in the central region of the grove of its pericarp.
One should meditate on the Śakti, whose form is the foundation (ādhāra), between the navel and the genitals;
and above that, the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), and above that, Ananta.
Above that, one should meditate upon the goddess Vasudhā, filled with four [elements], extending from the kanda to the navel,
divided into four parts.
Having meditated upon the Ocean of Milk at the navel, from that [ocean] a lotus arises,
endowed with a thousand petals and enveloped by a thousand rays.
One should place a seat resembling the thousand-rayed sun upon its back;
[the four qualities] are dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya as the fourth.
Having brought it down with its own mantra, one should place this tetrad in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya), extending as far as the domain of the northeast (īśāna).

One should then assign Adharma, as well as Ignorance (Ajñāna), Non-detachment (Avairāgya), and Non-mastery (Anaiśvarya) to the divisions of space beginning with the east and extending as far as the north.
These figures of men, radiant as the bandhūka flower,
are located in the northeastern direction and in the southeastern direction.
Between Yātu and Vāruṇa, and between Vāyu and Varuṇa,
are the fourfold groups beginning with the Ṛgveda and the collection of ages beginning with Kṛta.
Between the directions of Īśāna and Soma, between the directions of Antaka and Agni, between Yama and Rākṣasa, and between Soma and Sāmīraṇa. || 13 ||
Upon its summit is the Kālacakra, and in its center is the unmanifest lotus, whose stalk arises from the wind-element and is situated as the support for the transformations. || 14 ||
The elements reside in the power of support (ādhāra-śakti), while the subtle elements (tanmātrās) reside in the fire of time (kāla-pāvaka);
likewise, the senses beginning with speech are established as infinite and all-pervading.
O twice-born one, the ear and other senses are situated in the earth, the mind in the ocean of milk,
and the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) is supported within the lotus of infinite petals.

And twice eight [petals] are established upon the foundation beginning with Dharma; situated thereon is the Intellect (dhī), and above that, in the lotus, is Primordial Matter (prakṛti), which possesses the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas).
Time rests upon the three abodes; the state of the Puruṣa is within that which is called Bhāva.
O Lotus-born one, the object to be supported resides within its own modification, which is identical with its own essential nature.
It is itself obstructed at its beginning and end within the thread, like a cluster of gems;
first by means of the nature of the substratum, and thereafter by way of the form of the universe.
For in reality, it is indeed waveless above, being of the nature of various mantras;
and for the sake of quelling the karma of ritualists whose latent impressions have been cultivated, [it appears thus]. || 20 ||

And for those pierced by beginningless ignorance, who manifest their desires for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment or liberation, this limitation indeed exists only with respect to what is unreal. (21)
O Pauṣkara, for those who perceive reality, there is in truth nothing above, nor across, nor behind, nor before; nor is there any conceptualization of what is to be abandoned and so forth.
That power of the Blessed Viṣṇu, whose characteristics have been set aside by specific conceptualizations, is designated as the "common" (sādhāra) power. || 23 ||
Taking up the seed-syllable according to one's desire, as previously described, she possesses the power of the seat;
her form is both unmanifest and manifest, like a cluster of kadamba flowers around the sun.
Because it possesses the nature of future expansion and because it is the accumulation of all seeds, it is designated as "the tortoise" (kūrma) when its limbs are currently withdrawn. || 25 ||
He who, at the end of time, consumes the universe by means of the nature of Kālāgnirudra (the Fire of Time),
and whose deity is the Blessed One in the form of the Tortoise, worshipped by the world.
Not relinquishing its power and capacity as the Lord's energy, that very [principle] is again infinite, the imperishable sprout of the universe for all those possessed of conceptual thought. (27)
Just as a tortoise draws its neck upward into itself, so too that which has Śeṣa as its serpent-deity is sung as Ananta (the Infinite). || 28 ||
O Mahāmati, that which is the support for the four [elements] existing as seeds—that becomes the trunk of the fragrance; from it, manifestation proceeds as before. (29)
The Lord is the self of the syllable *bhūḥ*, in whom resides the deity named Abhimāna;
from him is manifested the fruit consisting of essence, characterized by nectar. (30)
O Lotus-born One, from him whose proud form is the imperishable ocean of milk comes this lotus, possessing the luster of countless jewels.
Know that his divine, infinite-petalled lotus, which is white and fully blossomed, possesses a manifest and eternal power characterized by burning.
O Lotus-born One, the intellect (buddhi) remains together with its eight modifications, distinguished by the former [categories] and consisting of one, two, or three qualities.
In this [Veda], the modifications of speech such as the Ṛg-veda and others are its presiding deities;
likewise, there are the four modifications of time, beginning with the Kṛta age. (34)
In that regard, form (rūpa) is indeed remembered as the supreme [nature] of all things, consisting of mere existence;
however, it is the other [nature], consisting of the parts, which is characterized by manifestation, cause, and substratum. || 35 ||
The third is characterized by the body of the deity named Abhimāna;
therefore, it has Vāyu as its presiding deity and consists of the subtle element of touch alone.
O Lotus-born one, from him whose manifest appearance was clearly distinguished by the marks of various wheels,
the sound whose deity is space (ākāśa) was produced.
That lotus-abode of Pradhāna, whose pure body is sung as having its manifestation of the wheel withdrawn into all its limbs, exists within the sphere of space.
Within whom all beings reside, in whom everything is established, and from whom [the world] emerges at the beginning of manifestation and returns to dissolution at the end. (39)
The succession of time proceeds, creating a distinction among all things that are in reality undivided, being divided only by means of mere words. (40)
Because the fourfold Brahman, whose multitude of qualities such as knowledge is eternally risen, eternal, and all-pervading, it is the supreme state.
Because it is complete and possesses the six qualities, time does not find its scope there;
O Great-minded One, from the word [Ahaṃ], [arises] the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) which has the Sun as its deity.
From that [ego], the mind was born with the moon as its presiding deity;
then, from the pervasive Self whose nature is manifest bliss, the intellect arose with light as its presiding deity.

This arrangement, beginning with the petals and ending with the pericarp, starting from the east and so forth, is known as the form of the principal lotus, consisting of the [three] qualities (guṇa). (44)

O one of great intelligence, that which is the imperishable cause of the principles beginning with intellect (buddhi) is called the Unmanifest (avyakta); it indeed possesses a form composed of non-differentiated qualities (guṇas). 45.
Having suppressed its own qualities, it proceeds established in itself;
indeed, having withdrawn all functions characterized by the internal self into the heart.
For from this, O best of the twice-born, all beings indeed arise;
and into this they dissolve once again. Therefore, this lotus is supreme.
The web of rays from the sun of consciousness, characterized by the grasped and the grasper, has transferred its own abode and its own power even into that [object] where it resides. (48)
O Lotus-born one, she who is named Vimalā is purity and the power of knowledge;
she who is named Prabhvī is sovereignty; and she who is known as Satyā is truthfulness. || 49 ||
O Lotus-born One, [the powers] called Nitya are indeed eternality, those called Prakāśa are luminosity, and those called Ananta are indeed infinitude. 50.
Indeed, by means of the power of grace, the supreme state of grace is to be known;
for that which consists of the two and four kalās exists as self-established. || 51 ||
It evolves and indeed returns once again;
by means of the distinction between the higher and the lower, these are the digits (kalās) of the conscious self (cidātman). 52.
O Lotus-born One, those whose supreme infinity has been proclaimed—listen now to the pure meditation upon all of them in their proper order. (53)
One should meditate upon the Lord known as the Support (ādhāra), who is tranquil, devoid of activity, white, situated with his face turned inward, and whose form embraces that which is supported. 54.

One should meditate upon the Tortoise, endowed with the tortoise-mudrā, having the face of a tortoise, possessing the luster of refined gold, holding a conch and a lotus, and standing in the svastika posture.
Constantly emitting from his body a terrifying and fierce radiance,
the Creator appeared like a mass of flickering flames surging upwards and outwards.
Then one should meditate upon the Infinite, who resembles infinite moons, adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods and embellished with a thousand arms. (57)
Adorning the ground of his own heart with his very palms joined as a cup,
he holds in his hands a white lotus, a conch, a rosary of beads, and a discus.
To one whose intellect fears a fall and whose mind is terrified,
he grants fearlessness, saying "Do not fear," even unto the abode of Brahmā.

One should meditate upon the Earth-goddess, seated upon a lotus throne with her hands joined in the *añjali* gesture, her limbs entirely adorned with jewels and gold, and radiant like the splendor of the rainy season. (60)
He was as white as a full-blown jasmine flower, bearing matted locks that were white and glossy,
blowing a white conch shell adorned with strings of pearls.
One should remember the ocean as having all its parts expanded, with its two thighs spread apart, and its knees and feet likewise extended. 62.
His palms and soles were radiant, dark like the ripe fruit of the *āmra* tree;
he had red eyes, disheveled hair, and a smiling face.
One should meditate upon the Lotus [Buddha], seated upon a lotus throne, surrounded by hundreds of rows of bees,
marked with the lotus gesture (padmamudrā), and possessing very long feet.
The four—Dharmajña, Ānanda, and the others—possess the luster of frost, clear crystal, pure pearls, and the moon; they have the shoulders and faces of lions.
Resplendent like blossoming rubies, coral, fire, and pomegranate fruits, they were inwardly colored by compassion and resembled the lords of the kings of kings. || 66 ||
Know that the four [elements] preceded by unrighteousness (adharma) are like two eight-year-olds, radiant like gold, campaka flowers, fireflies, and haritāla leaves. (67)
The Vedas are remembered as having the faces of horses and possessing the complete characteristics of men;
likewise, O Brahmin, the Yugas beginning with Kṛta have the faces of the lordly bull.
Resembling a well-ripened mango, flax flowers, and blue lotuses, as well as parrots,
they were all endowed with excellent garments, fine flowers, and beautiful ornaments.
All of them indeed hold a conch and a lotus, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
they have placed their heads upon the wheel that is to be established for the sake of the perfection of their own selves.
With their inner faculties surrendered to the Supreme Cause of the mantra,
[they beheld Him] situated in the midst of His own circle of rays, resembling the fire of the sun at the end of an eon.

One should meditate upon the Lord of Weapons, whose hands are joined with his own mudrās, who is leaping forth, and who is to be conceived as the unmanifest lotus, radiant like snow, gold, and fire. (72)
Peaceful, with eight arms, and gentle, he stands in the svastika posture;
possessing the luster of a crystal stone, he is the mass of consciousness, eternal and immutable.
One should meditate upon the formless Sun of Consciousness, the treasury of all powers;
for within His own glory abide all things, as they rest in that all-pervading Lord who is the foundation of the self.

O best of Brahmins, know that the being manifested by its own existence is distinct from the sattva of the qualities; it is the pervasive power, like a mass of flames arising from the tortoise-natured Self.
It was the personal domain of the Lord of Nagas; the earth was made of gold, and it possessed a divine essence like nectar, accompanied by surging waves.
One should fully understand the imperishable majesty of the milk-ocean, which is like the seed-vessel of a lotus, complete with its filaments and surrounded by petals. (77)
The excellent discernment of this tetrad beginning with Dharma is perfectly pure;
whereas the great power of ignorance consists in the [tetrad] beginning with Adharma, which is twofold within each pair. (78)

That which is to be abandoned through the great elaboration of speech, as well as the manifestation of the collection beginning with the Ṛgveda, and the [manifestation] of the Kṛta and other ages, up to the end of the great kalpa and down to a moment (ātruṭi). || 79 ||
Know that the manifestation of the wheel is indeed a rotation based on illusion;
for that immeasurable secondary function is the very nature of primordial matter (prakṛti).
This entire net of digits beginning with Vimalā is known as the manifestation of the Supreme Person;
it belongs to the Lord whose nature is mantra and is worshipped by the immortals. (81)
Indeed, that multitude of various mantras, endowed with their respective collections of powers, belongs to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, through the lords of those mantras. || 82 ||
O Lotus-born one, having thus understood dissolution, one should always abandon it;
for above that resides the manifestation of sound, characterized by the sun, moon, and fire.
O Mahāmati, that channel which is radiant with three lights and whose form is unmanifest sound exists above the three manifest wheels.
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), she went beyond the path of the sun;
then, piercing the netherworld (pātāla) by way of the gateway of the wind, she returned to her own domain. || 85 ||

Everything that is an object of volition is bound to and established within that [central channel], just as a cluster of gems is strung upon a thread; therefore, it is known as the "Middle Channel" (madhyamā nāḍī). || 86 ||
But within that aforementioned locus of the target, indeed inside that very [space], is the enclosure known as the moon and the sun, characterized by closing and opening the eyes. || 87 ||
There, having taken recourse to the lotus and the sun, the supreme Bhramarī resides;
she is the power (śakti) who gives birth to all mantras, belonging to the pervasive Lord whose nature is peace.
Resounding with a sound born of its own nature, which is known as the Śabdabrahman;
beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Ha', it bears the form of a continuous stream.
In the sky at the end of the Nāda resides the eternal Lord Ananta,
who indeed bestows boons and fearlessness, and is marked with the conch and the discus.
Endowed with two hands capable of supporting the three worlds,
he is peaceful, whose nature is pure consciousness, and who acts out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.
For he, though formless, has assumed a form with a body beyond compare;
therefore, one should perform the invocation—listen to how that is done. 92.

Having established [the mind] by means of its own power through its own essential nature, which consists of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, the unmanifest lotus [of the heart] is thus [attained]. 93.
O twice-born one, you remained in that state of pure, absolute equality for only a brief moment;
having now become the common manifestation of consciousness, your powers and faculties have reappeared.
Having correctly cast aside the characteristic dharma of egoism (asmitā), O twice-born one, it proceeds from that abandonment toward incomparable bliss. (95)
One should desire that mantra, which is self-luminous, incomparable, and imperishable, abiding within the space of light, yet to be delimited by the directions and other such categories. 96.
Immediately after assuming and relying upon the form of a digit (kalāmūrti), O Lotus-born One,
he then departed from that region of dense light into the midst of the sky.
Then, having sat comfortably upon his own seat through the power of fortitude,
[he should proceed] with his subtle body of knowledge, which conforms to the physical body of the elements.

Now, that which is the nature of the cluster of bliss (ānandakadamba), existing separately, one should color it with what is seen in the scriptures and with that which pertains to worldly conduct. 99.
By means of its own objective support and by means of the characteristics of the deity, it is like a gem endowed with various distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth. || 100 ||

Just as the omnipresent Lord assumes different forms through the distinctions of meditative absorption (dhyāna), so too does the supreme self, whose nature is the mantra, correctly manifest in this manner. 101.
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus is the imperishable light of consciousness, shaped like a *kadamba* flower bud, possessing a universal form and the luster of a jewel. 102.
Resembling a great jewel-lamp, with its radiance unbroken and vast, rays of light issued forth from his ear-cavities as if from openings for sound. (103)
Just as, O twice-born one, a mass of light issues outward from a jar that is full to the brim and contains a great lamp,
even so it is with the body.
O twice-born one, although the mantra-soul is imperceptible to the senses, the collection of rays belonging to the mantra extends outward through the channels (nāḍīs).

Nevertheless, by this very reasoning, it is perceived through direct perception that the fivefold set of qualities belonging to the external elements, such as earth and the rest, exists outside [the self]. (106)
Therefore, that which is beyond the senses must be perceived by him through direct perception;
for his quality is stability, and by means of that quality, she is indeed steadfast.
Through their mutual influence, one should ascend to that consciousness;
for whatever delight belongs to it is indeed perceived in water as well. (108)
O Sage, how could he possess that third quality otherwise?
Merely by remembering the mantra, there arises a great exhilaration of the mind. (109)
That supreme power of the Lord, which has transformed into the nature of form within fire—
that quality of fire known as "form" (rūpa)— abides within the essence of the mantra.
Since light cannot exist anywhere without heat,
O great sage, that which is the quality of touch belonging to air is indeed its own property.
The subtle quality belonging to air, which resides within the body of the mantra, arises through self-restraint by means of the internal organ alone. || 112 ||
Whatever emptiness belongs to space, that would arise from it;
for that quality, O Great-minded One, exists indeed conjoined within the nature of mantra. (113)

And because it cannot be grasped by the ordinary senses without meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), having thus previously understood the power of the mantra according to its true nature, [one should proceed]. (114)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs upon that [deity] so that, when the time for worship has arrived, it may be present with all its qualities complete. 115.
Then, one should worship with one's own mantras, without any distinction of location,
within that sphere of mantra which resembles a *kadamba* flower.
Now, through the undivided twelve-syllable mantra, she attains manifestation;
therefore, she is to be meditated upon as residing in the center of the heart-lotus.
That supreme Prakṛti is Speech, whose nature is consciousness and which is pure by essence;
she is filled by the Great Self, who is partless and possesses the state of a presiding witness.

Just as the gross and subtle bodies are related to the individual soul, so too, from the root mantra onwards, there are two aspects for the entire collection of mantras as previously described. || 119 ||
Without performing the karanyāsa (hand-assignment), one should mentally recollect the nyāsa upon the body;
likewise, one should perform the nyāsas of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
Then, one should visualize Gaṅgā descending from the sky-lotus in the center of the sky,
situated above, onto the head of the Blessed One, by means of that nectar-water.
One should indeed perform the auspicious visualization of all enjoyments, beginning with the *arghya*;
whatever enjoyment one intends, that very thing should be contemplated as consisting of nectar.
He was falling from the sky with great speed, bathed in moonlight,
appearing in those various forms born of nectar which were nectar itself in person.
One should contemplate the King of Mantras as expanded, joyful, and immersed;
then, having offered the *arghya* to the God of Gods according to the prescribed rite. (124)
One should perform the acts of proximity, suppression, and facing [the deity],
as well as the heart and other limbs, and the insignia such as the lotus.
The ornaments such as the crown and so forth, the powers (śaktis) such as Lakṣmī and others, Garuḍa, or whatever other forms reside within the body of the God; || 126 ||
All those who consist of light, abiding in their respective places as the pervader in that manner and situated within that body, are to be worshipped in due order. || 127 ||

O twice-born one, without the retinue and with their respective mantras for the arghya and other offerings—this is indeed the sacrifice of absorption (layayāga), O Brahmin, which is proclaimed as being performed within the heart and other centers. || 128 ||
Therefore, one should always worship the retinue residing within the body of the root mantra, whether in the support of the heart-cakra, in the [central] image, or wherever else.
This sacrifice, known as Layayāga, is concise and bestows all perfections;
the King of Mantras is in the center of the pericarp, while Lakṣmī and the others are in the filaments and so forth. (130)
O Nārada, all those [deities] are with form and are entirely separate; however, that which is designated as "enjoyment" (bhoga) exists through sacrifice alone, being distinct from them.
The worship of the lotuses and so forth is designated as the "office" (adhikāra).
Having performed the sacrifice called "dissolution" (laya) in this manner, as well as that called "enjoyment" (bhoga), [one attains the goal]. 132.
Then, one should worship the God in due order with offerings born of nectar,
beginning with the *susama* and ending with betel, all performed correctly as prescribed.
Having performed everything as appropriate, up to the offering of oneself, and having uttered mental shouts of victory, one should make this request: || 134 ||
Welcome to you, O Lord of Gods; grant me your presence, O Acyuta!
Accept this mental worship, which has been meditated upon according to its true nature.
But having ascertained that the Lord is well-pleased and inclined toward grace,
O best of the twice-born, one should commence the mental sacrifice in detail.
With pure, imperishable, and auspicious enjoyments born of mere volition—namely those consisting of touch, those known as services, and likewise those pertaining to food—he [is gratified]. || 137 ||
With vast and abundant forms arising from the seven worlds,
and possessing the most excellent characteristics as prescribed by the rules, (138)
Having thus offered those enjoyments with true devotion, he should recite the mantra mentally with a serene inner self. (139)

Then one should remember him bestowing elephants, horses, cows, and vehicles, as well as fine garments and ornaments, and causing [the devotees] to receive offerings presented within the sacred enclosure.
Having offered himself, along with his sons, his wife, and all his possessions, he bowed with his head, filled with tears of joy. || 141 ||
Having mentally formed the wish-fulfilling cow mudrā (kāmadhenumudrā) conjoined with the mantra, one should meditate upon it as that which fulfills all desires of Viṣṇu. || 142 ||
Then one should perform a special worship of Acyuta,
having extended the joined palms filled with golden flowers.
Having recited the root mantra with effort through the breath-control techniques such as *pūraka* and the rest,
[one should do so] until its manifestation, sounding like the resonance of a long bell.

Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is filled with a mass of quivering rays and possesses the splendor of hundreds of fires, suns, and moons, one should restrain him within the hollow of one's joined palms.
One should place that añjali upon the head of that very embodiment of the mantra;
one should again offer the arghya, and once more a beautiful añjali of flowers.

Having displayed the mudrā called the Root (mūla), one should begin the mental recitation (japa) without counting, according to one's capacity, by means of the instrument known as the bell (ghaṇṭā). 147.
And for Lakṣmī and the others who have entered the place of enjoyment,
one should mentally display the mudrā in sequence and perform the recitation once for each.
Having praised him thoroughly with purifying hymns and mantras, one should propitiate him;
O best of Brahmins, having thus performed the mental sacrifice in this sequence. (149)
One should perform such an auspicious fire sacrifice (homa) that bestows the fortune of liberation;
O Sage, one should meditate upon the abode of fire situated within the navel-center (nābhicakra). 150.
The triangle is completely surrounded by the unmanifest, which consists of the three qualities;
then, having churned the fire-drill of meditation, one brings down the fire of consciousness. || 151 ||
O twice-born one, it is perfectly pure, refined, and ever-blazing with upward-pointing flames;
because its essence is Vāsudeva, it dwells within the inner selves.
One should recite the root mantra as long as it remains within the range of hearing;
from that [place], one should draw forth the divine, supreme nectar of blissful clarified butter.

Having taken up that which has fallen from the waveless ocean of Brahman’s clarified butter (brahmasarpis) and the like, one should enter through the aperture of Brahman (brahmarandhra) by way of the path of nectar (amṛtamārga). || 154 ||
One should remember the mantra, radiant with light and augmented by the power of Brahman, as it flashes forth from the heart through the central path (madhyamārga) consisting of consciousness. 155.
That which resides like upward-pointing fuel within the fire of its own cause located at the navel,
shines intensely all around in the belly within the naturally blazing fire of Brahmā.
Having remembered that, one should imagine the nectar (amṛta) falling from the sky onto the top of the yantra, just as the clarified butter was previously brought by the twice-born. 157.
Having thus satiated the fire of consciousness (cidagni), which is of the nature of mantra, located at the navel,
one should again contemplate it as situated within the flame-tip in the lotus of the heart.

And while pronouncing the Lord of Mantras with a protracted vowel, endowed with meditative concentration, one should thus maintain a single-pointed focus upon that which resides in the two locations. (159)
Afterwards, one should deposit everything—including the nature of the mantra of the Knower, its various mantra-forms, and whatever has been performed as ritual action—into that [seat]. (160)
One should visualize the right hand as being filled with water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
in its center, one should recollect the partless mantra, radiant with a multitude of rays.
Having meditated upon the perfection of the fruit arising from the sacrifice in the form of Lakṣmī,
one should likewise recite the root mantra and visualize her within the center of the palm.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon the partless mantra above that;
placing the knees on the ground with the head [bowed], one should offer it to Viṣṇu. 163.
Then, O best of the twice-born, with a mind inclined toward serenity and being thoroughly satisfied, he respectfully made that his own and should have meditated upon it with devotion. (164)
But when the goal of human endeavor has been accomplished, whether in the heart or externally,
the host of mantras, having been recollected in due order, goes to dissolution in the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśvara).
Then, one should bring the manifestation of the mantra to rest within the power of one's own volition (saṃkalpa-śakti);
thereafter, together with that power of volition, one should likewise dissolve one's own form as the embodiment of knowledge (vidyā-mūrti).
One should dissolve the entire collection of creative powers (kalās) into one's own creative powers, and likewise into the Self;
then, as before, one becomes completely filled with a mass of bliss. || 167 ||
When he has formed the mental resolve, "I shall sacrifice externally," he then withdraws that manifestation and remains like the midday sun.
One should not dismiss the dancer as long as the external rites have not been performed;
for he must indeed be assigned to the objects such as the mandala and so forth. 169.
Having withdrawn [the elements] according to the order of creation, that which was previously described as the support dissolves by its very nature for the wise who know the reality. 170.
O Greatly Wise One, those who are free from action, perfected through their own deeds,
and whose souls delight in the eternal form, bring about the blossoming of others.
And for those who are devoted to the performance of mantras and are diverse in nature due to their lack of self-mastery,
it is indeed sustained by the power of Acyuta, whose essence never falls away.
O twice-born one, although this universe, which consists of the nature of the sixfold conceptualization, is pervaded by the Lord and sustained by His own power, [it remains as such]. (173)
Even there, O high-minded one, having overcome those living beings who inhabit it and whose bodies are sustained by his own power, he [attains] that state. (174)
"Yet he abides within that manifold self as the essence of various mantras"—thus has the nature of the substratum been described exactly as it exists. (175)
That through the thorough knowledge of which the exhaustion of karma occurs for those engaged in action—
this is the mental sacrifice that removes the wasting away of the disease of fever.
O twice-born one, it pacifies the afflictions of evil, brings about the cessation of worldly existence,
and through the yoga of constant practice, liberates one from the fall of the body.
But that man who, O Sage, performs this even once with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rule, I am pleased with him.
He exists as the foremost among all the sacrificial priests;
he shall deliver all his ancestors—those who have passed away, those yet to come, and those existing now. (179)

How much more so, then, for one who is constantly disciplined, whose mind is absorbed in that state, who stands upon the path of mantra-attainment, and who is endowed with faith and devotion? || 180 ||
There is no returning for him; he goes to the supreme state.
Knowing this, one should always perform the mental sacrifice with diligent effort. || 181 ||
This supreme secret has been spoken by me to you today, O Nārada;
it must never be told to those who are not disciples, nor to those who are not devoted.
This secret should be told to those devotees who are utterly terrified of worldly existence and whose inner selves are purified, after having thoroughly examined their true disposition. (183)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Mental Sacrifice," in the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) of the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Pañcarātra.
Śrīḥ.
The Sixth Chapter:
Having first performed a mental sacrifice according to this procedure,
one should thereafter perform the external ritual with action joined by devotion.
O Blessed One,
by your grace, that heart-sacrifice which destroys ignorance and bestows all perfections has indeed been understood by me, along with its theoretical knowledge and practical realization. || 2 ||
For what purpose should external worship be performed toward images and the like?
Explain this to me, O Blessed One, for I have a great doubt in this matter. (3)
Śāṇḍilya said:
O Brahmin, the latent impressions arising from the external world, accumulated over many births, are firm;
indeed, by these—which are themselves impure—the pure Self is rendered turbid.
That pure ritual pertaining to the mantra, which bestows the nature of peace,
is fully proclaimed for the purpose of [overcoming] arising and destruction.
Through both external and internal practices, he should become absorbed in that [state],
and the attenuation of firmly established latent impressions will gradually occur.
O Brahmin, whatever the practitioner is composed of while currently residing in the body, he shall become composed of that very thing upon the fall of the body; this is what has been declared by me.
Now, ascertain the procedure for the external arising sacrifice:
the deity, who abides in the space of the heart-lotus in the form of radiant light. (8)
Having brought him from that place, one should make him enter the eye;
one should then take recourse in that which was previously mentioned, namely the one named Vāsudeva. || 9 ||
Then, O best of the twice-born, with his pair of eyes fixed and reciting the mantra of Locanā, he gazed upon that entire [being].
Having established and gathered the requisites such as water and so forth,
one should meditate upon the weapon-mantra, radiant as the sun, upon the right hand.
Having burnt that collection of substances and defects while reciting that mantra,
O best of the twice-born, one should contemplate it all as having become ashes.
Then, having replenished that which was burnt by the defects with [the water] held in the left hand—
[water] equal to the full moon from the heart, raining down a stream of nectar— || 13 ||
Then, while reciting that mantra, one should contemplate [the deity] as radiant;
having thus [visualized] everything as burnt and then replenished, one should perform the practice in this manner.
First, one should burn him with the masses of the sun's fierce rays;
then, having visualized him as having become ashes, [one should revive him] with the rays of the full moon. || 15 ||
O best of beings, one should then further contemplate that which was burnt by the sun as radiant, through the falling stream of waves of nectar that nourishes it. 16.

Having bound the wish-fulfilling mudrā, which flows forth when conjoined with the mantra—[the mudrā] having the form of a cow, resembling the snowy mountain, and established in the supportless state. || 17 ||
By means of that [power], one should transform that entire web of enjoyments as it stands into nectar;
then the collection of substances, being stainless, becomes fit for sacrifice. || 18 ||
Having filled it with strained water and combined it with the water he has brought himself,
he should place the jar— which is useful for all purposes— to the north of himself, while reciting the Varma mantra.
Having placed all those great sacrificial implements that were previously acquired on the right side, one should set down the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) in the middle.
Its characteristics will be described in the chapter on the characteristics of images:
whatever leaves, flowers, and so forth may be seen situated upon the pedestal. (21)
Having gathered that with his hand and placed it in a pure spot,
[he should fan it] with cow-tails, yak-tails, peacock feathers, or kusha grass.
Having swept the auspicious seat with a clean white cloth,
he should thereafter sprinkle it with abundant water filtered through a cloth.
Having washed it with water using the twelve-syllable mantra preceded and followed by the *praṇava*,
one thus cleanses the support for worship with water.
First, one should render that [place] free from hosts of obstacles by means of the Astra-mantra flower;
then, having installed this [deity] there, one should worship it as consisting of the auspicious mantra.
For the sake of one's own spiritual accomplishment, one should fashion an image endowed with all requisites and possessed of all auspicious marks, made from metal or stone.
Having paid homage with the eight-limbed prostration, one should offer an arghya at the head,
followed by an auspicious handful of flowers accompanied by unguents.
One should worship Puruṣottama with devotion, together with his limbs and his retinue;
having indeed honored the God with water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamana). || 28 ||
O twice-born one, having removed the arghya and other offerings that have been consumed from that [place], and having offered salutations,
one should offer them to Viṣvaksena and purify [the area] with soft earth.
O Lord, one should wash [the image] with fragrant water using a brush made of uśīra grass and bamboo,
or, while reciting the root mantra, one should perform the three-fold path-cleansing.
One should cause the two well-washed garments of the God of gods to be put on;
for whatever flowers and other offerings have been consumed from the image of the Blessed One situated within the painting— || 31 ||
O twice-born one, having removed that [dust], he should wipe away the dust with a cloth;
or else, O twice-born one, he may do so after entering the sacrificial hall.
Having performed the placement [of mantras] for the auspicious seat and so forth, one should perform another [rite];
or else, at that very time, having performed the placement for the auspicious seat and so forth.
Having first performed the three paths according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform everything as stated for the image at the commencement of the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha.
Then, having washed the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings with water using the *astra-mantra*,
he should fill them with fragrant water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should place the ritual substances upon them according to the sequence and method prescribed,
in the corners and in front of the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) which has been covered with a cloth.
Or else, one should place the vessels upon the ground or on a support,
according to one's own prior rule, in the northwestern corner.

Having placed the water-pitcher for the *arghya* offering, one should then place the vessel called for *ācamana* (water for sipping) in the northeast, and the one designated for bathing in the southeast.
Having placed that which is designated as the *pādya* (water for the feet) at the southwest foot [of the deity],
one should place the second, the *arghya* (offering water), either in front of it or in its middle.
The arghya vessel should be placed in the southeast corner, the pādya in the northeast corner,
the ācamana water in the southwest region, and likewise the water for bathing in the northwest.

By the prior command of the Lord, one should deposit the substances for the *arghya* offering in the corners starting from the southeast (Āgneya), following the sequence of primary and secondary *arghya*, *pādya*, and so forth. || 41 ||
Sandalwood, moonstone, Bāhlīka, dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, tips of kuśa grass, rice, and sesame seeds; || 42 ||
One should place gold, silver, copper, gems, and fruits—
beginning with plantains— into the principal arghya vessel.
In the second [oblation], there should be four drops of curd, honey, clarified butter, and milk;
along with the tips of kuśa grass, bāhlīka, flowers, sesame seeds, and rice grains.
One should place dūrvā grass, viṣṇukrāntā, śyāmāka grain, śaṅkhapuṣpaka, padmaka, and kundareṇu into the vessel for the water for the feet (pādya). || 45 ||
One should place cardamom, cloves, and nutmeg, along with nutmeg fruits,
sandalwood, and camphor, into the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya).
One should add kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, campaka, vacā, kaccora, and mustā to the bathing water.
One should prepare those vessels according to the sequence of their placement; either by means of the specific mantras for each respective preparation, or else they may have been prepared previously.
Having filled [the vessels] with water and having placed the ritual substances (dravyas) in their proper order,
one should establish them upon their respective bases while reciting the specific mantras for each visualization.
Then, one should perform the rites of burning, nourishing, and so forth in their proper places;
at that time, these three [rites] should be performed for the vessels as well as for the objects of enjoyment. 50.
Having taken a flower there with his right hand,
he should meditate one-pointedly on the root mantra in its partless form.
Having poured that [water] into the arghya for sprinkling, and having likewise recited [the mantra] four times while muttering it,
he should lift it up again and cast it out from that place.
Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial altar, the acquired objects of enjoyment, and himself with that water consecrated by mantras, he should consecrate the arghya and other offerings.
Having worshipped them with flowers using the root mantra along with the scripture,
he should then worship them according to the prescribed rule using the root mantra together with its ancillaries.
One should worship the incense burner and the bell with incense;
attend now to the worship of the incense burner and the bell. (55)
At the base of the incense burner is the earth element; in the lotus is water;
in the wheel is fire; in the network of bells is air; and above the pericarp is space.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with those mantras, one should worship with those very mantras;
for they know that which is the wheel to be the heart-lotus, the hollow of the heart.
Those which are called the spokes in the wheel are known as the twelve channels (nāḍīs);
those small bells situated there, O Brahmin, should be understood as the subtle channels.
Those whose central power (śakti) is indeed coiled like a serpent, smoke-grey in hue, emerged after piercing through the egg. (59)
Arisen from the heart of the fire of time (kālāgni), she dissolved at the end of the Truth (satya).
Awakened by her, the Lord, who assumes the form of mantra, is the Self.
In its presence, [the fire] burns swiftly and without interruption;
now, understand correctly the true nature of the bell. (61)
Clearly, the Mātṛkā, whose form consists of phonemes, is eternally established there;
and therein the group of vowels, known as the twelve, is traditionally taught.
That very [mantra] is on the sixteen-spoked [wheel] along with the neuter vowels;
such, O best of the twice-born, is the threefold form of all the phonemes. (63)
That which is established in Vaikharī, preceded by Paśyantī in due order,
resting upon the spokes within the twelve-spoked [wheel], is indeed the supreme nature of speech.
That very [reality] exists eternally indeed in the sixteen-spoked [wheel], in those [petals] belonging to Vaikartana, and in the form known as the Middle (madhyamā). || 65 ||
O Great-minded One, that lotus which has a cluster of petals numbering twenty-four, consisting of the groups of letters, should indeed be fully understood as such. (66)
Know that the syllable 'ma' is the pericarp of the lotus;
and the syllable 'ya' is the conch, which is always held in the clenched fist within the house.

O twice-born one, having thus meditated upon the seven letters beginning with *ra* and ending with *ha*, which consist of the joints and the mace (*gada*), and likewise the letter *kṣa* preceded by the king of birds (*patatrirāja*), then... 68.
The power of the Lord, which is of the nature of the Śabdabrahman and characterized by the form of the bell, should be known as being indeed contained within the sixfold attributes (ṣāḍguṇya). 69.
Endowed with the quality of fire (tejas) and assuming the form of fiery substances—
know this to be the pair of qualities belonging to the presiding deity, known as Ghaṇṭā.
Indeed, those phonemes which are to be known based on this [vowel] must always be understood by practitioners longing for success during the time of constant worship. (71)
One should visualize the infinite Śaṅkha, joined with Kāla and Vaiśvānara, impelled by sound, resting upon a pearl necklace, and situated within the mouth of the Ghaṇṭā. || 72 ||
And that great wheel, O Great Buddha, is situated above, resting in the sky,
at that place where the twelve-fold sun is stationed.
Furthermore, in the form of the month, he abides within the solar rays;
indeed, the moon consists of the essence of nectar and possesses a body of sixteen digits.
Indeed, in all the fields of activity, the Wind himself [is present];
for he is the unmanifest collection of principles resting upon the lotus-leaf.

Know that the individual soul (jīva) resides in the filaments of the lotus, the Lord (Īśvara) rests upon the pericarp (karṇikā), the syllable Om (praṇava) is supported by the conch, and the Vidyā rests upon the mace (gadā). || 76 ||

O twice-born one, having meditated upon this host of deities— beginning with Garuḍa as the presiding deity of the vital breath— one should worship them with offerings starting from the *arghya* and ending with incense.
One should meditate upon the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as being face-downward and filled with the noise of people;
and above that, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus together with its stalk.

One should meditate on the Goddess in the center of that [lotus], which has scattered petals, is brilliantly white, and possesses beautiful filaments, rows of bees, and a pericarp; she is endowed with eight arms representing the eight groups of letters.
On the primary [face], within a span of four cubits, there is a mark such as a lotus,
a crystal rosary, and likewise a book of wisdom.
In her other two hands she displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
she is seated upon a lotus throne, with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Resembling the interior of a lotus, adorned with a garland of lotuses, covered with white ornaments, and wrapped in yellow garments. || 82 ||
She was vomiting forth a flood of mantras, endowed with the radiance of the flames of those mantras,
and was being praised by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, who were exponents of the Veda.
At the time of worship, one should always properly remember her being saluted by the ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas who act for the benefit of the worlds. 84.
For one who worships the mantra with this [method], success is not far off.
Having meditated thus, one should worship properly with the arghya and other offerings, and thereafter one should recollect [the deity]. 85.
Whatever [reality] of the Great Brahman of Sound resides within the space of the heart-lotus, it is eternally manifest, incomparable, and beyond the reach of practice.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to instruct others who are not devoted;
O Lotus-born One, this is the characteristic of mantras whose nature is supreme.
In the tenfold word beginning with the syllable 'ya' and ending with the visarga,
He exists in the form of various mantras within the body of letters.

The mantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, having been received from the mouth of a true guru, should be known by devoted practitioners intent on divine rites as residing in five locations. (89)

But in the case of an external image and so forth, [the visualization is performed] on the tip of the tongue, in the heart-lotus, in the crest of the incense smoke, and in the auspicious sound of the bell. || 90 ||
O Mahāmati, one should cause the light of one's own essential nature, which abides within the heart, to become uninterrupted through its central form. 91.
Know that the form of Vaikharī is again supported by the smoke of incense;
it is experienced as unbroken when the bell is being rung.

Having thus recollected her, he then [honored] her whose form was entrusted to Sumantra, who had been worshipped with offerings such as arghya accompanied by incense, and who was absorbed in meditation. || 93 ||
Then he should properly ring the bell, which is auspiciously sounded, awakened by mantras, the shaker of the three worlds, and the destroyer of all that is evil. (94)
For this is the swift awakening of mantras that have fallen asleep;
it is the warder-off of all obstacles and the purifier of all mantras. 95.
At the end of the Praṇava, this resonance indeed enters into dissolution within the power of sound (Śabda-śakti).
Mantras are said to have the phonemes as their body, and the deities have the mantras as their body. || 96 ||
Those who have awakened, rooted in the resonance of the bell, grant the accomplishment of their actions;
the power arising from the sound of another takes the form of the resonance of the bell.
O best of sages, having attained the nature of phonemes,
those phonemes have been fashioned into thousands of bodies of mantras of various forms.
But by her own will, through the power of this Śakti, and by her own capacity, she acts spontaneously for the sake of bestowing grace upon living beings—her devotees whose minds are purified. (99)
O tiger among sages, because they provide protection through contemplation (manana) and bestow their own state, they are therefore proclaimed as "mantras. || 100 ||
Those sounds are unmanifest and likewise formless;
when the bell is struck, they issue forth by the thousands.
For this very reason, O best of sages, she is celebrated as the Mother of Mantras;
she is the power known as Ghaṇṭā, as Vāgīśā, and as Sarasvatī. (102)
All mantras are established in speech, and that which is spoken is established in the mantra;
therefore, the entire universe, both external and internal, consists of the very nature of the mantra.
Everything is contained within the sound of the bell; therefore, one should ring it beforehand.
Now listen as I describe those times which have been mentioned for one's own [rituals]. 104.
Then, during the worship of the deities stationed at the gateway of Gaṇeśa’s pedestal, especially at the time of invocation and when offering incense, [one should recite] the mantras. || 105 ||

In the offering of lamps, the offering of arghya, as well as in the enjoyment of the food offering (naivedya), at the conclusion of recitation and praise, and when the satiation of the fire has commenced; || 106 ||
In the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), in the dismissal of the mantras, in the worship of Viṣvaksena, and in the presentation of his offerings. || 107 ||
Especially at the time of offering oblations to the deities,
there is no other prescribed movement for those desiring spiritual success than this.
Then, having offered incense accompanied by the sound of a bell for the vessels,
one should offer incense at the appropriate time, once for each [offering] such as the arghya and others.
In the case of a secondary rite, however, the wise one should employ the heart-mantra for the invocation, the presence, the confinement, and likewise for the worship. (110)
At the time of dismissal, one should always perform the offering of the *arghya* water from the vessel first;
with that water, one should likewise perform the honoring (*ārhaṇa*) and the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
One should perform the leading forward and taking up [of the fire], as well as the act of pleasing for the sake of propitiation;
furthermore, one should sprinkle all objects with water from another source.

Indeed, at the commencement of all undertakings and always upon their completion, [one should perform this] for the pacification of deficiencies and excesses, and for the pacification of errors in knowledge. 113.
The offering of that arghya to the pervasive Lord, whose nature is mantra, must be performed daily;
likewise, the rites for the pitcher, the secondary pitcher, and the sacrificial pit are performed during the worship of the weapon-pitcher with mantras.
O Great-minded one, regarding the worship of enjoyments, the teachers and others,
for the sake of the self-worship of the skillful disciple, and with respect to the worship of those stationed at the door— (115)
[He should worship] the deities of the palaces and seats, as well as the lineages of gurus, who are embodied in the form of emblems, limbs, retinues, powers, ornaments, and physical forms. || 116 ||
Likewise, there is the worship of the deities residing in the enclosure of the mandala;
as well as the binding of mudrās, the sprinkling of the hands, and the washing of those offerings. || 117 ||
At the time of recitation, one should likewise perform the worship of the rosary;
one should always offer water for the feet from the third vessel.
But from the fourth [offering] onwards, one should again provide water for sipping (ācamana) at the appropriate time,
as well as water for washing the hands, mouth-rinsing water, and water for cleansing the mouth.
One should perform the bath using the bathing water; this is the injunction for the officiant.
Having drawn out a little water from the second arghya vessel, [he should proceed]. (120)
Then, O Sage, having worshipped the mantras placed upon his own body in their proper order with ointments, flowers, and incense, he [proceeded]. 121.
Furthermore, the preceptor should never at any time take for himself any perfumes or flowers that have been prepared for the purpose of my worship. 122.
If the preceptor should, out of delusion or greed, withhold those perfumes and other offerings intended for worship, that worship shall become fruitless. (123)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the separation according to the prescribed rule;
having taken up the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other requisites, one should worship the deities stationed at the door.
Having gone outside the door, standing or even sitting,
[he should worship] Vāstu, Kṣetreśa, Garuḍa, Dvāraśrī, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍa.

Having worshipped the deities with water for the feet and other offerings, one should worship those residing in the temple, as well as those in the four-gated temple, in the pavilion, and in other locations. 126.
Then, at the three gates, [he should worship] Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Jaya, Vijaya,
Bhadra, Subhadra, and Gaṇeśvara.
When it becomes a subordinate limb for the host of deities beginning with the Gatekeepers and ending with Viṣvaksena, it is for men of little intelligence. (128)
For a person who is single-mindedly devoted, that failure to worship indeed causes mental distress;
for disciples engaged in their regular practice, it likewise constitutes an obstacle.

Therefore, for the sake of compassion toward him, worship performed with the thought that he is a servant of the gods—and even that which is devoid of devotion—is indeed ordained in this very manner. (130)
Bowing down, they receive with equanimity even that which is offered by a living being who has passed away;
for, having meditated upon the supreme good within their hearts, they grasp it with their minds through their intellect.
For all these are composed of Acyuta, their minds being offered to Him; such indeed is the worship for those who are single-mindedly devoted to the Guru.
There may indeed be a removal of contradiction because they are the servants of Hari;
having thus performed the sacrifice at the door, one should then offer flowers facing [the deity].
Having grasped [the water] with the thumb and three other fingers,
and having consecrated it with the Astra-mantra, one should visualize the discus (cakra) above it.
One should cast [the weapon] within the sacrificial hall—sharp-edged, blazing in form, raining down fire and thunderbolts, and the destroyer of the nets of obstacles. (135)
Then, out of compassion for him, one should expel that great web of obstacles from the interior of the house by means of that splendor.
One should visualize nectar emerging from one's own body, equal in brilliance to the moon;
even before the placement of the mantras, it possesses the radiance of fire for them.
Since it appears through that [mantra], by relying upon the flower-mantra, they emerge depending upon that;
therefore, they are on the left side.
Then, O Brahmin, one should raise the right index finger upward, joined with the *śikhā* mantra, possessing a radiance like a flash of lightning. (139)
Having recollected [the mantra] for the sake of pacifying obstacles, one should enter while rotating [the hand];
then, having sprinkled one's own seat with water from the *arghya* vessel.
O twice-born one, having struck it with the Astra-mantra and then with a flower upon its back, one should worship the collection of mantras beginning with Ādhāraśakti in due order. || 141 ||
Having sat upon the seat, one should begin the sacrifice with a concentrated mind;
or, at this juncture, one should perform the contemplation of all enjoyments.
Having established the auspicious seat from the base, one should then sprinkle it with water from the *arghya* vessel and cleanse it with the hand or with a *kūrca* brush using that same water.
First, one should make that [mandala] free from hosts of obstacles by means of the Astra-mantra flower;
it should consist of all the worlds and be the refuge of all the gods. (144)
One should meditate upon the King of Wheels (cakrarāja), which consists of the support of all and is inwardly absorbed;
one should then worship it with the syllable Om, followed by its own name, ending with "namaḥ."
Then, preceded by the offering of flowers, one should perform the mental placement (vinyāsa) of all the mantras there, according to the appropriate method.
Listen attentively as I describe how one should duly perform the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha with offerings of water for the guest (arghya), touch, incense, and garlands made from various flowers. 147.
The pedestal together with the image is declared to be the Yoga-pīṭha;
in the sacrifice of continuous contemplation (anusandhāna-yāga), one should likewise fashion the Yoga-pīṭha. || 148 ||
That is called the seat of the mantra; however, one should perform the placement of the mantra (nyāsa) everywhere, and place it beneath the pedestal of the deity residing therein.
Above that is the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti), and above her is the Tortoise known as the Fire of Time (Kālāgni);
upon its head is the one named Śeṣa, situated on the station of the Yoga-throne.
Having placed the earth above that, one should place the milk ocean in the shank;
the foundational lotus is in the knee, and above that, at the base of the throat, is the water lily (kumuda).

In the southeast and other directions, one should place that tetrad beginning with Dharma and ending with Aiśāna; however, in the east and other directions, one should further place the supreme [tetrad] beginning with Adharma and ending with the north.
One should thus arrange the Ṛgveda in the space between the east and the northeast;
the Yajurveda in the middle between the east and the southeast; and the Sāmaveda in the interior between the southwest and the west.
Then, in the middle of the directions of Varuṇa and Anila (the west and northwest), [he established] the Atharvaveda;

thereafter, in the middle of the directions of Īśāna and Soma (the northeast and north), [he established] the Kṛtayuga; and between the south and the southeast (Yāmya and Agni), [he established the Tretāyuga]. || 154 ||

The Tretā Yuga is in the middle of the southern direction; the Dvāpara Yuga is in the region between the north and the west; and the age known as Kali is, respectively, in the region between the north and the northwest. 155.
Beginning from the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and proceeding through systematic contemplation up to the end of the Yuga, one should first bestow the gross seat of the mantra-throne.
And having placed that group of sixteen again and again in the eight directions,
O Brahmin, it assumes a subtle form, extending from the eastern quarter to the domain of Īśāna.

There, in the upper middle region, one should indeed install the sixteen [deities] beginning with Dharma according to the previously stated rule—[deities] who are radiant and bearers of supreme forms. (158)
Upon its summit is the Kālacakra, situated on a band like the sky;
in its center is the unmanifest lotus, endowed with the three qualities (guṇas). || 159 ||
On its petals is the solar perimeter; in the filaments is the lunar mandala;
in the pericarp is the fire-wheel; and in its seed-syllable is the light-maker of consciousness.
And one should remember the pure Śakti near him in the eight directions:
the Lord’s Śakti of knowledge, his Śakti of truth, and his imperishable Śakti.

And having meditated upon the infinite power of illumination and the power of the Lord’s grace, as well as these [deities] in their aforementioned forms and their manifestations in due order, || 162 ||
Having assigned the respective principles (tattvas), one should perform worship with the arghya and other offerings;
and one should always display their mudrās upon a very stable pedestal.

O Pauṣkara, beginning from the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), the complete restraint of the entire collection of mantras is always ordained for all [practitioners] once they have become well-established.
O Lotus-born One, wherever a particular [deity] is appropriate, one should perform its placement (nyāsa) there, beginning from the earth up to the power of Īśāna’s grace.
The presence of the mantras should be established upon a movable seat alone;
however, a temporary restraint accompanied by worship is prescribed there.
Wherever the Lord of Mantras has been invited to sit facing [the practitioner],
one should arrange the placement of Dharma and the other [jewels] with respect to that eastern direction.
Since the Supreme Lord faces the practitioner, that seat is indeed of the nature of consciousness; it is perfected by means of this vehicle.
And for the pedestal that has attained union with the *calabimba*, the arrangement of mantras is prescribed just as it is for a movable pedestal. || 169 ||

The placement (nyāsa) of mantras is prescribed for those who are well-established and of a single origin, as well as for those who are well-established but of diverse origins; this is indeed declared in the Sthirapīṭha.

Of those [deities] associated with the primary and secondary seats (pīṭha-upapīṭha), together with their limbs (aṅga) and in their solitary forms, and of those with one or more limbs or feet, along with their images (bimba), in due order. || 171 ||
Having inferred [the procedure] according to the ritual rules prescribed for the mandala, one should perform it;
and thus, while the Lord lies upon this immovable seat (pīṭha), then— || 172 ||
One should worship Ananta above the sun-like Cit, who is endowed with power;
and one should worship Tārkṣya in the station of Ananta, mounted upon his vehicle.
Below the pedestal of the goddesses such as Lakṣmī and others, one should place the Lord of Serpents (Phaṇīśvara);
in its corners, Dharma and the other [virtues]; and above that, the unmanifest lotus (avyaktapaṅkaja).
Then, one should deposit the three abodes (dhāmas) within that [mandala] by means of the previously mentioned path;
furthermore, one should deposit the seats (pīṭhas) outside the [central] void, starting from the southeast corner.
The fourfold group beginning with Dharma, which has the nature of primordial wisdom as its form, is established in that very manner;
for it is indeed the collection of those [elements] in their reversed state.
It is accompanied by the distinctions of the Ṛg, Pūrva, and Sāman Vedas, as well as time;
it exists within the regions of those sacred seats (pīṭhas), in the mandalas, and in the ritual applications.
The worship of Vighneśa and the others should be performed starting from the northwest corner of one's own front chamber; the ground in front of that spot is the location for their seats.
From one's own northern [corner] to the western door-region, extending as far as the quarter of Vāyu, one should perform this for the sacrifices that possess pathways within the pathway. || 179 ||
