O Great-minded One, for those who have been released from the lines of the outer enclosure, there is no external fault when they are worshipped in a horizontal position. || 180 ||
Having placed mats made of darbha grass and clusters of flowers, one should then sequentially place drops [of liquid] upon them, arising from all diseases. || 181 ||
One should worship Gaṇanātha and Vāgīśā, and immediately thereafter the Guru;
then, with devotion, one should worship the Guru known as the Supreme (Parama). 182.

[He saw] the assembly of the eternally perfected ones (ādisiddhas), who were intent on meditation upon the Blessed One, possessed of eternal authority, and who had attained the knowledge of the true nature of the Blessed One. || 183 ||
There are four other Manus and seven ancient sages;
now listen in due order to their meditations. 184.

O twice-born one, one should meditate upon the elephant-faced deity, who has the luster of the campaka flower, is seated in the lotus posture, possesses a stout body, a single tusk, and a long trunk. (185)
One should meditate upon his right hand as granting boons and fearlessness, with a rosary resting in it; and the fourth left hand as resting upon a battle-axe.

One should visualize his two hand gestures (mudrās) with the hands granting boons and fearlessness; that which arises effortlessly from the clashing of the index finger and thumb [is the second]. 187.
White as a jasmine flower, the moon, or a conch shell, with her hands raised holding a conch and a lotus, or else with hands granting boons and fearlessness, or drawing a book. || 188 ||
Having meditated upon this Blessed Lady, who has two eyes and one face, adorned with golden earrings—she who is indeed the Śakti of the all-pervading Lord whose nature is sound. (189)
When well-practiced, she quickly grants the desired object of practitioners;
with the exception of Gaṇanātha, the others remain well-established and peaceful in form. (190)
Holding counting beads and the gesture of fearlessness, they bestow grace upon all;
all are seated in the lotus posture or adorned with circles of matted hair. || 191 ||
Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having displayed the mudrās in their proper sequence,
one should likewise request permission from them in due order.
Having taken that [image] upon his head, he should then invoke the Lord in the center of the inner sanctum (garbha-bhūmi) of the temple.
[It was] fashioned to his own proportions, soft to the touch, delightful, resembling pure crystal, blazing and exceedingly radiant. (194)
Likewise, he was illuminated by the jewels situated in the center of his circle of hoods;
reclining upon the couch of Ananta’s coils, he was clothed in yellow garments,
capable of creating the illusion of a mass of clouds at twilight.
Having mounted a lotus abounding in a thousand petals. || 196 ||
Whether lying down, standing, sitting, or even mounted upon a vehicle,
he was endowed with pure being alone, possessing a radiant luster.
With a body that was indeed beautiful, divine, and unchanging,
he incessantly emitted from his frame a light characterized by wisdom.
For those who meditate, it is great and destroys ignorance without effort;
it is adorned with divine, incomparable garlands, garments, and ornaments suited to itself. 199.

The faces of the directions were made manifest by the canopies of moonlight from her teeth, which were composed of consciousness, self-luminous, and mutually beautified by their mutual radiance. || 200 ||
His lotus feet were marked by white lilies that had risen along the lines [of his soles], and his face was occupied with dispelling the suffering of those submerged [in worldly existence].
His heart filled with compassion, intent on uplifting the world, he stands in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of his own body. (202)
With [hair] resembling thickly curled black bees or flowing collyrium, ashy-white as camphor, divine, and with interiors interspersed with flowers. || 203 ||
Adorned with beautiful hair crowned by a diadem and a tiara,
his eyes were like slightly reddened cow’s milk and pure blue lotuses.
With cooling glances that bring refreshment to the world,
he possessed beautiful eyebrows and a forehead, a handsome nose, and lips like coral with a gentle smile.
His shimmering cheeks were like the moon of beauty, serving to soothe the weariness of those meditators who were tormented by the fires of their past karma. (206)
Delighting [the world] with a herd of cows produced from the mass of his own moon-like teeth,
he was adorned by the region of his chin, which overflowed with the beauty of his face.
He bore a lotus-like face that was the support of a playful smile;
he had a neck like a conch shell, mighty arms, and a chest marked with the Śrīvatsa. || 208 ||
He has the body of a lion, large eyes, long arms, and a broad chest;
he is adorned with two hands that are reddish and marked with the signs of the conch and the discus. || 209 ||
Having placed his right great arm, which resembles the coils of a serpent,
as a pillow, with his left hand extended along the side of his hip.
His chest was marked by the Kaustubha gem, adorned with Lakṣmī and the Śrīvatsa;
his belly was the dwelling place for the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
With his lotus-like left foot slightly contracted and his lotus-like eyes open,
he lies on his back with his right leg extended.
It was radiant with a crown and tiara fashioned from many jewels,
featuring various clusters of gems resembling the rising sun.
His radiant crest-jewel shone brilliantly as it gleamed perfectly,
and his ears were illuminated by the luster of his jeweled earrings.
Adorned with hair-ornaments reaching to the edge of his forehead, he shone brilliantly with a beautiful tilaka-mark upon his brow. || 215 ||
It was adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings that resembled many rays of light,
and it was resplendent with a neck-ornament richly set with abundant jewels and pearls.
His chest was adorned with many various necklaces, beautified by diamonds, lapis lazuli, rubies, emeralds, and other gems. || 217 ||
He was resplendent with the Kaustubha gem, which resembled the rising sun, and he incessantly illuminated the entire world with his own splendors. || 218 ||
He was radiant with a broad chest adorned by the Vaijayantī garland,
and by various variegated strings of ornaments from which long strands of pearls hung down.
It was beautifully adorned with a shimmering golden sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*),
and it shone with great splendor, resplendent with brilliant, magnificent jewels.
Then, with a golden thread, he bound his belly;
likewise, he adorned the region of his navel with a lotus by means of his own chain of the world.
Adorned with a waistband shimmering with various rubies,
and embellished by a girdle-string composed of an intricate arrangement of many jewels.
He was clothed in shimmering yellow garments like many millions of suns, and adorned with anklets and other ornaments inlaid with many jewels. || 223 ||
Thus it was adorned with various other ornaments such as armlets and bracelets— beautiful, radiant, and appropriate for each.
Resembling a rain-cloud and possessing the luster of a mountain of split collyrium,
he was augmented by the undivided and full majesty of the sixfold royal policy.

The unborn, eternal Lord, the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, without beginning or end, the omnipresent Master who is directly the Lord of Lakṣmī—He is the object of meditation for yogis. (226)
One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, who is beyond the supreme, whose body is non-material and tranquil, four-armed, and as pure as clear crystal.
Having made one's hands fragrant with perfumes, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) upon that [image] which is marked with the four symbols of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

Having filled [the vessel] with perfumes, water for the guest-offering (arghya), and flowers while reciting the root mantra, one should cast a handful of flowers upon the head of Hari, who is seated upon the pedestal before oneself. || 229 ||
One should remember Him as facing oneself, peaceful and perfectly awakened;
in that state, one should perform the three [rites], such as the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), without the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa). || 230 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras beginning with the root mantra and ending with the Tārkṣya mantra;
one should illuminate [the deity] from the image elsewhere, and [then invoke] Hari into that handful of flowers.
With the root mantra joined with the word "āgaccha" (come),
[one should bring] the deity consisting of light from the heart-lotus by way of the right channel.
Having invoked that [deity] with the tip of the nose, one should cast it into the pedestal, the water-jar, and so forth;
into that sphere whose essence is the mantra, which resembles a kadamba flower.
Having assigned the limbs to the body without distinction of specific locations and having worshipped them here,
one should effect the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) and meditate upon that Lord of Gods as having attained manifest form.
There, one should project the limbs and other components as previously described using their respective mantras;
having thus invoked the Lord of Gods, one should offer the arghya with the desire for his presence.
Once again, having offered arghya to him with the heart-mantra accompanied by mudrās,
and having caused [the deity] to be present through the offering of arghya preceded by mudrās and the armor-mantra (varman), || 236 ||

But having completely restrained [the breath] with the root mantra together with its mudrā, and having brought [the deities] face-to-face while reciting the root and other mantras therein, [one should proceed]. (237)
Displaying the mudrās in that manner, one should offer salutation with the eight limbs;
however, in the sacrifice of many forms, [one performs] the invocation of the principal deities and so forth.
Likewise, for the sake of refreshing the invited deities, one should offer perfumes and other articles;
furthermore, there is the worship of the group of limbs (aṅga-gaṇa) of the arrays (vyūha) and manifestations (vibhava), beginning from the eastern root.
Afterwards, one should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) for the others in due order;
or else, [one should worship] the Supreme Lord in his embodied form, stationed within the sanctuary. || 240 ||
[One should worship] Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch and the discus, who was brought down by gods and siddhas, or established by seers or men endowed with devotion. || 241 ||
And one should worship that image with its own mantra, without the rite of invocation (āvāhana),
daily [drawing the deities] from the heart-lotus of the primary image into the action-images.
Those who travel to sacred fords, shrines, and other such places should perform some form of invocation every day into the images to be worshipped, [bringing them] from the lotus of their own heart.

One should perform the invocation as before; then, having worshipped those [deities] residing within that body by means of mantra-installation and so forth, they should be visualized like sparks emanating from that body.

Having meditated and brought [the deity] down into its respective places on the ground of enjoyment in due order, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should worship it here with arghya and other offerings; such is the sequence.
Here, on the twelve lotus petals starting from the petal in front of the Lord of Mantras and extending to the adjacent petal,
one should place the heart and the other limbs [of the mantra].
Outside the petals upon the pedestal, in the southeast corner of the deity, there is a lotus; in the northeast corner, a mace; and in the southwest corner, a radiant discus.
In the northwest is the Pāñcajanya conch near the mace;
on the right side is the diadem, and on the left is the Śrīvatsa mark.
One should place the Kaustubha gem near the lotus, the forest garland (vanamālā) on the right,
Śrī and Puṣṭi within the pericarp of the deity's lotus, and then the others.
One should place the bird-bannered god (Kārttikeya) in front of the pedestal, outside the circle;
now the meditation for all the limbs, sub-limbs, and so forth is described. || 250 ||
Just as the Lord of Mantras, when invoked, is visualized with a physical form,
so too should one visualize the heart-mantra as white as a water lily.
One should meditate on the head as being deep red, with the appearance of a mountain of rubies;
likewise, one should meditate on the form of the Śikhā-mantra as resembling a mountain of collyrium.
Just as a mountain of gold is heated on all sides by the sun,
so should one contemplate the armor-mantra at the time of meditation.
Surrounded by thousands of flames and possessing a brilliance like that of a magnet,
it is proclaimed as the weapon-mantra (astramantra) complete with all the powers of every missile.
The King of Mantras should meditate on the eye as resembling smokeless embers;
they are to be visualized as possessing their own respective colors, two-armed, and resembling human beings. (255)

In this very way, O best of eminent sages, one should remember the meditation on the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) as possessing auspicious characteristics; one should meditate upon them while they gaze at the face of the All-pervading Lord.
One should always meditate upon those forms that are standing as being standing;
likewise, those that are seated as being seated, and those situated on vehicles as being with their vehicles. (257)
One should indeed recollect with the intellect those who are lying down, sitting, or standing up;
hear now the meditation on their marks, ornaments, and so forth, in due order. (258)
A lotus as white as a jasmine flower, gentle with a slightly smiling face, uttering a sweet sound that brings pleasure to the sense of hearing. || 259 ||
A mace resembling a mountain of gold, slender, with eyes like blue lotuses, beautiful as if she were sixteen years old, a maiden in the bloom of fresh youth. || 260 ||
The King of Weapons should meditate upon [the deity] illuminating the expanse of the sky with a web of rays arising from himself,
while he himself leaps within the circle of his own radiance.
Waiting for the command of the Lord was Śaṅkha, who had short limbs and red eyes, who resembled the snowy mountain, and whose eyes were like lotuses. || 262 ||
He was vomiting forth the essence of the true scriptures and other teachings from his own mouths;
he wore a crown, had a gentle countenance, was golden-hued, and possessed a massive body.
Surrounded by splendors endowed with various forms and shapes,
he stood in the air, assuming the posture characteristic of the Vidyādharas.
Then one should meditate upon the Śrīvatsa mark, resembling a mountain of crystal,
seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana) with hands placed at its two sides.
And with his two principal hands, he bears the tortoise-mudrā,
as well as the Kaustubha, the lord of jewels, which has the form of a mountain of rubies.
One should meditate upon him illuminating the ten directions, standing with his feet joined together, and carrying at the center of his chest a casket formed by his own hands. || 267 ||
Likewise, another [garland] should clearly be visualized upon the head, held by the Blessed Lady; it is a garland of variegated colors, beautiful and enchanting. 268.
Endowed with all fragrances, gentle, with slightly smiling faces, they should be meditated upon as possessing their own natural luster, having two arms, and resembling [the form of] Puruṣa. || 269 ||
Those whose weapons are preceded by the crown, and who take the form of maces, garlands, and women—
all these leaders of weapons await the command of the All-pervading Lord.
Rising up and moving about, they stood in perfectly balanced postures,
their hands resting upon the slopes of their hips, intent on fanning with chowries.
Excluding the four [hands] beginning with the crown and including the lotus, the right hand of the others should be in the gesture of threatening the flood of the wicked. 272.
And at the time of meditation, one should indeed remember the well-known, formless, individual insignia of each [deity] upon the head of all [the others]. 273.
Lakṣmī has the luster of a red lotus, with eyes like blue water-lilies;
Puṣṭi is white as a mass of milk, her face agitated with bliss. (274)
The power of the enjoyer is known as Lakṣmī, while that called Puṣṭi is indeed designated as the agent;
these belong to him who has descended for the sake of enjoyment out of compassion for the worlds. (275)
Along with that very [seed-syllable], the two imperishable powers arose:
Raktatuṇḍa and Mahāprāṇa, whose eyes were marked by terrible frowns.
O Brahmin, one should meditate upon Garuḍa, who has the appearance of molten gold, is adorned with a circle of eyelashes, has the face of a vulture, and possesses a broad belly.
Then one should meditate upon them in due order, endowed with the forms as described:
the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), the Lotus, the Mace, and the Goddess Sarasvatī.
One should know Śaśāṅka, Śrīvatsa, Mālā, Ṣaṇmādhava, and the others, as well as Prāṇa and Patatri, as the deities of knowledge established within the principles (tattvas). || 280 ||
One should worship these according to the sequence of the presiding deities with water-offerings (arghya) and flowers:
on the eight-petaled lotus, the heart-mantra on the eastern petal, and the head-mantra [on the southeast petal]. (281)
The crest-mantra is on the southeastern petal, while the armor-mantra and the weapon-mantra are on the middle of the southern petal and the middle of the southwestern petal respectively. || 282 ||
The mantra for the eyes is on the western petal; the mantra for the belly and back is on the northwest;
the mantra for the arms is on the west; and likewise, the thighs and knees are on the north.
One should place the foot-mantra in the middle of the petal dedicated to Īśāna;
this same sequence applies even to a lotus joined with petals and sub-petals.
Alternatively, in this [mandala], the fourfold group beginning with the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya) should be placed on the petals of the cardinal directions;
the Weapon-mantra (astra) should be on the petals of the intermediate directions, and the Eye-mantra (netra) should reside in the filaments (kesara). || 285 ||
The subsidiary part (upāṅga) should be on the secondary petal; therefore, hear the rule for that:
one should place the belly upon the surface of the two [petals] situated near the front leaf. 286.
In the same manner, one should place the mantra of the back on the two western petals;
the two mantras of the arms and thighs are to be placed on the two southern petals.
Likewise, the knees and feet should be placed upon the two petals situated in the north,
within the six limbs in the form of mantras of the eight-petaled lotus.
One should place the heart-mantra in the east, the armor-mantra on the left, the head-mantra on the right,
and the crest-mantra in the west, upon the four remaining petals.
Having placed the weapon-mantra at the front of the pericarp and the eye-mantra on the filaments and the front petal,
one should worship as before and perform the placement of the lotus and other elements.
In lotuses with three petals and so forth, one should mentally divide the location at the base of the petals as previously described, into five, six, or twelve parts.
One should assign the limbs (aṅgas) according to what was seen on the back part of the Lord;
then, one should assign the limb together with the retinue on the right side.
Having divided the portion according to its nature, one should arrange it starting from the east and proceeding in order;
having taken recourse to the left side, one should begin from the direction of Īśvara as prescribed.
One should delineate the divisions of the directions as lunar, airy, and watery;
from those two, one should effect the arrangement of twelve positions according to the sequence of groups of six.
Having thus assigned the deities beginning with Dharma, who reside in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
when Śrī and Puṣṭi are present separately upon their lotuses in the sacrifice, [one should proceed as follows].

Even in the sacrifice for that specific office, there should be a separate seat and so forth, or it may be placed at the side, devoid of the branding marks of the sacrificial animals and the like. || 296 ||
Then one should provide him with enjoyments and worship him with all the excellent offerings, having presented the best seat to the omnipresent Lord who has been duly invoked. || 297 ||
Having offered a common footstool adorned with a soft covering and accompanied by the sound of a bell, one should present the *arghya* at the head of the mantra.
One should present a golden vessel for receiving the water for the feet, adorned with jewels, to the Lord;
likewise, the water for the feet, a cloth for wiping the feet, and unguents. (299)

One should worship Hari with vessels for receiving offerings, water for rinsing the mouth, fragrant ointments, and garlands, as well as with great lamps filled with ghee and other substances that burn without being extinguished.
One should worship the Lord with abundant fragrant and sweet incenses;
thereafter, one should offer the respectful oblation (argha), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and a mirror.
The cleansing rite (*niṣpuṃsana*) should be performed with the vessel, the rinsing water (*ācāma*), and the fragrance;
furthermore, it should be infused with powdered camphor and rubbed with sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*).
Having offered excellent betel-leaf together with areca nut,
he prostrated himself with eight limbs before his wife, children, and himself.
Having offered [the oblation] with a mind endowed with devotion immediately thereafter, one should then provide the requisites for bathing, seating, and other enjoyments;
and having performed the worship, one should touch the right foot of the deity with one's hand. (302)
Then, having grasped the left [hand] with the right or the left according to the mantra,
and having requested permission for the immersion, one should then prepare three paths.
Then, having offered two bathing seats for the God who has descended for the purpose of bathing, one should immediately provide a footstool.
With his head bowed in devotion, he should offer the arghya upon the [deity's] head;
then, having presented a golden vessel adorned with jewels as a recipient for the offering.
One should indeed offer water for the feet from the foot-basin to his two lotus-like feet,
as well as auspicious sandals, and then, at the conclusion of that, a bathing garment.
An excellent vessel filled with fragrant śāli rice for the sake of the mother,
a mirror with the luster of the full moon, and immediately after that, scented water.
Then, for the purpose of washing his hands, he should use an auspicious footstool.
(He should not touch any part of his body with oil that has touched his head.
Thereafter, he should use a tooth-stick made from a tree suitable for ritual use and free of milky sap. 308.

The vessel for rinsing the mouth, as well as the instrument for scraping the tongue, the water used for gargling and sipping, and betel-leaf perfumed with fragrances—[these are not to be offered]. || 309 ||
Having placed the oil and other substances required for the commencement of the bath nearby,
and having performed the worship of their respective vessels, one should then worship the oil.
Having covered the shoulder with a cloth, one should scatter beautiful flowers over the Lord;
then, one should pour the finest oil upon the head in the middle of the deity's crown.

Repeatedly twisting and squeezing [the oil], as well as scratching with the nails, and the removal of the oily residue through various applications, should be performed while scrubbing thoroughly. 312.
Having offered garlands of *ketakī* and lotuses, one should bind the hair;
then, having washed the hands with water and removed the cloth from the shoulder. || 313 ||
Having touched the oil, one should likewise massage the limbs and the minor parts;
thereafter, one should apply a highly fragrant powder made from wheat and śāli rice.
Mixed with the powder of *rajanī* and slightly saturated with *padmaka*, it should be applied for the purpose of rubbing; and immediately after that, one should apply *māṣī*.
Immediately thereafter, he provided warm water mixed with soap for the purpose of bathing, and sandalwood paste ground and infused with camphor for the purpose of anointing his face. || 316 ||
Then there was the bath with *āmalaka* fruit, as well as *lodhra*, *kāleyaka*, *varṇaka*, *keyūraka*, *tagara*, and *priyaṅgu*.
One should likewise offer fragrant water containing white mustard seeds, the essence of all medicinal herbs, and precious gems, as well as pure water in a thousand streams to Viṣṇu.
Then there is kāleyaka, and after that the lodhra-bath and the cosmetic paste;
O best of men, these are for the body, while others are for the head.
Alternatively, one should bathe the Lord with jars filled with milk and other liquids;
for the purpose of bathing, there should be abundant products of the cow: milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
Next, one should offer pleasing sugarcane juice, or in its absence, sugar-water;
then water infused with *dhātrī* fruit, and immediately after that, water infused with *lodhra*.
Water from red sandalwood, excellent water from turmeric, water from the granthi-parna leaves, and then water from tagara; || 322 ||
Then water from the priyaṅgu plant, after that water from the māṃsī plant, then water from white mustard (siddhārthaka), and thereafter water containing all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhi). || 323 ||
Then there is water with leaves and flowers, as well as water with fruits and seeds;
after that, scented water, and subsequently water with gold and jewels.
Immediately thereafter, it was mixed solely with the water intended for bathing in the waters of meritorious pilgrimage sites and rivers. || 325 ||
O Mahāmati, this should indeed be performed gradually, accompanied by water for honor and flowers, through the application of intervals between the various ablutions.
Then follows the washing with the water from the arghya-vessel accompanied by the offering of arghya;
thereafter, [the washing] with the remainder of the bathing water using materials such as gold and other substances.
A water-pot completely filled with water, containing turmeric and well-ground rice grains,
smeared on the outside, and adorned with garlands and other ornaments.
Having placed that [substance] in one hand and a small bowl in the other, he should whirl it over his head while it emits smoke from the white mustard seeds and then cast it outside. || 329 ||
Then, having offered a well-washed, large cloth,
he presented another garment for the purpose of wiping away the water from his hair and removing the moisture from his body.
Having offered two garments, one lower and one upper, scented with perfumes and incense, as well as a shoulder-cloth that is very fine, new, and white; 331.
Then one should make the head appear darkened, provided with moon-incense;
one should make the hair of the deity mixed with camphor powder.

Having meditated upon [the deity] adorned with devotion by means of enjoyments such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth—O Lotus-seated One, this is indeed the case for those who have previously performed various [rituals], as well as for others. (333)

One should perform the rites beginning with the bath for those [images] that are devoid of the precious gems and the Brahma-stone, either upon the ritual image (karmabimba) or, in its proximity, upon a mirror.
Having performed the request for the bath, one should perform the ritual worship (karmārcā) in his presence;
having placed [the deity] upon the bathing seat, one should perform everything [else] upon that [seat]. || 335 ||
In the absence of that [liṅga], one should offer the baths and enjoyments to the image in a mirror;
and while it remains in the painting, one should likewise offer the other enjoyments in due order. || 336 ||
And in their absence, taking them all with his hand and with his mind, he should offer them within the mandala and other such places; thus is the offering of enjoyments.
Or one may perform the sprinkling with the remaining materials, such as the arghya and others; this location is indeed behind the praṇāla and to the side of the bhadrāsana.

Having purified it with many jars of water and having caused the image of the Blessed One—whether together with its pedestal or without it—to descend into that [water], if it has been worshipped; || 339 ||
One should meditate upon the deity as leaping through the air, and then wash him completely;
thereafter, one should fill four jars with fragrant water once again.
Except for the bathing-pitcher, the ritual arrangement for the others should be performed as before;
however, one should perform the application of substances for the four [vessels] with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
Having consecrated all that with the Astra-mantra and the Root-mantra,
one should then prepare the three paths in sequence and offer the seat.

Having worshipped the Supreme Lord situated there in the third [mandala], which is inlaid with jewels, immediately thereafter with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), as well as the two sandals. || 343 ||
Water for sipping (ācamana) should be offered again, as well as a footstool;
and having anointed [the deity] with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like out of devotion, [one should proceed].
Having fanned him with a peacock-feather fan and likewise with a [other] fan,
he should then offer a golden, silver, or wooden seat.
Having offered to the God of gods a beard-comb that makes the hair beautiful, a pair of scissors for flowers and betel, and two white silk garments.
Anointment with powdered saffron, musk, and deer-fat;
then the sacred thread together with an upper garment, followed immediately by the crown and other ornaments. (347)
There was the most excellent ornament extending down to the anklets on her feet;
indeed, she wore a variegated head-garland together with a turban-wrapping. || 348 ||
Then one should offer loose flowers produced according to the season, strung together on garland-threads from the ears down to the feet.
Then one should give a beautiful bracelet and a protective amulet (pratisara),
variegated with minerals such as saffron and the like, or made from a white thread.
It was filled with soft cotton and stitched at intervals;
there was also collyrium with its applicator stick, and betel-leaf perfumed with fragrances.
A golden tilaka-mark on the forehead, mouth-perfume with rocanā,
flowers as ear-ornaments, and a large mirror for adornment— 352.
He scattered variegated flowers blazing with the luster of radiant jewels, and [he offered] lamps of great flames, filled with sesame oil and clarified butter. || 353 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should worship [the image] wrapped in unwashed, unblemished, and beautifully white dyed cloths, with cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients placed inside.
One should burn auspicious guggulu incense, mixed with camphor powder, fragrant and sweet in abundance,
and combined with refined incense.
With his arm moved gracefully by the pleasant sound of bells,
he [took] the sandals, the white umbrella, the palanquin, the chariot, and so forth.
The vehicle, extending as far as an elephant, was adorned with banners and a Garuda-standard;
immediately thereafter, his two mothers [received] white and black yak-tail whisks according to their respective wealth.
Placing his knees upon the ground and bowing his head,
he took [the offering] with both hands turned upward and presented it to the Lord of the World.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of fulfilling all enjoyments, [he should perform this] accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums and clay drums, and joined with shouts of "Victory! (359).
One should worship with various songs and dances accompanied by stringed instruments, as well as with flutes, horns, and other musical instruments that are pleasant to hear.
O Great-minded One, one should perform the recitation of the hymn-mantra beginning with "jitaṃ te";
it may be performed either separately or collectively, and especially in conjunction with the specific verses.
Then, O best of the twice-born, one should perform four circumambulations,
scattering flowers equally in the four directions.
With his heart full of devotion and accompanied by his internal organ,
he bowed with his back, head, hair, knees, forehead, chest, and hands all pressed together.
A householder should always perform a prostration accompanied by a circumambulation;
an ascetic, however, should perform a full prostration like a staff in every direction.
For those such as the *snātaka* and others, this very same [practice] is prescribed;
indeed, remembering the Lord of All with their intellect, they should prostrate themselves once upon the ground. (365)
If there is no space available, he should stand before the Blessed Lady;
with devotion and a focused mind, he should perform [the ritual] while joining his palms in the añjali gesture.
Remembering Hari, the Lord of All, with tremors in the region of the heart and the head,
[one should meditate] within the inner sanctum of Viṣṇu, in the half-pavilion at the entrance of the womb.
One should perform a series of prostrations without a series of circumambulations;
one should not rotate the body like a wheel, nor should one show the back.
One should exit by the rear side in the presence of the deity, the fire, and the guru;
for the back of the hand of the Lord residing in the fire is visible.
Even among many objects of enjoyment, one should first obtain the primary one;
thereafter, one should worship the festival image in that very same sequence. || 370 ||
One should perform [the circumambulation] with both knees and hands, or with the hands alone;
having performed the circumambulation of the knees, one should remain close within the presence of the Lord. || 371 ||

And likewise, the other [circumambulation] is performed in the reverse direction for the devotees' movement around the feet; having thus circumambulated and offered a handful of flowers, then— || 372 ||
Then one should also inquire after the Blessed One's well-being regarding the triad beginning with bathing;
or else, [one may do so] while offering the arghya-water and ācamana, along with arghya, perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Having performed the sacrifice, one should cause the deity to be honored with the *nīrājana* rite and offer the *arghya* to the Lord;
then, having presented a seat for the meal, one should proceed with the three paths (*mārgatraya*).

One should offer the water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamana), covered with an excellent cushion made of fine linen or cotton, together with the ritual vessel for acceptance.
Having prepared the libation and perfumed it with the arghya water, he then took the pure, fragrant water for worship from its vessel. (376)
Immediately thereafter, one should offer the madhuparka consisting of curd, ghee, and honey combined;
or likewise, one may offer all these together as a single portion, or even just the curd alone. || 377 ||

Then, cool, refreshing water and the powder previously mentioned should be offered for the purpose of sprinkling (niṣpuṃsana), followed by a further ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) for the Lord.
Having presented a well-adorned, beautiful cow wearing a garland, along with medicinal herbs filled with *śāli* rice, and a tree rich with garlands and fruit; (379)
First, one should present the image, then, having established it, perform the libation (tarpaṇa);
one should also offer the covering garment and the water for honoring (arhaṇodaka). || 380 ||
With divine and purifying food offerings arising from the six flavors, with fruits, and with many kinds of chewable foods piled high with jaggery and sugar-candy, all cooked in ghee; || 381 ||
With fruits mixed with jaggery, mung beans, and milk; mixed with turmeric, ghee, and sesame seeds;
mixed with curd; mixed with all [these ingredients]; and joined with the sweetness of honey. || 382 ||
One should gradually offer eight kinds of food, including cakes, along with savory juices, *rasālā* preparations, and well-boiled milk.
With purifying, cool, and sweet-scented drinks, as well as with various kinds of foods— those to be chewed, those to be eaten, those to be licked, and those to be drunk— in great abundance.
One should worship the unborn and immutable [Lord] with a mind purified by faith;
moreover, at each enjoyment, one should sprinkle it with water for the arghya offering.
Having performed a snap of the fingers joined with the mantra by means of both hands,
[one should do so] by means of the two dhāraṇās consisting of the sun and the moon.
One should properly prepare everything; listen attentively to how that is done:
first, one should burn it with the fierce rays of the sun. (387)
Having intentionally reduced myself to ashes, O Nārada, I was then restored by the rays of the full moon through the falling showers of waves of nectar.
One should further contemplate that which was burnt by the sun as radiant;
indeed, one should visualize the wife holding the wish-fulfilling mudrā, flowing [with nectar], and conjoined with the mantra. || 389 ||

Having offered flowers and the arghya water to her who has the form of a cow, who resembles the snowy mountain, and who stands upon the supportless path, one should touch her above with the hand of Viṣṇu.
Having touched the forearm of the right hand with the left hand,
one should then use that right hand with its fingers slightly contracted at the tips.
Then, O Brahmin, with his head bowed low, he should offer that [food] along with purifying, clear, cool, and sweet drinks. (392)

Immediately thereafter, [the deity] should be gratified with offerings accompanied by cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients, scented with refined incense and camphor, and mixed with coconut water.
Having rubbed [the body] with a powder of lentils, black gram, turmeric, and rice, and having washed it thoroughly with plenty of cold water; || 394 ||
For the purpose of the food offering and the ceremonial sipping of water, one should prepare excellent scented water, rendered pure with a cloth and white sandalwood. (395)
Having anointed himself with well-ground sandalwood paste mixed with camphor,
he [should place] sesame seeds and jewels upon a vessel made of gold or silver.
Then, having placed it in a vessel for the sake of the measure, one should offer it to the God, infused with cloves, *takola*, cardamom, cinnamon, and camphor. (397)
It was provided with many nutmegs and areca nuts, possessed of fragrant leaves,
mixed with camphor powder, and combined with pearl dust.
At the conclusion, one should bow down and offer betel leaf to the Lord of the World, accompanied by citron fruit and coconut fruit. (399)
Having indeed washed both hands with scented water drawn from the *arghya* vessel, so that they may become clear and perfectly stainless. (400)
Having purified those two [hands] with offerings of food, incense-bowls, and other vessels,
and having smeared them with fragrant unguents, they should honor one another with the *arghya* water.
Having displayed the mudrās and the mantras beginning with the root-mantra in their proper order,
one should worship them again with water for the guest (arghya), perfume, flowers, and incense.
Then, one should satisfy the deity according to the prescribed rules for the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña),
using either a rosary made of crystal or the joints of one's own fingers.
One should then place the vessel with water from the *arghya* vessel;
having smeared it with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one should set it upon an auspicious dish.
Having worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should then install the mantra there,
along with a seat provided with its base and surrounded by the [deities] preceded by Śakti.
One should meditate upon Viraja as having four arms, like another Nārāyaṇa, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and holding joined palms in reverence. || 406 ||
One should meditate upon that thread situated at the station of Brahmā as being like a topknot;
O Lord of Gods, remain present here, O Acyuta, remaining firmly restrained.
O Sage, having thus established the mantra upon the thread known as the rosary within this jewel-net called the Sūtra, for as long as the moon, sun, and stars shall endure. (408)
Once [the deity] is firmly established, one should indeed display one's own mudrā;
then one should perform recitation according to one's ability, either one hundred and eight times or more. || 409 ||
Having offered that to the Lord, he should thereafter perform [the rite] with speech, action, and mind, saying:
"O Lotus-eyed One, Soul of the Universe, Janārdana, whose form is the mantra! (410)
"O Lord, accept this recitation from me, a miserable one, forever.
Having spoken thus, he then offered the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the flower held in his right hand.
O Nārada, one should place [the seed-syllables] before Viṣṇu with the root mantra,
and then one should properly contemplate that shimmering garland of stars.
O tiger among the twice-born, she entered the mouth of the Blessed One, passed from his mouth into his heart, and then from his heart again by way of the sequence known as withdrawal (saṃhāra).
As before, one should unite each [element] with the Supreme through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); this procedure is prescribed for all [the centers], beginning with the heart. || 414 ||
There is no fault because it is an ancillary part of the ritual; otherwise, [it would be so] without that recitation.
Then, having offered incense, bowed, and praised the Lord of Mantras, [one should proceed]. || 415 ||
One should perform two circumambulations and likewise a prostration;
it should not be of an uneven number such as one, three, five, or seven. || 416 ||
For the Blessed Lord Hari is indeed equal toward all;
having worshipped those [images] which consist of the Blessed One with perfumes and incense, [he should proceed]. || 417 ||
Having worshipped them in due order and presented the food offering (naivedya), one should offer them their seats and other requisites, ending with the ritual portions (mātrā).
Having first offered to them [the ancestors] everything up to the end of the *tanmātra* at the conclusion of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*),
one should then present the offerings beginning with the respectful reception (*arhaṇa*) and ending with betel (*tāmbūla*) at this time;
thereafter, one should provide a bed and a seat, and then satisfy them with oblations into the fire.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The External Sacrifice," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
Prosperity!
Having laid down his weapons upon the seat and carrying the *arghya* offering, he should go to the fire-sanctuary;
then, having performed the worship at the entrance as before, he should enter.
There, having sat down according to the previously mentioned rule and being composed in mind, [one should perform the rite],
because for those who sacrifice with mantras, there is no accomplishment without an oblation in the fire-pit (kuṇḍa).

Therefore, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should always be prepared—whether according to the sūtras, mobile, or stationary—for the supreme primordial nature of the Lord’s fire-power consists of the flames and so forth. || 3 ||
The other primordial nature is the hearth, which takes various forms just like fires;
therefore, these hearths indeed possess the form of fire for the rite of oblation.
O twice-born one, those [mudrās] arising from the distinctions of the square and other shapes are for rites performed for specific desires;
they are characterized by a beautiful garland of jewels, the śrīvatsa, a crown, and ornaments on the limbs. || 5 ||
Resembling a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, and various arrows, as well as an axe and a ploughshare, they grant all accomplishments.
Having the forms of a collection of weapons beginning with the vajra, resembling water-pots and ritual jars,
all of them are provided with pedestals and fashioned with four, three, two, or one girdle.
They are marked with the wheel, lotus, mace, and conch, either individually or all together; they are endowed with their own beautiful limbs, which emerge from the eight sources.
The thirteen pits, measuring from twelve finger-breadths up to one cubit, may possess all shapes; they are mobile and devoid of girdles.
In the case of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), however, those prescribed for the mantra-satiation of devotees should measure from one to two cubits and be characterized by the appropriate marks.
Having drawn [the design] on the ground and filled it with grains, seeds, or even soil,
one should always complete the rite even in the absence of all ritual materials.
But in the case of a secondary or tertiary substitute, one must always act without contradiction;
this applies to the Prājāpatya, the Daiva, and the Ārṣa forms, when measured at half a cubit.
One should gradually increase the area by one finger-breadth at a time until the field for the purpose of the hearths (dhiṣṇya) becomes eight cubits in extent. || 13 ||
Thus, by the division of measures, there would be one hundred and eighty-one [types].
When the auspicious pit has been prepared in this manner, one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya). || 14 ||
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed rules either in a small cooking pot or in a bowl;
for a sacrifice numbering fifty oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be twelve finger-breadths in size.
In a fire-oblation of one hundred and eight [offerings], the measure shall be equal to a fist and a cubit;
and in a fire-oblation of one hundred and fifty, it shall be a cubit together with the little finger.
For a sacrifice of one thousand oblations, the pit shall be one cubit; for that called ten thousand, two cubits;
for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits; and for a crore of oblations, eight cubits.

Thus, having adorned and smeared that auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which possesses excellent characteristics and is proportionate to one's wealth, with pure pigments such as lime and the like; || 18 ||

If, at the time of commencing the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the purificatory rites have not been performed with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and preceded by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); || 19 ||
And once you have attained perfection, all of them shall become submissive to you in due order;
then, one should strike with flowers from the right hand while reciting the weapon-mantra.
The preceptor, having taken a clod of earth from one part within the center of the pit using a sharp instrument and through his knowledge of the science of weapons, [should proceed].

One should extract [the earth] with the thumb and ring finger while reciting the heart-mantra; having leveled it with the weapon-mantra itself, one should ensure that there is no unevenness of high or low.
One should sprinkle it with the Kavaca mantra, crush it immediately thereafter, smear it with fragrant water, and purify it with the Astra mantra. || 23 ||
With blades of kuśa grass consecrated by the weapon-mantra, excluding those that are sharp-tipped,
and with a pair of darbha stalks likewise empowered by the weapon-mantra.
And in the middle of that, taking hold of the eastern end with the tip of a blade of kusha grass,
one should draw a line extending toward the north, beginning from the southern direction.
Having first drawn the line of the bolt (the east-west axis), that which is equinoctial (the north-south axis) is indeed established;
upon that, one should clearly draw a set of three lines.

One should draw three lines with spaces between them, starting from the south and ending in the north, extending as far as the northern limit, with the first line pointing eastward. Or rather, one may draw three lines [as previously described]. || 27 ||
Starting from the western portion, one should lead that [line] facing east;
in its middle, there should be another triad of lines facing north.
Beginning from the inner part, there is one named Piṅgalā;
however, in the south and north, there are two, namely Suṣumṇā and Iḍā, which have the deities as their presiding lords.
Having then brought about purification with the Astra-mantra, one should wash it with water from the head-vessel (Śiras);
having dried it with the Kavaca-mantra itself, one should then gaze upon it with the Netra-mantra.
Having smeared [the vessel] and rubbed it with the Astra-mantra, and having worshipped it with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
one should then place two stalks of Darbha grass inside each and every portion of the liquor.

O high-minded one, having brought it to manifestation through the armor-mantra and the like, as well as by means of the four-way crossroads visualization, one should then perform the rite according to the rules with the heart-mantra.
A bundle of soft darbha grass, dried and crushed with a stone, mixed with powdered dried cow dung and together with sulphur (gandhāśman). || 33 ||

Having placed a quantity measuring one *droṇa* into the vessel and having spread it out, he [should then cover it] with darbha grass whose tips are uncut and which has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra. || 34 ||
One should adorn the entire wall of the pit with upright [ornaments],
and immediately thereafter, one should designate the axle-enclosure (akṣavāṭa) by means of the armor (varman).
Having worshipped [the lotus] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth, using the syllable Om (praṇava) in the center,
one should worship the navel, which resembles the moon, according to that same procedure.
Then, one should place a pavitraka made of darbha grass, consecrated with the śikhā-mantra and prepared with the preliminary anointing, at the junction of the four paths.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the heart-mantra,
one should then worship upon that [seat] the Vaiṣṇava throne, beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti).
Alternatively, one should worship the Śakti known as the Sole Support;
therein, indeed, is the Śakti named Nārāyaṇī, characterized by the brilliance of lightning. (39)
She had attained the state of being the very form of Lakṣmī, possessing a nature that was like nectar itself;
she was endowed with a beauty surpassing all others and was possessed of every power. || 40 ||
Having brought down through the path of eternal creation that which abides within all other things by virtue of its tenderness and beauty, [he placed it] in the lotus of his heart. 41.

Again, by means of the very sequence of meditation, [he should extract her] from the heart-lotus by means of the heart-mantra joined with her own name, preceded by the syllable Om and the word "namas. (42)

Having cast [the deity] from the center of the heart-lotus into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the exhaling breath (recaka), and having worshipped [it] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should display the lotus-gesture (padmamudrā). || 43 ||
Having taken up fire— whether from a forest, common (laukika), produced from a gem, or originating from a mirror— in a copper vessel or another [vessel], || 44 ||
Having now placed it to the northeast of the pit for the sake of purification,
one should strike it with the Astra-mantra and sprinkle it with the Śikhā-mantra.
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), having offered the meditation on nectar (amṛta-dhyāna), and then having covered [it] with the armor-mantra (varman),
one should recollect the root-mantra (mūla) and bring [the deity] into the interior of the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka).

Having drawn it forth from that [source] by means of the wind-form of the mantra, there emerges the sixth quality, which is indeed the quality named *tejas*, separated from the collection of qualities. (47)
This very essence of the Supreme Brahman is the commonality of all splendors;
having extracted it, one should place it within that previously consecrated vessel of fire.
Then, O twice-born one, taking the smokeless and intensely blazing vessel of fire with the right hand alone, or else with both hands— || 49 ||
Having whirled it four times, one should indeed cast it into the interior of the sacrificial pit;
then, one should meditate upon it as having attained oneness with the radiance of the mantra.

Having kindled the fire with dry sacrificial fuel consecrated by mantras of the weapons, one should perform the sweeping around [the fire] with the right hand while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra. || 51 ||
Indeed, proceeding in a clockwise direction with the palms of his hands moistened,
he moved sideways with his face cast downwards, not showing the backs of his nails.
One should sprinkle [the seat] with the water of the arghya offering, consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Then, one should provide a layer of kuśa grass that is even, with unbroken roots and tips.
In every direction, up to the northern quarter, and with intervals starting from the southern quarter,
there are four ponds, each fourfold and mutually concealed by their tips.
With the four weapons recited three times each in the four directions, [one should protect] from the eastern extremities and the front part as far as the northern region.
O twice-born one, [the pillars] should be four each in the east and west facing north, and likewise four each in the south and north facing east.
Having brought it down, one should perform the placement of the substances above that, on the right side of oneself,
by means of the application of two pairs.

Having placed together in one place the four items— the enclosing sticks (paridhis), the heap of fuel, the raft-like mat (taraṇḍikā) with its darbha grass removed, and the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva)— he should arrange them.

Then, one should place together a garland, incense, honey-mixture (madhuparka), seeds, silk cloth, hair that has been cleansed by fanning, a seat (viṣṭara), clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Immediately after that, having placed four vessels for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), a pair of praṇītā vessels, a water-pot (karaka), and the vessel for the arghya offering; || 60 ||
Having placed this other set of four in front,
[he should prepare] fuel-sticks of the measure of a span and an abundant amount of dry firewood.
Having placed the eyelash-cloth, the sweat-removing cloth, and the heart-cloth on the left side,
one should bring everything to a state of purification with the *arghya* water accompanied by the Astra-mantra.

Having fashioned eight purifiers (pavitrakas) made of wood, resting upon the first girdle on the eastern side outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should place the eightfold [mantras] within them.
[He perceives] the Goddess Prakṛti, beginning with the earth and ending with the ego (ahaṅkāra),
through her fourfold nature as the pervasive one, by means of the distinction between manifestation and dissolution.

O Great Buddha, having worshipped that [image] consecrated by the Great-Souled One with a prostration consisting of his own name followed by the word "pada," and with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), [verse 65].
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others, seated upon silken mats, within the four directions of the four girdles, from top to bottom.
By means of the yoga of dissolution even in the intermediate directions, from the bottom up to the top,
they should likewise be worshipped in sequence with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth.
Then, those situated at its base, arising from the *brahma* tree and other such trees,
are clearly visible with their leaves and bark, extending even further down than the navel-ring.
One should worship the four enclosing sticks (paridhis) with the Śikhā-mantra: two with their tips pointing east and west, and two with their tips pointing north and south. || 69 ||
Then, O Sage, one should offer seats; upon them, with the heart-mantra, one should always worship the world-protectors situated in their respective directions on the back [of the seat]. (70)
Having wound the darbha grass counter-clockwise from the root for a span's length,
and having made a loop two finger-breadths beyond that, one should wrap it three times around the tip.
Having placed it in the noose and having stretched it from the base through the strands two or three times,
one should trim the excess tips to make them even and cut them with a nail-less blade.
Having performed the *upayāma* rite, one should place that [ladle] between the left thumb and forefinger;
and the consecration with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be performed with *kuśa* grass blades placed at the front of the *upayāma*.
Having purified the *sruk* twelve times with hot water and the ritual blade (*śastra*),
O tiger among the twice-born, one should likewise purify the *sruva* in two ways.

In the same manner, one should indeed heat the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the *śikhā-mantra*, and then strike them with the *astra-mantra*, accompanied by offerings of *arghya*, flowers, and a seat.
Then, for the sake of the accomplishment of the rite, the object of measurement (prameya) of the sacrificial ladles (srucaḥ) must be known:
it is the infinite one in the form of a hundred-petaled lotus, held within the fist, bearing infinite faces.

And having remained within as the nature of the seed-self, he then [manifested] upward-facing that which consists of the seven aggregates, the internal elements, the vital breaths, and the great wind.
Impelled again through the aperture of Brahma by the power of His respective will,
it entered the seven netherworlds and the Nagas, taking the form of the earth-lotus.
Relying upon which, he who is of the nature of nectar remains within the water;
abiding in the lattice of the arrangement of the wheels, he possesses the splendor of the three forms.
Then, Vāyu holds the form of a conch and the treasury of the kingdom;
thereafter, Space (Kha) is the primordial presiding deity, which is seedless, unborn, and unshakeable.
Listen so that you may understand what is to be known regarding the other, the *sruva* ladle:
Varuṇa himself, the very embodiment of nectar, exists in the form of the water-pot (*kalaśa*). (81)
That weapon, abiding as the stalk, effects the removal of obstacles;
and the moon, which nourishes the world, is situated at the tip as the lotus. (82)
For that capacity known as Ānanda is to be understood as belonging to the Supreme Lord;
it is real, immeasurable, the object of knowledge, and this infallible reality.

But at the time of consecration, having invoked [the deity] constantly during the satiation with the excellent mantra, one's own name, joined with the *praṇava* and accompanied by the word of salutation, [should be used]. (84)

O Brahmin, having worshipped all [the deities] either with the heart-mantra or by honoring them with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and perfumes, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the collection of mantras.
Then, having filled two vessels made of gold or other materials with water purified by [the mantras], one should place two sets of grass-seats (viṣṭara) within them.
Having fully worshipped the root mantra together with its injunctions in one [vessel], and that weapon-mantra in the other, he should proceed from the beginning with that [mantra].
Having poured with the *sruva* ladle in a clockwise direction and having set it down,
he should again fill it with water together with the second [ladle] on the north.
Having set it aside in a corner of the quarters, having worshipped and bowed to it,
the twice-born one should sprinkle the stream of clarified butter with that weapon-mantra and strike it.
Know that the prior touching of the clarified butter contained in the vessel with blazing *darbha* grass is the consecration known as *adhiśrayaṇa*.
That which is called "relying on an adjunct" (upādhiśrayaṇa) is said to be its liquefaction;
it is the transferring [of the substance] into another vessel for the removal of defects. (91)
For this is the act of making [the vessel] clear: having taken it up again with the raised hand, one should place it carefully in front upon the support. || 92 ||

Having first turned [the vessel] around with the *sruva* spoon, one should take four bundles of *darbha* grass, each measuring twelve finger-breadths in length, according to the count of four, three, two, and one.

Having grasped [the instrument] with the palms turned sideways and upwards at intervals, one should press it with the pair of the ring fingers and thumbs so that the middle [of the tongue] becomes bent. || 94 ||
One should bring them back four times for the sake of sovereignty; one should lead them four times by means of alternating intervals, indeed facing one's own fire.
One should cast [the materials] into the center of the sacrificial pit with the Praṇava repeated the prescribed number of times;
or else, one should pour them in three portions using two blades of Darbha grass while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having performed the submerging and emerging [of the breath], one should then place a pavitraka made of darbha grass into the middle of that, for it is a means of purification.
Having purified the eyes with the tips of kuśa grass endowed with luster,
one should perform the conjunction with the heart-mantra and the taking of the hand (upayāma) therein.
O Brahmin, this beholding—whether by the eye or by the heart—is an act of gazing performed with the splendor residing in the heart that has come into view. 99.
Having thus beheld it, one should thereafter remember that which resides within the belly of the armor;
for one should remember this veiling (avaguṇṭhana) as situated above that.
Situated in the center of the lunar disc and accompanied by the dhenu-mudrā, one should contemplate the mantra of the Sun’s daughter, radiant with the luster of a hundred shimmering moons. 101.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Mantras situated within that [lotus], resembling the Himālaya mountain;
and by the floods of nectar flowing from it—both lunar and produced from the celestial cow (Kāmadhenu)—[one should perform the sprinkling]. 102.
Having rendered it immortal with the Kavaca mantra, one should place the clarified butter in the north;
this rite known as Amṛtīkaraṇa has thus been fully explained to you. || 103 ||
O twice-born one, having performed the purificatory rites for the common clarified butter (ājya), you should then perform all the appropriate consecrations for the fifteen [oblations]. 104.
O twice-born one, first with flowers gathered from a sacrificial fire, or with a seat, or with a dipping-spoon (sruva),
or with flowers sprinkled with clarified butter, or with ghee itself, one should perform the rite with a focused mind.
One should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning with conception and ending with marriage;
for indeed, [this] is the entry of that which was external into the hollow interior of Śrī’s womb. 106.
Know that, O Sage, the first sacrament is indeed conception;
it is the power residing in the womb, born of fire, which arises from the union of the vital breaths.
That which is the subtle, imperishable flow of consciousness (cit) belonging to her, who is insentient in form, gradually [emerges] through the power of the Lord's energy and consciousness. || 108 ||
Having recollected this, one should offer clarified butter with the previously mentioned heart-mantra;
indeed, the "puṃsavana" (the rite for begetting a male) occurs through the directing of the power of consciousness into the fire.
Immediately after [the birth-rite], one should perform the sacrament known as the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) for the fire;
for all the unmanifested parts situated within it, such as the head, hands, and so forth, [are thereby consecrated]. || 110 ||
Those who, being awakened, resort to their respective limits of action—for them, that conceptualization of division is declared to be the "sīmanta" (the parting of the hair). || 111 ||

O twice-born one, for the sake of the birth-rite of the fire, one should offer oblations once as before; and for the fire that has emerged from the womb, there is the ritual consumption [of the sacrificial food] after it has been bathed.
That birth-rite (jātakarma) should be performed with gold, honey, and clarified butter;
for the sake of the naming ceremony (nāmakarma), one should offer oblations with a ladle filled with clarified butter.
O twice-born one, once the fire has been produced with effort by Vāsudeva and others, one should mark it with a well-known name; this shall be the rite of naming (nāmakarman). || 114 ||
For the purpose of the annaprāśana rite, one should perform the oblation as before;
thus, for the Vaiṣṇava fire purified by these consecrations, one should proceed with diligence. || 115 ||
That which consists of the feeding with food preceded by the recitation of mantras is called annaprāśana; and that which is the binding of the tuft of hair before the fire is called caula. || 116 ||
That which constitutes the fitness of the fire for oblations is known as the initiation (upanayana), as well as the Vedic vows, the Godāna ceremony, the return home (samāvartana), and marriage. (117)
Having performed this, one should again meditate upon the seven tongues of fire within the sacrificial pit where the fire is kindled in nine sections and the flames have risen high.
One should contemplate the triad of words known as Īśa, Prāg, and Anala;
likewise, in the three words pertaining to Yātudhāna, Vāruṇya, and Vāyanya.
Three tongues are to be understood, situated from the middle toward the south and north; one more is to be fully known—learn them now in their proper order.
Havyā, Kavyā, and Dhūmrā—these three indeed abide in the eastern direction;
while Kālī, Manojavā, and Karālī are in the west.
Know that one among them is indeed called Lelihā; know that in the remaining three places,
one should meditate upon the seven tongues in sequence as red, white, blue, black, yellow, crimson, and resembling lightning.
[They should be worshipped] with their respective seed-syllables, or with their own names, or with their names together with seed-syllables. || 123 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should meditate with these mantras in their proper sequence:
Prabhā, Dīpti, Prakāśā, Marīci, and Tāpanī. (124)
Karālā and Lelihā are situated pervading the sacrificial pit;
these three, beginning with Prabhā, are recorded as being in the direction between the northeast and the southeast.
The three beginning with Marīci are located in the south-west, west, and north-west;
one, named Lelihā, is situated in the middle of the northern direction and the south.
Having thus understood the classification of tongues for the rite of fire,
one should place [the oblation] after meditating upon the fire within the sacrificial pit as having the form of a [marked] linga.
Then, [he should contemplate] her who gave birth to him, having emerged from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by way of the path of flames,
possessing the radiance of the manifestation of supreme bliss, through the nasal aperture up to the distance of twelve finger-breadths.
Then, by means of the yoga of descent, one should visualize [the deity] entered into the heart;
having worshipped the fire with the heart-mantra and with pure offerings of arghya and flowers. || 129 ||
O twice-born one, [one should worship] in due order with incense, a lamp, curds, sesame seeds mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata), food accompanied by edibles and fruits, and clarified butter (ājya).
Having thus performed the worship according to the ritual procedure, or then by means of one's own mantra;
One should satisfy them according to one's ability, with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other offerings, in the proper sequence. || 131 ||

Or, with clarified butter alone, one should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) numbering one hundred thousand times, after which [the deity] has been worshipped with flowers and other offerings. || 132 ||
With the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles joined in the *upayāma* position, and with them positioned above and below,
one should cause the oblation to enter the mouth of the fire by means of the union of the two ladles in the *sampuṭa* gesture.
One should perform the pouring of the stream in a clockwise direction until reaching the center;
then, one should likewise lead the stream of clarified butter back to its original starting point.
O twice-born one, having displayed the heart-mudrā or the fire-mudrā,
he should then worship the fire as being of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, as previously described.
And as before, one should meditate upon the Fire-god, possessing form yet radiant with the formless,
pervading all directions through the power and vigor of one's own yoga.
Having the form of a kadamba flower, resplendent with its own radiance,
it filled the entire basin from all sides with every possible shape.
Thus, indeed, [he is] expanded, pervasive, formless, and brilliantly radiant;
then, within the fire in the middle of the sacrificial pit, which possesses a mass of flaming tresses. || 138 ||
One should mentally contemplate the seat as it has been described;
then one should perform its worship with flowers, incense, and sandalwood paste.
Then one should perform the binding of the mudrās for the assembly of deities on the throne;
thereafter, having brought down the Supreme Lord from his heart into the midst of that [assembly].
From the water containing blue lotuses, one should offer a handful of flowers to the Lord with his own mantra;
one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord as complete, together with his limbs and his distinctive marks.
One should perform the rites of facing [the deity], bringing [the deity] near, and restraining [it];
indeed, one should perform everything as before, preceded by the offering of the *arghya*. || 142 ||
Just as there is meditation upon the root image, so it should be within the midst of the fire;
one should meditate on the vehicle-bearer in the vehicle, situated as it is in the place of fire.

When he is seated, one should likewise meditate on him as seated; when he is reclining, one should likewise meditate on him in that state—possessing the reddish luster of a ruby, to be remembered in the abode of fire.
Having displayed the respective mudrās for all the mantras beginning with the root mantra,
one should thereafter worship the entire Lord with the arghya, perfumes, and other offerings.

O Sage, having properly placed the collection of sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) in a vessel according to the previously mentioned procedure, or else by means of the nature of absorption and enjoyment, one should worship them with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Then, having made his report to the Lord with his head bowed low,
he offered eight, four, or even two pieces of fuel-wood.

O best of the twice-born, having taken wood produced from the *brahma* and milk trees that has been sprinkled all over with clarified butter, and having divided it into two parts with the root mantra; 148.
Having placed one in the south and another in the middle of the southeast direction,
he should place one at rest in the southwest position and likewise another in the north.
Then one should cast the āghāra libation of clarified butter, obstructed by the station of Vāyu (the northwest);
then, from the base to the tip of the fuel-stick, one places the fuel-stick situated upon the other fuel-sticks. 150.

Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, one should contemplate the thousand-rayed Sun within it by means of its seed-syllable; then, one should place it to the south of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 151 ||
Having meditated upon the other ladle as being filled with the syllable named Soma,
one should offer that [oblation] toward the north of the lunar disc.
One should indeed offer clarified butter with fuel-sticks according to the prescribed number;
know that the two eyes of the fire consist of the nature of the Sun and the Moon. || 153 ||
The space between these two is indeed known as the mouth of the fires;
there one should first offer seven pieces of fuel in succession.
One should indeed offer into the fire four pieces of wood, each well-prepared and soaked in ghee;
having first smeared them with saffron and other substances, they should be designated as "wood" (kāṣṭha) and then sacrificed. 155.
Garlands, incense, honey-mixture (madhuparka), seeds, food, and clarified butter are offered in their respective order;
therein, this specific rule is prescribed for the offering of food and the placing of sacrificial fuel (samidh).
Having first prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the consecrated fire and placed it before him,
one should then open its lid, look at it, and subsequently sprinkle it with the water of the arghya offering.
Thereafter, one should touch [the vessel] with four stalks of darbha grass along with fire;
then, in the middle of that, one should pour four ladles of clarified butter (ājya) while reciting the mantra. || 158 ||
Then, taking the sacrificial ladle (sruk), one should offer four oblations there in the same manner;
then, one should take a mouthful of food measuring four finger-breadths.
Having placed that [ladle] within the womb [of the fire-pan], one should offer clarified butter as before above it;
then, one should cast four oblations of food into the fire.

Again, having carefully taken four ladlefuls of clarified butter (ājya) into the fire, and then having performed another oblation as before with a different [ladle] sprinkled with clarified butter; || 161 ||
One should give the four [offerings] in this very same manner according to the previous procedure;
having offered the oblations of food, one should then offer those known as the clarified butter (ājya) oblations. || 162 ||

Whatever is offered to the image, that same kind should also be offered as an oblation; one should offer each drop of clarified butter individually from the middle of the *sruva* ladle into the cavity of the *sruc* vessel. || 163 ||
One should offer individual fuel-sticks of food at the beginning and the end,
as well as one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
One should perform [the rite] a hundred times, fifty times, or a quarter of that, according to one's ability;
then, one should likewise offer oblations with unbroken grains (akṣata) and sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter.

One who desires success should, at the time of recitation as well as during the fire-oblation, perform [the rite] with half, or joined with a half-part, or even more, for those standing at the forefront. 166.

One should perform the svikṛt offering with a single mouthful of the first portion of food, using those optional rites which yield certain fruits when performed according to the specific place and time. || 167 ||
With sesame seeds, ghee, milk, or curd;
with milk-rice, prepared cooked foods, edible offerings, seeds, parched grain, and rice. || 168 ||
With roots, fruits, and tender shoots that are highly praised, and with fragrant flowers such as land-lotuses and white jasmine, O twice-born one. || 169 ||
With guggulu mixed with clarified butter, or with śrīveṣṭaka,
as well as with fresh dhātrī fruits and auspicious blue lotuses.
With very white and whitish-red lotuses, with beautiful bilva fruits, and with blades of dūrvā grass whose tips are unbroken and as pure as the fine tusks of an elephant. || 171 ||
With fuel-sticks produced from *brahma* trees as well as from milk-exuding trees,
[the oblations] should be combined with *amṛtā* and milk, and consist of pieces of *udumbara* wood soaked in honey.
For they should have uncut tips, be unbroken, and be free from thorns;
all of them should be provided with the three sweets, or alternatively, mixed with ghee. || 173 ||
All various kinds of food, as well as sandalwood and other such items, should always be offered into the midst of the fire along with sacrificial fuel sticks.
In the Lakṣahoma, tooth-sticks, betel-leaf, and items free from pungent alkaline substances, as well as seats and other such articles, are to be provided. 175.
Avoiding honey, salt, drinking water, pungent substances, and oil,
and using sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, one attains peace as well as all spiritual accomplishments.
An oblation of clarified butter, milk, and curd bestows satisfaction;
however, with milk-rice, prepared foods, and edible delicacies, nourishment shall always be attained. (177)
O twice-born one, when the king of mantras is gratified with seeds, grains, and rice, the Supreme Lord, being pleased, always bestows the highest good. || 178 ||
An oblation performed with young shoots, fruits, and roots bestows satisfaction;
it wards off untimely death and brings diseases to their pacification. || 179 ||
O Brahmin, when propitiated with land-lotuses and other flowers such as the white ones, he bestows incomparable good fortune before long.

The health of the twice-born is secured by offerings of guggulu resin with clarified butter, as well as auspicious dhātrī fruits, sugar, and bilva fruits sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 181 ||
With lotus seeds smeared with clarified butter, one quickly bestows prosperity;
one who desires subjugation or worldly enjoyment should perform the fire-oblation with blue lotuses.
Through an oblation of dūrvā sprouts, one shall obtain an increase in longevity;
and an oblation with auspicious fuel-wood and black gram (māṣa) is the powerful means that bestows peace.
The oblation of sesame seeds is praised when performed with the seal of the lion's face;
likewise, an oblation of one karṣa of clarified butter, and especially of milk, is recommended.
An oblation of curd is the measure of a śukti; that of milk-rice is a handful (prasṛti);
the measure of solid foods is half a mouthful; and for edible snacks, it is according to their own natural size.
Thirdly, one should perform the oblation of roots and tubers according to their own proportions,
and for all seeds, one should perform the oblation with a handful.
One should offer five grains of rice from the tips of the fingers,
and likewise fruits and sprouts in their natural measure.
Pills of guggulu the size of a jujube fruit should always be offered in the fire-sacrifice;
or, if available, one may offer them the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit. || 188 ||
O best of Brahmins, the blades of dūrvā grass should be four or eight finger-breadths long;
the fuel-sticks should be the measure of a span (prādeśa), cut evenly, and possessed of bark.
The colors, smells, sounds, and shapes of the fire,
as well as its modifications and the directions of its flames, are to be perceived for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action.
