O twice-born one, for the purpose of victory, a fire that possesses the excellence of the luster of a ruby, resembling lac-dye, or having the color of a young parrot, is praised. 191.
A fire resembling an indragopaka insect, or red in hue, is auspicious;
likewise, one that resembles Indra’s bow (the rainbow) or has the luster of saffron is most excellent.
Fire is desired here by the color of red varieties of flowers;
the fragrance of fragrant substances and the smell of ghee are auspicious signs of fire. || 193 ||
One who gives long life has the fragrance of a lotus, and one of excellent vows has the fragrance of bilva;
however, for malevolent rites, one with a pungent odor is always prescribed as the sacrificial fire.
A sound of fire that resembles the resonance of a cloud, a lute, a conch, or a drum leads to success; therefore, any other [sound] would be a cause for failure.
The shape of an umbrella is considered the best, as are those resembling a banner and a chowrie; so too for celestial chariots, canopies, palaces, and the bull. 196.
Furthermore, by its shape, it grants success for swans and peacocks;
when the fire appears reddish with diminished flames, [it is auspicious]. (197)
The acquisition of a broken royal stone is auspicious if it has the luster of crystal; likewise, if it possesses the same form as previously described and is turned clockwise. || 198 ||
In that way, the fire becomes a bringer of success;
even if it is of a despised color, such as pigeon-grey and the like. (199)
If the fire then reverses its direction, it is a sign of great misfortune;
at the conclusion of the oblation, for that reason, one should indeed perform more than a hundred additional oblations.
Irregular flames, as well as those resembling the crest of fire and those shaped like a woman and so forth, bring auspiciousness;
short, short-and-tall, or long flames are said to bestow success.
Smooth, turning to the right, and with a sound that mutes other noises—
this [voice] is always auspicious, even if it is devoid of other qualities.

One who desires the fruits of the sacred scriptures should offer oblations into a fire that is blazing with flickering flames, free from smoke, endowed with its natural qualities, pleasing to the heart, and conducive to satisfaction. (203)
A fire that has little luster and little form, which is accompanied by sparks, and which is devoid of flames and smoke, does not bestow success. || 204 ||
If one offers oblations into a fire that is unkindled, smoky, or not properly kindled, there will be a failure of his ritual action;
however, this is not heard [to apply] when the rite is for the purpose of malevolent magic (ābhicāra).
O best of beings, if the mantra— which is foul-smelling, yellow in color, licked by [the tongue], and inauspicious— enters the body of light when it has been satiated, [it becomes auspicious].
The Lord, the bestower of the earth, bestows knowledge before long; established in radiance, he swiftly consumes the enemies by means of his manifest supremacy.
The all-pervading Lord, when ascending in the Marīci [flame], quickly bestows the destruction of enemies;
the mantra, when ascending in the Tāpinī [flame], grants the pacification of all afflictions.
O Sage, if the mantra is offered libations while situated in the Karālā state and remaining in the Lelihā state, it shall effect the eradication of opposing forces.
It grants one's desired object and, at the end of the body, the supreme state;
one should always utter "svāhā" during the oblation and "vauṣaṭ" during the full oblation.
One should employ that very [syllable] in rites for peace, as well as in rites of subjugation and nourishment;
one should use *svadhā* in ancestral rites and the syllable *phaṭ* in rites of destruction.
For the purpose of inciting enmity, [use] "huṃ"; for subjugation, "hrīṃ"; and for the attainment of liberation, "namas.
At the conclusion of the ritual fire-offering (karmahoma), one should fill the sacrificial ladle (sruk) with clarified butter.
And in the absence [of sufficient materials], one should fill [the vessel] with abundant substances for the oblation;
thereupon, one should place ghee on top, followed by the water-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth. || 213 ||
Beginning from the base, the *sruk* ladle, together with the *sruva* spoon, should be worshipped;
the substance mixed with clarified butter is placed within the bowl-like cavity of the *sruk*.
Then one should meditate on [the self] as resembling a flowing moon; thereafter, one should extract the full [mantra].
Having restrained it at the base of the handle of the sacrificial ladle—that is, at the navel of the body—one should contemplate it.
One should extract the partless Lord of Mantras, whose form is like the full moon,
from one's own body upward from the base by means of the power of the vital breath (marucchakti).
Having established that great stream of nectar upon the support of Īśvara,
one should contemplate it falling into the lotus of the *sruk* by way of the path of the nasal junction.
One should pour forth a stream of clarified butter accompanied by nectar, like a shower of wealth,
either into the middle of the mantra or into the aperture of Brahmā.
One should correctly visualize [the deity] having fully entered within the heart-lotus;
by means of that [deity], one should meditate upon the mantra expanded by a stream of Brahman. 219.
Satisfied, joyful, nourished, and indeed contented toward the practitioner, she is truly endowed with the utterance of the mantra and possessed of a physical form. || 220 ||
O best of the twice-born, endowed with meditation, this [knowledge] has been fully imparted;
it eternally bestows all perfections and increases the fortune of liberation.
For the successful accomplishment of the rite, [the oblation] should be offered into a fire containing much dry fuel;
it is to be offered once for multiple applications, but not at every individual action.
Then, one should worship the Lord of Mantras with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should display all the mudrās in sequence, beginning with the root mantra. || 223 ||
One should perform the refinement of the primary materials with one-fourth of the total weight of the metals;
for the decorative marks and ornaments, such as those representing Lakṣmī and others, it should be half of that.

Or else, O best of the twice-born, [one should worship] with half of that [measure] for the heart and other [limbs] in all the beloveds of the Supreme Lord, and with half of that again for the others.
One should offer all the emblems, ornaments, and so forth, in sequence;
or alternatively, one may offer each of the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra individually.
Then one should perform the dismissal (visarjana), having offered the arghya together with incense;
those mantras which were worshipped in due order while residing in the locus of enjoyment (bhogasthāna). || 227 ||
And one should contemplate them as having entered the body of the principal mantra, just as rivers enter the ocean or as tongues of flame enter between other flames. || 228 ||
O twice-born one, one should contemplate that gross form consisting of the mantra, which is the locus of all mantras, as having entered into the subtle, presiding essence of the heart. (229)
But others [regard] that [reality] as subtle and consisting of both aspects in the manner previously described;
they regard it as the Supreme, whose nature is throbbing radiance, and which rests in the supportless state. || 230 ||
O best of beings, one should meditate upon [the deity] having entered the heart-lotus by way of the path of the joints (sandhi) through inhalation accompanied by mantra and mudrā. 231.
O twice-born one, one should permeate the body from the feet up to the head with that mantra which has entered [the body], even without deliberate effort.
The deity whose image trembles becomes pleased with his mantra;
having thus dismissed the Lord of Mantras together with the binding of the mudrās.
The mantras of the shared seats and those of Gaṇeśa are always [recited];
however, for the Guru and the others, half [the portion] is prescribed due to the libation for their insignia.

And, O Brahmin, one should perform the dissolution of these according to the sequence of creation, for those who protect the three worlds while stationed at the gates and those who serve Hari while stationed on the ramparts. (235)

Following the lineage of the gurus, one should cast this half by half in due order, or according to one's own capacity, once each; or, at the end of all the years, one should cast the full amount below.
Then, O twice-born one, Viṣvaksena should be gratified with devotion using sesame seeds and unbroken rice;
one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ."
Having worshipped according to the rule, he should perform its dismissal;
then, having worshipped the fire, he should offer libations according to his ability. || 239 ||
Having cast a handful of flowers into the vessel while recollecting the fire-mantra,
one should apply four vertical *puṇḍra*s using water churned with the *hā* syllable.
With the mantras of the head, armor, and heart, one should fashion the shape of a lamp flame on the forehead, the two shoulders, and the heart, using the ashes from the sacrificial pit.
Having first touched the heart with the *Jvālā* mantra and the eyes with the *Astra* mantra,
and having offered forgiveness and paid obeisance according to the prescribed rule, one should then dismiss it.
Having smelled [the substance], one should deposit it into the stomach according to the sequence of descent;
then, for the consecration of the established fire, beginning with the circumambulation by fire (paryagnikaraṇa) and so forth.
One should indeed perform the dismissal (visarjana) when the smoke has ceased;
having wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, one should place the *sruk* into the fire and [rinse] it with water.
Having filled [the vessel] from the arghya-pātra, one should perform a circumambulation outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
starting from the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa) with an unbroken stream of water.
Then, having cast the *pavitraka* upward with his hand, he should place the remainder upon the head; finally, he should set down the *sruc* ladle with its opening facing downward.
On his left side,
having removed the water from that pair consisting of the *viṣṭara* and the *sruva*, he should worship it.
Having indeed withdrawn [the ritual materials], he should proceed to the house of worship carrying the arghya;
he should then pay homage to the Lord of the World by prostrating with the eight limbs.
Having filled both hands with flowers placed upon them,
one should meditate on the partless, deep-sounding [deity] augmented by nectar.
One should cast [the offering] smeared with abundant light onto the head of the mantra:
"O Lord, you who abide in the midst of the fire, you have been gratified by this oblation through my devotion. (250)
Having offered the oblation to the Lord and performed worship according to the prescribed rule, take into yourself that potency which resides in the materials of the sacrifice. 251.
One should meditate upon that which has been received with a serene inner self.
O twice-born one, this has been stated in brief as the propitiation of the mantra. (252)
This should never be spoken to those who have not been initiated, nor to those who lack devotion,
nor to those who do not perceive the truth, nor to those whose minds delight in derision.

But it should be spoken to one who knows the true state of being, to one who knows the samaya, to one who has sons, to a practitioner, to a guru, or to one who is devoted, affectionate, and free from envy. (254)
To that Lord who is devoted to truth, dharma, and vows, who is of upright conduct and established in the teaching—
having thus completed that oblation, [he should worship] the Lord with water for honor, perfumes, and other offerings.
Having worshipped [the deity], one should then perform the distribution of portions for the ancestors;
this has been explained in detail by the God of gods specifically in the section known as Pauṣkara. || 256 ||
O best of Brahmins, this procedure for the birth from the lotus has been declared;
now I shall describe that procedure to you according to the method taught by the Sātvata. || 257 ||
O Brahmin, that which is performed daily before the one to be propitiated should be known as the highest form of distribution among all ritual acts. || 258 ||
Through sharing with the ancestors, a man becomes free from his debt;
by that act, they too attain incomparable satisfaction, even according to the power of their own karma.

Whether invited, or arrived spontaneously, or one who has been constantly accepted as a guest—such a lord of the twice-born who knows the five times (pañcakāla) and is devoted to the six duties (ṣaṭkarman). || 260 ||
Having first performed his ablutions and other rites,
O Brahmin, being self-restrained, he should again purify his hand with water for the arghya offering and then lie down.
Having struck [him] with the flower-arrow empowered by the mantra-weapon,
and then having gazed upon everything while reciting the eye-mantra (netramantra).
Having seated [the deity] before the Blessed One upon a seat presided over by the Praṇava,
which has been honored, spread out, and purified— either facing [the practitioner] or with the face turned north— 263.
And having likewise directed him toward the gaze of the north,
so that he is pierced by the spreading rays from the eyes of the Lord of Mantras.
Having worshipped him with mantras and meditated upon him, one should remain with speech restrained;
they too, being well-disciplined, must be devoted to silence.
O Lotus-born One, having established the Lord of the World in the sky of the heart-lotus like the sun, [one should offer] from the vessels of a worthy recipient into the vessels [of others]. (266)
Having thus established the foundation with previous effort in this ritual,
one should offer gifts within the inner altar (antarvedikā) for the sake of the ancestors.
That place where the best of the twice-born have been seated is known as the *antarvedī*, even though it is situated outside;
it is that which lies within the two [lines]. (268)
Whatever gift one may offer to the ancestors through a worthy recipient, that indeed becomes divine and stainless, for it is performed by relying upon consciousness itself. || 269 ||
O Lotus-born One, they remain there, sharing [the merit] at that very time;
therefore, O Puṣkarasambhava, it is by the power of the donor's resolve.
One should place it upon a seat for either one person or many;
furthermore, the seat should be made of wood, free of knots, and woven from many blades of kuśa grass. || 271 ||

The Kuśa grasses are known as the body hairs of the omnipresent Lord, whose body consists of the limbs of sacrifice; all those very hairs are the channels (nāḍīs) extending throughout his elemental body.
The rays within the bodies of living beings are indeed all the powers of the embodiment of consciousness;
for this very reason, O best of Brahmins, there is the seat of kusha grass for the ancestors.
But whatever is given with devotion after that time, following what has been prescribed for those invited at the time of the śrāddha, becomes indeed identical with Brahman.
O Lotus-born One, in former times, for the sake of those men who did not know the Self, you ordained this net of kuśa grass as a means for their ritual actions.
For those for whom Brahman is omnipresent and the Lord Acyuta exists in reality as the essence of their state of being in the form of mantra, there is indeed no further need for anything else.
Therefore, the twice-born man should place the kuśa grasses with their tips unbroken and their roots facing north;
for the divine region is designated as the north, while the region of the ancestors is known as the south.
O twice-born one, those immortals constantly cause the ancestors to flourish by means of their own nectar-like potency, under the very guise of the darbha grass path.
Therefore, the host of ancestors dwells there, resorting to the southern portion;
for in this way, they likewise reside in the northern portion of men in the form of a fraction of the *cit* (consciousness).
O twice-born one, you are that stainless, eternal, and imperishable digit known as Immortality (Amṛta), which has taken its seat [within all].
For this very reason, whatever is known by those from Brahmā downwards, O twice-born one— [is but a reflection of you]. 280.
And that which is given to the ancestors is done with the left hand,
while addressing Hari— the unborn source of the universe, whose self is the mantra.
And they offer libations of water to the ancestors;
yet, because those [offerings] depend upon them, that which was stated is not the cause. || 282 ||
And for those, O Mahāmati, for whom the supremacy of the task at hand flashes forth within them preceded by the propitiation of mantras; || 283 ||

By the power of their own subsequent [attainment], and by virtue of the direction of the preeminence of those mantras, that which is performed with a non-conceptual mind becomes inexhaustible. || 284 ||
But, O Puṣkarasambhūta, those men on earth who act having firmly resolved in their hearts that [you] are difficult to find are indeed rare. (285)
In the direction of the womb (south) of the pit, or above the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha),
or nearby in front of it on the ground, [one should perform the rite] with water for respectful offering (arghyavāri).
Having sprinkled [the ground] with the Astra-mantra, one should spread kusha grass with its tips pointing south;
upon that, one should pour water mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken grains (akṣata) using the Pitṛ-tīrtha.
O twice-born one, since these two— the tips of the kuśa grass and the end of the spreading— should be scattered with darbha tips consecrated by the Astra mantra and the Praṇava.
It is the generator of the entire web of enjoyments in the three worlds, especially of that substance which is offered to the ancestors and purified by faith. || 289 ||

The Lord himself, whose nature is the self of the sacrificial animal, has manifested in the form of Agni and Soma as the embodiment of the principles of ritual action for the sake of establishing his own identity. (290)
That splendor exists as joy in the form of sesame seeds, yet by its own nature it is not [perceived as such].
For this very reason, O twice-born one, it is so for both the unawakened and even for the awakened.
When sesame water reaches the limbs during the performance of a śrāddha rite, it provides supreme protection for that śrāddha; these two [mantras] are for those who are constantly engaged in counsel.
Having thus understood the sesame-water, characterized by radiance and bliss, through the specific knowledge of its true nature possessed by those who know the mantras; 293.
Above the stars, one should meditate upon the forms of Puruṣa and the others, endowed with their respective characteristics, from the top down to the bottom in due order.
They praised their fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers, as well as their deceased ancestors,
according to their respective lineages.
One should not offer to the gods food that is mixed with remnants, nor the first portion of the cooked food collected in the vessel,
but rather [an offering] consisting of honeyed oblation along with blades of darbha grass and sesame seeds.
Having purified it with fire by means of the heart-mantra using the tip of a blade of darbha grass,
[the soul] becomes free from defects, possesses the nature of consciousness, and has a radiance equal to the three abodes.
O high-minded one, one should meditate on the defect inherent in the substance as burning everything on all sides— that food which is intended for the satisfaction of the deities and the ancestors.
And that ritual procedure was performed by the consecrated fire of old; then, upon leaves of *tāla* and *kadalī* trees that had been previously washed, [the offerings were placed]. (299)
Having divided the food into four parts and placed them with the syllable *praṇava*,
one should sprinkle the four food vessels— or the four morsels— with water.
Then, for the satisfaction of all, having offered it to the deity, he should respectfully satisfy the ancestors with that food, such as the rice-balls (piṇḍas) and other offerings. || 301 ||
Having first understood the state of those previously unseen [entities] through their names in the heart, and likewise having known the prior condition of those whose true nature has been seen; 302.
O Brahmin, as before, with mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svadhā*, preceded by the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), and accompanied by their respective names. (303)
Thinking, "I shall prepare the funeral ball (piṇḍa)," one should then proceed as before;
with the Praṇavas, the southward-pointed blades [of grass] are sprinkled with water and sesame seeds.
One should place blades of darbha grass, representing the channels (nāḍīs), above the funeral cakes;
one should then meditate upon [the deities] as having entered into them through the paths of the channels in due order.
Then, saying "I invoke the ancestors," he [invokes] those standing to the east above the sacrificial grass (staras),
sequentially with his own four mantras, according to the principle of absorption (apya-aya).
One should worship them according to the rule with offerings such as water for the feet and perfumes;
then, preceded by the mantra, one should offer water with sesame seeds, mentioning their names and lineages.
One should then offer [the water] from the Arghya-pitcher to all of them in due order,
with the head bowed low and both knees placed upon the ground.
Placing both hands upon the forehead and with a one-pointed mind, one should recite this:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O ancestors; salutations to you, O supreme among men. (309)
Salutation to those who dwell at the feet of Viṣṇu; svadhā to you, O ancestors, salutation!
Salutation to Hari, the lord of the ancestors, whose self is Agni and Soma. || 310 ||
O Viṣṇu, salutations to you whose self is the drinker of the true soma; salutations to you whose self resides upon the sacrificial grass.
For from the beginning of saṃsāra, O Acyuta, the Janakas have been Agniṣvāttas.
You are the grandfathers who drink the Soma, and you are the other great-grandfathers;
salutations to you, the Blessed One, the embodiment of the ancestors, and to Acyuta.
O Blessed One, to Nārāyaṇa, to Haṃsa, to Viṣṇu, whose self is the three Puruṣas—
except for You alone, I neither bow nor do I worship anyone else.
"O Lord of All, I do not satisfy anyone else; I invoke no other.
Having thus praised the assembly of ancestors with supreme devotion," (314)
When possible, one should perform the honoring of the physical form [of the deity] and, in due order, that of the assembly of twice-borns seated before it. || 315 ||
O best of the twice-born, having performed the investigation with respect to both [the deity and the ancestors], or with respect to one of them,
one should meditate upon the divine state situated in the present, and the ancestral lineage in the past, in due order.
Then, having arisen by himself through the syllable Om (praṇava) into his own true form,
he stands in the middle between two [channels] situated transversely, positioned not far apart and facing one another.
O twice-born one, facing either north or south,
he should place the mantra upon the heart from the heart, according to the orientation of that northern face.

One should [meditate upon] the form of the wind and the ether, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with the word "namas," as the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) of a twice-born man seated at the tip of the Piṇḍa. || 319 ||
Or, having meditated on her as having emerged outside through her own independence by means of great effort from among many [deities], one quickly attains oneness with her. || 320 ||
Having caused [the breath] to dissolve into its own power, it indeed proceeds toward the characteristic known as *ūṣman*;
having thus performed the movement of the vital breaths within the body of the Brahmin who represents the ancestors.
As before, when [the breath] is restrained within bliss, one should feed those who have the form of the ancestors;
then, having seated the four [officiants] upon their seats for that purpose.
Having attained their goal in the supreme reality, the Brāhmaṇas and the Pāñcarātrikas [should be seated],
two facing eastward and two facing northward.
In the absence of these [materials], one should place a single [substance] facing north,
or else pour something for the purpose of the water for the feet (pādya) at the feet, starting from the right.
Then, one should perform their worship in sequence, as in the case of the Cāturātmya,
with offerings such as the arghya and unguents, up to the final concluding oblation (mātrā).
At all times appropriate to each occasion, they should remain free from all that is unworthy of acceptance;
moreover, being well-restrained, they should be devoted to silence.
Then, with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra, or with a wooden stake, or with smooth powdered stone, or with a club empowered by one's own inherent power; || 327 ||
One should fashion that seat outside [the mandala], its length being one śama greater than [the mandala's] and its width being one śama;
as before, one should bring it to a state of purification. || 328 ||
O twice-born one, he should also place there blades of kuśa grass with unbroken tips and roots facing north;
and there, moreover, he should especially scatter sesame seeds and water.
One should place there vessels consecrated with mantras over which weapons have been recited;
all of them should be circular, preferably made of gold or other precious materials if available.
Then, the vessels should be made of plantain, lotus, or *tāla* leaves,
or else of auspicious leaves, provided with darbha grass and water for the weapons.
And upon them he should place foods and eatables, even those that are sweet,
as well as solid foods, fruits, roots, curd, milk, and so forth.
O Seventh One, there were refreshing drinks, milk-based sweets with water,
and other functional beverages produced according to their respective seasons.
And for the purpose of spreading [the seat] before the vessels,
an immortal stream should be poured by the right hands with water that has been drawn up.
Those ancestors who, being restrained in speech and having attained their goal, eat the food within Janārdana in his embodied form,
thereby attain eternal satisfaction.
Therefore, those intent on action should avoid silence that is characterized by uncertainty; rather, that which is auspicious and free from deviation should be practiced in all matters. (336)
When silence is maintained through unarticulated nasal syllables consisting of bodily gestures and signs,
or by merely closing the lips, that silence causes the destruction of spiritual accomplishment.
That which exists within all things by one's own intellect and spontaneously, without being taught by words— that is silence (mauna), which bestows all accomplishments.
Therefore, indeed, for those who partake in the Śrāddha during a divine rite or a rite for the ancestors,
one should offer everything like a food offering (naivedya) before them within the prescribed boundaries.

If all remain restrained in speech until the time of the final sipping of water (ācamana), and if even a single portion of food is offered for the sake of their satisfaction, [then that alone suffices]. // 340 //

One should first remember the word "om" for the ancestors, followed by the word "asmat," and then "to the ancestors"; at the end of that, one should recollect "this is the arghya," "this is the pādya," and finally "svadhā. (341)
At the conclusion of every ritual service (upacāra), one should indeed remember "namas" in this way;
or one may say "namaḥ svadhā," or else "svadhā" ending with "namaḥ. || 342 ||
In this very way, O most excellent one, homage is due solely to him who performs what ought to be done for his own kinsmen who are equal to himself. (343)
O twice-born one, when [the name] is uttered, the reversal is always prescribed as "svadhā";
for the renunciant himself indeed bestows [the fruit] upon those who seek its results. (344)
He must always perform the salutation ending with "svadhā";
for he who desires fruit gives [the offering] to those who constantly seek no fruit.
But at the conclusion of the utterance of "svadhā," that [offering] is always designated as "namaḥ.
Thus, O twice-born one, having distributed [the offerings] among the ancestors according to his own desire, [he should proceed]. 346.
Having asked again and again about satisfaction by means of the mouth of the vessel,
he then placed a handful of water, which was like nectar, into his hand with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should bestow that which is equal to the full moon; it is to be meditated upon while reciting its sixteen digits, distinguished by the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a' along with the anusvāra.

"O Lotus-born One, the mantra consisting of the letter 'sa' followed by the letter 'na', with the 't' situated before it and accompanied by the star (the bindu), is said to be the designator of the full moon. (349)
Before washing his hands, he should drink [the water] as before,
by which the power of the food— situated within the vessel of nectar— becomes imperishable.
O Brahmin, you too should perform the act of nourishment for the assembly of ancestors and gods;
having washed your hands from the wrist down with black gram flour and other substances.
Having sipped water and properly withdrawn the remnants according to the rule,
and having purified the ground, he should place water with sesame seeds in his hand.
Then, having risen, one should first perform the act of pleasing before the Blessed One, [saying]:
"May the Blessed One be pleased with me first, and likewise the assembly of ancestors. (353)
The divine array stationed within the body, beginning from the feet, lead this food to immortality, with Viṣṇu at their head. (354)
The gods, the rivers, as well as the cows, Sūrya, Soma, Bṛhaspati,
and the blessed Mādhava, who is the embodiment of mantra, consisting of honey, and great— 355.
O twice-born one, having applied an ointment to the seat, he should prepare it so that, by abiding in this food as honey, it may indeed bring satisfaction to the ancestors. 356.
For on that very portion of the earth,
O Lotus-seated One, is the abode of all the ancestors even now, upon that ground where their funeral cakes are offered.
As long as there is no withdrawal of the physical remains of those who have departed from life,
and as long as the rites dedicated to them are properly performed, they continue to travel [in that state] until the end.

Having granted a blessing from his own place, he offered through the intellect of the performer of the śrāddha—along with water and food, and accompanied by sesame seeds and the power of the mantra—an offering of nectar. (359)
The path for your return has been made secluded by the power of the sacred mantra known as Nārāyaṇa, which has been rendered into a Brahman through its ritual application.
Having mounted their respective senses as chariots, they departed satisfied for the abode of Acyuta.
Thus, one should perform action within the temple dedicated to the worship of You, which is so well-expanded.
Furthermore, in other difficult circumstances, the king of mantras, having been entreated, should depart;
meanwhile, one should first purify the site through rites such as striking it and so forth.

One should further meditate upon the mantra as resting within the power of pervasion (vyāpti-śakti) and situated in a reservoir of water; having first performed the worship, one should carry out all [subsequent rites] before it. || 363 ||
A meal intended for the gods and the ancestors in the house of the Blessed One is not forbidden to the best of the twice-born; otherwise, it would cause contradiction. (364)
By this very rule, one should always, and especially during a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice,
perform the distribution of portions for the ancestors with devotion and according to the prescribed rites.

Or, having performed the rites ending with the offering of water and sesame seeds, he should give half of that— measured by a single mouthful— with fruits and roots according to his capacity, to cows or to a mendicant.
Because that which is offered when Acyuta is worshipped with divine great mantras—whether it be small or abundant for the sake of the ancestors—becomes inexhaustible for them. || 367 ||
Having properly worshipped the omnipresent Lord, who resides in the primary image, with offerings of water, perfumes, and other articles,
[one should do so] in all courtyards, temples, and sanctuaries.
When the forms of the arrayed manifestations have been installed for the sake of beauty,
likewise [the installation occurs] upon the gate-towers, the gates, the directional deities, and in the pavilion.
And when they have attained their presence, one should perform constant worship according to one's capacity, using sixteen services, or thirty-two, or even more. || 370 ||
The practitioner should likewise perform [the rites] with the mantras of the [deity's] forms during occasional ceremonies as well;
thereafter, he should perform the bathing and other [rituals], ending either with recitation (japa) or with fire-oblation (havana).
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a sacrificial pit situated at the foremost point of each respective image;
however, there [in that location], one should not perform ritual worship of the icon, nor the ceremonial bathing, nor the festival and other such rites. || 372 ||
The offering of oblations (balidāna), as well as the ritual of ascending the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) and so forth,
should not be performed anywhere— especially not in images that are dependent on others.

In those [vessels], one should perform only the daily consecration (nityābhiṣeka), or else the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) or the offering (nivedana), for those [vessels] endowed with colors such as white and so forth. || 374 ||

Together with the worship of the root-abode (mūlālaya), the preceptors should perform the rite of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) as an ancillary part within the dependent temples (paratantra), having consecrated it through the preliminary ritual of adhivāsa.
And likewise in all the *pūraka* [breaths], as well as in the *āgrayaṇa* and other [rituals],
and also in the host of attendants such as Khageśa and Viṣvaksena.
In houses where [the deity] has been installed, the formless Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), Viṣvaksena, and the others are worshipped like the embodiment of their refuge. || 377 ||
Of the lords of the Kumuda and other gaṇas who dwell in the gates and enclosures, and of the other attendants residing in the great seats (mahāpīṭha). || 378 ||
At the beginning of the daily festival worship, one should offer the bali-oblation three times a day to Viṣvaksena,
whether he is with form or without form, together with his attendants.
Or else, having worshipped [the deity] and offered oblations with the remaining materials, one should then perform a perpetual festival (nityotsava) accompanied by all types of ornaments.
O Lord, preceded by the offering of oblations (bali) to the deities of the courtyard and the gates,
Sanaka [is established] by you in front of my daily festival worship.
The offering of oblations (bali) for the deities of the door-panels has been described;
tell me specifically their divisions, which grant all accomplishments.
Śāṇḍilya said:
I shall explain to you in detail the daily festivals and other rites; listen, for by performing them, the desired fruit arises for the devotees. (383)
The image for the purpose of the perpetual festival should be made of gold or silver, or else of copper or brass;
it should not be too tall and should have four arms.
And it was established and worshipped in the past in accordance with the original image, adorned as beautifully as possible with garments, ornaments, and garlands. || 385 ||
Having projected the power (śakti) residing in the primary image onto that [object] by means of mantra,
one should worship it thoroughly with offerings such as water for honor (arghya) and flowers, as well as with enjoyments ending with incense.
When the deity has been propitiated by trustworthy persons in self-manifested shrines and other such places,
the practitioner should choose another person to perform the rites of offering oblations and so forth.
Formerly, at the door of the inner sanctum and likewise in the front pavilion, [he was worshipped] with a blazing lamp accompanied by the sounding of bells. || 388 ||
Having worshipped the door-keepers with offerings beginning with the arghya and ending with incense, and having then presented the respectful offering (arghya) with water,
one should thereafter offer food and subsequently the water for libation (tarpaṇa).
Having offered betel-leaf in sequence with their respective mantras in due order,
[he should offer] a vehicle made of gold or other materials in the first courtyard in front.
Having adorned it as beautifully as possible with fragrant flowers, radiance, linen cloths, white and other garlands,
one should perform the auspicious rite for the offering of bali upon it.
Having placed [the image] facing the east, he circumambulated it clockwise within the courtyards, accompanied by white and other colored umbrellas, and by peacock-feathered banner-staffs. || 392 ||
With banners, chowries, and beautiful palm-leaf fans;
with courtesans, temple-maidens, singers, and collections of musical instruments. || 393 ||
With the sounds of kettledrums and tabors accompanied by the resonance of Vedic chants,
and with such ornaments as these, [the ground] was smeared with cow dung.
In a mandala measuring one cubit, preceded by the offering of bali, [one should worship] the deities of the doors and enclosures who have been visualized in their respective directions. || 395 ||
One should perform the fixed festival according to the procedure to be described;
then, upon the pedestal, there is the worship of Viṣṇu and the beings together with their attendants.
Having performed this, one should scatter the remainder as a water-offering (bali) for the sake of satisfaction;
then, having circumambulated the seat, one should divide it into four parts or likewise into two.
Having gratified [the deity] with dance, song, and other offerings, one should cause the Lord to enter within;
likewise, one should do so respectfully in the spacious outer courtyards. || 398 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon the decorated chariot, one should perform the circumambulation;
then, having descended from the vehicle and offered the sandals, [one should proceed]. || 399 ||
And having seated [the deity] upon an auspicious throne situated on the floor of the main pavilion,
[one should worship] with water for the feet, the respectful offering, and water for sipping, as well as with ointments such as sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped with various kinds of garlands, incenses, and betel-leaves as the final offering, one should establish it in its own place for the sake of pacifying fatigue. || 401 ||

Having first established the Śakti and having joined it to that root, one should worship it with offerings such as water for honor (arghya) and perfumes, and bow down preceded by hymns of praise. || 402 ||
Where a regular festival is performed according to rule at the three times of day, there shall be constant and complete prosperity for both the king and the kingdom. (403)
In the absence of a physical image (balibimba), when it has not been brought into proximity due to some cause,
one should then perform the daily festival using either a tuft of grass (kūrca) or a food-image (annamūrti).
Having performed the withdrawal of everything without exception, including the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and so forth,
and having bowed to and praised the Lord of Gods, [he should proceed] from the reception of the water for the feet (pādya).
Having taken the water from washing the feet, one should sprinkle it upon one's own body;
and the leaves and flowers that have been used for eating, one should place upon one's own head.
When the sacrifice to the gods has been performed with flowers, water-offerings, and perfumes,
and when devotees who observe the mantras have brought their offerings with humility.
By constantly holding [the breath] at the crown of the head, misfortune is destroyed, and one attains fame, splendor, prosperity, health, and spiritual perfection. || 408 ||

Thereafter, having petitioned the Supreme Lord for the sake of maintaining his physical body and having received His permission, he should perform the subsequent sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.
Having entered a secluded dining area free from defects,
he should then indeed light a lamp placed in a vessel filled with ghee.
Then, having smeared a square mandala there with cow dung,
one should install a wooden plank or similar object in its center while reciting the syllable Om.
Having washed his feet and sipped water for purification, he should sit down in their midst;
then, taking all the food intended for consumption along with the offerings (naivedya) placed in the vessel, [he should proceed].
Having offered it to the deity and purified it with water, it becomes the embodiment of truth, invisible, and the destroyer of all defects in food. (413)
The fourfold self and the cultivation to be practiced are [to be understood] by the mind;
the one known as the witness of the essence of flavors is established in the state of sweetness within food. || 414 ||
The Lord Pradyumna is in form, while the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) is in valor;
I am the enjoyer, the Self, the unborn Lord Vāsudeva himself.
This is that immortal Brahman; this is imperishable life;
this is knowledge, this is vigor, and this indeed is the splendor of Viṣṇu.
This very one is the unbroken moon, abiding himself in the form of food;
that Blessed One, as the self of the rain-cloud, exists for the sake of establishing the persistence of condiments.
The Supreme Lord, the Eater, indeed enjoys [the objects] through the nature of the fire within the heart;
because he is favored by that power, I am a person subject to material nature. || 418 ||
In this way, the giver of food is to be known as the eater of food, and the food stands before him;
furthermore, through the external offering of clarified butter, it attains full awakening.
In whatever way the lord, the fire residing within the body, approaches through water,
it becomes the cause for the sixfold essence of food and for the six tastes.
The self, though non-Ātman by nature, becomes Ātman through its slight identification with that [divine] instrument;
having brought the self into a state of direct presence, one should then slowly offer the food as an oblation.
Then, having consecrated it with the *praṇava* four times, one should drink a handful of that water;
thereafter, one should offer four oblations of food into the cavity of the mouth using that very same water.
First, one should offer four oblations using the outer joints, with regard to the fourfold nature;
then, by virtue of regarding the threefold nature, one should offer three oblations.
Then, with a focused heart, one should eat morsels of food while reciting the root mantra;
finally, with mouth and hands purified, one should drink water consecrated by the mantra.
Or else, that water may be one that has flowed from the lotus-feet of his meditation,
or it may be water previously consecrated for him while he was established in the form of an image.
For it destroys all sins, brings about the destruction of all defects,
pacifies all afflictions, and always bestows all happiness.
O best of sages, this is more purifying than all sacred fords and mantras;
therefore, after the meal, one should first perform the libation for the *hārdha* fire.
Constantly devoted to heartfelt devotion, one who bestows clarified butter should drink [the water] slowly with the Brahma-tīrtha, three or four times in succession. || 428 ||
Having sipped water for purification, he should again proceed to the house of the Blessed One,
having placed his mind, intellect, and ego upon the surface of the earth.
Like a tortoise, one should always keep the four feet and the head as the fifth in that very place,
moving in a clockwise direction in this manner at all times.
One should pay homage with the eightfold prostration while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra;
at that place, worship should be performed at the twelve times according to the detailed ritual for the spirits.
There, one should perform the morning worship endowed with its eight limbs,
or having completed it even without the final two limbs.
The preceptor should always perform, at his own discretion, the distribution among the ancestors and the secondary sacrifice as prescribed during the midday worship.
At the three times of day, one should practice both the eight-limbed and the six-limbed [yoga];
for those seeking yoga, there is the study of scripture and yoga known as "inner" (adhyātma).
Now, it is stated that one should perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) at those respective times:
having prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra), one should sit down before the Lord.
One should study the scriptures and reflect upon the meaning of their statements;
then, when the time for twilight has arrived, one should bathe as far as the hips.
Having washed [the feet], one should then change one's garments;
one should perform the evening worship consisting of six limbs, concluding with the offering of bali.
Having performed the recitation according to one's ability, and then having retired to one's bed,
one should place the external deity within oneself, established in the state of the supportless.
Indeed, with a mind that is neither striving nor yet ceased from activity,
you shall now fall asleep together with him.
Then, having risen at midnight, with sleep and fatigue conquered,
he performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) using the very water contained within his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

Then, for the sake of the manifestation of yoga, one should practice Vaiṣṇava yoga in a well-concealed, solitary place, free from the pairs of opposites and possessing auspicious characteristics. || 441 ||
Having subdued pride, he should fix his mind on the welfare of all beings,
remain devoted to the gods, the sacred fires, and his gurus, and always take delight in the true scriptures.
Abandoning malice toward living beings, refraining from theft, and with his senses restrained,
he sat upon a very beautiful seat endowed with auspicious marks.
But [a vessel] made from auspicious wood, twenty-four finger-breadths in length and twelve finger-breadths in height, even when wiped with a well-washed cloth— 444.
Covered with soft kusha grass and a sacred skin,
seated there, one should constantly practice the limbs of yoga.

That breath control (prāṇāyāma) which is performed by means of the four [stages] beginning with exhalation (recaka), distinguished by their respective measures (mātrā), is proclaimed as the minor, the middling, and the superior. || 446 ||
One should perform withdrawal (pratyāhāra), which is the restraint of the mind;
for the intellect, the mind, and the ego—by these three, the mind is proclaimed. (447)
Nevertheless, one should diligently practice the withdrawal of the mind;
for the mind is said to be of four kinds, and it is conquered through withdrawal. 448.
It abides on the path of the target, and never otherwise;
meditation is the accomplishment of the target, and that is proclaimed as reflection (cintana). || 449 ||
Thereafter, for the sake of removing evil, one should also maintain the dhāraṇā;
it is fivefold, as before, according to the arrangement of each individual mantra. (450)

One should perform the recitation (japa) with eyes closed, consisting of the seed-syllables (bīja), clusters (piṇḍa), and words (pada), which express the mantra for the sake of realizing that which is expressed. || 451 ||
Indeed, that which was previously described according to the prescribed method is declared to be threefold;
yoga also is said to be threefold—listen to it from me in its entirety.

The first is the natural (prākṛta), the second is the human (pauruṣa), and the third is the divine (aiśvara). Reasoning (ūha) is celebrated as logic (tarka); know that it is the faculty of investigation. || 453 ||
Samādhi, however, is proclaimed as bliss consisting in the attainment of one's own true nature;
it is devoid of the utterance of mantras and has abandoned all objective focus. || 454 ||
When the portion of the Brahman-element, freed from ritual injunctions, is discerned, one attains the Supreme Person upon the perfection of meditative absorption. || 455 ||
From the beginning of breath control (prāṇāyāma) up to the end of meditative absorption (samādhi),
it is proclaimed to be established according to the distinctions of measures (mātrā), being twofold and threefold.
Seated upon a yogic posture, one should perform the ritual exactly as prescribed;
one should secure the four yogic postures with a yogic belt. || 457 ||
Having assumed one of these— either the paryaṅka, the kamala, the bhadra, or the firm svastika posture— one should keep the body straight and gradually [proceed] upwards.
With the joints of his limbs relaxed, having broad thighs and a fine neck, he should place both arms level above him and slightly bend his head. || 459 ||
The hips and the middle of the thighs should be positioned like a tortoise,
with the left hand placed upon the right, or likewise the right upon the left.
Having placed the two hands palm-upward, one should employ the *kacchapī* [mudrā];
the neck, however, should extend from the heart to its end, being neither too rigid nor bent. || 461 ||
One should slightly close the eyes while gazing at the tip of the nose,
covering the mouth as if with a cloth, and not letting the teeth touch one another.
One should practice yoga with the "embryo" (sagarbha) or, when well-restrained, without the "embryo" (nirgarbha);
then one should agitate the vital air called prāṇa, conjoined with the mind.
Prāṇāyāma is proclaimed to have four divisions, beginning with recaka;
one should always strive to conquer the mind, which is difficult to defeat even for gods and dānavas.
Even if the mind is restrained by force through practice and detachment,
one should nevertheless exert effort in the avoidance of limiting adjuncts.
They should be understood as being of two kinds: those that are proximate and those that reside in the mind.
The proximate ones are produced by location or produced by mental impressions (vāsanā). || 466 ||
One should remain with eyes closed, free from all sensory engagement, in a place not infested by gadflies or mosquitoes, devoid of noise, and free from odors. || 467 ||
Thus, one who is properly established in the focal point should renounce all adjuncts born of sensory contact, as well as the various [impurities] arising from latent impressions. (468)
One should always withdraw the mind that is distracted among all objects;
then that mind, which has become pervasive, should be understood as being characterized by tamas.
That mind which has moved away from passion and so forth due to practice is known as rajasic; it is described as virtuous when it is closely attached to the sphere of the objective.
O one whose wealth is austerity, one should know that [the state] beyond the qualities (guṇātīta) is then attained through absorption;
one should perform such meditation as this, which is "with-embryo" (sagarbha), during the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇanigrahe).
And it is further stated that there are three kinds of destinies for yogins:
the Sakala, the Niṣkala, and Viṣṇu as the third, who is of the supreme form.
That other [aspect] is to be known as threefold: sound, the formless void, and the embodied form of the God of gods; one should contemplate this as the visible form. || 473 ||
Thus meditation has been fully described; it should extend as far as the limits of space.
One should meditate upon the focal point for as long as that focal point does not [itself] become the object of meditation.
For when existence has reached non-existence, the "other" is said to possess intrinsic nature (sasvabhāva).
Having first dissolved the gross, one then [dissolves] the subtle, and after that, the supreme.
In this way, the mind dissolves along with the object of focus and its limiting adjuncts;
one should meditate upon the form of the God of gods within the sphere of the heart-lotus.
Then one should contemplate another object of focus, first gross and then, beyond that, subtle;
as one practices in this manner, an excellence of qualities arises.
O tiger among sages, this yoga is declared to be common [to all], originating from Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest and whose nature is light and bliss. (478)

Because he is beyond the senses, incomparable, of the nature of existence and consciousness, eternally manifest, possessing two arms, having a single form, and with hands granting boons and fearlessness. || 479 ||
From the existent Brahman, who is the nature of the fourfold self, who is perfected through the sixfold policy of sovereignty, and whose essential form is supreme bliss and perfect tranquility; 480.
For the sake of favoring devotees,
he has descended by his own will in forms such as the supreme manifestation (paravyūha), which is as radiant as a lamp lit from another lamp.
This manifestation of the single and manifold forms has been revealed;
having concentrated the mind thereon, the yogi [attains] the cultivation of consciousness. (482)
One should practice yoga by means of that very mantra-word;
he who does so in this manner goes, in the course of time, to that which is higher than the highest.
For one who desires to attain it quickly, yoga is prescribed—
namely that supreme, great, eternally arisen state which was previously revealed to you.
Having meditated upon that which is to be expressed by the twelve-syllable mantra, the wise one should apply himself;
meditating on the eternal Brahman at the tip of the nose or on the ground, he should perform the recitation in two ways.
One should revolve the mantra four times on the tip of the tongue in water, six times in fire at the palate,
and likewise eight times in air at the middle of the tongue.
Likewise, having meditated upon the twelve-syllable mantra ten times at the root of the tongue and in the void,
one should recite it sixteen times after meditating upon it in the pit of the throat and in the mind.

One should recite twenty-four times over the region of the chest, which is the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva); then, at the end of the chest, over the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), one should recite eighty times again.
O Lotus-born One, at the time of performing the rite, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred times combined with half;
thereafter, indeed, one should mutter two hundred times through the lotus-petal [nostril] without agitation.
Or, from the presiding deity (adhyakṣa) down to Vāsudeva, one should unite [the breath] within the space of the heart for four hundred [mātrās];
or else, one should join it upwards in the sky, ending at the nāda within the heart.
Or likewise, one should practice with the Praṇava in the channel, or by means of the syllables of the Praṇava;
thus has yoga been described in many ways through specific mantras. || 491 ||
Thus, he who practices yoga, ever-disciplined and concentrated,
attains the supreme state, which is eternally manifest and free from affliction.

Having thus concentrated the self by means of the self and performed the act of recitation, one should continue until, through the non-differentiation of the knower and the known, one attains identity with that [reality]. (493)
Just as a yogi attains stability in a meditative absorption (samādhi) that is free from any object of perception, so too,
through the absence of practice, he then becomes one with Brahman, as if it were a state of worldly existence.
Then, having abandoned the sequence of meditation postures, one should practice the conquest of fatigue;
thereafter, having offered a seat for the bed, immediately following that of the primary deity (mūlamūrti). || 495 ||
One should install the deity, who is endowed with powers such as Lakṣmī and resides within the sacrificial form, upon that [image] which is adorned in all its limbs.
Having offered the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamana) along with the gift-receptacle,
he should thereafter anoint [the deity] with sandalwood paste and other unguents.
Having offered fragrant flowers, garlands, and the like, as well as lamps and incense,
one should present various kinds of foods, beginning with cakes, along with milk and fruits.
Then, having offered water for libation (tarpaṇa), betel-leaf prepared with fragrant substances, and the various ritual components (sāṅga) to the God of gods according to one's means; 499.
Afterwards, one should deposit everything therein, including whatever has been performed as ritual action;
one should contemplate that right hand as being satisfied, accepted, and complete. (500)
In the midst of that, having meditated upon the partless mantra which consists entirely of a mass of rays, and upon the attainment of the fruit arising from yoga in the form of Lakṣmī; || 501 ||
Having fully recited the root mantra, one should likewise visualize it in the center of the palm;
furthermore, one should contemplate the partless (niṣkala) mantra above that.
Placing his knees upon the ground along with his head, he should offer it to Viṣṇu;
then, by means of that [offering] which is oriented toward grace, it is made one's own.
O best of the twice-born, it should be meditated upon with great devotion by one who is fully contented,
whether after having performed renunciation or the accumulation of merit, and having properly completed what was to be done.
And by means of the mudrā that conforms to the form of the mantra, the renouncer should seal [the seed] so that it does not bring forth fruit for the sake of worldly results. || 505 ||
And when the time for the final conclusion of the fruit has arrived as impelled by destiny,
it is not fitting for us to remain with our goals unfulfilled while others who seek the fruit have achieved theirs.

Having offered arghya accompanied by incense, one should then perform the dismissal (visarjana) of the image that is eternally established, even without [the presence of] land, water, and so forth. (507)
One should remember that the mantras residing in the places of enjoyment, when worshipped in their proper sequence,
have entered into the body of the principal mantra.
Just as rivers enter the oceans or as flames merge within other flames, so too, O twice-born one, is that gross form consisting of mantras, which is the locus of all mantras. (509)
One should meditate upon that which has entered into the subtle, the perceptible, and that which possesses both natures;
indeed, into that supreme [reality] of the previously described form, which is both subtle and dual-natured. || 510 ||
Therefore, having shown a stainless mirror before him, one should display that supreme, throbbing form which rests upon the supportless state. || 511 ||
One should meditate upon [the deity] having entered the heart-lotus by way of the path of the joint (sandhimārga);
and having remembered that [deity] as the Supreme Self within the sky of one's own consciousness in the heart.
One should meditate upon the deity as resting, endowed with its own intrinsic nature,
within the six types of images such as those for ritual action and worship, for the sake of attaining the eternal and other states.
When the daily morning worship has been duly established, one should,
according to one's capacity, re-engage the empowered [deity] from the primary image as before.
Having worshipped them thoroughly with the previously mentioned offerings beginning with arghya and flowers and ending with tāmbūla,
one should again install [the deity] at its respective base where it was previously placed.
For the sake of worship during daily, occasional, and other rites performed with a ritual image (karmabimba) and so forth,
the knower of mantras, having reached the beginning of each respective rite, should invoke [the deity] into the root-mantra and so on.
Having completed those rites upon them according to the actual purpose,
and having transferred [the merit] to the primary image, one should dismiss them from there.
Having first offered the mantras and the contents of the arghya vessel and other vessels according to the preliminary ritual,
one should then place all the remaining arghya and so forth together with that which has already been consumed.
Having offered [the oblation] to Viṣvaksena with water purified by the hand, and having mentally withdrawn the two-fold nyāsa from his own body; || 519 ||
One should perform the withdrawal of everything without exception— the arghya and so forth,
as well as that which pertains to the sacrificial altar, the fire-pit, the ritual grass-covering, and all else— by virtue of the purpose of the sacrifice.
Immediately after the smearing, one should throw everything into the water;
that which was previously mentioned should not be kept for long in front [of the fire]. 521.
One should offer some food as an oblation (naivedya) to the deities who are the embodiments of the mantras, with the exception of flowers and fruits;
then, reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should perform the closing of the door-panels.
Having stationed the Cakravartin, the lord of birds, there for the sake of protection, the practitioner should go to his bed and sleep;
then, having risen in the morning, he should proceed as before.
One should perform everything as previously described, including the awakening,
worship, and so forth, for one day, three days, seven days, a fortnight, or even a month.
Whoever performs worship according to this rite, endowed with devotion and faith, shall go to the supreme abode; how much more so for one who is permanently established here?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire-Rite, the Distribution to the Ancestors, the Daily Festival, and Other Rituals," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the Śrī-Pāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ!
The Eighth Chapter: Sanaka said,
"O Blessed One, tiger among sages, omniscient one, best among speakers!"
That worship of those headed by Garuḍa which was previously described; || 1 ||
Therefore, now reveal this in detail and at length.
Śāṇḍilya, listen; I shall explain to you correctly the ancient method of worshipping Garuḍa.
By the mere knowledge of which the practitioner attains his desire—that [knowledge] of Viṣṇu, known as Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is endowed with the power of supreme wisdom. || 3 ||
That which is called the power of knowledge (jñānabala) is the form (mūrti) whose nature is the support of all;
this is known as the greatness (mahima) of the Creator of the world, who is the Lord of Birds (Vihageśvara). || 4 ||
It destroys all diseases and fears, and it is a thrower of all enemies;
therefore, the knower of mantras, having installed it in the temple, should worship it daily.
One should construct a pavilion in the shape of a temple on the first or second courtyard in front of the main shrine.
It is endowed with four gates, possessed of three groups,
or else accompanied by six groups, and adorned with all ornaments.
The main hall should be three times as high as it is wide, or half as high, and very spacious;
it may be of the Brāhma, Divya, or Divyamānuṣa type.
Having established an image made of metal or stone as prescribed,
one should worship it daily at the three times of day, following the final worship of the primary form.
Listen now to the specific procedure for its performance, preceded by the mantra, in due order:
first, having extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), immediately thereafter the word "bird" (pakṣin). || 10 ||
The great five-syllable mantra is proclaimed to end with "svāhā";
its syllables, together with the bindu, are preceded by the syllable "oṃ."

Now, understand that the limbs [of the mantra] are to be recited with the fourth [vowel] ending in each, along with the [seed-syllables] beginning with knowledge (jñāna) and the [mantras] beginning with the heart (hṛdaya), extending from the eye (anetra) up to the weapon (astra). 12.
If one consumes it with the root mantra first and without transposition, it shall become a destroyer of poison;
this very mantra has been proclaimed as difficult to obtain even for the gods. (13)
O best of sages, this is known as the five-syllabled Gāruḍa mantra;
its five limbs should be formed with the syllables preceded by the bindu (m) as before.
With this mantra, complete with its ancillaries, [the deity] should be installed according to the ritual procedure,
whether the image resides in the primary temple or is situated upon a vehicle.
The form of Garuḍa remains either standing in the vehicle, or ready to depart,
or indeed seated upon the bed or the throne, or otherwise well-established.

The characteristics of the deities of the door-panels will be explained specifically in the chapter on meditation, and their characteristics will also be clearly stated in the section on the raising of the banner. || 17 ||
Knowing this, O twice-born one, he who is devoted to that mantra should bathe at the proper time with its specific mantra and perform the washing of the feet.
Having sipped water according to the rule and having entered the palace, he sat comfortably on his own seat, facing either the east or the north. || 19 ||
Having performed the purification of the hands, the binding of the directions, and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma),
and having completed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to rule, one whose body is infused with mantras [should proceed].
Then, having bound the mudrā of the Lord of Birds within the lotus of the heart,
[one should contemplate] the fourfold-natured God who abides in the abode of his own bliss.

Having brought down [the deity] from the portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, which is filled with complete wisdom and power, and having worshipped it as before until the end of the recitation (japa) with offerings of nectar; || 22 ||
Then one should worship with the external offerings previously mentioned, consisting of an accumulation of enjoyments,
as well as with the food for the deities remaining in the vessel, or else prepared separately.
For that purpose, as before, one should prepare five vessels for the arghya and so forth;
or else, two [vessels]—one for the water for washing the feet (pādya) and one for the water for bathing (snānīya)—in a single [vessel].
Whether for the *arghya* and *ācamana*, or for one or the other,
the knower of mantras, having worshipped the mantras previously assigned to his own body, [should perform the rite] in its entirety.
Then, at the four doorways, one should worship Vāstveśa, Kṣetranātha, and Dvāralakṣmī with their respective mantras, using offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with incense.
Then, one should arrange the seat for the group beginning with Caṇḍa as before;
thereafter, one should arrange the eight [deities] beginning with Dharma, or the two groups of eight, following the remainder of the previous sequence.
Above that, one should duly worship the Kālacakra and the fourfold [mandala] beginning with the lotus,
as well as Gaṇanātha and the others, with perfumes and other offerings.
Having previously worshipped with mental offerings in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one should invoke [the deity] from his own abode into the heart-lotus of the image by means of his own vidyā.
Having duly performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the ornaments marking the limbs,
[he should worship] with the power named Satyā on the right, who is identical in form to Balaśakti.
And likewise, a rosary, a cluster of Mandāra flowers, and a jar containing nectar, with the Lord of Serpents starting from the right [side]. (31)
One should thus place the insignia, namely the crown and the forest garland;
immediately thereafter, the serpents beginning with Ananta are to be placed.

The power (śakti) previously mentioned, which consists of the nature of strength and dharma, should be manifested by displaying the mudrā of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), and then one should perform the sacrifice of dissolution (layayāga). || 33 ||
And the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga) should be performed upon the surface of the lotus-seat;
on the lotus petals starting from the east, the [limbs] beginning with the Heart should first be worshipped.
And in the intermediate petals, their weapons are to be placed with colors as before;
in form, beauty, ornaments, and so forth, they are like the bodies of the root mantras.
In the corners of Agni, Śarva (Nairṛta), Rakṣas (Vāyu), and Vāyavya,
[one should place] the four items beginning with the rosary for the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), as well as a crown and a forest garland.
Having placed [the first four] in front, behind, and likewise on the south and north,
the remaining lords of serpents, beginning with Śeṣa, are to be arranged in due order.
To the south of Vihageśa, upon the pericarp, is the one named Satya;
these [five] have the nature of the vital breaths: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. || 38 ||
Outside the central lord of birds, starting from the east and proceeding in order, are Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya, the lord of birds. || 39 ||
This fivefold manifestation of the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa) is as follows:
the four beginning with Satya are in the cardinal directions, while Vihageśvara is in the corners. || 40 ||
Now listen specifically to their lineage:
from the region of Ācāṅghri onwards, every member of this line possesses a human body. (41)
He has two arms, is white as snow, and is the deity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
He is Suparṇa, with the luster of a ruby, stainless, and possessing golden eyes. || 42 ||
Garuḍa, however, has a golden luster, with curved eyebrows and eyes like those of Varuṇa;
Tārkṣya indeed has squinting eyes and resembles a rain-cloud during the monsoon.
The fifth has eyes like molten gold and a variegated luster;
these four-armed deities, headed by Suparṇa, are indeed of gentle form and unperturbed.
All of them were footed with wings, adorned with circles of feathers, pot-bellied, with well-fleshed limbs, and decorated with earrings and other ornaments. || 45 ||
With curved eyebrows, well-rounded eyes, crooked beaks, and white faces,
they are established through their lordship over the vital airs such as the *apāna*.
The fifth [mudrā] here is Mahābalā, who has a large body and a red beak;
it is formed with both hands joined by inserting the two thumbs into the hollows made by the fingers.
All those foremost of birds held handfuls of flowers;
Suparṇa, however, held them with his two hindmost hands, starting from the right.
Garuda, however, bears those two [hands] in reverse order, holding a cluster of mandāra flowers and displaying the seal of wonder. (49)
The fifth lord of birds, Tārkṣya, always holds Kadrū on his right and the jar of nectar on his left in the two rear positions. || 50 ||
In his right hand he holds a jar of nectar, and in his left, the Lord of Serpents;
such is the nature of the eternally manifest manifestation (nityodita-vyūha) as well as the quiescently manifest manifestation (śāntodita-vyūha).
Garuḍa, who bears the names of all five vital airs beginning with prāṇa and apāna, serves specifically as both an attendant and as the emblem upon the banner.
In the same way, these [states] should be applied to the other states such as deep sleep;
they correspond respectively to the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva. (53)
From Satya up to Tārkṣya, these [names] are to be taken respectively within their various other forms;
specifically, from Satya onwards, they are to be applied to Keśava and the others in groups of three.
The fifth among the forms beginning with Pajhana is Vihageśvara, belonging to the all-pervading Lord whose body consists of the Parātpara, the Paravyūha, and the intermediate Vyūhas.
Furthermore, because he is the source of manifestation, desires to protect the world,
and is the cause of the birds (khaga), he was previously called Khageśvara.
Thus has the power of the Gāruḍa array been fully proclaimed to you;
outside of that are Kumuda and the others, and beyond them, in order, are Śakra and the rest.
Outside of that, the attendants of Bhūteśa, such as Utkaṭa and others,
should be worshipped in groups, or else in a circle of offerings (balimaṇḍala) in front of him.
Alternatively, the followers of Garuḍa should be worshipped at the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha),
as they protect his devotees and even the divine abodes.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the worship with the seats and other requisites as prescribed,
using either the sixty-four services or the other thirty-two.
Or, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior [devotees], one should offer it with the sixteen services;
that food and other offerings thus presented are always for the benefit of men who are ill.
One should distribute and bestow [the medicine] upon barren women, kings who desire victory, and those whose bodies have been afflicted by poison. 62.
One should worship him especially during the month of Ārdrā;
and during festivals, one should carry him in procession with special festive worship.
Thus has been correctly described the supreme worship of Garuḍa;
O Sage, tell me now what else remains to be heard after this.
O Sage Sanaka, knower of all dharmas, O Blessed One, lover of devotees!
In ancient times, the worship of Viṣvaksena, the enemy of obstacles, was ordained.
If you are gracious, please describe that procedure in detail,
as it was formerly taught by Śāṇḍilya in the great scripture named Pauṣkara to the one born from the lotus (Brahmā).
"The worship of Viṣvaksena has been declared; listen to it duly, O Sage.
Pauṣkara said: "For what purpose, O Blessed One, did he speak of the Lord who destroys obstacles? (67)
Viṣvaksena, who is the supreme cause of all the lords of obstacles,
is to be worshipped when Acyuta has gone to the land of enjoyment.
"With which substances and by what rite does he perform worship when propitiated? The Blessed One said:
"The afflictions of living beings are destined to arise and act as obstacles to the true Dharma. (69)
I do not consider auspiciousness for those caught in saṃsāra to come from sacrifices, rituals, dharma, and the like;
rather, it belongs to those who are weary of such activity and who discourage others from pursuing it.
And they all flee, O twice-born one, afflicted by the fear of the blazing wheel, due to some previously accumulated karma of their own.
He enjoys the twofold fruit of the sacrifice standing before him;
indeed, Viṣvaksena is always there for its protection.
At the proper time known as the conclusion of the sacrifice, or on the second occasion,
one should perform the sacrifice with an undisturbed mind for the attainment of the fruit.

With the remnants of the offerings, unfading and beginning with the *arghya*, and with all the enjoyments consisting of ritual services such as ornaments and the like, [he worshipped] because of the completion of the sacrifice. || 74 ||

With food offerings such as madhuparka and other oblations presented to the principal image, and with those remaining after being given to the twice-born, but excluding what one has consumed oneself; || 75 ||
Likewise, with other [dishes] placed within the serving vessels, not yet announced to others,
prepared, endowed with heat, and drenched in sweet ghee.
Paiṣkara said:
Who is this one of incomparable prowess, from whom even those obstacles capable of uprooting the three worlds flee to a great distance in the mere twinkling of an eye? (77)
The Blessed Lord said:
That form of the all-pervading Self of the Fourth State (turyātman) which is known as Kālavaiśvānara is indeed proclaimed as Viṣvaksena, whose face is that of a twice-born deity.
Established through the distinctions of the Āhavanīya and other fires for those who sacrifice in the ritual,
it takes up the oblation purified by the Ṛgveda and satisfies the entire world.
Thus, having obtained from the guru’s own form the transmission consecrated by mantra, [the disciple proceeds] from the sattvic sacrifice consisting of mantra, which is permeated by Brahman.
And out of a desire to bestow grace upon them, he himself quickly distributes [the offerings] to all the gods who dwell in every world, even those who have not been invited. 81.
Having thus understood his majesty as residing in manifest form for the sake of attaining the fruit,
one should worship him daily at the three junctions of the day, concluding with an offering of oblations.
Having first performed worship in due order upon the individual [deities] and the other substrates, such as those occurring prior to the annual festival and on other special occasions, || 83 ||
O Lotus-born One, one may perform it either briefly, or up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa), according to one's own capacity or wealth; or else, one may do so perpetually in great detail. 84.
Having placed water in a leaf-cup, or in a vessel, or in a flawless jar,
one should worship it with oneself situated in the northern part and offer it.
Then, in another vessel consecrated with that same mantra, one should take a portion from the food offering as well as from what remains within the *caru* vessel. (86)
Having set aside a portion of the rice together with curd, clarified butter, and condiments,
it should be consecrated with water containing kuśa grass, along with fragrant paste, flowers, and the arghya offering.
O Lotus-born One, having consecrated it many times with that heart-mantra,
one should recite its root-mantra while endowed with meditative visualization and contemplation.

O Pauṣkara, having placed the vessel previously prepared, having poured [the contents] into it and covered it, or having recited the Praṇava eight times over it along with the name [of the recipient], [one should perform the rite]. 89.

One should always and everywhere, even without the previously mentioned ritual procedure, perform the sacrifice using a single vessel containing water, accompanied by an offering of food (naivedya), and submerged in water. 90.
Furthermore, one should scatter that [water] on the ground, into a well, or into a pond and the like,
so that it does not come to the enjoyment of crows and other such creatures, just as a lotus-born [being] would not [be consumed by them].
Since that which is purified by the six mantras increases primarily [in merit], therefore it is forbidden for sinners, and especially so for those who are sinless. 92.
Having understood this, the practitioner of mantra should worship with effort using that mantra;
therefore, I shall declare the mantra along with its ancillaries—listen attentively as it truly is. (93)
The seed-leader called Prāṇa is indeed pervaded by Anala;
