endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds, it has ascended above Ūrjā. (94)
Then, having taken up the Vārāha [mudrā], which adorns both the earth and the sky, one should subsequently place the foot upon Viṣvaksena while offering salutation. 95.
This mantra of Viṣvaksena is indeed proclaimed to begin with the Praṇava;
its former seed-syllable is that which is devoid of the vowel 'ū'. (96)
One should lead the group of limbs (aṅgas), distinguished by the six long vowels beginning with 'ā', accompanied by the Praṇava, one's own name, and the six Jātis. || 97 ||
This [image] of Viṣvaksena, along with its ancillary parts, should be consecrated according to the prescribed rite using this mantra together with its limbs, beginning with "namas svāhā. (98)
Either in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure,
in the direction between Īśāna and Soma (the northeast), in a temple facing south.

When the inner sanctum (garbhamandira) is conceived as being higher than the primary abode (mūlālaya) or lower, or in the divine Brahma-sthāna, [the measurement] shall be according to the proportions of the primary image (mūlabera). || 100 ||

The worship of the imagined [deity] with substances such as stone, wood, or clay, etc., constitutes the primary ritual (mukhyakalpa); the secondary ritual (anukalpa) takes place in the front pavilion (agramaṇṭapa).
Having brought down [the deity], whether formless or embodied, from the sky onto the pedestal constructed with three tiers in the previously mentioned corner of the ground; || 102 ||
One should satisfy [the deities] solely with offerings of oblations (bali) and water,
in the case of those who have entered the four stations within the activities such as the mandalas.
During the time of worshiping the deity whose form consists of the external arrangement (paravyūha) and so forth,
even though he is within the temple, he remains in his own place in the pavilion.
Worship should be performed according to the rules from the day of commencement;
however, at the conclusion of all rites, when the Lord has entered the mandala and other sacred spaces.
Once each [deity] has been released into its own abode, the practitioner of mantras, having meditated [on them] from the center of the mandala,
should worship according to the rules on the second day as well.
For the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One, one should especially worship him while he is situated in the temple,
according to the prescribed rites, with offerings presented as oblations.

One should daily satisfy with all offerings such as *arghya*, as well as betel leaves and other items, those beings residing in water, on land, and elsewhere, who have become part of that [offering]. 108.

Then, for him who was staying in the palace, having fashioned a special image according to his body's proportions out of materials such as gold and so forth, in accordance with the prescribed ritual; || 109 ||
Whether fierce or peaceful in form, capable of destroying obstacles, having four arms or two arms, and either seated or standing; || 110 ||
One should worship an image with two arms, or one fashioned with four hands or otherwise, with festive worship when special occasions have arrived. (111)
When a festival such as a hunt arrives, wherever the lord may go, he should lead him there for the sake of accomplishing his goals without obstacle. (112)
I shall describe his meditation exactly as it is; listen, O best of beings!
It has the luster of nine fresh dūrvā sprouts and bears a slight yellowish-green brilliance.
He had four fangs, four arms, and four cubits in height; he possessed the four states of existence, was complete in all his limbs, had the shoulders of a lion, and was adorned with a broad chest.
Adorned with a navel cavity that slopes to the right, he possessed arms reaching to his knees; he was glorious, bearing matted locks of tawny and white hair. || 115 ||
With eyes tawny like molten gold, flat-nosed and broad-bridged, adorned with rows of long white nails, and possessing curved eyebrows; 116.
His face and cheeks were broad, his entire body was covered with hairs that resembled the crescent moon and were as red as fresh kiṃśuka flowers. || 117 ||
He was endowed with a pair of ears that were beautiful, long, broad, and prominent, and adorned with ruby earrings. || 118 ||
Adorned with a lofty crown and beautified by necklaces and other ornaments,
he is clothed in variegated silk garments and decorated with diverse garlands and jewels.
His radiance was a thousand times greater than the twelve suns at the time of universal dissolution;
his eyes were slightly turned upwards and cast obliquely.
His teeth possess the luster of jasmine and the moon; his face is slightly smiling, naturally gentle and stainless, yet tinged with the wrath of Māyā. || 121 ||
Standing in a posture with his feet placed in a graceful, swaying motion,
he was meditating upon the supreme state by means of his own inner organ alone.
On the left hand, from the thumb to the little finger, there are three creeper-like lines;
one is raised and applied to the tip of the nose. || 123 ||
He is endowed with this mudrā which bestows fear of the six obstacles;
he holds a discus and a conch in his hands, and carries a mace hanging down from him.
With a hand resting nonchalantly upon the slope of his hips,
[he beheld] the God who assumes such a form and possesses manifold wondrous exploits.

One should meditate on the Āgneya [mantra] as having a fierce form, with the luster of fire, displaying fangs and the threatening gesture (tarjanī), yet free from fear and possessing the characteristics of peace. || 126 ||
With his primary right hand he grants fearlessness to his devotees,
and with his left hand held in the same manner, he holds a dangling mace.
Holding the discus and conch respectively on his right and left rear hands;
thus has the four-armed form been described—now understand that of the two-armed one.
Excluding the two, the fierce and the peaceful,
as previously described, one may instead contemplate either the pair mentioned before or the second pair.
Or else, it may be devoid of the mace, or resting upon the left hip;
whether in a standing posture or a seated one, it is placed upon the region of the left thigh.
Either with the *gopanī-mudrā* or with the *kaṭakākāra-mudrā*, [the hands] rest behind the back of the seat with both palms. (131)
Grasping the upper end of the mace, which is shaped like an elephant’s club,
he stepped upon the eastern petal with his two feet, taking his seat upon the pericarp.
Or, having established [the deity] upon the pericarp as before, adorned with other ornaments, one should thus place a single [deity] according to the rule within these specific meditations. (133)
One should worship with one's own mantra at the times previously mentioned,
for the purpose of worshipping the four locations in the center of the maṇḍalas.
Then, once the mantras have been worshipped and assigned to their own abodes,
[the practitioner should perform the ritual] within a square city situated between the directions of Īśāna and Soma, or else within the city itself.
In the space freed from the splendor of the doors, adorned with three lines, within that, situated upon a half-moon, is a lotus endowed with eight petals. || 136 ||

When this [mantra] has been appointed with universal sovereignty by Acyuta for the sake of the wise, and is constantly honored according to the rule, the practitioner attains his desired goal. || 137 ||
Therefore, having bathed according to the previous injunctions with his own mantras,
and having washed his hands and feet or performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having purified one's own body by means of the *dhāraṇās* through its presiding deities, and having again performed the imposition (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) starting from the hands; 139.
As before, having likewise brought down the Lord from the abode of bliss and worshipped Him within the lotus of the heart as the partless Self according to one's own requirement; 140.
Having meditated upon that very [deity] as having become the totality, one should worship externally;
having established the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings as before within one's own body. (141)
Having worshipped the mantras placed at the southern and northern doors,
[one should worship] those known as Bala and Prabala, who resemble Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa.
Having worshipped Vāyuvega, who possesses great vital power and resembles Garuḍa at the front of the door, according to the previous ritual, he first offered him a lotus-seat.
One should first meditate on the fivefold or ninefold [mandala], extending from Dharma up to Ananta, covered by the sattva element; thereafter, one should meditate on the lotus alone.
Having invoked that deity into him, stimulated by meditation within his heart, and having performed the rites of presence and so forth, preceded by the binding of ritual gestures (mudrās). || 145 ||
Having worshipped thoroughly with water-offerings, flowers, and other items according to the procedure for the yoga of dissolution,
one should [worship] that [deity] situated in the center of the pericarp, beginning with the heart-mantra, as if it were the principal mantra.
And those situated within the coverings of the lotus-petals lack that specific form and luster;
however, meditation on white and other colors is prescribed everywhere for the limbs.
[He meditated on] the power called Action, which is of the nature of fire, whose synonym is Svāhā, who assumes the form of Lakṣmī, yellow in color, and adorned with all ornaments. || 148 ||
She is always seated in a posture corresponding to her beloved, or else standing firmly;
she holds two chowries by means of the right and left hands. || 149 ||
This mantra, ending with "hrīṃ kriyāyai svāhā," is thus proclaimed;
by means of this [mantra], [the power] from the luminous body of the Lord, the destroyer of obstacles— || 150 ||
Having brought him down on the left side at the conclusion of the sacrifice for enjoyment, [there appear] Gajānana, Jayatsena, Harivaktra, and Mahābala. || 151 ||
And the fourth, O Lotus-born one, is known as Kālaprakṛti;
these four are indeed the lords of the Gaṇarājas, possessing fierce forms. || 152 ||
Waiting for his command were those with white yak-tail whisks raised aloft,
as well as Vināyaka and the other foremost lords of obstacles.
One should place those who constantly obey the commands of these lords of the Gaṇas,
stationed outside the lotus in the intermediate corners beginning with Īśāna.
Gazing at the face of the Lord, they stood with their postures identical to His;
likewise, all were marked by the same hand gestures (karas), yet they were devoid of the ritual seals (mudrās). || 155 ||
Understand that their meditative absorption (dhyāna) is distinct from their physical bodies:
[it has] the face of a formidable lordly elephant, four tusks, and three eyes. || 156 ||
With a neck like a conch shell and four arms, possessing the splendor of ten thousand full moons,
he was adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, girdles, and strings of beads.
One should meditate upon the elephant-faced one, rich with various garlands, perfumes, and garments, and possessed of incomparable prowess; thereafter, one should remember Jayatsena.
He had the face of a great horse, the luster of a mountain of ruby,
eyes like molten gold, and a body of manifold wonders.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the horse-headed [form], whose head is covered with a mane, resembling molten gold, and possessing a gurgling sound from the sky. 160.
O Brahmin, one should meditate upon the face of the King of Beasts, which possesses the speed of the wind at the end of an aeon,
and which is named Kālaprakṛti, like a mountain of collyrium.
His face was formidable with fangs, his beard and eyes were tawny, he wore fierce fish-shaped earrings, and his nose was sunken like that of a fish. || 162 ||
O Brahmin, these lords of the hosts of kings are indeed endowed with all the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), extending from their feet up to their necks.
One should remember whatever object serves as an ornament, beginning with those previously mentioned, in the three [stages];
one should perform their worship by their own names, preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava).
Homage to the one born from the lotus, for the sake of attaining the fruits of various siddhis—
whether by groups of eight times eight, half of that, or half of that again, according to one's preference.
For the sake of the swift accomplishment of one's rites, one should worship with eight [offerings]:
the food and other items presented to him, as well as the water for honor (arghya), garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth.
Wise men, for the sake of attaining success in this world and the next, should not give anything to anyone else;
rather, by that [act], it is permitted for those who depend on him and for all living beings.
Above them, their movement is perpetually obstructed by the quarters of space;
for this very reason, they bring about the loss of wealth for those who enjoy [the fruits of their labor]. (168)
Indeed, they always destroy the entire multitude of hopes;
therefore, he who gives to others while eating himself is the lowest of men. (169)
Or if, out of delusion, he neglects it, that base man goes to hell;
therefore, one who desires his own welfare must always practice its avoidance.

One should likewise throw that [offering] into a hole in the ground or into a pond and the like, so that it does not come into the possession of crows and other such creatures, O Lotus-born One. (171)
Since that which is purified by the six mantras increases even through its predominance,
therefore it is forbidden for sinners, and especially so for those who are sinless.
Thus has the worship of Viṣvaksena been correctly explained to you. If there is anything further that ought to be told, please tell it to me.

Sanaka [established] whatever image was fashioned from stone, metal, and other materials and consecrated for the lords of the enclosures, Kumuda and the others, who reside in the gates and the surrounding walls. (174)
Tell me, Śāṇḍilya, what should be done in each instance regarding their worship,
for the deities of the door-panels who are well-established in their own abodes? (175)

Or else, [one should perform it] three times a day, twice a day, or once a day in times of distress, with moving [images] or those fashioned from gold and other materials, according to the prescribed rule. (176)

One should perform the worship with its respective mantra through the eightfold service (aṣṭopacāra) for Viṣṇu, who exists in the form of the supreme manifestation (paravyūha) and others, within divine abodes and the like. || 177 ||
Temples, images, walls, gate-towers, gates, and pavilions;
kitchens, water-halls, and pavilions for flowers and other offerings. || 178 ||
Wealth, grain, clothing, dwellings, garlands, sacrificial offerings, and seats;
likewise, the limbs of the body, houses, cow-pens, and stables for vehicles. (179)
Or those who extract new, old, or lost [images], as well as the coverings for village streets and so forth, for the purpose of parading them during festivals; || 180 ||
Abounding with trees laden with fruits and flowers, provided with ponds and wells, and adorned with resting pavilions and watering places for livestock. || 181 ||
Those who, out of devotion, create gardens for the Lord of the World, and those who provide the necessary means, such as fields and shops; || 182 ||

At that very moment, for those former worshippers who were now attendants—along with their female and male slaves, their families, and those residing in the temple of the god—[the fruits of their merit ripened]. || 183 ||
Those who provide sustenance through their constant livelihood for the pleasure of the Lord—the one whose limbs are his own forms—and for the host of his attendants; 184.
Those who adorn their bodies with everything from their feet to the tips of their crowns, and who possess palaces, gate-towers, and other structures made of gold; 185.
There were beds, seats, vehicles, and various chariots, all large and fashioned on every side from gold and excellent jewels. || 186 ||
He gave elephants and excellent horses, as well as the implements for sacrifice,
beginning with vessels for water for the feet and guest-offerings, and including the acceptance of water for washing the feet and other honors.
Likewise, a noble seat (bhadrapīṭha) endowed with the characteristics of lamps and incense, a pair of vessels, a bell, a rosary, and so forth. || 188 ||
Umbrellas, white fly-whisks and various other such items, sandals, wooden shoes, and numerous footstools; || 189 ||
And various oblation-pots with lids and auspicious marks, made of gold, silver, and copper, together with containers for betel-leaf. || 190 ||
Those who offer all the vessels suitable for worship—such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and whatever other implements there may be—to the Lord of the World; || 191 ||
Filled with fear, they protect the property of the gods and the wealth of the gods, praising the definitive meaning established by the scriptures and other authoritative traditions. || 192 ||
Those who indicate the meaning of the Vedānta initiate the true devotees;
those who compose treatises on that subject in their respective vernacular languages [also do so]. || 193 ||

They should be known as the best of devotees; they [should be honored] in divine shrines and other such places, according to the distinction between movable and immovable [images], whether made of metal or stone. || 194 ||

They possessed forms and gestures consistent with the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life; they stood with palms joined in reverence, or were otherwise characterized by their proper proportions. || 195 ||
Marked on their right and left arms with the discus and the conch,
they are seated comfortably or standing well-composed in the midst of lotus pedestals.

Having fashioned [the image] according to the prescribed rule, standing upright or in the Vaiśākha posture as is appropriate for its beauty, one should proceed toward the east in either a pavilion or a maṇḍapa.
In suitable palaces prepared before the Lord,
according to the available space, either on the left, the right, or the rear.
Having installed them with their respective mantras according to the rules, one should worship them with faith;
hear now those mantras for the rites of installation and so forth. (199)
Or else, [I am] by means of *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, *īśa*, *ātman*, and *tāraka-brahman*;
or again, I am that very *tāraka* with the final *visarga*.
They should be joined with the name by means of the first, the second, or the third [syllable] together; now hear from me the sacrifices along with their constituent parts (sāṅgayāga). || 201 ||

Having divided one of the two [mantras] beginning with Tārā into six parts, one should utter the [mantras] beginning with Jñāna and the others, such as Hṛdaya, ending in the dative case, at the end of those [six]. || 202 ||
Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of these very limbs joined with the support of the Praṇava, one should daily worship the devotees who are supremely righteous.
This rule has been proclaimed for devotees who are dependent on others; however, for those who are independent, it may be performed at a land-grant, in a forest, or on a riverbank. (204)
Having diligently fashioned a celestial palace complete with a rampart, adorned with floors as desired, and embellished with carriage-roads; || 205 ||
Or for those inhabitants of the world of the Blessed One who have gone to another land, he appears in a visible form or an invisible one, having attained a likeness to the gods. || 206 ||

Having established [the deity] according to the prescribed rite in a temple, whether in a human location, or in a divine-human location, or in a purely divine location that is nevertheless dependent upon the human realm. || 207 ||

Having brought down the consciousness from the sentient being situated within the unmanifest lotus of Viṣṇu’s seat of mantras, [one should place it] into the heart-lotus of the devotee's form. || 208 ||
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should always worship with the mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga).
This is the specific procedure for invocation, whether [the deity] is living or not. 209.
In all cases, [the worship is performed] with the eight [offerings] beginning with the unmanifest lotus, or with sixteen,
[increasing] in sequence by the aforementioned abundant enjoyments ending with betel.
On the birth-anniversary of each of them, their special worship must be performed;
having done so, the great festival of the mounting of the lotus-bannered [Viṣṇu] should be celebrated there.
The banner should be raised during the festival of the Supreme Lord (Paratantra) together with the Deity;
likewise, hymns composed by devotees, which expand upon the meaning of the Upanishads, should be recited.
One should cause the deity to hear [the hymns] according to the rules with devotion, preceded by songs;
one should then cause that offered food and other provisions to be given to the singers.
Thus, the entire worship of you and your retinue, including Vainateya and the others, has been explained, which bestows the fruits of various supernatural attainments (siddhis). || 214 ||
This must be guarded with great effort, especially from those who are nihilists;
however, reveal it to those devotees whose souls are constantly engaged in their daily duties.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Retinue beginning with Garuḍa and Viṣvaksena," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrīpāñcarātra Pārameśvarasaṃhitā.
Śrīḥ.
Chapter Nine:
Śāṇḍilya said:
Thus, the best among those who know the mantras should perform worship during the three periods of the day.
And worship is not prescribed as being deficient in any of the three times, but rather as perpetual.

O best of the twice-born, in palaces that were manifested by themselves in the past, the primary time for worship would be the three periods of the day; beyond that, it depends on the desire of the builder.
And one should increase it gradually according to one's means,
O best of sages, until it reaches the twelfth period.
Furthermore, among the three times,
the time of dawn is indeed the most excellent for the proper placement of mantras upon oneself and one's hands and body.

One should daily perform the mental sacrifice (hṛdyāga), the purification of the locus, and the sacrificial session pertaining to the elements at dawn; in other cases, it may be done according to one's desire.
One should always perform the ritual bathing (snapana) and the offering of oblations (balidāna) at the three times [of day];
however, the worship of the seat of the image (mūrty-āsanapūjā) should be performed at the four times.
At five times there should be the ritual placement (nyāsa), and at six times the act of oblation (havana);
from the times beyond these, worship shall consist of concluding with recitation (japa).
The ornaments, the seat, and so forth should be arranged in the same sequence as before; one should not perform it otherwise than in the manner already described. (8)
In the primary ritual procedure,
however, one should perform the daily and occasional worship services in their proper sequence, concluding each with its respective fire offering (homa).
But in the case of a secondary ritual (anukalpa), [the procedure] ends with the recitation of mantras for those sacrifices that are not followed by an oblation;
likewise for sacrifices ending with the offering of oblations, such as the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites. || 10 ||

O best of sages, having performed each respective sacrifice up to the recitation of mantras (japa) in due order, one should thereafter perform the corresponding oblations (homa) in sequence according to the prescribed rule.
Indeed, in the secondary sacrificial rites (anukalpa-yāga) proclaimed for times of distress,
one should offer a seat, water for honor (arghya), then water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and a gift (pratigraha).
Having offered perfume, garlands, as well as lamps and incense in their proper measure and sequence,
one should then, according to the prescribed rule, offer food at the conclusion in due order.
Now, O twice-born one, understand in due order the division of the twelve periods beginning with Kālādi, extending up to the three times (past, present, and future), according to the nāḍikās.
Having first performed the daily obligatory rites according to the rules, preceded by a bath, starting from the Brāhma-muhūrta for two and a quarter ghaṭikās; 15.
In the morning worship, there are ten and one-quarter nāḍīs;
thereafter, four nāḍīs are for each of the two sacrifices.
Then, for one's own daily rite, there should be three and a half nāḍīs;
afterwards, for the midday worship, there are seven and a half nāḍīs.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, the sacrifice of the forenoon lasts for two ghaṭikās;
thereafter, the sacrifice of the afternoon shall last for three ghaṭikās.
The time for private Vedic study (svādhyāya) shall be two ghaṭikās from that point;
the subsequent half-ghaṭikā is for one's own evening ritual.
Then, for seven and a half nāḍikās, there is the Pradoṣa sacrifice;
thereafter, one should perform two sacrifices during four ghaṭikās.
After the midnight sacrifice, there shall indeed be a period of three nāḍikās;
furthermore, O Brahmin, one should perform worship for two ghaṭikās.
Then, at dawn, the sacrifice should last for two and a half nāḍikās;
after that, there should be a rest of four nāḍikās preceded by yoga.
Where there is worship at twelve times, this determination of time applies;
where there is worship at eleven times, this sequence is stated.
The worship at dawn should take place after the midnight sacrifice;
or else, one may omit a single period of time following the evening worship.
The time for rest shall be exactly six nāḍīs;
however, when worship is prescribed during the ten periods, then [it is as follows]. || 25 ||
After the midday worship, the afternoon worship should take place;
likewise, there are nine and a half nāḍīs for the midday worship. (26)
At those times when worship is prescribed during the nine periods,
one should omit only a single sacrifice prior to the midnight worship.
O best of the twice-born, when ten nāḍīs are reduced by half, that is the time for the evening worship (prādoṣika-arcanā), wherein the sacrifices are ordained during the eight periods of the day.
Then, after the dawn [rite], one should omit one sacrifice;
at that time, in the dawn sacrifice, there are thirteen nāḍīs with their parts. || 29 ||
O best of the twice-born, when the sacrifice is performed at the seven times—
namely, at dusk, midnight, and likewise at dawn during the night— then [the fruit is attained].
At that time, the period of midnight consists of four nāḍikās;
however, the final [period] consists of four ghaṭikās diminished by half.
When worship is prescribed during the six periods of time, three divisions of the day are traditionally recognized:
the forenoon, the midday, and the afternoon.
At that time, three and a quarter nāḍīs constitute his morning ritual;
however, four and a half nāḍīs constitute his midday.
The five periods are declared to begin at dawn and end at midnight;
the remaining ghaṭikās are prescribed for yoga and rest.
These four periods, excluding the afternoon, are proclaimed;
at that time, the period for private Vedic study (svādhyāya) shall consist of five ghaṭikās.
Morning, midday, and evening are the three times in their respective order;
at those times, the remaining ghaṭikās are for one's own ritual duties.
In the case of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), there may be only one time, namely the midday;
or, O twice-born one, according to one's capacity, there may be two times: the midday and the night.
Where there is an abundance of obstacles, there likewise is an expansion of power;
thus, the ritual of sacrifice to the Blessed One is performed with great magnificence.
Wherever many forms are worshipped in detail, one should perform the rites there by applying one's own intelligence through inference. || 39 ||
But at the time of the primary [observance], O Great-minded One, there is an increase of the nāḍīs;
however, during the twilights, there is a contraction according to the requirements of each respective rite.
O Mahāmati, he who always worships during these aforementioned times obtains the fruit of worship in its entirety.
One should act with diligent effort so that there is no lapse of time;
for if this [instruction] is spoken when the time has already passed, a great fault will arise. || 42 ||
Thus has been described the arrangement of the channels (nāḍikā) in a location conceived by humans;
the same applies to locations that are self-manifested (svayamvyakta) and others, as well as those established by sages (ārṣa) or in later times.
O Brahmin, the determination of the four periods of time should be made;
hear now the specific rule regarding this, even in the case of fixed rites.
On occasions preceding the annual festival, on various incidental rites, at the conclusion of the Pavitrārohaṇa ceremony, and on various optional (kāmya) rites; || 45 ||

And likewise, regarding expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), [they may be performed] due to such faults as the collapse of the kingdom, or because of the vastness of the sacrifice, or due to incapacity and the like. || 46 ||
O Brahmin, when the specific time prescribed for each respective rite has passed—even by a moment—no fault occurs due to the power of that particular sacred place. (47)
By Brahmins devoted to the true scriptures, dedicated to the five daily observances, solely intent on the fourfold divinity, and who are exclusive qualified aspirants. || 48 ||

According to the path taught in the divine scriptures, [one should worship] with the previously mentioned pervasive and slow-moving [mantras] beginning with the twelve syllables, joined with the limbs (aṅga) and subsidiary limbs (upāṅga), and so forth. || 49 ||
And wherever a sacrifice is performed, especially in that regard,
the fault of transgressing the proper time never exists at all.
Nevertheless, observe the distinction regarding the lapse of time:
those who have constructed temples by means of mixed castes performing sacrifices; || 51 ||
O Brahmin, whether it be obligatory rites, optional rites, or occasional rites—indeed, in all various types of ritual acts, as well as in those known as expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). || 52 ||
If even a single muhūrta of the time prescribed for each respective [rite] is exceeded, a great fault shall accrue to both the performer and the preceptor, as well as to that location. || 53 ||
When the time has been determined by castes who have no other refuge,
the commencement of the morning sacrifice may even take place at the eighth part of the night.
The midday [period] should not exceed two praharas plus one-eighth;
nor should the commencement of the evening [period] extend into the eighth part of the night.

The commencement of the midnight worship does not take place during the thirteen nāḍīs [after midnight], nor does the commencement of the dawn worship take place during the nineteen [nāḍīs after sunrise]. (56)
If there should be a transgression, there would be fault for the triad beginning with the agent;
regarding occasional rites and the like, the determination of the fault shall be as previously stated.
O Brahmin, understand from me regarding a place established by Śūdras:
the commencement [of the rite] should be at dawn during the day, and one must not let a portion of the watch (yāma) pass by.
The commencement of the midday [rite] shall not exceed two and a quarter praharas;
at night, the commencement of the evening [rite] shall not transgress one watch (yāma). || 59 ||
The commencement of the sacrifice at midnight shall not exceed fourteen nāḍīs;
however, if it exceeds twenty [nāḍīs], it must not extend into the dawn.
For the performer who has kinsmen, as well as for the place and the preceptor,
there shall be fear from the portents and so forth, just as before, in the event of transgressing those respective rules.
Determine the division in the place established by the six Vaiśyas:
indeed, two nāḍīs after sunrise at the commencement of the sacrifice. (62)
One should not let the midday period pass, for it consists of twenty-eight nāḍīs;
nor should one let the triad of rites beginning with the evening at night be transgressed.
The commencement of worship at midnight should not exceed two watches;
likewise, the commencement of worship at dawn should not exceed twenty-one nāḍīs.
The triad beginning with the *naimittika* [rite] must not exceed its [prescribed] time;
for if it should be exceeded, [misfortune falls] upon both the performer and the teacher, as previously stated.
For one with kinsmen, there shall arise affliction from great diseases and the like;
there shall be the destruction of grain in the dwelling and calamities caused by the great elements. || 66 ||
Henceforth, I shall describe that which was ordained by the Kṣatriyas who were conversant with the true scriptures:
the commencement of the sacrifice should take place at dawn, and one must not let half a watch (yāmārdha) pass by.
O twice-born one, the commencement of the midday [offering] should not exceed two yāmas, nor should the commencement of the evening [offering] exceed half a yāma. || 68 ||

The commencement of a sacrifice at midnight lasts for sixteen nāḍīs; it is not [performed] during the three watches of the night, nor on other occasions such as those for specific events (naimittika). || 69 ||
If one should let the prescribed time pass due to negligence, there would be the fault of regional unrest and so forth, as well as for the three previously mentioned [factors]. (70)
Understand from me this which has been devised by Brahmins devoted to the five times (pañcakāla):
the commencement of the sacrifice must not exceed the first five nāḍīs. || 71 ||
One should not begin at midday after twenty nāḍīs have passed, nor should one begin in the evening after six nāḍīs have elapsed. || 72 ||
One should not let the worship at midnight pass beyond seventeen nāḍīs;
nor indeed should one let the worship at the end pass beyond twenty-four nāḍīs.
Nor does the time for the performance of occasional rites and the like ever pass away for him;
yet, he may transgress any such rule as has been stated by anyone at all.
There may be defects such as the displacement from one's station for the triad beginning with the Preceptor;
however, observe the specific rule regarding a site conceived by the sages. (75)
The commencement [of the sacrifice] should not exceed six nāḍīs before the morning offering,
nor should the commencement of the midday offering exceed twenty-one nāḍīs.
O twice-born one, the commencement of the evening sacrifice should not exceed seven nāḍīs;
nor should the sacrifice at midnight exceed eighteen nāḍīs.
The animal sacrifice should not exceed five sets of five nāḍīs;
if it should exceed this, the performer will suffer affliction from loss and disease.
In that place there shall be drought and great danger to the location;
understand this regarding a site consecrated by those who have attained perfection in mantra. (79)
The commencement of the morning sacrifice should not exceed the first watch; likewise, the midday rite should not be delayed beyond one and a half watches after noon. (80)
The commencement of the sacrifice should not exceed the evening watch;
nor should the midnight sacrifice extend beyond nineteen nāḍīs.
One should not exceed twenty-six [verses], nor should one omit the final worship. If these two are transgressed, the performer will suffer the loss of a son.
In the Sthāna [mansion], there will be the destruction of wealth and the affliction of disease for the kingdom;
now I shall describe the commencement of the sacrifice in the Divya [mansion]. || 83 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should not exceed eight nāḍīs [after sunrise],
nor twenty-two at midday, nor eight in the evening.

O best of sages, one should not perform the sacrifice at midnight with twenty offerings, nor with twenty-seven at the final [time]; yet if, through negligence, one should exceed these limits, [one must perform expiation].
The ruler of the country will constantly suffer from afflictions such as fever and other diseases;
there will be destruction of grain and other assets in that location for the inhabitants of those respective regions. (86)
Now, O twice-born one, listen to the rule regarding the time for the self-manifested shrine at Sthāna:
the commencement of the first sacrifice should not take place during the ten ghaṭikās.
Midday should not exceed twenty-five nāḍīs;
the commencement of the evening sacrifice should not exceed ten [nāḍīs]. 88.
One should not let the final worship at midnight pass beyond twenty-two [muhūrtas];
nor should one ever let it pass the time of sunrise.
O twice-born one, if one should transgress [the rules] either through negligence or intentionally, there will be humiliation by enemies and affliction by great diseases and the like. (90)
There will always be affliction by disease among the subjects of the ruler of that land;
there shall be no prosperity for that region, and rain will be withheld from that country. (91)

One should not let the time for the prescribed obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, nor for those rites performed on account of specific astrological signs and the like, pass by in the human world.

In the triad beginning with the Ārṣa [nakṣatras], one should perform that which was prescribed for the preceding part; however, upon the passing of that [part], one should do so in the immediately following part. || 93 ||
If that time passes, there would be a fault, as in the case of missing a regular obligation;
however, one should perform the rite prescribed for the subsequent part of the day at that very same time.
One should perform the rite prescribed for the forenoon during midday;
and that which is prescribed for midday, one should perform during the afternoon. (95)
One should perform the rite prescribed for the first watch of the night during the middle watch;
that which is prescribed for the middle watch, one should perform during the last watch.
In the case of a self-manifested [liṅga], the rite prescribed for the eastern part should be performed;
however, in the case of a medium-sized one, it may be as stated for the western, the eastern, or even the middle part.
O twice-born one, if one must perform a rite according to a secondary rule (anukalpa), one should perform that which was prescribed for the forenoon either at midday or in the afternoon.
One should perform [the rite] during the first watch of the night, or in the middle, or even in the last;
however, one should carry out the ritual of the stars during the eastern part of the night.
One should perform the ritual pertaining to the lunar day (tithi) during the latter part of that day;
likewise, when there is a discrepancy or an excess of asterisms (nakṣatra), one should act at the end of the lunar day.
If even there, this new moon day should occur after the *saṅgava* period, one should perform that rite on that very day; otherwise, it should be performed on the preceding day.
In the past, one should perform the sacrifice to the Blessed One during the northern course [of the sun];
thereafter, within an interval of sixteen nāḍīs, the concluding oblation is performed.
O best of sages, the bathing ceremony and other rites should likewise be performed during the equinox in the month of Caitra;
furthermore, one should perform the sacrifice to the Blessed One even earlier, during the southern solstice.
The rites beginning with the ceremonial bath and ending with the fire oblation (homa) should be performed within the first sixteen-nāḍī interval;
however, according to the secondary alternative (anukalpa), one should perform them subsequently within the next sixteen-nāḍī interval.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] in the month of Āśvayuja and also at the equinox;
one should act as at the commencement of the northern solstice during those four transits of the sun.
Whatever karma was caused by the [auspicious] lunar mansion and whatever was occasioned by the moment, having generally brought that to completion with remaining power, it is thus. (106)
When that auspicious time has arrived, one should permanently complete the remainder;
having worshipped the deity with offerings such as the arghya, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire. || 107 ||
That which is prescribed for the day should be completed on the very day;
that which is prescribed for the night should be completed on the very night.
O twice-born one, whatever rite is prescribed for whichever day and night,
that indeed must necessarily be completed during that very time with diligent effort.
A great festival should be observed at all times and must not be neglected;
the time for the festival should last until the rising of the sun.
O best of the twice-born, in the primary ritual procedure, the time for a pilgrimage to a sacred site during the day should be within twenty nāḍīs after [sunrise] at a place established by humans.
In the case of a secondary rite (anukalpa), however, the time extends until sunset;
in the case of a primary rite (mukhyakalpaka), it should take place during the day at a self-manifested or similar sacred site.
In the secondary alternative (anukalpa), however, it should take place during the first half of the night;
even in the primary alternative (mukhyakalpa), it may be at night if the commencement of the solar transit (ayana) or other such occasions occurs.
O best of Brahmins, the time for the ascent of the sacred thread upon a mortal body occurs during the twenty-finger-breadth interval (nāḍī) of the day.
In a naturally manifest place or similar location, one may perform [the ritual] until sunset;
however, one should never perform the donning of ornaments at night.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
even for one situated in four places or in two places, [the rite should be performed] precisely before that time.

Having performed the worship of the deity, including the ritual bathing and other rites up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa), with abundant service-attendant offerings that are tangible and heart-pleasing. || 117 ||
O Mahāmati, having properly prepared [the body] with milk, ghee, and other specific substances, the wise practitioner should then take up the rosary and perform the recitation (japa). || 118 ||
As long as the moon and other celestial bodies remain visible after being released from Rāhu, one shall obtain infinite fruit from worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and other such rites. || 119 ||
Otherwise, the action would be fruitless for the agent, resulting in affliction by disease and the like;
for this reason as well, that which is declared to be occasional (naimittika) is impermanent.
By the power of the auspicious time alone, one should act in this manner even there;
one should perform all optional rites at their respective appropriate times.
Otherwise, those rites will not be accomplished in a short time;
however, one should always perform them at sites such as Svayamvyakta.
One should indeed perform the expiation when that which is caused by it has arisen;
either at that very moment, or at the conclusion of the rite, or within three days.
According to the weight of that [substance], its commencement or completion should take place within five or seven days; otherwise, one should double the duration.
One should indeed perform expiation at places such as those self-manifested;
O high-minded one, this applies even to the fourfold group of sites beginning with the self-manifested.
The commencement and the establishment of walls, gate-towers, and so forth, as well as specifically the installation of ritual icons (karmabimba). || 126 ||
The procedure for the restoration of the dilapidated, as well as the re-consecration, the sowing of sprouts, and the raising and lowering of the banner. || 127 ||
One should perform [the rite] even at a moment that is auspicious, under a favorable asterism, and in a favorable lunar mansion;
yet if one transgresses those [optimal times], a fault shall arise, and one should perform the propitiatory rite for that.
If the twelfth lunar day is present for only a single digit (kalā) on the thirteenth day, one should perform the ritual;
indeed, the laying down to sleep and the awakening again take place at the conclusion of the rite.
In various rites such as the Pavitrārohaṇa and others,
there shall never be any fault if a Muhūrta is exceeded.
But where worship of the Lord is performed by qualified practitioners using unique, pervasive mantras, according to the path taught in the divine scriptures; || 131 ||
In that regard, there may be a restriction of time according to the path taught for the divine abodes;
however, wherever two of these [conditions] coincide, the time is that of the Siddhas.
Wherever one [of these three] occurs, there it shall be treated as an archaic (ārṣa) form, as in the case of the "place" (sthāna);
this applies in due order to all the aforementioned places. || 133 ||
The temporal rule that has been stated for obligatory rites is twofold, distinguished by the primary and the secondary alternatives; [the following concerns] the transgression of that.
Having indeed pacified those defects, one should perform those [rites] at the subsequent time, so that no loss of merit ever occurs. || 135 ||

In that manner, one should always perform those rites in their proper sequence; for when both the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites are to be performed at the same time, [one should act accordingly]. || 136 ||

Having first performed the occasional rite (naimittika), one should afterwards perform the regular rite (nitya). For when both the occasional and the irregular [rites] coincide with the regular rite, they must be performed simultaneously. || 137 ||

First one should perform the occasional rites (anitya), and after that, the obligatory and occasional rites (nitya-naimittika). When both an occasional rite and a rite for a specific desire (kāmya) have arisen, however, the rite for a specific desire should be performed first.
And even among all these, when the rites known as expiations (prāyaścitta) arrive at the same time, the expiation should indeed be performed first. || 139 ||
One should always perform those rites only after completing [the primary ritual],
provided they are extensive due to the availability of wealth and so forth, such as occasional (naimittika) rites and the like.
Then, one should perform that which is occasional as well as that which is permanent prior to that specific time;
in that case, the fault of transgressing the proper time shall never occur.
Where there are many instructors and many attendants,
many forms of the object for each respective ritual task come into being.
In that case, one should indeed perform all the rites at one and the same time;
however, the fault of exceeding the proper time exists there just as before.
O twice-born one, the characteristics of the presiding deities (deśikas) in the self-manifested [shrines] and others will be described hereafter;
now listen as the characteristics of the presiding deities in the various types of images (mūrti-bheda) are being pointed out. 144.
One should always conceive of four types of teachers for the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest and all-pervading, as prescribed by the scriptures.

The lords of teachers should likewise arrange eight or twelve [deities] in the military array (vyūha), as well as in other forms, and indeed in the same manner for the embodied forms of the Vaibhava [manifestations].
And the practitioners (sādhakas) should likewise always be sixteen, O twice-born one;
or, when there are independent means of wealth, there should be twelve practitioners.
O Mahāmati, when these ten independent Avatāras have been established in their temples, ten officiants should be appointed for them. (148)
Even if they are joined with the conduct described above, they are nevertheless more numerous;
therefore, this conceptualization is superior there, whereas elsewhere it is useless.
These ten, however, are never to be conceptualized as being absolute;
one should never conceive of the number ten in relation to the "beyond-the-beyond" (parāt para) and so forth. 150.
Even when the descent [of the deity] is not independent, one should not conceive of a number of ten;
however, I shall explain the number of attendants in detail further on. (151)
Thus, for the wise one who has set out for the sake of others without contradicting his own welfare, the times have been declared in due order for that single path. 152.

Likewise, for one who has been initiated and whose mind is devoted to the established doctrine, there is now always an engagement in ritual action for its own sake by those two [the body and the mind].
Now listen to the division of time for the daily rites;
the five periods of time, beginning with *abhigamana*, have been proclaimed. (154)
The first is called "approaching," and the second is designated as "taking up";
this was asked by the Lotus-born One regarding the division of times.
The fourth is called Svādhyāya, and the fifth is designated as Yoga.
Thus was the division of the times asked about by the Lotus-born One.
O Brahmin, that very same [teaching] was spoken by the Blessed One himself through Nārada with distinctions;
it is now being recounted here separately in due order, O twice-born one.
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, I desire to know, together with the distinctions of time, the true nature of the mantras, the Siddhāntas, and the other Āgamas as they truly exist. (158)
The Blessed Lord said:
O best of the twice-born, time is one; however, due to the influence of its own operations, it appears as if divided to those agents who are destined for union with the Blessed One.
That which is indeed reckoned as a day and night, consisting of sixty *nāḍikās*, should be divided into five unequal parts starting from dawn. || 160 ||
Having reached the Brāhma-muhūrta, the knower of mantras, being self-restrained and pure,
should purify his own body by means of the āyāmas and other practices as prescribed.
Then, having assigned the mantra-deities to his body,
he should perform the worship of the mantras until the conclusion of the recitation and hymns, or until the appearance of the sun.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship with enjoyments such as flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth;
when the eighth part of the day has passed, one should perform it preceded by a bath.
As before, one should perform the mantra-based worship until the third watch;
thereafter, in the fourth watch, one should engage in the study of the scriptures. (164)
Having performed reflection accompanied by hearing and exposition according to the desire of one's own intellect,
when the sun has set, one should enter the hall of worship.
One should properly perform the worship of the mantra, accompanied by recitation (japa) and meditation;
thereafter, having approached the bed, one should remember the Lord of Mantras within the heart.
Having passed the portion of the night and then rising from his bed,
he should indeed practice the yoga of Māntraṇa within the lotus of the heart as before.
Having reached his bed and awakened once more, O Lotus-born One,
he should rise, leave his couch, and then perform what was previously prescribed.
Know this division of time, along with its manifold elaborations, as previously described.
O Lord, it is heard that there is but one Time in the world, and no other. (169)
"You have designated five times; what is this? I have a doubt regarding this.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Nārada, it is indeed a single time, devoid of division," || 170 ||

From dawn until the end of night, there is indeed a fivefold division; this should be performed according to the specific requirements of each rite, for many distinct times are not prescribed. || 171 ||
Nārada said:
Tell me the characteristics of actions performed at a single time, by the thorough knowledge of which I may become one who has accomplished his purpose. (172)
The Blessed Lord said: O Brahmin, beginning from the morning hour during the day, one should engage in recitation, meditation, worship, and hymns, accompanied by action, speech, and mind. (173)
One should approach the source of the world, and that is known as "approaching" (abhigamana).
Thereafter, having risen, one should perform the gathering of flowers, fruits, and other such items. (174)
The supreme hour is the cause for the completion of the sacrifice to the Blessed One;
it is indeed designated as its material substrate, resting upon the stages of the ritual time. || 175 ||
Then, O Brahmin, the practitioner should worship the Supreme Lord with the eightfold yoga; that period of three hours (prahara) is traditionally known as the time for sacrifice. || 176 ||
O best of sages, know that the portion of time consisting of hearing, reflection, exposition, and accompanied by recitation is designated as *svādhyāya* (self-study). 177.
When the end of the day has arrived, having performed worship, one should practice yoga;
and at the end of the night, one should practice it again, with intervals of rest placed between.
This fifth portion of time, known as Yoga, bestows the perfection of Brahman;
previously, I heard in its entirety from Nārada the supreme sacrifice to the Blessed One.
"I wish to know its constituent parts again according to their divisions.
The Blessed Lord said: "From the internal sacrifice of the mind and so forth, up to the offering of one's self. (180)
O Sage, the first limb of that sacrifice is the great approach by name, as well as the worship with all enjoyments such as water for the hands (arghya) and flowers. (181)

Know that, O Nārada, worship performed with external offerings, such as that which is done with curds mixed with honey and clarified butter, or with animal sacrifice, is designated as "enjoyment" (bhoga).
O Sage, that third limb of sacrifice is indeed the fourth: the worship with food, which is the giving away of what has been offered according to the previously mentioned rule. || 183 ||
The fifth is traditionally known as the *sampradāna*, which is an auxiliary of the sacrifice;
the sixth is the propitiation of the fire, and the seventh is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyāga*). || 184 ||
The eighth is the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga) known by the name Prāṇāgnihotra;
thus has everything been told that was requested by you. || 185 ||
"Indeed, he shall soon bestow his own station upon those who are devoted to it"—thus has it been declared in due order, together with the distinctions of ritual action. (186)
The division of the five times applies to both types of qualified practitioners;
however, in this regard, there is indeed this distinction for the sacrificer whose resolve is true.
For one who is solely devoted to the Four-Selfed One and whose mind is fixed on the fundamental Dharma alone,
the final sacrifice for overcoming obstacles should be preceded by the placement of the breath-extensions (āyāma).
Whatever has been declared here should all be avoided with effort, for the sake of attaining one's own desired goal, by following the path prescribed by the Sātvatas and others. (189)
Even for a disciple who has been initiated and is authorized for worship, everything previously described, beginning with the *āyāma*, is prescribed for him as well. (190)
Thus has the distinction of time been correctly explained by me to you;
by the knowledge of which, O best of beings, it is fitting for one to perform every ritual action.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Division of Times for the Twelve-fold Worship," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrīpāñcarātra Pārameśvarasaṃhitā.
Śrī.
The Tenth Chapter: Sanaka [says] that worship was previously described at the time of the sacrifice to the Blessed One.
A brief summary of the world and other elements situated within the parts of the palace.
O best among speakers, I desire to hear in detail their true nature, their names, and especially their locations; please tell me.
O Great-minded one, Śāṇḍilya [described] all the palaces, which are divided into many varieties,
in detail, beginning with the Vṛtta and Āyata types.
I shall describe the arrangement of the worlds, the paths, the principles, and the deities,
after having compressed the entire earthly realm down to the surface of the earth.

In this manner, one should remember the Bhuvarloka as it is situated upon the pedestals of the palaces, extending as far as the knees; and the Svarloka, which lies above those, extending further upward.
Beginning from the region of the sacrificial grass (prastara), it extends to the great peak-land;
Janaloka is situated upon its altar, and that cosmic egg is known as Tapoloka.
One should remember that world known as Satya-saṃjña within the topknot (śikhā),
and one should likewise contemplate its ancient pervasion throughout the seven worlds.
Then, one should meditate upon the pervasion consisting of the paths in their proper order;
remembering the sixfold path situated within the jar, the pedestal, and the stone, one should perform worship.
One should contemplate that which exists within as the seed pervading the paths of time;
from that seed, having become a sprout, it subsequently attains manifestation.
From the stone supporting the pitcher up to the pedestal of the temple,
the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā) should be meditated upon everywhere according to its actual state.
The path of the womb (garbhādhvan) extends as far as one can see with the feet;
the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) extends to the end of the *śukanāsa* (the frontal projection); the path of reality (tattvādhvan) extends to the edge of the altar (*vedikā*).
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) extends from the [first] digit (kalā) up to the throat; above that is the path of principles (tattvādhvan).
Having thus established the pervasion of the paths, one should then place the principles (tattvas).
O twice-born one, having joined the principle of earth upon the surface of the feet,
one should place the principle of water on the seat and contemplate the fiery principle in the shanks.
From the region of the neck up to the principle of air (vāyutatva), and above that, space (ākāśa) resides at the summit; from that region, however, it proceeds in due order.
One should place the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and the rest down to the soles of the feet;
on the sides are the two nostrils and the two ears, while the skin is declared to be the Sudhā [deity]. 15.
The two eyes should be the windows, the tongue the altar called Bhadra,
the nose the śukanāsa, and the mouth is declared to be the door.
The hands are to be known as the pillars, the feet as the pedestals, and the pot as the base;
the anus is the water-outlet, while the generative organ is situated between them. || 17 ||
The mind is to be known as the inner void; pride resides upon the stone of Brahmā.
The intellect is to be known as the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and primordial nature (prakṛti) is that which lies within it.
The twenty-fifth should be known as the Supreme Person (puruṣa), the image.
Thus, when the principles (tattvas) have been deposited, the deities are to be deposited in sequence. || 19 ||
Beneath the supporting stone of the jar is the king of serpents named Ananta, adorned with a circle of hoods numbering one thousand. || 20 ||
Above that is situated the wheel adorned with a thousand spokes;
know that stone, which is designated as the support of the pitcher, to be all-pervading.
The power of capacity (sāmarthya-śakti) is universal, partless, and belongs to the Supreme Lord;
O twice-born one, those nine jars are situated above that.
In the center of those four situated at the intermediate directions,
one should place Lakṣmī seated upon a lotus throne, surrounded by the treasures (nidhis).
And for the other four [jewels] as well, the king of gems known as Kaustubha is accompanied by the lords of the treasures with their own mantras and their own names. || 24 ||
The Blessed One, whose self is all-powerful, should contemplate within himself the partless one, whose form is sound, by means of the six-syllabled mantra. (25)
There, one should place the supreme Śakti, who is capable of sustaining the universe, in the middle of the lid of the central jar. (26)
One should remember Prabhā, the sovereign of all, as the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in the cardinal directions;
and one should remember her, characterized by bliss (ānanda-lakṣaṇā), in the collection of manifest intermediate directions.
The power called Kriyā, which is imperishable and the progenitor of the pure group [of letters],
resides within this ninefold enclosure as the domain of the Lord, beginning with the Name.
O Mahāmati, they are to be contemplated as pervading everywhere, dwelling in a sequence of the radiance of knowledge;
likewise, there is the light of infinite power.
Sarvagā, Brahmovadanā, Dyotakī, Satyavikramā,
and Saṃpūrṇā— these are said to be the powers that sustain the universe.
The eight powers (śakti) should be installed outside that [mandala] in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
they are to be placed in sequence upon the eight stones, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
The eighth among the twice-born is named Bala, Vīryavatī, Nityā, Anantā, Sthirā, Dhruvā, Styā, Dhṛti, and by name Sthiti.
Within the stones, on the ground, a group of six should be placed in sequence, beginning with the first letter and ending with the final letter of the alphabet. (33)
One should contemplate the pervasion by means of the syllable *kṣāṃ*, and outside of that, the ring-finger [seal].
Then, upon the base of the *masūraka* [pedestal], there is the group of eight [deities] beginning with Dharma.
O Brahmin, when four lotuses are thus arranged in the corner regions above that, then [the deities] are situated upon those lotuses.
The forms beginning with Vāsudeva [should be placed] from the southeast to the northwest;
then, in the area below the pedestal, a discus with the brilliance of the fire of time (kālānala).
In the region of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), however, there is a lotus resting upon the three abodes;
in its center is the Person consisting of consciousness, endowed with all powers. || 37 ||
In the four directions of the pedestal, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise to the north and west, Ananta, Vihaga, Ambhoja, and Cakra are situated in order.
Then, in the four directions beginning with the east, one should install Vāsudeva and the others, or alternatively, Puruṣa and the others, in sequence upon the lotus-feet.
The wheel, consisting of the support of all, rests upon the root of the branches;
it abides in the pair of branches whose nature consists of knowledge and action.
Parabheśvara, the primordial one, is situated upon the udumbara post above the door;
he is all-pervading, and behind him, in the middle of that space.
O best of the twice-born, when the two door-panels of the gate were fashioned, the entire Dharma, complete in its four quarters, remained present there, O foremost among the virtuous.
For these two deities, Kālabaiśvānara and Apāmpati, are stationed at the two side-panels by means of their southern and northern positions. || 43 ||
O Great-minded One, when the two Śukanāsas have been fashioned together with their limbs,
one should establish Agni and Soma as their vital breaths and will within the two windows.
Then, in the pair of shanks and likewise in the intermediate spaces, there are Kāla, Viyat, Niyantṛ, Śāstra, and Nānāṅgalakṣaṇa. (45)
The lords of the sciences, as well as Śiva together with Rudra and his attendants, the assembly of the Prajāpatis, and Indra along with his retinue. || 46 ||
The seven ancient sages, other planets surrounded by stars and the like, all the clouds, the nāgas, and the foremost of the apsarases [were there]. (47)

The medicinal herbs, the sacrificial animals, and all the sacrifices with their constituent parts; the lower sciences (aparavidyā) and the higher science (paravidyā); and likewise the fire and the wind. || 48 ||
The Moon and the Sun, Water and Earth—these groups of deities, numbering twenty-four, should be meditated upon in their proper order. (49)
The images of Keśava and the others are situated at the base of the pillars;
on both sides, they rest upon the foundation of the wall near the śukanāsa.
One should install Gaṇeśa and Yoganidrā, starting from the south;
above that, situated upon the surface of the eaves (kapota) of the designated area of the lintel (prastara).
The group of nine [deities] of the nose, as well as those intermediate stages—
indeed, all these should be established in that [place] and in those [stages] respectively.
The discus and conch, the mace and lotus, the plow and pestle,
the arrows, the Śārṅga bow, the sword and shield, the staff, the axe, and the thunderbolt.
The noose, the goad, the mallet, and the thunderbolt, together with the spear, [are to be placed] in the square palace and also in the square-long [hall]. (54)
One should place Garuḍa above the stone slab in the four corners; O high-minded one, he is to be meditated upon above that on the altar.
Through these associations with the eastern direction and so forth, he is then the one-horned body;
the god is the dwarf-bodied Trivikrama, who pervades all.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa;
Rāma holding a flaming axe, and another Rāma, the wielder of the bow. || 57 ||
Then the Lord Kalkī, the knower of the Vedas, who reclines upon Pātāla, is the Awakened One;
thereafter, the Tortoise, the supporter of Pātāla, is to be meditated upon at the surface of the neck. || 58 ||
The Boar, the Man-Lion, and indeed the Stealer of the Nectar; the Lord of Śrī with a divine body, the Embodiment of Beauty, and the Sustainer of Immortality. || 59 ||
The conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the great one who carried away the Pārijāta tree;
the Lord of the World, whose soul is peaceful, Dattātreya, the Great Lord.
"O best of the twice-born, [it was said] that the Blessed One was lying beneath a nyagrodha tree;
then, having divided the summit of the peak into three equal parts," (61)
O best of the twice-born, as far as the pedestal supporting the pitcher,
the remaining deities of the manifestation (vaibhava) should be meditated upon in sequence on the lower part.
The Lord is Ananta, the Divine One; he is Madhusūdana, whose essence is Śakti;
he is Kapila, the presiding deity of knowledge; he is Viśvarūpa, the one who moves through the sky. || 63 ||
Kroḍātman, Baḍabāmukha, Dharma, Vāgīśvara,
and the god Ekārṇavaśaya— these are remembered as the twelve.
Dhruva, however, is all-pervasive and is situated in the position above that;
above him, Pajhanābha stands as the pervasive one.
The Supreme Person, the Blessed One, the support of the world, the Lord of the universe, the Eternal One, is to be worshipped at the mouth of Śukanāsa. (66)
Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the universe, the infallible one;
he is the eternal first principle, even for the gods, who are like travelers on the path through the worlds.
They were placed upon the palace and remained there after having stepped across it;
however, in that part of the palace structure where the śukanāsas (parrot-noses) were not fashioned, they stood as they were.
There, one should first meditate upon Vāsudeva at the tip of the nose;
when three parts of the nose remain, the three beginning with Acyuta are situated there. || 69 ||
Or else, O best of the twice-born, they are Puruṣa and so forth, or Narasimha and so forth, or Varāha and so forth, or Dharmamūrti and so forth, in their respective order. || 70 ||
Alternatively, Paraśurāma and the others should be remembered in their proper sequence;
all of these may be accompanied by their Śaktis or may be alone. (71)
Upon the surface of the altar-platform, adorned with trees possessing leaves and creepers,
one should place a six-spoked wheel that bears thousands of flames of splendor.
Then, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva and the others within the *sāmalasāra* [sections];
in front of them, the discs (*cakras*) are to be visualized in their proper order. (73)

Indeed, in the pitcher of Śukanāsā, there is the stainless [state] known as "the peaceful," as well as that which has arisen from the peaceful and arisen again; beginning with Nara and ending with Kṛṣṇa.
In the corners of the inner circle, from the southeast to the northeast and west,
is the Lord, the Master, who has assumed the form of a boar and bears the body of Śeṣa.
O best of Brahmins, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa in the form of Nṛsiṃha likewise resides in the parts of the temple as they have been described in sequence.
Whichever limb has not been prescribed among those that serve as the supports for the deities, or wherever it may be in excess, one should perform it there as well. || 77 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities in their respective locations according to one's own understanding;
or rather, one should avoid the sacrifice to the deities for a limb that is not prescribed.
O best of the twice-born, the seven worlds, as well as the abodes and the assemblies of reality, and the deities, should be meditated upon by practitioners as being formless.

Likewise, when a celestial chariot (vimāna) has been consecrated by perfected beings (siddhas) and gods, there is, however, no branding or other such marks upon the bodies of the brahmins therein. (80)
O best of Brahmins, their locations were determined according to the prescribed rule,
after carefully examining even the constituent parts of the celestial chariots.
One should worship with a mind full of attentiveness and preceded by meditation upon the images on the emblems and so forth, as well as upon the various parts of the temple. 82.

O best of Brahmins, because the characteristics and other attributes are examined even in those whose forms are unmanifest, and also because of dreams and so forth, through the instruction of the supreme teacher. || 83 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should examine [the matter] with effort according to the facts;
O twice-born, even when the characteristics and so forth are deficient or even reversed.
O best of the twice-born, one should not perform the marking and other rites otherwise;
for one should not examine the marks with the intent of performing them incorrectly. (85)

However, if one examines the primary marks and so forth for the purpose of altering them, and once that has been done, it shortens one's lifespan; by means of those [altered] marks, one goes to hell. (86)

Therefore, with every effort, one should [ascertain] the characteristics and other features of the forms situated in celestial chariots (vimānas), even those that are self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) and so forth. || 87 ||
Having thoroughly examined their positions as well as the components of their celestial chariots exactly as they exist, and having thus determined their forms, [he proceeded].
One should perform the worship clearly with each deity's own specific mark, such as their insignia,
and with each deity's own respective mantra.
O best of beings, that self-manifested and most excellent [liṅga] within the palaces—the Lord, the Divine, in that very form—resides right here in his own village. (90)
There, the Lord himself, who is compassionate toward his devotees, is ever-present;
even when defects such as old age arise, he never deserts them.
These supreme powers of the mantras each occupy their own respective locations; though situated within the temple, they are preceded by self-manifested forms.
The forms of the Lord should be correctly understood through the previously mentioned yoga;
their manifestation is clearly evident throughout the three worlds by means of weapons, mantras, and banners.
They too bear a multitude of marks upon the range of their feet,
on the forehead, on the shoulder-cloth, on the back, and on the two palms of the hands.
One should specifically examine the multitude of various marks upon the mass of body hair on the head for the sake of determining the spiritual status of those engaged in ritual action. || 95 ||
One should worship them with designations fixed to their respective forms, for those whose multitude of marks on the feet and so forth are not clearly manifest. (96)
O high-minded one, one should worship those pervasive mantras,
preceded by the twelve-syllable mantra, using whichever single mantra is desired.
Having understood this correctly, the knower of mantras who performs worship in such a manner obtains the fruit of that worship; otherwise, he experiences the opposite.
All these, beginning with the worlds, have been described in sequence for the occasions of propitiating the God of immeasurable splendor. || 99 ||
Having performed the worship of the deities stationed at the door,
one should thereafter worship them with their own names, preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with the word "namaskāra."
O best of the twice-born, with water for the guest-offering (arghya), anointing unguents, garlands, and incense,
[he should worship] in front of the God of gods, outside the entrance.
Or, having gone to the region of the inner mandala, one should worship in due order; thus, in whichever temple-structure there may be, by the best of practitioners. || 102 ||
O twice-born one, whether worship is performed once a day, twice a day, or thrice a day,
the omnipresent Lord is always present there as long as it is done constantly.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, a practitioner who longs for spiritual success should perform the worship of Viṣṇu preceded by that adoration. 104.
Whoever always acts in this way with devotion, being single-mindedly intent on nothing else, shall soon obtain their desires both in this world and in the next.
He who, seeking liberation, performs [this rite] goes to the supreme state. Sanaka especially [praised] temples that were self-manifested from of old. || 106 ||
"You yourself highly praise this self-manifested temple;
what would its true nature be, and what would that of others be as well? (107)
And what is the nature of his greatness that I now wish to know—that this world which is seen here has been fashioned by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu?
(108) Śāṇḍilya said:
"That which is seen here as this world was created by the māyā of Viṣṇu. (108)
Divided by many distinctions such as time and others, and possessing various forms,
its manifestation occurs indeed during the day, and its dissolution at the arrival of night.
Know that a thousand divine yugas constitute his single day; his night should be understood to be of equal duration. Thus, when the night has ended—
But when the day was proceeding toward the time characterized as the twilight,
O bull among sages, [the sun] did not abandon its own cause for the sake of its effect.
By the power of the yoga of knowledge, the heart-lotus—enveloped in immeasurable majesty—was impelled through the aperture of the navel by that [breath]. || 112 ||
But the form of representation-only (vijñaptimātra), abiding within one's own internal organ, resembles a thousand suns and has a thousand moon-like filaments. 113.
And within it was a golden stalk of great luster containing a thousand fires;
in its center was the mental Brahmā, the four-faced one, who was created by him.
O Brahmin, he is the creator of the world’s prosperity, the eternal embodiment of knowledge,
perfected in all purificatory rites, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Endowed with the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) and possessed of the creative energies of desire to emit,
he was not recognized as such once he had fallen into a state of pride.
Having acquired the notion "I am," he was defiled by passion;
and when that [notion] had vanished, Pauṣkara's mind then [became clear].
O twice-born one, because of that perversion, the creative impulse did not proceed;
he who knew the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done became troubled in mind. || 118 ||
Then, with a serene mind, Prajāpati performed most difficult penance,
desiring to behold the lotus-eyed Lord before long.
Then, O best of the twice-born, as Brahmā was performing his austerities, O foremost among the wise, the thought arose in him for the purpose of praising Hari.
Then the Lord Brahmā, with palms joined in reverence, recited this supreme prayer:
"Obeisance to you, O Heart of Brahman; obeisance to you, O Primordial One of Brahman."

O best among those who have attained the goal of yoga, O treasury of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, O all-pervading Lord, O inconceivable creator of the manifest and the unmanifest, you who abide on the path of security! 122.
O Viśvabhuj, the inner self of all beings, not born from a womb;
I am born of your grace, O self-existent one, the abode of the world. 123.
From you my first birth was mental, honored by the twice-born;
that which was my second birth here in ancient times was from your eyes. (124)
And by your grace, O Lord, my third great birth was through speech;
and my fourth birth, O All-pervading One, was truly through hearing.
My fifth birth from you is said to have been from your nose;
my sixth birth was produced by you as being born from an egg.
And this is my seventh birth as a lotus-born one, O you of immeasurable luster; for in every creation, I am the son [of Brahmā], devoid of the third quality (tamas).
The first is the lotus-eyed one, fashioned from the primary qualities;
you are the Lord, the source of power, and the creator of all beings.
You are the refuge of those who perform the five-fold ritual; you are the Pāñcarātrika.
Indeed, by you I was created, though I am beyond the speech and the vision of the Vedas.
"O Lord of Gods, O Lord of the World, what power do I have to create this entire world, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient? (130)
Thus praised, that Blessed One, the Puruṣa whose face is turned in every direction,
revealed to him his own divine and unsurpassed form.
Seeing him, the lotus-seated Brahmā was filled with great joy;
overcome with tears of bliss, he stood bowing with palms joined in reverence.
Then the lotus-eyed Lord of the World said to him:
"O son, create all beings from your mouth as well as from your feet."
"O you of excellent vows, I shall bestow upon you longevity, strength, and splendor;
and receive from me this Veda known by the name Sātvata. (134)
Therefore, establish the entire Kṛta Yuga according to the prescribed rule,
once the work of creation for all living beings has been accomplished.
Between the great divine abode and its manifest form,
he exists by means of his own self-manifested, divine, and stainless form.
Reclining upon his bed of the serpent Ananta, the lotus-eyed Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest, will manifest himself before you.
Worship that Lord of Gods, who resides within the celestial chariot and is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all the worlds. (138)
