One should worship Vāsudeva, the supreme Person who is affectionate toward his devotees, with the twelve-syllable mantra and with enjoyments such as tactile objects and the like. || 139 ||
And with various services that touch the heart, they act according to their respective offices out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (140)
In the manner described by the scripture known as the Mahopaniṣad,
that which shall attain renown in the world through the words of the Pauṣkara.
Since this has been spoken by you concerning Pauṣkara, it shall indeed be renowned as such;
and I shall speak of that [Pauṣkara] as "Mahāvibhūti" in another age.
When this first Kṛta Yuga among men had passed away,
Brahmā then paid homage to the god Harimedhas.
And Vrahnā took up the foremost [sacrificial vessel], together with the *Saniṣat-saṃhitā*,
using mantras for the commencement of the ritual and others consisting of twelve syllables.
O Brahmin, it is endowed with divine [qualities], joined with the twelvefold inner self (adhyātma),
and grants as its sole fruit the attainment of that [state] even to those who lack desire for authority.
It is solely devoted to the fourfold nature (cāturātmya) and has emerged from the mouth of Vāsudeva.
In this way, that Blessed One, the God, [revealed] the primordial, eternal Veda.
Then, O Brahmin, having instructed Brahmā of immeasurable splendor and having bestowed upon him the power, energy, and capacity for the work of creation that leads to his welfare; || 147 ||
He went to the further shore of darkness, where the unmanifest is established;
then the boon-granting god Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [appeared]. || 148 ||
Then he created all the worlds, both stationary and moving;
having thus created the entire universe, the lotus-seated one [Brahmā] did so once again.
"When shall I behold the god who acts for the welfare of the worlds—the auspicious deity reclining within his celestial chariot, clothed in yellow garments? (150)
Thus absorbed in thought, he performed a most difficult penance;
thereupon, a divine and most wonderful celestial chariot appeared.
Illuminating all directions with its stainless radiance,
it was provided with footstools, a base-platform, and a carpet.
It was endowed with divine limbs ending with the neck, the summit, the altar situated thereon, the jar, and the crest, and it was beautified by divine ornaments. || 153 ||
Seeing that [palace], which was square yet elongated and adorned all around with parrot-beak (śukanāsa) ornaments, he was overwhelmed with tears of joy and felt great reverence. || 154 ||
With all his limbs covered in horripilation and his eyes dilated with joy, he rose up in agitation, bowed down, and stood with palms joined in reverence. || 155 ||
Upon the pedestals and other parts, up to the pinnacle, and upon the components of the celestial chariot (vimāna),
the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ and ending with Satya are situated in sequence.

O best of the twice-born, among the paths, there is the group of six beginning with the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and ending with the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan); and there is the collection of principles (tattva), beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa.
Having assumed the very nature of existence, he beheld it established [therein];
then, he gazed upon the host of deities in due order.

On the foundational part of the pedestal (pīṭha), however, is the king of serpents named Ananta, as well as the wheel (cakra) and the assembly of powers (śakti-saṅgha) such as Sāmarthya and Śakti. || 159 ||
Likewise, there is an eightfold group of powers beginning with the radiance of knowledge (jñānabhāsā);
the first eight are possessed of strength and vigor, while the latter eight are characterized by stability.
O best of the twice-born, [one should place] the wheel of letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa';
then, from the region of the pedestal, the sixteen [squares] beginning with Dharma.
The wheel is the light of the fire of time, and the lotus rests upon the three abodes;
in its center is the Person consisting of consciousness, endowed with all powers.
In the four directions, one should place Ananta and the others; then, in the group of feet, Vāsudeva and the rest in the cardinal directions, and Sudarśana at the base of the branches.
In the reality consisting of knowledge and action, the Supreme Lord is at the beginning; on the upper branch of the Udumbara tree, and upon its back, indeed, is Dharma.
O twice-born one, one should worship Kālāgni on the two door-panels and Varuṇa thereafter;
one should worship Icchā and Prāṇa on the two pillars and the śukanāsā, and on the two windows.
Then Agni and Soma are the shanks; in the twelve internal spaces, from Kāla down to Vasudhā, and at the tips of the shanks, Keśava and the others [are placed].
Within the group of nine nostrils, and also within the space between them, the collection of weapons beginning with the discus (cakra) exists in the form of a living being. || 167 ||
On the face of Śukanāsā is the Lord Vāsudeva, the Master of the World;
on the three remaining nostrils, Acyuta and the others are situated in successive order. || 168 ||
On the surface of the altar, adorned with leaves and other ornaments,
one should place the Sudarśana discus with its six spokes along with its spear, within a set of four jars.
O Brahmin, in front of those discus-bearers beginning with Vāsudeva, one should place the four deities beginning with Amala in order, from east to west. || 170 ||
O Brahmin, from the Adhyakṣa up to the first Mūrti, within the jars of Śukanāsā, there is indeed that which consists of all worlds and likewise that which consists of all paths.
"Consisting of all reality and likewise consisting of all the gods"—
having thus beheld the celestial chariot in this sequence, his heart was filled with joy.
Then, having circumambulated him and prostrated with all his limbs like a staff upon the ground out of devotion, he paid homage to Puruṣottama in four ways.
Then, considering himself to have achieved his purpose, he entered the interior of the celestial chariot and stood in the middle of the inner chamber.
Fashioned according to his own proportions, soft to the touch, and enchanting;
resembling pure crystal, it was blazing and exceedingly radiant. (175)
Likewise, he was lying upon a bed of the coils of Ananta, illuminated by the jewels situated in the midst of his circle of hoods, and was clothed in yellow garments.
Endowed with absolute goodness, he possessed a radiant luster,
with a body that was beautiful, divine, and unchanging.
Constantly emitting from the body a light characterized by knowledge, it effortlessly destroys the ignorance of those who meditate; it is truly great.
Endowed with garlands, garments, and ornaments that were appropriate to themselves, peerless, consisting of consciousness, self-luminous, and mutually delighting one another. || 179 ||
The faces of the quarters were made manifest by the canopies of moonlight from her teeth, and the soles of her lotus-feet were marked with white lilies rising from lines [of beauty]. (180)
His face was occupied with pacifying the suffering of people submerged [in the ocean of existence], his heart was filled with compassion, and he was intent on uplifting the world. || 181 ||
He stands in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of his own body,
with [hair] resembling thick, curled blue bees or molten collyrium.
It was adorned with divine, hair-like ornaments that were grey as camphor, interspersed with flowers, and crowned by diadems and crests.
His eyes are like slightly reddish cow’s milk and pure blue lotuses;
by his cool glances, he is the cause of refreshing the entire world.
With beautiful eyebrows and forehead, a fine nose, and lips like coral glowing with a gentle smile, her radiant cheeks were like the moon of beauty. || 185 ||
He gladdened the meditating sages, who were afflicted by the fires of their past karma,
by refreshing them with a mass of rays arising from his own moon-like teeth.
He bore a lotus-like face, beautified by a chin that was the outflow of his facial splendor,
and serving as the locus for a playful smile.
He had a neck like a conch shell, mighty arms, and a chest marked with the Śrīvatsa;
he possessed lion-like shoulders, large eyes, long arms, and a broad chest. || 188 ||
Adorned with two reddish hands marked by the conch and the discus, he rests his great right arm, which resembles the body of a serpent, upon a pillow. 189.
With his upper arm extended along the side of his waist,
his chest marked by the Kaustubha gem, and his breast adorned by Lakṣmī.
The lotus-eyed one, whose slender abdomen contains the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has his left lotus-foot slightly bent.
With his right leg extended and lying slightly supine,
he was radiant with a crown and diadem inlaid with many jewels.
It was brilliantly illuminated by a perfectly shimmering crest, adorned with various clusters of jewels resembling the rising sun.
His ears and crest were radiant with the light of a jeweled ear-ornament,
and he was adorned with youthful decorations hanging down to the edge of his forehead.
He was resplendent with a beautiful tilaka upon his forehead, and adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings that rivaled the brilliance of many suns. (195)
It was adorned with abundant jewels, pearls, necklaces, and throat-ornaments,
and beautified by diamonds, lapis lazuli, rubies, topazes, and other gems.
His chest was adorned with many various necklaces,
and he shone with the Kaustubha gem, which resembled the rising sun.
He was incessantly illuminating the entire world with his own splendors,
and his great arms were resplendent with the Vaijayantī garland.
It was beautifully adorned with a shimmering golden sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), variegated with various jewels and hanging with strings of pearls.
It was fastened around his waist with a brilliant golden cord, set with magnificent, radiant great jewels.
It was beautified by a waistband shimmering with various rubies and adorned with a girdle-string composed of an intricate arrangement of many gems.
He was clothed in shining yellow garments like many millions of suns, and adorned with anklets and other ornaments set with various jewels. || 202 ||
Thus it was adorned with various other ornaments, such as armlets and bracelets, which were appropriate, beautiful, and radiant.
Resembling a rain-cloud in the monsoon and possessing the luster of a mass of crushed collyrium,
it was augmented by the undivided and complete majesty of the sixfold royal policy.
The unborn, eternal object of meditation for yogis, the cause of the birth and other states of the world, the Lord without beginning or end, the manifest husband of Lakṣmī, the Sovereign. || 205 ||
Vāsudeva, whose body is beyond the ordinary, who is peaceful, and who is higher than the highest,
was being praised by Sanaka and other Siddhas residing in Janaloka.
With his two unblinking eyes, as if drinking her in with thirst,
he gazed upward with a joyful soul, bowing down again and again.
Having praised him with various hymns in a voice faltering with joy,
he then took that great divine celestial chariot upon his head.
The lotus-seated one, O Brahmin, went to his own abode;
there he worshipped with the twelvefold knowledge of Brahman.
In the meantime, O best of Brahmins, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there with great magnificence for the sake of the high-souled Pauṣkara.
But when the desire to know had arisen regarding the scripture named Pauṣkara,
O Brahmin, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, then manifested himself.
He caused the lotus-born Brahmā to receive this great Mahopaniṣad scripture, which is renowned as the root Veda; from that [scripture], this work has flowed forth.

O Brahmin, it bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation; it contains the essence of the meaning of all scriptures, is endowed with various manifestations, and is accompanied by other forms. || 213 ||
Endowed with various manifestations and accompanied by different appearances,
[the Lord is attended] by Lakṣmī and others, as well as those known as Śaṅkha, Cakra, Garuḍa, and the lords of the directions.

O best of the twice-born, it is filled with mantras consisting of groups of syllables fixed upon weapons, as well as seed-syllables (bījas) in the form of piṇḍas and words composed of technical designations (saṃjñās). || 215 ||

It is endowed with various arrays of mantras and various meditations, along with mandalas such as the Bhadraka and others, which are designated according to the enumeration of the principles (tattva). || 216 ||
Likewise, it is endowed with fourteen arrays containing the single Aja within each, joined with twenty-six spokes, and likewise with nine lotuses and wheels. || 217 ||
O Brahmin, [these are] together with the eighteen cakras known by their respective names, beginning with the dvāravaka and ending with the sahasrāra, along with their causes. || 218 ||
It is perfectly established with a form that is indeed concealed by a covering, resembling a great forest of clouds, and existing as a variety of reflected images. || 219 ||
It was further adorned with various ritual implements such as the bell,
the large and small sacrificial ladles, as well as fire-pits endowed with diverse characteristic features.

O best of the twice-born, it is completely fulfilled through the rites beginning with the installation ceremony, including those performed at the end of the annual festival, as well as the daily, occasional, and optional rituals.
It was endowed with temples arising from various types such as the self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta), for the sake of his authorized function and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. || 222 ||
Then, according to the path described therein, by means of various accumulations of enjoyments— consisting of daily, occasional, and optional rites, as well as various great festivals— || 223 ||
There, performing worship every day, the Grandfather of the worlds,
honored by the world, carried out the various affairs of the worlds.
Then, O Brahmin, when the Manvantara named Vaivasvata had arrived,
there was a king named Ikṣvāku, born of the solar dynasty.
The high-souled one, ever a yogi, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
with a tranquil mind, desired to behold Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe.
Having assumed the garb of an ascetic, he went to the forest to practice austerities;
having entered it, he performed penance, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits. || 227 ||
In the summer, that great ascetic passed his time standing in the midst of five fires;
during the rainy season, he remained without shelter; and in the winter, he stayed within the waters of a lake.
Having again restrained all the senses within the heart,
one should cause the mind to enter Viṣṇu while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.
As that high-souled king was muttering prayers while subsisting on air alone,
the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, appeared before him.
Then, beholding the four-faced one, the lotus-born Brahmā, who had arrived, he bowed with a spirit of devotion and gratified him with hymns of praise. || 231 ||
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, the creator of the world, the Great Soul;
salutations to you, the four-faced one, who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras. || 232 ||
Thus praised by Brahmā, the creator of the world, he spoke to that best of kings,
who was peaceful, devoted to austerity, and had renounced the great pleasures of sovereignty.
O King, the Sun, the illuminator of the world, is your grandfather;
and Manu, the father of all the Vasus, is always worthy of honor.
Your father and grandfather performed intense austerities in the past;
having surpassed those very same austerities, you now abide in penance, truly free from desire.
"For what purpose, O best of kings, have you abandoned all royal enjoyments and perform such severe penance? Tell me, O high-minded one. (236)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the king bowed to him and spoke these words,
desiring to see Madhusūdana through the power of his ascetic practice.
"I shall perform penance here, O Brahmin, [meditating on] the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace.
Thus addressed, the lotus-born one spoke to the king as if smiling.
O King, the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa cannot be seen through ascetic penance;
nor can the unborn Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, be beheld by those such as I.
"How much more so for one like you! Contemplate that Mādhava is indeed the Lord.
Listen as I relate to you this ancient, meritorious tale. (240)
O Great King, in former times, desiring to behold the eternal Vāsudeva at the beginning of creation, I performed most rigorous ascetic penance.
At the conclusion of my ascetic penance, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees,
being pleased, appeared before my very eyes, O lotus-eyed one.
Having bowed down to the lotus-eyed one, I praised him with various hymns;
thereupon the Lord, bestowing upon me welfare, strength, and splendor, prepared to create the world.
Then he taught me the primordial, eternal Veda known as the True Tradition (Sadāgama), which is the root that reveals the Supreme Brahman. || 244 ||
It is divine, bestowing success, and brings peace to the masters of all crafts;
it exists within a celestial chariot possessing divine characteristics at the conclusion of the creation.
The lotus-eyed one, reclining upon a couch of infinite splendor, will manifest before you; worship him with special devotion.
O Lotus-born One, [this should be done] with the twelve-syllable mantra according to the path taught by Pauṣkara, following the procedure that will be described hereafter.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Supreme Self and Master of the Universe, vanished;
thereupon, a divine and most wonderful celestial chariot appeared.
I have also obtained a scripture called the Mahopaniṣad;
therein resides Vāsudeva, the Lord of the gods, the Master of the universe.
O best of kings, I worship according to the procedure prescribed therein;
therefore, I grant you that which is the abode of bliss for Keśava. (250)
"O King, having abandoned this severe asceticism, go to your own city;
for the protection of subjects is the duty of a ruler, as is asceticism. (251)
"O best of kings, I shall send a perfected celestial chariot from heaven, yoked with twice-born brahmins who are devoted to sacred truth and know the five divisions of time. (252)
There, propitiate the Lord of Gods, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, who lies upon the serpent Ananta, with all auspicious external and internal offerings. (253)
O best of kings, by worshipping the God with the twelve-syllable mantra according to the procedure taught in the Pauṣkara, and with various sacrifices, [he attained his goal]. 254.
Free from desire, O tiger among kings, protect your subjects according to dharma;
through the grace of Vāsudeva, liberation shall be yours, O king.
Having spoken thus and having instructed that protector of the earth in the Pauṣkara scripture according to the proper sequence, the Creator once again became invisible to him.
O twice-born one, as Ikṣvāku sat reflecting upon the words of the lotus-born Brahmā,
that celestial chariot appeared before the king.
Having seen that auspicious [image] of Mādhava and Ananta accompanied by Brahmādatta and the twice-born, and having bowed to Puruṣottama with supreme devotion, [he departed]. || 258 ||
Having paid homage to the sages and the elders, he took them and departed for the city,
watched by the citizens, the people, and women who were filled with splendor.
Then, while they were scattering parched grains, the king [beheld] his own spacious palace,
which was indeed a beautiful Vaiṣṇava celestial chariot.
Having established [the image], that best of kings, with his soul purified, worshipped Hari—
who had been honored by those twice-born brahmins— according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the Pauṣkara.
The beautiful-limbed women of human birth, having rubbed themselves with yellow sandalwood and fashioned fragrant garlands, spread their affection for him. || 262 ||
The citizens likewise gave camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and so forth;
they brought and gave to the king flowers suitable for Viṣṇu.

Having installed the images representing the various ritual purposes according to the prescribed rules, and having seated them extensively in their respective locations as they have been described; 264.
Then, with all eightfold sets of offerings numbering sixty-four, which are entirely natural, primary, accompanied by their subsidiary enjoyments, and various ritual services; || 265 ||

O Brahmin, having thus worshipped Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World and the Supreme beyond the supreme, with fragrant substances that touch the skin and those known as heart-pleasing [incenses], [he attained his goal].
With supreme devotion, he caused the annual festival of the God to be celebrated for a very long time through recitations and Vaiṣṇava hymns at the three junctions of the day.
And likewise, the annual rites and various occasional ceremonies, their specific procedures, and their respective locations [were described]. (268)
And I shall describe in detail further on the various types of festivals and so forth;
having gratified Hari, who embodies all the gods, with enjoyments. (269)
Free from desire, through the practice of giving and righteousness, he attained supreme knowledge;
performing sacrifices, protecting the earth, and worshipping Keśava.
Having procreated sons for the sake of his ancestors and finally cast off his body,
he meditated upon the stainless God and attained the station of Viṣṇu.
And thereafter, this was obtained in succession by the Lord himself,
Rāma, the lotus-eyed sovereign of all, together with his three brothers.
He who, remembering "I am a human," is the slayer of the Rākṣasas;
he who [destroys] the terrible night-ranger of the mind, which has ten sense-organs for its mouths.
With a net of arrows of discernment, he brings embodied beings to tranquility;
he who has accomplished his purpose knows the divine and supreme nature. || 274 ||
He gave to his beloved Vibhīṣaṇa, who acted for his pleasure,
a celestial chariot endowed with divine characteristics, preceded by instruction in the scriptures.
Taking that head upon his own, he departed toward his own country;
when the sun had reached midday, he arrived at the bank of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā). || 276 ||
He caused the Moon to descend onto the Ananta-pīṭha in the middle of the Candra-puṣkariṇī pond;
for at the sacrifice of Dakṣa, the Maker of Night had been humiliated by Rudra. || 277 ||
He made his dwelling upon its summit, where he performed great austerities;
it was there that the lotus-eyed Lord, assuming the form of a dwarf, [performed his deeds].
He indeed attained by himself the refinement of right conduct,
whereby he reached a divine, preeminent celestial chariot known as Śrīrahaṅga.
Having resolved, "He shall establish himself here," the Lord of the World commanded Gaṇeśa and Yoganidrā for the sake of protection.
Having brought it there, Vibhīṣaṇa placed the celestial chariot in their midst;
then he worshipped Hari, who had already been honored by those twice-born brahmins.
With various delightful objects of enjoyment, such as tactile sensations and the like,
that powerful one made an effort to rescue him.
At that time, he was not able to move him even slightly from that state;
then, lamenting and filled with grief, he fell indeed upon the earth.
Seeing Vibhīṣaṇa distressed, lamenting like one who is helpless,
the Blessed Lord Raṅgin then spoke with a mighty voice.
The Blessed One said:
"O noble one, knower of dharma, this region is indeed delightful in my estimation;
lying here, I shall take delight in gazing upon you."
Together with these exclusive devotees who are intent on my worship,
O Vibhīṣaṇa, grant them permission and do what is pleasing to me.
And make these Brahmins, who are devoted to the five daily rites, your worshippers;
and make them well-provided with fields, gardens, houses, and other such things.
Do not be dejected; go quickly to Laṅkā, O night-stalker!
There, with your purposes fully accomplished, enjoy prosperity that never fails.
Thus addressed, he made those [disciples] very prosperous with fields, gardens, houses, and so forth,
and established them as followers of the Ekāyana path, devoted to the five times of daily worship.
Then, afflicted by the misfortune of mortals and for the welfare of the Brahmins, Vibhīṣaṇa departed once again toward Laṅkā. || 290 ||
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of establishing the gods, the Lord of the Stage (Raṅgeśa) took delight there on the riverbank, reclining in the theater-hall.
Then that best of rivers, embracing him from both sides,
moved along as a woman might embrace her long-lost beloved husband with both her arms.
For this is a great divine abode, and the inhabitants there are divine;
likewise, this river is divine, as is this lake with its divine bathing-places.
That self-existent celestial chariot is indeed endowed with infinite power;
even Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā are powerful beings who can assume any form at will.
And they all protect that region with unblinking eyes;
those who dwell there are outflows [of merit], free from food, and characterized by goodness.
Uttering sweet speech that brings delight to the ears, no suffering such as hunger or thirst befell those dwelling there. (296)
There is neither internal nor external affliction, nor old age, nor lack of discernment;
they are endowed with knowledge of the three times and are free from all desires. (297)

They are perfected in the knowledge of the seven categories of reality, they do not sacrifice to other deities, they are devoted to the twelve internal [disciplines], and they are dedicated to the five periods of the day. || 298 ||
Worshipping him day after day, they indeed dwell right there, devoted to the six duties and with their minds fixed upon Brahman. (299)
There dwell stainless men of firm vows,
as well as gods, lords of the asuras, and chief sages, who are ever desirous of the divine state.
Abiding there, they assume various immobile forms;
even one who is insane becomes tranquil, and even one who is deaf becomes clearly perceptive.
O best of sages, even Brahmā is unable to fully comprehend the greatness of that region; how much less so, then, those such as myself? (302)
This supreme abode, known by the name Śrīraṅga, is endowed with divine characteristics and is celebrated as being self-manifested. || 303 ||
Here is present in person the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama, the lotus-eyed Supreme Self, the infallible Hari, for the sake of his devotees. 304.
Furthermore, even though he is constantly present in various other places,
Vāsudeva himself, whose essence is the knowledge of mantras, remains personally present there.
Nevertheless, it indeed attains prominence here by virtue of its strength, just as the sun reaches its peak intensity upon arriving at the summer season. || 306 ||
Without ever abandoning its own essential nature, the Lord of the Universe likewise undergoes no alteration here through such defects as the divisions of space and so forth.
Due to the greatness of his eternal presence, time proceeds in this world in an ever-increasing succession until the end of the kalpa.
Incomparable in prosperity, splendor, fame, and ritual action, she who bestows the pacification of the wicked through her power, and who indeed grants spiritual perfection along with it. (309)
O best of men, those living beings who desire liberation and those who desire fruits attain their respective desired goals right here in this world, which are imperishable.
In this world, all those devoted to ritual action always perform all their rites in the evening, at dawn, and at midday, with their minds ever directed toward the celestial chariot.
Thus, [it is] in the field of Puṣkara, on the peak of Mount Tota, on the portion of the earth known as Purāṇa, and also in that named Madhubhāṇḍa. || 312 ||
The Lord, the self-manifested Master of the universe, the blessed lotus-eyed one, remains present there out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. || 313 ||
O best of the twice-born, the God of gods, the Lord of the World, having been thus installed in certain sacred fields by the foremost of the wise, remains present there.
O Brahmin, when installed according to the prescribed rites by certain lords of men whose minds are nourished by devotion, the Lord of the Universe becomes present there.
Thus, by means of the forms of the Blessed One, characterized by various configurations,
and through various specific manifestations according to various functions.
The entire universe has been filled in its entirety out of a desire to bestow grace upon all;
it is self-manifested as well as established by perfected beings and the gods.
It was established as the embodiment of mantra by the foremost sages, as well as by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Rākṣasas, and the chief Asuras. (318)

One who is skilled in the scriptures should worship the deity installed by men according to the procedure taught in the divine scriptures and following the path described in the words of the sages. || 319 ||
O twice-born one, there too one should worship with those who possess knowledge, who perceive the truth,
who are solely devoted to Vāsudeva, and who are free from devotion to other deities.
But those established by lords of men who were liberated through the mixed scriptures, endowed with intense devotion, and skilled in the piercing [of the centers] and other rites; || 321 ||
One should worship the Lord of the gods according to the path taught in the divine scriptures;
for in that place where worship is performed according to the method spoken by the sage, [the goal is attained].
Even in that case, if one wishes to perform worship by way of the divine path, one should abandon the path of the sages and worship by way of the divine path. || 323 ||
The greatness of the storehouse shall endure for a period lasting until the end of the kalpa,
wherein worship and other rites are performed perpetually by way of the divine path.
In that regard, O Mahāmati, having abandoned the divine [method], one should never perform worship and so forth according to the path taught in the words of the Sage.
If, however, through delusion, that Brahmin of bewildered mind should perform it,
his devotion will depart before long along with the very seed of its practice.

O best of Brahmins, the mantras, the ritual procedures, and the supernatural powers will all turn away from him; yet, in this very life, he shall quickly attain the cessation of rebirth at the end of his body.
The king goes to a terrible hell and the kingdom perishes;
therefore, with every effort, one should not abandon the divine path. || 328 ||
But where worship is performed by means of a tamasic path, even there, worship performed by means of a rajasic path alone shall be the bestower of success. || 329 ||
Even where worship and other rites are performed constantly by one of the royal temperament (rājasena), worship performed there with a purely sattvic disposition always bestows auspiciousness. (330)
However, wherever worship and other rites are performed daily according to the *sāttvika* method, one should not perform the worship and so forth by means of the *rājasa* path. || 331 ||
Where worship and other rites have been commenced by way of the rājasa path,
one should not perform worship and other rites there by way of the tāmasa path.
There may be a mutual intermingling of various passionate (rājasa) statements; however, in all human speech, that which is non-contradictory should be accepted.
Sanaka would not perform the installation and other rites merely according to that procedure,
nor [the rites] you have described for the purpose of worshipping divine abodes and the like. (334)

I wish to hear the scripture in its true essence, according to its divisions such as the divine and others, so that by knowing it, I may turn away from the fault of confusion regarding the scriptures. (335)
Śāṇḍilya [received] that scripture which was spoken by the Lord Vāsudeva himself,
composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter and distinguished by its concise and expanded sections. || 336 ||
Know, O best of beings, that it was likewise set in motion by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and others, and it prevails even in the divine worlds; know that to be the divine. 337.
Know that the scripture which was composed by the gods headed by Brahmā and Rudra, as well as by the sages whose wealth is austerity, is what is spoken by the Munis.
Know that this [knowledge] is threefold, according to the distinction of *sāttvika* and the others;
having understood the multitude of objects as they truly exist from the Lotus-eyed Lord. (339)
That scripture which has been composed to explain that [reality] is remembered as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
Therefore, once the collection of objects has been understood, having relied upon even a small portion of it, || 340 ||

O best of the twice-born, having understood in truth that which has been composed as an awakener of the multitude of objects that are [only] revealed by one's own intellect, [one should proceed]. 341.
From the Lord of all lords, [I have received] this scripture joined with extensive treatises;
by the grace of its condensation, through the unfolding of my own intellectual reflections, [I shall now explain it]. 342.
O twice-born one, that which was composed by Brahmā and others, as well as by the ṛṣis—
having heard it from Brahmā and the rest, I have [presented] it once more in a condensed form.
Know that everything produced from one's own conceptual construction is characterized by passion (rājasa);
it is twofold, distinguished as the Pañcarātra and the Vaisvānara. || 344 ||
That which is performed solely through one's own conceptual constructions is indeed *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness);
whereas that which is performed by men alone would be *pauruṣa* (human effort).
Sanaka said:
O best of speakers, tell me in detail those characteristics by which I may truly understand the distinction between the words of the Blessed Lord and others. (346)
Śāṇḍilya said:
[That hymn] which is rich in meaning, free from doubt, clear, concise in syllables, and stable, [is dedicated] always to the All-pervading Lord who exists in the form of the fourfold Self. (347)
Wherever "otherness" (paratva) is proclaimed as being intrinsic (svābhāvika), and wherever it belongs to other mantra-forms, that [otherness] is indeed adventitious (aupādhika). || 348 ||
The distinction of states, beginning with the fourth (turya) and ending with the waking (jāgrat), has been revealed therein for the sake of compassion toward devotees of the Fourfold Self. || 349 ||
Therein is revealed the sovereign power of the all-pervading Śaktīśa,
as well as the powers of the Lord of Birds, who are adorned with the ornaments of his limbs and marks.
But where the essential nature, divided by the distinctions of *laya* and so forth, is expounded through the fourfold method beginning with *bīja*, *piṇḍa*, and *pada*, O best of beings; (351)
Wherever mantras are employed in the rite of installation, there the procedure for piercing is prescribed, as well as the daily worship. || 352 ||
O twice-born one, it has been declared that the complete [ritual] pertains primarily to the primary image;
however, whatever among those rites, such as bathing and so forth, is impossible to perform there, [that alone is omitted]. (353)

But that [reflection] exists within the interior of the object when preceded by the ritual image; it is prescribed in mirrors and such, O Great-minded One, because of the absence of that [interiority] elsewhere. (354)
O twice-born one, by means of the five-fold concentration (dhāraṇā) consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, as well as by the two-fold concentration, [one attains success]. || 355 ||

In this [system], where purification of the material elements occurs through what is called burning and satiating, it establishes for itself the fact that its own source is rooted in the traditional scriptures (āgama) and the Vedas (śruti). || 356 ||
That word of the Supreme Lord is indeed established by command and bestows liberation;
O Great-minded one, such is the scripture arising from words that are to be accepted. (357)
Know that to be the complete revelation of the true path and the doctrine of injunction;
and by virtue of its authority, whatever else may be inferred according to the facts [is also to be understood]. (358)
It must be carried out without contradiction between what precedes and what follows, without critical inquiry, pleasing to all, subtle, and incapable of being definitively determined. (359)

Whatever collection of meanings spoken by the Supreme Lord exists as it truly is, and whatever purifying discourse of the sages serves to bring about recognition [of that reality], [is this work]. 360.
That which praises the supernatural powers (siddhis) and even promotes them,
disregarding the fundamental form [of the deity], is entirely devoted to the ritual worship of the physical image.
The daily worship has been declared,
as well as the primary dimensions and characteristics of the images of Brahmā, Rudra, and the other deities.
Wherever the installation of the Lord of the worlds is prescribed, there indeed the worship of the material, insentient objects is also ordained. (363)
O best of Brahmins, it is there that the five mantras beginning with Parameṣṭhin, which denote the principles (tattvas), the directions, and time, are indeed applied in their proper sequence.
The pentad beginning with *sthāpana* and ending with *pratiṣṭhā* has been proclaimed;
those beginning with *yāga* and ending with *haristoma* are celebrated as seven. || 365 ||
Where there are likewise seven sacrifices, those are the qualified practitioners in their respective order;
it has been stated that where [the rite] is established, there is the arrangement of the sixteen-fold nyāsa.
Know all this to be of the nature of passion (rājasa), as spoken by the sages;
for it is directed toward the Blessed One without, however, constituting a limb [of the ritual]. 367.
And likewise for the gods headed by Brahmā and Rudra,
as well as for the Mothers and Durgā, wherever they indeed exist in their own independent capacity.
Know that the statements of the sages which prescribe mantras, meditation, measurement, characteristics, and likewise installation, are called tāmasa. 369.

A statement composed by a human being is traditionally defined as that which is purposeless, incoherent, trivial, merely a display of verbal flourish, and incapable of carrying out the initial assertion. (370)
O twice-born one, that which contradicts the meaning of the Supreme Lord’s words is to be abandoned; it is a mine of misfortunes and leads to hell. 371.

O Brahmin, that which is required for the divine state among the words of the sages beginning with those concerning the *sāttvika* nature should be diligently grasped; that which is non-contradictory should be accepted.
O high-minded one, having inferred among them according to the sequence beginning with the *sāttvika* [qualities],
and employing well-known meanings, you should understand the distinct and coherent sense.
Moreover, if human speech is to be accepted, it should be like the words of a sage;
for Sanaka and others proclaimed these scriptures as being of divine origin by means of these very indicators.
O best of the twice-born, they have been embraced and provided with manifest names;
indeed, I have a great curiosity to hear them—please tell them to me in their respective groups.
And how they are to be understood by those of limited intellect without confusion—
namely, the Śāṇḍilya, the Sātvata, the Pauṣkara, and likewise the one called Jaya. || 376 ||
Understand that such treatises as these are divine;
so too are the Saṃhitās of Īśvara and of Bharadvāja. (377)
Likewise, there is the Saumantavī, that which is known as the Pārameśvara, the Vaihāyasī Saṃhitā, and the scripture born from Citraśikhaṇḍin. || 378 ||
Likewise, O best of beings, know that the *Jayottara* and other such words of the sages therein are truly characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*). 379.
The Tantra known as Sanatkumāra, as well as that named Pajhodbhava, Satyāpi, Tejodraviṇa, and likewise Māyāvaibhavika. || 380 ||
Understand these and others to be truly of the nature of *rajas*—namely, the *Pañcapraśna*, the *Śukapraśna*, and the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*. (381)
Understand these and other such [states] to be specifically characterized by tamas;
therein, that which pertains to puruṣa is to be known by the very definition previously stated. || 382 ||
Having correctly understood the distinctions among palaces and treatises, as well as those beginning with the divine, which have been duly elucidated, one should perform everything accordingly. (383)
He who performs worship and other rites without understanding this intermixture indeed perpetually creates confusion for the entire world. (384)

Therefore, O twice-born one, even in times of distress, a seeker of his own welfare who is learned in the scriptures should not cause a confusion of the scriptures, especially for the sake of his own lineage. (385)
All that was asked has been told; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Deities of Temples such as the Self-Manifested," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
Śrīḥ!
The eleventh chapter: O Brahmin, the method of worship during the daily festival has been fully described by Sanaka.
The meditation and other rites for those deities of the door-panels are now described in sequence.
"I desire to know, O best of Brahmins; tell me in detail.
Listen, O son of Śāṇḍila, for I shall speak that which I have been requested by you. (2)
Beginning from the deities of the palace gate,
one proceeds in due order until reaching the final udumbara tree situated below the exterior of the palace gate.
The two lords of the site and the field stand in order from right to left;
he has a white face and a dark body, possesses two arms, and holds a vessel of jewels.
With his right hand alone, he is the refuge of all the immortals;
he possesses a splendor equal to the white lotus and is adorned with garments, garlands, and unguents.
O Brahmin, the Vāstupuruṣa should be meditated upon with his hand raised, holding a mallet;
one should meditate on Kṣetreśa as having two arms, with a golden luster, garments, and a garland.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with a staff in his hand and a massive body,
he was the protector of the sacrificial ground, holding his fist with his left hand.
With their bodies adorned by earrings and other ornaments,
these two gazed at the face of the Lord, overflowing with intense splendor.
She possessed the luster of molten gold and wore garments resembling coral;
she was adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, caskets, crowns, and other ornaments.
Adorned with ornaments, her eyes resembling white lotuses,
and her face like the stainless, perfectly full moon of autumn.
One should meditate upon Lakṣmī, who holds a lotus and a water-pot,
seated upon a lotus, above the door-post on the Udumbara pillar.
Resembling the rising sun, broad-chested, and four-armed;
tall with elevated shoulders, his limbs were well-proportioned yet not excessively fleshy. || 12 ||
He had a slender belly and a deep navel, adorned with a line of body hair;
his face was formidable with fangs, and he bore tawny beard and matted locks. || 13 ||
With eyes honey-brown, endowed with curved creeper-like eyebrows, with long and swaying ears, a broad nose, and a smiling face; (14)
Adorned with earrings, decorated with necklaces and armlets, with a turban bound upon his forehead and further embellished by a sectarian mark (tilaka). || 15 ||
Clad in white garments and adorned with garlands, one should meditate upon him holding a raised discus in his right hand and a blazing mace in the other.
And she is seated upon her hips, resting on the surface of the earth;
in her left hand she holds a conch shell, and in the other, a rosary.
Thus the fierce leader of the hosts, unconquered by prowess, was enraged and capable of destroying tens of thousands of obstacles in an instant. (18)
The one to be meditated upon is at the base of the right door-jamb of the inner sanctum;
in that very place, on the western side, one should worship Pracaṇḍa in such a manner.
However, there may be a reversal by means of the left and right arms;
that which is prescribed for the left arm of Caṇḍa applies to both arms.
Having visualized that [form] on the right or having imagined it there,
one should meditate upon Garuḍa, with the luster of gold, at the position of the front of the door.
With curved eyebrows and large, round eyes adorned with circles of eyelashes,
he had a protruding belly and well-nourished limbs, and was decorated with all kinds of ornaments.
He was resplendent with ornaments such as a crown and anklets, wearing blue garments and adorned with various garlands. (23)
He stood before the God of gods upon the ground with palms joined in reverence—
the two-armed Lord of Birds, named Satya, who possesses the luster of snow.
One should meditate upon the deity of the vital breath (prāṇa) as being situated in the center of the circle of offerings within the wheel,
established in the form of a person with all his limbs complete.
With a protruding belly and adorned with rows of wings,
he held a rosary in his right hand alone.
With one hand raised and the other adorned with earrings and other ornaments, he was clothed in dark-blue silk garments and anointed with dark-blue garlands and unguents. || 27 ||
He was constantly gazing at the Lord with untroubled eyes;
then, [he saw] two [beings] stationed at the pair of door-frames of the front pavilion.
Resembling the interior of a lotus and possessing exceedingly terrifying prowess, they were like Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, adorned with the ornaments of arm-emblems. || 29 ||
Having meditated upon and worshipped with single-minded devotion the two attendants Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, who wear red garments, possess red garlands, and are anointed with red unguents; || 30 ||
One should worship the lords of the Kumuda and other groups in the first enclosure;
furthermore, two Gaṇanāyakas are to be worshipped in the eastern and southeastern directions.
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, with serene faces and eyes, resembled the snowy mountain and were in the prime of their youth. (32)
O twice-born one, their limbs were smeared with various ornaments, they were adorned with various earrings,
decorated with various garlands, and they wore various crowns.
With limbs smeared with various perfumes and adorned with various garments, the right hand of the Lord of the Gaṇas named Kumuda is to be meditated upon. || 34 ||
Adorned with a fly-whisk resembling a ray of the moon,
one should meditate on the second right hand as bestowing fearlessness.
For others who have taken refuge [in him] for the sake of destroying worldly existence, there is the teaching of his virtues;
and his very first left hand is raised with a blossoming lotus. (36)
One should meditatively contemplate the supreme hand of those situated outside as being silent and indicative of fear;
indeed, one should contemplate these in the reverse manner for Kumudākṣa.
Indeed, for the others as well, it is exactly the same with two hands each;
both Puṇḍarīka and Vāmana possess the splendor of the consumer of oblations (Agni).

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) or meditated upon the two hands bearing the Garuḍa-banner, and having done so as previously described for the rest, one should place them in the south and also in the southwest.
He who is named Śaṅkukarṇa and he who is designated as Sarvanetra—
these two, both with complexions like the campaka flower, are intent upon raising the peacock-feather fans.

Of the Lord Mahāvibhūti, [the attendants] Sumukha and Supratiṣṭha are situated in the west and northwest directions; of the All-pervading Lord (Vibhu), they are situated in the north and northeast directions.
One should visualize Mudga and Śyāma holding sunshades in their hands;
know that for those whose remaining hands have not been specified, they hold the [lotuses] mentioned previously, such as the white water-lily (kumuda). 42.
Mānava and Pṛśnigarbha were stationed in the sky over the earth;
they shone with the luster of molten gold and were radiant with their jeweled caskets and crowns.
O twice-born one, they have faces made terrible by fangs and wear various garlands;
there also is the one named Mānava, adorned with wings and serpents.
His right hand is adorned with the king of conchs;
upon its back, on the wrist, it rests playfully between the fingers and the thumb.
She is called Akṣamālā, who always bestows all accomplishments.
In her principal left hand is a discus, and behind it, held upright, is a mace.
O twice-born one, one should meditate on this in the reverse manner of Pṛśnigarbha; having visualized [the serpent] extending from the waist to the hand, it is without the two serpents of the wings.
O Brahmin, these internal states of the Blessed One have been declared by me;
with their minds absorbed in his being, they [attain him] through action, mind, and speech. 48.
It was crowded with millions of supreme beings endowed with the six qualities beginning with knowledge,
as well as with infinite perfected ones (siddhas) seeking the highest state.

Adorned with garments, ornaments, fragrant unguents, and the like, they all resembled white water-lilies, for they were decorated solely with the vertical *puṇḍra* mark fashioned from white clay. || 50 ||

O twice-born one, by means of that which resides on his forehead, all the lords of the hosts such as Kumuda and others, as well as all other attendants beginning with the Bhūtas, [were likewise empowered].
In this same way, the Āvṛti gods and likewise those stationed at the gates, as well as his Brahmins and those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, [were all present]. || 52 ||
O twice-born one, they should always be adorned with twelve or four vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) fashioned from either clay or sandalwood.
Dark as the flax flower, adorned with yellow garlands and garments, wearing yellow turbans, fierce, and possessing arms decorated as before. || 54 ||
And one should worship the two attendants named Jaya and Vijaya on the two sides of that door; they possess fierce forms, are difficult to behold, and are hard to overcome.
Starting from that point and extending outward to the end of the gate,
one should divide the field of the second enclosure into six parts, and then [further] into five in the fifth.
O Brahmin, having fashioned Garuḍa on the portion, or having meditated upon him,
one should install him— shaped like molten gold, with eyes and eyebrows knit in a terrible frown.
He had broad fangs, a broad snout, broad limbs, and a broad belly;
his chest was adorned with the sprouts of wings, and he was graced by a circle of feathers.
Adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, earrings, and crowns,
he was dressed in blue garments and decorated with various garlands.
O twice-born one, his limbs were smeared with various fragrant unguents, he was adorned with eleven serpents,
and he held his hands joined in añjali, filled with clusters of flowers.
Having raised his right knee and placed the other upon the seat,
he sat comfortably in a relaxed posture, awaiting the command of the Lord.
Then, the tenfold group of principles consisting of the individual soul (karmātman) attained perfection,
endowed with qualities such as omniscience and power equal to that of the Lord.
It is indeed separated from ordinary suffering and united with the Lord;
for, by means of its capacity to carry one across existence, it gradually removes the veils.
O best of the twice-born, Upendra is stationed in the eastern quarter;
in the southeast is the one named Tejodhara, who is difficult to overcome.
In the southwest is Mahākarmā, in the west is Mahāhrada;
Agrāhya is in the quarter of the wind (the northwest), and likewise Vasuretas is in the north.
One should remember the witness residing in the north-eastern Vardhamāna, who dwells in the sphere of the sky and is known by the name Ādhāranilaya, situated below everything.
These [deities] have the luster of the color of crystal, are adorned with white garlands and garments,
and hold a rosary, a discus, a conch, and likewise a mace.

Indeed, holding [the weapons] beginning with the primary Dakṣa and ending with the primary Vāmā with their four hands, they are perfectly symmetrical and adorned with crowns and other ornaments. || 68 ||
Dispelling the nets of obstacles with their splendor,
those of great majesty all stood in their respective postures, their eyes opened in meditation.

Alternatively, these [deities] are two-armed; they hold the ten [objects] beginning with the vajra in sequence with their right hands, while holding the [emblems] of the world-protectors with their left hands. (70)
Alternatively, they may hold a rosary in the left hand and grant boons and fearlessness;
or, with their complexions, bodily ointments, and so forth, they may resemble Indra and the other gods.
One should install these two groups known as the Gatekeepers (dvārapāla) within the space on both sides of the second gopura door, starting from the left.
The two lords of treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, are situated atop their treasure-vessels;
they have thick tusks and well-tamed forms, possess two arms, and are permeated by the Blessed One.
O twice-born one, they possess curved creeper-like eyebrows, slightly elevated chests, pendulous bellies, well-fleshed limbs, and short hands and feet. (74)
Resembling conch shells and lotuses in luster, they wear blue and white garments and garlands, and are adorned with various ornaments such as crowns and the like. (75)
With their right hands they held lotuses,
and with their other hands, turned upward, they held their own treasures.
Alternatively, O twice-born one, he may hold in his two left hands the gestures of granting refuge and fearlessness, and in his two right hands,
a conch or a lotus.
The Lord of Treasures (Kuvera) should hold either a lotus or a conch in his left hand;
or he may hold both a conch and a lotus upon his head above his crown.
Or, according to the desire of the practitioner, he may also hold the conch and the discus;
having raised his right knee and made the other [the left] the seat. (79)
In this manner, for the Śaṅkhanidhi and the Padmanidhi, it is the reverse;
one should remember them as being fixed at the two door-panels, starting from the south.
And they were as pure white as jasmine buds, dressed in garments of blue silk,
their bodies adorned with flowers having the hue of deep blue lotuses.
Resembling the previously mentioned Gaṇas in name, they are Bhadra and Subhadra;
they stand at the two sides outside that gate, situated within the gopura.
One should install these two lords of the Gaṇas after meditating upon them or having fashioned them;
or else, if these two are two-armed, then [they belong to] the right side of Bhadra.
The left hand, joined with the index finger and slightly bent, rests upon the tip of the mace and is positioned above the base of the mace. || 84 ||
O Brahmin, the right foot is turned upward while the left foot rests upon the ground;
this is what has been described regarding the hands and feet of Bhadra’s two left [hands].
That [gesture] of Subhadra, which belongs to Dakṣa, would be on the left according to Dakṣa’s teaching;
however, his left hand should be joined with the gesture of wonder (vismayamudrā). 86.
Caṇḍa and Prajaṇḍa, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, as well as Jaya, Vijaya, Bhadra, Subhadra, and Gaṇeśvara. || 87 ||
These eight lords of the Gaṇas are indeed identical in their bodies, faces, and forms, as well as in their ornaments and weapons, even though they lack radiance, flowers, and garments. || 88 ||
They are fully prepared to sever the web of obstacles for their devotees—which exists in every direction and yields the fruits of saṃsāra. (89)
All were facing one another, standing in uniform positions,
accompanied by tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of lords of the Gaṇas who bore bodies of various colors.
In the third enclosure, they are subsequently surrounded by those devoted to the propitiation of Acyuta, one by one,
according to the sequence starting from the east.
O twice-born one, one should place the ten guardians of the world, beginning with Indra;
one should meditate upon Purandara, who resembles the sun and possesses four arms. 92.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, who is mounted on a goat, is red in color, holds a spear in his hand, stands upon a well-whetted elephant, and brandishes a very sharp thunderbolt. 93.
It was filled with thousands of rays, as radiant as a thousand suns;
it was mounted upon a great buffalo and possessed a luster like that of a mountain of collyrium. 94.
One should meditate upon the god Pitrīśvara, who holds a club made of subhūma wood in his hand, whose face is formidable with fangs, and whose luster is like a black cloud. || 95 ||

One should meditate upon the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who sits upon a formidable corpse-throne, wielding a sword, possessing a brilliance like that of a pearl, and holding a raised noose in his hand. 96.
The lord of the waters, seated upon a makara, was accompanied by thousands of naga maidens;
he resembled a dark blue cloud and was marked by the cloth of his great banner. || 97 ||
One should meditate upon the god Samīraṇa seated upon a deer, and upon Soma accompanied by the hosts of stars, white as a conch shell or cow’s milk. 98.

One should meditate upon him as seated on the back of a large hare, holding a cool-rayed weapon (the moon) in his hand, his limbs smeared with white ashes, possessing three eyes, and having a bull for his vehicle. || 99 ||
One should meditate upon Īśāna, the wise one, holding a trident in his hand;
and one should contemplate Halāyudha, mounted upon a tortoise, situated in the direction of Pātāla.
The white one with a thousand hoods, the serpent-king named Ananta, [held] the discus being whirled and Prajāpati with staff in hand. 101.
One should meditate upon the eternal, unborn, and all-pervading Lord as seated in the sky, mounted upon a swan;
all these [deities] have four arms and are adorned with rosaries. (102)
Contemplating the supreme reality, with their hands raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
their limbs smeared with divine ornaments and endowed with celestial garlands and garments.
O twice-born one, they possess divine forms and carry divine fragrances,
with splendors like those of the red, white, black, yellow, and blue campaka flowers.
Likewise, they were adorned with garlands, unguents, and garments as precious as sky-crystal, the sun, and royal gems.
Adorned with various ornaments such as caskets and crowns, O Brahmin, the bull-bannered Lord should be known as four-armed from these [descriptions]. (106)
"Others among the immortals may have two arms, granting boons and fearlessness," so it was stated regarding the Lords of the World by you, O best of the twice-born. (107)
At the root of the branch on the southern side of the door of the third enclosure is Sudarśana, four-armed, with a short body and blazing radiance. || 108 ||
With eyes red as krodha-flowers, smeared with the blood of Daityas and Dānavas, dancing and intoxicated with pride, he stood within the interior of the thousand-spoked wheel. || 109 ||
With a mouth formidable with fangs and joined by curved creeper-like eyebrows, it had the appearance of the fire at the end of an aeon and was encircled by its own rays. || 110 ||
In his pair of right arms, he holds the Sudarśana discus with the foremost one,
and with the other, a mace resting upon the ground.
He holds a conch in his principal left hand and a rosary in the other;
he is adorned with necklaces, armlets, earrings, a crown, and other ornaments. (112)
Adorned with various white garlands, garments, and the like,
he eradicated obstacles by means of his own blazing splendor.
Then, O high-minded one, O Brahmin, he should remember Garuḍa well-established at the foot of another tree, resembling molten gold. (114)
With a gentle face, rolling eyes, and a red beak, he was most terrifying;
he had a large belly and was adorned with a long tail and a circle of wing-feathers. || 115 ||
Clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and red unguents,
his face was formidable with fangs, and his eyes were crooked with a frown.
Wearing a variegated tunic, adorned with the lords of serpents, and embellished with various ornaments such as a crown; || 117 ||
That which is proclaimed for the left side of the wheel regarding the two arms shall be on the right side of this [deity], and that which was stated for the right side shall be on the left. (118)
The vajra, the śakti, as well as the staff, the sword, the noose, and the banner;
the trident called Śiśira, and likewise the plow and the mace. || 119 ||
Situated in the fourth enclosure according to the sequence starting from the east, listen now to their meditation in due order. (120)
He holds a vajra as hard as a diamond, marked with long white claws;
his face is terrifying with fangs, and his eyes blaze like gold. || 121 ||
She possessed the radiance of lightning, her face and eyes were like extinguished fires, and she repeatedly emitted a deep, rumbling sound like that of thunderclouds. 122.
One should meditate on Daṇḍa with his fists clenched, red-bodied and red-eyed,
the very embodiment of wrath, biting his own lower lip with his teeth.
One should meditate upon Nandaka, who is adorned with rays of light, dancing,
resembling the autumnal sky, and biting his row of teeth.
He held a noose bristling with a multitude of coils, terrifying with a tongue like lightning;
it was white as a garland of gold, possessed a formidable mouth, and had blood-red eyes.
[He beheld] a banner resembling an autumnal cloud, with curved eyes,
illuminating the entire world by its own splendor, and formidable in its power.
He was cool as frost, resembling the moon in luster, with full limbs and a broad body;
he bore a mass of matted locks, was gentle, and had eyes like white lotuses.
The trident, possessing a terrifying form, shone like a thousand rising suns and was encircled by rays resembling the fire at the end of an aeon. || 128 ||
Resembling a twilight cloud, possessing a plow and fearsome eyes,
with emaciated limbs and uplifted shoulders, he had a body as hard as a diamond and was preeminent in strength.
The pestle was as white as a jasmine flower, gentle, with a face slightly smiling;
it uttered a sweet sound that brought pleasure to the faculty of hearing. || 130 ||
Resembling blue, red, white, yellow, fire, and collyrium, and having a luster equal respectively to gold, the moon, snow, and the sky. || 131 ||
Adorned with beautiful garlands, unguents, and garments, they were equipped with divine ornaments and their heads were marked with their own respective signs. || 132 ||
Threatening the host of the wicked with their right hands,
while resting their left hands upon their hips, they stand in perfectly balanced postures.
Having meditated upon Gaṅgā and Yamunā on the southern and northern door-panels of the fourth enclosure, one should worship them in sequence. || 134 ||
She was like the Gaṅgā born from the feet of the Blessed One, resembling a white water-lily, and endowed with the qualities of fresh youth, beauty, and delicacy. || 135 ||
She has blue body-unguents and garments, is adorned with blue garlands, possesses two arms, a gentle countenance, and eyes resembling lotuses. || 136 ||
Adorned with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments, [it is for those] scorched by the miseries of saṃsāra who desire to ascend to the supreme state. || 137 ||
By her own splendor, she washes away the mud of latent impressions and karma, carrying a water-filled pitcher in her right hand alone. (138)
With her left hand she was threatening ordinary people;
she resembled the Yamunā in the luster of a blue gem, with dark, curly hair.
She is adorned with white unguents and garments, and decorated with white garlands;
the right hand is known to display the tarjanī mudrā, while the left holds a water-pot.
But everything else that was spoken regarding Gaṅgā should also apply here, O Mahāmati;
[he is] red-eyed, of great heroism, immeasurable, and most beautiful. (141)
Vīrahā, Vikrama, Bhīma, and Śatāvarta as the eighth;
these are situated in the fifth enclosure according to the sequence of the directions starting from the northeast (Aiśvarī). || 142 ||
One should meditate upon him who resembles the moon, red-eyed, and preeminent in strength;
who wears blue garments, blue garlands, and blue unguents.
Possessing great heroism, a massive body, and a yellow complexion, he has mighty arms;
he wears garments the color of coral and is adorned with red garlands and unguents. || 144 ||
One should recollect him of immeasurable fame, preeminent with immeasurable power,
having a green form and wearing yellow garments, garlands, and ointments.
One should meditate upon him as most beautiful, with lovely limbs, resembling a pearl,
and adorned with garments, garlands, and unguents that have the luster of the flax flower (atasī).
One should meditate upon Vīraghna, known as Vīrahā, who has the luster of a campaka flower, is adorned with bāhlīka flowers, and is decorated with red garments and garlands. 147.

One should meditate upon Vikrama and Vikramāvāsa, who resemble the belly of a blue jay, are clothed in garments as white and radiant as jasmine and the moon, and are adorned with white garlands and unguents. || 148 ||
One should meditate upon Bhīma, who is of terrifying form, resembling molten gold,
clad in white and reddish silk, and likewise endowed with fragrances and garlands.
One should meditate upon Śatāvarta, who is dark as the flax flower,
wearing yellow garments, and adorned with yellow garlands and perfumes; indeed,
these two-armed deities have their minds delighted within.
Likewise, with all his right hands, he held a blazing axe.
Holding excellent, radiant conchs in their left hands, they wore beautiful earrings;
they were symmetrical with well-proportioned limbs and possessed a tranquil appearance. || 152 ||
All were stationed in their respective places, radiant with their own splendors;
they had serene faces and gentle countenances, and were capable of uplifting the three worlds.
Adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, and armlets,
they were intent on observing his commands and were the pacifiers of the faults of the wicked.
By your great power, you effortlessly and playfully cast down the gods, asuras, and great serpents,
being the sole hero and without any companion.
These door-deities at the four doors of this enclosure are capable of perpetually revolving [the wheel] as far as the realm of Brahmā. 156.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) by means of a paired application, starting from the eastern gate in due order:
Vajranābha and Harīśa in the east, [and their counterparts] in the south and north.
One should meditate upon the one named Vajranābha, whose radiance is equal to a hundred suns, and who performs the gesture of prohibition with his primary right hand. 158.
With his second [hand] he holds a cane-staff, with the third a wheel-king, and with his principal left hand, it is placed against the slope of his hip. 159.
Holding the king of conchs with the second [hand] and likewise the thunderbolt with the third, as well as various ornaments of gold. (160)
Wearing red garlands and garments, and anointed with red unguents, he likewise represents Lord Hari, devoid of the gesture of prohibition. || 161 ||
However, it is marked by the hand known as the *praveśābhinaya*;
for with this, he indeed effects the exclusion of those who are not devotees. (162)
Furthermore, another [guard] grants entrance to the devotees;
such is the purpose of the pair of doorkeepers at every gate. (163)
That which was taught by Dakṣa belongs to Vajranābha; for Hariśa, it proceeds to the left.
Everything else that is situated on the first left [hand] belongs to the right hand.
To the right and left of the south, one should fashion Dharmādhyakṣa and Niyantṛ, resembling Antaka (Yama) and adorned with arms as before. || 165 ||
Clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents, they hold a staff and a mace in their hands, yet are devoid of the thunderbolt and the discus. || 166 ||
To the west, starting from the south, [the faces] are Śuddha, Akṣama, Amṛta, and Ānanda;
in one hand there is an arrow and a bow, and in another a noose. 167.
The first four hands should remain unfurled as before;
indeed, they always resemble those of the Lord of Waters in form. (168)
Clad in blue silk garments and adorned with blue garlands and unguents,
the two lords of wealth, Sudhānanda and Mudaka, are situated in the north, east, south, and west.
Holding a sword and a mallet in their hands, the remaining four [deities] are as previously described;
the form of these two hands should be identical to that of the Moon.
Clad in garments dark as the flax flower and wearing garlands and unguents, these men were adorned with various ornaments like Vajranābha himself. (171)
O bull among sages, listen now in due order to the meditation upon the deities of the sixth enclosure, specifically those stationed at its gates, according to their true nature.
O Brahmin, these deities, situated in the sixth enclosure from the east to the northeast, have taken recourse to a form of radiant energy.
Time, the Ordainer, and the Restrainer; the scripture characterized by various limbs;
the lords of knowledge; and Śiva together with the Rudras and his attendants. || 174 ||
The assembly of Prajāpati, as well as Indra with his retinue, are situated in order as before at the four principal gates. (175)
The discus, conch, lotus, mace, plough, club, arrows, and the Śārṅga bow— these should be meditated upon in sequence, possessing the luster of lightning, snow, and jasmine.
With garments, garlands, and ointments resembling yellow, blue, white, red, and the color of cow’s milk, as well as those with the luster of green arsenic and the dawn-red; || 177 ||
Adorned with ornaments made of every kind of jewel,
they were possessed of great strength and great heroism, having one face and two arms.
All these leaders have their heads marked with their own respective symbols,
and they threaten the flood of the wicked with their right hands.
Leaning on his hip with his left hand, he stood in perfectly balanced postures;
firm in his vows, many-headed, large-bodied, and possessed of great strength.
He who has conquered anger, who is invincible, possessed of great energy, and who strides with three steps;
who is incomparable, the slayer of the wicked, radiant, all-seeing, and difficult to overcome. 181.
The uneven, dense, and unfailing [regions] consist of sixteen secondary entrances,
beginning from the middle of Śakra and Agni and extending to the interval between Śakra and Īśāna.
White, crimson, golden, honey-colored, tawny, red, white, and black;
red, yellow, flaxen, gold, crimson, bright, white, and black. 183.
Adorned with fine garments, garlands, ointments, and ornaments appropriate to their castes, and possessing conduct consistent with their names, they carried conch shells and mallets. || 184 ||
By the very sequence of right and left, they are the causes of entry and prohibition;
in an instant, they possess the power to perform the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
One should worship these aforementioned [deities] in their proper sequence, as before:
the seven ancient sages, the other planets, and those surrounded by the stars and so forth. || 186 ||
All the clouds, the nāgas, the most excellent hosts of apsarases, as well as the medicinal herbs, animals, and all the sacrifices along with their constituent parts and supplements; 187.
In the seventh enclosure, they remain in a subtle form as before:
Saṃbhava, Prabhava, Pūrṇa, and Puṣkara. || 188 ||
Ānanda and Nandana, as well as Vīrasena and Suṣeṇa—these two each stood at the main door-posts on the right and left sides respectively. 189.
Saṃbhava is white in color, while Prabhava resembles a kunda flower; Pūrṇa has the appearance of red, and Puṣkara is intensely red.
Ānanda is yellow in color, while Nanda is said to have the luster of gold;
Vīrasena has a dark complexion, and Suṣeṇa resembles collyrium.
O best of Brahmins, they have two arms or four arms; their bodies are adorned with crowns and armlets, and they hold maces, or they bear the conch, the discus, and the mace.
As before, with another hand they prevent entry;
with mouths formidable with fangs, they are capable of both restraint and grace. (193)
He is the maker of security, the maker of auspiciousness, the wise one, the performer of oblations, and the creator of beings;
he is the fire at the end of the age, the devourer, as well as Saṃvarta and Bhīṣaṇa.
Saṃkrandana, Animiṣa, Śataparvan, Śatānana, Audumbara, Prākṛtika, Dvirāma, and Aṃśumālin as well. || 195 ||
This group of sixteen, beginning with Dṛḍhavrata and the others, is like that of the doorkeepers; they are distinguished by their colors and are endowed with six arms. (196)
By means of the left and right [hands], [the hands] at the back are endowed with the conch, mallet, lotus, rosary, boon-granting gesture, and fear-dispelling gesture, facing east and west. || 197 ||
Adorned with various colored garlands, turbans, garments, ointments, and ornaments, it is enriched by the valor of the previously mentioned host and is capable of performing all rites. || 198 ||
For the sake of protecting those eight splendors, Śatamanyu and Virocana are inconceivable, unassailable, and possess names that are immeasurable. || 199 ||
Amarṣin, Mahābhūta, Ke, Arka, and Rākṣasa as the eighth;
these are situated in order on the beautiful sides of the side-doors between Indra and Agni.
Standing alone, these heroes are the warders who forbid entry;
they possess the luster of blue, yellow, hibiscus, dark, black, vermilion, and the moon.
Possessing great strength and great heroism, their prowess was exceedingly difficult to overcome;
they were adorned with various kinds of garments, garlands, ornaments, and unguents.
Adorned as was fitting with other ornaments not previously mentioned,
they possess the majesty of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) and have four hands each, arranged in due order.
On their backs, to the right and left, they are endowed with a discus and a conch;
their two upper hands rest upon the top of a mace. || 204 ||
One should worship these, beginning with the lords of the beauty of the main doors and side-doors, in due order:
Vidyā, Aparavidyā, Pāvaka, and Māruta. (205)
The moon, the sun, water, and earth—these are the deities of transmigratory existence;
they abide in subtle form upon the ground of the external enclosure. 206.
Amareśa, Virūpākṣa, Sudharmiṣṭha, Niyāmaka, Sarvasattvāśraya, and thereafter Atigahana. || 207 ||
Mahārājeśvara and likewise Dhanādhyakṣeśvara—these eight lords of the Gaṇas are the chief gatekeepers there. || 208 ||
All [the deities] are to be meditated upon as four-armed; however, Amareśa and Virūpākṣa hold a thunderbolt and a cane-staff in their two principal hands. (209)
With their backs and hands blazing with discs and conchs, resembling saffron and collyrium, they had distorted faces due to their fangs. || 210 ||
By means of the union of south and north, and endowed with the exchange of their marks,
they stand on the right and left of the door, respectively as the one who permits entry and the one who forbids it.
They were most righteous and disciplined, possessing a beautiful dark-blue luster;
they held formidable staffs in their hands, yet were devoid of the thunderbolt weapon.
Holding the other [elements] as they have been described in sequence according to the rule, he is the refuge of all beings, profoundly deep, dark, and white. || 213 ||
However, these two nooses-holders are adorned with arms as before;
Mahārājeśvara is red, and Dhanādhyakṣeśvara is black. (214)
Joined with the weapons of Śiśira, they were another triad just as before—possessing great strength and great heroism, and causing fear through their wicked defects. || 215 ||
Difficult to look upon and difficult to assail, they were slayers of Daityas and Dānavas, adorned with various costly garments and ornaments and unguents. || 216 ||
It is the great bull, abundant, profound, and within the range of the vital breath;
it is a limb of yoga, the abode of yoga, eternal, and unshackled. || 217 ||
Tārakāntarita, Tāra, Virāma, Viṣama, as well as Duratikrama, Durgraha, Sudhūmra, and Anilāśana. (218)
One should place them at the side-gates of that [mandala] according to the previous method, as radiant as the colors of the aforementioned gatekeepers. (219)
This group of sixteen, however, is provided with four hands,
beginning from the secondary left hand and ending with the primary left hand.
He holds a conch shell and a cloth in his hands, is intent on the gesture of warding off, and performs the gesture of entry; he is adorned with garments and garlands of various colors.
Adorned with various ornaments and joined by various positions,
he holds a rosary and acts as the usher for those who have sought refuge.
O best of sages, one who would prohibit others should likewise place [the name of] Devavrata, Nirātaṅka, Bhīma, and Puruṣa. (223)
O best of sages, [he praised] Ugra, Vīreśvara, Ramya, Ariṣṭa,
Anirviṇṇa, Yugāntāṃśa, Śatānanda, and Śatānana.
One should place each of these— Tejodhara, Viśālākṣa, Yugāṃśa, and Devanandana—
one by one within the sixteen beauties.
Resembling the Lord of Upadvāra in complexion, though devoid of his [specific] marks, he likewise possesses four hands, positioned from right to left on the back. || 226 ||
Holding the conch, discus, and mace, with his primary right hand reaching out,
he is the restrainer of the wicked and the opener for those who are sinless.
Adorned with various garlands, garments, turbans, ornaments, ointments, and the like; possessing infinite and inconceivable majesty; they are the refuge for all living beings. || 228 ||
Skilled in various weapons and missiles, endowed with diverse forms of knowledge,
having cast down many lords of the Daityas, they are intent upon the protection of the virtuous.
In the palace provided with two doors, both [guardians] stand in subtle form at the sides of the other door, while the two principal ones are stationed at the main entrance.
One should install the fourfold forms, which consist of the nature of origin and dissolution, at every corner of the enclosure wall, beginning from the southeast corner.
Likewise, one should sequentially recollect the forms of the other manifestations and their consorts,
as well as the mantras of the weapons and the rest.
One should offer oblations at the four corners outside the temple with the name of Bhava, because no other deity is remembered as being distinct from Bhava.
Outside of them, one should place the Lord of Weapons (Hetirāj) according to the sequence of the directions with his own mantra,
illuminating [the area] by means of his own multitude of rays.
