Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should perform the worship with offerings such as water for the guest (arghya), garlands, and sandalwood paste, which have been purified by inspection and other rites, accompanied by mantras and mudrās.
The deity named Vāsudeva, whose very body is the six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya),
[assumed] a temple in a gross form for the sake of benefiting those engaged in ritual action.
Having attained that which is rich in all-knowing activity and the support of all principles, the Lord, ever abiding within the image, bestows grace.
Therefore, one should sequentially place the eight external principles—beginning with Earth and ending with Intellect (buddhi)—upon the eight walls that constitute its constituent parts. || 238 ||

The temple is conjoined with the limbs; the primordial nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas). The image situated therein is the individual soul (jīva), and the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) resides within that.
Therefore, having meditated upon these principles (tattvas) as presiding deities (adhidaivata) in their respective order,
one should then worship them as pervading everything everywhere.
Indeed, by means of the lotus of Kālacakra, which consists of the support of all, which is the locus of all principles, and which destroys the poison of all defects; || 241 ||
Having enclosed the abode together with its wall on all sides, both below and above,
one should worship it while performing the *Hnādayī* mudrā along with the *Cakra* mudrā.
Having displayed [the deity] in all directions, one should envelop it with the armor-mantra (kavaca); likewise, in the case of the rite for a single image, it is adorned with a single door. || 243 ||
In the case of a palace, this procedure should be performed once the layout of the quarters is finalized;
in a house provided with four doors, [the rite is done] in the pavilion situated at the front of each directional door.
In the Sarvatobhadra enclosure and also in the Aghanirmocana,
as well as in those called Sadadhvan and Dharmākhyā, each provided with two pairs of gates.
This specific procedure for the placement of the groups of gatekeepers is now demonstrated:
Caṇḍa and the others, ending with Subhadra, are located at the four doors of the temple. (246)
They should be deposited in sequence, as before, in pairs;
they are situated in two pairs upon the door-lintel (udumbara) above the doors, respectively.
The goddesses Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā, whose characteristics were previously described, as well as Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya, are stationed at the front corners. || 248 ||
Anirvartin, Mahāvartin, Darpahā, Sarvajit, Sthira, Jayanta, Bhayakṛt, and Mānin—these are the eight, O best of the twice-born. (249)
Stationed at the side of the door-pillar of the pavilion in the cardinal direction were Anirvartin, Mahāvartin, Kṛṣṇābha, and Śukasannibha. (250)
Darpahā and Sarvajit possess the luster of white and red gold respectively;
Sthira and Jayanta always possess a radiance like that of dark collyrium.
Bhayakṛt, Mānin, Piṅgala, and Pāṇḍurojjvala—
all of these have two arms, and with their right hands— 252.
When they are to be meditated upon as four-armed, these lords of the Gaṇas hold the conch Nandaka in one hand and possess fierce prowess. || 253 ||
With their primary right hands they hold swords and cane-staffs;
likewise, in their left hands they hold conch shells, starting from the back and proceeding toward the right.
In their two hands they bear wheels and lotuses, blazing with light;
they are endowed with various garments, garlands, turbans, ornaments, and unguents. || 255 ||
With hands and feet crossed and possessing a reversal of the marks, he is powerful and has a body of nectar; he is present in every limb and faces in all directions.
Śubhrāṅga, Varada, Vāgīśa, and Śabdavikrama—these four, being specific forms of Pāñcajanya, stand in pairs respectively. (257)
At the four gates of the Sarvatobhadra palace, as before,
those with two arms should be visualized holding [the mudrā] with their right hands.
All four hold maces in one hand and conchs in the other; they resemble the bandhūka flower in color. || 259 ||
Others, resembling cuckoos, were adorned with every ornament;
by their great strength, they had cast down the gods, asuras, and great serpents. || 260 ||
Solitary heroes and without companions, they are capable of constantly traversing as far as the realm of Brahmā with effortless ease, as if in play.

The Lord of the Universe, the Enjoyer of the Universe, the Universe itself, the Soul of the Universe, the Eye of the Universe, He whose feet are the universe, whose arms are the universe, and likewise the Performer of the actions of the universe. || 262 ||
These are to be known as the guardians at the directional gates of the second enclosure; they have two arms, arranged according to their left and right positions. (263)
Equipped with maces, swords, and missiles, and adorned with crowns and caskets,
they are red, tawny, white, dark, crimson, yellow, and black.
Resplendent with garments of every color, ointments, garlands, and ornaments, they are peerless heroes, acting without assistance, and warding off all defects. || 265 ||
On the inner sides of those two doorways, joined to the left and right,
one should sequentially install the lords of the treasures facing toward the temple.
Then there are Śaṅkhapadma, Mahāpadma, and the one named Śatadhāmā;
furthermore, he is known as Akhaṇḍita, Santata, and Anantadhāra. (267)
The first two are proclaimed as "Sarvadvāra" (All-Doors) and have been described previously;
the color, form, and other attributes of the remaining six will now be stated in order. || 268 ||
Red, black, golden-hued, white, crimson, and the color of tamāla;
they are endowed with all the characteristics described for the lords of the treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
The lords of wealth, gems, gold, the eight metals, grain, and riches, as well as the masters of all medicinal herbs and treasures, are seated comfortably upon thrones above them.
Adorned with all ornaments, they bestow upon their dependents whatever is desired;
then, at the doors of the third enclosure, they are arranged in pairs.
One should place them in sequence on the southern and northern branches;
the discus and Garuḍa in front, and the plow and palm tree on the south.

In the west are the Śārṅga bow and the Makara; in the north, the Nandaka sword and the Ṛśyaka; and for the discus, the lord of birds (Garuḍa), and the stars, there are also the Śārṅga bow and the Nandaka sword.
O twice-born one, the colors, forms, and other attributes previously described for their respective positions shall now be stated for the other three, beginning with Tāla. || 274 ||
The palm tree is the banner, representing the ego-sense of time beginning with the elements;
the fish is described as the seed of the universe, hidden within all its limbs. (275)
This entire world of suffering is like a deer, and saṃsāra is fickle by nature;
having meditated upon these in their subtle form, one should worship them in due order. || 276 ||
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Godāvarī, and likewise the great river, as well as the Vitastā, the Narmadā, the one called Jambū, and the Sarasvatī. || 277 ||
The rivers are situated in order at the directional gates of the fourth wall;
the description of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, including their colors and forms, has been stated previously.
Other than those two, there were others of equal [status], yet lacking the splendor of their complexions;
they possessed a radiance like white, reddish, dark, golden, and white kunda flowers. || 279 ||
They possessed the bold attire of the intoxicated, adorned with various ornaments;
their limbs were variegated with all kinds of minerals and resplendent with every sort of jewel.
Holding nectar-pots with two hands, they are as described before;
thus has been declared their station at the gates of the quarters and the gates of the pavilions.

In the case of single-formed [temples], the gates and other features belonging to the cardinal-directional form, as well as those situated above the enclosure walls, are declared to be common to all. || 282 ||
If both are located at the outer gateway, they should be visualized or installed on either side of the branches of the *sarvasāla* door-panels.
Those endowed with the characteristics as previously described should be established in their respective order;
having thus meditated upon and installed the lords of the enclosures, one should worship them. || 284 ||
Those who have arisen from meditation should be depicted in their own forms within their respective pavilions at the locations of the seats;
for that purpose, the courtyard area should be divided into either three or five parts.
Having set aside one-third or one-fourth [of the space] from the center toward the outside,
one should construct a pedestal or a sanctuary in all directions or in a single direction.

When the two bases, the lower and the upper, remain as previously described, platforms (pīṭhikā) constructed from stone, brick, or other materials, measuring one cubit in width, should be prepared. || 287 ||
All of them should be half that height, adorned with every ornament,
either square or perfectly circular, and they may be worshipped individually.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities of the village and other sites upon mandalas smeared with cow dung and the like, located in their respective directions.
The pedestals (pīṭhas), possessing the characteristics previously described, should be made according to their width and height;
or they may be made with half that measurement, provided it does not conflict with the chariot procession (rathayātrā).
Thus, the lords of the obstructions, stationed upon their respective pedestals in their own directions, stand facing the temple for the purpose of dispelling evil defects. || 291 ||
O bull among sages, listen now to the installation of the lords of the Gaṇas at the entrance and in the sacrificial hall of one who has entered the four stages. || 292 ||
The two deities known as Vāstu and Kṣetreśa are stationed at the eastern gate as before;
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are stationed above the gates in sequence.
The deities Vajranābha and the others are located two by two on the door-panels of the cardinal directions;
and Saṃbhava, Prabhava, and the others are in the vases at the eastern and other gates.
And the supreme group of eight elements, beginning with Kumuda, which is internal, occupies the region of Bhramaṇī by means of a pair of gates situated within. || 295 ||
O twice-born one, Suparṇa, the one named Cakra, Satya,
and Kaumodakī should be placed in order at the very base of the doors.
Satya is situated on the golden staff, but he is located in the western direction;
O twice-born one, the deities beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Subhadra are positioned in pairs in the directions starting from the east.
By means of the southern and northern [lines], they reach the base of the archway pillars;
the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) stands upon the archway, situated between the two wheels.
When the banners were white, the king of birds known as Satya appeared;
when they were crimson, it was Suparṇa; and when they were tawny, it was Garuḍa. || 299 ||
In those [images] having the color of royal stone, he is established under the name Tārkṣya;
in one with banners of various colors, the Lord of Birds (Vihageśvara) is to be worshipped. || 300 ||
Indra and the other guardians of the world, preceded by hosts of Siddhas,
and their weapons such as the thunderbolt, stood outside in their respective directions.

One should act in this manner according to the primary ritual or during other specific occasions; or else, according to the secondary ritual, one should worship Caṇḍa and the others, preceded by the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) and so forth.
Having placed [the deities] exclusively at the doors, one should worship up to Garuḍa;
or, the Lord who has birds as his vehicle should be worshipped along with his weapons at all the doors.
In various types of installations, as well as in the rite of restoring dilapidated temples, in all great festivals, and in the act of hoisting the banner; || 304 ||
In the planting of the auspicious sprout, in the rites of purification and so forth, and likewise in the ritual of consecration with the infinite jars and other implements; || 305 ||
O twice-born one, [this applies] constantly to expiations that are occasional, such as the ordeal by scales and others;
to the primary rites for pacification and the like; and to other rites performed for specific desires.
One should perform [the rite] according to the procedure prescribed for the primary kalpa, and otherwise in other cases;
likewise, the hosts of Siddhas, Indra and the others, and their weapons, [should be worshipped] in due order.
These guardians of the world-quarters, surrounded by their own armies,
always occupy their respective stations according to the well-known eastern arrangement.
O Great-minded One, because they act as guardians of the directions, the stability of those infinite mantra-forms of the Blessed One remains firm from the beginning of creation until the end of time.
Established in their own places, they pay homage, worship, and recite [the mantra];
they also attend upon them perfectly with offerings such as banners and other ritual services. || 310 ||
For the sake of attaining liberation, they eternally protect [the world] together with their many followers, and they bestow strength and vigor upon their devotees.
They incessantly destroy the flood of obstacles for those who perform sacrifices with mantras,
and they protect the twofold increasing fruit of the mantra.

The power-seed (*śaktibīja*) of the Lord of the Universe, which possesses an authority that is without beginning, assumes a tenfold nature for the sake of establishing the directions; its unmanifest state consists of the eight directions.
The deities of existence, such as Kāla and others, reside on the three outer *trisāla* grounds;
because they are the means of accomplishing that [state], they are always fixed in the previously mentioned directions and divisions.
The deities Vajranābha and others are the guardians of the world-quarters and the gates;
likewise are Amareśa and the others, beginning with Saṃbhava and Prabhava. || 315 ||

Stationed in the directions and gates according to the well-known traditional sequence, there is the group of eight beginning with Kāla and ending with Yama, followed by the group beginning with Indra and ending with Rudra. || 316 ||
The Controller (Niyantr) is at the end of the principle of Time (Kālatattva), and beyond that is the well-established Space (Viyat);
one should place them in order in the northeast and southeast corners, and the southwest and northwest.
Indeed, having placed the two—knowledge and ignorance—within the fire and wind situated in their own places, and having assigned the moon and the sun to their positions in the north and south; 318.
One should place the water located in the western part upon the earth in the eastern part;
likewise [one should place] Kumuda and the other guardians of the enclosures, as well as Lohitākṣa and the others.
Excluding Vajranābha and the others, there are twenty-four door-keepers;
furthermore, there are other groups of door-keepers as well as groups located at the corners of the hall.
In the prescribed order,
the lords of the Gaṇas, beginning with Kumuda, reside in cities, villages, and other habitations, facing the direction of the Blessed One.
And in the temple of Pālikā, remaining according to the directions spoken by the Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas),
one should thus perform the offering of bali to the deities at the three junctions of the day.

One should not offer an oblation to those deities mentioned by the Sāla tree who reside in the door-enclosures of houses where a Sāla tree has been intentionally planted, nor to those mentioned by a Sāla tree that was not so intended.
Having installed them according to the prescribed rite at the time of each respective consecration,
one should perform the offering of oblations together with the procession of the deities.
Having thus prepared everything, including the ground above the great seat (mahāpīṭha),
and having ascended it after it has been washed, one should face either the east or the north.

Then, having summoned the attendants known as the planets— the lotuses, etc., in the directions above that, and the Kumuda and others within— along with all living beings, [he should perform the ritual].
Having honored that [deity] with water, one should scatter the remainder of the bali offering;
thereafter, having sipped water according to the rules and bathed, one may enter the house.
For the worship of those who are lords of all the gates and dwellers in the groves (oṇa), the mantra is said to be their own name joined with the prostration (namaḥ) and the praṇava (oṃ). || 328 ||

One should apply the word "Viṣṇu" at the end of the name "Tārā," according to the prescribed sequence, for the attendants who are spirits residing in the great seats (mahāpīṭha) and whose nature is that of householders.
The mantras located in all the corners are declared to end with *phaṭ*;
all the mantras combined in the rite of fire-offering (*homakarman*) end with *svāhā*.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with those mantras and services such as the water-offering (arghya) and so forth,
one should display the mudrā known as the "threatening finger" (tarjanī) to the lords of the enclosures (āvṛti).
The group of door-keepers, beginning with Caṇḍa, has been described immediately following;
they are situated above the enclosure of Dharma and the others for whatever reason. || 332 ||
If the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) is impossible for those residing there,
one should perform it by doubling the offerings in the directions starting from the northeast of the Sarvatobhadra mandala, in due order.
In the primary ritual as well as elsewhere, according to one's capacity, on the ground of the enclosure,
one should satisfy the deities of the outer enclosures by repeatedly performing the offering.

One should assign [the offerings] for the guardians of the main gate and the side gates at that gate, and for those mentioned in the context of the Great Seat (mahāpīṭha) within the mandala situated at the front of that gate. || 335 ||
However, there is no fault in transitioning between those who have arisen from meditative absorption; for what reason?
Because [the practice] proceeds according to the stated sequence at the respective locations of the doors of the obstructions. || 336 ||
Furthermore, the movement of those residing in the form of substances would bring about undesirable results;
thus, one should offer the bali-oblation to the deities of the veil at the three junctions of the day.
One should perform that [rite] in the presence of the image intended for the perpetual festival, accompanied by dance, song, and the like, and joined with the resonance of the Vedas. || 338 ||
But when an image intended for constant festivals falls to the ground during its procession,
one should perform an excellent consecration bath and carry out a rite of propitiatory oblation.
Having placed that image upon a vehicle, one should perform a perpetual festival;
the practitioner, even if his mind is weary, should observe the vow for twelve days. || 340 ||
If [the site] is defiled by a schism or other such faults, one should recite one's own mantra ten thousand times;
having then properly restored it according to the rules and performed the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa), [one may proceed]. || 341 ||
Having performed the festival and concluded the remainder of the rite, the practitioner, with a weary mind,
then began a fast and remained steadfast in the vow of celibacy.
Then one should recite four hundred thousand repetitions of one's own mantra;
for that, [the duration may be] three nights, six days, twelve days, or two fortnights. || 343 ||

Having diligently observed the vow, O best of the twice-born, one should practice the giving of gifts to worthy recipients according to one's capacity, such as cows, land, gold, and other such things. (344)

If, by chance, a breakage occurs in the large [image], then, using the interior of the [new] image, one should perform the bathing rites and so forth, as well as the offerings of oblations (bali) consisting solely of [the prescribed substances]. || 345 ||

Having completed the remainder of the ritual action and performed the dismissal of the mantra, one should undertake the observance of the vow according to the procedure for the restoration of the dilapidated [temple]. || 346 ||
One should perform forty thousand recitations over four nights and so forth, until absorption into the image is achieved; thereafter, one should again perform penances such as the *kṛcchra*.
O twice-born one, having performed the vow before the day of commencing the image, and then on the eleventh day, [one should perform it] before the deity on the very day of commencing the image.
Having honored twelve preceptors with equal value for each individually,
he should give them twelve gifts, such as cows, land, or sesame seeds.
In the presence of these [deities], one should again begin the preparation of the image;
or else, having prepared the image, one should perform the sequence beginning with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā). || 350 ||
Furthermore, one should perform the gift of cows, land, gold, and so forth;
and if public reproach has arisen, one should again observe a vow. || 351 ||
One should practice as long as public scandal remains quiet, and one should observe the vow until the time when the mind has attained clarity. 352.
O Brahmin, when a fracture or similar damage occurs to other images as well, the procedure for expiation is exactly the same. || 353 ||
Thus has the expiation for a Śūdra who is a worshipper been declared;
for a Vaiśya, however, it is double this, while for a Kṣatriya, it is triple.
A fourfold penance is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the event of breaking or other damage to images installed by human beings. (355)
When such [a defect] has arisen, this expiation is prescribed for the practitioner alone;
however, in the case of an image of the Lord made by a seer (ārṣa), that same [expiation] shall be doubled. || 356 ||
When the image has been consecrated by the gods, that [merit] becomes threefold;
when the image has been consecrated by a Siddha, this shall be fourfold. || 357 ||
O twice-born one, when a division or similar defect occurs in self-manifested images,
the expiation shall indeed be fivefold as previously described.
The image of the all-pervading Lord may be of two kinds: self-manifested in the form of *sālagrāma* stones, or otherwise made from stone and other materials. (359)
The expiation prescribed for both cases is the same;
however, O twice-born one, there is this specific distinction regarding self-manifested [liṅgas] and others. 360.
While the worship is in progress, one should perform acts such as meditative concentration;
all rites such as expiation should be performed with particular care. || 361 ||
However, for all images—whether self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) and so forth—even without being consecrated by a mortal, whichever one among them has been obtained [is suitable]. || 362 ||
O Brahmin, at the time of acceptance, [one should accept] even that which is devoid of auspicious marks and the like, or that which is broken or cracked, exactly as it stands. || 363 ||
Having accepted [the deity], one should worship it constantly; no fault exists for him.
[This is] the determination of those various forms in the image of the Śālagrāma stone. (364)
Having correctly ascertained [the defects] by means of the respective established signs, one should perform the proper worship;
afterwards, when an auspicious [result] has occurred, one should perform the expiation.
The practitioner, with a mind rendered lean through effort, should diligently apply what was previously taught,
even when distinctions such as those caused by thieves, spirits, enemies, fire, and so forth have arisen.
Even if the images are carried away by cats or other creatures, or if damage such as breaking occurs, the practitioner should perform the previously mentioned rite.
Starting from that day, one must diligently perform penance;
for even the sinful karma previously accumulated has its cause therein. (368)
Therefore, for the sake of its pacification, or indeed for the pacification of the censure [incurred], one must diligently perform the expiation prescribed previously. (369)
Otherwise, O twice-born one, he would become a sinner on account of this transgression;
therefore, even when such an act has been committed through negligence, one should perform the expiation.
For a division intentionally committed, there is no atonement through penances;
that most wicked and extremely foolish person must certainly be punished. || 371 ||
Whether the breach was caused by one's own negligence or even by another being, if the practitioner, overcome by remorse, does not perform what has been prescribed, [he must perform the rite]. (372)
Likewise, he too must first be punished and then undergo penance;
otherwise, being unfit, he would become something else.
Even while concealing that fault and its various distinctions,
both punishment and penance must be prescribed.
When such divisions and the like have arisen, there will be fear for the king and the kingdom;
to pacify that, one should perform sacrifice at the Kumbhasthala and other sites for seven days.
Alternatively, for one week or three weeks, the penance prescribed for the fault of schism and so forth applies when the image is installed and consecrated. || 376 ||
But in the case of an unmanifest [image], O twice-born one, one should perform a fourth part of what was prescribed;
however, if an image previously stolen is recovered again, [the penance is as follows].
One should diligently perform the remedial rites as prescribed for the sake of the goal;
now hear specifically regarding the defects that arise when a wound occurs on the images. || 378 ||
A wound located in the circle of the sense organs (indriyacakra) brings misfortune to the performer;
one situated within the mantra from the neck down to the navel-lotus causes the death of a son.
On both sides of the wife's back, situated from the navel down to the genitals, there is a location which, when occupied, brings about the destruction of one's brother. || 380 ||
O twice-born one, a wound on the young children of the sons causes their destruction; likewise, a wound from the navel down to the anus brings ruin to the sisters. (381)
Wherever there may be a wound from the root of the thigh to the knee, there will always be a loss of wealth, grain, and cattle. || 382 ||
From the knees down to the soles of the feet, he bestowed his blessing upon the circle of servants,
both out of compassion for them all and for his own satisfaction.
O Lotus-born One, the agent should restore what has been wounded to a state of being unwounded; however, listen to me regarding the remedy prescribed for minor wounds. (384)
One should apply the melted [metal] of the variegated image with white, red, and other purifying pigments, which have been perfumed with fragrances and consecrated with the weapon-mantra.
For images made of clay, however, [the restoration] should be performed with clay mixed with honey, clarified butter, and milk,
combined with silk cloth and sprinkled with gold water.
O Brahmin, one should effect the joining of that which is made of wood; listen:
in the case of a split or a break, one should join it with two [pieces of] wood using a tool and an implement. || 387 ||
When a wound had been inflicted upon those born of stone, the rubbing against a whetstone was performed with a jeweled probe set in gold.
However, in the case of large stones fashioned by humans, abandonment is prescribed in every way when there is a great injury; but in the case of self-manifested images and the like, it is not so.
In the case of stone images that are split or broken, one should join them together with gold-encrusted bands so that they become more firmly secured. || 390 ||
Alternatively, one should properly join those [limbs] with golden ones;
likewise for those made of wood or metal, and even for those that are self-manifested (svayamvyakta) and so forth. 391.
In the case of a fissure or a breakage, the meditative absorption (samādhi) should be restored by itself, like a reflection on a polished stone;
even in the case of one born from a jewel, one should practice meditative absorption in exactly this same way.
An image of Śālagrāma stone that is split, broken, or extensively damaged, as well as one with minor damage, should be made very firm by binding it with golden bands. || 393 ||
One should bind [the mantra] into an image made of metal; listen now regarding its installation in a mortal [image].
Indeed, for a purely golden one, one should cast it into the field according to availability. (394)

O Mahāmati, the powder made of gold and jewels, consecrated with the twelve-syllable mantra, must otherwise be applied when the image has risen [from its base], for only then will the wound be properly healed.
One should fill it with its own metal mixed with a small amount of gold;
one should perform this same procedure for the primary rite even in the case of a self-manifested (svayamvyakta) image and others.
O twice-born one, for the sake of beauty, regarding the images of other forms that are installed in palaces, pavilions, or gate-towers (gopura) and so forth; || 397 ||
Whenever any division or other alteration occurs among the arrays and manifestations of the omnipresent Lord, one should restore them exactly as they were.
The practitioner should perform the installation and other rites according to the proximity of each respective deity;
having carefully considered the required expiation, he should then carry it out. (399)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Meditation on the Deities of the Doors and Enclosures, the Atonement for the Falling or Breaking of Offerings and Images and for Deficiencies in the Limbs, and the Repair of Wooden and Other Images," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Pārameśvarasaṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ.
The Twelfth Chapter: Sanaka said,
"When there is a sudden cessation of one's constant virtuous activity,"
Likewise for one who is devoted to yoga through bathing and other practices, and for one who performs occasional rites. || 1 ||
O Great-minded One, [this applies] to those devoted to the various festivals of the year,
as well as to those who practice the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such virtuous observances.
[He described] truly the [wives] of those established in the four stages of life and of the [four] castes,
as well as those of superior, middling, wealthy, and even inferior means.
For devotees who practice faith and self-restraint toward the Lotus-eyed One, and whose minds are intent upon His worship for as long as life lasts, [there is no rebirth]. || 4 ||
O bull among sages, I now wish to hear the means of protection for those who are devoted to that mantra, exactly as it is.

O one of great intelligence, having extracted the essence from everywhere, I, Śāṇḍilya, shall properly declare that by which, when performed, devotees attain the state of having fulfilled all their duties.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, with a mind full of vigilance,
he for whom even enjoyments are impossible without the realization that they are illusory.

For one who, lacking the necessary capacity, undergoes the falling away from the *kṛcchra* and other penances due to the affliction of diseases such as fever, and for whom there has arisen a deficiency in the daily observance; || 8 ||
O Great Sage, hear what is ordained as beneficial for each person who has not attained the Cāturmāsya without its independent practice.
For the enjoyment of tactile pleasures, there is indeed a measure of wealth;
and for those things that reach the heart, there is food drenched with sacrificial oblation.
He is the seed of various secondary enjoyments and the fulfiller of vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. || 11 ||
The observance of the four-month period is joined with special worship;
it is beautiful, auspicious, like a pearl necklace, and variegated with the sacred thread.
It brings peace to devotees at all times, fulfilling every desire, just as the horse-sacrifice fulfills the desires of the Brahmins through its daily performance. || 13 ||
The Rājasūya sacrifice is the ornament of kings and likewise of devotees,
just as the Kaustubha gem is the most excellent ornament among all ornaments.
In the same way, that which is to be known as the *pavitraka* (purifier) exists within the web of enjoyments;
it fulfills for the devotees the activity pertaining to the Supreme Lord. || 15 ||
Since he eternally bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, who indeed is superior to him?
Through constant devotion, he truly grants the state of being in the same world (sālokya) to his devotees.
It bestows proximity (sāmīpya) endowed with various supernatural powers (siddhi) upon practitioners,
and it grants union (sāyujya) within the self of one's own mantra to the foremost of practitioners.
O Brahmin, once that northern solstice has passed, one should perform [the rite] during the middle of the Cāturmāsya on an auspicious day, free from all defects.
Time is also declared to be threefold, characterized by the four-month period from the fifteenth day of Āṣāḍha until that of Kārtika.
That period, ending with the lunar month, lasts for as many days as there are in a full moon;
it begins from the transit [of the sun] into Cancer and continues until the end of the sun's passage through Libra.
The time consisting of eight fortnights is called the solar *madhyama*;
it is characterized by the four-month period beginning from the eleventh day [of the lunar month]. || 21 ||
Know that time to be indeed Vaiṣṇava, the most excellent, which bestows all perfections;
until the attainment of this time, however, there may be some obstacle.
Indeed, another period must be spent in fulfillment through the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances;
and in the interim, the completion of the sacrifice must be accomplished according to the prescribed rules.
When the rainy season has set in, [this] must be performed by those dwelling within the belly of the three worlds—
humans, gods, and Siddhas— who stand at the forefront of their duties.
For indeed, with faith, they engage for a year in this great and highly intelligent undertaking pertaining to the Supreme Lord.
At that time, when the Lord was reclining upon His bed, the sky was filled with flowers and fruits and hung with clouds accompanied by cranes.
The surface of the earth was adorned with white, blue, and red lotuses, and the forests, groves, and gardens were verdant with grassy meadows and the like. || 27 ||
In a place endowed with rice crops and the like, beautified by the waters of ponds,
the Pavitraka rite performed for the infinite Viṣṇu bestows supreme satisfaction.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should perform that with effort during the middle of the Cāturmāsya, specifically on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
O twice-born one, one should perform it at the beginning and at the end, on all the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs), on all the solar transits (saṅkrāntis), or on the full moon days (paurṇamāsīs).
On all new moon days, as well as on the third lunar days,
and on the eighth day in the month of Nabhasya when it coincides with the Rohiṇī asterism, O high-minded one.
The first, the second, the fifth, the thirteenth,
the tenth, and the eleventh— on these days as well, one may act according to one's preference.
In the dark fortnight they are inauspicious, but especially so in the bright fortnight;
the Moon, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury—these should be known as bestowers of auspiciousness.
Now hear from me the lunar mansions for the Pavitrārohaṇa and other rites:
in the three Uttarās, in Revatī, Aśvinī, and the Bharaṇīs. || 34 ||
Likewise, under Punarvasu, Hasta, Rohiṇī, and Śravaṇa,
as well as under the asterisms sacred to Viṣṇu and at all auspicious moments.
On the twelfth day of rising during the four-month period,
which is the divine Ṣaḍaśītimukha, whoever should place [the image] upon it— || 36 ||
That sacred thread of the source of the universe purifies his own lineage—past, present, and future. (37)
There, the lotus-eyed Hari, the Supreme Self and the infallible Lord, is personally present for his devotees through various manifested forms. (38)
O Great Buddha, although it is thus, Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is mantra, indeed remains eternally present and personally manifest for his devotees. (39)
Nevertheless, because of the power of the desire for that [result] in that action, the Lord, the King of Mantras, assumes proximity through the ministering mantra. (40)
Just as the sun, having reached the summer season, attains its intense heat without abandoning its own nature, so too does it become closer in proximity to the Lord. || 41 ||

Indeed, for the sake of the persistence of the worthy recipient, the place, and the time from their creation onwards, the sacred thread (pavitraka) is used; for it is impossible [to perform the rite] otherwise.
The rite should be performed with devotion by those intent on action, so that it may become complete;
one should avoid the Pavitrārohaṇa of Viṣṇu for others as well.
O twice-born one, for that purpose, one should construct a pavilion in front of the temple,
either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure.
Whether in the third enclosure, or the fourth, or even the fifth;
if it is not found at the foremost [point], it should be located elsewhere according to one's desire in the appropriate direction.
It may be square or even rectangular, extending from east to west or from north to south, according to the builder's desire.
Likewise, the pavilion should be twenty-two cubits in measurement, facing either east or toward whichever direction is desired; such would be the most excellent.
O twice-born one, the middle pavilion should measure eighteen cubits,
while the inferior one should be twelve cubits in measurement.
Beginning from five cubits and increasing by two cubits each time, up to a limit of twenty-one cubits,
there shall be nine types according to these measurements.
Alternatively, one should know that the best [measure] is ten cubits, the middling is eight cubits,
the inferior is six cubits, and the small is three cubits in length.
Or it may extend up to thirty cubits, or twenty-five from six cubits;
for when these are being constructed, they should be made according to one's wealth.
The base may be provided with a pedestal (upapīṭha) or be a simple plinth (masūraka);
above the plinth are the pillar and the entablature (prastara), which constitute the threefold division.
It is endowed with the pigeon-like mode (kapotavṛti), or else it is devoid of the aforementioned shapes;
it is surrounded by one, three, five, seven, or more varieties of walls. || 53 ||
It may be endowed with the ornaments mentioned for each specific part, or it may be devoid of them;
it may be constructed of stone, brick, wood, or even earth.
It may have one door, four doors, or be provided with two doors;
it may be joined with walls, or unjoined, or even provided with corner walls. || 55 ||

Or, for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the rite, one may construct a beautiful structure made of reeds and wood, consisting merely of a water-shed (prapā) and devoid of the characteristics previously mentioned. || 56 ||
One should construct a wall provided with windows, adorned with doors, and covered on top with a canopy. || 57 ||

O twice-born one, having thus constructed the pavilion according to the rules of the architectural treatises (śilpaśāstra), with the dimensions of the site contracted or expanded in accordance with the builder's desire; 58.
O Brahmin, for the sake of the sacrifice, one should then prepare a very beautiful altar within that [enclosure];
it should be firm, level, of that same shape, and slightly sloping toward the northeast. (59)
And one should especially choose ground that is highly elevated and resembles a mirror,
so that it does not become level with the pavilion of the earth.

The courtyard for the sacrificial grounds of the minor rites consists of eight units, increasing by one unit for each successive category of small-scale sacrifices, up to a height of two finger-breadths per finger.
The elevation of the ground surfaces, which are measured by their own intermediate dimensions, ranges from nine finger-breadths up to fifteen finger-breadths.
For those of superior stature, the height [of the image] should be made starting from sixteen finger-breadths up to twenty-four finger-breadths, according to the previously mentioned increments. 63.
And this height has been described by you for the various grounds;
however, in terms of width in all directions, it should indeed be one quarter, one half, or one cubit.
First, one should construct the bases with bricks and other materials;
then, having filled the middle of that space with earth mixed with a small amount of sand.

Having examined it for hair, insects, and the like, and having struck it [with a pestle], immediately thereafter, until it possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, or especially so. || 66 ||
Having examined for seven days a delightful site that is elevated in its center, she should not grant it until it becomes fit for sacrifice according to the prescribed division. || 67 ||
Above that, one should construct an altar provided with many steps, and equipped with archways according to one's means and desire. || 68 ||
With purifying sacrificial wood— firm, straight,
and even— he constructed archways at the four directions, endowed with the proper characteristics.
O Brahmin, one should place three [deities] outside the doors or inside them;
alternatively, one may properly install three in each of the cardinal directions.
Having determined the extent of the pavilion to be either five or seven [units],
one should decorate these with gold, jewels, and other materials, provided that one has the means.
Or else, O twice-born one, the four archways (toraṇas), starting from the east and ending in the north, should be made from the wood of the śrīvṛkṣa, udumbara, vaṭa, and plakṣa trees.
There should be four archways (toraṇas) in the four directions, or indeed only one for each; the height of these archways is considered to be equal to the length of their pillars.
The width [of the structure] should be measured by the distance between the two pillars,
or indeed always by a measurement slightly exceeding the height of the pillar's capital.
O best of those who know the Vedas, one should place those two staffs on the ground; their position must always remain within the pillars for those whose nature is vision.
O Brahmin, the measurement of the height of the gateways from their base to their pinnacles was exactly as they stood externally. (76)
It is equal or double in length, situated upon the shafts,
positioned between two wheels, and adorned with a circle of feathers.
At every archway, one should place Garuḍa standing upright,
as well as the incarnations beginning with the Fish (Matsya) and many other manifestations.
One should draw [the mandala] in the four directions according to the procedure described by Citra, together with hosts of sages, perfected beings, and gods who behold many wonders. (79)

With many islands, mountains, forests, and gardens; with numerous leaders of deer herds; and with lakes filled with cranes and white lotuses, [the place was] inhabited by those intent on water-sports.
By sky-faring beings joined with their consorts, by kings, by Vidyādharas and others, and by Brahmins whose minds were tranquil and who were devoted to meditation on the Self. || 81 ||
By means of these and other endless activities arising from various sources,
that entire sacrificial hall should be diligently made delightful.
One should smear it with lime or, immediately thereafter, decorate it with mirrors, chowries, cloths, and various brilliant silk garments. || 83 ||
With bells, crescent moons and other ornaments, and charming parasols;
with uplifted plantain trees, betel-nut palms, and sacred, sturdy branches of trees.
With bronze vessels filled with honey, clarified butter, curd, and excellent milk, along with bowls of śāli rice, gold, and auspicious fruits. (85)

With parched grains, white mustard seeds, and vessels of seeds endowed with the six flavors, as well as with excellent fragrant substances such as cinnamon and cardamom, and with betel leaves and areca nuts; || 86 ||
With madhūka, badara, and drākṣā; with sugarcane and the fruits of the triphalā;
and with many seasonal flowers from various groves.
With various such multitudes of purifying enjoyments, and with a sacred canopy that is very white and radiant; || 88 ||
One should then decorate the top of that with the marks of a wheel and a lotus;
afterwards, one should wrap each of the pillars individually with various silk cloths.
One should attach banners there, arising from the distinctions of colors such as white and so forth, starting from the northeastern direction and extending to the wind-god's corner (the northwest).
Thus, by means of the division according to passion (rāga), and again from the western portion as far as the limit of the southern direction, there is a second set of four.
A single lotus of all colors should be placed upon the canopy at the navel;
furthermore, it should be placed outside the altar in the eight directions of the pavilion.
Starting from the southeast corner up to the northeast corner,
one should make four [sections] colored white, reddish, yellow, and black.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, from the northern quarter as far as the western direction,
a similar set of four banners is likewise proclaimed.

One should fashion three Vaijayantī banners on the arch situated in the eastern direction; they should have the luster of the color of royal stone (sapphire) and be approached by the lord of birds (Garuḍa) bearing the discus.
One should place three banners on the archway: one with the luster of crystal in the south, one with the brilliance of vermilion in the west, and one with the radiance of gold in the north.
Each archway (toraṇa) there should be provided with four banners of white and other colors; there may be one, three, or five of them.
O twice-born one, having thus constructed a new pavilion for the purpose of sacrifice, the length of the banners shall be half the height of the archway. 98.
Then one should decorate the pavilion that was previously prepared for the special assembly of rites beginning with the ceremonial bathing and ending with the festival. 99.
When this has been done, thereafter one should successively smear the altar, together with its archways, with sandalwood and other fragrant substances, radiant with color.
Having anointed the altar entirely with pure sandalwood paste,
he likewise anointed the first archway with that very same paste prepared from Bāhlīka.
One should make the southern direction smeared with musk;
then, one should have the western direction made white with frost and powder.
Having anointed with pure saffron while standing in the north,
[he should offer] a mound made of milk, sandalwood, and saffron.
With water mixed with powdered turmeric and *harīvera*,
and with sacred, fragrant medicinal herbs, [he should sprinkle] the doors and the area of the pavilion.
Then, O twice-born one, he should fumigate it with many various incenses;
thereafter, he should enclose it on all sides outside with a curtain.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the north of the pavilion beforehand;
or else, O twice-born one, it may be elsewhere, provided it is situated at the front of the sacrifice and avoids the forbidden directions.
In the three directions desired [for the ritual], one should construct a fire-pavilion (anala-maṇḍapa) provided with exits for smoke and adorned with various sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). || 107 ||
It should be well-furnished with moist, beautiful leaves and arches (toraṇas) and so forth;
or else, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics in the cooking house.
Or if it were something previously prepared for some other incidental purpose;
having done so, O twice-born one, he should then proceed to gather the necessary materials.
On either the seventh or the fifth day prior to the day of the ritual,
having first performed the planting of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should then commence the rite.
Then, O tiger among the twice-born, on the tenth day, one should cause all the ritual materials that are required to be brought into that sacrificial pavilion.
Thereafter, one should perform the decoration and so forth; listen attentively to how that is done.
Their form is indeed twofold, distinguished by the categories of subtle and gross. (112)
With his entire being, he always protects his devotees in all their auspicious activities arising from mind, speech, and heart. (113)
Therefore, its essential nature as it truly is must be fully understood, as well as the fruit that comes to devotees through the completion of that [practice]. 114.
That which is the unbroken, white expanse of the infinite flow of the source of the world,
itself undergoes division through its own manifold nature by those who are ignorant.
Know that the "world-thread" (jagatsūtra) is indeed like a golden thread and so forth;
it bears the majesty of the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya) by means of its nature as a protective amulet (pratisara). || 116 ||
But when it is colored by the passion for knowledge, it is joined with the effects born of vigor;
enveloped by the fiery mantras, it is completely subdued by power.
Sovereignty is [the power] in ritual service, while it is imperishable through its capacity for prosperity;
thus has the sacred thread (pavitraka) of the Lord of the World been fully understood. 118.
When Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord of the Brahman, is thus established in the form [of the image],
that which is given according to rule with devotion bestows the state of the Blessed One.
Understand how that gross, distinct [entity] is to be conceptualized by means of those categories of objects established within the sphere of conventional usage. (120)
The thread should be fine, firm, white, and of excellent quality; it should be prepared by a girl born of a Brahmin lineage, or by a disciplined elderly woman.
Or it may be prepared by a pure widow;
it should be made of linen or silk, and be free from hair, down, and the like. || 122 ||
Having taken whatever has been obtained and having thoroughly washed it with water,
one should first perform its purification by means of this burning as well.

O twice-born one, having looked [at the disciple] and recalled the root mantra, one should perform it fourfold; or, when there is a requirement for the fourfold nature, one should perform it eightfold.
But by means of the cognition of its origin and dissolution, it is characterized as differentiated by distinctions,
existing in three or four qualities through its presiding presence in Keśava and the others.
One should avoid using uneven threads for the sacred thread (pavitraka) of Viṣṇu, who is himself even;
for that rite of the pavitraka is uneven for no one. 126.
O best of sages, sacred threads (pavitrakas) should be made from those well-spun fibers for all the mantras, beginning with the root mantra.

O twice-born one, one should first fashion the ornaments for the mantra-form residing in the pitcher with threads that are one and a half times the length of the *śama* units in width and arranged in the form of garlands.
One should perform the first [rite] with one hundred and eight [recitations], the second with double that, and the third with triple; in this manner, one should carry it out according to Vyāsa.
The first [section] consists of thirty-six knots; the second is remembered as being double that;
one should make the third triple that, O Mahāmati, in this very manner.
And for the Lord situated in the mandala, as well as for Him who has entered the fire and for Him who resides in the image—understand the distinction regarding these sacred objects. || 131 ||
And he should place a garland upon his head with knots as desired, and a second one hanging from his shoulders down to his kneecaps. || 132 ||
Extending from the head down to the feet, it is three times as wide;
from the head down to the pedestal, it is the sacred forest-garland (vanamālā). || 133 ||
One should indeed fashion a beautiful separate pedestal according to its own proportions;
for the images and the sacred threads (pratisara), however, no fixed rule regarding their size is prescribed.
O best of sages, if possible, the previously mentioned measurement for the forest-garland ornament should be doubled or even tripled. 135.
One should construct it endowed with one thousand and eight sūtras, or half of that, or a quarter, according to one's financial means. || 136 ||
O twice-born one, when the primary image is situated on a plastered wall or a cloth painting,
one should perform the fivefold rite of adorning the festive image.
At that time as well, one should arrange the ornaments of the primary image as before,
but on the cloths covering the images, they should be the very first ones.
In the state of manifestation, one should contemplate the Lord of the Gods of gods, endowed with five necklaces, possessing threads of various forms, and adorned with pearl necklaces. || 139 ||
For all [the threads], knots should be made at equal intervals of three finger-breadths;
without counting them, they should be properly fashioned like citron fruits and be auspicious. (140)
The forest garland, joined with one hundred and eight knots,
serves as an invitation for the All-pervading Lord who has descended into the four stations.

The purificatory rite (pavitra) is like the primordial one; it may be performed once for each [deity] or twice for each, for all the ritual images as well as for the gate-towers (gopura) and so forth. || 142 ||
For those who constantly worship the established forms of the mantras, which remain in their presence,
one should indeed perform all the rites, beginning with the highest, in the primary ritual procedure.
One should fashion a substitute similar to that, whether by means of a medium or a superior one;
or indeed, two by two, or even one by one, in the case of a secondary option.
O twice-born one, [he described] the limbs and the secondary limbs, as well as the marks,
the ornaments, and likewise the powers of the Lord of Birds.
O twice-born one, as before, one should demarcate three, or two, or two each, or even one each,
according to one's desire, by means of threads produced from whatever number is intended.
When there is the wealth of other deities who are members of the mandala, [one should provide] a collection of ornaments with deep [qualities] accompanied by the rotation of the sutras. 147.
One should prepare the collection of purifiers (pavitrakas) with threads knotted as desired,
and likewise for the retinue of Viṣvaksena and the others.
There are indeed two for the mantra and the weapon-vessel, one for the mandala, two for the sacrificial pit and the fire, and two for the seat of the scripture. || 149 ||
Of the Lord who is the essence of speech and the reality of sound, and of the great-souled ones who possess the limbs of ritual action beginning with the bell and the rosary; || 150 ||

For the deities of the sacrificial pedestal and so forth who reside in other lands, and for the four beginning with the Guru who utter the repeated cry of "Hari," [one should perform the rite]. || 151 ||
For the best of the twice-born and the other castes who constantly meditate upon Acyuta—
whether they be householders, students, ascetics, or forest-dwellers— (152)
Of the elders, such as Janaka and others, who knew the true nature of the Blessed One;
of their kinsmen, led by his brothers, whose souls were devoted to Nārāyaṇa. || 153 ||
[He spoke] to his wife, who was bowed with devotion and intent on the worship of Hari,
as well as to his kinsmen, friends, and those who serve the abode of the Blessed Lord.
And [he saw] his followers who were devoted to him, who desired the fourfold selfhood, who were servants well-disposed toward him, and who performed sacrifices to Puruṣottama. || 155 ||
For the sake of increase, for fitness alone, and for purification,
[one should perform it] with threads and knots of the desired measurements.
Or else, O best of sages, one should prepare a collection of purifiers for the four types of ascetics, beginning with the preceptor, as well as for householders. || 157 ||
Successively by twenty-four sūtras, then by sixteen, then by twelve, and likewise by eight and three. || 158 ||
The purificatory threads (pavitrakas) should be prepared with knots according to the number of the [mantra] threads;
and for the worshipper and the preceptor, one should make two ornaments each. || 159 ||
This has been declared as the gross method; now hear the subtle method.
First, the ornament for the image is prescribed according to the measurement of the head. (160)
Having fashioned it very beautifully with four hundred and thirty-two well-proportioned thread-turns (sūtrāvarta), || 161 ||
Having tied a collection of knots in this [thread] measuring twenty-seven units,
one should fashion the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*) extending from the navel upwards to the extent of the [upper] body.
And having composed a second [work] of the Sūtras, O Best of Sages, consisting of three hundred and twenty-four [verses]. (163)
It is recorded that it should be surrounded by double the number of knots within its interior, beginning from the region of the shoulder and extending as far as the two feet. (164)
O best of the twice-born, one should fashion it with eye-threads reduced by one-third, along with clusters of threads and triple-stranded knots; thereafter, [one should fashion] another. 165.
With one hundred and eight threads and likewise with knots, [he should mark] from the head and the initial descent down to the Vaiṣṇava pedestal. || 166 ||
Then, by means of threads, clusters of knots, and various internal compartments,
one should fashion another fourfold [mandala] according to the measurement of the mandala.
The first [measurement] should be by the span; the second is by the span with the thumb extended;
the third should be equal to the cubit; and the fourth is equal to the rim [of a wheel]. || 168 ||
O best of the twice-born, there are eighty-one coils of threads,
and the knots are likewise equal in number to the measurement of the fire-pit.
O Mahāmati, one should fashion the three ornaments as appropriate,
using threads numbering one hundred and eight, or half of that, along with their knots.

O best of the twice-born, one should provide ornaments that are perfectly even and very beautiful for the foremost of the twice-born; for the other Brahmins, half of that [should be provided]. || 171 ||
This is remembered as the primary ritual procedure (kalpa); now hear this secondary procedure (anukalpa).
This first one consists of one hundred and eight threads.
The second [section] should be less by one-fourth; the third by half of that [the first];
and then one should fashion the fourth by one-fourth of the first. || 173 ||
One should fashion the ornament for the fire-altar using one-third less than the fourth part;
for the foremost of the twice-born, it should be made from twenty-seven threads.
O twice-born one, for Brāhmaṇas, one should perform [the rite] with nine threads;
it must never be done above the breast or below the navel. || 175 ||
Through these three sūtras, know this to be the subtle ritual procedure for other devotees of the Teacher of the World; now hear this supreme ritual procedure.
O Sage, for the pervasive Lord who has entered the four stations,
[the rite is performed] with one hundred and eight repetitions, or indeed with half that amount, or even with a quarter.
One should make an ornament of the threads, either one by one or three by three;
for the great-souled ones, the number of recitations, oblations, and so forth, may be complete or deficient. || 178 ||
For this very reason, he equalizes the portions for the devotees and the ministers;
he should then form a heap of those [grains], marked by the number of threads. || 179 ||
Then, having by chance devised a collection of ornaments for other patrons using fetuses accompanied by a whirling of threads, [he proceeded]. (180)
Then, O Brahmin, that group of purifiers belonging to the God of gods, who is established in four places, was proclaimed, beginning with the foremost one.
O best of beings, one should fashion an interior arrangement for that entire [structure] using gold,
excellent gems, camphor, sandalwood paste, and saffron.
Together with all kinds of medicinal herbs, mixed with cinnamon, cardamom, and other such substances,
along with various purifying materials, a cord, and a wick.
It has the appearance of a citron, like a fresh *āmalaka* fruit or a conch shell;
its internal cavities, moreover, are connected by an unbroken thread.
For the sake of understanding the divisions, the other [mandalas] of all the forms should be arranged nearby, according to one's available resources. (185)
One should fashion the construction of the womb using the collection of materials mentioned previously,
as well as two ornaments for the womb for the worshiping Guru.
O Blessed One, this has been prescribed through the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) and the cultivation of identity [with the deity];
therefore, for others, it should be constructed without a womb (agarbha) according to the proper sequence.
One should fashion the inner circle of the womb-section,
adorned with bāhlīka gems, and having decorated it with gold, one should further embellish it above with silver.
Or it may consist of gold, with its base fashioned from the trimming of purifying grass, and adorned with the conch, lotus, mace, discus, rosary, and the Śrīvatsa mark, among others. || 189 ||
Whether for one person alone or for many, according to the extent of one's wealth—having thus prepared the purificatory materials, O best of the twice-born, in due order. (190)
Having placed it in a wide-mouthed vessel made of metal, covered with cloth, or alternatively in a very beautiful vessel made of bell-metal or clay; || 191 ||
O best of the twice-born, having placed the entire collection of ritual ornaments consecrated with mantras upon one palāśa branch, and the worldly ornaments upon another, [he should proceed]. 192.
Then, having covered it with a very white, unwashed cloth, and having bound it with a firm, very white thread. || 193 ||
Having placed those sacrificial substances within that vessel in the center,
the preceptor, having performed his ablutions and daily rites according to the previously prescribed rule, [should proceed].
Accompanied by the lord of preceptors, they went into the presence of Mantreśa and worshipped the Lord of the Gods with arghya, perfumes, and other offerings in due order.
Having petitioned the God of gods, saying, "May there be no obstacle for me," he then received permission from him with his head bowed low.
When the onset of night had begun, he, prepared with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and flowers,
suddenly [heard] the sound of the Veda being chanted along with the recitation of hymns and auspicious verses by those who read them aloud.
O Brahmin, having performed the worship of the door-keepers with the sounds of conchs and trumpets, and with flowers accompanied by the arghya offering, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
One should recite this mantra in a loud voice:
"Homage to the divine Brahmā, the infallible and the imperishable. (199)
To Viṣṇu, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and whose body is sound,
[he] entered the place where the water-pot was kept and sat upon an excellent seat nearby.
Facing the east, he should recollect the mantra as before while contemplating its pervasive presence;
then, seated according to the rule, he should perform the rites up to the end of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
Having first performed the purification of the hands and so forth, one should subsequently prepare the arghya and other offerings;
having done this as before, one should then worship the assembly of mantras born of the body.
Two pairs of full water-pots, either made of gold or silver,
or else of copper or clay, provided with lids and sprouts of leaves.
Adorned with fruits such as jewels and encircled by a thread,
they should be placed on seats of śāli rice on both sides at each door.
One should arrange three small bowls and three shallow dishes at each corner;
likewise, one should place three small water-jars at each corner.
Then one should perform the sacrifice at the door, starting from the east and proceeding to the north and west,
with water for the guest-offering (arghya), touchings, garlands, and incense mixed with guggulu resin.
O twice-born one, Vāstvīśa, Kṣetranātha, Dvāralakṣmī,
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Garuḍa are stationed at the eastern gate.
In the south are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ; in the west are Jaya and Itara;
and in the north are those named Bhadra and Subhadra, starting from the south.
When one performs the rite of consecration (pavitrārohaṇa) upon the primary image,
then [the sequence] for the deity situated in the mandala begins from the east and proceeds to the north and west.

When the arrangement of the deities stationed at the gates occurs in a processional image (yātrābimba), then their arrangement is said to be according to what was previously [established] for them. || 210 ||

O Brahmin, having first sprinkled with the primary arghya water that five-fold cow-product (pañcagavya) which was previously kept in a separate vessel, one should then consecrate it with the [mantras] beginning with the Hṛdaya.
Having offered water with kusa grass using that [same] weapon-mantra, one should first consecrate it;
or else, one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) by means of the five Upaniṣad-mantras.
Then, having brought [the elements] to the state of fitness by means of the two hands themselves, which consist of Agni and Soma,
one should thereafter purify the earth.
One should sprinkle with this root-mantra mixed with water that which was previously brought forth,
while meditating upon that very same [deity] through a silken purifier (pavitra).
Then, having taken all kinds of seeds and grains together with white mustard seeds, one should empower them with the Astra-mantra and meditate upon them as being identical to the Astra itself.
For the pacification of obstacles, one should swiftly cast [the materials] in the ten directions;
then, having gathered them with a large bunch of kuśa grass, one should indeed place them in the eastern direction.
Or, having placed it in the northeast direction according to the desire of the sacrifice,
one should draw the King of Weapons (hetirāṭ) with sandalwood paste and other substances, enclosing that [mantra] within it.
Having meditated on the discus above the pavilion, the lotus on the surface of the earth, the mace and the goddess in the Nigama, and the conch in the eight directions; 218.
One should then install, by means of mantra, either a mace in the form of a spear that has a body shaped like a rampart and is filled with various flames, or simply the mace alone.
When this is done, the destruction of obstacles will then be perfectly accomplished.
Then, having taken a staff that is firm, pure, uniform, and without blemish— || 220 ||
And a beautiful jar made of clay, or else of gold or silver,
filled with jewels, gold, garlands, perfumes, fruits, and all kinds of medicinal herbs.
Abounding with the branches of auspicious trees, adorned with silk ribbons, garlands, and perfumes,
it was provided with a stream of water filled with filtered liquid— truly new.
Smeared with sandalwood paste and other unguents, surrounded by unbroken grains of rice, and encircled on all sides with threads, one should scatter offerings over it and place it there.
That body of the deity bestows subjugation, strength, and splendor;
then, one should consecrate the *vardhanī* vessel with the weapon-mantra and the discus-mantra.
Combined with the materials previously mentioned and wrapped all around with thread,
one should invoke [the deity] to the right of the Lord of Mantras and to the north of the water-pot.
Having arranged them there all around, one should place eight water-pots,
provided with sprouts, covered with lids, and wound with thread.
Having prepared the seat for the Lord within the pitcher as before, one should duly invoke the Lotus-eyed One into its center according to the prescribed rite.

Having performed everything as before, beginning with the *sannidhi* (invocation of presence) and ending with the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), including the *sannirodha* (withdrawal), one [should perform it] for that [deity] located in the southern direction.
Having meditated upon and worshipped according to the prescribed rite the form of his body as a weapon,
which destroys the entire web of obstacles that persist until the completion of one's karma.
Standing with palms joined in reverence and holding a weapon, he should thus entreat the God:
"O Lord of the Universe, please accept this sacrificial hall constructed by me. (230)
O Lord, maintain the presence of the ritual components until completion;
then, one should lead an unbroken stream of water from the weapon-mantra along the wall.
One should remember that [path] from the eastern portion by way of circumambulation up to that foot, O best of the twice-born; or else, from the northeastern direction up to that foot.
Having rotated two water-pots behind [the deity], either simultaneously or separately,
one should place the water-pot joined with the *vardhanī* vessel and scatter the upward-moving offerings.
Having offered the *arghya* to those two, one should worship them again with flowers and other offerings;
then, having consecrated a pair of unwashed garments with the Astra-mantra, indeed— (234)
Having perfumed both of them with incense and the like, and having wrapped them [in cloth],
one should then place a bhadrapīṭha (auspicious seat) upon it, scattering upward-moving [flowers].
One should place the scripture and the mantra-vessel upon that;
or, having prepared a pedestal with four, three, two, or one layer of rice grains, one should set them there.
One should place rice grains of that same measure or half of it above that;
or one should place sesame seeds of a quarter of that measure or equal to it above that.
Above that, having spread out a pair of auspicious unwashed cloths,
one should place a water-pot equipped with a lid upon them.

As before, one should worship the Lord of Gods with His weapons, following the sequence beginning with the seat; one should perform the divine activity while, during the kumbhaka breath-retention, remembering the All-pervading Lord.
Since no other benefit is appropriate, this ritual involving a jar must be visualized by the practitioner specifically for the purpose of protecting the woman. 240.

Then, having brought the Blessed One down and worshipped him upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the ritual manual, one should perform everything as before, ending with circumambulation and prostration. || 241 ||
In the mandala and during the jar-sacrifice (kumbhayāga), one should perform the sprinkling and bathing rites;
thereafter, accompanied by the sound of Vedic chanting, one should proceed to the abode of the deity.
Then, having gone to the temple, one should worship Acyuta, the Supreme Person, the lotus-eyed one, after bowing down with the eight-limbed prostration.
One should bring all those suitable items—arghya, water for touching, garlands, incense, and so forth—as well as whatever has been offered during other acts of worship. || 244 ||
Having first taken up flowers and honored them with his head,
he offered them to Viṣvaksena, consecrated by the mantras of the weapons.
Having purified the image of the Blessed One along with its pedestal by means of waters,
and having cleansed the temple, one should worship the God of gods.
With baths consisting of milk and the like, or those preceded by the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree, as well as with other unartificial offerings presented according to the prescribed order. || 247 ||

O twice-born one, when the primary image (mūlabimba) is situated on a plastered wall or a cloth painting, one should especially perform all the rites, ending with circumambulation and prostration. || 248 ||
Then, one should perform everything especially for the image of the deity;
O Brahmin, by merely performing its ritual bathing in the presence of this [liṅga], [all benefits are attained]. || 249 ||
Whether for the image designated for the ceremonial bath, or for the daily and occasional rites,
one should perform all other rituals up to the purification at the primary image.
But in the case of an image intended for perpetual festivals, one should perform that festival at that time;
O Brahmin, in their absence, [one should perform it] in a mirror placed near them.
One should perform merely the ablution,
and then one should perform that festival upon a seat made of a cluster of darbha grass, or on a discus, or even within the water-pot.
All else should be performed as before, but in the case of the primary image (mūlabimba), one should proceed accordingly;
then, having gone to the fire-hall, one should consecrate the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as previously described.
There, having consecrated the fire according to the previously mentioned rite, one should indeed perform the libation with mantras using the consecrated fire. || 254 ||
One should cause the sacrificial oblation (caru) to be cooked on the hearth with milk, clarified butter, and rice while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra;
then, having lifted it out and purified it with clarified butter, one should present it in the proper sequence.
Then one should offer as an oblation one part of the images located at the kalaśas;
or else, having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) prior to the commencement of the sacrifice.
Having performed the worship of the pitchers, the ground, and the images in due order,
one should then satisfy everything, ending with the gifts to the twice-born, into the fire.

After offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should then proceed to the presence of the image, O Brahmin, on the same day as that upon which the [consecration] was performed in the previous year. || 258 ||
Recalling from the beginning of that day the withdrawal of the sacred thread (pavitraka),
he should worship the entire sacrifice with offerings of water for honor (arghya), flowers, and oblations (bali).
In that same manner, one should then offer clarified butter (ājya) in sequence until the final full oblation;
then, having established the front of the mandala, one should perform the binding of mudrās and so forth.

Having performed prostrations and so forth, one should then take a single purifying thread (pavitraka) that has been perfumed with incense and fragrance, and place it at the four locations of the deity.

Having offered [the oblation] in due order and presented incense preceded by the arghya water, you, the imperishable one, are eternally satisfied by the enjoyments consisting of your own bliss. || 262 ||
"Nevertheless, unsatiated by my devotion, I worship you for the sake of my own spiritual perfection.
Having thus informed the God, he then [purified] the water of the *arghya* offering with the Astra-mantra.
Having consecrated the entire collection of materials with water, preceded by ornaments, using either śāli rice, or taṇḍula rice, or sesame seeds, or all three together; || 264 ||
Or, having prepared a pedestal or a ground surface consisting of four, three, two, or one *bhāra* [of materials],
one should place it in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), relative to the east of the site.
Alternatively, in the western direction, according to the teacher's wish, [he should be seated] with white garments and with armor consisting of unbroken grains. || 266 ||
Having consecrated it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should cover it with the armor-mantra (kavaca);
in this manner, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of all substances everywhere.
Then, one should offer at the sacrificial site the eight arrows together with their feathers and constituent parts, consecrated with the Astra-mantra, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having wrapped it four times with a firm thread of five colors or one that is very white, starting from the interior, one should encircle the sacrificial pavilion.
While recollecting the armor mantra (varmamantra), one should likewise circumambulate the temple four times from the outside and encircle the fire-sanctuary in the same manner.
Then, the most excellent of teachers, having himself requested the assembly devoted to the five times (pañcakāla), should encircle [the area] as before.
Furthermore, tomorrow, in your presence and with devotion, I shall worship the Lord before a multitude of Vaiṣṇava ascetics who are devoted to the six duties.
"Therefore, out of a desire to favor me, you should remain present;
for when thus entreated by them, you should indeed grant your permission."
Facing east and seated upon his seat, he should drink the *brahmakūrca* water poured from the hand of the Guru, and thereafter he should consume the remainder of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

One should drink water from kusa grass infused with gold and gems, over which the heart-mantra has been recited, as well as the auspicious water from the feet of the Blessed One, which removes all sins. (275)
Thereafter, he should consume betel-leaf and a tooth-stick;
then, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should effect the complete integration (sakalīkaraṇa) of his body.

Having extracted the mantra situated on the ground, having placed it in the pitcher, in the fire, and within oneself, and having stood upon a woolen rug provided with a blanket and a layer of kuśa grass; 277.
One should recite the excellent mantra along with its ancillaries, chant auspicious and supreme hymns,
and narrate the meritorious story concerning the Lord of All, after having prepared the pitcher and the mandala.
Whether it be a single lotus, many lotuses, or a wheel with a lotus and so forth—the characteristics and other details of these were personally proclaimed by the Blessed One. (279)
O twice-born one, on another day, the God of gods properly performed the rite for Puṣkaraja at Pauṣkara, or else he drew a mandala and [prepared] a water-pot.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having gone near the ornaments,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) by means of fumigation and sprinkling.
