Having meditated upon a twelve-spoked wheel with blazing radiance in his right hand, joined with the twelve digits (kalās), and the sun situated within it; 282.
One should visualize that [impurity] as being burnt by the mass of those rays and reduced to a heap of ashes;
thereafter, one should generate the entire collection of mantra-purifiers without exception.
One should visualize a white lotus endowed with sixteen petals in the left hand;
in its center, one should meditate upon the moon, possessed of its full digits.
O twice-born one, one should meditate upon [the deity] emitting a downpour of nectar rain; with that nectar, one should saturate the accumulated ashes.
One should again contemplate all that which has arisen from the midst of the ashes;
having meditated upon it as consisting of the five elements, one should further contemplate it as being all-pervasive.
Having sprinkled [the materials] with the root mantra, touched them, and then gazed upon them,
those suitable for the water-pot (kumbha) should be placed in one [vessel], and those belonging to the mandala in another.
O twice-born one, some are suitable for images, while others are for fire-offerings;
O best of the twice-born, yet others are indeed suitable for mantras.
Having placed each alms-bowl separately according to the quality of the bowls obtained,
one should afterwards cover them with a well-washed, new cloth.
Those vessels for the ornaments should be tied individually and in sequence with a firm, very white thread. || 290 ||
Having covered them as before, one should pass the night in vigil;
then, at dawn on the eleventh day, having bathed and worshipped Janārdana, [one should proceed].
Having invited them and gone to his home, he, being self-restrained, prostrated himself before the Brahmins who were devoted to Viṣṇu, firm in their vows, and preceded by his own teachers. || 292 ||
Those who, devoted to their own duties and intent upon the rites for the God of gods, worship the Lord Acyuta even when a time of calamity has arrived; || 293 ||
Then, certain other Vaiṣṇavas—friends, relatives, and kinsmen—assembled;
and then, at the onset of night, the proclamation of an auspicious day began.
Accompanied by the auspicious sounds of conch shells and the voices of Brahmins reciting the Śākuna hymn, one should enter the temple of the deity.
Then the preceptor, together with the presiding priests (mūrtipas), having adorned the image of the deity with garments, garlands, ornaments, and ointments, [proceeds]. || 296 ||
Having placed [him] upon a vehicle and gone forth with conch shells, kettledrums, and trumpets, as well as with palm-leaf fans, umbrellas, and various white chowries; || 297 ||
The lord of men should have the deity installed in the pavilion according to the prescribed rite; then he should place the deity upon an auspicious throne provided with four legs.
Having installed the deity, one should worship him with special rites according to the injunctions;
then, having offered the great oblation, one should satisfy [the deity] from the midst of the fire.
Then, at the time of the afternoon twilight, or when night had begun, amidst all auspicious rites such as the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha) and others, [the ceremony proceeded]. || 300 ||
One should cause the Lord of the World, the God of gods, to enter the sacrificial pavilion at the western part of the sacrifice,
onto a golden auspicious seat.
O twice-born one, having placed the deity facing the Lord present at the sacrifice, one should adorn him from above with a canopy made of pearls.
Alternatively, on the tenth day, one should place the pervasive Lord (Vibhu) residing in the image within the sacrificial hall;
those consisting of the Ṛgveda, facing east and west, should be joined to their respective seats.
And on the south, one should station those versed in the Yajurveda facing north;
and having seated those who know the Sāmaveda in the western part facing east.
And together with the Brahmins of the Ekāyana school, who were characterized by the designation "Mūrti," he [then saw] those in the northern quarter who were devoted to their daily obligatory rites.
Having then established all those who know the Atharvaveda in pairs, listen further, O best of the twice-born, to another injunction in detail. (306)
Having first positioned the best of the twice-born facing westward while seated upon a throne,
he was adorned with flowers, garments, turbans, and finger-rings.
One should cause him to recite the meritorious Ṛg-vedic mantras that are composed of the Lord and known by those who know the mantras;
then, while he is looking toward the northern direction from his position in the southern direction.
The preceptor should cause that collection of Vaiṣṇava Yajus-mantras to be recited; meanwhile, one who is skilled in the Sāmans, standing in the western direction, should sing the pure Sāman hymns.

Then, standing in water, facing south, the knower of the Atharva Veda, being devoted, should recite in their entirety the mantras declared in his own branch that bear the marks of knowledge. || 310 ||
Each one, surrounded by a circle of disciples, was worthy [of initiation] in due order;
so too were those ascetics devoted to the Lord who follow the Pāñcarātra tradition. || 311 ||
One should place four trustworthy Brahmins and others in the direction of Īśa (the north-east),
and those who are single-mindedly devoted, even if they are not trustworthy, in the direction of Agni (the south-east).
Having seated the devoted Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas in the southwest, as well as the Vaikhānasas,
he [should then proceed] with four handfuls of water toward the northwest quarter.
O Sage, at that time, four Śiśus who are full of the Blessed One, belonging to the Sātvatas and characterized by exertion (sārambhin), should be employed in the four directions.
And their followers, O best of sages, were fourfold: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (315)
And he should cause the ascetics who have previously attained realization to recite the supremely purifying mantras arising from the Ekāyanīya branch, according to the Pāñcarātra tradition.
While performing their own rites, they recite their respective mantras and converse;
beginning from the east and ending in the north, there are four [disciples] preceded by the Guru. || 317 ||

Many were knowers of the sacred conventions and experts in the Sātvata doctrine; according to their own capacity, they had performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) and their hands were adorned with meditative gestures (mudrā).
They should mutually conceal their own secret seals with their own garments;
others, intent on song and dance, should stand in front as reciters of hymns. || 319 ||
Outside, they were accompanied by throngs of bards and likewise by drummers;
all the other Vaiṣṇavas, moreover, were behind them and on their flanks.
Having thus performed the installation for all [the deities] in their proper order,
he then [performs it] for the God of gods who is established in four locations.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the worship in sequence as before;
having reached the vicinity of the water-pot, one should perform the formal offering (vinivedana).
And for the purpose of summoning various distinct enjoyments and splendors,
there is the tooth-stick, betel with its accompaniments, mouth-perfume, and a fine mirror.
Having offered fragrant substances such as sandalwood and fruits such as nutmeg and cloves, he then placed them before the Lord of the World on his right side.
Guggulu resin and refined incense, a bright lamp placed in a copper vessel, a beautiful golden necklace for adorning the eyes, and a bracelet; || 325 ||
In a metallic vessel filled with honey and clarified butter,
one should place the sixfold great image of the deity along with yellow pigment and collyrium, within a white and red cloth covering the eyes.
And in the western direction, one should likewise offer to the Lord water from a sacred river,
water from a holy bathing place (tīrtha), water from a mountain, as well as mountain herbs, bilva fruits, and the like.
O best of beings, one should offer grassy meadows and blue darbha grass in a copper vessel or a vessel of iron to the Lord of lords, the Supreme Being, in the northern direction.
Garlands, the seven medicinal herbs, seeds, and fruits;
vessels of sesame and rice, milk, curd, clarified butter, and sugar. || 329 ||

The group of fragrant substances consists of cinnamon, cardamom, and so forth; the minerals consist of red ochre and the like; coconut with its fruit is included; and all products derived from sugarcane are also [fragrant]. || 330 ||

O twice-born one, it should be offered in a shining bronze vessel according to what is available, or in a leaf-cup made of sacrificial leaves; however, if these are unavailable, it may be offered in any vessel.
Betel nut with its shell, betel leaf for one standing on dry land,
a tooth-stick, white garments along with upper cloths, sacred threads, and sandalwood paste.
Then, having likewise offered those ornaments and vessels individually to the image, to the fire, and to the four directions; 333.
When one performs [the ritual] with the primary image situated in four places, then everything should be arranged in front of it. || 334 ||
Having placed [the offerings] up to the ornaments and presented them in due order,
[one should offer] that which is perfumed with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.

One should offer a fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka) to the one who has entered the four stations; thereafter, one should perform the offering of water for the feet (arghya), flowers, and incense, and execute the binding of the mudrās. || 336 ||

At the beginning, middle, and end, one should recite the supreme mantra along with its ancillaries for the complete pacification of any deficiencies; thereafter, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite the following verse.
One should invite the mantra of praise beginning with the two-fold Praṇava:
"O infinite one, consisting of all mantras, eternally present and imperishable. (338)
O Lord of the yoga of qualities and the primary [nature], whose body is the enjoyment of meditative realization;
O Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Brahman, Lord of the vital breath, you who possess four forms! || 339 ||
O All-pervading One, O You who have not fallen from Your true form, O Omniscient One, Supreme Person!
From this moment until the day of Your departure, [protect us]. (340)
O Lord, endowed with a multitude of various mantras, abide near me— within the divine image,
the true form, the water-pot, and upon the ground of the mandala.
In the thread for counting [beads], in the rosary, in the fire, in the form of the Guru, in the bell, on the seat of the weapon, and in the ritual implements; || 342 ||

In all those who possess the forms of single-minded twice-born ones, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth, and in the various attendants of Viṣṇu who delight in [the performance of] births and rituals; || 343 ||
Indeed, for those who are purified by faith, skillful, and have you as their sole refuge,
there is [the efficacy] of past rites such as ritual bathing and the like.
For the pacification of occasional, constant, and incomplete [impurities], and for your pleasure, I shall today perform [the rites] according to the scriptures. (345)
The rite of the purifier (pavitraka) fulfills all ritual actions;
therefore, today [perform] the worship consisting of the offering of mouth-perfume and other such services.
Perform everything up to the end of the oblation for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), making it entirely your own;
I worship you with devotion through my capacity during this vigil, O You who transcend all powers.
"O Blessed One, you have been informed by the Brahma-sutras and the Agamas, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; you know everything that dwells within the heart. (348)
"Out of affection for me, your devotee, you should grant me your favor this morning.
Having thus invited him, one should prostrate before Aja on the ground with the eight limbs of the body. (349)

Having circumambulated [the deity] four times while recollecting the mantra in his heart, [he should worship] with songs, dances, and so forth, along with hymns accompanied by Vedic recitations. || 350 ||
One should pass the night in vigil accompanied by shouts of "Victory!
Then, having bathed during the Brahma-muhūrta and performed the auspicious rites of protection (kautuka-maṅgala), [one should proceed]. || 351 ||
Having first performed the daily rites for a single officiant, one should then perform the sacrifice at the eastern gate with great magnificence.
One should worship [the deity] residing in the water-pot as before, and then, in due order, that which resides in the mandala;
thereafter, one should worship the Lord of the God of Gods residing in the image with all his specific attributes. || 353 ||
With the twenty-five substances beginning with milk, duly consecrated, and with various other ablutions and enjoyments consisting of edible foods and the like; || 354 ||
With various services such as seats and other articles of touch, which are heart-pleasing by name and fashioned in many different varieties; || 355 ||
Having thus performed the sequence up to the conclusion of the *japamudrā*,
one should afterwards satisfy [the deities] residing in the fire, duly and in proper order.
Then, O twice-born one, having gone into the presence of Bhūṣaṇapātra and having honored him,
he opened the protective vessel.
Having observed and taken up [the materials], and having gone to the vicinity of the jar,
the collection of limbs for the propitiation shall become unmanifest yet real.

The third, however, consists of both; likewise, having reflected upon the triad beginning with the internal (ādhyātmika), one should perform recollection within that [third] by means of the intellect, focusing on the heart.

In that regard, the collection of mantras and mudrās, numbering sixty-four and consisting of the unmanifest which is free from attachment to enjoyments, is proclaimed as the ultimate reality. || 360 ||
The vows of Vedic recitation, singing, instrumental music, and so forth, as well as the observances (niyamas), various occasional gifts preceded by festivals, and other incidental rites. || 361 ||
These, possessing both forms, bestow the goals of human life and grant delight to Janārdana, the source of the universe, who has the mantra as his body.
That which is their imperishable form—resplendent, consisting of consciousness, and pure—is to be contemplated within the wombs [of all beings]; it is subtle and thereafter luminous.
O Great-minded one, that which resembles the sun, the moon, and fire, and is conceived as having a limited measure, should be meditated upon at the locations of the various knots within the granthi.
The third [level] is gross, conventional, and universal;
it should indeed always be cultivated with respect to the designated collection of threads.
Having thus characterized the internal pervasion, one should thereafter contemplate the imperishable mantra-pervasion known as the "presiding deity. (366)
That form which is inseparable from the four, which is like nectar, filled with a multitude of various appearances, both manifest and unmanifest, and imperishable; || 367 ||
O great-minded one, one should constantly contemplate the presence of the triad consisting of the crown, the garland, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem, as the presiding deities themselves.
That which is the aggregate of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—is a beautiful and auspicious form that brings complete satisfaction to his devotees. (369)
One should consider its state as the presiding deity (adhibhūta) within the range of a yojana;
having meditated upon this, one should then utter the root mantra.
With hands raised, one should recite that mantra adorned with the *praṇava*, which is the stainless and supreme *tāna* (melodic extension), O God, that is the means for attaining you. (371)
The practice revealed by you is endowed with devotion and faith;
indeed, you have explained the means for its unimpeded accomplishment.

By your grace, this work called the *Pavitra*, which is according to my ability, has been composed by me for the sake of those devotees whose souls are purified and who are devoted to both knowledge and action.
Now, meditate upon that Supreme Lord as is appropriate;
for from Him comes action that is more auspicious, and indeed, stainless knowledge.
You alone are indeed the various injunctions, the collection of mantras, and the aggregate of ritual substances;
you are the attainment and the fulfiller who completes those rites that were previously incomplete. || 375 ||
O Blessed One, by this truth, may all your ritual activities be unimpeded for you, who are free from deceit and afflicted by the destruction of worldly existence. (376)
"O Blessed One, you have been petitioned; my longing for you is supreme, except for your own satisfaction and the granting of perfect knowledge. (377)
"O son, even when a time of calamity has arrived, ritual action and knowledge must not be abandoned by me intentionally; you know all that in its true essence. (378)
O Lord, because you have not been properly honored with appropriate enjoyments at the proper time and in the proper manner, there is distress in my heart on that account.
Worship with the enjoyment of sensory objects, oblations of clarified butter, and libations—
none of these are of any use to you, for you have already accomplished all that was to be done.
"Indeed, this entire [teaching] has been sown in a fertile field for all my purposes;
knowing this as it was in the past, it will surely bear fruit through immortality. (381)
It was accepted from the mouth of my guru, O Lord, Sovereign of All; yet it does not flash forth clearly in my intellect as it truly stands, nor has it been fully realized.
Through the actions of mind, speech, and body, from night until dawn, [the self is inactive] due to the lack of independence, the incapacity [of the senses], and the instability of the mind. (383)
O Lord, due to obstacles such as cold, heat, wind, rain, and fevers,
the constituent parts of the ritual that correspond to Your own nature have failed to be fully accomplished.
Since this daily practice culminates in the attainment of supreme bliss prior to [renewed] worldly activity, it is therefore not possible for the immortals, as has been stated. (385)
To fulfill that purpose, however, the most important worship is the rite known as Pavitraka, which has been prescribed by you for every year. (386)
Whatever pure [deed] has been performed by me through direct perception, yet remains incomplete due to the lack of ritual application (kriyāyoga), lead that to complete purity for me. || 387 ||
Whether through ignorance or lack of knowledge, whatever has not been performed by me as prescribed—may all that become complete; may you always be fully satisfied. (388)
Oṃ, O Imperishable Lord of the World, O Janārdana whose form is mantra!
Protect me, O Lotus-eyed One; forgive me, O Lord, be gracious. Oṃ.
Having thus uttered the root mantra together with the marks of the heart and the other [limbs], one should then place it upon the head of the all-pervading Lord, whose nature is mantra.
[He is] the embodiment of all-knowing activity, enjoyment, and virtuous resolve;
thus [he is visualized] both within the mandala and situated inside the temple. (391)
O best of the twice-born, one should thus offer two purifiers for the fire;
or else, one may place the crown at the beginning, and the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha in the middle.
And on the third [digit], one should place a forest garland with these mantras: "To the crown for the king of lotuses; [I am] myself surrounded by ruby-colored [gems]. (393)
Come to this purifier; be quickly present here.
Salutations to you, O Śrīvatsa; come, O Kaustubha, om, salutations! || 394 ||
O you of pure luster, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, abide in this purifier;
O Vanamālā, come here and be present within it. (395)

Listen further to another injunction regarding the purificatory rite (pavitraka) which has been prescribed by me for the Source of the World: at the outset, one should meditate upon the entire [deity] as a twice-born (dvija). 396.
But that ritual which lasts for a full year, from dawn until the end of night, arising from meditation, partless, and perfectly bestowing liberation—[that is the true one]. (397)
Having recollected the partless mantra through the sequence of pure recitation,
one should unite that thread with the mantra, and likewise the mantra with the thread.
Having unified it with one's own self, one should indeed offer it at the head of the mantra; then, taking up another thread, one should place within it that which is both with and without parts.
One should meditate for a year upon the ritual action that constitutes the very nature of meditation;
and having recollected the mantra, which possesses both forms and is worshipped in the water-pot (kalaśa), [one should perform the rite]. || 400 ||
Having performed the connection as before, one should offer the purifying thread (pavitraka);
then, O Brahmin, one should bring forward the third, the protective cord (pratisara). || 401 ||
One should remember all external annual rites in their entirety,
as well as oneself being worshipped from the foundational level up to the supreme limit.
By means of the sequence known as absorption, enjoyment, and authority, with his entire being,
he [perceives] the complete Lord of Mantras, whose form consists of absorption, enjoyment, and sovereignty.

O twice-born one, having remembered [the mantra] and performed the reconnection (sandhāna), one should then offer the protective cord (pratisara) along with water for honor (arghya), flowers, perfumes, garlands, and incense.
One should perform worship by encasing each of the ornaments individually,
interspersing them with the ringing of the bell at every interval.
It is provided with all kinds of gems, the five auspicious substances (pañcagavya), flowers, unbroken grains, and fruits;
it is endowed with excellent fragrances, the arghya offering, darbha grass, parched grain, and white mustard seeds. || 406 ||
One should joyfully shower many clouds of rain, or simply a rain of flowers alone; one may also sound conch shells and other instruments. (407)
One should offer [the thread] to the mantra, the weapon, and the pitcher, excluding the meditation;
having thus first offered the purifying thread (pavitraka) to that which resides in the pitcher, O Brahmin. (408)
O Nārada, according to this procedure, one should first offer three auspicious purifiers (pavitraka) to the deity residing within the maṇḍala, and then to the place of enjoyment (bhogasthāna).
One should offer [these] to all the mantras, either three or one as desired;
having worshipped the image equally, one should then present the ornaments.

In the ornament known as the garland of forest flowers (vanamālā), one should perform the contemplation beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta) according to the very sequence stated for the water-pot (kalaśa), or else as prescribed by another injunction. || 411 ||
Having performed everything from the *parā* [level] up to the gross (*sthūla*), one should offer it;
O best of beings, the placement of the flowers for the crown and so forth is as previously described. (412)
In this regard, O Brahmin, there is indeed this distinction: one should invoke the four [deities] beginning with Kirīṭin in sequence upon the four ornaments.
Endowed with a radiance equal to the sun, remain here in this head-ornament together with your retinue, O Lord of the gods named Kirīṭa.
O Śrīvatsa, you who resemble the full moon and are beloved by the Blessed One, come; you have been fashioned as an ornament upon the chest of the Source of the Universe by me. (415)
O Lord of jewels, beloved of the Blessed One, you have been fashioned as an ornament for the chest of the Source of the Universe; come, O Kaustubha! 416.
O auspicious one, beloved of the God of gods, come to the Vanamālā, which is strewn with flowers from the [sacred] elements and adorned with coral and jewels. 417.
O twice-born one, with these four mantras, he should invoke in succession the limbs, the subsidiary limbs, and likewise the insignia. (418)
Then, one should gradually offer the purificatory materials (pavitra) for the ornaments, the Śaktis, and Garuḍa in their proper order, and thereafter for the pedestal (pīṭha). || 419 ||
In this very same manner, one should offer [the oblation] to the pervasive Lord residing in the primary image, and likewise to all the ritual images, such as those of Lakṣmī and the others. || 420 ||
Having bestowed ornaments in due order upon the other images of the limbs and the retinue, he should proceed to the abode of Agni.
One should offer ornaments to the pervasive Lord stationed in the fire as before;
however, when the placement of the *pavitraka* occurs, it should take place at the primary image (*mūlabimba*). || 422 ||
O Brahmin, if the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is permanent, it may be used for both the regular (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites;
however, one should offer the ornament into the fire, but not perform the oblation (homa) with it.
Since renunciation is prescribed as the highest ornament,
it is not fitting to seize what has been consumed without first removing the fault of its seizure.
Having placed [the deity] upon the heart of the preceptor who has been worshipped like a god,
and likewise having placed it upon the hearts of each of the other preceptors as well.
Then, O twice-born one, having given [the initiation] to the practitioners, as well as to those who are parts of the sacrifice,
and then to those whose nature is the scripture, and likewise to others in due order.
Thereafter, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) and standing facing the deity, one should recite the great mantra once, which increases all ritual actions. || 427 ||
The destruction of transgressions against the pledges occurs even by the mere recollection [of this];
therefore, one should cause the deity situated in the three places to be proclaimed in due order.
O Supreme Lord, whether intentionally or unintentionally, the observance of my vows has not been performed by me due to some obstacle or fault. (429)
Because of this, O Janārdana, my mind suffers an exceeding torment of a burning nature,
since I am afflicted by the fault of having violated the agreement.
O Lord, that which was previously taught by you out of a desire for the welfare of your devotees—that bright and purifying [teaching] which destroys all faults—has been performed by me. (431)
Be gracious to me and grant me protection; indeed, abandon this anger born of delusion, for I am sinking in the ocean of existence and have fallen away from my commitment.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Soul of Mantras! Be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
Protect, protect us, O Lord of the three worlds, O Keśava, destroyer of affliction! 433.
And by your grace, O Lord, may no fault regarding the observance of my vows arise for me;
today let there be the successful completion of my obligatory and occasional rites.

Upon hearing this with devotion from him who is afflicted by saṃsāra, the King of Mantras shall swiftly lead him to the state of perfection and destroy the faults arising from the violation of commitments.
Then, with coverings and gifts gathered according to his means, together with sacred threads, upper garments, umbrellas, and sandals; || 436 ||

O Brahmin, one should worship those who have previously been attained [as gurus] and likewise those beginning with the ascetics (yatis), using various kinds of food, incense, water offerings (arghya), ritual sprinklings (ālabhana), and so forth.
O twice-born one, [he described] the five ending with the Vaikhānasas, as well as the four beginning with the Brāhmaṇas,
the five beginning with those devoted to Yoga, and likewise other Vaiṣṇavas.
First, [he should perform the worship] of the mantras arising from the Ekāyanīya branch, and likewise of the mantras consisting of the three Vedas (trayī) and their hymns (stotra). || 439 ||
And a proclamation should be made by Brahmins in the presence of the Lord, accompanied by the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, as well as by the music of trumpets and songs. 440.
One should please the Lord with dances, other sounds, and auspicious rites;
thereafter, the preceptor, having placed the festival image upon a vehicle, [proceeds]. || 441 ||
One should cause the temple to be circumambulated according to the sequence of pradakṣiṇa, as prescribed in the rules for the great festival and endowed with all auspiciousness.
Then one should offer a prayer to the ascetics of purified soul:
"By the power of your grace, may there be fulfillment of my mind. (443)

"May there be no violation of the samaya for me regarding all the constituent parts of the ritual. To this, everyone should respond with "So be it," accompanied by the rhythmic clapping of hands (tāla). || 444 ||
Having questioned them, O best of the twice-born, he should partake of a fine meal preceded by the offering of food (naivedya), accompanied by his kinsmen and servants; that is the special rule.
O twice-born one, having established the purifying cord for one night, three nights, or seven nights, one should then perform the renunciation (saṃnyāsa). || 446 ||
Or else, O Brahmin, having first placed the ornament upon the image,
one should wait until the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika has arrived.
And having removed the garlands and other offerings, he should present new ones day by day,
until they reach the day of the anniversary, provided that they do not become withered.
Having first performed the great worship (mahārcana) and concluding with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should gradually withdraw [the ritual] either by oneself or through the self of the Guru.
Having taken the consecrated vessel and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
he knelt with both knees upon the ground and prostrated before the preceptor.
Having first honored him with water for the feet, flowers, and other offerings, and having prostrated himself, he should present that vessel, saying: "O Lord, please grant me your favor. (451)
The blessing for oneself or the pleasure of the Blessed One should be expressed by the teacher for him,
according to tradition and according to the scriptures, through the grace of the Fourfold Self.
"O son, may your annual duty be well completed! Having thus spoken, they then poured [the water] upon the head of him who was seated on his throne. || 453 ||
Having consecrated two water-pots with mantras that bestow good fortune and liberation,
one should perform the dismissal of the Lord, preceded by worship, according to the proper sequence.
One should worship Viṣvaksena along with his limbs (attendants) and offer libations immediately thereafter;
subsequently, having withdrawn everything, this dismissal (visarjana) should be performed. || 455 ||
Whatever has been offered to him, one should indeed cast into deep water;
thus the fault incurred by transgressing a prior agreement over the course of a year [is expiated]. 456.
O Sage, it indeed quickly attains destruction through the rite of Pavitrāropaṇa;
for it protects [the practitioner], since it guards one from falling despite existing faults. || 457 ||
It especially protects the twice-born and performs its function in full;
even when the practitioner is devoid of ritual action, it does so—therefore, it has been called "Great" by me.

This sacrifice, called the *pavitra*, which is characterized by the previously stated definitions, protects one who has fallen due to the omission of ritual acts when performed according to the rules. (459)
Then, O Brahmin, one should remember the sacred thread (vapu-traka), the ornament born of the thread;
whether out of ignorance, or delusion, or due to neglect in the performance of the rite. || 460 ||
Whether due to atheism, or from egoism, or because of the obstruction of the agents, or from the attainment of another Vaiśeṣika state, or from defects such as sleep and so forth; || 461 ||
Or if, out of fear of missing the proper time, or for some other reason, one should offer the *pavitraka* after having performed an incomplete sacrifice; || 462 ||
At that time, the ritual of the Lord of Mantras would become tamasic;
the ruler of the land and the preceptor would both incur a tamasic result. || 463 ||
Then there will be affliction by diseases such as fever for the inhabitants of that region;
or, O Brahmin, [the king] may be seized by haste or defiled by the menstrual flow (rajas). || 464 ||
If one performs a sacrifice for the deity and then offers the purifying thread (pavitraka), that action shall be of the rājasa type, and its fruit shall indeed be of that same nature. || 465 ||
When, being free from the previously mentioned defects caused by ignorance,
one has performed the sacrifice perfectly complete, one should then worship with ornaments.
Then the performer and the preceptor shall obtain the fruit declared for the purificatory rite;
then the annual ritual shall become most complete. || 467 ||
Then there may be protection for one who has fallen due to the omission of ritual duties;
therefore, having performed the worship of the Lord properly and in great detail, [one should proceed]. || 468 ||
When that auspicious moment has arrived at its conclusion, the preceptor,
with a tranquil mind and acting with diligence, should properly adorn the Lord with ornaments.
If, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, even a single auspicious moment cannot be obtained,
then one should place the purifiers upon another [vessel] according to the prescribed rule.
Then, for the pacification of the fault of transgressing that [rule],
the Guru should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times, as well as the weapon (astra) mantra.
One should recite eight times the Lord of Mantras, which destroys the faults of the samaya;
this should be done in all sacrifices when a muhūrta has elapsed. || 472 ||

O tiger among sages, the ritual for the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) has been described according to the lunar day, asterism, and weekday, as well as when auspicious moments and other favorable signs occur.
One may perform that [rite] either in a Vaiṣṇava temple alone; hear from me regarding that:
starting from the day on which the auspicious moment (puṇyakṣaṇa) and so forth occurs. || 474 ||
Having performed the sowing of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) as before seven days prior, and having likewise performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) two days beforehand; 475.
Then, on the day of the ritual, having performed the bathing rite during the Brāhma-muhūrta,
he should worship the Lord situated in the four locations as before.
Or, even if it is only the image, when the auspicious moment pertaining to Viṣṇu has arrived, one should worship the Lord with sacred threads according to the requirements of the time.
But when the consecration (pavitrāropaṇa) takes place for the image alone, then the worship prescribed for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) should be performed for that very image. || 478 ||
Likewise, one should avoid [the ritual] even when it has entered the fire within the mandala of the jar;
however, once this muhūrta has passed, [one may proceed] with the extensive sacrifice to the Blessed One.
Having performed that [rite] at another moment, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times along with its root;
to pacify all defects, one should recite it twenty-eight times.
O high-minded one, when that moment of conflict has passed, the preceptor should offer a thousand oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, or unbroken grains.
Having placed the purificatory items upon another [vessel] according to the rule,
one should then perform the first consecration bath upon the original group of nine.
Or a second or a third time, according to the will of the Guru;
or else, having recited ten thousand times the root mantra along with its ancillaries, one should afterwards [perform the rite] with sesame seeds and other materials.
One should offer one thousand oblations for each [deity] with three [mantras];
thereafter, one should recite the excellent mantra fifty-four times.
Thus has the procedure been described for a site established by mortals, as well as for self-manifested sites and others, during the consecration of sacred objects and similar rites. || 485 ||
In all occasional rites, and especially in those that are obligatory, if the auspicious moment (muhūrta) passes, or even if that specific time is exceeded; 486.
O twice-born one, there is no fault in what was previously stated, especially in that case;
for [the rite] cannot be accomplished by anyone other than through the extensive sacrifice to the Blessed One.

When that [period] consisting of moments and so forth has passed during the exertion against obstacles, he should perform all those respective rites at another time according to the prescribed rule. || 488 ||
To pacify those defects, the wise person should perform the recitation of the great mantra—once, twice, four times, eight times, or ten times. (489)
It may be divided into twelve, sixteen, or even twenty-eight parts,
according to the gravity and specific requirements of each particular ritual act.
Or rather, one should perform additional recitation until the mind becomes serene;
thereafter, I shall explain the specific atonements in detail.
The possibility of defects has been declared there, as well as the time limit;
since it has been described in detail therein, it is not elaborated upon here.
Thus has this ritual for the Pavitrārohaṇa been correctly described,
O Brahmin, when the pavitra has been prepared by devotees intent on the performance of mantras.
A certain specific rule must be observed with great effort until the most merit-bestowing eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika. || 494 ||
O bull among sages, another subtle method will be described, whether performed upon a solitary image or one situated within the sacrificial temple. (495)
Or, when [the deity] is established in the temple and has been consecrated on the tenth day,
one should arrange the application of ornaments within the mandala of the water-pot, excluding the pot itself.
At that time, one should also perform it for the deity residing in the fire, which has been consecrated as before;
then, one, two, or three purifiers (pavitra) should be offered to the Lord.
Or if they have been prepared according to the distinctions beginning with the "excellent" (uttama) and so forth;
O best of the twice-born, this applies when there is an absence of materials or if there is an incapacity. (498)
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the twelfth day, one should, according to one's capacity,
O best of the twice-born, provide ornaments for the image of the Lord while observing a fast.
With threads fashioned according to one's desire, with knots likewise made as one wishes,
or else with the night-illuminating substance (niśārocanā) or with the mineral used for purifying [the threads].
O Brahmin, one should duly dye the knots with something, having filled the interiors with flowers, or otherwise using only [the dye] itself. (501)
O Brahmin, having worshipped the omnipresent Lord as before, with the image present before him, one should offer ornaments and utter this mantra: (502)
"O Brahman, please accept this Brahmāsūtra which has been composed by me for the purpose of completing my [past] actions, so that no fault may accrue to me. (503)
Having spoken thus, one should then place the sacred thread (pavitraka) upon the object of worship;
and having praised the Lord of the Gods of gods, one should do so with diligence on the second day.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then perform its withdrawal;
now the specific procedure for the Pavitraka sacrifice at home is being described.
Whether [the deity] resides in the image, in the mandala, or even in the four locations,
one should offer the three purificatory rites, or each one individually, according to one's desire.
Thus has been described, O best of yogins, the supreme Pavitrārohaṇa rite,
which always protects the devotees on earth from deficiencies, excesses, and other such faults.
By performing this with devotion, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a knower of the Vedas;
and a Kṣatriya becomes illustrious, possessed of exceedingly fierce power, and endowed with an unbroken lineage. || 508 ||
The Vaiśya shall be endowed with wealth and grain, and the Śūdra shall become a partaker of happiness;
indeed, this is the fruit of infinite gifts of cows, land, and gold. || 509 ||
For as many years as one has given throughout their entire life, for a hundred years thereafter,
that man shall obtain the full fruit of the supreme lifespan.
Having reached the abode of Hari at the appropriate time through his own intellect,
and properly remembering the Lord of All, he completely casts off the body.
Being fanned by celestial women with moon-bright vehicles and being likewise honored by the immortals, he goes to heaven.
He who, free from desire, performs the offering of ornaments for the pleasure of the Lord, may enjoy all the pleasures arising within all the worlds. (513)
Having attained the world of Viṣṇu, he remains there for many hundreds of kalpas;
then, after a long time, he indeed returns once more to human birth.
He is born at an auspicious time, in an auspicious place, and into a most excellent family; and when childhood has passed, his faculties are fully manifest.

But when the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva) has been awakened through the power of the repeated practice of the Ṛgveda, one should become devoted to Nārāyaṇa in deed, mind, and speech. || 516 ||
Constantly devoted to ritual action, wise, dedicated to Brahman, and possessing truth as his prowess;
he was a worshiper of no other deity, pure in soul, and free from the company of the wicked. || 517 ||
Freed from disease and sorrow, endowed with sons, wife, and other kin,
and liberated from untimely death, he attains stainless knowledge.
Having reached Śvetadvīpa, which is very difficult even for the gods and other wise men to attain,
he beheld there the Lord of the Universe.
That person who is devoted to those rites attains the state of the Supreme Brahman;
for they behold the Brahma-sūtra of the Lord of the Universe being superimposed upon the Paśyantī [level of speech]. || 520 ||
Those who rejoice in this manner together with one another attain the supreme goal,
as do those who hear this sacred rite which destroys all sins.
And they obtain that merit which arises from sacrifices and charitable works;
for a woman who has no other refuge, when urged by her husband, [attains the same]. || 522 ||
Devoted to him, virtuous, and upright in deed, thought, and speech,
she was ever free from malice toward her husband and indeed departed together with him.
Or if a twice-born man places the purifying thread upon the source of the universe, he shall indeed obtain fortune and auspiciousness without delay. || 524 ||
At the end of her body, she attains the status of being worshiped by celestial women and gods;
yet she is perceived as being below those headed by Arundhatī.
O Lotus-born One, at the end one attains that knowledge by which one goes to the imperishable state,
and by which one delivers one's kinsmen from their evil deeds.
O Brahmin, he who, being devoted with affection, gives an ornament in the name of the ancestors such as Janaka and others, becomes a minister of the all-pervading Lord whose self is the mantra. (527)
They go from an evil state to a happy state, just as by means of the bones of [the sage] Dyusindhu;
just as [the attainment of] immortality is for the gods, so is the water of the Ganges for men. 528.
Just as the *svadhā* offering is for the ancestors who perform ritual acts, so indeed is this sacred thread (*pavitraka*)—rich in ritual action—a purifier that increases prosperity. (529)
It destroys all faults and fears, annihilates all calamities, bestows all happiness, and reveals all secrets. || 530 ||
Having performed the act of completing the penances, gifts, vows, the prescribed daily rites, and the enjoyments of all sacrifices without remainder; || 531 ||
On another day, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the worshipful mantra on the fourth or even the seventh day, at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or at a confluence of rivers.
In a river flowing to the ocean, or in a natural pool, or in a lake,
for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord and for the destruction of one's own suffering.
For the delight of the immortals and for the satisfaction of the ancestors,
for the nourishment of all beings and for the welfare of the worlds.
For the sake of pacifying the calamities of the land and for the welfare of cows and Brahmins,
one should perform the ritual bathing according to the rules, especially upon an image at a sacred site (tīrtha).
Or, in the absence of that [specific] image, one should perform [the rite] upon the image used for daily bathing;
and indeed, in the absence of the image dedicated to the daily festival, one should perform it upon that [other image].
In the absence of those [lotus stalks], however, there are auspicious purifiers made from clusters of darbha grass;
O Brahmin, listen attentively as I explain the procedure for this correctly. (537)

Having previously taken a blade of darbha grass with many branches, its tip unbroken, and possessing roots, but not yet flowering, while facing east, he [should recite] the syllable *praṇava* before the ground.
Then, by that very [means], one should establish its root as before;
that liquor which remains subordinate to it becomes powerless. (539)
Having propitiated him, one should remember the Lord of Mantras as pervading [all things] with his great self;
know that to be the supreme manifestation of the Self, which is called "direct perception. (540)
That stalk which is lofty, containing many internal chambers, and is the most excellent among stalks—
endowed with qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest— it is by means of that [stalk] that the principle of the Person (puṃstattva) is conceived.
Its designator should be applied as having two characteristics and being joined with the *haṃsa*;
it is preceded by the mind (*citta*) and consists of four parts, each with four external sections. || 542 ||
Then, the face should be composed with its own words, ending in the unmanifest;
it is pervading, characterized by subtlety, and begins with the *praṇava* and ends with *namaḥ*.
In this manner, one should then bind the five [organs] beginning with the ear by their own names;
thereafter, the organs of action, and then the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra).
Then, having indeed bound the pentad of the elements ending with earth,
one should bind it like a basket with the remaining stalks.
Now, [the soul] departs from the limit of its emergence without the mass of tufts of hair, and from a certain point slightly above that, so that it does not indeed return again. || 546 ||

The collection of chapters has been arranged in many ways according to the enumeration of the principles (tattva), through the division of the various chapters and by means of one or another structural analysis. || 547 ||
Since change arises [from that], one should therefore bind it firmly;
having thus prepared the *pavitraka* made from a cluster of *darbha* grass at the outset. (548)
Therein, the meditation on the mantra is investigated as it truly is;
having worshipped with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and flowers, and having adorned [the deity], one should recite this. || 549 ||
O Blessed One, you alone are the sacred ford; you alone are the supreme sanctuary.
I know this entire world to be truly presided over by you alone.
And even there, you have prescribed the auspicious ritual procedure;
that I shall now carry out today, desiring to show you favor.
Having thus informed the Blessed One, the supreme embodiment of mantra,
one should place him upon a leaf-plate or, alternatively, upon a vessel made of *brahmaya*.
Preceded by the sounds of Vedic chants, conch shells, and auspicious music,
he led [the image] to the vicinity of the sacred ford and set it down there on the bank.
Taking that vehicle facing east and the purificatory grass (pavitraka),
one should place it upon the palm of the left hand as if it were situated within a mandala of the earth.
Having held it by its middle portion with his right hand,
he should descend into the midst of the water and immerse himself together with it.
At that very time, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) located throughout the three worlds indeed quickly assembled there in their entirety.
Wherever the mantra-soul remains for even a moment in a body of water for the sake of protection,
there occurs the convergence of all sacred abodes and holy fords.
How much more so when the Blessed One, Adhokṣaja, whose form is mantra, bathes at the request of the practitioner with a mind intent on bestowing grace upon all? (558)
The wise man who, knowing the truth, reaches a sacred ford (tīrtha) by this rite and bathes his kinsmen and others, they shall soon attain [the desired goal]. || 559 ||
The fruit of the sacred ford is obtained without effort through the grace of the one whose form is mantra;
however, that ritual procedure should be devoid of vehicles and musical instruments.
O one of great intelligence, know this distinction regarding this action:
that which is common, indestructible, consisting of consciousness, and devoid of form. (561)
Having meditated upon that swan of the individual soul (jīvahaṃsa) as connected with specific knowledge,
and having remembered the sacred thread (pavitraka) in that same form, it should then be immersed in water.
In this manner, the bathing on the seat (viṣṭara) must always be performed by him alone for others, or by many for many, even when they are situated at a distance.
O Mahāmati, when the ceremonial bathing is thus completed on the second day,
one should place him upon a consecrated chariot and worship him according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the festival known as the Yātrā, preceded by the distribution of food, accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music, and joined with a night vigil. || 565 ||
For one night, two nights, or three nights with devotion, at the end of the year, one should perform the festival consisting of the ritual bathing and other rites. || 566 ||

He who performs [this] for the Lord of Mantras attains supreme accomplishment (siddhi), whether during the ritual of lulling to sleep or awakening [the deity], or during the annual festival. || 567 ||
Likewise, O twice-born one, [this applies] to the rite of consecration with a thousand jars,
as well as to the planting of sprouts and the donning of the mantra-limbs as ornaments.
In various types of consecrations, even in the rite of restoring dilapidated temples, in principal expiatory rites, and also in the Tulābhāra and other such ceremonies; || 569 ||
In this manner, regarding such signs as well as those desired ones,
and at times such as the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and others, one should perform the rite preceded by sacrifice.
Regarding the arrangement of the sacrificial pavilion and the ritual of worship at the four locations,
there is indeed this specific procedure to be performed on the day before the day of the rite.
The preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) should take place during the night, and the ritual act should be performed at dawn;
however, in the case of festivals, the adhivāsa occurs on the very day the commencement begins.

O best of Brahmins, one should perform that rite at night, preceded by the worship of the water-pot and other items; in the case of flower-sacrifices, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) immediately.
And prior to the sprinkling, there should be the acts consisting of burning and nourishing;
or rather, that [burning] may occur everywhere immediately, according to the requirements of place and time.
O twice-born one, during the ritual of sleep (prasvāpa), one should perform the excellent sacrifice named Svastika;
however, during the ritual of awakening (prabodha), one should perform that called Viveka, or any one of the [other] Vyūhas.
For in the festival, O Brahmin, there is either a single lotus, or many lotuses, or a circle of lotuses,
adorned on all sides by those who are like mere axes.
Or even by those hidden within a scythe, or resembling lotus petals, having the shape of blue lotus leaves, or appearing like barley or anthills. || 577 ||
Or one may perform the sacrifice known as Navanābha, for it is the most excellent of sacrifices;
or else, [one may perform it] in sequence for those [deities] ending with Kumbhodara, such as Vṛtta and the others.
Of all nine images, each one [should be worshipped] every day,
beginning from the first day up until the ninth day.
Or one may perform the sacrifice known as Vyūha, provided with nine lotuses;
or else, from a four-petaled array up to an eight-petaled lotus.
Of the nine Vyūha-sacrifices, each one is performed in due order;
the rule known as the "ninefold number" applies to that festival of equal count.
On another day, whether fewer or more days have passed, or on the ninth day during a festival,
the procedure for the single lotus and so forth shall be common to both.
O twice-born one, in the flower sacrifice performed at all times, one should fashion a lotus-wheel joined with the petals of the citron fruit within the infinite vessel.

Likewise, for the planting of the desired sprout, one should employ the wheel-lotus (cakrāmbuja) in various consecrations; in those [consecrations], one should install the Lord within the wheel-lotus.
O twice-born one, whether in an array of whatever form is desired, or in that called Bhūtāvāsa, or in the one known as Dhruva which is eternal; || 585 ||
For it is exactly thus, O Mahāmati, in all rituals such as the restoration of dilapidated temples,
and indeed in all rites preceded by the formal acquisition of land.
But when an occasion for expiation has arisen, such as the occurrence of caste-confusion (saṃkara) and the like,
one should always fashion a lotus-wheel joined with the desired spokes.

The same applies to the Tulābhāra and other such rites; alternatively, they may be performed according to one's specific desires during the two or four transits, beginning with the transit into Aries. || 588 ||
In the *Sadadhva*, the *Dharmākhyā*, the *Vasugarbha*, the *Krama*,
the *Sarvakāmya*, the *Amitraghna*, the *Āyuṣya*, and the *Balabhadra* [Tantras], respectively.
One should worship the imperishable, lotus-eyed Lord during the period of health,
as well as during the two solstices known as Mānasa, which bestow the power of eloquence.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, it is indeed Jaya and Ananta;
on the two twelfth days, they are named Supratiṣṭhā and Buddhyādhāra in the first two [months]. || 591 ||
On other auspicious lunar days known as Amogha,
and under favorable constellations, one should perform sacrifice in the Guṇākara shrine.
One should indeed perform the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) in the sacrifice known as Śaṅkhodara, or the worship of the God of gods in the sacrifice called Śāntika. || 593 ||
In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), the all-pervading Lord should be worshipped either according to the specific sacrifice, or within the Kaustubha gem, or within the garland of forest flowers.
One should worship the Lord for the purpose of protection, for the destruction of enemies, or for health;
likewise, one may worship Him during the rite of nourishment known as the "half-moon" or when the lunar disc is full.
In the sacrifice called Kaja, or in the Kumbhodara rite,
one who seeks dharma should constantly worship Janārdana, the God of gods.
One who seeks wealth should constantly worship the deities of the six paths in the [mandala] called Dharma, or in Aghanirmocana, specifically the mace Kaumodakī within the lotus.
One who desires specific fruits should perform the sacrifice named Vasugarbha, or alternatively the Sarvatobhadra, which is called the bestower of all desires. || 598 ||
Victory and the attainment of sovereignty [result from] the hundred-spoked mixed wheel-king;
or the thousand-spoked mixed [wheel], or the mixed lotus-wheel-king. (599)

One who seeks liberation [should contemplate] the lotus of the wheel in the sacrifice of supreme bliss, which is filled with desire, number, and flavor, and culminates in the thousand-spoked [lotus]. 600.
It is adorned with spokes numbering one thousand, or else it is the Miśracakra (Mixed Wheel), embellished with that same number of spokes. || 601 ||
In all these sacrifices and in all ritual acts whatsoever,
one should worship Vāsudeva, the eternal Lord of the World.
The ritual of sleep and the ritual of awakening, the annual festival,
the consecration of the sacred thread, and likewise the various rites of installation.
Regarding the rites for the restoration of dilapidated temples, the performance of the *tulā-puruṣa*, *bhāra-puruṣa*, and other such acts,
as well as the primary expiatory rituals (*prāyaścitta*), these are excluded from [the category of] ordinary ritual acts.
O best of the twice-born, in all other rites known as occasional (naimittika),
one should worship the deity in an alternative manner (anukalpa) without using a water-pot or a mandala.
The method of atonement is indeed diverse, divided into three groups according to the classification of superior and so forth, [performed] in the pitcher, the mandala, and the ground. || 606 ||
One should sacrifice to the deity in the fire using the image according to the most excellent of methods;
one should sacrifice to the Lord situated within the fire of the pitcher and the mandala according to the middling method.
O twice-born one, in that lowest [form], one should worship the omnipresent Lord in the water-pot and in the fire;
or one may worship the Lord in the image and in the fire according to the teacher's wish.
One should bathe the medium and supreme [deities] with ablutions arising from the supreme division;
one should bathe the Lord with the four divisions mentioned previously.
In due order, one should satisfy the Lord in the four [fires] beginning with the middle-middle and ending with the lowest-lowest; in the other fire, one should likewise satisfy the All-pervading One.
In all expiatory rites,
one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the suitability of the place, time, one's own capacity, the material substances, and so forth.
O best of Brahmins, learn from me the number of days for all expiatory rites, including the worship performed at the four locations and the tenfold types [of service]. 612.
Forty days, thirty, twenty, fifteen, ten, and finally one day, in this sequence. (613)
Thus, the number of days is proclaimed to be of eighteen kinds;
or, according to the ninefold division beginning with the "most excellent of the excellent" (uttamottama), it is ninefold.
Then, following the sequence of two by two, the final [period] consists of two and one days;
the various types of penance have been mentioned here incidentally. (615)
"I shall indeed explain it in detail further on, O Mahāmati.
Thus has the purifying rite been correctly described by me.
Beyond this, O best of sages, what else do you wish to hear? (616)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Pavitra," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
Śrīḥ!
The Thirteenth Chapter: Sanaka [speaks] while the Lord of the World is lying down in the midst of the Cāturmāsya.
O best among the wise, you have described the ritual for ascending the sacred grass (pavitrārohaṇa).
What is this so-called "sleeping of the god"? What deity will sleep?
For what purpose does the god sleep? Tell me likewise what the ritual procedure is. || 2 ||
What are the mantras? What are the observances? What are his vows and what is his ritual action? What is to be accepted and what is to be abandoned while the Lord Janārdana is asleep? (3)
O Śāṇḍilya, listen; I shall tell you that which is more secret than the secret itself.
Formerly, [the Lord] was gratified by the power of my penance through Yoganidrā.
Thus entreated by the words "Honor my body," the Lord of the worlds looked at his own chest, which was occupied by Lakṣmī.
His arms were beautifully adorned with the conch, the discus, the sword, the Śārṅga bow, and other weapons; and from below the navel, he was supported by the bird Vainateya.
His head was covered by a crown and his pair of ears by two earrings;
then, being well-pleased, he respectfully bestowed upon his eyes their proper place.
"Delighted, you shall go to dwell for the four months of the rainy season";
hearing those words, even Yoganidrā’s hair stood on end with joy.
O lord of the twice-born, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, he made his eyes the abode of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow to an exceeding degree.
Then, at the beginning of that very day of the month known as Kaumuda,
the Lord, the Sovereign of All, honored her as she stood before his eyes.
Sleeping upon the couch of the serpent Śeṣa in yogic sleep, the great sleep,
his feet washed by the crests of the waves of the milk-ocean waters, he remained composed in meditation.
His two feet being gently massaged by the lotus-hands of Lakṣmī,
Janārdana awakens when the winter season has set in.
O twice-born one, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, though he indulges in that sleep by his own will for the sake of performing his activities, the Lord does not fall into insentience.
Just as an ordinary person who is asleep, with a defiled mind, becomes an agent of no actions whatsoever, being overcome by yogic sleep (yoganidrā). || 14 ||
The Creator of the world is not such [as you think], for he is immeasurable, eternal, awakened, omniscient, constant, unborn, and the Supreme Lord. || 15 ||
His defects such as sleep and the like constantly come under control;
for when the stainless Acyuta is fast asleep, he is indeed free from the defects of sleep and so forth.
All the rites for the four castes ceased entirely:
marriage, the binding of the sacred thread, the tonsure ceremony, and initiation. (17)

One should avoid performing sacrifices, entering a new house, the gift of a cow, the worship of deities, the consecration of images, and whatever other meritorious rites there may be during the southern course of the sun (the winter solstice).

One should avoid that month which is non-transitional (asaṅkrānta), whether in the context of divine or ancestral rites; it is considered impure and defiled, being devoid of the sun's transit. || 19 ||
He performed the occasional rites month by month as well as the annual festivals,
joined with special sacrifices, except for those that complete all [the requirements].
During these four months, no other occasional (naimittika) or optional (kāmya) rite should be performed;
rather, those four months should be spent by resorting to the vow of fasting (abīṣṭavrata).
Listen further to what else should be done by those proficient in devotion to the Blessed One:
one should construct a bed-chamber in front of the temple of Viṣṇu.
From the first six cubits up to the limit of fourteen cubits, it should be provided with pillars,
smeared with plaster, and beautifully colored with various pigments.
Likewise, one should fill the upper portion of the wall with various forms created by painting,
such as the images of Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Candra, and Arka, as well as other [deities] fashioned by wise artists.
O Brahmin, he was attended by all those belonging to the eight classes of beings who remained in a state of submission—
by brahminical sages, perfected beings, and humans, as well as by other devotees and even by the asuras.
And by various Apsarases, adorned with all ornaments and with palms joined in reverence, [the Lord was praised] as they stood face-to-face before the God of gods. || 26 ||
Having thus prepared the bedchamber adorned with garments and other ornaments,
O twice-born one, one should then occupy the place of Brahmā within it.
On the ground, one should use stakes made from auspicious sacrificial wood, measuring one, two, four, or eight cubits in length, with their respective lengths being equal at the corners. || 28 ||
The altar should be made very smooth and provided with four archways;
above that, however, there should be a canopy adorned in its center with a lotus.
One should adorn it with hanging flower garlands, bells, chowries, and mirrors,
as well as with ornaments made of gold and silver, such as water-bubble-shaped pendants and the like.
It was variegated with pearls, sapphire, lapis lazuli, and rubies,
as well as with various white and other colored cloths, banners, and standards.
It is joined with elevated pillars in the eastern and other directions known as Khagendra, Tāla, Makara, and Ṛśya, and it is endowed with full jars at the corners.
She was surrounded on all sides by various collections of vessels filled with seeds, fragrances such as cinnamon and cardamom, and shining with excellent fruits.
One should prepare an altar for the Teacher of the World, strewn with various flowers, anointed with sandalwood and other unguents, and covered with variegated cloths. (34)
Having thus first prepared a beautiful bedchamber, he should provide a bed endowed with auspicious characteristics and its frame variegated with gold and jewels. (35)

It was adorned with figures of eagles, palm trees, sea-monsters, and rishyas situated at the cardinal points; it was joined with mouths like those of sea-monsters and possessed feet resembling those of tigers.
Alternatively, O Brahmin, one should arrange a bed for the primary form of Viṣṇu to the right of the inner sanctum, or in one's own home as a secondary alternative.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, having previously prepared everything according to his means and having gathered all the necessary materials, on the tenth day—
Having prepared the aforementioned sacrificial pavilion according to the previously stated rite,
the one known as the Lord of Teachers should enter it at the onset of night on the eleventh lunar day.
One should perform worship as before in the water-pot, on the mandala, and upon the ground;
then, having entered, one should perform worship in the primary form (mūlamūrti) as previously described.
Therefore, one should perform [the rite] upon the processional image (yātrāmūrti) when it is fit for bathing;
otherwise, one should satisfy the mantra with seven pieces of fuel wood (samidh) in the fire, in due order. || 41 ||
Having reached the sacrificial pavilion, he should pass the night in vigil;
then, when the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, he should rise from his bed.
Having bathed and performed his daily rites,
O Brahmin, he should then complete the previously mentioned mandala by means of various colored powders.
Having first worshipped the Kumbha and Maṇḍala in due order,
one should thereafter [worship] the occasional image (naimittika-bimba) in the western part of the pavilion.
Having established [the deity], one should perform the sacrifice properly with manifest enjoyments arising in their proper sequence,
numbering sixty-four, consisting of various items fit for consumption.

Then, O Brahman, having thus performed the worship with tactile offerings known as "heart-pleasing" (hṛdayaṅgama), one should perform the ritual specifically according to the rules up to the end of the oblation (homa). || 46 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should offer oblations to Indra and the other guardians of the world;
then, having dismissed the Lord of Mantras who resides in the pitcher, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit.
One should worship Viṣvaksena along with his limbs (attendants) with offerings in the center of the maṇḍala;
thereafter, one should cause that manifestation of the Blessed Lord to enter within the temple.

O high-minded one, having caused the primary image to enter [the temple] according to the procedure prescribed for festivals and adorned with all ornaments, one should then proceed with the invocation.
Having worshipped with the water of honor (arghya), with scents and flowers, and with very beautiful incense,
one should invoke [the deity] from the primary image (mūlamūrti) into the image intended for the bed.
Having brought her to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice, one should bathe her in due order,
having adorned her with brilliant ornaments ending with anklets.
She was anointed with sandalwood, moon-fragrance, and bāhlīka, adorned with flowers,
veiled with a cloth for the eyes, and well-perfumed with refined incense.
O Sage, one should worship with all one's wealth and with various purifying offerings; or else, O Brahmin, the preceptor may perform it as permitted by the Guru.
First, one should worship this form preceded by the ritual bathing;
then, when the onset of night has arrived, the preceptor, together with the practitioners, [should proceed].
Having circumambulated the palace four times by whichever vehicle is preferred, or having circumambulated all the surrounding enclosures; 55.
And together with the brahmins who follow the Ekāyana Veda, those lords of the twice-born who observe the five-fold daily rites,
who are steadfast in the Siddhānta, devoted to its prescribed duties, and absorbed in the Blessed Lord.

O twice-born one, having performed the worship of the door-keepers with offerings of water for the guest (arghya), flowers, perfumes, and unguents, while reciting auspicious verses and holding flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) in their hands. || 57 ||
O Lord, abode of Lakṣmī, sovereign one who reclines upon the couch of enjoyments, quickly destroy the multitude of my sins and the web of obstacles. 58.
Reciting this mantra correctly, joined with the syllables *praṇava* and *brahman*, one should enter the bedchamber while recollecting the mantra in one's heart. (59)
Then, having placed the image facing east upon a golden seat in the western part of the sleeping chamber—just as it was when it was in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha)—[one should proceed]. || 60 ||
Having placed it facing the door and seated himself there,
O twice-born one, he should then sprinkle the surface of the bed with the five products of the cow.
Having smeared it with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood,
one should fashion an auspicious svastika of subtle characteristics in its center.
O Sage, one should fashion it with white, reddish, yellow, and black minerals,
or with the fourfold colored powder produced from jewels.
It was provided with a head-pillow, furnished with a bolster and a pillow-case,
equipped with side-cushions, and provided with a footstool.
Having prepared a bed provided with a canopy-cloth resembling a spread of moonlight, and well-perfumed, he likewise placed [the image] upon it. (65)
O twice-born one, the image should be placed upon its bed in the primary icon with its head facing either north-east or east, according to what is appropriate.
Then, O Brahman, having taken up a region in that southern direction,
on that most auspicious bed, white as the moon— || 67 ||
O high-minded one, [visualize] the King of Serpents, white as snow, jasmine, or the moon, possessing a crown of a thousand hoods, residing within the ocean of milk. 68.

Having meditated upon [the deity] with the syllable *praṇava*, one's own name ending in a vowel and accompanied by the nasal bindu, and having worshipped, praised, bowed down, and propitiated [them]; || 69 ||
Having established that image therein, either alone or together with Śrī, one should [install] one's own seed-syllable purified by mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Lakṣmī. (70)

Having set forth [the mantra] with his intellect according to the sequence of the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga), by means of the twelve syllables joined with the words of his own name. || 71 ||
Having offered perfumes, garlands, and incense to the Lord reclining on the couch,
one should worship Him according to the previously mentioned rite with all the enjoyments as prescribed.
Then, O twice-born one, having consecrated a new pit within, one should summon the splendor (tejas) into it and deposit it with this mantra: || 73 ||
O Hutāśana, O Lord, O carrier of oblations, come;
establish your presence for four months in this sacrificial pit and in this jar. (74)
Then, having invoked the Lord of Gods, one should offer libations in the prescribed sequence as before;
having completed the fire sacrifice and performed worship with the arghya and other offerings, one should recite this: || 75 ||
When you, the Lord of the World, are asleep, this entire world is asleep;
when you awaken, the whole world, including all that is mobile and immobile, awakens. || 76 ||
Having spread a white silk cloth over it and perfumed it with incense, he should offer worship upon it with flowers, incense, and ointments. || 77 ||
One should place the power of thought that encompasses all sentient beings [in the left];
on the right, however, one should place the form named Abhimāna, with a chowrie raised.
Thus, on the left [side], Jñānā holds a palm-leaf fan raised in her hand;
Nidrā is at the position of the head, intent on massaging it with her hands. (79)
Cradling with her lotus-hands the one who dwells at the region of the lotus-feet,
she took hold of the two divine feet— Śrī herself, who rests upon a treasure-vessel.
Bliss is the form of Brahman; the God, the Supreme Deity, [resides] within that.
Her eyes were filled with wonder born from the bliss of remembering Him. (81)
They should be worshipped with their own name-mantras preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava). [The image may be made of] silver, gold, copper, or bronze. (82)
In the matters of lying down and rising, each preceding one should be considered more auspicious than the following;
if a king should act in reverse order, his kingdom perishes. (83)
In the absence of all these, one should then perform it upon a seat made of a cluster of darbha grass;
for in this manner, O best of the twice-born, having established the bed of the God, [one should proceed].
In the presence of that very deity, a person should personally undertake the observances with his own voice for the four months of the rainy season, until the time of the deity's awakening.
Whether a woman or a man, one who is devoted to Him, seeking righteousness, and firm in his vows,
should undertake these observances, beginning with the cleansing of the teeth.
I shall describe the fruits for those who perform these acts individually:
by avoiding jaggery, O Brahmin, a man becomes sweet-voiced.
One obtains a long lineage by abstaining from the use of oil;
O Brahmin, by abstaining from anointing the body, one is born with beautiful limbs. (88)
By renouncing pungent oil, one shall attain the abode of Śakra;
by renouncing scented oil, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune. (89)
By renouncing the enjoyment of flowers and other such things, one becomes a Vidyādhara in heaven;
but he who practices yoga shall attain the state of Brahman.
He who avoids anointing himself with musk, saffron powder, sandalwood, and other such unguents shall not incur deformity or foul odor. (91)
By abstaining from betel, one who enjoys such pleasures becomes possessed of a red throat;
by the renunciation of ghee, he attains loveliness and his entire body becomes smooth.
By the renunciation of fruits, the wise man becomes possessed of many sons;
by the abandonment of foot-unguents and the avoidance of head-massage [he gains these benefits]. (93)
Radiant and a performer of brilliant deeds, he becomes the manifest lord of wealth;
by the discipline of consuming curd, milk, and buttermilk, a man attains Goloka. || 94 ||
By refraining from the *sthālīpāka* offering, one attains the status of being Indra’s guest;
and by not eating cooked food, one obtains long-lasting progeny. (95)
Sleeping on a mat upon the ground, one becomes an attendant of Viṣṇu;
by always avoiding honey and meat, one is forever a sage and forever a yogi.
By such renunciations as these, one becomes a possessor of dharma and a delighter in dharma;
by fasting on every other day, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
For one who plucks out their nails and body hair, there is a daily bath in the Gaṅgā;
for one who observes the vow of silence, his command shall be equal to that of the Lord's.
One who is proficient in these twelve syllables shall attain the supreme state;
by chanting the name "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," one obtains the fruit of reciting a hundred names.
By bowing at the feet of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit born of the gift of a cow;
by the touch of the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
O Brahmin, that man who performs the smearing and sweeping in the temple of Viṣṇu shall remain for the duration of a kalpa; of this there is no doubt. || 101 ||
He who recites hymns of praise while performing a hundred circumambulations shall go to the city of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot drawn by swans.
One who performs singing and instrumental music for Viṣṇu shall attain the world of the Gandharvas;
having performed a divine circumambulation, he shall go to the abode of the Apsarases.
He who constantly enlightens the people through the diversion of sacred scriptures shall, in the form of Vyāsa, go to the city of Viṣṇu at the end before Viṣṇu himself. || 104 ||
Having performed worship with garlands of flowers, one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
that man who bathes in the morning does not go to hell. 105.
He who refrains from food shall obtain the Pauṣkara bath;
by bathing in the water of the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Hari, he shall attain a stainless body.
O Brahmin, by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
the man who eats from leaves obtains the fruit of Kurukṣetra. || 107 ||
By eating constantly from a stone slab and bathing at Prayāga, one obtains the merit thereof;
by abstaining from food for two watches of the day, one is not overcome by diseases.
The God, being thus gratified by these and other such vows, attains satisfaction;
and in whatever region a devotee of Him spends four months, [there he is honored]. || 109 ||
With a noble mind, by means of various vows and great observances, he shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for an entire kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
Having explained to the eminent brahmins who had eaten what the rule for the four months of the rainy season was, he gave them that as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having given [the gifts], he should dismiss the Brahmins, and then he himself should eat;
or he may practice the observance of eating only at night during those four months.
Thus, O twice-born one, the wise man who performs this practice shall attain infinite merit; for him, the Cāturmāsya vow dedicated to Viṣṇu reaches its completion.
He would indeed have accomplished all that was to be done and would not become a human again;
at the end of that [existence], having attained birth in the home of the pure and the prosperous, || 114 ||
