Having understood the scripture as the sole path and having correctly performed the thirteenfold ritual arising from it, one attains the Blessed One. || 115 ||
Having thus resolved upon the other observances enjoined by the scriptures, one should perform daily worship, as well as the ritual sprinkling and the smearing [of the ground]. (116)
The offering of incense and lamps with clay, or with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like, and the production of a breeze by means of a fan. || 117 ||
The ritual was performed with cool water mixed with moonbeams and sandalwood, along with plantains, fruits, and white water-lilies, interspersed with red and blue lotuses. || 118 ||
Having brought about the cessation of perspiration, one should perform worship repeatedly, along with sweet-sounding songs accompanied by flutes and lutes. || 119 ||
Thus, when two months had passed and the roar of the clouds had subsided from the sky,
O Brahman, on the twelfth day of the month of Bhādrapada, at the onset of night— (120)
Relying upon a slight awakening, the God of gods, Adhokṣaja,
indeed performs his rotation for the sake of the stability of the immortals.
Having cast off her as she lay on her back, he embraced her with his right arm,
and resorting to yogic sleep, he brought about both the creation and the dissolution [of the world].
Then, having removed the veil of the sky from the orb of his moon-like face, [he revealed] the mass of seed-syllables of the universe situated within the wheel of wind.
And on the twelfth day of the month of Āśvayuja, the Supreme Lord,
having abandoned his divine bed during the night of Kārttika, remains [awake].
Then Amarānātha, the king of birds, having risen and taken his stride,
acted for the sake of pacifying the defects of all the pathways of the multitude of worlds.
He, whose nature is immeasurable, wanders about gladdening the gods and others, and bringing joy to this world by [establishing] the path of dharma for those of virtuous deeds. 126.
In this manner, his devotees should perform those great deeds of his through various festivals, gifts, prayers, vigils, and hymns of praise. || 127 ||
They sported with graceful gestures accompanied by dance and song, joined with laughter; they were well-disposed, self-controlled, and bowed down before the Lord.
O Brahmin, those who remain in one place with unwavering minds should always perform the circumambulation preceded by a special sacrifice. (129)
In the same manner, at the time of dawn, the seat is prepared;
thereafter, one should perform the awakening of the Lord while He remains upon His bed.
O twice-born one, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika,
the wise man should duly perform the formal vow (saṃkalpa) as previously described on the tenth day.
Likewise, on the eleventh day, one should issue an invitation to the twice-born;
having performed worship as before for the Lord established in the four stations. (132)
At night, the preceptor, together with his companions, should keep a vigil with meritorious narratives and songs preceded by hymns of praise. || 133 ||
With savory and sweet dances, with joyful jests, with shouts of victory, with prostrations accompanied by the clapping of hands. || 134 ||
Having fasted and bathed, being pure, he worshipped the Supreme Lord with offerings consisting of foods filled with the six flavors and with abundant ritual services.
On the twelfth day, during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should awaken the Lord, who is the embodiment of the mantra, with offerings of water for honor (arghya), ointments, garlands, and refined incense.
Awaken, O Lord of the World! Awaken, O Supreme Lord!
Awaken, O Lotus-eyed One, out of compassion for your devotees! 137.
O Lord of Gods, since you have awakened, O Supreme Lord, I shall perform before you here those sacrifices that belong to the worldly realm. (138)
O Lord of the World, you are always the sovereign by name at the forefront of all sacrifices,
and not when other gods are being worshipped.
May the completion of the sacrifice take place when you have satisfied the fire;
for all the gods who have fire as their mouth, and that very fire itself, has been placed within your mouth. 140.
Brahmā himself in the world of Brahmā, the inhabitants of heaven in heaven, the sattvic beings in the world of humans, and the nāgas and others in the netherworld (rasātala). 141.
These [senses] are always awakening You for the sake of accomplishing their own purposes;
O Eternal One, abandon Your yogic sleep and show compassion. 142.
Reciting the mantra, "May awakening come to me, not non-awakening," he chanted:
"Arise, O Brahmanaspati! Upward [to] that Jātavedas! (143)
"Vishnu strode through this [universe]; in three places he planted his step. His station is gathered together in the highest heaven; Svāhā! || 144 ||
He was conquered by that exalted speech, through its application both collectively and individually, accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and large drums. || 145 ||
O Great-minded One, with the loud and various words uttered by the throngs of bards, and with the repeated cries of "Great Victory! Victory! that were proclaimed again and again; || 146 ||
Then, having awakened [the deity] from his bed with hymns characterized by the nature of awakening,
and having worshipped him with offerings of water for the feet, scents, and so forth, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
Having filled the mandala with the desired colors and consecrated it,
one should first perform the worship of the jar and the mandala according to the prescribed rule.

Thereafter, one should worship the Festival Image (utsavamūrti) in the western part of the maṇḍala with full and appropriate enjoyments, preceded by the great ceremonial bathing (mahāsnapana). || 149 ||

Having performed the fire-oblation according to the rules, O twice-born one, he should satisfy [the deity] on all sides with verses arising from the Ekāyanīya Śākhā that directly expound that [truth]. 150.
With divine mantras such as the *balā* mantras, which are all-pervasive and accompanied by the *praṇava*;
and with various kinds of hymns and mantras originating from the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas. || 151 ||
Then, while various songs, dances, instrumental music, stringed instruments,
and so forth are thus proceeding, he should go to the bedchamber.
O great sage, having awakened him according to the rules, one should bathe the Lord as before; and having worshipped him with devotion in the proper sequence, [one should proceed]. (153)
O Brahmin, with great collections of riches, flowers, incense, and unguents, with various kinds of food offerings, preceded by hymns of praise and musical instruments— || 154 ||
Thereafter, one should offer special oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite;
afterwards, that consecrated image of the festival should be removed from the sacrificial pavilion.
Having brought [the image] from the chariot onto vehicles as desired,
and having stationed it either in front of a palace or at the beginning of a village, one should cause it to be circumambulated.
Or, having first established it upon the crooked base, O twice-born one, he should cause it to be whirled by courtesans together with the devotees of the Lord and the citizens. 157.
[He was surrounded] by wandering mendicants and celibate students, who were devoted to silent recitation and praise,
led by the foremost of the twice-born, endowed with virtuous conduct, and dedicated to that [duty].
All of them were auspicious, wearing white garments, with banners raised in their upper hands, holding yak-tail fans in their [other] hands, and with flags uplifted in their palms. || 159 ||

Others had hands holding blue and white lotuses; other twice-born ones held cane-sticks; others held parched grain and white mustard seeds; and still others had their palms full of unbroken rice grains.
With hands holding incense burners from which the fragrance wafted beautifully,
others with hands bearing fruits and flowers, and still others raising full water-pots.
And by others always holding water-pots in their hands, bearing maces and discs, holding conchs and parasols, and carrying staffs and ploughs. || 162 ||
With those intent on proclaiming the Ṛgveda and the Brāhmaṇas, as well as those devoted to recitation and praise,
and with efforts made by female deities, there was a festival including dance, song, and other performances.
One should cause pathways to be made on all sides with various kinds of musical instruments;
one should burn fragrant incense and guggulu resin mixed separately with clarified butter.
And those seeking wealth should be satisfied with stores of riches according to one's ability, O twice-born one, as the divine vehicle of Brahmā wanders about. (165)
But whatever gift one who is devoted to the five times (pañcakāla) may give, even if it be very small,
that gift becomes multiplied a thousandfold and attains expansion therein.
He who worships with devotion the God seated upon the Brahma-vehicle with offerings of flowers, roots, and the like, as well as fruits, roots, and wealth; || 167 ||
That gift becomes multiplied a hundred thousandfold; there is no doubt about this.
Mustard seeds, unhusked rice, and flowers should be placed before and behind the Lord. (168)
O best of the twice-born, these should be cast upwards and into the eight directions;
such is the Brahma-chariot of Viṣṇu, which destroys all obstacles. (169)
Whether he wanders anywhere—in a village, a town, or a city—that region shall become free from sin, and there shall be no fear of famine. || 170 ||
Nothing is obtained through premature death according to the law; likewise, calamities, afflictions, and the like always pass away in due time.
Thieves perish there, and unrighteousness does not prevail;
the king shall be endowed with dharma, and likewise the people shall be devoted to dharma. || 172 ||
All become happy, freed from suffering and grief;
having thus circumambulated [the deity] and then cast a handful of flowers, || 173 ||
Having descended from the chariot, one should first empower the mantra through the adhiṣṭhāna of the cakra;
then, having formed the mudrā, one should worship with arghya, fragrances, and other offerings, and subsequently perform japa.
Then, one should offer an auspicious full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with clarified butter and other substances for the satiation;
and with offerings such as water for honor (arghya), incense, and primary gifts, one should ask Puruṣottama for forgiveness.
Then, having led [the disciple] to the sacrificial hall and prostrated himself again and again,
the Guru likewise went into the presence of the deity in the form of the couch.
Having circumambulated him four times, one should prostrate on the ground with the eight limbs;
O twice-born one, having thus gratified the Lord of the World, one attains the path of Brahmā and other higher realms. || 177 ||
Having established [the deity], one should now devoutly circumambulate the temple in due order;
then, having entered the inner sanctum, one should stand at the doorway facing the Lord.
Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, one should then lead [the deity] inside;
having prostrated before the primary image (mūlamūrti), one should then worship it with the guest-offering, scents, and other articles. || 179 ||
One should dismiss the mantra residing in the image of the sleeping form from that [sleeping] image;
thereafter, one should dismiss that worshipped image of the festival from the sacrificial pavilion.
One should cause [the deity] to enter the inner sanctum by way of circumambulation, and having thoroughly worshipped the deity residing in the primary image with arghya and other offerings. || 181 ||
Having praised and petitioned that Adhokṣaja, who transcends all qualities,
[he did so] further by means of this festive occasion and through sacrifices, worship, and other rites.
"O Blessed One, may you be pleased with me by what has been accomplished.
Then, having dismissed him, [he placed the vessel] in the center of the circle of jars.
Having performed the sacrifice to Gaṇeśa, one should perform his dismissal;
this applies even in the secondary ritual (anukalpa) for the deity whose function is circumambulation. || 184 ||
First, having offered libations to the Lord of the Gods residing in the Kumṇa-maṇḍala-kuṇḍa,
one should thereafter perform the circumambulation.
Alternatively, one should likewise perform the sacrifice to Vighneśa;
indeed, having first placed the Lord upon his bed at the primary time, one should proceed as before.
Then one should dismiss the deity residing in the pitcher, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit;
likewise, having offered a vehicle, a vessel, and an umbrella along with a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Brahmin, one should sleep on the bed of one's own guru, or in the absence of the twice-born, on that of the God of gods, the Lord who has assumed his root-form. || 188 ||
Placing both knees upon the ground and with palms joined in reverence, one should recite this:
"O God, Lord of All, through this beginningless action, [I seek] the entirety... (189)
"May people attain an auspicious state and enjoy supreme joy"—
having thus informed the Lord, one should then gratify the Brahmins.
O best of the twice-born, one should then perform the concluding rite (anuyāga) according to one's ability, providing various kinds of food, drink, and other offerings,
accompanied by kinsmen and servants.
One should perform the awakening of the deity lying on the bed according to this procedure;
however, when the worship of the four locations takes place in the case of the primary image (mūlamūrti). || 192 ||

Then, when the festival-form [of the deity] has been worshipped, one who is skilled in the scriptures should perform that festival; and when the sleeping-form [of the deity] has been worshipped, he should perform the rite of laying the deity to rest.
But in the absence of the manifestation for the procession, worship should take place at the primary image;
at that time, the ceremonial bathing should take place at the bathing image.
O best of the twice-born, at that time the rite should be performed upon a bed;
in its absence, however, that rite is beneficial when performed upon a couch of *darbha* grass.
Having prepared a seat upon the seat for the sake of protection, slightly smaller [than the previous one],
then there should be the ritual of the Weapon-vessel (śastrakumbha) and its festival for the Lord of Mantras (mantreśa).
Alternatively, one may perform the rite upon the seat of the Wheel-King;
in the absence of a physical vessel for the bathing, the bathing should take place in a mirror. || 197 ||
In the absence of that [image], one should offer [the ritual] and then deposit the jars in sequence;
thus has been described the deity's lying down and awakening. (198)
O twice-born one, all this that has been stated may not occur at the proper time due to lack of independence, incapacity, or perhaps the absence of wealth. (199)
In this manner, one should perform [the rites] on all the twelfth days throughout the year;
but when the year has passed, one should observe the restraint during the four-month period while remaining in a state of sleep.
The devotees must carry out the concluding rites at the end of the enjoyment of the Tulā festival;
whoever prepares a bed for Viṣṇu according to the previously mentioned rule [attains great merit]. || 201 ||
He shall soon obtain fortune as well as incomparable good luck, along with his sons, wife, and family, never at any time [deprived] by anyone. || 202 ||
Neither woman nor man shall suffer any separation;
they attain incomparable merit and obtain a long life. || 203 ||
The sick man is freed from disease, and the frightened man shall indeed be freed from fear;
he becomes unconquerable by all enemies and worthy of worship by all people. (204)
Having enjoyed various pleasures, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu—he who worships Viṣṇu with devotion as He reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa. || 205 ||
Keśava is pleased with him either by his wealth or by his devotion;
and at that time, whatever men remain there— || 206 ||
Their sins go to destruction, and at the end they go to heaven;
indeed, that Vaiṣṇava who hears this ritual for the bed [attains these rewards]. (207)
Indeed, by this method, he who performs the awakening of Viṣṇu effects the instantaneous destruction of his threefold sin. || 208 ||
O twice-born one, he who performs this rite every year according to this rule attains all his desires without exception and gains a long life. (209)
Indeed, that awakening of the Lord occurs in birth after birth;
he awakens happily, being entirely free from all defects. || 210 ||
O Brahmin, that man who is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu is worthy of being saluted by all his kinsmen and others; he shall indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
On whichever day the Lord Ananta sleeps or awakens upon his bed of the serpent in the ocean of milk,
for those who observe a fast with undivided minds on that very day—
Situated upon the shoulder of Garuḍa, it bestows a happy rebirth upon men.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Festival of Sleeping, Reclining, and Rising," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Pārameśvarasaṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ.
Chapter Fourteen:
O Brahman, please explain in detail the procedure for the ritual bathing of the [deities], Sanaka.
From which knowledge all the constant and occasional rites become complete and perfect. || 1 ||
Śāṇḍilya said:
Listen, O child of great intelligence, with an attentive mind, to the procedure for ablutions which has been composed with many divisions. (2)
One should construct a pavilion for that purpose in front of the temple,
either in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure.
Either in the third enclosure, or in the fourth, or even in the fifth;
or in the southeast, the south, the southwest, or the west.
O twice-born one, one may perform all the measurements and other rites in the northwest, the north, or the northeast, according to one's preference, just as in the sacrificial pavilion.
Without the sacrificial ground, there is no wine, nor the altar above it; likewise, there is no consecration of the jars, nor their installation, nor the ritual bathing.
It is indeed appropriate; as it is for one [teacher], so should one act by inferring [the rule] accordingly—whether there be four teachers, O Brahmin, or six, eight, or even twelve.
The patron, together with the preceptor, should choose those who are learned in the scriptures and proficient;
however, when there are many, a fixed number for them has been prescribed.
In the absence of those aforementioned numbers of experts,
one should select four, three, or even just one such Brahmins.
One should select four, six, eight, twelve, or sixteen practitioners who are skilled in the scriptures and proficient in the aforementioned rites.
Thus, in all sacrifices—whether obligatory, occasional, or for self-perfection—the prescribed number of teachers and practitioners has been declared. || 11 ||
One should never disregard the prescribed number, even in times of distress;
if one disregards it through delusion, there will be danger for both the king and the kingdom.
In the western part of the third section of the east-facing pavilion,
one should prepare the bathing pedestal by relying on the central line.
That which was situated in the east should be placed facing west; that from the north facing south;
and that from the south facing north, each according to its prescribed characteristics.
O best of the twice-born, when one intends to perform the ritual bathing upon an image or similar object used for bathing, one should then construct a pavilion in this manner.
O best of the twice-born, when one constructs the pavilion in front of the primary image, at that time one should not construct a bathing pedestal.
O best of sages, O twice-born one, on the seventh, the fifth, or even the third day prior to the day of the ceremonial bath, or indeed on that very day.
Having offered the sprouts, one should then begin the ritual bathing;
provided that on the preceding day, one has performed the consecration (adhivāsana) of the water-jars.
At that time, one should perform the tying of the protective thread (kautuka) during the first watch of the night;
if it was obstructed on the previous day, one should perform it on that very day.

O Brahmin, when one performs the consecration of the water-pot (kumbhādhivāsana) on the day of the ritual, then on that very same day one should perform the tying of the protective thread (kautukabandhana). || 20 ||
Then, at dawn, the preceptor, having performed his ablutions and being of serene mind,
entered the pavilion together with the attendants devoted to his service.
O Brahmin, facing either the east or the north, one should sprinkle [the area] on all sides with darbha grass together with śalākā stalks and mixed with sahadevī.
One should smear [the area] with fresh cow dung, starting from the east and ending in the northeast and west,
using only filtered water and a new cloth.
O Brahmin, one should sprinkle [the site] in all directions with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water mixed with kuśa grass.
For the ritual bathing (snapana), it is prescribed that there may be one, two, or even many preceptors (deśika).
All of them wore new sacred threads, were adorned with every ornament,
wore new upper garments, possessed turbans, and were endowed with the qualities of their preceptors.
There were many established in their religious observances as well as attendants;
O Brahmin, wherever anything might be suitable for the ritual bathing, they were present there.
Having gathered all that together and brought it into the pavilion,
the preceptor, who has mastered the scriptures, should thereafter commence the ceremonial bathing.
Know that ablution (snapana) is twofold, distinguished as supreme (para) and inferior (apara).
The supreme is said to be tenfold, according to the distinctions of the primary [elements] and so forth. || 28 ||
Know the first to be Pradhāna; the second is remembered as Para;
the third is Parasūkṣma, and the fourth is Parasthūla. || 29 ||
The fifth would be the subtle-superior; the sixth is the subtle-subtle;
the seventh would be the subtle-coarse; and the eighth would be the coarse-superior. || 30 ||
The ninth is both gross and subtle, and that which follows it is grosser than the gross;
know that the latter is fourfold, for each one exists in nine ways.
O best of the twice-born, by means of the highest-of-the-high distinction,
this commonality stands among these various divisions of the supreme and the non-supreme.
The ritual bathing known as Anantakalaśa fulfills all [desires];
it is performed for these aforementioned principal [deities], preceded by the laying down of the ritual cord (sūtrapāta).
O best of beings, listen in due order to everything up to the final extraction:
[the image] may be made of metal, wood, or clay, and should be very beautiful. (34)
Having placed a water vessel in the north-eastern direction of the pavilion, and having washed the altar with water, one should cover it with new cloths. || 35 ||
Then, one should perform the laying out of the lines (sūtrapāta) in accordance with the number of jars,
in the middle of the pavilion on a field as wide as the prescribed measurement.
O best of Brahmins, having taken hold of the eastern part of the pavilion, or alternatively,
having established the west, one should lay down four lines from west to east.
One should lay down five threads running from south to north;
when this is done, O twice-born one, there arise twelve squares here.
The width of each [pillar], however, should be one tāla, or a prādeśa, or a hasta, or an aratni, according to the proportions of the pavilion. || 39 ||
And for the sake of the living beings, having thus adorned all the jars everywhere above and on all four sides with flour-dust, || 40 ||
One should construct a pedestal within the compartments using either rice or *vrīhi* grain;
indeed, for each of those compartments, one should prepare [the pedestal] with a measure of one *āḍhaka*.
O Brahmin, one should prepare it with three *prasthas* and a half, or with three *prasthas* alone,
or with two and a half *prasthas*, or even with two *prasthas*.
Or else, O twice-born one, it may be with two prasthas, or with one and a half prasthas,
or with one prastha, or with half of that, or even with a quarter of it.
Then, having fashioned a pedestal that is either four-cornered or circular,
it should be made of gold, silver, or copper, and must be free from defects.
The jars should be auspiciously smooth, without holes, twenty-four finger-breadths in height, and likewise in width at the middle; their necks should be three finger-breadths high.
There, the face is considered to be six finger-breadths [in width] and three finger-breadths [in height];
O best of the twice-born, the girdle is known to extend all around for three finger-breadths.
Or else, O Brahmin, all of them may be half that measure, provided they are first increased in height; or they may be of the highest quality, filled with a drona-measure of water.
Then, the lowest-of-the-low pitchers (adhamādhamakumbhas) are successively less by one-eighth part, starting from two prasthas down to those that hold only one prastha of water.
Thus, these [altars] should be constructed according to one's wealth, endowed with the aforementioned characteristics;
they should be situated upon the wheel-base (cakrādhāra), wide and shaped like the belly of a tortoise.
O twice-born one, their necks were marked with the Pāñcajanya conch, their faces were like lotuses,
and they were adorned with circles of Kaumudī garlands suspended above and below.
Adorned with the faces of all the goddesses beginning with the letter 'Ma', they carry streams of nectar;
they are further embellished by rivers, oceans, auspicious trees, and various garlands. || 51 ||

Alternatively, when the primary materials are unavailable, they may be made of clay; however, in the case of a substitute (anukalpa), they must be devoid of cracks and fissures, and provided with the wheel-base and other [required] parts. || 52 ||
Shaped like ripe bimba fruits, free from dark spots, not double-tapped but well-tapped, they are of a single color and possess a beautiful sound. (53)
Having gathered it, one should wash it thoroughly with pure water on all sides;
then, one should carefully wrap it with thread at intervals of one finger-breadth each.
In the western direction, one should consecrate the water jars starting from the location of the central jar;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with śāli rice, or on a bare sacrificial mound.
One should spread kusha grass there with their tips pointing eastward and northward;
having placed the water jars there with the Tāra mantra and worshipped them with flowers.
Having placed those very same [blades] face downwards in a row,
and having spread kuśa grass over them, one should [place the vessel] facing eastward with the *parameṣṭhi* mantra.
Then, having displayed the darbha-mudrā and having sprinkled [the area] on all sides with scented water, one should scatter unbroken grains (akṣatas) with the Viśva-puruṣa mantra.
Having turned [the vessels] back and facing them [toward the practitioner], O best of sages, one should lift all the jars individually and place them in their respective positions in due order. (59)
One should perform all the rites, beginning with the deposition on the jars (kumbhanyāsa), using the twelve-syllable mantra;
having purified [the materials] through inspection and other means by means of the heart-mantra (sahṛdaya).
One should consecrate them one by one with the twelve-syllable mantra;
thereafter, one should worship them with that same mantra using water for honor (arghya), garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth.
One should perform the ritual of bringing that [offering] according to one's ability;
having then completed it with fullness, learn now that sequence of materials. 62.
In the three rows, from west to east, there are four in each;
therein, on the southern row, the western pitcher is situated.
Water from the dhātrī fruit, and immediately after that water from the lodhra tree;
water from red sandalwood and the excellent water from turmeric.
Then, one should likewise arrange [the offerings] in the middle row:
first the water with knots and sprouts, and then the water with *tagara*.
Next is the water of priyaṅgu, and after that the water of māṃsī;
likewise, this same quartet should be placed in the northern row.
Then there is water with white mustard seeds, followed by water with all medicinal herbs;
then water with all kinds of gems, and after that, pure water.
One should place there a broom made of kuśa or darbha grass, sixteen finger-breadths in length;
the knot should measure one finger-breadth, while the base should indeed be twelve finger-breadths.
One should know that the remainder is the tip; this is the characteristic of the *kūrca* [brush].
Alternatively, the knot may be four finger-breadths [in length], and the tip indeed two finger-breadths. || 69 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should make the base twelve finger-breadths in length;
for a Brāhmaṇa it should consist of four darbha blades, but for a Kṣatriya, three darbha blades.
The *kūrca* for Vaiśyas should consist of two *darbha* blades, and likewise for women and Śūdras;
or else, for all of them, the *kūrca* may be made of four or seven [blades].
Thereafter, O best of sages, one should worship with the root mantra and the twelvefold [mantra],
using water for the guest-offering (arghya), sprinkling, flowers, and incense.
Having covered them in sequence with the prescribed rites and wrapped with threads, one should wrap each jar with cloths if one possesses the means.
Having covered it on all sides with a new cloth, facing either east or north, and having performed worship as before, he should then commence the fire-oblation (homa). || 74 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of fuel sticks and other materials individually,
and then having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should consecrate the water jars with mantras.
O twice-born one, the bathing of all [the deities] is prescribed with the root mantra,
using jars filled with pure water in successive intervals.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the offering of the water of honor (arghyadāna) for the ritual substances;
their extraction is proclaimed to follow the very sequence in which those substances were deposited. || 77 ||
This primary [form], consisting of twelve jars, has been described;
it is the cause of all, while the others are its effects, O best of beings. (78)
Then, with water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and water containing all medicinal herbs; || 79 ||
Then, it should be filled in due order with water from seeds, water from fruit, water scented with perfumes and flowers, and finally with water containing gold and jewels.
This supreme group of twelve pitchers which has been described is filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugarcane juice.
It was filled in succession with the waters of all medicinal herbs, fragrances, jewels, fruits, and flowers,
and finally with pure water alone.
This group of twelve jars is declared to be the supreme subtle [form];
they are filled with milk, curd, ghee, honey, all kinds of fragrant substances, and scented water.
Also with water containing all medicinal herbs, with water from leaves, flowers, and fruits,
and with water from seeds combined with water containing gold and jewels.
Know this vessel, which is filled in succession with the waters of various sacred rivers,
to be twelvefold in nature and gross in form.
And other [measures] such as the laying of the thread should be treated as primary in these three cases.
When the site is divided into five parts, there shall be twenty-five sections. || 86 ||
Outside, in the sixteen pitchers arranged according to the sequence beginning with the east,
there should be milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugarcane juice.
Indeed, the ten items beginning with the dhātrī fruit and ending with all medicinal herbs,
followed by leaf-water, are placed within those eight jars.
First [he offers] water with flowers such as *prāgādī*, then water with fruits and seeds, followed by scented water, and likewise water with gold and jewels. || 89 ||
The water of the merit-pond is placed within the wine as pure water;
its extraction is declared to follow the very same sequence as the placement of the substances. || 90 ||
O best of the twice-born, this bathing performed in sequence with twenty-five jars containing the ritual substances is remembered as the subtle and supreme rite.
Having arranged twenty-five squares as before,
one should place pure water in the center, and outside of that, according to the arrangement of Indra and the other deities.
The first [vessel] was filled with milk and water; the next with pure water;
the third with jewel-water; and another with gold-water.
Another [vessel] mixed with perfumes and provided with fruits, flowers, and water, filled with rice seeds and water, is proclaimed as the eighth. 94.
Outside of that, the eight jars are situated in the eight directions:
in the east, water with dhātrī fruits; then, in the west, water with pathyā.
In this case, powdered *galūcī* [is used]; in another, *vibhītaka* water;
likewise, water boiled with *kumārī*, and also water from *vyāghrī*. (96)
In one case there is water from a city well, and likewise in another, honey-water;
in this matter, the removal [of the obstacle] is prescribed according to the sequence of depositing the substances.
O Great-minded One, [this applies] to the vases situated in the inner enclosure, in sequence, by means of the five mantras beginning with Satya and the three beginning with Siṃha. (98)
Having consecrated each one seven times starting from the east and so forth, one should consecrate the jars situated outside of them with the Cakra-mantra and the Hṛdaya-mantra and the others.

O Sage, one should bathe [the deity] in sequence with water-pots belonging to the Brahmins situated within the Gāyatrī, while the rites of worship performed by those in the second enclosure are done with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Then one should sprinkle [the disciple] with water alone over which the Astra-mantra has been recited;
or else, one should perform everything according to the very path previously described.
This is considered to be extremely subtle when measured by ten or seven *kumbhas*.
The area is four cubits, three cubits, or two and a half cubits. || 102 ||
Having prepared a space of two cubits, that half should be divided into two parts;
with one part one should fashion the pericarp, and with the other two parts, the sixteen petals.
Then, O Brahmā, one should place the petals;
and upon the pericarp, one should arrange a quartet of jars situated in the four cardinal directions. || 104 ||
First with water and flowers, then with scented water;
next with golden water, and another with water containing all kinds of jewels.
O Sage, having first begun from the eastern leaf and established sixteen other jars right there within the domain of the northeast, up to that point; 106.
First, one should fill it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) alone;
second, with cow urine; and third, with water mixed with cow dung. || 107 ||
O Brahmin, with the ash of the three sacred fires as the fourth, and furthermore with water,
and with earth from the horns of an elephant, a cow, and a bull, and from an anthill and a riverbank.
O twice-born one, the sixth jar should then be filled with earth from a field of śāli rice, from the middle of a river, from a cluster of lotuses, and from a mountain.
Know that the seventh is with mustard-water and the eighth with all medicinal herbs;
the ninth is with milk, and the tenth is said to be with curd.
O twice-born one, the eleventh [offering] is with clarified butter, the twelfth with honey;
the thirteenth is with all [kinds of] seeds, and the fourteenth with all [kinds of] fruits. || 111 ||
Another [mandala] is made with all kinds of grains, and the sixteenth with all fragrances;
having first extracted those situated on the petals according to the sequence for the placement of substances.
Thereafter, one should likewise carefully extract those [seeds] situated upon the pericarp;
having first consecrated each individual jar with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Then, O best of the twice-born, one should bathe [the deity] with each of the root mantras in succession, accompanied by twenty jars. 114.
This has been declared as the subtle and the gross; now hear the detailed account of that which is other than these.
Having laid down five threads extending from east to west, || 115 ||
One should lay down eleven threads from south to north;
when this is done, there will indeed be forty squares.
There, beginning from the row in the western direction, in successive order from south to north, there are four jars for each [direction]. (117)
Having performed the placement (vinyāsa), one should fill those [vessels] in sequence with the substances; understand that [as follows]:
the triad [of vessels] is filled with the previously mentioned substances intended for the foot-wash (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya). 118.
[The earth] originating from mountains, rivers, clay, and riverbanks, as well as from lakes, anthills, mountain peaks, and places scarred by the tusks of elephants; || 119 ||
Cow dung produced from fields, or from the horns of bulls, or from rice paddies, as well as that produced from lotus thickets, is of one kind; while in other cases, it is simply [cow] dung.
Likewise, others, having placed the ashes of the three sacred fires—arising from a forest conflagration or from a kitchen—into a water jar; || 121 ||

In another [vessel], however, there should be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) combined with water infused with kuśa grass, along with ghee, a jar of oil, and a ladle filled with water. || 122 ||
In one [vessel], there should be water decocted from palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, śamī, and red sandalwood;
in another, however, there should be water decocted from the three myrobalans (triphalā). || 123 ||
Vacā, śatāvarī, kanyā, vyāghrī, siṃhī, kṛtāñjali, golomī, siṃhalomī, kuṣṭha, and likewise bhūmyañjana. || 124 ||
And Mahāgaruḍavegā, O best of beings, as well as Kalaśā, Mahānīlā, Galūcī, Sahadevī, and Śatāvarī [are to be placed] in another jar. || 125 ||
Viṣṇukrāntā, Kārkoṭā, Sāṃhā, Vahniśikhā, Yaṣṭī, Varāhakarṇī, and Gajapippalī are [to be used] in another [preparation]. (126)
In another [vessel], he should place auspicious fruits such as the *śrīphala* and other purifying fruits,
as well as jars of curd, milk, and clarified butter, along with two jars containing honey and sugarcane juice.
And one should place the roots of lotuses in another jar,
especially those of purifying trees that yield milky sap.
In one [vessel], a cluster of blossoms provided with leaves, flowers, and fruits;
and in another, a collection of flowering creepers such as the *jāti* and others. || 129 ||
Rocanā, the two types of Rajanī, Bālamoṭā, and Pajhaka—these five, as well as Darbha and Dūrvā sprouts, [should be placed] in another [vessel]. || 130 ||
In another jar, he should indeed place a heap of rice sprouts, along with siddha-dhārthaka,
white and other grains, priyaṅgu, and that which is known as gandha.
One should place [the herbs] together with *nāgakeśara* in the other jar;
seven domestic plants and seven wild plants [should be placed] in the two jars.
Bāhlīka sandalwood, resin, and camphor—these four constitute one group; however, others hold that there are auspicious minerals in yet another set.
One should place copper, Jāmbūnada gold, and other such materials, as well as a great heap of jewels; and in two places, one should set coral clusters and pearls.

Then, he should place a vessel for the *arghya* water in one spot, and two vessels containing water from a river-tirtha in another; furthermore, a jar of all medicinal herbs and a jar of very cool water.
These forty are known as the jars of fragrant flowers;
this sequence of depositing the substances and their extraction is considered the supreme gross [level]. || 136 ||
O twice-born one, forty jars filled with cool water have been displayed, both large and small. (137)
That which is accompanied by exactly forty jars filled with scented water is proclaimed as the "very large" (sthūlasthūla). || 138 ||
O twice-born one, one should then perform the ritual for laying the lines and the sequence for placing the water-pots (kumbhas),
as well as the extraction of these two [the lines and pots], which is unlike that of the gross [elements] and so forth.
Furthermore, whether by the power of devotion and faith or according to one's means,
one should perform the threefold gross division in a twofold manner.
In the secondary rite (anukalpa), one may use half of that, or a quarter, or even an eighth;
or there may be four jars, or two for each [of the deities], or two for each.
O best of Brahmins, even if there is only one jar for each [deity], it should consist of all the prescribed materials;
beyond the nine jars that are completely filled, nothing else is required.
One should perform all that by reflecting upon it according to the path taught for the primary [form];
thus, O Brahmin, the tenfold divisions have been revealed. (143)
O best of beings, hear now the divisions of the other [mandala] in due order:
when the field has been made square and divided into thirty-one parts. || 144 ||
There are nine hundred and sixty-one squares;
having established three rows in the center, one should erase the two rows on either side of them. (145)
Having again established three rows outside that for the sake of the path,
one should erase two and establish seven more for the sake of the path.
Or, having divided each [section] into nine or three parts, O twice-born one,
he should sprinkle them as before for the sake of the paths in a crowded place using water-pots.
Gradually, one should place jars in those compartments as before:
with ghee, warm water, jewel-water, and fruit-water. || 148 ||
Iron-water, cleansing-water, scented-water, and unbroken-grain water, as well as barley-water ending with the Īśāna [deity], starting from the middle and placed in the central [vessel]. 149.
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for rinsing the mouth, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be offered in sequence;
these are placed in pairs and fours within the middle of the enclosures.

From the northeast to the end of the north, for those situated in the intermediate directions, one should place curd, milk, honey, and likewise astringent decoction in the center, following the sequence starting from the southeast. (151)
Thus, seventeen [offerings] are declared to be combined with the primary substances;
the remaining sixty-four are accompanied by pure water.
Thus, O twice-born one, eighty-one pitchers are situated in the center;
thereafter, forty-nine pitchers are placed in those eight directions.
There, one should sprinkle water from the central jars as well as those situated in the cardinal directions—namely, jujube-water, sugarcane juice, and coconut water. (154)

O best of sages, one should sprinkle the auspicious water called "Śāntivāri" into the Brahma-pitchers situated in the intermediate directions, following the sequence starting from the eastern direction. || 155 ||
From the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśa), there are three hundred and eighty-two remaining jars,
likewise increased by four.
O best of the twice-born, [one should fill it] with fragrant and cool waters;
thereafter, within the central group of nine, from the center toward the northeast and west... || 157 ||
One should worship the nine forms beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Varāha, in due order, with water for the guest-offering (arghya), anointment, garlands, and incense. || 158 ||
Outside of that, one should worship [the deities] in the Brahma-pitchers of the nine squares,
starting from Keśava and ending with Vāmana, in pairs, according to the sequence of the directions beginning with the East.
Then, O Great-minded One, there are forty-nine pitchers.
One should worship the four [deities], beginning with Śrīdhara, in the Brahma-pots.
O twice-born one, one should worship the four [deities] starting from the east and ending with the north, from Agni and ending with Īśāna, and from Nara and ending with Kṛṣṇa.
Having placed tufts of grass as before and having covered them with small bowls,
one should then cover each individually with new cloths.

Thereafter, one should worship the god Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the five products of the cow, clarified butter, and curd. || 163 ||
Milk, honey, and astringent decoction; warm water and fruit-water;
water for sprinkling, water with unbroken grains, jewel-water, and iron-water. || 164 ||
And scented water, barley water, molasses-water and sugarcane juice, as well as coconut juice, the water of pacification, and auspicious water. || 165 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should perform the ablution of the Lord according to this sequence;
O twice-born one, the ablution for all [the deities] is prescribed with the root mantra.
Alternatively, beginning with the water for the feet and ending with the scented water, one should offer [the oblations] with the verses of the Puruṣasūkta and with the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. (167)
O twice-born one, the fourfold set beginning with barley-water and sugarcane juice, ending with the rite of pacification,
[is performed] with the mantra "tvaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and "viṣṇornukaṃ".
O best of sages, one should bathe [the deity] with auspicious water and the like,
and one should consecrate the Lord of Gods with the primary pitcher.
One should consecrate him with those jars of pure water while reciting the mantra;
for each substance, however, there should be an offering of arghya, anointment, and garlands performed with a cloth.

And having worshipped him thoroughly with incense, he should then perform the consecration; whatever water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), as well as perfume, garlands, incense, and lamps [he should offer]. || 171 ||
One should offer everything in due order, or only the *arghya* alone;
[the latter] being joined with four hundred, seventy, and three [units respectively]. (172)
This bathing of the jars is indeed declared to be the most excellent of all;
that which is inferior is performed with sixty-four jars, ending with pure water.
That which is performed with water-pots (kalaśas) constitutes the superior or middling [type of bath];
likewise, a row of four [pots] would be inferior compared to what was previously determined.
This bath is appropriate when there are eighty-one [deities] in the center, forty-nine in the cardinal directions, and four in the intermediate directions. || 175 ||
O twice-born one, it was accompanied by jars placed in the portions designated for Brahmā and the gods, along with the remaining one hundred and sixty jars filled with pure water. || 176 ||
O Brahmin, that [mandala] which is devoid of pitchers becomes inferior;
however, it becomes excellent when provided with two hundred pitchers situated in the four directions. || 177 ||
O Brahmin, when the bath is performed as before, but with eighty-one [verses] instead of the four deficient ones, it becomes the "middling-superior" (madhyamottama). || 178 ||
That which is deficient by jars numbered as eight times eight (sixty-four), filled with pure internal water, would be the middling-liquor (madhyama-madya). || 179 ||
It is provided with eighty-one jars in the center,
forty-nine in the cardinal directions, and nine in the middle.
Devoid of the remaining pure water-pitchers, it is the middling-inferior [type];
one should arrange the site here as being deficient by eight rows. || 181 ||
And with eighty-one jars, O twice-born one, it is exclusively as before;
this is proclaimed as the inferior-superior ablution. || 182 ||
However, that bathing which is performed with thirty-two jars filled with pure water placed upon peacocks is considered mediocre. || 183 ||
O best of the twice-born, that which is devoid of the sixty-four jars filled with pure water situated in all directions would be the most inferior of all.
Having divided the field here into nine or seven parts, one should press [the ground];
two or four parts are left over for the purpose of installing the water-pots (kumbhas). 185.
Thus the first [type] has been described in nine ways; now hear, O best of beings, about the second:
when a square field has been divided into eighteen parts, || 186 ||
Alternatively, O Brahmin, having arranged six rows of sixteen squares each in the middle, one should then erase two [squares] for the path outside of that, O twice-born.
Or else, one should place four [vessels] outside of each of those;
having deposited the pitchers in them as before, one should pour in the ritual substances.
Then, in the four jars in the center, there is water containing all kinds of jewels;
in two [jars] pearls, in one in the eastern direction, and in one situated in the south-eastern direction.
O Brahmin, there is a vajra in the two southern [squares], a gomedaka in the one immediately following,
an indranīla in one, and then a puṣyarāga in the two that follow.
In the western [direction], however, there is one made of coral;
in the northwestern, indeed, one made of ruby; in the two northern, one made of moonstone; and in the other (the northeast), one made of coral.
O twice-born one, in the second enclosure, clarified butter is placed in two jars in the east;
in the jar situated in the south-eastern corner, there is indeed that which is comparable to fire.
Milk is in the two [vessels] situated in the south; likewise, the cleansing (mārjana) is in the southwest.
Curd is in the two situated in the west; the perfume is located in the northwest corner.
In the two northern directions, there should be honey; in the northeast corner, there should be astringent decoctions.
The remaining eight jars are to be filled with scented water. 194.
Thus, O twice-born one, there are thirty-six jars situated in the middle;
however, outside of that, there are twenty-four jars for each cardinal direction.
O twice-born one, there are sixteen jars situated at each of the intermediate directions;
and in the center of those jars situated in the eastern direction— || 196 ||
In the northern quadrangle, one should place the arghya; likewise, the pādya in the southern and western [quadrangles];
the ācamana in the northern [quadrangle]; and the pañcagavya in the central quadrangle. (197)

In the four directions starting from the southeast—namely, the southeast, south, southwest, and northwest—oil is placed in the center; molasses is in the southwest (Nirṛti); and water with sesame seeds is in the northwest (Vāyu). || 198 ||

The unbroken [grains] are placed in the vessel situated in the direction of Īśa; indeed, there are one hundred and twenty-eight [vessels], while the remaining jars are filled with scented water. || 199 ||
The sequence for extraction is intended to extend from the *arghya* offering up to all the gems;
first the *arghya*, then the *pādya*, then the *ācamana*, and after that the *pañcagavya*. (200)
Oil, molasses-water, sesame-water, and unbroken-rice water; likewise clarified butter, water for sprinkling, milk, and the water for rinsing. || 201 ||
Curd, fragrance, honey, astringent decoction, and likewise pearl—O twice-born one, these eight, beginning with the diamond and ending with all other gems, are to be offered in sequence. (202)
Combined with two hundred and four jars,
this is declared to be the bath known as the "most excellent of the excellent."
When the field has been made square and divided into fourteen parts, there will be one hundred and ninety-six squares here.
Having established four rows in the center, one should sweep them;
and one should place four [seeds] each in the outer pathway. || 205 ||
There too, for the purpose of placing the water-pots within the compartments, one should establish one hundred and eight; the remaining ones should be wiped clean.
As before, having placed the jars upon them, one should deposit the ritual substances;
one should place a collection of jewels in the center and four jars [around it]. || 207 ||
O twice-born one, to the south of the eastern meridian-line, place a pearl in the pitcher;
to the south of this, there should be a diamond and a gomedaka gem in sequence.
O twice-born one, there is sapphire and topaz in the two [gems] situated in the west; likewise, there is beryl and moonstone in the two situated in the direction of Soma (the north). 209.
O twice-born one, coral [is placed] in the pitcher to the north of the thread extending from east to west;
thus, there are twelve pitchers in the eight directions surrounding the center.
O best of the twice-born, there are twelve jars for each direction;
in the midst of those, within the four jars starting from the eastern direction— || 211 ||
The arghya, oil, water for the feet, water with gulāla for rinsing the mouth,
water with sesame seeds, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and unbroken rice grains— these are placed to the west of Īśa.
The remaining sixty-four jars are filled with scented water;
the sequence of extraction is prescribed as beginning with the *arghya* offering and ending with all the jewels.
In this manner, with one hundred and eight pitchers, [the mandala] is of superior or middling quality;
it is made square and divided into thirteen parts.
Having placed the fifth of the rows in the middle, one should wipe it clean;
then one should place three [units] each in the outer path. || 215 ||
In the center is a jewel-pitcher; then, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, there are pearls, a diamond, a gomedaka gem, and a sapphire.
Puṣyarāga, brahmarāga, candrakānta, and vidruma—these are held outside that [circle], in the eastern direction and so forth, as the analogical [ornaments]. || 217 ||
Milk, water for washing, curd, perfume, honey, astringent decoction, and the remaining eight [substances] are filled with fragrant water. || 218 ||
Thus, O Brahmin, there are twenty-five jars situated in the center;
outside of that, in the eight directions, there are eight groups of nine.

In their midst, one should offer in sequence: water for honor (arghya), oil, water for the feet (pādya), jaggery-water, water for sipping (ācāma), sesame-water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise unbroken rice grains (akṣata). || 220 ||
O twice-born one, the remaining sixty-four [pots] situated from the eastern direction to the northeastern direction are filled with fragrant water and likewise provided with jars. || 221 ||
With ninety-seven [units], that becomes the highest and lowest;
indeed, when the field is divided into fifteen parts, there are [these] divisions. (222)
O best of sages, there are two hundred and twenty-five rows;
five of these are in the center, and one should erase two outside of that.
O twice-born one, having gone outside that [area], he should establish a triad for the sake of the pathway;
in the center of that, however, he should place a jewel-pitcher within the four [vessels] situated in the cardinal directions.

The eight jewels, beginning with pearl, are placed in pairs according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east and ending in the northeast; outside of that, they are placed upon the eight jars.
O twice-born one, there is a group of eight substances beginning with ghee and ending with decoctions;
and for the nine [groups] beginning with Aindra, O twice-born one, there are eight in the middle.
From the *arghya* offering up to the *akṣata*, in sequence from the northeast to the west;
the remaining sixty-four jars are filled with scented water. || 227 ||
This [mandala], provided with eighty-five jars, shall be of medium-superior quality;
in the medium [variety], however, there is water containing jewels, and outside of that, eight jars.
Combined with substances such as pearls and so forth, as before, outside the nine [vessels];
thus, with eighty-one jars, there shall be the "middling-middling" [arrangement]. (229)
When the field is divided into seven parts, there are forty-nine squares here; one should then place the pitchers.
As before, there are twenty-five jars joined with substances;
the remaining twenty are filled with pure water. || 231 ||
Thus, with forty-nine jars, there is the middling-inferior [consecration];
ten [types of substances], beginning with jewels and ending with decoctions, are joined [to these]. (232)
Eight [offerings] combined with scented water constitute the lowest of the superior;
that which is devoid of the eight pure waters would be the middle of the lowest. || 233 ||
That which consists of a set of nine jars joined with a collection of substances beginning with gems and ending with coral is the lowest of the low. || 234 ||
Thus the second division has been proclaimed; now hear the third.
Having divided the field into seven parts and established it as before, || 235 ||
Then, standing facing north, one should bind the Praṇava;
one should place its mudrā upon the pitcher in the center with the mantra known as Jitaṃta.

Facing east, he should place the divine jars with eight-syllable mantras starting from the eastern direction; facing northeast, he should place the human ones with twelve-syllable mantras, numbering sixteen.

O Brahmin, facing west and north, one should place the paternal mantras with the utterance of "phaṭ"; having formed their respective mudrās, [one should place them] from the center toward the north-west.
O Brahmin, in the five jars, one should likewise offer water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping,
as well as the five products of the cow and clarified butter, in sequence, with the five Upaniṣads.

In the four corner-pitchers (vidikkumbha), starting from the southeast and ending in the northwest, one should place curd, milk, honey, and warm water, using the mantras that denote the forms [of the deities].
O Brahmin, with four jars placed outside in the four directions,
[one should place] decoction water, cleansing water, fruit water, and wiping water.
In the four jars from the southeast to the northeast,
one should place water containing gems, water with all metals, water with *kuśa* grass, and water with barley flour.
O best of Brahmins, one should gradually pour the eight jars filled with pure water and containing the substances mentioned for the eight syllables.

Beginning from the center of the fire in the east, extending toward the northeast, the east, the center, and the west, one should [draw] with the mantra known as the *praṇava* alone; then, outside of that.
In the four directions of the jars, however, there should be scented water, flower-water, that which is known as the "comparative" (aupamānika), and likewise water with *āmalaka* fruit. || 245 ||
In the four pitchers, following the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya),
one should place water with unbroken rice, water with sesame seeds, water with barley, and water with rice grains.
Then, O twice-born one, with the Dviṣaṭka mantra and the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
he should fill the remaining sixteen vessels with pure water in due order.
Having thus completed [the ritual], and having prostrated with the añjali-mudrā,
one should perform everything beginning with the sacrifice to Vāsudeva and the others, exactly as before.
The extraction [of the mantras] is proclaimed to follow the very sequence of the deposition of substances (dravyanyāsa).
O best of the twice-born, one should indeed offer everything with the root mantra, or else [as specified]. || 249 ||
From the hymn addressed to Viṣṇu, one should offer water for the feet and the arghya;
with the mantra "āpo vahantu," one offers water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana); and with the Gāyatrī, one offers the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 250 ||
Then, O Brahmin, one should offer clarified butter with the mantra "ghṛtaṃ śukramasi," and thereafter one should offer curd with the mantra "dadhi krāvṇa. || 251 ||
"O Kṣīra, cause us to swell!"—thus [one should address] Pāthodvāta; "O Madhu, [be] honey"—thus Āditya; and "O Śukra"—thus, O best of sages, one should address Uṣṇāmbhas.
Then, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the water of decoction while reciting the verse beginning with "śaṃdasaspatiṃ" and the mantra "śanno devīḥ. || 253 ||
One should offer water with fruit using the mantra "gaṇānām," and one should perform the ritual wiping with the mantra "tvaṃ viṣṇuḥ. || 254 ||
Then, with the mantra "agna āyāhi vītaye," water containing gems;
with "iṣetva," iron-water; and with "agnimīḷe," water containing kuśa grass. || 255 ||
Then, with the mantra "kimittah," he should offer groats mixed with water;
subsequently, he should offer eight libations of pure water in sequence with the mantra "āpo asmān. (256)
One should offer the eight substances beginning with fragrant water with the *Mānastokīya* hymn;
the remaining sixteen offerings should be presented in order, verse by verse, with the *Puruṣasūkta*.
In this way, with forty-nine jars, it is the most excellent of the excellent; with sixteen outside jars made of pure materials, it is the excellent-middle. || 258 ||
Among those situated there, that which is devoid of the corner pitchers (koṇakalaśa) would be inferior;
[the arrangement] where eight vessels of scented water are placed within the location of the pure water [vessel] is [the best]. || 259 ||
Devoid of all the vases situated in the outer enclosure,
yet endowed within with twenty-five [vases], it is the middle-superior [mandala].
In the human [world], that which is devoid of the four directions is the middle-middle;
therein, that which is devoid of all the jars situated there is the middle-lowest. || 261 ||
That which consists of nine jars is considered either inferior or superior;
thus the third [type] has been described. Now listen, O best of beings, to the fourth. || 262 ||
If there is a single jar situated in the middle, that would be the lowest of the low;
thus has the third been described. Now listen, O best of beings, to the fourth. (263)
When divided into seven portions, there are forty-nine parts:
clarified butter, warm water, jewel-water, and fruit-water. || 264 ||

Iron-water, cleansing-water, scented-water, and water with unbroken rice grains, followed by barley-water; beginning from the center and ending with the northeast, [these are placed] in the central [vessel].
Water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping (ācamana), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
as well as curd, milk, honey, and astringent decoctions (kaṣāya), [should be placed] in the cardinal and intermediate directions outside of that.
And likewise, water with rice, sugarcane juice, coconut water, and the water of pacification [should be placed] in the four directions according to the sequence starting from the east. || 267 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should place auspicious water in the four corner-pitchers;
the remaining twenty-four parts shall be empty.
The mantra-worship as well as the extraction [of the deity] is performed just as in the *adyottamottama* [rite];
for this is proclaimed as the *uttamottama* ablution.
Having divided the space into five parts and arranged twenty-five jars with the root mantra, one should then sprinkle them.
Facing the east, self-controlled and purified, he should place the ritual substances;
he should fill the central pitcher, dedicated to Brahmā, with water for bathing.

Then, in the human portion, in the four directions beginning with the east, [he offered] water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and likewise the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 272 ||
Clarified butter, curd, milk, and honey—beginning from the southeast and proceeding through the middle of Indra and Agni, ending in the west between Īśāna and the other [deity]. || 273 ||
Warm water, decoction, water for sprinkling, fruit-water, sesame-water, jewel-water, metal-water, and kuśa-grass water. || 274 ||
Then, in the divine portion, as before, in the four directions,
there should be water with fragrance, water with flowers, water with *aupamānya*, and water with *āmalaka*.
From the southeast to the northeast, there should likewise be unbroken rice grains and water,
as well as coconut juice, sugarcane juice, and rice-water.
And thus, with twenty-five jars, the highest and middle [offerings] are prepared;
and in the middle section, the water for washing the feet (pādya) is arranged from the east to the northeast and west.
The arghya, the ācamana, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
ghee, curd, milk, honey, and warm water, should indeed be offered in sequence during the intervals.
Astringent water, cleansing water, fruit water, wiping water, jewel water, iron water, kuśa-grass water, and warm water. || 279 ||
Then, in the divine portion, from the east to the north-east and west,
[he places] perfumed water, water with flowers, water with raw rice grains, and pure water.
Unbroken rice, water, sesame-water, barley-water, and rice-water;
these are prescribed as the "extraction" (uddhāra) offerings, beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the rice-water. || 281 ||
Thus, with twenty-five [substances], the bath is both supreme and inferior;
on the ground divided into seven parts as before, clarified butter is placed first, and the water of pacification last.
The bathing with twenty-one jars is considered middling and superior; O best of men, there, the area is divided into nine compartments in three ways.
From the center to the northeast, one should place curd, milk, honey, as well as unguents and powder; then, in the four corners [of the mandala]. (284)
Warm water, scented water, flower water, and auspicious water—their extraction is proclaimed to follow the very sequence of the placement of the ritual substances. || 285 ||
In this manner, with nine jars, there shall be the "middling-middling" [type]:
clarified butter, milk, curd, honey, as well as scented water and gold-water. (286)
Water containing jewels, water with medicinal herbs, and rice powder, placed respectively in the center and ending in the northeast direction—this constitutes the middling-inferior [type]. || 287 ||
In the middle of the four directions, there is a group of five made of the five precious gems;
and from the southeast to the northeast, there is a set of four jars.
This [mandala] would be inferior or superior depending on whether it is filled with pure water;
in the center is jeweled water, and there are four jars in the cardinal directions. || 289 ||
O best of beings, when combined with pearls and other gems in pairs,
this [consecration] performed with five jars shall be of the lowest-middle grade.
In the center of the water for all the nights, there are two jars in the two directions, east and west; therein, in the eastern one, are the four items beginning with pearls.
O best of the twice-born, the four [gems] beginning with topaz are indeed placed in another [vessel];
thus, the lowest of the low rite of ablution is performed with three jars alone.
Thus, thirty-six further subdivisions have been revealed;
one should perform everything previously as before, preceded by the consecration of the jar (kumbhādhivāsa). || 293 ||
The supreme deity of clarified butter is remembered as the god Vāsudeva;
Saṅkarṣaṇa is the deity of hot water, and Pradyumna of precious water.
O twice-born one, the Lord Aniruddha is the deity of fruit-water,
while Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is the mantra, is the deity of metallic water.
Hayagrīva is for the water used for sweeping; Viṣṇu is for the fragrant water;
Nṛsiṃha is for the water with unbroken rice grains; and Varāha is for the water with barley. || 296 ||
Lord Keśava is remembered as the deity of the water for washing the feet; Nārāyaṇa is the deity of the arghya offering;
and Lord Mādhava is the presiding deity of the water for sipping.
Govinda is the deity of the five products of the cow; Viṣṇu is the deity of curd;
and the one known as Madhusūdana is remembered as the deity of milk. || 298 ||
The Lord known as Trivikrama is the deity of honey, and Vāmana is the deity of the decoction;
the Blessed One known as Śrīdhara, however, is the deity of the syrup.
O twice-born one, Hṛṣīkeśa, the god of gods, is the presiding deity of sugarcane juice; Dāmodara, however, is the presiding deity of coconut water. 300.
The Blessed One Pajhanābha is the deity of Śāntitoya;
likewise are Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa.
From the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśa), the deities of the auspicious waters [are worshipped];
in the rite known as "cleansing" (parimārjana), however, the conch shell should be placed above them.
O twice-born one, there should be a lotus for water mixed with kusha grass, a mace for flour, a forest garland for water with flowers, and a discus for water with medicinal herbs.
The crown is the presiding deity for water with *āmalaka* fruit;
the *kaustubha* gem for water with sesame seeds; and the *śrīvatsa* mark for water with rice grains. (304)
The deities of the eighty-one Śuddhodāna [mandalas] consist of an eightfold group beginning with Kānti and ending with Unnati, proceeding in order for each direction. || 305 ||
Externally, in the forty-nine pure waters,
there are in sequence the powers (śaktis) beginning with Svadhā and ending with Gāyatrī, who are indeed the presiding deities (adhidevatās).

O best of the twice-born, for all other types of ablutions, there are eight [vessels] each in the directions starting from the east, and likewise in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast.
The presiding deities of the boundary lines and the ploughs are Hṛṣṭi and Śuddhodā; Garuḍa is the deity of the water-pots, and Śeṣa is the deity of the measuring-line. || 308 ||
Of brooms, he is the Supreme Brahman; of chowries, the King of Chakras;
of garments, Vāsudeva; indeed, he alone is all of these. (309)
One should perform sweeping and sprinkling, as well as smearing with cow dung;
one should mark the lines for the layout and decorate all around with powdered flour.
The knower of mantras should perform the five [rites] with the twelve-syllable mantra;
the practitioner of mantras should consecrate the water-pots with the five Upaniṣads.
There, one should place the water-pots (kalaśas) in the compartments with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
there, one should fill them in sequence with the names denoting the presiding deities of the substances.
One should cast kūrca-grass into those [vessels] with the Dviṣaṭka-Brahmavidyā mantra,
and one should worship the presiding deities of each respective substance within those very substances.
Afterwards, the practitioner, knowing the mantra, should establish the wheels with the wheel-mantra;
then, the knower of the mantra should cover them with cloths using the twelve-syllable mantra.
The knower of mantras should remove the cloth with the root mantra;
having cut the threads with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and having saluted with that same [mantra], || 315 ||
Having lifted it up, one should likewise place it in the hand of the Guru with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī;
O twice-born, whatever mantra has not been prescribed here for each specific rite [should be used].
The wise one should perform each respective rite with the twelve-syllable mantra;
or else, all rites may be performed with the twelve-syllable vidyā.
O Mahāmati, the collection of substances for the *arghya* and other offerings for the aforementioned supreme divisions of ablutions has been stated; now that of others is being described. (318)
Viṣṇuparṇī, dūrvā grass, lotus, and śyāmāka grain—these four, O best of the twice-born, are the constituent parts of the water for the feet (pādya). || 319 ||
Fragrant substances, flowers, unbroken grains, fruits, barley, white mustard seeds, sesame,
and the tips of kusha grass— these indeed are the eight components of the arghya offering.
Lavaṅga, jāti, and takkola are for the rinsing of the mouth;
likewise, cow dung juice, cow urine, milk, curd, and ghee [are used]. || 321 ||
These five are the constituent parts of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in their entirety;
likewise, [the wood] of the Śamī, Udumbara, Bilva, Palāśa, and Vaṭa trees.
The bark-extract from the Khadira, Aśvattha, and likewise the Vikaṅkata tree constitutes a decoction that removes all sins.
Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, campaka, vacā, kaccora, and mustā are proclaimed as the "all-healing herbs" (sarvauṣadhi). || 324 ||
The young shoots of the *palāśa*, *bilva*, *vakula*, *kadamba*, mango, *śirīṣa*, as well as those of the *nyagrodha* and *aśvattha* trees, constitute "leaf-water. (325)
Flowers produced from the *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *jāti*, *nandyāvarta*, and *utpala*; and those arising from the *padma*, *campaka*, and *kunda*—these are "flower waters. (326)
Plantains, wood-apples, mangoes, jackfruit, citrons, coconuts, emblic myrobalans, and citron-melons—these are the "fruits and waters. (327)
O Brahmins, these eight constituent parts are indeed declared to be the fruits:
barley, wheat, rice, paddy, mung beans, and millet. (328)
Māṣa and nīvāra are declared to be the limbs of the seed-water;
likewise, bāhlīka, sandalwood, camphor, and agallochum [are its parts]. || 329 ||
Or else, O bull among sages, there are four fragrant ingredients:
sandalwood, saffron, spikenard, and likewise nutmeg. (330)
Uśīra, kuṣṭha, agaru, gandhāmbhas, and aṅga constitute the group of eight;
likewise, sūryakānta, padmarāga, and indrakānta.
Vaiḍūrya, as well as magnetite, indranīla, coral, garuḍa, puṣyarāga, crystal, and brahmarāgaka; || 332 ||
The diamond, pearl, and limbs [are the gifts] of the Ratnoda; or else, O twice-born one, the diamond, pearl, ruby, coral, and topaz. || 333 ||
These five, including the water of jewels, have indeed been described to you;
they constitute the second set of nine for the subsequent ablutions.
In that regard, there are pearl, diamond, gomedaka, sapphire, topaz, ruby, moonstone, and coral. (335)
Indeed, these eight components of the "jewel-water" (ratnāmbhas) have been declared:
sahadevī, śirīṣa, rajanī, and sūryavartinī. || 336 ||
O twice-born one, the six components for cleansing are: *sadābhadra*, tips of *kuśa* grass, gold, silver, copper, lead, and tin. (337)
The five components of the "iron-water" (lohavāri) have indeed been declared:
sesame, white mustard, wild rice, barley, and bamboo-seed. || 338 ||
The six limbs, including the *tulasī* leaf, are likewise peaceful;
as are the sprouts of *indravallī*, the lotus, and the *aśvattha* tree. (339)
One lotus and four ingredients [constitute] the "Auspicious Water":
earth from a river, a pond, an anthill, and a mountain. (340)
O best of the twice-born, the objects for purification have been declared:
the conch, the discus, the tortoise, and likewise Vainateya. (341)
One should fashion an image out of metals; this is called the "analogous" (aupamānika) rite.
All the pitchers of pure water should be combined with a single part of sandalwood. || 342 ||
Alternatively, there is the vessel named Anantakalaśa, which fulfills all requirements;
listen now to its detailed procedure in due order.
One should construct a pavilion as before, forty cubits in length and thirty-two cubits in width, provided with four doors and other such features. || 344 ||
It should be well-adorned with banners and other ornaments as before,
or one may simply provide a water-station (prapā) located in a place according to one's preference.
One should construct a pavilion for the sacrifice near that [shrine] as previously described;
having performed the sowing of seeds (aṅkurāropa) on the day specified, prior to the day of the ritual action.
Having gathered all the necessary materials for that purpose,
the preeminent teacher, being well-composed, should bathe thoroughly and perform his daily rites on the preceding day.
Adorned with various ornaments and new garments, wearing a white turban and upper robe, and decorated with variegated garlands; || 348 ||
It should be accompanied by four or eight such noble practitioners, equal in number, skilled in the scriptures, and adorned with waist-cloths and other ornaments. || 349 ||
And by many attendants, their faces and noses covered with other very white cloths, who were skilled in various specific applications.
When the time for the *aparāhṇa* has arrived, having performed the worship of the door-keepers, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion;
there, one should worship the deity in the water-pot (*kumbha*) and other vessels. || 351 ||
Or, O best of sages, one should worship the image in that very place after having gratified the fire as before; then, having obtained permission, proceed in due order.
But according to the rule for the secondary procedure, having entered the temple and worshipped the primary image with water offerings, anointing, and garlands; || 353 ||
Then, having obtained permission with incense, one should proceed;
after first worshipping the door-keepers, one should enter the bathing pavilion.
One should sprinkle [the site] on all sides with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the twelve-syllable mantra;
likewise, one should scatter various kinds of flowers in every direction.
Then, having placed white mustard seeds in the center of the pavilion,
one should divide the field, measuring twenty-two and a half cubits, into five parts.
Each one further becomes ninefold, making forty-five;
and the rows of squares shall likewise be twenty-five.
Two thousand [units], and then in the center, for the purpose of placing the jar, one should arrange eighty-one squares and sweep them clean. || 358 ||
There are two rows around the central path, and outside of that,
in the four directions beginning with the east, there are eighty-one squares.
One should arrange a path along the sides; there shall be two rows [of squares].
In the four corners, however, there are forty-nine cells.
There, one should also arrange eighty-one [squares] according to the middle [series];
having established a group of nine from the center, one should omit one row on each side.

Having established six [units] in each of the cardinal directions and six in each of the intermediate directions outside the two rows, and four in each [of those directions], one should sweep away the remaining [units]. || 362 ||
Outside of that, one should erase two rows [of squares] all around for the pathway (vīthī);
then, one should carefully construct sixteen squares for the corners.
One should erase one row at a time on its sides in the four directions;
by means of two rows, there shall be three inner sections for the doors and three outer ones.
On the five sides, however, for the sake of beauty, there are two [lines] outside the four;
within that, in three rows, there are thirty-three squares.
Having brought them into unity with the streets, one should place each one outside,
