numbering sixteen in the middle of the doors and corners.
O Great Sage, having set aside twenty-five squares on each side, one should erase one row at a time, alternating with the other.
O twice-born one, having thus prepared the locations for the jars for the purpose of their placement, one should then make them perfectly level with white fragrant powder.
One should fashion straight lines with a width and height equal to a thumb;
then, having scattered colored powders into the squares, one should fill in the doorways.
O best of sages, one should adorn the pathways everywhere with that very yellow [pigment], along with clusters of creepers provided with various flowers. (370)
Then, having collected one hundred and eight jars marked with the previously described characteristics, he should indeed offer clarified butter while reciting the root mantra.
Then, by means of the Gāyatrī mantra, having placed two jars each at the four gates starting from the eastern direction, and having worshipped Kumuda and the others; || 372 ||
Having worshipped the compartments with various flowers accompanied by mantras,
one should diligently prepare pedestals using all kinds of grains.
O twice-born one, one should place two blades of *kuśa* grass at the top of each of those [jars] with the root mantra;
having wrapped them with thread, the jars should be prepared as before.

Having washed them with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should place them in their respective compartments starting from the syllable *Tāra* (Om). One should place the Kuśa grass with its tips pointing downward upon the back [of the vessel] with the *Parameṣṭhin* mantra.

Then one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using *kuśa* grass and the *puṃs* mantra; thereafter, one should scatter all the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the *viśva* mantra. || 376 ||
Then, having turned them upward, one should gradually and with effort wash them with filtered water scented with sandalwood and other fragrant substances. || 377 ||
O Brahmin, one should fill all of them in sequence with scented [substances];
specifically, the central pitcher among the nine located in the center of the eighty-one [pitchers].
Sūryakānta, padmarāga, vaiḍūrya, candrakāntaka, ayaskānta, indranīla, pravāla, and likewise gāruḍa. || 379 ||
Topaz, crystal, ruby, and sapphire;
diamond, silver, pearl, and copper as well. || 380 ||
Having deposited all these outside that [area] upon nine wooden planks,
one should place them in order within the central jars, starting from the east and ending with the northeast.
One should arrange these sixteen substances by pairing them in twos;
as for the remaining seventy-two in number, one should place pearls upon them.
In the center of the ninety-one [worlds] situated in the east, within the central region, [there are the worlds] named Kadalī, Panasa, Āmra, Kṣīrikā, and Badara. || 383 ||
Thereafter, one should place the fruits of the mātulaṅga, kesara, havya, and jambīra upon the nine wooden pieces outside of that.
From the east to the northeast, [he should plant] the citron, the pomegranate, the orange, the jambīra, the takkola, and likewise the jujube tree. (386)
One should place the *kṣudrapūrva*, the *panasa*, the *kadalī*, and the *mocaka* in order within the jars of liquor, using the method of pairing them. (387)
One should place jujube fruits in new wooden vessels and jars,
as well as uśīra, saffron, māṃsī, and sandalwood.
One should place murā, harivera, kuṣṭha, and agaru in the eighty-one squares in the southern direction; these are all the Viśvas. (389)
In the middle, within the central jar, and in the remaining central jars according to the sequence starting from the east, one should place the fruit produced from each individual [seed].
And one should apply sandalwood paste to these eight [spots]:
the ocean, the pond, the well, the tank, and the lake.
One should place the waters of rain, rivers, and snow into the central Vāruṇa jar; each of the remaining [elements] should be placed in the middle jar.
And in the remaining eight groups, one should place pure grains:
barley, wheat, rice, paddy, mung beans, and millet. (393)
One should place black gram and wild rice in the ninth pitcher, which is the middle one;
in the remaining pitchers and the jars of liquor, one should place each type of grain in sequence. || 394 ||
One should present the perfected waters in the groups of eight;
one should fill the forty-nine [vessels] of the fire-group with clarified butter in the group of nine.
In the six [pots], having placed cow urine, cow dung, milk, and curd according to the sequence beginning with Indra, one should place warm water in the corners.
Having placed oil in the central ninth vessel in the southwest (nairṛta),
one should place molasses-water in the remaining forty jars.
In the center of the nine [vessels] of the Vāyavya group, one should place mustard oil;
and in the remaining jars, one should place sugarcane juice.
One should place honey in the forty-nine [vessels] dedicated to Īśāna;
in the remaining ones, one should place coconut water or its milk. || 399 ||

Among the twenty-five [deities] beginning with Indra, [one should place the waters] from the field, sacred fords, the ocean, and the mountains into the first and middle jars; and [the waters] from the cave known as Sūkara and from the elephant [into the others]. (400)
One should take earth from an anthill and from the horn of a bull to fill [the remaining vessels];
for each of the other eight, one should place a single portion, and in the sixteen, fragrant water.
Sahadevī, vacā, śatamūlī, śatāvarī, kumārī, galūcī, siṃhī, and likewise vyāghrī. || 402 ||

Having placed [the seed-syllables] in the second middle pitcher, one should place them one by one in the outer octagon according to the eastern sequence; in the sixteenth [pitcher], it should be as before.
The middle jar [should be filled] with the inner bark of Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Jambu, Bilva, Palāśa, Śirīṣa, and Madhuka. || 404 ||
In the third [circle], having filled eight [petals] with individual [mantras] as before, [one fills] sixteen with those produced from Palāśa, Bilva, Vakula, Kadamba, Āmra, and Śirīṣa flowers.
Having cast sprouts from the Nyagrodha and Aśvattha trees into the fourth jar,
one should place sixteen [sprouts] in the middle jar and in the eight [surrounding jars], distributed as before.
Having filled the middle [section] with flowers born of the *mallikā*, *jāti*, *vakula*, *nandyāvarta*, and *priyaṅgu* species, as well as with *padma*, *campaka*, and *kunda* blossoms. (407)
One should place the *kalaśa* with the five [substances] distributed separately; the remaining eight [vessels] are as before.
[The substances are]: white mustard (*siddhārtha*), black mustard (*sarṣapa*), black gram (*māṣa*), and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) derived from a cow. (408)
One should place indrayava, veṇuyava, and the seeds of śamī and śyāmāka into the sixth pitcher situated in the middle, and [the remaining items] into the eight [other pitchers] in due order.
Those substances are to be distributed individually as before; the remaining sixteen are sesame, wild sesame, cumin, and black cumin. (410)
Having placed atasī, śatapuṣpā, and likewise kuṭhāracchinna,
as well as ṛṣibīja, in the seventh central jar.
O twice-born one, as before, place sixty grains each of śyāmāka, śāli rice, and wild rice (nīvāra) in each of the sixteen [vessels] on the outside of the eight.

One should place sprouts of dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, indravallī, and pippala in the center and in the eight [directions] during the eighth [day]; in the others, they are to be placed separately as before.
In the ninth [section], one should place the roots of kuśa grass, uśīra, sugarcane, kāśa, uśīra, śarapuṅkha, agaru, and pāmārga. || 414 ||
When the pitcher is situated in the middle, [the rites] for the eight [directions] are performed in reverse order; for the others, it is as before.
[The materials used are] the leaves of *tulasī*, black *tulasī*, *granthi* grass, and bamboo. (415)
For *bhṛṅgarāja*, *bilva*, *śamī*, *ketakī*, and the two types of *jāti*, [the proportions] are ten, eight, and eight respectively; for the remaining [plants], it is as stated previously. (416)
One should take the tubers known as mustānagara and mustā, as well as those of the kuvalaya, kumuda, and utpala, and the śītalīyaka tuber. (417)
One should place the roots of the white water-lily (kalhāra) and the kaśeru in the eleventh;
these [should be placed] in the middle pitchers, and in the others in sequence as before. || 418 ||
In the twelfth [month], one should place sprouts of mung beans, black gram, niṣpāva, śimba, rice, barley, āḍhaka, and kuluttha beans.
O twice-born one, in the eight central jars, as before, [place] the sixteen [herbs] distributed [among them]:
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Sadābhadra, Viṣṇukrānti, and Ekaphalā. || 420 ||
Likewise,
one should place the sprouts of balā, kharamañjarī, sahā, and sahadevī into the thirteenth jar.
Having placed them individually upon the eight [petals], one should perform the remaining rites on the other [parts] as before;
[namely,] Śvetārka, Brahmadaṇḍī, and likewise Brahmasuvarcalā. || 422 ||
Having placed *saraktā*, *viraktā*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *sthirā*, and also *paraṇḍa* in the fourteenth jar in the center; || 423 ||
One should place those [fragrances] separately on the eight [petals] as before, and on the others, one should place *surabhi*, lotus filaments, and *nāgakeśara*.
Patra, melā, tvak, latā, and likewise kastūrikā,
as well as jātīphala— these five are indeed placed in the middle of the tenth.
Having deposited [the mantras] individually into the eight jars, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
Gold, silver, tin, iron, lead, and mercury— || 426 ||

O twice-born one, having placed a copper vessel and a bronze vessel in the sixteenth [vessel] situated in the center, and having distributed them separately among the eight [other] jars as before, [one should do so] in the sixteen [vessels]. (427)
Having thus arranged the ritual substances in sequence with a well-composed mind,
he should then, for the purpose of worshipping the deity, [proceed] to the southeast corner.
One should arrange the collection of materials for the *arghya* and other offerings, as well as the *madhuparka*,
and then, in the southwest corner (nirṛti), upon a mound made of river-sand and rice flour.

One should place dūrvā grass, aśvattha leaves, white mustard seeds, and likewise unbroken grains (akṣata), as well as garlands and the eastern pitcher, for the purpose of the lustration rite (nīrājana). || 430 ||
Likewise, for the purpose of anointment, there should be powder made from wheat and śāli rice, mixed with the powder of turmeric and slightly perfumed with lotus-scented water. (431)
O bull among sages, he also brought camphor paste and flour-cakes, as well as sandalwood for smearing on the face, which had been infused with ground camphor. (432)
One should apply ground āmalaka fruit, combined with campaka, murā, māṃsī, and haribera, for the purpose of bathing the head. || 433 ||
Then, in separate vessels in the northwestern corner,
[he should place] a washed cloth, a casket, and a container for flowers, garlands, and so forth.
Then, O twice-born one, in the northeast corner, there should be iron rods,
iron balls, and likewise a pair of tongs.
Whatever else may be useful, one should place it according to one's preference;
this may be stated either in its entirety or as situated in whichever corner is desired.
In the ninth square situated in the center of the eighty-one central squares,
one should worship Vāsudeva within the pitcher (kumbha), starting from the east and proceeding in order.

One should place the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva in the centers of the nine groups situated in the cardinal directions according to their order of manifestation, and [the remaining four] in the centers of those situated in the intermediate directions.
One should worship those very [deities] from Īśa to Vahni according to their process of dissolution;
one should truly worship them in the middle of all the pure water-pitchers.
But for those of the nine outer directions, [the offerings are] in the pure waters (śuddhodaka) according to the sequence of the directions:
Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya, the lord of birds.
In the four groups of nine [deities] extending from Agni to Īśāna, one should worship those very same [deities] in sequence within the pure waters. || 441 ||
In the eighty-one [vessels] situated in the directions, according to the sequence starting from the east,
and in the thirty-six central jars, one should proceed in due order.
O Brahmin, the deities beginning with Pajhana and ending with Vedavid are to be worshipped according to the ninefold arrangement, starting from the center and extending to the western direction.
In the center, one should worship the one whose form is Kalkin within the pitchers of pure water;
outside, one should worship the Lord within the nine pitchers of pure water.
Then, beginning from the southeast corner and so forth, in the four corners, there are those known as the Pātālaśayana and others,
within forty-nine groups of nine squares each.
In the middle [positions], one should place the first [four] among the four triads of Keśava and the others;
in the jars situated at the cardinal directions, one should place the second [four] in all four.

In the sixteen [petals], one should worship the sixteen weapons, beginning with the discus (cakra) and ending with the vajra, in sequence, placing the third [weapon] in each of the intermediate directions. || 447 ||
Thereafter, one should place the Śakti in the four squares situated at the corners;
then, among the twenty-five [deities], one should first worship Aindrī on the right.
O twice-born one, one should worship Lakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity, in the central jars;
Pusti (Nourishment) on the eight [jars] outside of that; and Kānti (Beauty) on the sixteen [jars] further out.
And in these and other twenty-five [deities], one should proceed;
one should worship this triad of three for each of the powers, beginning with Prabhā. || 450 ||
There too, one should place [the deities] on the fifteenth [petal], and externally on the sixteenth;
one should worship the triad of Kirīṭa and others on the twenty-fifth [petal].
One should likewise [worship] the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, and the forest garland (vanamālā),
in sequence with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Vanamālā.
Having offered twenty-eight oblations of clarified butter according to one's preference,
and having then given the full-offerings (pūrṇāhuti), one should touch the jars according to the rite of the residual drops (saṃpāta-vidhi).
Having covered them all with circular lids according to the sequence previously described,
one should afterwards cover each individually with new cloths.
Having again offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should present the bali-offering to the spirits in the various directions;
the sequence for the extraction [of the image] is held to extend from clay up to all kinds of precious gems. || 455 ||
O Great-minded One, having first sprinkled [the deity] with water-jars from the east to the northeast while reciting the mantra "viṣṇornukaṃ," and then having performed the consecration; || 456 ||
Then, O Brahmin, with a single earthen pitcher placed in the center, one should [arrange] sixteen pitchers outside it, starting from the east and proceeding in due order. || 457 ||
O twice-born one, this same sequence applies to all twenty-five [tattvas];
with the mantra "pra tad viṣṇuḥ," one should perform the consecration with water from the root-mantra.
With the mantra "pratatte viṣṇuvāsa," he should [bathe the image] with water mixed with decoctions;
and with the mantra "yasya triṣpūrṇe," he should do so with jars provided with sprouts.
With the mantra "tadasya," he [should perform the rite] with jars filled with flowers;
and with the mantra "tāvām," accompanied by white mustard seeds and other such items. || 460 ||
With the mantra "pravaḥ pāntam," one should offer water mixed with sesame seeds and other substances;
and with the mantra "paro mātrai," one should offer water containing sixty or other such items. || 461 ||
Then, with water containing the roots of *kuśa* grass while reciting "na te viṣṇo," and subsequently with water containing *tulasī* and other plants while reciting the mantra "irāvatī. || 462 ||
Therefore, with the mantra "ato devā" combined with the bulbs of *mustā* and other ingredients,
and with [vessels] filled with sprouts of mung beans and so forth using the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," || 463 ||
Then, with the mantra "trīṇi padā" and water from the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* plant and others, and subsequently with the mantra "viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi" and water from the white *arka* plant and others; || 464 ||
Then, with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should bathe [the deity] with fragrant waters such as those from the Surabhi cow;
thereafter, with the mantra "tad viprāsaḥ," one should bathe [him] with iron-infused water.
First, one should perform the ritual bathing with eighty-one jars according to the sequential method;
the order of bathing proceeds from the east through the center, ending with the ninefold arrangement.

First, with the nine verses beginning with "For the great sacrifice" (uru-yajñāya), and with the verse "O Indra and Viṣṇu, you have made firm," situated in the direction of the Fire (the southeast). || 467 ||
With the nine verses beginning with "iyaṃ manīṣā," one should consecrate [the image] with the Yāmya [mantra];
thereafter, with the Nairṛta [mantra] beginning with "vaṣaṭ te viṣṇu. || 468 ||
O Great-minded One, by means of this Vāruṇa hymn beginning with "tisro vācaḥ," and by the medicinal mantra and the ninefold Vāyavya hymn, [the rite is accomplished].
With the nine verses beginning with "starīr atvad abhavatī" from the Soma section, and with the verse beginning with "yasmin viśvā" situated in the northeast direction— 470.
One should bathe [the image] with this verse beginning with "parjanyāya" using the central vessel;
thereafter, one should bathe the Lord with eighty-one vessels dedicated to Yama.
One should proceed in sequence with the mantra beginning with "sahasraśīrṣaṃ devaṃ" and ending with "santataṃ sirābhiḥ. (472)
O best of sages, one should bathe [the deity] with these eight mantras in the nine directions starting from the east;
however, one should perform the bath with all of them together using the central mantra.
One should perform the consecration with eighty-one jars of Varuṇī water,
using the hymn beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ" and the nine verses starting from the east.
One should perform the consecration with the mantra "yā āpo divyāḥ" using waters originating from ponds, wells, tanks, the ocean, lakes, and rain. || 475 ||
Then, one should bathe [the image] with river water while reciting the verse beginning with "yāsāṃ rājā," and subsequently with cold water while reciting the mantra beginning with "yāsu rājā."
Then one should consecrate him in due order with the four [mantras] preceded by Samudrajyeṣṭha, with the middle one, and then with eighty-one auspicious jars.
With the mantra "yad imā" from the Śākvara hymn, consisting of nine verses,
and with the mantra "yasyauṣadhi," situated in the direction of fire (the southeast), [he should perform the rite].
With the mantra "Sākaṃ yakṣma" [he offers] in the south; with "Anyā vo" in the southwest;
with the mantra "Yāḥ phalinī" in the west; and with the ninefold [mantra] in the northwest. || 479 ||
One should release [the disciple] from the curse with the nine verses beginning with "mā śapathya aditiḥ," while standing in the direction of Vāyu;
and one should purify him with the verse beginning with "āpaḥ punantu," while standing in the direction of Soma. || 480 ||
With the mantra "oṣadhīḥ somarājñī," one should perform the rite for Īśāna;
with the mantra "yā oṣadhīssomarājñī viṣṭhitā," one should do so in the center. || 481 ||
Then one should consecrate him with forty-nine jars of fire,
with the Gāyatrī, with the six [verses] of Indra, and with "Gandhadvārām" from the south.
In the west, [he worships] with the six verses beginning "payasvatīroṣadhayaḥ," and after that,
with the verse "dadhikrāvṇa" and the Saumya-hexad.
The rivers flow perfectly with the Sūkta and with clarified butter;
one should perform the consecration with forty-nine jars dedicated to Nairṛta.
Then, one should bathe [the image] with oil using the *tejo'si* and other Yajus formulas,
and subsequently with jaggery-water using the twelve-syllable mantra in the previously prescribed order.
With the mantra beginning with "tejasī," [one should offer] into the wind;
with sesame and mustard [seeds], and then with all sugarcane juices using the twelve-syllable mantra.
With the mantras beginning with "madhu vātā," using jars filled with honey,
and then sequentially with coconut water using the previously mentioned mantra.
Thereafter, one should sprinkle it with hot water from the southeast (Agni) to the northeast (Īśāna) and west,
using water that has become hot at that very moment by the casting of well-heated iron balls.
One should rub the Lord with *drupadā diva* mantra;
one should apply *āmalaka* (myrobalan) to the head with the *mānastoke* mantra. || 489 ||
Having washed [the image] with many pure and fragrant waters,
one should then bathe it in sequence using eighty-one central jars.
With this verse beginning "sahasraśīrṣe," one should perform the rite using nine jars dedicated to Indra,
eight of which are placed in the eight directions and the second [central jar] with the middle [verse].
Likewise, with two [verses] at a time from the Ṛgveda, and then by groups of nine and seven respectively,
one should recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta in its entirety, very slowly.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with the central group of nine [verses],
or alternatively, in sequence, with the mantras beginning with "sarvasya vaśinam" (6.50).
By means of the eight pitchers situated in the cardinal directions according to the *Mahopaniṣad*,
and by that single [pitcher] located in the center with the words "Nārāyaṇa alone," [he should worship].
Or else, O best of the twice-born, one should bathe [the deity] with all the pitchers in sequence, using the twelve-syllable mantra, beginning with the clay and ending with all the jewels. 495.
Thus has the extraction been described; now hear, O twice-born one, the sequence of the ritual acts:
having performed his bath at dawn and having completed the auspicious rites for protection, || 496 ||
Then the preeminent teacher, accompanied by other teachers, having entered the temple and performed the daily rites as before, [proceeded]. (497)
Having reached the sacrificial pavilion and filled the mandala with powders,
and having performed the worship of the pitcher and the mandala, he entered the temple.
Then one should worship the primary image with offerings such as the arghya and other enjoyments;
likewise, having invoked [the deity] into the bathing image from that [primary image], one should worship it in the same manner. || 499 ||
Having worshipped and adorned it with various garments, garlands, and ornaments,
he placed it upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, equipped with all manner of decorations.
O Brahmin, having placed [the deity] upon the bathing throne according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should lead him to the bathing pavilion by the path described before. (501)
Having worshipped [the deity] duly in sequence up to the offering of self-surrender,
one should then perform the binding of the auspicious thread (kautuka) for the God of gods.
One should prepare an auspicious mandala with cow dung in front of the deity;
having adorned it with flour-dust, one should place small earthen vessels (pālikās) in the corners.
Having fashioned a pedestal out of rice grains,
one should place upon it a vessel made of gold or silver, filled with polished śāli rice.
Adorned with betel leaves measuring one *svāri* or half that size,
one should place above that a fourfold thread made of silk.
Having consecrated it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and worshipped it even with flowers,
he should place that vessel upon the head of the one intent on service.
Afterwards, one should cause the disciple to circumambulate the pavilion clockwise;
if it is inside the temple, it should be endowed with all auspicious features.
One should perform four circumambulations either in the first enclosure or in the second; however, in case of difficulty, one may perform two.
One should place that vessel upon the support in front of the deity;
then, having made the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), one should worship the deity with arghya and other offerings.
Then, having performed the *pratisara* rite and having perfumed it with fragrant incense,
one should bind the protective amulet (*kautuka*) upon the right hand of the God of Gods.
Having honored them further with water-offerings (arghya) and other gifts, he should satisfy the twice-born,
as well as the initiated Vaiṣṇavas led by the preeminent teacher, with betel leaves.
The preceptor himself should take half of that rice and other materials;
in this manner, the binding of the protective thread (kautuka) should be performed in all sacrifices.
If the ritual for the water-pots was not performed by you previously, then for what reason should all of that be performed at that time? (513)

Having worshipped him in sequence with the enjoyments beginning with the bath and seat and ending with the application of ointment to the face, one should then bathe him with the water-pots according to the prescribed method.
One should fill all the jars with the remainder of the bathing water;
however, another jar should be filled with substances through their successive combination.
Having bathed [the image] with pure water, one should worship it with garments, the arghya offering, and other rites.
Having thus bathed it according to the rules, [one should offer flowers] filled with the powder of rajanī.
According to the path described in the *Kautuka*,
one should proceed with twenty-five, or nine, or five jars that have been consecrated beforehand.
Or else, one may offer that powder upon the head of the deity while reciting the Dviṣaṭka-Brahmavidyā,
and then worship him further with water-offerings (arghya) and other rites.
Then, having rubbed it over all his limbs, O twice-born one, he should cause it to be placed upon the heads of the devotees after giving it to Viṣvaksena with that mantra.
One should perform the ritual bath with a thousand streams of vomited water;
then, having offered sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should [bring] the Lord from the pedestal.
Having brought the seat of ornaments, one should worship it according to the sequence beginning with the seat,
using various enjoyments involving touch and ritual services as before.
And with various heart-pleasing and captivating names, having thus worshipped until the end of the gift to the twice-born or until the end of the oblation; || 522 ||
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle as before,
one should then enter the interior of the temple by proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Having deposited that image there and installed it in its proper place,
one should likewise worship the primary image with offerings such as the arghya and other enjoyments.
Having offered the performed ritual action, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana);
thereafter, that festival image [should be adorned] with various garments.
Then that festival image was likewise adorned with various garments,
many beautiful ornaments, and highly fragrant garlands.
Having adorned [the image] and placed it upon a palanquin,
one should bring it into the assembly pavilion according to the procedure prescribed for festivals.
Having placed him there upon a golden, spread-out, and auspicious seat, or, O Brahmin, upon a throne provided with various colorful coverings; || 528 ||
One should worship according to the very path described in sequence,
especially with various enjoyments beginning with tactile sensations.
Then, having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis) and performed everything in due order up to the gift to the twice-born, one should satisfy [the deities] in sequence within the fire.

Having performed all the rites beginning with the formal dedication (samarpaṇa) to the God, the Lord of the Universe, and having placed Him upon a vehicle or similar conveyance accompanied by every auspicious rite; || 531 ||
Having caused [the image] to descend from the vehicle and so forth, one should lead it into the temple;
then, having seated it in its proper place, one should worship it with water for the hands (arghya), perfumes, and other offerings.
Having thus worshipped the primary image,
one should offer the performed ritual action with the water remaining from the bath, which is contained in the ritual jar, in the proper sequence.

Having sprinkled water upon all the deities stationed at the doors as well as those situated in the surrounding enclosures, and having worshipped them according to the sequence of offering oblations; || 534 ||
Having offered the bali-oblation and consecrated Gaṇeśa with the remainder,
one should worship him with arghya, perfumes, and other offerings, or else according to the secondary ritual (anukalpa).
At the conclusion of the worship, there is the bathing of the deity,
the sprinkling of the deities, and the consecration of Gaṇeśa.
Then, O twice-born one, the sacrificer should perform [the rites] according to the sequence of yoga;
he should satisfy both the teachers and the practitioners with various kinds of wealth. || 537 ||
One should satisfy all other Vaiṣṇavas according to one's capacity,
and one should cause food and other provisions to be distributed freely to all people without restriction.

In this very same way, for all ablutions (snapana), one should omit the ritual sequence [of the main deity], as well as the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the attendants and the offering of oblations (balidāna). || 539 ||
And when one has the means, one should perform the ritual of the Great Oblation (mahāhavis),
following the sequence beginning with the primary rites, including the fivefold ablutions.
O Brahmin, one should perform this in the daily rite as well as in the occasional rite;
thereafter, [one should meditate upon] the pentad beginning with the most subtle and ending with the grossest.
The ritual for the installation of deities such as Cāturātman and others should be performed during the solstices,
the equinoxes, and during eclipses of both the moon and the sun.
In the primary ritual procedure (mukhyakalpa), one should perform the snapana rite as the first and most excellent of the best;
in the secondary procedure (anukalpa), however, it is the middle one, while the four [remaining] types beginning with the inferior follow.
O best of sages, one should arrange the four transits situated between the two solstices by means of the sequence of rotation.
One should begin on the day the festival commences and conclude at its end;
that which is designated as inferior or superior, or the intermediate one, should be performed according to the secondary rule (anukalpa).
In the case of a great sacrificial rite (mahāhavirvidhāna), however, one should perform that [rite] even if it is deficient;
or, according to the requirements of place and time, one may perform a second set of nine.
One should prescribe the third or the fourth [part] in due order;
in all matters concerning expiations, one should apply all of these accordingly.
Among those, I shall describe in detail further on the various types of ablution;
the procedure for these ablutions, according to the path taught in the divine scriptures, has been correctly and fully explained. What else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Ritual Bathing," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the glorious Pārameśvarasaṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Prosperity!
Fifteenth Chapter: Sanaka [speaks] by way of the manifestation of the self-manifested celestial chariot (vimāna).
O Brahman, the installation has been indicated; tell it to me today in detail.
Śāṇḍilya said: Listen, for I shall declare that for which you have requested;
it was spoken by the Blessed One himself in the great scripture named Pauṣkara.
The installation of the high-souled Pauṣkara by Vāsudeva has been described in great detail; it is spread everywhere and established in many ways.
Having extracted the essence from all [scriptures], I shall speak it to you through the grace of that [essence],
by means of divine words originating from the primordial Veda, which directly express the True Brahman.
The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) performed with the *bala* and other mantras grants that [highest] state;
it is accomplished by means of the mantra prescribed in the Siddhānta, together with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), and with the *bala* and other [offerings]. || 5 ||
That which is called *sthāpanā* (the rite of installation) bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is performed with the root mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*), accompanied by knowledge and meditation.
O Brahmin, the installation has been prescribed as bestowing the fruit of mantra-siddhi,
by means of mantras declared in the Veda known as Ekāyana and by other mantras consisting of the three Vedas.
That initiation which is performed with the mantra as declared in the Siddhānta, together with its ancillaries,
bestows the fruits beginning with *ṛddhi* along with worldly enjoyments.
Together with divine mantras such as the *Bala-mantra* and others consisting of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*),
that [rite] shall yield the fruit of the six measures of statecraft (*ṣāḍguṇya*) along with the fruits of the signs [of the zodiac].

O Great-minded One, the installation [of the deity] is performed with the root mantra together with its ancillaries, accompanied by the mantras preceded by the Ṛg and Sāman verses, which are joined with one's own pervasive power.
She bestows all enjoyments and, at the end, likewise grants the fruit of the mantra,
through the mere recitation of the Vedic mantras according to their proper occasion and characteristics.
Dhāraṇā, which consists of meditation upon the Lord together with the placement of mantras (nyāsa),
should be performed by the preeminent teacher for the sake of his devotees toward the Supreme Lord.
That [state] is to be understood as common, like a sacrifice, bestowing all enjoyments;
through the sequence of time, even for those who have no desire, they all yield supreme fruits.
Thus, through the division of mantras, she is proclaimed to be sevenfold.
The best of the twice-born, a sacrificer for the Blessed One, was always devoted to her and his mind was fixed upon her. (14)
Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, contemplating the six internal subjects,
he is the knower of the manifest Supreme Self preceded by its manifestations.
He whose supreme steadfastness is established in the divine mantras such as the *balā* and others, and who performs the renunciation of actions through direct supervision in due order; || 16 ||
For one who always possesses the power within their heart for that form and for devotion to it—which are eternally established—that [deity] shall grant its presence. || 17 ||
The Lord of the World, the Supreme Self, the infallible Master, exists in the form of mantra;
therefore, the installation was performed by him as the primary officiant. || 18 ||
Know that this is the primary ritual procedure for consecration, which bestows the fruits described;
it is for one who was previously devoted to the dharma of the three Vedas, who has received initiation, and whose senses are conquered. (19)

Know that the installation performed by one who knows the mantras, is skilled in ritual action, and understands the reality of the meaning of the Pañcarātra, is indeed an alternative procedure (anukalpa). || 20 ||
Of the Supreme One who is higher than the highest, whose nature consists of four aspects, of the arrays such as the Tranquil and the Arisen, and of the entirety beginning with Keśava; || 21 ||
Likewise, [he is the master] of those whose forms are dissolution, who possess a single uniform nature;
and likewise, he is the master of the entire world, which consists of a single seed-nature. || 22 ||
Of the all-pervading Vāsudeva, whose nature is eternally manifest, and likewise of his three manifestations beginning with Acyuta. || 23 ||
That which consists of the union of the Supreme, who possesses a fourfold nature and whose own form is both quiescent and emergent, is proclaimed as *Pratiṣṭhā*.
That which is characterized by the union of the fourfold Self—the pillar of knowledge consisting of the pedestal and the Brahma-stone—while it gazes toward the four directions; || 25 ||
You are to be realized as the well-established foundation that fulfills the array of the directions;
you are the power of fortitude by your own form, which is unmanifest and of imperishable nature.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of stability and for the purpose of ritual practice, she has become a stone of Brahmā; she is established upon all the stones of Brahmā down to the earth.
In the past, that formless [principle] indeed pervaded everything from the very root;
thus, the material form, both embodied and formless, was grasped as characterized by a pillar.

For the sake of favoring the social classes, for the stability of the sequence of the directions, for the purpose of distinguishing between the lower and the upper, and indeed for the attainment of perfection once again. (29)

In order to remove the insentience of the universal seat of reality (tattva), and for the sake of attaining perfect consciousness of the principles (tattvas) which possess distinct forms, [this is taught]. || 30 ||
And the logical principle, characterized by the single nature of the fourfold self, is grasped within each distinct entity of that one immutable seed. (31)
Their continuous state of abiding is indeed their final foundation, for these fourfold beings are inseparable from the pillar of knowledge. || 32 ||
The installation of those looking toward the four directions has been described;
likewise, that of those looking toward a single direction and those installed in rows. || 33 ||

And that installation, O best of the twice-born, should be understood as being as previously described for all [deities] beginning with Keśava, whether they are separate or in the form of a military array (vyūha). || 34 ||
O twice-born one, when a multitude of manifestations, numbering two or more, abide within a single universal seat by the will of the One; (35)
The specific rite called *pratiṣṭhā* is declared to be the installation (*sthāpana*);
it is the unmanifest form of the principles, permeated by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
O twice-born one, during the rite of consecration known as *adhivāsa*, which pertains to the divine form called *cala*, one should always maintain the realization of oneness with it.
Whether by means of immovability or again by means of movement through excellent mantras,
[the rite is performed] together with its limbs and its characteristic marks, indeed according to one's desired wish.

For the sake of propitiation, one should again withdraw that [deity] which was placed from the heart into the [disciple's] heart, either constantly or at another time, once the purpose has been accomplished. (39)
Through the transformation of easily understood existence and through stainlessness, the temporal existence of things is known as "limitedness" by virtue of its delimitation. (40)
The specific procedure for its installation has been fully described;
it is performed when the consecration of the Brahma-stone and the pedestal (paiṭhika) have been completed. || 41 ||
When bathing alone has been performed for the purpose of pacifying defects in craftsmanship, using ointments, massages, earth, ashes, cow dung, and so forth; || 42 ||
When the gift of the eyes has been completed and the supreme bathing has been performed,
the Guru, with many attendants, forcibly raises [the image] by means of the ritual forms and the water for the feet.
O twice-born one, that which was just now performed according to rule as the consecration-mantra for the dwelling is the third; through the adamantine cement, there is eternal oneness.

When the rising of the ascendant has arrived, by means of the recitation of the mantra-installation and through the contemplation of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), there likewise occurs the stabilization of that which is established. || 45 ||

On the interior walls of the palaces and in the sky and other such places, the lords of practitioners have inscribed [the mantras] for the sake of accomplishment, specifying the limit of time for success. (46)
O twice-born one, the ritual placement of mantras for the mobile image and for the seated image should always be performed for the sake of worship, even in the case of a ritual image. 47.
That [ground] is called "trembling" (pracala), as well as "unstable" (sthitasthāpana);
it is excessively defiled by defects such as fissures in the earth and floods of water. (48)
Having extracted [the image] and joined it again in this place characterized by auspicious marks, the re-establishment resulting from that correct installation is declared as *saṃsthāpana*. || 49 ||
When a seat has been rendered utterly defiled by defects such as lightning strikes and falls, and once it has been thoroughly cleansed and restored to a state free from blemish; || 50 ||
O Mahāmati, an image and so forth, equal to that [liṅga] and rich in auspicious marks, should be duly installed upon another new pedestal according to the prescribed rite. || 51 ||

One must understand its specific distinctions, namely its installation and removal, according to the divisions of the primordial form and so forth, and through the classification of the mobile and the immobile. || 52 ||

The specific types of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and so forth are proclaimed to be eightfold, pertaining to the primary forms (ādimūrti) and other forms [of the Lord] reclining upon the couch of enjoyment (bhogaparyaṅkaśāyin). || 53 ||
O best of sages, that which is the ritual application on the pedestal according to the rules should be understood as *saṃsthāpanā* (establishment), as well as *āsthāpanā* (installation). || 54 ||
For those who are seated or standing, the installation (sthāpanā) is declared to be performed in that same manner.
The dispatching of the images seated upon Garuḍa has thus been fully described.
It is proclaimed to be fourfold through the distinctions of the reclining posture and so forth;
furthermore, know it to be twofold according to the unity or plurality of the image (bera). || 56 ||
Whether it is made of stone, gem, or even metal, that which is fashioned [as a linga] is always devoid of the scope for all daily ablutions and the like. (57)
Even when worshipped with ritual action by the goddesses, whether standing or seated, the form is established alone; know that to be the "single-bera" (ekabera). || 58 ||

However, an image made of clay or wood, provided it is equipped with ritual implements and ornaments, may be used for daily bathing and all other rites, whether or not it is accompanied by the Śaktis. (59)
That which is produced from jewels, vajras, and other stones is suitable for the ceremonial bathing of the *nimitta*;
however, that which is used for the daily constant bath, together with the ritual image (*karmārcā*), is for the purpose of the perpetual rite.
The large image, whether accompanied by Lakṣmī and others or without them,
is capable of undergoing all the prescribed ablutions, such as the daily and occasional rites.
O high-minded one, know that this triple form, which is always accompanied by the powers (śaktis) such as Lakṣmī and others, constitutes the many images (bahuberam). 62.
As for that image made of variegated materials, which rests upon a wall, wood, or cloth, and is provided with a ritual image (karmabimba) during rites such as the daily ablution; || 63 ||
Furthermore, the image made of clay, as well as the threefold type produced from painting,
should be provided with a mirror and other items during the daily and occasional ritual baths.

Know that this [initiation] is of four kinds, according to the lineage of the action-image (karmabimba) and in accordance with one's wealth and desire; it possesses many distinct varieties of deities. || 65 ||
It may be large, as appropriate, whether standing or seated,
or even lying down or traveling in a vehicle, according to one's desire.
The various types, beginning with Bahuberā, are proclaimed to be fivefold;
as for the other ritual images (karmabimba), they are headed by the processional image (yātrābimba).
For the sake of various specific rites, two types of shrines—one with many images and one with a single image—and also two [other types] should be conceived according to one's means. (68)
Listen to the procedure for the installation common to all forms, which is endowed with the characteristics as previously described and includes the temple together with the image. (69)
Having first determined the direction according to one's preference,
one should then construct the sacrificial pavilion on that plot of ground.
Due to its absence in the three directions, or due to its absence in the intermediate directions,
it extends from the northern to the southern direction across the desired locations.
It should be suitable, pure, auspicious, free from defects, and elevated;
it should be fifty-three cubits in length and sixteen finger-breadths in width. || 72 ||
Its width should be fourteen cubits according to one's means, or twelve cubits wide and forty-six cubits long. (73)
O best of the twice-born, it should be thirty-eight cubits in length, joined with two or four finger-breadths,
or else ten cubits in width.
It should be thirty-four cubits in length and a half, nine cubits in width,
and thirty cubits in height, augmented by sixteen finger-breadths.
And its width is eight cubits; thus it may be of five kinds:
seven, six, five, and likewise four and a half cubits.
The pedestal should be four cubits in size in each of the five pavilions;
in every pavilion, one should construct a set of five earthen pedestals.
O best of Brahmins, having excluded the intermediate spaces by one-sixteenth of their own width for all [the elements], one should then determine their height.
O Mahāmati, each [deity] should occupy its own twenty-fourth part;
the remaining space all around should be the pathway (vīthi). This is the arrangement of the pedestals (pīṭha).
One should erect pillars of that same width and height at the corners; having raised them to that measurement, they should be placed upon the tops of the [lower] pillars.
And other staffs, devoid of carvings, were spread out horizontally;
O Brahman, the entire courtyard was provided with archways in the four directions.
The archway (toraṇa) should be one-third the width of the pedestal (pīṭha);
the height of all [archways] is traditionally held to be three times their width. || 82 ||
All the discs, Garuḍas, pillars, and arches, numbering three, four, or five, were constructed according to the proportions of their respective internal spaces. || 83 ||
All those possessing auspicious marks should be buried in the ground after being dug;
they should be square at the bottom and eight-sided in the middle portion.
Circular and with upper portions divided into equal parts—having thus constructed the pavilion for the sacrifice to the Lord, which is the source of all ritual actions. || 85 ||
And above the seat in the northern direction, one should construct a pedestal marked with a lotus;
it should be circular or square, well-characterized, and known as "Prakāśa. || 86 ||
Marked with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus on its girdle-land, that which stands near it is for the purpose of consecrating the ritual substances. (87)
In the middle [mandala], on the pedestal, is the worship of the mantra-weapon and the water-pot;
the fourth is for the placement of the bathing pots along with medicinal herbs.
In that [hall], there is another bed; the fifth is the bathing seat, provided with a *bhadrapīṭha* and equipped with all materials for bathing. || 89 ||
O twice-born one, it should be filled with sand, and provided with doors, windows, panels, and bolts. (90)
Having thus prepared the great enclosure wall along with its temple for the purpose of consecration,
he then left a space all around it, equal in measure to the site of the palace.
One should draw eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the cardinal directions, together with the boundary line (samekhala) and the pedestal (sapīṭha);
or, according to the secondary rule (anukalpa), one may construct them outside the vessel in the eastern direction.
On its western side, however, there may be [shrines] with pedestals and arches, or with pillars, each on a separate pedestal and distinct from one another. (93)

O Brahmā, hear now concerning the various arrangements of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the cardinal and intermediate directions for the rite of installation of the deities beginning with Cāturātman. || 94 ||
For the increase of great wealth, good fortune, longevity, and health;
for the accomplishment of all undertakings; and for the removal of obstacles. || 95 ||
O sinless one, know that through this inversion, equanimity leads to liberation;
it is endowed with two pairs of maces, like the four directions or the four stages of life. 96.
O Brahmin, place the discus in the southern direction, the conch in the western region,
and the lotus in the northern quarter, with its petals facing as desired.
Then, having prepared a pit in the southeast that resembles an aśvattha leaf, one should make it triangular as before, free from lotuses. || 98 ||
The sacrificial pit for the purpose of the *homa* rite is located in the northwest direction; it is octagonal, known as the *dhiṣṇya*, and its shape resembles a half-moon. 99.
Having drawn [the diagram] in the northeast, marked with the appropriate characteristics, now attend one-pointedly to another arrangement. (100)
In the eastern quarter, on the pedestal, there is a circular mark in the shape of the Kaustubha gem;
in the southern direction, there is a discus, while in the western direction, there is a bow in the form of the Śārṅga.

In the eastern quarter, one should fashion a lotus-shaped [mandala] for Āpya, and likewise a garland-shaped one in the position of Vāyu; in the northern direction, it should have the form of a lotus, and in the direction of Īśa, the form of a Śrīvatsa.
The width of the *śamamāna* (the measurement of the inner wall) for all [the temples] has indeed been prescribed;
having set aside one-twelfth part from that for the sake of the lip (*oṣṭha*) outside, [the remaining is used]. || 103 ||
One should make the binding of the girdle perfectly level and equal to its width; everything, including the girdle itself, should measure two finger-breadths (śama). 104.
In the central region, however, the site should be circular or square and well-characterized;
indeed, that very [site] should be outside the northeast quarter of the temple ground.
O high-minded one, this [rite] is appropriate when being performed for the propitiation of all ritual acts,
as well as for the deities who are limbs of the site and for the lords of the worlds.
Having thus performed [the rites] for Vighneśa, the door-keepers, Kṣetreśa, and the Earth,
one should decorate the sacrificial pavilion along with the fire-pits as previously described.
It should be square with four doors, encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass;
or, if those are unavailable, it may face whichever direction one prefers.
From fourteen cubits up to thirty cubits,
and again from six cubits downwards, [the proportions] depend upon the measurement of the image itself.
In the middle of those [sections], a platform (sthalā) should be constructed with two-sevenths of that [measurement] and then with eight [parts];
it should be Samantabhadra, very smooth, and paved with bricks and the like.
Beginning with heights equal to a palm tree in this general rite, the [height] is low by a gradual increase of finger-breadths, or by a decrease of those same [fingers]. 111.
The mandala for all [deities] should be in the center with two, three, or eight parts;
it is square, has four doors, and is adorned with wheels and lotuses. || 112 ||
The bed is in the south, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is in the north, and the fire is as before;
it is auspicious, measuring two cubits with a girdle, and marked with the wheels and lotuses. || 113 ||
Below that, one should fashion a square area adorned with a girdle of maces;
likewise, on the southern side, one should make it marked with the sign of a discus.
It should be circular in the west and north, charmingly marked with a lotus;
it should be marked with a conch in all corners, and their measurement should be as described for the upper part.
All four pavilions measuring ten cubits [in width] have a single girdle;
however, in this case, everything extending upwards must possess a girdle.
Below that, all the pavilions (maṇḍapas) are situated with a single pit (kuṇḍa);
their first [enclosure], including the girdle (mekhalā), should be twenty-two finger-breadths.

In a six-cubit house, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) starting from a reduction of two finger-breadths up to sixteen finger-breadths; or indeed, it may have additional girdles (mekhalā).
First, it should be eight cubits high, then increased by half a cubit; thereafter, one should decrease the height for the four [sizes] beginning with thirteen cubits.
The eightfold [measurement] consists of seven, five, and four finger-breadths respectively;
there shall be no reduction for those ending at six cubits when they are less in height.
In this manner, the width of the bath-houses was equal to their height;
moreover, they were adorned in the middle with sand-pavilions.
Extended by two or four double-handfuls (aṣṭahasta) and raised as before,
these bathing-pools should be constructed in three directions from the front cow-stable for the desired auspiciousness.
One should construct a principal, well-proportioned pedestal, equal to half the height of the image, provided with a couch,
and serving as a hall for the vision and the gift, together with auspicious water-pots.
One should fashion the entire area of the ritual ground, adorned with corner pillars, surrounded by beautiful windows, and endowed with wheels and other features as previously described.
It should be very stable with firm feet, capable of holding bathing water,
and half as long as the sand pedestal according to the initial sequence.
Having increased it by half a cubit and decreased it by four finger-breadths,
and having made its width half of its own length, one should thus construct it together with a spout.
With that [mudrā], one should adorn the central sand-pedestal;
indeed, for the sake of the doors in the directions of the sacrificial hall, one should do so there in the intermediate spaces as well.
The decrease elsewhere, starting from a *kalā*, occurs by means of the addition of half a *śama*;
one should construct arches outside with strong, well-consecrated wood.
They should be five cubits increased by half a cubit;
one should not practice a reduction of them except when there is a specific reason for doing so.
From the tenth [measurement], one should cause five cubits to enter the ground;
for those increased by half a cubit, one should increase them by two units at each stage.
The distance between them should be one-third of the remainder left after subtracting the entrance from the length;
the entire wheel-banner (cakradhvaja) should be fashioned complete with cloth, garlands, and a festoon.
Just as this entire body, though its limbs are distinct, is perceived as one when smeared with yellow pigments such as lime and with sandalwood paste and the like; || 132 ||
In the sacrificial hall, without the constant presence of wealth or fire, the ritual site (kṣetra) measures thirty-five cubits and is extended by one-fourth of its own measure. || 133 ||
In the middle of that, one should prepare seven platforms measuring four cubits each;
the interval between these platforms should indeed be made equal to one tāla.
One should indeed make the courtyard within the enclosure one *vihasta* by means of a single reduction;
sequentially, from a measurement of eight *aṅgulas*, one should omit two *aṅgulas* at each step.
The distance between the elevations and the depressions is two *golaka*s;
in this very same manner, the height of all [the others] is proclaimed. (136)
The measurement for the surrounding pathway (vīthi) here is derived from its own pedestal;
or, in case of a constriction, one may construct it from the first of the two previously mentioned pavilions.
In the center is the mandala-pedestal; to its southern side should be the bed, and nearby the place for the installation of the ritual jars.
Thus, in the vicinity of Vāmana, there is the satiation of the mantras with enjoyments;
and for the supreme ones, there is the offering of the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma.
The bed for seeing and giving should indeed be placed in another location;
for it is beneficial for the accomplishment of one's resolve, as well as for knowledge of place and time.
Having understood this, one should perform everything—neither deficient nor excessive—that which is appropriate, non-contradictory, pervasive, and purposeful. (141)
Having reflected upon each case in every instance, one should act without a mind of greed;
for what has been prescribed may or may not actually come to pass for the gods.
Therefore, the wise person does not falter without what has been stated;
indeed, the filling of gaps in the performance of what has been taught is considered the supreme [duty]. (143)

Accompanied by devotion to the deity and purified by faith, as previously described, [one should offer] the space of the eight directions of the temple to the guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ), as has been ordained. || 144 ||

Then, one should perform the oblation either on sacrificial mounds or in fire-pits, or else personally in one's own pit for that purpose; furthermore, others [should perform it] according to the four Vedas.
Or, one may perform the entire rite oneself, due to the absence of suitable officiating priests (mūrtipas) and the lack of necessary materials. || 146 ||
O twice-born one, having thus newly constructed a pavilion for the sake of sacrifice and having adorned it with various kinds of ornaments as previously described, [one should proceed].
Having first established the eight banners on the east and other directions according to their distinctions of white, red, and so forth,
one should likewise place them again in the center of the altar in the manner of reabsorption.
Listen further to another rule regarding the construction of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa):
it should be thirty cubits in length from east to west or north to south, starting from the temple (prāsāda). 149.
One should construct the pavilion with twelve cubits more than that;
it should be square and elongated in the center, where there shall be five altars.
It was five cubits on all sides, with no space left between each cubit, provided with a series of circumambulatory paths, and adorned with canopies and other ornaments. || 151 ||
On the altar situated in the northern direction, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics;
having placed all the implements for the fire-oblation upon it, [one should proceed].
Then, on the next altar, the twice-born should open his eyes;
on the middle altar, however, there is a single lotus within the mandala.
O best of sages, having spread out a variegated bed on the fourth day,
one should then perform the ritual bathing on the fifth day in the southern [direction].
One should construct four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the four directions of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and one should also construct four sacrificial pits all around the temple (prāsāda). || 155 ||
Having gathered all the necessary materials for that purpose, being well-composed,
on the seventh or fifth day prior to the day of the ritual, || 156 ||
Having offered the sprouts, the most excellent of preceptors should then commence the ritual on the day prior to the principal day. || 157 ||
Having bathed, wearing white garments and garlands, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), with a perfectly tranquil mind,
and having completed his daily rites, he should be adorned with all ornaments for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Equipped with all the ritual implements and provided with water for the guest-offering and the foot-washing,
he should take up the auspicious jar while meditating on Acyuta within his heart.
And together with the Brahmins who follow the single path and are devoted to the true scriptures,
as well as those beginning with the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda, who from their very foundation are permeated by the Blessed One.

Accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, conchs, and the like, they recited the sacred Vedas, beginning with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, in a praiseworthy manner. || 161 ||
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should recollect the pervasive presence [of the deity] in one's own seat, perform worship, and sit down.
Near the central pedestal, facing east on the western foot, he should place an auspicious jar upon the base in front. || 163 ||
Having seated the Brahmins, preceded by the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda, as before, the auspicious collection of materials is joined with more substances than those previously mentioned. || 164 ||
And whoever is suitable for a particular purpose, one should introduce him there;
he should be a teacher of mantras, well-disposed, and of great intelligence. (165)
O Brahmin, one who is skilled in ritual action should be employed on all occasions;
indeed, he should be self-controlled, single-minded, and composed.
Having himself investigated the substance, he remains with undistracted mind throughout the rites of offering and worship—
from their initial commencement to their conclusion in the ritual of nyāsa.

Having performed everything in sequence, beginning with the purification of the hands and ending with the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa), one should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) recited.
One should cause the first four mantras—beginning with Oṃ and ending with the Pavitra—to be recited, together with the Puṇyāha formula and accompanied by the three Gāyatrīs. (169)
Then, he should likewise recite the Ātmānuvāda, the Ātmavyūha,
the Viṣṇusūkta, the Śākuna, and the Śivasaṃkalpa.
The Śrīsūkta, the Śaṃsūkta, and likewise the Bhadrasūkta, as well as [the hymn] beginning with "adbhiḥ" and ending with the mantras of gratification (prīti). || 171 ||

Having proclaimed "An auspicious day!", "Welfare!", and "Prosperity!", together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), he should sprinkle [the site] with the hundred-streamed water using the mantra beginning with "sthānāni" and so forth. || 172 ||
In this manner, the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) should take place in all sacrifices;
one should perform the sacrifice for the three locations in sequence according to the previously stated rule. || 173 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should then place the Blessed One, the source of the world, within the central image,
and subsequently perform the installation of the archways and the banners.
The tetrad beginning with Truth (satya) is to be known in the center, as well as the eight banners;
one should worship them according to their emergence and dissolution, starting from the east.
Furthermore, O gods, you who are attentive, should cause the Ṛṅbhayas to recite [the mantras] there, at the fourfold archways in the four directions beginning with the east. || 176 ||
One should worship Suśobhana, Subhadra, and Sugandha in sequence;
then Suhotra, and thereafter Cakra, together with Vihageśvara. || 177 ||
O best of sages, one should worship above each archway;
or alternatively, there may first be worship of these [deities] together with those stationed at the gates.
Then, one who knows the Sāman chants should cause the female gatekeeper to recite the Sāman;
thereafter, he should proceed surrounded by those bearing the Sāman, carrying water for the guest-offering (arghya) and flowers, acting as the embodiments of the Vedic hymns.
Wherever Viśveśa resides, accompanied by the pedestal and the Brahma-stone,
there one should perform the gazing upon them, as well as the striking and other rites.
Then, one should bathe [the deity] with water-pitchers consecrated by the Cakra-weapon mantra,
as well as with white mustard seeds, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), earth, and ashes.

Then, having stirred [the body] with ant-hill earth and water, and with the water of the *cakrāṅka* herb, and having worshipped and rubbed it, one should wash it with the water of the *astra* [mantra]. || 182 ||
Having honored him with the arghya offering,
he should then place consecrated white mustard seeds in the disciple's right hand and cause him to recite the following verse.
Likewise, he should bring all the *rakṣohan* (demon-slaying) amulets for the *pratisara*;
having wrapped them all around and placed them upon the excellent chariot, [he should proceed].
While he recites the commencement of the ritual, one should place four Brahmins each, preceded by the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda, on his right and left sides respectively. 185.
Recalling the Astra-mantra before him, he himself should proceed while destroying obstacles,
accompanied by dancers, singers, musicians, panegyrists, and readers of auspicious texts.
With the reciters, they should chant the verse "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame" along with the Ṛgvedic hymns;
at the end of those, however, they should recite "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe. (187)
In the same manner, having gratified those who seek gold and other gifts according to his capacity with the Śākuna Sūkta accompanied by the Śrī Sūkta, he should cause them to enter.
Then, having descended from the chariot or other vehicle onto the sacrificial ground,
one should place the image upon a portal constructed of solid wood and settle it there.
Then, on the bathing ground, one should perform oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds with the Astra-mantra;
or else, having previously brought the pedestal (pīṭha) together with the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā).
Having placed [the deity] upon a pedestal on the ground at the altar,
one should then bring the image and install it upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
Listen as the specific procedure for installing a large image is described: as before, having established it in the workshop for the sake of purifying its form. (192)
Having bathed [the image] according to the prescribed rite and performed the opening of the eyes,
one should then carry out the grand ceremonial bath (snapana), either the full ritual or with abundant water alone.
Having performed a brief worship of the bathing-rites, the ritual stones, and so forth,
he should raise [the deity] with many vessels containing water for the feet (pādya) and place it upon the chariot.
Then, having brought him with great effort into the interior of the palace,
he seated him upon a throne according to the rules, preceded by the proper arrangement of jewels.
One should then perform all ritual actions upon the large image; indeed, the suppression of mantras is traditionally taught to be accomplished there at the base of the [small] linga. || 196 ||

O highly intelligent one, whatever [rites] may be there prior to the great ablution (ābṛhatsnāna), all that should be completed up to the full vessel (pūrṇāhuti) at the very beginning; thus has it been understood. 197.

In this way, O best of sages, one should perform auspicious work so that the auspicious moment does not pass away; for such is the case with those who have previously performed various deeds, as well as others.

One should complete the rites beginning with the ritual bath for those [images] that are free from flaws such as precious gems or Brahma-stones; however, in the case of a ritual image (karmabimba), one should perform them either near it or in a mirror.
Even for those [deities] without a ritual image, one should perform the rites beginning with the entry and ending with the festival, even during sleep and so forth, upon the seat. || 200 ||
When one performs the consecration together with the Śaktis, the ritual images, and Garuḍa and the others, it must indeed be performed together with the primary image (mūlabimba). || 201 ||
At that time, one should cause those images to enter the sacrificial ground;
having thus caused that image to enter, the preceptor, being well-composed, [should proceed]. || 202 ||
Then, having reached the center of the mandala, one should present the image there, saying:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, [this is] for the sake of worship unto you alone. (203)
"I shall fashion this image after performing the consecration at the end of the night"; having thus announced, one should set out separate jars for the purpose of bathing. (204)
Alternatively, on the third day prior to the day of the ritual work, having brought [the stone] from the land of action (karmabhūmi) together with the Brahma-pīṭha stone; || 205 ||

Having established the Lord of the Gods of gods upon the sacrificial ground, in the water-pot, on the site of the mandala, and in the fire, one should worship Him according to the previously described method.

Having performed the consecration (adhivāsa) of all the substances, such as the sacrificial cakes and so forth, exactly as they are situated, and having made the formal offering of the image to the deity; || 207 ||
When the following day has arrived, the Guru should commence the ritual bathing;
or else, on the third day, having performed the worship in sequence as previously described.

Having entered the workshop for ritual action, one should approach the Lord of the World, who resides in the three places, at the time of the afternoon meal for the sake of purifying the form of the image. (209)
Having bathed it according to the prescribed rite and subsequently consecrated it in water for a night,
the preceptor, having performed his daily rituals when the following day arrives, [should proceed].
Having raised that image from the water, one should cause it to enter the sacrificial ground. Sanaka,
O best of speakers, has thus explained the ritual of the preliminary consecration in the water (jalādhivāsana) according to the rules.
"Since you desire to hear it, explain it correctly and in great detail.
Śāṇḍilya said: I shall speak; listen attentively to this ritual for the preliminary immersion in water."
For the sake of the purity of the temple, and indeed for the purity of the image, and for the pacification of any deficiency or excess in the measures of height, width, and circumference. || 213 ||
For the purpose of nourishing the world and for the attainment of all perfections, one should perform this before the commencement of the rites for installation on an auspicious day. (214)

One should perform bathing with the five products of the cow and so forth, as well as worship, fire-offerings, and the recitation of one's own mantra; for if this has not been done previously with effort, [the rite will not succeed].
For some reason or other, one may dwell there in water—whether in rivers, long ponds, lakes, mountain springs, or pools. || 216 ||
When possible, one should perform the water-dwelling according to the prescribed rule;
if it is not possible, [one may do so] in a wooden tub or a vessel made of metal.
Or, as the case may be, in another vessel such as one made of clay, containing a small amount of water, at the edge of a cremation ground, submerged in salt water. (218)
In that which is pungent, astringent, or bitter, and defiled by froth;
near a sacred tree (caitya-vṛkṣa), or in the vicinity of a low dwelling. || 219 ||
One should not cause [the image] to dwell in water in places such as these that are defective: where there is a change in color, where it is very small, saline, or covered with pebbles. || 220 ||
One should consecrate [the materials] in water for one, three, or five nights,
or perform the consecration in water immediately, according to the requirements of place and time.
On the third, fifth, or seventh day prior to the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
having entered the ritual hall during the afternoon, || 222 ||
Then, having sprinkled the image with the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
one should strike it with long white mustard seeds and sesame seeds consecrated by the weapon-mantra.

Having bathed [the image] for the sake of purifying its form with the six substances beginning with white mustard seeds, and having adorned it with ornaments such as garments, jewelry, and flowers; || 224 ||

Having bound the auspicious thread as before and placed [the image] upon a chariot or similar vehicle, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments as previously described; || 225 ||
Accompanied by various dances, songs, and other auspicious rites,
one should circumambulate the village, the city, or the palace.
Having whirled it around, he should bring it to the vicinity of the water together with the image-keepers;
then, having set it down from the chariot or other vehicle near the water at the water-shed (prapā), [he should proceed].
Then, having seated him upon a seat facing either east or north,
[one should prepare] an auspicious pavilion in the middle of the water, capable of withstanding wind and rain.
It was provided with four pillars, adorned with four arches,
furnished with canopies and banners, and encircled by a garland of darbha grass.
It was endowed with various fruits and sacred branches of trees,
joined with strings of pearls and adorned with garlands of flowers.
Having first caused it to be prepared with lamps at the corners and adorned with chowries,
one should then have the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) made.

Having first performed the purification of the waters as previously described, one should then place within them an auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) provided with a coverlet, in accordance with the proportions of the image.
Above that, one should prepare a mantra-seat together with its cushion;
having visualized Ananta above it, one should worship him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, and other such items. || 233 ||
With a mantra of twelve syllables, one should offer the *arghya* and likewise the *pādya*, as well as the *ācamana* water,
scented perfume, the sacred thread, and the upper garment for the image.
Having offered ornaments, garlands, lamps, and incense in due order, and having performed the offering of clarified butter, one should meditate upon the process of withdrawal.
I shall now describe the sequence of reabsorption; listen attentively.
Having meditated upon the Self as the all-pervading, omniscient, and imperishable Viṣṇu— (236)

Endowed with devotion, one should perform the supreme consecration (adhivāsana) of Viṣṇu; having established the life-force (jīva), which is the presiding deity of the image, by means of the syllable Om (praṇava). || 237 ||
Having ascended and attained oneness with himself, Lord Hari, the sovereign of all,
he dried up the earth with his wind and burnt it along with its seeds by means of fire.
Having drenched it with water and dried it with air, one should dissolve it in fire;
then, having withdrawn the fire by means of air, one should lead the air to the state of space.
Having thus withdrawn in sequence the internal and divine organs, together with their objects, which are established in the subtle elements (tanmātras), the teacher [proceeds].
Having withdrawn the ether into the mind, and the mind into the ego,
one should then lead that ego into the Great Self (mahat), and finally bring even that into oneness with the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta).
One should meditate upon Him who is peaceful, infinite, in the supreme void, partless, whose form is knowledge,
and who abides in supreme bliss with a tranquil form.
In that which is the unmanifest, the dissolved, the self-abiding, and whose nature is its own essence—
therein Vāsudeva is to be known as the soul of all, the lord who creates all.
Having withdrawn the earth and the other elements into that very [image], the preceptor,
having meditated in this manner according to the rule, should wrap the image with a cloth.

Having covered [the deity] with divine garments, all the darbha grasses, garlands, and other offerings, the preceptor, together with the image-guardians (mūrtipas), should recite the four pervasive mantras.
Taking [the vessel] from the shore together with those reciting the Śākuna hymn as well as other Vedic texts, and with others intent on proclaiming the sacred tradition (āmnāya), [he departed].
One should oneself place that image in the middle of the water upon a pedestal, with its head toward the east and its face toward the north, using the mantra beginning with "ambhasya. (247)
Having caused various kinds of drums to resound in the ten directions,
accompanied by shouts of victory, songs, and other music, preceded by the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon oneself in due order, one should bind the two directions with the Astra-mantra;
then, having looked with the Netra-mantra, one should veil [the self] with the Kavaca-mantra.
Having visualized the world-protectors outside this place on all sides,
and then having reached the bank, one should wrap the water-pot with a thread.
Having placed it wrapped in two new cloths, with a lid and sprouts of leaves,
one should likewise place a water-pot to its south.
One should place the jars all around, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna;
they should be provided with cloths, lids, gold, and tufts of grass.
Having invoked Viśākha into the large pitcher (kumbha) and Sudarśana into the small jar (karaka),
and having worshipped them with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites, one should invoke Indra and the other deities into the eight pitchers.
One should place a water-pot (kumbha) and a small vessel (karaka) at the head-region of the image;
and one should arrange eight consecrated jars (kalaśas) around it in due order.
Having placed oil-lamps in the corners that have not been extinguished, one should display the wheel-mudrā as well as the protection-mudrā. || 255 ||
From this point forward, one should certainly not perform sexual intercourse in that water;
such is the case for the immersion of images made of wood, metal, or stone. || 256 ||
In that case, it would be a direct manifestation; otherwise, there would be an infusion by means of a shadow-image.
I shall explain the procedure for that; listen attentively to how it is done. 257.
One should perform the bath for the sake of purifying the form upon the mirror;
