furthermore, O Brahmin, one should perform all other rites upon the image as previously described. (258)
In front of the image of the deity, for the purpose of consecrating it with the shadow (chāyādhivāsana), one should place a water trough or a basin made of iron. || 259 ||
For the collection of grain, one should fill a vessel made either of clay or wood with scented water that has the luster of pure crystal.
O best of the twice-born, having prepared a seat as before, one should fashion an auspicious *kūrca* made from a cluster of *darbha* grass consisting of twenty-eight blades of *darbha*.
The lord of preceptors, having invoked the Teacher of the World there according to the ritual procedure,
worshipped him with offerings of water, fragrance, and so forth, and indeed recalled the sequence of dissolution.
One should place the *viṣṭara* (seat-grass) in the middle of the water with its tip pointing eastward;
then, having displayed the *cakramudrā*, one should install the jars and other items as before. || 263 ||
O best of Brahmins, for the Śaktis as well, there should be a seat as before;
or else, one should fashion a kūrca from three blades of darbha grass according to the prescribed rule.
However, for each of those [deities] individually, one should cover every limb of the image on all sides with a new cloth, serving as a mere protective shade. || 265 ||
Having sprinkled water all around, one should scatter white mustard seeds upon the ground;
with the mantra "rakṣohaṇa," one should perform protection on every side. || 266 ||
Whatever has not been mentioned here, all that should be performed as before.
In the case of an image made of clay or situated on a wall, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) is performed by means of its shadow. 267.
Having entered the palace, the preeminent teacher should perform [the rite];
for others, having constructed a pavilion for the sacrificial hall as previously described, he should act. || 268 ||
Or, in that place, the Guru should construct a hut as a dwelling in the shade; this applies when there is the means for images made of wood, metal, or stone. || 269 ||
One should perform the consecration of the water in a vessel such as a wooden tub;
even then, one should carry out the ritual residence in the water within the pavilion.
Or else, one may perform it in a specially prepared pavilion for bathing;
or rather, it should take place in the sacrificial hall upon the ground designated for bathing. || 271 ||
Having thus performed the ritual immersion in water, the supreme preceptor should gather whatever materials have been acquired for the purpose of the consecration.
Having gathered all of that together, one should then cleanse the palace with sweeping, smearing, and other such rites; thereafter, [one should do so] in the sacrificial hall.
Whatever ornament has not yet been made, he should have it all fashioned;
[he should punish] those who are atheists, those who have broken the bounds of propriety, and those who revile the gods and Brahmins.
Others who are afflicted with foul diseases, those who are censured, as well as backbiters, heretics, those of base conduct, those born in the inverse order, and those who are envious; || 275 ||
Then, on the day of the ritual, during the afternoon, the preceptor himself should forcibly expel from there those who are greedy, foolish, and ignorant. (276)
Having reached the place for the ritual immersion in water together with the image-bearers (mūrtipas),
he should lift the image from the water, as well as the primary pitcher and the other jars.
Having dismissed the deities residing therein, one should then place that image upon a seat on the bank facing east and wash it with waters.

O Great-minded One, if it is made of iron, for the sake of purification, one should perform the sequence of emanation as before according to the ritual rule using water infused with *titriṇī* fruit. (279)
Having adorned that image with captivating garments, ornaments, flowers, and other such items, one should place it upon a vehicle accompanied by conchs, kettledrums, and other musical instruments.
Having circumambulated the village or the temple, one should bring [the deity] back;
having descended from the vehicle and other conveyances, one should install [the deity] in the sacrificial hall. || 281 ||
At the previously mentioned time, the Guru should subsequently begin the ritual bathing;
having first entered the temple with the image-protectors (mūrtipās), he should proceed to the drawing and other preliminary rites.
First, one should lift the consecrated grass mat from that water,
and then remove the garments, ornaments, and garlands from the image.
On the pedestal prepared for the placement of the bathing jars,
the twice-born should establish the previously mentioned gross supreme ablution.
A separate bathing pavilion was constructed with effort, extending from the eastern direction to the western limit; right there, to the left of the God of gods, [the bathing took place]. || 285 ||
One should place the station of the Yātudhānas starting from the southeast corner;
the bath called Sthūlaparā is [placed] there, while the Sthūlasūkṣma is behind it.
Starting from the northeast corner and extending as far as the southeast region,
on the right side of the deity, from the northeast to the west of the northwest.
One should establish the bath called Sthūlasthūla according to the sequential method;
on the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should perform the bath known as Sthūlapara.
On the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should perform the bathing (snapana) categorized as gross and subtle;
on the fourth day, the bathing known as "gross-gross" (sthūlasthūla) should take place. || 289 ||
Then, on each respective day, the Guru should perform that specific ablution.
Thus, having established the bathing jars in sequence as before, [he should proceed]. (290)
Then, at the conclusion of that offering, one should prepare the bed in two ways;
however, one should first prepare the bed for the purpose of opening the eyes.
Then, one should sprinkle the pedestal with the twelve-syllable mantra,
having spread out abundant darbha grass with its tips pointing either eastward or northward.
One should place five *bhāras* of fine rice, or half that amount, upon a woolen blanket, whether it be circular or square in shape. || 293 ||
One should arrange various colorful pillows as parts of the bed,
having placed auspicious jars situated in the eight directions.
Then, one should prepare a bed for the purpose of consecrating the image;
above the altar, at half that height, one should fashion a svastika mandala.
Then, having strewn darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward, using either dust, flowers, or the four highly radiant protective coatings; || 296 ||
One should place there five measures of śāli rice;
half of that amount of pure rice, and likewise half of that amount of sesame.
Having placed [the materials] one above the other, he should then set upon them parched grain;
[he should prepare] a very firm wooden structure, smooth and provided with four limbs. || 298 ||
Then, one should place upon that [altar] a bed known as a *khaṭvā*, which is provided with four legs, rectangular in shape, and wide. || 299 ||
O twice-born one, he should provide a fine cotton cloth and a soft bed along with its furnishings; or he may provide merely the bed itself. (300)
Then, having avoided a bedstead or cotton-wool, one should place a fresh garment made of new cotton over a woolen cloth, which rests upon parched grain and a jeweled blanket.
One should place a linen garment in the middle, and over that, a multicolored cloth,
provided with a pillow for the head and a footstool.
All the garments were brand new, bright white, provided with pillows for the cheeks, scented with fragrant incense, and equal in fragrance to the scent of flowers. || 303 ||
From Indra to Īśāna, the pitchers should be wrapped with thread,
filled with water, level, smooth, provided with lids, and accompanied by cloths.
One should place those [offerings] joined with sprouts of excellent jewels upon heaps of grain;
and [one should place them] with the emblems of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and banner, respectively, for Indra and the other [deities]. 305.
One should place a golden Śrīvatsa, Garuḍa, and tortoise upon them;
and in the intervals between the jars, one should set auspicious objects atop the grain.
Likewise, one should place the *pālikās* covered with cloths in the corners;
having thus prepared the pair of beds, one should worship beneath them.
One should worship the infinite support of all, the omnipresent Lord above that, through the yoga of origin and dissolution, according to the sequence beginning with the east. || 308 ||
One should cause [the disciple] to recite the mantra known as Sarpasāman, which consists of the power of knowledge;
having offered oblations one hundred and eight times, one should then apply the root-mantra accordingly.

Then, having offered oblations into the collection of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with purifying colors such as white and other auspicious pigments, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess in the mandala; || 310 ||
One should consecrate [the vessel] situated within the water-pot near each individual fire-pit;
then, through the yoga of origin and dissolution, one should indeed sacrifice to the fourfold self.

Alternatively, having offered the weapon-mantra (astra) over lakes and other such sites situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions for that purpose, one should cause [the disciple] to recite the full [mantra] from the full and the full. || 312 ||
Having thus completed everything— consisting of the single path, composed of the Yajurveda, and immediately following the *āśrāvita* call— one should proceed into the presence of the image.
Having worshipped the image with water for honor and other offerings, the Guru should begin the ritual bathing;
first, he should do so with the water from the auspicious jar using the Astra-mantra.
Having sprinkled the image, one should then bathe it with clay and water;
thereafter, one should cause the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras and the Bala mantras to be recited there.
Then, with a pot of cow dung, one should cause the cows to drink here;
by means of this auspicious recitation, they shall be made to drink with the mantra "bhūtistama."
Thereafter, one should cause a dog to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
then, having worshipped it as before according to the rules with water from the camasa vessels, [one should proceed].
Having washed it with pure water and then consecrated it, one should worship it;
this is declared to be the bath for the purpose of destroying defects caused by craftsmanship. || 318 ||
Then, O Brahmin, having put on two garments, one lower and one upper, he went to the bed that had been prepared for the purpose of opening his eyes. || 319 ||
There, O twice-born one, one should cause the image to lie down with its head toward the east;
then, one should cover the image on all sides with blankets and other such materials.
Having first placed a golden vessel filled with an āḍhaka measure of grain upon a heap of grain, one should fill it in due order.
Then, with honey and clarified butter in a vessel of honey,
[he beheld him] situated in the center of the solar orb, resembling ten thousand suns.
Having meditated upon and worshipped the Lord of Mantras, O Mahāmati, [one should place him] in another [vessel], situated in the center of a lunar disc and endowed with the dhenu-mudrā. || 323 ||
By means of the mantras, one should meditate upon the Saurabhīya [deity], possessing the brilliance of a hundred shimmering moons;
within that, one should remember the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśa), resembling the Himālaya mountain.
One should meditate upon the discus as thoroughly consecrated by the streams of nectar flowing from it— both that produced from the moon and that from the cow—
while reciting the mantra beginning with "madhuvāta."
One should consecrate the ghee and other substances with mantras and then cover them with a cloth;
likewise, there should be a golden or silver probe eight finger-breadths in length.
Or, O best of the twice-born, there may be a single golden needle;
one should place the eight kinds of grain around it in the vessels.
Having brought cows and auspiciously formed maidens adorned with ornaments,
he should place them at his side and cause them to be proclaimed with the sound of the Vedas.
Having himself fashioned a golden probe, consecrated it with mantras for the eyes,
and smeared it with honey, he should slightly scrape the right eye with it.
Recalling the supreme light with the Netra-mantra,
the preceptor should scratch the left [eye] with that [needle], either smeared with clarified butter or made of gold.
The artisan, having bathed and been looked upon with a weapon consecrated by that mantra, shall manifest [the image] correctly according to the path prescribed by the ritual rules. || 331 ||
One should cause him to recite the Vāruṇa Sāman along with the Cāndra Sāman;
then, one should gradually fill both eyes with honey and clarified butter.
Then, one should offer oblations with that same root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
for the sake of pacifying burning sensations and other ailments, one should meditate upon the lunar disc upon his head.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] with a stream of nectar while reciting the heart-mantra ending in *dyanta*;
then, having removed the covering cloth, one should show the honey and clarified butter.
O twice-born one, one should present the eight kinds of grain, cows, and maidens standing before him,
as well as honey, clarified butter, and two rods, to the artisan.
The practitioner, longing for spiritual success, should bestow upon the preeminent teacher eight kinds of grain, cows, as well as beds and their furnishings.
Alternatively, one should present all the honey and other offerings to the Preceptor;
likewise, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) should be given to the others and the image-guardians (mūrtipās) according to one's capacity. || 337 ||
If the primary image is made of clay or is situated on a wall, one should enter the temple there and perform the rite of opening the eyes.
In this way, the opening of the eyes of the Śaktis, such as Śrī and the others, occurs. Having thus opened the eyes, one should thereafter [proceed] with the image.
One should perform the burning and nourishing rites with the Astra-mantra and the Heart-mantra;
one should then install the twelve-syllable mantra up to the head for the sake of the Mūrti, as previously described.

Then, one should bring the image to the seat previously prepared for the purpose of bathing—a seat consecrated by sprinkling and other rites and endowed with the reality of pervasion (vyāpti). || 341 ||
Having caused [the deity] to descend upon a pedestal endowed with the sequence beginning with the support (ādhāra), which has been smeared and well-worshiped,
one should wrap it in two garments, one below and one above.

Then, with the heart-mantra [repeated] while rotating through the twelve [syllables], one should bathe [the deity] with the pitchers raised in succession and cause the Brahmins to recite the Vedic verse beginning with "oṣadhīnām. || 343 ||
Immediately after that, [he recites] the Ṛgveda hymns beginning with "yā oṣadhayaḥ" and so forth;
thus, when the vessel has been sprinkled by the remaining ten [hymns], || 344 ||
Then, at the four pitchers, one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed according to rule by four bearers of the [divine] forms, while they recite the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda hymns.
One should cause him to recite the *uduttama* from the Ṛgveda, the *adraviṇa* from the Yajurveda, then the *vāruṇa* from the Sāmaveda, and thereafter the Atharvaveda for one who knows the Sāmans.
Then the very great teacher should cause him to recite the verse "ayaṃ te varuṇaśca" and the purificatory verse "pavitraṃ te," as well as the Yajus formula "vasoḥ pavitram. || 347 ||
Then, having joined together those who follow the single path, he [performed] the *pavitra* rite for you,
as well as the four *pāvamānī* hymns, with the image-keepers assembled in a group.
At the end of that, having arranged the supreme mantra "bhagavān," one should then recite the purifying mantra: "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame. || 349 ||
Then, having sprinkled [the disciple] with water from the jar consecrated by all the *vibhava* mantras, he should do so again with the *vyūha* mantras and the supreme mantra. || 350 ||
Having bathed and worshipped [the image], one should offer more than a hundred oblations;
then, having performed the pervasion (vyāpti) properly with the Praṇava, one should cause [the disciple] to recite.
"Do not depart" is from the Ṛgveda; "O Agni, [grant] life" is composed of the Yajus;
for that which is the Sāman is the out-breath and in-breath; therefore, salutation indeed to Prāṇa. || 352 ||
Then, the worshipper, joined in meditation, should properly recite with his intellect this supreme mantra, "yātavya," which has the Brahmins as its sole refuge. || 353 ||
I invoke the Lord of Lakṣmī, whose pair of feet are bowed to by hosts of immortals, the cause of the universe, the immeasurable,
the primordial one with eternal form, seated upon the seat of the Praṇava.
Possessing the brilliance of a thousand full moons, suns, and fires.
He is the supreme object of meditation for those who know all principles, the one to be known by them,
possessing a gentle form like that of Varāha, Kapila, and Narasiṃha,
with his limbs adorned by the Śrīvatsa mark and the great jewel Kaustubha.
Holding in his hands the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the trident, and the discus.
O Blessed One, although you are indeed all-pervading,
I invoke you just as one fans the wind with a fan;
for fire remains hidden until it emerges from the friction of wood.
For even though you have been invoked, you likewise approach the worship.
O Mālādhara, O Acyuta, O All-pervading Lord, O Embodiment of the Ultimate Truth,
O Lord of the Omniscient, O Supreme Sovereign, O Omnipotent One! Come to me, show me compassion, and accept this image.
Accept this worship today out of a desire to show me favor.
Then, having wiped [the deity] with a cloth, one should worship with the enjoyments previously mentioned;
then, beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should cause the Ṛg and Sāman verses to be recited.

One should satisfy those who know the Sāmaveda with the mantra "arcāmi te," the chanters of the Sāmaveda with "arcata tvam," and those who know that [the Lord] as the Blessed One (Bhagavān) by offering oblations into the fire.
The preeminent teacher should offer seven pieces of sacrificial fuel (samidh) into his own fire-pit;
thereafter, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with clarified butter.

Having performed the libation until completion, he should then extract a spark from the fire and cast it into the consecrated sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the various directions that were prepared beforehand.
In the same manner, having extracted and worshipped those situated in the intermediate directions in due order,
one should then install them in the four cardinal directions according to their respective origins.
The four [classes of] twice-born, beginning with the Vāsudevas, who follow the single path, perform their respective tasks in countless ways through their own names, such as Abhidha and the rest.
With seven previous offerings of fuel-sticks, along with sesame seeds and rice mixed with clarified butter,
one should likewise perform the sequence of oblations starting from the wind-god and ending with Īśāna.
First, having consecrated the four [Vedas] beginning with the Ṛgveda, one should likewise place them;
or else, one should install them starting from the northeast (Īśa) up to the northwest (Vāyu).

With those [mantras] dedicated to Acyuta, as well as the purifying ones prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, the oblation should be performed according to the rules with a mind full of devotion. || 366 ||

Having thus offered oblations into all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in sequence, the preceptor should then perform the rites for the previously mentioned guardians of the directions, beginning with those stationed at the gates.
Having performed the oblation according to the rules in the sacrificial pit previously prepared for that purpose,
and having praised [the deity] with the *jitantu* mantra, he should again cause the Sāman-knowers to recite it.
Having recited the twelve-syllable mantra known as the Rathantara together with the Gāyatrī Sāman, and having formed the mudrā and offered salutation, || 369 ||
Then, with his eightfold limbs, he addressed the Blessed One, the creator of all beings,
in this very form through a distinct manifestation of his body.
"Bring joy to the citizens who do not know the truth, by means of you who have entered within them for a short time indeed. (371)
They attain liberation from the sins arising from thousands of previous births;
for thus is the Blessed Lord, the sovereign who acts for the benefit of the worlds.
Having offered the arghya, fragrance, garlands, incense, lamps, and food offerings,
and having presented the water for sipping (ācamana) and the arghya once more, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Accompanied by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory," joined with the sound of the Vedas,
along with the resonance of conchs and musical instruments, the beating of drums, and songs.
Having placed [the disciple's] hands and feet at those of the God of Gods, the preceptor should then cause him to recite the mantra "uttiṣṭha" together with the Ṛgbhaya.
Having performed the mantra-rite with the requisites for the journey upon a stable Brahma-chariot, well-yoked and provided with milk, clarified butter, curd, and boiled rice; 376.

For the sake of abundance, security, and peace, one should have him recite the Vāmīya hymn together with offerings of excellent food and fruit; immediately thereafter, [one should address] fear. (377)
O Mahāmati, one should recite the Vāla-mantra five times;
having restrained it from beginning to end by oneself, one should recite the Kavaca-mantra with the heart-mantra.
One should cause the offering of the bali-oblation to be whirled in all directions;
as before, one should perform the casting of lotuses, gold, and vajras.

And worship should be performed as is appropriate for the divine sense-bases (āyatana) and for ascetics who observe the five-night vow, as well as for those who are celibate students (brahmacārin). || 380 ||
And for those devoted to the six duties, there is the giving of gifts even to the destitute;
[this applies] as long as one proceeds for a hundred steps while the mantra-image is mounted upon a chariot. || 381 ||
The worshipper who is constant, whose desires are fulfilled, and who is firm in his vows, obtains through the sound of musical instruments from that chariot the fruit of a hundred sacrifices.

Then, having stationed the chariot at the location of the archway (toraṇa), one should worship the Lord with water for the feet, the arghya offering, flowers, and incense; and after bowing down, one should cause [the scripture] to be recited.
Reciting the entire Puruṣasūkta, including the twelve-syllable mantra "uttiṣṭha" along with the seed-syllable (sa), he should lead [the deity] into the sacrificial hall. || 384 ||

The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should cause the image to lie upon the bed with its head toward the east while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra, and then perform the Yātrā-homa sacrifice.
Then, upon that jar situated in the form of a wheel at the region of the head,
which possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, one should worship the Eye [of Śiva] enclosed within the Astra-mantra.
One should worship the eight auspicious objects with their respective names, beginning with the east,
within those eight jars that have been previously established there.
Vāsudeva and the others are to be worshipped according to their power of emergence and dissolution;
or else, that which pertains to the lakes and so forth is the weapon-form located in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Alternatively, Vārāha is in the east, Nārasiṃha in the south, the god Śrīdhara in the west, and Hayavaktra likewise in the north. (389)
In the southeast is Rāma Bhārgava, and in the southwest is Rāma himself;
Vāmana is in the northwest, and Viṣṇu is in the domain of the northeast.
Then, having worshipped these [deities] by their own names with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and perfumes,
one should thereafter worship the Lord seated upon the bed with arghya, flowers, and other offerings.

Having given a covering cloth for the armor that has been perfumed with incense, one should then perform the rite of nourishment (āpyāyana) for the deity seated upon the bed by means of the root mantra. || 392 ||
The preceptor, seated near the feet of the deity,
being a knower of mantras, should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the image of the god.
O best of the twice-born, having performed the festival for the written [image] and so forth, for the mantra-image, for the image situated in the temple,
or for the ritual image on a seat, one should proceed accordingly.

Having caused [the deity] to sleep upon the bed as before, and having entered the temple, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and other rites according to the procedure to be described. || 395 ||
Now attend to that detailed procedure:
having placed a handful of flowers along with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains upon the seat (396).
One should place the twelve-syllable mantra from the top of the head down to the feet;
one should then establish the positions of the limbs and sub-limbs in the locations beginning with the heart.
Then, [one should place them] on the heart, the head, the crest, the two shoulders, the middle of the hands, the two eyes, the abdomen, the region of the back, and the two arms. (398)
Then [he should worship] the two thighs, the pair of knees, and thereafter the two feet;
then the discus in the right hand of the deity and the conch on the left. (399)

In the left hand, one should place the mace and sword; or alternatively, on the right and left [hands], one should sequentially assign the insignia-mantras for the insignia, beginning with the discus.
Immediately thereafter, one should place the crown upon the region of the head and the Śrīvatsa below the neck on the left side of the chest.
Having placed the Kaustubha gem upon the heart and the forest garland (vanamālā) around the neck,
one should place Śrī on the right side and Puṣṭi on the left.
Now, learn from me regarding the placement of the four-armed deity, beginning with the discus and others, at the root of the thigh of Vainateya.
One should place a lotus in the primary right hand and a mace in the left hand;
in the other right hand a discus, and in the other left hand a conch.
One should assign the other insignia-mantras according to their proper application;
in the case of other [deities] such as the six-armed one, they are to be assigned in sequence starting from the primary right hand.

One should place all the insignia-mantras (lāñchanamantra) according to their respective positions; having thus established them, the form of the Blessed One bears the insignia such as the discus and so forth.
In the same manner as the sequence in which the marks are to be placed upon the hand, one should likewise assign the mantras beginning with the *kirīṭa* everywhere, as previously described. || 407 ||
Then, in the twelve limbs beginning with the feet, one should likewise place the mantras of Dāmodara and the others,
along with their respective Śaktis, characterized by pervasion as before.
Then, one should meditate upon [the deity] by means of the seed-syllable of Īśvara as it exists in its true state;
likewise, one should do so with that most excellent mantra, which is identical from the feet upward.
But by the same process of dissolution as before, that very supreme state [is reached] through the all-pervading Self, which consists of internal light and has speech as its essential nature. 410.
Having understood him to be perfectly tranquil, all-pervading, and like an ocean without waves,
one should cause the followers of the Pāñcarātra to recite the *Vidyāṅgadā* and other such texts.

Immediately thereafter, one should cause [the disciple] to recite from the Ṛgveda the mantra known as *dhāraṇā*, which involves the renunciation of the body, namely "jīmūtasya" and "nāsadāsīt. || 412 ||
Having offered oblations in this sequence, O Great-minded One, by the count of one hundred and fifty, using sesame seeds as well as clarified butter with these mantras.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* as before, characterized by the ritual withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), one should then meditate upon that supreme Brahman as it has arisen, just as previously described. (414)
Indeed, by its own nature consisting of all powers,
which is essentially vigor and strength, it is just as fragrance exists within the substance itself.
Just as a seed exists in the form of a tree and the ocean in the form of bubbles,
so too does that power which is indefinable exist within its own mirror of power.
O high-minded one, having taken hold of the Lord of the Universe who is established [within him],
he assumes a body in the form of mantra through his own sovereignty for the sake of perfect worship.
The expansion of that which has attained diversity, and the loss of luster of the collection of seeds of consciousness as it proceeds [toward dissolution]. (418)
Even though it has been manifested, it is obscured by a more powerful,
formless, and dense thicket of ignorance, which consists of the eternal and the non-eternal, and is itself stainless in its nature.
Having thus recollected the root mantra, one should visualize [the deity] seated upon the lotus at the heart of the image,
endowed with the rays of the six powers, and possessing a body composed of those very substances.
One should remember [the deity] withdrawing [the universe] by the very path previously described;
then, one should again remember that stainless essential nature (svarūpa) through its embodied form (mūrti).
When that Supreme Lord, having attained autonomy through the nature of mantra, likewise leads [the soul] by means of the aforementioned method, then [this occurs]. || 422 ||
One should cause all the Brahmins to recite, "The god with a thousand heads," and they should cause them to read the mantra beginning with "O Ordainer, O Overseer."
"Who has eyes on all sides," and "he becomes one who must be approached";
then follows "Two birds," and after that, "From that god... (RV 1.22.20). || 424 ||
One should recite the Puruṣa Sūkta from the Ṛgveda, then "tataḥ paratamām," followed by the eternal "kālakalety" mantra. || 425 ||
"This intellect is sevenfold"—one should recite this here and now;
thus has the investigation of the mantra, known as the Supreme (parā), been described.
O best of sages, the subtle state of consciousness is now described;
next is the intermediate piercing, followed by the manifestation of the circle of deities known as the *vyūha*.
O best of sages, having worshipped [the deity] even subtly at the feet, heart, and head with flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should then prostrate with mudrās.

Having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to one's capacity with sesame seeds and other materials, beginning with a hundred offerings, amidst all ritual activities. || 429 ||
Having recollected each individual rite,
the performer should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root-heart mantra as recited in the ritual manual.
O twice-born one, until dawn and for the sake of completing the rites,
you should then pour the water of pacification (śāntyudaka) over your head at the conclusion of the fire-oblation.
Having offered that very water upon the head of the image with the root mantra, one should perform the recitation of the ritual mantras according to one's ability. || 432 ||

And when the offering (bali) to the spirits has been made, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should perform a fire-oblation (homa) of either one thousand, one hundred, or eight oblations in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), each with their own respective mantras. || 433 ||
The preceptor should indeed cause that water of pacification to be placed upon the head;
then he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) according to the ritual procedure as seen in the scriptures.
O Brahmin, O Sage, that mantra which has entered into the image, or resides in a cloth painting, is indeed the partless and pure state known as Dhyāna, by which it is always present.
Nor has it been withdrawn until it has first been withdrawn entirely by the teacher who knows reality, according to the method of the sequence of withdrawal. (436)

O best of the twice-born, the Guru resides within his own pure and unmodified essential nature, having established the presence of the Primordial Self upon the lotus composed of the rays of his own heart. (437)
In this very way, having indeed conceived of the image as imperishable, devoid of parts,
and possessing a body of awakened consciousness and wisdom, just as it is.
Two paths consisting of the Suṣumṇā, having the form of the blazing sun, arise from a single point within the sphere of the heart-lotus. (439)
Like the luster of a gem, they abide as pervading both above and below;
having contemplated them in the self, so [one contemplates them] in the Deity, and likewise in the self. (440)
Then, O Sage, one should go from one's own body to the heart-god by way of the right nostril path, and enter [the deity] through the left path.
Just as the incomparable Self has been experienced within one's own heart by oneself,
so should one meditate upon that sphere of consciousness situated within the heart.
Having seen that great [light] filled with bliss, inlaid with its own rays,
and solely intent on coming and going, one is then capable of abiding in Brahman within the self.
Unity with the consciousness residing within the body of the deity must be accomplished for as long as the duration of the state of motionlessness within one's own body. (444)
But that which is experienced by the self alone, O Brahmin,
through its own movement, is then manifested in two ways by time, which is of a single nature.
Just as [the deity] is in oneself, so should the practitioner emerge from the deity;
he should enter the deity by the right path and himself by the left.
O tiger among sages, this yoga consists of the heart, which is radiant in form and overflowing with the nectar of knowledge, as well as the image produced from material substances. || 447 ||
O Brahmin, it is the manifester of the entire network of channels from the feet to the crown of the head, by which the Lord of All becomes manifest within this image.
I shall now describe that yoga; listen with one-pointed attention.
The practitioner, free from mental fluctuations, abides in the center of the lotus of the heart. || 449 ||

Through the application of the utterance of the mantra, as before, one should go to the state free from affliction by means of the upward flow; therefore, it is known that [the state] proceeds from that. 450.
Uninterrupted, unwavering, and unshaken, it yet undergoes agitation by its own will,
just as a lamp that is most steady may nonetheless tremble when not shaken.
Just as a silkworm proceeds by taking hold of its own thread, so too does the one who possesses the power of consciousness, relying upon that very power, [emerge] from the lotus of the heart. (452)
Then, by means of his own *māyā*, the teacher should lie down as before;
having beheld the lotus-heart of the deity together with that [deity], indeed.
Then, having cultivated consciousness through the power of awakening, one should proceed from there;
having reached that "twelve-finger space" (dvādaśānta), one reaches what is called the "knowable," which is not the nose.
From that foot, however, by means of the previously mentioned method, one should take refuge in the divine heart;
then, indeed, having entered from that divine heart into one's own heart.
Having come from the heart by way of the central channel to one's own eyeball, and having thus focused upon the deity and gazed at each other; || 456 ||
One should remember oneself as pierced by the light of the deity, and one should contemplate the Lord of Devas as distinct from oneself everywhere by means of the light of the self. || 457 ||
Know that this concentration on the Lord, which is distinct yet characterized by a single essence, bestows all sovereignty at all times upon images indeed. (458)
Now I shall explain the contemplation of sound, which is the vision of the singular wonder, by means of which the mantra indeed attains identity with the Bimba.
Having himself become the nature of unshakable universal consciousness,
[he perceives] all those entities produced by words, which range from the subtle to the most subtle.
Perceiving them through the word "universal cognition" as having attained oneness, yet prior to conceptualization and devoid of even the mere word arising from all [concepts], || 461 ||
And that [object] comes before him, arising from his volition, as a word whose substance is sound-and-form and which possesses supreme power. (462)
O Sage, know that which is the sound upon an object, which has ascended the path of conceptualization and clearly manifests while remaining within, to be the *madhyama* [speech]. (463)
He who resides in the pericarp of the heart-lotus, and who manifests within the paths of diligent effort as well as in the sciences arising from the instruments of the senses. 464.
That sound is called "gross" (sthūla) by virtue of its nature as the signifier and the signified;
furthermore, it is [also called] "extremely gross" (atisthūla) with respect to the domain of speech. || 465 ||
And it attains manifestation within both perceptible and imperceptible entities;
for that sound is indeed the grossest, residing in all worldly discourse. (466)
Therefore, having first made the mind firm in the conviction that "the body consists of the *śam̐da*," the practitioner should then meditate upon the image as being of that same nature. || 467 ||
Through the yoga of the withdrawal of sound, the Guru whose self is joined with unwavering yoga enters into the reflected image conjoined with Brahman.
O Brahmin, by means of the application of the sequence previously described, one should indeed behold the future Śabdabrahman as it gradually transforms through its universal nature.
The image established by him bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; O best of men, having thus performed the ritual recitation of the mantra for the image, [one should proceed].
Then, indeed, one should diligently undertake the union of mantras;
it is the body of soundlessness, whose essence is sound, eternally arisen and free from ailment.

By means of all the mantras, one should [visualize] the Lord of the World, whose essence is mantra, situated within the heart-lotus of the [divine] image and likewise pervading the heart-lotus located in one's own heart. (472)
And [one should contemplate] the form of a throbbing star, as well as its pervasion by all mantras;
the Lord of the World, whose self is mantra, situated within the lotus of the heart of the image. (473)
The best of practitioners should remember Him as performing both creation and dissolution;
He alone is to be known as the Supreme, most subtle, and partless (niṣkala). || 474 ||
And everything indeed must be understood as being of a dual nature;
it should be known as abiding in the essence of sleep within the night of consciousness. (475)
Then, at the dawn of the group of principles (tattva), one should remember the awakened God as if arising with his consort from the state of enjoyment, descended from the supreme plane.
One should meditate upon that as having stepped upon the seat of the enjoyments of all three times;
and having visualized the deity established upon the ground of enjoyment as being in a state of stability. (477)
The power of support (ādhāra-śakti) is indeed the stability of the all-pervading Lord who consists of mantra;
therefore, one should contemplate the pedestal of the Brahma-stone and the image as unified. 478.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform worship by means of various incenses;
having first performed the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) in three ways according to the previous sequence.

O Brahmin, without the placement on the hands (hastanyāsa), everything has been explained according to the method of dissolution (layayukti) as the subtle conjunction; now hear the gross [method], which is another procedure. || 480 ||
One should also clearly recollect the well-formed, perfectly complete worshipful body of the God of gods, composed of jewels and gems, yet devoid of [external] ornaments. (481)

Together with the networks of channels and their constituent parts that are to be adopted as one's own body, and with the elements—such as the moon, sun, and fire—as well as the innate qualities beginning with knowledge; || 482 ||

That which is other than the collection of principles ending with earth, arising from the cause of qualities, and that great non-existent image which exists depending upon substance—[these are the objects of perception]. (483)
There, in the space of the heart-lotus, the mantra—blazing with the luster of jewels—is placed through the contemplation of Brahman; it bestows the corresponding fruit.
For those agents who are devoted to faith, it always leads to a firm and supreme realization of the Brahman with respect to every form, by way of its fruit.
By virtue of which one finally attains the knowledge that illuminates the Self—listen now to all this as it has been explained in great detail. || 486 ||
As before, however, by means of the concentrations (dhāraṇās) through the application of the process of withdrawal,
one should dissolve that image into the supreme, unchanging essential nature.
Then, having gradually emanated it, one should meditate upon the image consisting of light;
thus, having contemplated what was previously described, which is the manifester of the multitude of channels.
Then, one should meditate upon the manifestation of those channels in great detail;
indeed, seventy-two thousand channels have been proclaimed. || 489 ||
Of those, there are ten principal ones, and likewise ten winds;
namely, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and another.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and the illustrious Pūṣā;
Alambusā and Kuhū, and Kauśikī is remembered as the tenth. || 491 ||
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, as well as vyāna and udāna;
and nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 492 ||
Having brought [the breath] in, one should perform the triad; in the rite for the gods (daiva), there are the pūraka and kumbhaka.
By means of pūraka, all the channels (nāḍikāḥ) are filled; of this there is no doubt. || 493 ||
Then the heart-lotus will undergo expansion;
O twice-born one, restrained by the kumbhaka breath, it becomes turned upward.
Then, having recollected the state of the channels along with the vital breaths, as well as that of the lymph, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and bone; || 495 ||

Having recollected the elements in their sequential order up to the end of the white element (śukladhātu), and having recollected within [the body] the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire in the heart-lotus; 496.
O best of beings, from the feet up to the aperture of Brahmā, one should properly effect the placement of all the limbs, as well as the primary elements and the principles (tattvas). || 497 ||
From the feet up to the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), and sequentially up to the Unmanifest (avyakta);
or [the dissolution] of the elements beginning with earth occurs from the feet up to the Unmanifest, or up to the earth itself. (498)
O twice-born one, one should meditate on the Pradhāna from the crown of the head down to the middle of the eyebrows;
one should remember the Intellect (dhi) in the center of the palate, resembling a mass of vermilion. || 499 ||

One should perceive the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) at the root of the palate as having the luster of the color of the moon's rays, like a firefly moving through the sky, and resembling the juice of safflower.
O twice-born one, one should remember that mental reality within the space between the palate and the throat, which steals the luster of a royal gem and resembles a kadamba flower. (501)
One should meditate upon the five equal syllables from the throat up to the heart-lotus;
then, one should contemplate the five [senses] beginning with hearing as blazing like shimmering stars.
From the heart center down to the navel, at a distance of five steps as before, one should duly install the five [deities] beginning with Vāk (Speech) in their respective order. || 503 ||
From the navel to the end of the bladder-head, upon five very level footprints, [the elements] begin with the subtle element of sound and end with the subtle element of smell. (504)
Endowed with their respective qualities and possessing the radiance of shining light,
they are located at the root of the thighs, then in the middle, then at the junction, and finally below that.
Then, at the end of the vital points (marmas) in the staff and throughout the entire foot,
one should contemplate the five elements in sequence, ending with ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
One should meditate upon the sphere of space as having the color of collyrium without form;
that of air as blue and yellow, and that of fire as honey-yellow.
The watery [element] is like a pearl, while the earthly is red and yellow;
or else, one should perform the arrangement of the principles (tattvas) in this very same manner. 508.
Having placed the primordial nature (prakṛti) in the heart, as well as the intellect, mind, and ego-sense;
and having placed the subtle element known as sound in the throat, heart, and navel.

The letter *tā* joined with its own inherent vowel (*a*) is located at the head; likewise, the one called "contact" (*sparśa*) is at the end of the throat together with air (*vāyu*), and the one called "form" (*rūpa*) is conjoined with fire (*vahni*). (510)
From the throat down to the navel, one should place [the element] called *rasa* together with water;
from the navel to the knees, and from the knees to the ends of the feet, one should likewise place them.
Then, by means of fragrance, one should place the earth element in its own respective location;
likewise, one should place the organs of perception and the organs of action in their proper order.
Alternatively, one should place the Pradhāna from the top of the head down to the chest;
one should contemplate the Buddhi at the navel and the Ahaṅkāra resting at the base of the hips.
From the two thighs comes the subtle element of sound; the one called touch resides in the region of the joints.
From the two shanks comes the subtle element of form; that known as taste is located in the two ankles. (514)
One should [place] that which is designated as fragrance upon the two feet, conjoined with meditation on its own seed-syllable;
or else, listen to the sequence of positions for the arrangement of the seven principles.

From the ankles, knees, hips, chest, throat, the hollows between the eyebrows, and up to the cranial aperture— these are, in sequence, the seven earths of the elements beginning with earth, ending with intellect.
Or else, the region up to the navel is pervaded by the four great elements beginning with earth and ending with air; above that, it is again pervaded by space.
One should contemplate that [the breath] fills the interior of the heart and, directed toward that [object], reaches up to the crest-lock (śikhā);
it should be mentally visualized as pervading everything from there up to the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta).
One should, however, place the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), which is another synonym for Pradhāna. Now, understand the procedure for the twofold arrangement of the principles. || 519 ||
One should contemplate Pradhāna from the crown of the head down to the navel;
one should remember the group of Tanmātras from the navel down to the feet.

Or else, [one should meditate on] the Pradhāna as manifest, all-pervading, and assuming a divine form; or one should place the mantra consisting of all the principles (tattvas), or that mantra alone, within his heart. || 521 ||
The primary principle (pradhāna) should be joined as the undivided cause of the principles (tattva);
thus, one should perform the arrangement of the principles according to one's desire. 522.
One should also assign the six qualities, beginning with knowledge, to the heart and other centers; O best of sages, one should perform the unification with the Lord as previously described. (523)
Then one should perform the previously mentioned investigation of sounds;
likewise, one should place them according to the distinction of phonemes and the distinction of their points of articulation.
O twice-born one, one should dissolve the syllable *ma*, which has the form of a *kadamba* flower, into the crest;
and the syllable *ā*, with the luster of saffron, into the region of the crest.
The syllable *i* on the circle of the face has the appearance of molten gold;
the syllable *ī*, however, in the region of the throat, possesses a radiance like that of the kunda flower or the moon.
One should visualize the syllable *ukāra* at the region of the collarbone, possessing the luster of pure crystal,
and likewise the syllable *ūkāra* on the chest, having an appearance like vermilion.
One should place the syllable *ṛ* in the heart, white in color and of great radiance;
the syllable *ṛ* in the region of the stomach, possessing a luster like lac juice.
One should place the letter *lṛ* at the region of the navel, resembling molten gold;
one should place the letter *lṝ*, which has a dark-blue luster, at the region of the penis.
The letter *e* (ekāra), shining like molten gold, rests upon the pair of thighs; the letter *ai* (aikāra), resembling an evening cloud, is located on the pair of knees.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, the syllable *oṃ* is white in color on the two shanks,
and the syllable *au* is red in color, located on the two ankles.
O Brahman, one should place the letter *Aṃ*, which has a luster like a magnet, upon the two feet;
and the syllable *Aḥ*, which has a luster like a ruby, upon the big toes of the feet.
One should place the syllable *ka*, red in color, located on the forehead;
and the syllable *kha*, resembling yellow, situated in the region between the eyebrows. (533)
The letter *ga* is in the nose, having a form like frost;
the letter *gha*, white in color, is situated in the place of the teeth.
One should place the syllable ṄA, resembling the autumnal sky, in the region of the chin, and the syllable CA, red in color, in the vicinity of the nape of the neck. (535)
The letter *cha* on the back [of the body] resembles blazing fire;
the letter *ja*, situated at the region of the hips, has a luster like a mountain of gold. (536)
The syllable Jha, resembling pure crystal, is at the root of the thighs;
the syllable Ña, with a luster like a ruby, is at the tips of the ankles of the feet.
O Brahman, one should visualize the letter *ṭa*, resembling snow in appearance, situated between the two eyebrows;
and the letter *ṭha*, which is red in color and of great splendor, located in the eyes. (538)
The syllable Ḍa, of yellow color and great luster, is on the two cheeks;
the syllable Ḍha, possessing a radiance like that of a sapphire, is situated on the pair of jaws.
One should visualize the syllable *ṇa* on the pair of breasts, having the luster of yellow orpiment,
and the syllable *ta* on the pair of ears, resembling coral and stone.
One should visualize the syllable *tha* on the pair of shoulders, shaped like a campaka bud,
and the syllable *da* between the arms, resembling a blazing fire.
One should place the syllable *dhakāra*, possessing the luster of a swarm of fireflies, on the forearms; and the syllable *nakāra*, with a radiance like that of lotus petals, upon the hands.
The syllable *pa* is located in the pores of the skin, resembling the petals of a lotus;
the syllable *pha* is situated in the armpits, with a luster like the clouds at twilight.
The syllable *ba* is on both sides, with a radiance equal to the full moon;
the syllable *bha* is situated in the region of the thighs, resembling a heap of blue collyrium. || 544 ||
One should place the letter *ma*, resembling the autumn sky, upon the base of the conch, and the letter *ya* of smoky color upon the Pāñcajanya conch. (545)
And the syllable *rakāra* in the thousand-spoked wheel, resembling a red lotus;
and the syllable *lakāra* in the mace, possessing a brilliance like lightning. || 546 ||
One should place the syllable *va* within a lotus, possessing a luster like an autumnal cloud;
then, having placed the syllable *śa* in the blood, it has a form appearing like nectar. (547)
The syllable *ṣa* is in the heap of bones, resembling the blood of a hare;
the syllable *sa* is in the region of the flesh, with a radiance like snow or a jasmine flower. (548)
The letter *ha* is situated in the region of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), having the form of pure crystal;
the letter *kṣa* pervades everywhere, possessing the radiance of the sun and the fire Vaiśvānara. (549)
Alternatively, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa in this very manner:
having placed the letter *a* on the palate, and likewise the letter *ā* on the mouth.
Having placed *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, likewise *u* and *ū* on the two ears, *ṛ* and *ṝ* on the two nostrils, and *lṛ* and *lṝ* on the two cheeks; || 551 ||
One should remember the vowels *e* and *ai* in the row of teeth, and *o* and *au* located in the lips;
likewise, one should place *aṃ* on the forehead and the *visarga* on the tongue. (552)
Having placed the letter *ya* upon the skin, one should place the letter *ra* in the eyes;
the letter *la* on the nose, and the letter *va* at the tips of the teeth. (553)
Having placed the letter śa in the ears, likewise the letter ṣa in the belly, the letter sa in the region of the hips, and the letter ha in the heart; || 554 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should place the letter *kṣa* at the region of the navel;
the *pa*-group is the first [limb], while the *ta*-group is the second.
The *ṭa*-group and the *ca*-group are declared to be the two shanks;
all the *ka*-group [consonants] should be known, O best of the twice-born, as the fingers. (556)
Having thus performed the conjunction of the phonemes, thereafter one should place the twelve-syllable mantra from the top of the head down to the feet.
One should establish the placement of the limbs and sub-limbs in the locations such as the heart and so forth,
having performed the sequential nyāsa starting from the wheel and ending with Vainateya, just as before.
Then one should install all the branding-mantras (lāñchanamantra), beginning with Dāmodara,
as well as the mantras of their respective powers (śakti), in the same manner as before.
Having performed everything in sequence, beginning with the withdrawal [of the elements],
one should then meditate upon that supreme Brahman residing in the heart as before.
Then, having performed the application of mantras according to the previously mentioned method,
one should recite "The Deity with a thousand heads" and the subsequent verses in their proper order.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, this gross contemplation has been described by me to you among these aforementioned forms of contemplation, beginning with the supreme (para).
Having first performed the ritual union (sandhāna) according to the teacher's will,
he should then worship the Lord of Gods in his resting state, following the procedure for the image.
O twice-born one, [he was honored] with various seats and other articles for physical contact, with diverse ritual offerings,
and with heart-pleasing items such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
And with foods such as *paramānna*, as well as with pure drinks and various other enjoyments, in due order.
But having first completed everything ending with the act of giving, and then having brought [the deities] into the presence within the mandala and worshipped them with great magnificence— 566.
One should satisfy the deity together with his limbs (aṅgas) in the fire, preceded by seven pieces of fuel;
the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should also offer oblations in their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍas) according to the prescribed order.

In the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the directions starting from the east, the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) are prescribed in order for the trees palāśa, vaṭa, khadira, bilva, and udumbara.

In the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast (āgneyī), there should be those produced from the Pippala and Plakṣa trees, as well as those originating from the Nyagrodha and Kāśmarya trees. || 569 ||
In other cases where a greater number of sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) is prescribed,
if those specific materials are unavailable, fuel sticks made of Palāśa wood are considered suitable in all instances.
Four cows should be stationed facing north in the southern [direction], assuming the forms of the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Godāvarī, and Yamunā. (571)
With his own milk, he should cook the sacrificial oblations (carus) and likewise the offerings;
first, he should cook one āḍhaka of śāli rice with milk.
One should offer *kṛsara* in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, rice mixed with *gulā* in the western fire,
turmeric-rice in the northern fire, and pure rice in the other fires.
There should be one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] with sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials;
or half of that, or even a quarter, according to the requirements of place and time.
Sesame, rice, barley, bamboo, oblation-grains, and seeds [are used] in sequence;
one should perform the rite with sesame in the other fire-pits, or with those [other grains] everywhere.
Having drawn water from the pitcher containing one's own image with the mantra into a vessel,
it should be offered in succession upon the head of the [divine] image by all [the priests], beginning with Ekāyana.
Then, O twice-born one, with a brush made of four blades of darbha grass,
and with water from the branches of the palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, and bilva trees— || 577 ||
The image-protectors (mūrtipās) should properly sprinkle [the deity] with water from the jars placed upon the altar,
while the preceptor (ācārya), standing in the corner region, sprinkles with water using a cane branch.
Thereafter, having fully gratified the mantra together with its retinue with abundant clarified butter and other offerings, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having thus purified the entire sequence of principles (tattva-paddhati) according to the procedure for initiation, the teacher, remaining in the supreme state and being well-composed, [should proceed]. || 580 ||
Having thus mentally approached with a perfectly pure mind, one should cause the Blessed One, residing within the image, to hear this mantra in due order. || 581 ||
O Adhokṣaja, O Nirañjana, you must remain present here for the sake of the perfection of my devotees who preceded me. 582.
Then that Blessed One, the lotus-eyed mantra, having awakened,
should be meditated upon by the practitioner face-to-face with the preceptor while raising the image.
Then the practitioner, having performed prostration with the eight limbs, [worships] the earth and the other elements which have entered into the form of the image as its own body. || 584 ||
Furthermore, for the sake of fulfilling the purpose and for the sake of consolidating the meaning, one should indeed pacify the defects that have arisen from the very beginning. || 585 ||
For the purpose of nourishing the mantras, one should perform a fire-oblation with substances,
using twelve oblations for each of the four "heart" [mantras].
Having touched the clarified butter from the feet up to the knees, one should first perform the oblation; likewise, one should offer the curd from the navel down to the region of the knees.

One should offer oblations by mixing together milk from the navel up to the throat, honey from the throat upwards, and [clarified butter] from the head downwards; then, having touched the entire body, one should offer it all.
Having first offered [the oblation] with ghee, and thereafter having consecrated the pedestal and the *brahma-śilā*—which is distinct [from it]—with the root mantra, just like the image; || 589 ||
Or else, whichever deity presides over the vital breath (prāṇa) for a particular person,
one should wrap that [image] with variegated garments and then [worship] the wheel with the mantra.
The oblation for the Brahma-stone should be performed with a number of Gāyatrī verses exceeding one hundred and eight; half of that number should be offered separately by the Bahvṛcas and others.

Then, by means of the Ekāyana mantras beginning with "In the navel of the Unborn," [one perceives] the path and so forth, as well as the elemental form or the object of enjoyment, existing as non-different [from Him]. || 592 ||
Having established the deities' seat as the pīṭha within the intellect,
one should then offer oblations with the Praṇava itself, followed by the Vyāhṛtis.
O wielder of the plow, [the worshipper] should then satisfy that very [deity] with another mantra ending in the *praṇava* (Om), and likewise with the oblation mantra (*havana-mantra*). 594.

The restraint of those who have been gratified should be performed with their own names, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *svāhā*, as well as by others; indeed, it should be done until the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
One should perform worship with a concentrated mind, through extensive ritual action,
along with recitation, for all one's own deities within their respective forms.
Likewise, for those [deities] whose nature is sound and for those who are embodied,
as well as for the temple made of sacred syllables, one should proceed in due order at the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) surrounding it.
Having first performed all the purificatory rites for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the presiding deities (mūrtipās),
one should perform the oblation according to the rules, using the previously mentioned materials in the proper sequence.
Having performed this and then stationed the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) in the various directions,
one should satisfy them with milk-rice (pāyasa) in the vicinity of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Then, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of gold and other materials according to one's ability;
having received the fee, those [brahmins] should then recite the mantras for their gratification.
Standing near the image, O Brahmin, one should recite this mantra once the auspicious moment has arrived, having firmly restrained the Teacher of the World: 601.
"O Blessed One, omniscient one whose nature is compassion, please wait a moment;
I shall install your Brahma-throne in the palace."
Then, having praised the Lord while He is sleeping, having veiled Him,
and having worshipped and paid obeisance to Him, one should cause everyone to enter there.
Or likewise, he should cause the Brahmins— who follow various single paths such as the Ṛgveda and others—
to recite the mantras arising from their respective branches according to the sequential method.
He should cause those who recite hymns of praise, those devoted to dance and song,
and others such as lute, flute, and drum players to enter.
O Brahmin, one should assign the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) located in the intermediate directions during the recitation of the *praṇava*,
but one should assign the guardians of the forms situated in the cardinal directions during the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, having formed the protection mudrā, he should display it in all directions;
thereafter, he should have the fasting patron lie down upon a bed of darbha grass.
Then, O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining success in dreams, the preceptor should sleep on the sacrificial ground with his head toward the east;
having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), he should pass the night in vigil.
When the night has turned to dawn, having performed the ritual acts such as bathing and so forth,
the preceptor, most learned in the scriptures, should thereafter commence the installation.
Once the sacrificer has awakened, the preceptor should ask him about the dream, whether it was auspicious or inauspicious;
at that time, for the sake of pacifying any inauspiciousness, the guru should perform a fire-oblation.
O twice-born one, one should offer a hundred, a thousand, or eighty, or as many as one is able, of sesame seeds mixed with honey, clarified butter, and milk, along with fruits. (611)
With the name itself encased by the weapon-mantra (astra) and joined with "svāhā," one should utter the words "destroy the defect, destroy! followed by the name ending in "-nasanam. (612)
Alternatively, one should perform the fire-oblation with either clarified butter alone or with the lion-mantra.
Having thus brought about the pacification of bad dreams, one should proceed with the ritual installation.
One should cleanse the palace both inside and out with branches of darbha grass;
having scattered flowers along with unbroken grains, one should again incense it with guggulu resin.
Then, O Brahmin, the preceptor, accompanied by artisans bearing his own image and holding arghya, flowers, and unbroken rice grains in their hands, should proceed to the interior of the temple.
One should destroy the obstacles residing there with empowered *siddhāryaka* mantras consecrated by weapons;
or, according to this procedure, one should first dig a pit in the center of the east.
For that purpose, one should divide the inner sanctum (garbhageha) by means of the laying of lines;
O best of sages, listen attentively to its procedure as it truly is.
In a palace with a single door,
the measurement of the inner sanctum is determined as extending from the door to the western wall, stretching north to south.

One should properly divide [the offering] into seven parts: the first is remembered as that of the Piśācas, the second is the portion of humans, and the third is designated as belonging to the gods. || 619 ||
The Vārāha is to be known as the fourth; likewise, the other three in sequence—the Deva, Mānuṣa, and Paiśāca—are to be known, O best of the twice-born. (620)
Alternatively, one should divide it into nine parts extending from south to north;
the first portion is known as Paiśāca, and the second is remembered as Mānuṣa.
The third and fourth parts are designated as belonging to the gods;
beyond that, the fifth part should be known as belonging to Brahman.
The four others—the divine (daiva), the human (mānuṣa), and the piśāca—are respectively [assigned] to the four gates of the palace, situated in the four directions with equal steps. || 623 ||
One should divide [the area] into seven parts; the central portion shall be designated as Brāhma.
Then, in successive order along the rows, there shall be the Divya, Mānuṣa, and Paiśāca [sections]. 624.

Alternatively, O Brahmin, having divided it into eight parts, one should place the four-footed Brahma-mantra in the center; then, there shall be three rows [of mantras] designated as "divine" and so forth, in their proper sequence.
Alternatively, one should divide the womb into nine parts using squares for all directions;
the central square shall be the Brahma-square, or it may consist of two rows.
The divine [seat] should be in a row; that which is designated as divine is in a row.
The human is outside that row, and the piśāca should be outside of that.

Alternatively, having divided [the space] twice by eight, one places four feet within the Brahma-square; the divine [portion] is outside with a row of five, and the divine [portion] again with three rows.
Two rows [of pillars] would be for the human [style], while the piśāca style arises from three rows;
even in a house with a single entrance, one should arrange them in this manner or surround it [with rows]. || 629 ||
In the central square of the abode called Brāhma, which has four gates,
there is the installation of the Four-Selfed One (Caturātman) as he gazes toward the four directions.
O best of the twice-born, in a temple with a single door, there should be a single image;
it may be divided between the portions for Brahmā and the deity, or between the divine and the human [portions].
One should establish [the deity] either in a Brāhma, a Daivika, or a Divya receptacle, or in one that is both Mānuṣa and Daiva, according to the distinction of the fruits [to be obtained]. || 632 ||
One should establish many images in the four-gated temple,
either in the portions belonging to the gods and Brahmā, or in those for the divine and human [deities].
O twice-born one, [this occurs] within the three divisions ending with the human realm— beginning with the Brahma realm—
or whether it pertains to the divine or that which pertains to the human.
In accordance with the proportions of the pedestal and the image, and according to their magnitude,
the Brahma [shrine] should always be located at the four gates of the temple.
Among the three divisions beginning with the Brahma-world and ending with the human realm, the [first] is considered the highest;
that between the Brahma and divine realms is middling, while the lowest is traditionally taught.
Know that it exists in three ways, through the divine and the human portions respectively:
either in the Brahmanic, or in the Brahmanic-divine, or in the divine [portion] which rests upon the Brahmanic.
O Brahmin, whether for divine or human beings, or for those who are divine or dependent on the human state, a seat is prescribed; likewise, it is ordained even regarding their place.
One should place the vehicle at dawn, whether it belongs to the divine or the human realm;
however, according to the rite for a single image (ekabera), it should be placed before that [image] in two portions.
O best of sages, for the purpose of propitiation, one should prepare an altar; and this should be done whenever there is the installation of images, such as festival icons and others. (640)
One should divide the space between the two walls into three equal parts, or into seven, eight, nine, or ten parts, with the foremost portion being the uppermost section.
Or [divided] twice by eight; however, in the middle, one should successively discard three parts.
Then, among the remaining [sections], there are four, three, and six on the right side.
O Brahmin, one should install the festival image together with the Goddess on the left side, and sequentially in the other sections, accompanied by the images of the sacred fords (tīrtha).

The image for the purpose of constant festivals, as well as the marriage-thread ceremony for the bed; and the image for the purpose of the ceremonial bath at auspicious signs, and the marriage-thread ceremony for that [image] when it is young. || 644 ||
For the sake of propitiating the deity, while the bathing of the principal image is being performed with abundant water in both of the central sections, || 645 ||
Just as images of deities used for festivals and the like are not touched by drops of bathing water, so too should one perform their installation. 646.
When there is a lack of space in that location, one should place all the images in the outer portico; and if there is still a lack of space even there— || 647 ||
Whether in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure,
having made the site very spacious, one should avoid the top of the temple and the inauspicious directions.
One should perform [the ritual] in three directions as desired, or in the intermediate directions as desired,
or on the site of a training ground, or in a well-examined, auspicious location.
One should install the image for the procession according to the prescribed rite together with the Goddess;
one should never install any other images outside at any time.

O best of men, the preeminent teacher who knows the scriptures, even when performing many types of rites such as the auspicious bathing and other ceremonies, should act appropriately on a grand scale.
When the primary image (mūlabimba) has been installed, one should perform the rites in exactly this same manner;
for the purpose of the daily festival, there may even be an image without a ritual action-image (karmabimba). || 652 ||
One should always place both [the main image and the portable image] somewhere inside the temple, provided that the primary image is not unsuitable for the ritual of constant bathing. || 653 ||
All images, whether for processions or for permanent installation, should always be placed within the inner sanctum; they must never be placed outside.
In the procedure for many squares, having divided that [area] into seven parts at its front and set aside one part,
[one proceeds] then with two squares to the south.

One should place the festival image (autsavabimba) in the fourth bathing chamber; the ritual image (karmabimba) should be to its left, along with the arrangement of the pilgrimage-site images and so forth. || 656 ||
The altar (vedi) should be established in the portion other than that, or even in two portions;
or else, having set aside the Piśāca portion in front, it may be in two portions.
Having established the [central] image, one should then place the locus of the ritual image above it;
on its right side, however, one should install the processional image (yātrāmūrti).
Then, the placement of the others on the left side is prescribed;
one should place them in the fifth square when the area is divided into eight or nine parts.
The action-image (karmabimba), however, is located in the ninth square when divided by sixteen;
for all other images, one should perform the installation as previously described.
Now listen as the specific detail regarding the central image lying down is told:
when the space between the two walls is divided into seven parts, it should be placed in the foremost part as before.
Having given four parts on the right side,
one should establish the ritual for the auspicious thread (karmakautuka) either in the fifth or the fourth part.
When divided into eight or nine parts, it should be at the sixth or even the fifth;
or when divided into sixteen in the front, it should be at the twelfth or the eleventh.
One should place the *karmakautuka* on either the tenth or the ninth [finger];
for the others, the placement should be as before, on the right and left [fingers]. || 664 ||
For the sake of propitiation, the altar should be established as before;
it may be divided on all sides into seven, nine, eight, or sixteen parts.
In front of the primary image, either in a row or in a second [line],
one should perform the installation of all the action-images as previously described.
O best of Brahmins, the altar for worship should be established as before;
or else, one should always worship the deity upon a pedestal (pīṭha). || 667 ||
Having placed a jewel-stone upon the pedestal in the center, one should set it there above;
O twice-born, that is where the installation of [the deity] accompanied by the Goddess takes place.
Having left a space for the pedestal on either side of the main image,
one should perform the installation of the goddesses together with their pedestals.
One [finger] should be placed on the left or the right; two should be placed on the right and the left;
and four should be placed in sequence on the right and the left. || 670 ||
O best of beings, wherever the mobile image is to be installed in the palace,
one should construct an altar in the center and place it upon that.
Alternatively, having established a pedestal in either a divine or human [shrine],
and having placed that image upon it when the time for worship has arrived— 672.
Having placed a Bhadrāsana in the center and having seated [the deity] upon it,
one should worship it daily and then place it back upon the pedestal.

In a place such as a self-manifested celestial chariot (vimāna) or one consecrated by perfected beings (siddhas), and likewise in those established by the foremost of sages—listen to the specific rule regarding these, O best of beings. (674)

The image of the Blessed One, together with its pedestal, known as the "Root" (mūla), was formerly installed; whatever the distance may be from that location, [one should measure] the interval between the two doors of that place. || 675 ||
Having divided that [area] into three perfectly equal parts starting from the side of the door, there shall be the three divisions in sequence: the Paiśāca, the Mānuṣa, and the Divya.
Starting from the right wall, one should divide the divine portion equally into seven parts up to the left wall; then, indeed, starting from the right side, [one proceeds].
One should place the *karmakautuka* on either the fifth or the fourth [finger];
on its right side, however, it should be accompanied by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.
One should place the festival image and station it on the left side;
all other images should be arranged according to the proper sequence and order.
Having divided [the space] sevenfold from the door to the western wall, one should set aside the two sides of the door and then divide [the remaining area] into two parts again. || 680 ||
Having performed the third divine rite seven times between the two walls, it becomes the place for the installation of the ritual images and other icons, as previously described. (681)
O Brahmin, attend to the ritual procedure for that bed as well:
one should employ the ritual image during the fifth or sixth part of the day.
The installation of all other images should be performed as previously described;
in the case of a self-manifested shrine with four doors, one should divide the area around it sevenfold.
Having abandoned the Paiśāca and Mānuṣa [sites], on the third divine (Daivika) step,
either in the foremost part or in the north, according to the Īśvara-prāgvaṃśa layout.
Or one should place the ritual image in the divine northeast quarter,
having installed it upon a single pedestal within the womb of the temple.
Alternatively, one may arrange the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva, or those beginning with Keśava,
or the entire collection of manifestations (prādurbhāva) in the form of a row.
In that regard, this distinction according to the divine method is now described; listen.
From the door up to the walls, it extends from south to north.
When the embryo has been divided sevenfold, one should establish it in the forms of rows within the stations beginning with Brahmā, by means of the very path previously described.
In that case as well, one should place the southern direction first and end with the northern;
and wherever one places them in the form of a circumambulation, there [the sequence] is sevenfold.
When the womb [of the altar] has been divided all around, one should assign the principal image to the center of the Brahma-section,
