or surround it on all sides in both the divine and human sections.
And one should install all other forms according to the sequence of the enclosures;
however, in the installation of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), Vāsudeva is placed in the center.
Outside of that, in the divine row, one should place Saṃkarṣaṇa in the south,
Pradyumna in the western part, and likewise Aniruddha in the north.
In the same manner, one should likewise assign the fourfold group of the Cāturātmya mantras, each conjoined with its own respective cause, to those who have entered into other forms.
In the fourfold group of deities and in the nine forms consisting of the nine mūrtis,
one should place Vāsudeva at the beginning and in the middle, and in the four cardinal directions starting from the east.
The four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva are to be installed in sequence within the two central positions in the rite known as the installation of the five forms (pañcamūrti). 695.
Then, having established Vāsudeva in the center,
one should place the four [deities] ending with Nārāyaṇa, preceded by Saṃkarṣaṇa, in the four directions.
In this manner, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhāna) sequentially even for a group of seven;
however, in the consecration of the nine forms, Vāsudeva should be placed in the center.
Outside of that, in the eight positions situated in the divine portion,
there are in sequence the eight forms beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ending with Varāha.
In the consecration of Keśava and others, one should place Vāsudeva in the center,
having divided the divine portion according to the method described for the twelve-spoked [mandala].
One should install the deities beginning with Keśava, numbering twelve, starting from the east; or else, in the row of humans, one should place them in the four corner sections.
Having abandoned the other sections, one should place [the deities] in order starting from the east;
indeed, in the event of a narrow space, one may do so for both divine and human [images].
Listen to the fruit resulting from the distinction between these places when they arise together at one time:
in the portion of Brahmā there is liberation, while in the divine portion there is the increase of one's station.
The attainment of the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation occurs when one relies on the divine in the morning;
the attainment of the fruits of divine portions occurs when one relies on the divine among human beings.
From the portions of the gods and humans comes the fruit pertaining to this world and the next;
and from the portions of the wise and Brahmā comes the eightfold quality pertaining to this world.
But listen, O twice-born one, to the distinction of the fruits resulting from the performance of many types [of rites]:
the attainment of the six qualities, beginning with knowledge, occurs in the state of Brahman. (705)
The attainment of all desired fruits occurs in that which pertains to the gods and is based on Brahman,
as well as in that portion belonging to the gods and Brahman among both divine and human beings.
The fruit regarding both those dependent on humans and the divine has already been stated;
this applies when [the image] is installed within the divisions beginning with Brahmā and ending with the human. || 707 ||

O Brahmin, the prosperity of the site, the sacrificer, the king, and the kingdom shall increase; now the distinction of the fruits resulting from the performance of rituals and the installation [of images] is being described.
In the Brāhma period, which is divided into seven parts, the installation [of the deity] should take place in the fourth part;
in the fifth part, it bestows liberation and grants the fruit of proximity [to the deity]. (709)
When the fifth [section] is divided into eight parts, there is a group of eight qualities;
however, in the sixth part lies the *sthāpana*, which bestows the fruit of *sālokya* (residing in the same world).
When divided into nine parts, the result would be exactly thus;
when that same [result] is divided sixteenfold, the ninth part is a group of six qualities.
O Brahmin, the installation [of the image] on the tenth, twelfth,
or eleventh day swiftly bestows residence in the world of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, when the seventh part of the day is divided into seven, the installation [of the image] should take place during the fourth;
it bestows right discernment, righteousness, and mental serenity.
Installation in the sixth part increases nourishment and good fortune;
it bestows victory over untimely death and brings about an abundance of strength and enthusiasm.
When that [space] is divided ninefold, the result would be exactly the same;
but when it is divided eighteenfold, O twice-born one, the ninth part is to be established.
It bestows the attainment of divine enjoyments without delay;
its application occurs in the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth parts. (716)
It bestows abundance of wealth and grain as well as the attainment of land;
thus, one should employ it on all sides for the sake of a devotee who possesses a portion of Brahman.
It eternally bestows the fruit of absolute liberation in the supreme divine state;
likewise, it grants enjoyment and brings about an abundance of strength and vigor.
In the divine northeastern quarter, however, its installation bestows longevity, health, sovereignty, and indeed victory for kings. (719)
It brings about great prosperity for the site as well as for the district;
its establishment in a gentle and divine place bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the row known as the divine Brahmā, however, the installation should be performed as in the case of the divine [deities];
wherever the placement of the images is prescribed for a particular position, [that is how it should be done]. || 721 ||

Having divided each of those into two and established them in the lunar portion (amṛtāṃśaka), the stated fruits are accomplished; however, in the fiery portion (āgneya), they are reversed if performed otherwise.
O Brahmin, within the temple, there is the installation of the processional image for the duration of a year, as well as for the site, the patron, the king, and the realm. (723)
It bestows great fortune and splendor day by day;
O Brahmin, this indeed is the fruit of the middle face in the pavilion of the mouth. (724)
O Brahmin, the fruit will be meager in the first enclosure and other such locations; the same result applies when others are installed as well.
O Mahāmati, for all the images, beginning with the primary image,
one should [place them] in their respective locations as prescribed, whether through negligence or intentionally.
If it is abandoned and established in another place, then that location, the sacrificer, the king, and the kingdom shall all perish. (727)
All the people living in that region will be afflicted by diseases and other ailments;
there shall be drought, famine, and oppression by enemies.
Therefore, one who desires the welfare of the kingdom, as well as his own and that of the king,
should not act in such a way as to cause a displacement from the positions as they have been described.
Even when the image is fixed in place due to a fault preceded by negligence or laziness, it remains immovable; however, this applies to a stationary image, excluding one that is mobile.
Having established [the deity] in its respective place as prescribed, one should worship it;
especially so in the case of a self-manifested (svayamvyakta) image or one installed by perfected beings (siddhas) and others.
One should install the mobile image in the palace within its respective place;
if it is broken, one should perform the rite again when the middle [image] has been restored by means of inspection.
Having washed [the site] with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and smeared it with sandalwood paste and the like using the Hṛdaya-mantra,
one performs the "blocking" (nirodhana) of the mantras by means of jars placed upside down in a pit.

Having performed the worship as prescribed, up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), according to the previously stated procedure and with focused mind during each respective transit (ayana), one should consign [the deity] there.
Generally, however, one should place a stone slab measuring six, five, or four *golakas*, which has slightly protruded from the pedestal and is well-stabilized on the ground. (735)

One should cause [the deity] to be installed there with its own mantra, reciting: "O you who were formerly established by the nine apertures for the sake of liberation, may you be established here by the seat (pīṭha). || 736 ||
Then, one should place five [substances] each, starting from the east, according to their respective powers;
among the materials in the stone pits, there should be diamond and gold.
Then, on the right side, there should be yellow orpiment, ushira root, and rice;
as well as sapphire, green vitriol, sandalwood, and sesame seeds.
Pearls, silver, mercury, and likewise the eastern [substances], as well as uśīra, mung beans, and the red lotus in the north. (739)
One should first place twenty pieces of bell-metal, royal stone, and king-ratna together with chickpeas in the middle, and then outside of that.
Likewise, in the intermediate directions, by means of the yoga of dissolution, other [substances] are likewise [to be placed] individually:
iron, beginning with lapis lazuli, as well as the discus-marked and the mica.
In the northwest direction, there is ṣāṣṭika rice, topaz, and myrobalan; here also are red ochre, the śārikā bird, and lentils; then, in the southwest direction— 742.
Mahānīla, vaṅga, as well as pāṣāṇamākṣika, barley, and agaru, and likewise sphaṭika in the southeast. || 743 ||
Copper, realgar, wheat, and Śaṅkhapuṣpī—these should all be placed in the middle; thereafter, one should prepare that group of pits.
Having covered it with plaster and having worshipped it, one should cause him to recite the mantras along with their auxiliary limbs at every step, as well as the Yajurveda and the six Vedāṅgas.
Above that, O Mahāmati, one should place the pedestal, having set it into its cavity; and above that, indeed, is the wheel made of the eight metals.
The support for which has been specified by its particular name among the twelve, and which is its own,
is a golden lotus above that, or one made of copper or brass produced from it.
For this pentad, situated in its proper order within the fourfold self, one should install Ananta upon the wheel, and indeed Mīna and Kūrma upon him.
The Tortoise and Ananta are for the Fish; the Fish and Ananta are for that [Tortoise];
for all [the others] the lotus is prescribed, and one should place Ananta for that [lotus].
Having installed the circle of the Śaktis, beginning with Lakṣmī, during the rite of establishment,
and having performed the ritual up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) within this rite.
In the pavilion of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), one should perform the ritual in exactly the same manner;
as before, the rite with darbha grass and water should be performed together with the bearers of the images.
Now I shall describe another method; listen to it now.
O Brahmin, one should first consecrate and then install the Brahma-stone.
O twice-born one, having first made a surface slightly less than the size of the pedestal— level, smooth, firm,
and divided into nine squares— one should place a lotus in each square.
Having properly drawn the lines, one should dig out the pericarp (karṇikā) in all [the sections];
in the center of the womb (garbha), one should dig according to the measurement of the stone's height and its width.
Having moved it along the path of that previous sūtra toward the northern direction,
one should also make an auspicious pit there in the middle, measuring six finger-breadths.
In that [place], however, there was a water-pot made of gold or silver, filled with jewels,
measuring four finger-breadths in size, and shaped like a conch shell.
Having consecrated it with the heart-mantra and established it with the Gāyatrī,
one should place a lid upon it and likewise apply a plaster of lime over the top.
Having offered [the oblation], the Guru himself, having first consecrated the *brahmaśilā* with mantras and assumed a state of all-pervasiveness, should install it facing eastward. (758)
One should meditate upon that all-pervading stone, whose form consists of both the support and the supported;
therein, one should contemplate the placement of all the paths by means of the root mantra.
O twice-born one, having thus performed that placement, you should afterwards place jewels and other such items upon it; listen as to how this should be done. (760)
A golden fire-altar, likewise an infinite silver one, and a golden earth;
a lotus made of eight metals in the center upon the Brahma-stone.
In the lotus-seated [deities] starting from the east and proceeding in order up to the domain of Īśāna,
there are the vajra, the sun-crystal (sūryakānta), and likewise the sapphire (indranīla).
O best of sages, [the gems are] mahānīla, and beyond that the pearl; then the puṣyarāga, and after that the padmarāga. || 763 ||
Having placed lapis lazuli in the northeast, one should place crystal in the center; and in the east and other directions, silver, copper, tin, lead, and brass.
Having placed copper, iron, and bell-metal, with gold in the middle, as well as realgar, yellow orpiment, chinapiṣṭaka, and kuṣṭha; || 765 ||
Srotoñjana, darada, saurāṣṭrī, and hemagairika; for the liquor, however, one should take rājapāṣāṇa and pārada from all [of these]. || 766 ||
Wheat, wild barley, as well as mung beans, black gram, chickpeas, O tiger among sages, horse-gram, and lentils; || 767 ||
Having placed in sequence the eight [substances]—white mustard seeds, sesame seeds, hrībera, turmeric, māṃsī, sahadevī, and likewise vacā—in the center; || 768 ||
One should extract the series of roots, beginning with *viṇṇukrāntā* and ending with wine (*madya*), [using] *balā*, *moṭā*, *śyāmāka*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*. (769)
If even jewels are unavailable, a pearl is recommended;
and if even metals are absent, gold is considered the best alternative.
If even the minerals cannot be obtained, green vitriol (haritāla) is superior;
if all the seeds cannot be obtained, the rice seed (śālibīja) is praised. || 771 ||
If all these items are unavailable, one should place gold everywhere;
in its absence, however, one should place silver or pearls.
O Brahmin, one should first apply an ointment made of ghee and milk that has been previously prepared, and indeed do so in all hollows.
After placing a new, well-washed *dukūla* cloth upon that [surface],
one should apply a smooth inner coating of plaster and then set down the pedestal.
O best of Brahmins, having aligned that [image] as before with a stone,
one should then place the great golden Gāruḍa image into the cavity of the pedestal.
Milk, curd, clarified butter, parched grain, honey, flowers, and fruits, as well as all perfumes together with all medicinal herbs, O best of Brahmins. (776)
One should meditate upon the seat as before, endowed with all [the principles] beginning with Dharma;
then, one should further place thereupon the pervasive presence consisting of the seat of consciousness.
Having consecrated each [oblation] individually with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra recited from the heart,
one should perform the offering in whatever specific rite is required.
Then, until the completion of the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), the Guru should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and encircle the temple with a cord quadrupled in length.
One should cover it with a new cloth as well as with a garland of darbha grass;
thereafter, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion together with the presiding priests (mūrtipās).
One should wait for the auspicious moment; however, as long as that time does not arrive, one should pass the interval by means of diversions, fire offerings, laughter, and recitations. || 781 ||
O Brahmin, when the rising of the auspicious moment (lagna) has arrived, one should awaken the Lord while He is lying down;
having honored Him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), fragrant unguents, garlands, and so forth, one should recite this [hymn]. || 782 ||
O Supreme Lord, withdraw your own fiery form consisting of mantra and assume gentleness for the sake of maintaining stability.
Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; arise, O Supreme Lord, and step upon this seat for the sake of showing me favor.
Then, having extracted the mantra-form whose sleep has been abandoned by means of the heart-mantra,
one should forcibly raise it up together with the bearers of the forms by means of the form-mantra.
One should lift up the pitcher along with its contents, situated near one's own sacrificial pit;
those performing the directional fire-offerings (diśāhoma) should lift it up together with auspicious rites.
The preceptor should proceed in front, carrying eight jars representing the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras),
holding them in an unbroken stream with a flow no thicker than a blade of grass.
Or else, while scattering many various kinds of jewels,
along with many different types of flowers mixed with parched grain and other offerings.
Those who carry the image immediately thereafter are the bearers of the form, so that others do not pass between the preceptor and the image. (789)
Others, bearing eight jars and those who carry auspicious objects,
should also go around him while reciting the Śākuna.
The sacrificer, however, should remain silent, holding kuśa grass in his hand and bowing;
other attendants should follow behind them.
Having emerged through the gateway, one should perform four circumambulations of the pedestal of the temple,
having stationed oneself before the door.

Having offered water for the feet, the respectful oblation (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamana), one should cause [the disciple] to enter with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra); then, those who know the ritual should have him recite the Vedic branches and so forth, ensuring he does not touch them.
Following that, [he recites] "the city with four wheels" and "the eleven";
then, with a white silk cloth consecrated by armor-mantras, [he performs the protection]. || 794 ||
First, one should encircle the stalk of the lotus-feet with the *śikhā-mantra*, having balanced Agni and Soma by means of the *praṇava* at the beginning and end. (795)
With the root mantra, one should firmly establish the image above the pedestal;
in the rite of installing the deity, the center of the door must not be bypassed.
It should not be placed in front of him, nor at his side, nor behind him;
the best of teachers should subsequently avoid the wind from the left.
And one should cause the two mantras, *pratiṣṭhā* and *liṅga*, to be recited in sequence,
while firmly maintaining one's own form as peaceful and consisting of Brahman.
Even where the installation is prescribed solely for the Brahma [quarter], there too one should resort slightly to the divine portion on the left. || 799 ||
Since he has emerged for the benefit of all with a nature endowed with the six qualities,
he should therefore be brought slightly down from the station of Brahmā to the portion of the gods.

Indeed, for the sake of attaining the fruits such as liberation, that which is already within one's hand must be relinquished without further deliberation; let this curiosity be cast away from the heart.
Having offered the water of honor (arghya) to all the limbs with the mantra, one should then recollect the root mantra;
thereafter, indeed, with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra recited over it, one should apply the vajra-ointment.
The Guru, with his head bowed in prostration, should first utter the syllable Oṃ and then perform the rite of unification for the Bimba, the pedestal, and the stone slab. 803.
O Blessed One, you have been propitiated for the benefit of practitioners;
therefore, out of compassion, you should dwell here forever. (804)
"O Lord, wherever you abide, there success is not far off for the foremost of practitioners;
this was indeed stated by you in the past. (805)
Therefore, remain forever steadfast, ever-contented, compassionate, supreme, and great;
remain always intent on bestowing grace as long as the moon and stars endure.
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, one should then offer the arghya water upon the head and the feet of the primary image fashioned from materials such as clay.
O twice-born one, in the worship of the ritual image or on a seat made of darbha grass,
one should perform the rite of awakening and likewise the act of circumambulation.
Having entered the temple, the master of adepts, being composed, should perform all other rites in due order at the root and the branch.
Then one should perform the subsequent piercing (anuvedha), starting from the base (ādhāra) up to the crest (śikhā),
by means of the thread of capacity and power, according to the sequence of the Lord.

When that [power] exists, even if the reflection and so forth are lost, as well as the movement [of breath], the multitude of mantras does not abandon him, and after some time, [it becomes manifest]. || 811 ||
Whether unawakened or awakened, whatever man installs an image made of another substance in that sacred abode, [he incurs a fault]. || 812 ||
And immediately thereafter, it arises permeated by that cognition;
such a state exists in this triple world, O wise one. (813)
Having meditated upon the root mantra, which possesses the characteristics of the utterly tranquil Brahman, she exists as the sense-bases (āyatana) as far as the moon and stars.
One should contemplate that everything from the foundation (ādhāra) up to the tip of the banner (dhvajāgra) is pervaded by it;
having thus performed the general integration (sāmānyasandhāna), one should practice the pervasion of the paths (adhvavyāpti). || 815 ||
One should effect the pervasion consisting of the path of the worlds (bhuvana-adhvan) residing within the temple and the pedestal,
interwoven with other paths such as that of the words (pada-adhvan) and others which are the very nature of existence.

For everywhere, O Brahmā, it is indeed abandoned by the all-pervading characteristics of the other worlds, as well as by the other [characteristics], except for that portion belonging to the world of earth. (817)

And because of the predominance of rajas and tamas, and only slightly of the quality of sattva, they are indeed of a nature consisting solely of the quality of sattva, while others are for that very reason [not so]. (818)
The Bhūrloka stands separately within the group of paths beginning with Pada;
and there are three Padas upon the stone known as Kūrma and Brahman.
When the deposition of the jewels has been performed, another [deposition] beginning with the waking state is to be placed;
the path of mantra, conjoined with the fourth Brahman, is on the image-seat.
O best of the twice-born, having placed [the breath] from the feet up to the navel, one should then contemplate the path of the principles (tattvādhvan);
thereafter, from the navel up to the crown of the head, one should contemplate the path of the digits (kalādhvan).
In that lotus of the aperture of Brahmā, upon the ground of the syllables of Brahmā,
resides the supreme Brahman— the universal, eternal, and all-pervasive Lord— within the pericarp.
Having thus performed the pervasion of the paths, one should meditate upon the root mantra in its gross, subtle, and supreme aspects; the gross aspect is sixfold, extending as far as the stone.
Likewise, one should perform the subtle placement upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and the supreme placement upon the form of the image;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the deities at the base of the seat (pīṭha).
O Mahāmati, one should never perform the ritual arrangement of these articles conducive to worldly existence within the mantra-image.
O best of sages, however, above the pedestal (pīṭha), one may install the deities of the manifestation (vibhava) even without this foundation (pratiṣṭhā),
arranging them one above the other as before.
Beginning with the designation of the jar (ghaṭa), one then proceeds to the supreme worship;
for it is indeed by virtue of the arrangement of all the deities in this manner.
The placement (nyāsa) consisting of wish-fulfilling gems becomes the bestower of success when performed;
thereafter, one should perform the establishment of the principles (tattvas), following the establishment of the primordial nature (prakṛti).
Like the sun, it [the consciousness] manifests the objects of knowledge through waves of cognitive bliss,
generating manifold delights from its support up to the summit of the head.
One should behold the image consisting of mantra, possessing a manifold and wondrous form;
thus it is the source of all arising and the bestower of the fulfillment of one's intentions.
Having established the image, which is a tree consisting of mantra, with a stainless mind,
[he should worship] its branch consisting of wisdom— the most excellent and lofty of ascetics.
O twice-born one, the practitioner should meditate upon [the world] pervading the infinite sky,
by means of that incomparable nectar which has indeed flowed forth from it.
One should always meditate upon the tree consisting of the mantra-form as being full of sap,
O Nārada, [nourished] by the water of the earth and that which arises from the sky.
The branch of the mandāra flower is indeed exactly like that and not otherwise;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the image according to the prescribed rule.
One should perform the threefold placement (nyāsa) of the Lord consisting of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal,
whether he is standing, sitting, lying down, or even moving.
O twice-born one, one should perform the three-fold nyāsa upon all these as well;
or else, when standing, one should perform the nyāsa of stability, and when seated, that known as creation.
O best of the twice-born, while lying down, one should perform the withdrawal of the placement (saṃhṛtinyāsa);
one should establish the limbs and sub-limbs in their respective locations, beginning with the heart.
One should install the other marks and so forth, ending with Garuḍa;
then, one should worship everything there by means of the ritual of dissolution (layayāga).
One should again worship the wheel of mantras situated on the seat through the sacrifice of enjoyment;
then, one should worship the assembly of mantras belonging to the seat in reverse order.
O best of men, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of creation up to the power of the foundation (ādhāraśakti),
one should superimpose the word "Lord" (svāmin) upon one's own name, or even the supreme [name].
Then, preceded by "Harikeśa" and joined with "Tāra," the guardians of the images and others should indeed say: "May it be well-established. (841)
Scattering handfuls of flowers and unbroken rice grains from all sides, everyone standing there should say: "May it be well-established! (supratiṣṭhitam astu).
O twice-born one, he should cause them to recite the mantra beginning with "āt-bhā-hārṣe," followed by "saha vai pratiṣṭhāsi," and then "viśvasya mitram" and so forth, up to the Ekāyana.
"Oṃ, let there be salutation; and thereafter, together with those beginning with the Ṛgveda:
'Oṃ, repeated salutations to Brahman,' and likewise, 'Victory be unto you! (844)
Accompanied by shouts of victory, the preceptor, together with everyone, should chant a hymn that is enchanting to the ear with loud and resonant voices.
O best of Brahmins, know that by this all-pervading one who has become the individual soul and whose form is the mantra, everything is established once he is established.
Having first performed the ritual of consecration (adhivāsa) and so forth together with the primary image (mūlabimba),
one should install the ritual images (karmabimba) and others in their respective places as prescribed.
One should likewise install the Śaktis, such as Lakṣmī and others, according to the prescribed rite;
and in the temple as well, one should install the previously mentioned [deities] beginning with Loka, in their proper sequence.
Even when that portion of the moment has passed, the king of birds must be established—
he who was previously consecrated by his own mantra, bathed, and anointed.

O best of beings, because [the reflection] exists together with the power of cognition and the original object (bimba) when objects are distinct, whether they are situated near the original object or elsewhere.
While [the deities] are always proceeding as auxiliary parts at that time,
[the offering] should be performed entirely until the end of the oblation, preceded by meditation and worship.
By itself, it attains a state of commonality with the ritual action through its own corresponding nature.
Therefore, having raised [the deity] from that sacrificial chamber and taken hold of it like an image (bimba), [one should proceed]. || 852 ||
Having circumambulated the deity clockwise as before at the stage of installation, one should place the pentad beginning with Vajra into a single cavity for liquor. || 853 ||

That very same [deity] is also to be placed above; furthermore, the support that was previously mentioned should be established as before, and the cosmic path (adhvan) is to be placed upon its pedestal.
Likewise, one should cause the Brahmins to recite the king of mantras, "Suparṇo 'si," which is to be cultivated within the body and characterized by specific consciousness.
Having first worshipped that very [linga] with weapons in the Śāṅkara [space],
then either between Soma and Īśāna, or in the courtyard, or in its specific location.
Alternatively, having installed Viṣvaksena within the sanctum, whether he is situated upon an image or on a pedestal, according to the procedure prescribed for the aerial chariot; || 857 ||
The best of preceptors should duly install all the deities stationed at the doors as well as those situated in the enclosures, in the same order as previously described.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with water from the pitcher, one should proceed to the abode of the god;
then the omnipresent Lord is to be bathed with pitchers placed at the rear.
Together with all those bearing their respective forms in due order,
and indeed together with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn and the recitation of the Gāyatrī.

First, however, [the knower of the Yajus] should sprinkle with the *ṛṅmaya* [mantra]; thereafter, he himself, being learned in the Yajus, should sprinkle with the six mantras revolving from the heart and so forth, which have been rotated four times. 861.
Then, being himself a knower of the Sāman, he should bathe [the deity] with six other jars; thereafter, he himself, as an Atharvan, should perform the rite with that same [formula].
Thus, with the jars being turned clockwise while reciting purificatory mantras at intervals,
the ritual bathing should immediately follow together with those belonging to the Vaikāyanīya lineage.
Then, one should bathe [the deity] with a water-pot using mantras consisting of the four forms, which have been repeatedly meditated upon; having taken the remainder, indeed, with that pot.
Having performed one hundred rotations of that [mantra], today, with the root-mantra together with the form-mantra,
one should indeed pour the arghya upon the head of the God of gods and cause it to be recited.
Having indeed conquered all [the obstacles] with the weapon-water (astra-udaka),
and having purified the palace, he went to the vicinity of the water-pot (kumbha).
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods there according to the previously mentioned sequence,
and having performed worship in the mandala, one should then proceed to the presence of the image.
There, one should especially worship the deity— excluding the ritual bath—
with various articles such as seats and other services that involve physical contact.
With heart-pleasing foods such as milk-rice and the fourfold types of offerings, as well as with abundant other kinds of food, including both solid and soft delicacies. || 869 ||
O best of the twice-born, having performed [the rites] in sequence ending with the final dedication (sampradāna),
one should especially offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and to those who bear his form.
Having first offered seven handfuls of fuel into the fire in due order,
one should bow to the deity and inform him through action, mind, and speech.
O Lord, you who reside within the image and whom I have brought before me through fire and other means— O Acyuta, that [conduct] of mine must be forgiven.
Having thus prostrated, made his request, and received forgiveness,
he went out before [the king] and [described] the palace that had been built from its foundations up to its pinnacle.
Having circumambulated the deity and prostrated with the eight limbs,
and having taken the vessel for the water offering (arghya), one should go outside the temple.
Having worshipped the vehicle, which consists of the Blessed One, with bathing and other rites, as well as the previously mentioned door-keepers and the lords of the directions; || 875 ||
Thereafter, one should offer the bali-oblation in the same manner as before,
and then proceed to begin the offering of the bali for the multitude of spirits.
May the beings devoted to the Blessed One who dwell outside the temple accept the food offerings and the purificatory materials here,
as well as those who are their followers.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation in sequence, he should then cause all [the students] to recite the mantras in order: "Ṛgvid," "Hiraṇyagarbha," and "Yā devāḥ. (878)

One should likewise perform the *sāman* chants along with the *anna-sāmans* and those consisting of the cow (*dhenumaya*) for the sake of the offering, circumambulating clockwise through all the enclosures.
Having performed [the rites], the preceptor should afterwards sip water (ācamana) and enter the temple;
for the sake of pacifying any deficiencies or excesses, he should offer one hundred oblations ending with the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Heart-mantra accompanied by the Weapon-mantra,
one should mutter the mantra of the Wheel outside that [deity], enclosed at its beginning and end.
In the mandala, in front of the principal image, for the purpose of filling all deficiencies,
he should then cause the deity to hear [his request], standing with his hands joined in the añjali gesture.
Standing at the gateway of the palace with my knees upon the ground,
this which has indeed been performed by me today was set in motion by your power.
And by that very [water], the performer should be consecrated with the water from the jar;
he should give for four days, preceded by fire-offerings and gifts.
By the giving of gifts on the day of commencement, and by the offering of oblations and worship, the entire three worlds, beginning with the earth, attain satisfaction. || 885 ||
For four days thereafter, one should perform worship as before—beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and the others—in the water-pot, the mandala, and the fire. || 886 ||
The sevenfold world-system, beginning with Bhūḥ and ending with Satyaloka,
attains satisfaction through a seven-day period of giving, fire-offerings, worship, and other rites.
When the fourth day has arrived, having removed the garlands and other ornaments from the jar,
the mandala, and the image, one should then perform worship in the sacrificial hall.
Having first completed the conclusion of the mantra for the oblation as performed previously,
and having sipped water and offered the bali-offering, he should then proceed to the temple of the deity.
There, having worshipped the Lord as before with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with the bath,
[they should proceed] with jars from which the cloth has been removed, placed upon a pedestal of grain.
Furthermore, with waters consecrated by the heart-mantra and filled [in the vessels],
together with the bearers of the forms, one should proceed as before through the method of alternating placement at intervals.
One should indeed perform the ritual of bathing and other rites according to the prescribed procedure;
then, in the waterless temple, one should worship again as before.

Having worshipped Acyuta with offerings beginning with a seat and ending with the formal gift (saṃpradāna), one should form the mudrā, recite the mantra, offer praise, ask for forgiveness, and go outside. || 893 ||
One should personally offer a hundred, a thousand, or one hundred and eight oblations with the King of Mantras itself,
according to the method of reciting the Saṃhitā together with its limbs and retinue.

The Mūrtipas [should perform] one hundred recitations each with the Gāyatrīs preceded by the Praṇava; likewise, those who know the Ekāyana [Veda] should perform an equal number with their own respective [Gāyatrīs]. || 895 ||
Then he should cause the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) to receive the complete Ṛgveda and the others;
at the conclusion of that, he should then have them recite the Ekāyana in due order.

One should personally offer [the oblation] with the mantra "From fullness, fullness" (pūrṇāt pūrṇam), or with the mantra beginning "Thou art full" (pūrṇam asi), accompanied by a salutation and including all its constituent parts.
Then, with offerings, he should satisfy all those who have appeared in the past;
having entered and sipped water, he should thereafter ask forgiveness from the deity residing in the pitcher.
As before, one should worship Viṣvaksena, who resides in the maṇḍala and subsequently in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), with the desired and remaining offerings in the prescribed order.
One should adorn the images of the preceptor and his predecessors with bracelets and other ornaments;
or one should offer sacrificial materials to the preceptor or the preceptor’s son. (900)
Or else, the twice-born preceptor himself should perform the consecration;
thereafter, it should be distributed in due order among the image-keepers and others.
In this manner, the preceptor should perform [the rites] in all sacrifices;
and for the sake of attaining the desired goal of perfection, he should bathe with the avabhṛtha bath.
This has been declared for the practitioner who desires the propitiation of the mantra—the installation of the mantra-form wherein he may abide and attain perfection. (903)
I shall now briefly describe the fruit for the patron (yajamāna) regarding the installation [of the deity],
from the site of the temple grounds up to the pinnacle of the flagstaff and the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
O best of the twice-born, it was endowed with all necessary implements and, in all its coverings, was completely composed of all atoms.
For as many times as the number [of recitations] that arises, for that long the performer shall dwell;
enjoying pleasures in the world of Viṣṇu, he goes at the end to the supreme state. || 906 ||
O learned one, the Brahmin who performs the rite shall indeed become the sovereign of all branches of knowledge;
the Kṣatriya who acts as the patron of the sacrifice shall become the ruler of all lands. || 907 ||
A Vaiśya who performs a sacrifice shall be abundant in wealth and grain;
a Śūdra who performs a sacrifice shall rejoice together with his kinsmen.
By birth and by knowledge, she shall become exactly like this for women;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom. || 909 ||
Whatever the practitioner desires, all that he shall attain;
for those devotees who are free from desire, their devotion remains unswerving.
Furthermore, that which is eternal knowledge, together with its inherent nature, is proclaimed as the installation of images fashioned by oneself. (911)
Having thus installed the image in a temple or in one's own home,
from that time forward, one should worship that icon every day.
For as long as the period for the restoration of the dilapidated lasts, one must not, according to the prescribed rules,
allow the omission of worship— whether through negligence or intentionally.
O twice-born one, one must not omit any prescribed rite for each respective image, nor any of the rituals such as the ceremonial bathing that have been ordained.
One should indeed perform each respective rite upon that very ritual image, provided that the manifestation of the image for the purpose of that specific rite is present. || 915 ||
One should not perform the transposition of those various specific rites, for in their absence there would be the fault of the ruin of the kingdom and other calamities. || 916 ||
Whatever ritual form is appropriate for that specific place and time should be present there;
one should perform every such ritual form in that context.
Furthermore, there are two types of ablutions, consisting of the regular (nitya) and the occasional (naimittika);
likewise, there is the procedure for the regular festival (nityotsava) and the occasional festival (naimittikotsava).
The procedure for pilgrimage and these five rites indeed [are thus];
then one should perform the rite of lying down and rising upon the *kūrca* grass mat.
Alternatively, when a consecrated image intended for beauty is being worshipped—thus it has been stated regarding one image being present. (920)
When two images are present, having performed all other [rites] according to their respective distinctions of action as appropriate, one should perform [the ritual] accordingly. || 921 ||
Having reflected thus, one should perform [the rites] once that respective image has been revealed;
indeed, this applies to all ritual images when they are present there.
At that time, one should not effect an exchange of those images;
for then, when an image made of superior metal is obtained for the sake of beauty, [the original] would be lost.

In that case, when [the deity] is established with colored powders (varṇas) upon clay for the sake of elevating one's own lineage (khakula), one should never perform the ritual procedure prescribed for a [fully consecrated] image (aṅgabimba). || 924 ||
If a king should act through negligence, the kingdom perishes—especially in the case of a self-manifested, divine, perfected, or even a ṛṣi-made [liṅga]. || 925 ||
One should not perform a transposition of the ritual images in their respective places;
for such is the nature of those images, O best of Brahmins. (926)
Whether endowed with the proper characteristics and measurements or devoid of them, and whether produced from superior metal or arising from inferior sources. (927)
Such things indeed come to pass; a wise person should not act otherwise.
One should not create another defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), nor likewise another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
One should not employ a different substance, nor should one perform a different ritual action;
one should not apply a different mantra, but should do everything exactly as before. || 929 ||
If one should cause a perversion of the marks and so forth, O Mahāmati, there would be the destruction of the king and the kingdom, as well as that person's own lineage. (930)
One should not perform any reversal of the primary characteristics and so forth even in the case of the root image;
therefore, one should not practice such reversals in the ancient site.
Thus, even in the human realm, one should never at any time perform the ritual known as "Jīrṇa" prior to the reversal of the [auspicious] marks and other characteristics. 932.
O twice-born one, whether in a place that is self-manifested or otherwise created by humans, or in a temple or image that is undigested [by time] or lacking a limb; 933.
One should not create another abode by destroying that which was previously situated;
nor should one create another *bimba*, if one should conceive of it out of delusion.
The performer would be deprived of his own self, as would the king along with his lineage;
there would be great danger for that kingdom and its monarch. || 935 ||
Now, the procedure for restoration is being briefly described;
first, hear the rules for restoration regarding a site constructed by humans. (936)
O Great Sage, whatever form of the Blessed One is produced from clay, stone, wood, or transferred onto cloth and other materials—of each such form [there is a specific result]. (937)
Whether it be worn out, or suffering from a fracture of the limbs, or wounded in various places—
one should repair that which is fit for repair, but one should abandon that which is unfit.

But that image, having been abandoned without the materials of the constituent elements, one should cast it into a deep reservoir of water or into the ocean according to the prescribed rite. || 939 ||
Or, O Brahmin, one should bury it in the ground according to the requirements of place and time;
provided that the ritual procedure has been performed correctly from beginning to end.
Even when defects such as the breaking of limbs have properly occurred, as long as there is the capacity for rejoining, one should never abandon [the practice]. || 941 ||
For that [small image], its abandonment or destruction causes increasingly greater affliction;
however, the abandonment of large images, such as the *bimba* and others, is not appropriate. || 942 ||
In particular, it is not appropriate to discard superior vessels made of gold, silver, or copper; therefore, one should perform the joining (soldering) of them. || 943 ||
If it remains unfit despite one's efforts, one should perform its abandonment;
then, with material of the same kind, one should fashion another image. || 944 ||

O best of the twice-born, by means of those various metals produced from the substances of the elements—metals of their respective kinds that have been reduced to formlessness—the former metals [are transformed]. (945)
Or, O Mahāmati, it may be made of various superior metals;
or else the image may be made of silver, gold, or excellent copper.
One should join it with great effort and never abandon it;
that which is made of inferior copper is indeed composed of brass (ārakūṭa). || 947 ||
One should discard that pair if it is unfit for rejoining;
once discarded, one should cast that image away by the same route as before.
Then, O Mahāmati, one should fashion the interior of the image out of silver, gold, or whatever material of superior quality is appropriate for that particular type.
Indeed, one should perform exactly this same procedure for all ritual images made of clay, wood, stone, or even those fashioned from precious gems. (950)
If [the temple] has been destroyed for some reason, one should construct a children's house or the like,
leave that [site], prepare another [location], and perform the installation of the image there.
Pay close attention to the specific requirements regarding divine or perfected sites;
however, when the primary clay image has become worn out by water or other elements, [the following applies].
Or, in that case, one should diligently perform the rejoining of missing limbs;
likewise, one should carry out the rejoining even for those devoid of color.
One should never discard clay, wooden pegs, cords, and so forth; when an image made of metal has become worn out, one should restore it with gold and other precious materials.
When an image made of iron has decayed, one should repair it with gold;
likewise, one should perform the restoration of an image made of precious gems.
Whatever has become worn out and is to be discarded, having abandoned each of those, O Brahmin, one should thereafter apply oneself to the next; one should not act otherwise.

One should not perform that ritual action in the house of a child, nor should one perform that [specific] rite while obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and other such rituals are currently underway. || 957 ||
One should perform everything previously mentioned according to one's available wealth;
likewise, one should not act otherwise even regarding the characteristics and other such details. (958)
O best of men, even those individuals upon whom the marks were not clearly manifested likewise bore their own marks upon the forehead or the shoulder-cloth.
Whether on the back, or on a cloth for the limbs, or on the palms and soles of the feet, or on the head—
one should examine it in each of those places.
Therefore, an individual devoid of defining characteristics never exists;
this is likewise true for those born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes. || 961 ||
Maudgalyāyana and others, as well as others likewise, must by all means not be devoid of those marks; therefore, [the image] should be endowed with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
With metals heated in the fire and consecrated by their respective mantras,
and honored with offerings of water for the guest, perfumes, and so forth, they should be marked in an instant.

Even those Brahmins and others, as well as Śūdras, who possess the threefold knowledge, are endowed with wisdom, and are firmly established in the conduct prescribed for them—when they have thus acquired these characteristics. || 964 ||
At that time, O high-minded one, they should be known as qualified for the hearing of the *samaya* and all other ritual requirements prescribed in the scriptures.
The implements of sacrifice, such as the arghya-vessel and others,
should likewise be joined with the appropriate marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth, according to their respective requirements.
Likewise, all vehicles, seats, and so forth belonging to the Lord [should be offered] with diligence;
however, all one's own personal requisites, including the seat and other items, should be excluded.
Ornaments such as bracelets and so forth, ending with the finger-rings, and everything removable from the head, beginning with the turban—[all these he should give]. 968.
One should mark [the animal] with the wheel and other signs; its cattle and so forth should also be marked.
Its trees and so forth should likewise be marked, just like those belonging to the Brahmins and other castes.
They should be marked, as appropriate, with the signs of the discus, conch, and so forth;
those who perform worship and the like, being thus marked with the discus and other symbols, are indeed fit for ritual action.
Those [images] marked with the signs of other deities are unfit for ritual use;
likewise, that form of the Blessed One in which no mark is visible [is unfit]. (971)
Even there, O twice-born one, one should not perform the imposition of characteristics according to one's own whim;
that manifestation, exactly as it exists, is to be worshipped by means of the all-pervading mantra.
All others who were previously unmarked should be marked;
thus is the perfect consecration of the deity fully proclaimed. || 973 ||
O Brahmin, for the purpose of protecting the site—at that time or at any other time—whether on the roof of a palace, in the courtyard, or anywhere else; (974)
One should establish the formless Cakra there upon the summit,
while the embodied [form], having sixteen or eight arms, should be placed in the courtyard area.
One should fashion the formless [mandala] with twelve spokes, or eight spokes, or six spokes;
likewise, one should place the conch and other weapons upon the corners and so forth.
Whether in the second enclosure or even in the third enclosure, the construction of the mandalas of the wheel and so forth will be explained further on. (977)
When the installation is performed together, as before, no division of ritual acts occurs;
when the installation is performed separately, one should perform every rite according to the prescribed rule.
At the time of installing each [image], one should mutter the mantra corresponding to its respective name;
one should cause those who know [the ritual] to recite such [mantras] as "Vidyā" or "Gadā. || 979 ||
One should cause the Bahvṛcas to recite the two ṛcs beginning with "camūṣacchayena" and "pnaviṣṇo," and afterwards, the Śākuna Sūkta.
One should recite the mantra "dhṛtordhvapuṇḍraḥ kṛtacakre" for the Kaṭhas,
and these Yajurvedic mantras beginning with "pavitraṃ te vitatam" for others.
And he causes the Sāmavedic priests to recite "pavitraṃ te agniḥ" and the Atharvavedic twice-born ones to recite "ebhirvayam urukramasya."
Having established [the image] according to the rules with these nine jars,
he should then bathe it with the eight mantras residing in the Brahma-sūkta.
By means of the mantra "The god who is the controller of all," which was previously established, [the deity is invoked];
however, by means of the mantra situated in the southeast direction, it is said that [the deity] does not exist in the outer enclosure.
The verse beginning with "yannābhipadmādabhavat" was uttered by one standing in the south,
while the verse beginning with "dhṛtordhvapuṇḍra" was uttered by one belonging to the Yātudhānas.
On the right arm, O Brahmin, it is said by the one situated in the west;
and on the left, it is said by Viṣṇu, who is stationed in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest). || 986 ||
"Viṣṇu is the Lord who has the male as his primary [nature]," according to the Soma-lineage; but "this Great Upaniṣad," according to the Īśāna-lineage. (987)
With all these mantras together, one should sprinkle with the central jar;
one should perform the sprinkling upon the wheel situated at the top of the temple.
Then, for the sake of all-encompassing peace, one should recite the eight mantras previously mentioned that reside within the Mahopaniṣad, or else the Puruṣasūkta. || 989 ||
Whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform it all as previously stated. Thus the installation has been correctly explained; what else do you wish to hear?
O best of sages, you previously described the *nīrājana* rite for the daily worship and other rituals; please explain its procedure to me in detail.
Śāṇḍilya said:
O Brahmin, now listen to the procedure for the lustration rite (nīrājana) in the context of daily, occasional, and even optional worship.
Finally, for the sake of pacifying all defects and for the sake of total protection, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord with baths and offerings. || 993 ||
One may provide even the most basic of enjoyments mentioned in connection with the ornaments and the seat, or one may do so in both cases, according to one's wealth and desire. || 994 ||
Or else,
O best of the twice-born, one should perform that every day at the time of dusk, specifically before beginning the evening worship.
Alternatively, one should perform it before the offering of lamps during the worship;
or else, one should perform it at the conclusion of the worship, ending with the food offering (naivedya). || 996 ||
That [gift] is also said to be threefold, according to the distinction between the *sāttvika* and the others;
at the conclusion of a bath and at the conclusion of a sacrifice of enjoyment, the two [types of gifts] are *sāttvika*.
One should perform the rite designated as *rājasa* every day at evening;
that which is *tāmasa* consists of the offering of lamps at the beginning of the worship and the presentation of food offerings at its conclusion. (998)
One should construct a temple for one of them, but not for all three;
likewise in the case of a self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) image or one consecrated by other deities.
In a temple built by the foremost sages, one should practice the *sāttvika* form;
in one established by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, it becomes *rājasa*. (1000)

When it is established by Śūdras or women, one should practice that which is called Tāmasa. Now hear properly, in due order, the procedure for these [forms of worship], beginning with the Sāttvika. || 1001 ||
O twice-born one, the pitcher should be filled with the water remaining after the bathing;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. (1002)
It should be smeared on the upper part with well-ground turmeric and rice grains,
and it should be joined at the neck region with a garland and a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
Having placed that [bell] in the left hand, one should hold a bowl in the other,
filled with a profusion of flowers and provided with the fire from an incense burner.
Having once whirled [the offering] over the head of the God of gods, together with mustard seeds or incense materials while they are smoking, || 1005 ||
One should have it discarded outside the door by a person who has been initiated and is intent on service, or by a pure woman. || 1006 ||
At the conclusion of the bath and enjoyment, one should always perform this lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
having filled a water-pot with the substances previously mentioned.
Alternatively, having taken water from the arghya vessel, or even using only water that has been strained again,
one should place white mustard seeds inside it and make a decoration around the neck.
O twice-born one, one should smear [the image] on all sides with aloe-wood paste, with garlands of aśvattha sprouts, and also with unbroken grains; alternatively, with turmeric ground into a paste.
Then, one should place a bowl filled with flowers upon his face,
after first lighting lamps produced from consecrated fire.
O twice-born one, according to one's means, [one should offer] twenty-four or more lamps, raised four finger-breadths above the cooking place.
Having placed a lamp in a basin, one should set it down together with its vessel,
always positioned upon a support in front of the God of Gods.
The practitioner should then worship it with water for the guest (arghya), perfumes, garlands, and incense using the heart-mantra;
thereafter, he should worship it with only arghya and flowers.
O twice-born one, at the conclusion of the sipping of water (ācamana), he should offer the arghya to the Lord of Mantras;
or else, he may offer the arghya, the anointing, the garland, the incense, or indeed the arghya alone.
The attendant, having lifted the lamp-vessel with both hands,
[should move it] starting from the right foot of the deity and ending with the other, the western one.
One should rotate all the limbs in one way, or two ways, or three ways,
while reciting either the Netra-mantra or the Hṛdaya-mantra according to one's preference.
Having thus rotated the pitcher, one should dismiss it as before;
thereafter, one should offer the arghya water upon the head of the God of gods.
Now listen to the procedure for that very purpose when the lamp is brought from the place of cooking. || 1018 ||
The attendants, having been initiated, well-disciplined, and properly bathed,
shall cover their faces and the openings of their nostrils with a cloth.
All of them wore white turbans and were anointed with white sandalwood paste;
they had spread out golden vessels according to their preference.
Then, having prepared vessels made of silver, copper, brass, or even bell-metal, according to one's means.
Likewise, they may be one, three, five, seven, nine, or eleven;
or two, six, sixteen, or by the number twenty-four. || 1022 ||
O great sage, having reached the kitchen, he first performed the consecration of the fire there; then, in their midst, he [prepared] lamps with wicks for the vessels.
Then the attendants, having lifted those vessels with their hands, should again light them— each four finger-breadths in height and filled with ghee.
In front of that, the courtesans should proceed in a single file,
while the devotees of the Blessed One should go along performing dances and songs.
In front of him were those intent on sounding conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments;
and in front of them were the staff-bearers, intent on clearing away those people who were untouchable.
People carrying lamps for them should go around them on all sides;
thus, having approached in due order, they should stand in the presence of the deity. || 1027 ||
Then another initiated brahmin, having brought a water-pot as before, together with a small bowl placed upon it, should kindle a fire from one of those [fires]. || 1028 ||
Having brought [the materials] from the place of cooking and having set up a lamp, the best of practitioners should then place it upon a stable support. 1029.
O best of the twice-born, having worshipped the jar as before and the Lord of Gods thereafter,
one should then whirl the jar in that same manner as previously described at that time.
The twice-born, stationed in the directions starting from the east, should perform the recitation of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures;
meanwhile, the courtesans should perform a dance in the presence of the God of gods.
Let all the singers sing auspicious songs,
and let the reciters of hymns offer praise with the highest of voices.
They should cause the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and so forth to resound on all sides;
in this manner, one should indeed perform the study of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures everywhere.
Having thus rotated the pitcher and handed it over to the attendants,
he should then show them the lamp-vessels and the other items in their hands.
Having seen [the deity] correctly, one should then offer the arghya upon the head of the god,
while attendants carry vessels preceded by the water-jar.
Following the sequence of circumambulation, together with the courtesans and others as before,
they should cast [the offerings] either outside the gate or further outside the outer gate.
Alternatively, having gathered those women who have been assigned [to the task], who are well-bathed, wearing clean garments, and whose minds are purified by the twice-born; || 1037 ||
Having applied a tilaka on their foreheads and adorned with all ornaments,
O best of the twice-born, they should proceed by the very path already described.
Alternatively, before the time for the ritual application and even before the kitchen,
one should take the lamps and vessels for the women according to the prescribed method.
They should bring [the items] before the Lord in accordance with the desire of the creator;
thus one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), ending with the ornaments and the seat. || 1040 ||
Alternatively, one should rotate the pitcher accompanied by eight lamps;
or in that case as well, the pitcher should be joined with a small vessel containing fire.

O best of the twice-born, one should cause the image to be circumambulated while it is emitting smoke from white mustard seeds and is devoid of lamps; thus is the Nīrājana rite described for a single-liṅga image.
In the worship of multiple forms, having offered the arghya and other offerings individually to all the forms in sequence, beginning with the principal form; 1043.

O twice-born one, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for each [deity] with a single water-pot, or else for all of them together with a single pot, as previously described. || 1044 ||
Thus, those people who perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord, the All-pervading One, and who provide assistance in that rite, [attain the highest merit]. || 1045 ||
They will undoubtedly become completely free from passion and ignorance,
provided they abandon that [water] in a jar touched by unworthy people.
Having established another lamp, one should perform that [offering] with it;
if, among the lamps, even a single lamp should go out. || 1047 ||
If, due to negligence, the force of wind, or similar causes, one fails to inform [the preceptor] beforehand,
a loss of prosperity occurs later, as does affliction by disease and other ailments.
Therefore, having suddenly ignited [the lamps], one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
thus is the *nīrājana* performed, even without conch shells, dance, or song. || 1049 ||
If it were [performed] alone, it would be fruitless; therefore, one should perform it together with them.
Thus is described the Nīrājana rite, known by the name Sāttvika.
O best of brahmins, the rājasa nīrājana is now described.
Having prepared the vessels as before, women well-adorned [should be present]. (1051)
Equipped with waist-bands and preceded by their attendants,
they reached the kitchen and lit the lamps among them.
Having lifted their vessels with their hands, they emerged from the kitchen;
forming themselves into rows, they approached as before accompanied by songs and other such performances.
They should place them on the ground in front of the God of gods;
then, upon their bases, one should worship those vessels with water for honoring (arghya) and other offerings.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the primary image and the other images according to the prescribed rule,
[one should worship] with offerings of water for honor (arghya), touching, flowers, and so forth, or indeed with water for honor, water for the feet (pādya), and the like.
The practitioner, having performed the worship of the God of gods in due order,
being well-composed, the worshipper should lift up the lamp-vessels.
First, for the primary image (mūlamūrti), one should rotate [the vessel] three times from the feet up to the head;
or alternatively, one may rotate each of them three times.
One should perform the same rite for other forms as well;
likewise, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) separately for the two goddesses, Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.
O best of Brahmins, one should perform the study of the Rigveda and other Vedas as previously described; then, having again accepted the offerings presented by the women, [one should proceed].
O twice-born one, they should cast [the lamps] upon the offering-stands according to the previously mentioned rule;
thus, O Brahmin, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) at the time of evening.
Alternatively, one should then cause the previously mentioned jar, provided with a wick and a lamp, and accompanied by offerings of fish, meat, and other oblations, to be carried around.
Alternatively, having circled the water-pot together with the lamp-vessel,
one should thereafter perform the circling of the five balls of food.
Thus has the threefold Nīrājana, known as the Rājasa, been described.
Now, attend to the Nīrājana called Tāmasa. || 1063 ||
Having reached the kitchen, either a woman or an attendant, taking a single vessel made from the aforementioned materials, [should proceed]. || 1064 ||
O twice-born one, having placed four morsels of food and four handfuls of dūrvā grass in the four directions within that vessel, [one should proceed].
One should place those four [substances] separately in four vessels,
having brought them into the presence of the God of gods by the path previously described.
Thereafter, the practitioner should place the vessel upon the support;
having worshipped that vessel with the *arghya* flower while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the practitioner [proceeds]. || 1067 ||
Having offered the arghya, pādya, and ācamana to the God,
he should then offer a ball of food (piṇḍa) situated toward the east, as well as a handful of dūrvā grass.
Having whirled it above the head of the deity with the *cakra*-mantra,
one should then cast it toward the eastern direction of the God of gods.
In this manner, having whirled that which is situated in the southern direction, one should cast it toward the south;
having whirled that which is situated in the western direction, one should cast it toward the western quarter.
Having circumambulated the one situated in the north, he should cast [the ashes] in the northern direction;
he should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) on the deity with the ashes arising from the lamp-vessel.
Thus one should perform the Nīrājana rite prior to the offering of lamps;
the vessel, made of gold or other materials, should be twenty-six finger-breadths in width.
Having fashioned a well-rounded base, one should construct a lotus with a pericarp in its center;
upon the eight petals and within the pericarp, one should prepare a hollow for the lamps.
One should light lamps there, six finger-breadths in height,
filled with white mustard seeds, curd, dūrvā grass, and other grains.
Having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the practitioner takes up the vessel,
circumambulates it three times, and places it with both hands upon the head of the deity.
Outside the enclosure of the wall, one should cast [the offering] toward the north during the day;
even before the food-balls have been moved forward, at the end, with the ashes from the incense.
O twice-born one, one should enclose [the deity] with protection;
thus should the lustration rite (nīrājana) always be performed for the Lord at the conclusion of the offering.
Thus the Nīrājana has been described as being of two kinds, the one called Tāmasa;
all [the rites] such as singing and dancing should be performed here as previously stated.
At the conclusion of the bath, one may perform the study of the Rigveda and other such recitations;
however, one should always avoid performing worship with offerings such as the *arghya* water at that time.
O twice-born one, except at evening time, one should never perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) for the God of gods during any other rite of lustration (nīrājana).
The Nīrājana rite known as Sāttvika should be performed wherever it has been established;
one should never perform it in a Rājasa or Tāmasa manner.
Whether it be of a rajasic or tamasic nature, wherever it has been performed,
one should perform the nīrājana known as sāttvika according to one's desire.
O Great-Minded One, one who desires the complete fruit from the sacrifice to the Blessed One should never practice anything contrary to the path that has been taught. (1083)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installation," in the section on Ritual Action (Kriyākāṇḍa) of the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the venerable Pāñcarātra.
Prosperity!
The sixteenth chapter: Sanaka has fully understood the installation of the mantra-icons according to the prescribed rule.
I now wish to hear about the performance of the great festival.
Śāṇḍilya said:
O bull among sages, I shall duly proclaim the Great Festival (Mahotsava).
That which is called "Sava" is declared by the wise to be suffering. || 2 ||
Because all prosperity arises from it, it is called a festival (utsava).
That great festival is threefold: obligatory, occasional, and optional. || 3 ||
That which is performed every year is the obligatory (nityaka) rite;
it is also performed during earthquakes, the burning of the quarters, and when great portents occur. || 4 ||
During a famine, when the kingdom is afflicted by disease, likewise in times of danger from enemies,
during droughts everywhere, and when stars fall from the sky— 5.
O best of men, when the limbs of the Blessed One’s image laugh, they move;
and when it weeps, the image wanders from its seat.
Whatever one performs for the sake of pacification when there is a reversal of the moon and sun, or in other such circumstances, that is called occasional (naimittika).
A ritual performed for the sake of one of the four aims of human life is a "desirable" (kāmya) festival; it bestows the fruit that was intended.
O bull among sages, know that each festival is threefold according to the distinction of superior and so forth, as well as in its festive splendor.
That festival which is performed [on specific occasions] is declared to be the highest;
that which consists of the daily bathing of the image is proclaimed as the middling.
That which exists for the purpose of perpetual festival in the image is the lowest;
that which is in the jar, on the seat, or on the wheel is designated as the "manifest" (ābhāsa).
Furthermore, another threefold classification is stated:
at the time of circumambulation, [the image] is first [placed] to the east of the procession image (yātrābimba). || 12 ||

O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining perfection through meditation, one should use images of the lords of the spirits (Bhūteśas) such as Kumuda and others, either painted on cloth or fashioned from materials such as gold.
Likewise, for the sake of protection in accordance with his power, he was accompanied by Heti;
and indeed, for the sake of fulfilling all requirements, he was also with Garuḍa.
O Brahmin, that festival at which one should regularly perform the offering of bali in villages and other such places is known as the "Uttama" (the Supreme). || 15 ||
O Mahāmati, even before the commencement of the wandering [of the ritual],
one who is formless should offer food in the presence of the image intended for the perpetual festival.
Together with the Cakrarāja, or indeed alone, having offered the bali according to the prescribed rite in the presence of the image of the Lord; || 17 ||
Having first brought the *balibimba* and other images into the temple,
one should thereafter perform the circumambulation of the image intended for the procession.
Whether in a village or even in a city, that [place] is designated as "middling";
having first offered an oblation in the presence of the Cakrarāja.
Wherever a divine procession (devayātrā) takes place, it belongs to the younger [tradition];
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished by the primary (mukhya) and the secondary (anukalpa) methods. || 20 ||
Where the worship of the Lord is performed daily in the water-pot, the mandala, the image, or the fire, that is proclaimed as the primary ritual procedure (mukhyakalpa). || 21 ||
That in which worship is performed in the image (biṃba) and in the fire (vahni) is the secondary ritual procedure (anukalpaka).
Each of these is traditionally held to be threefold, according to the distinctions of supreme (para), subtle (sūkṣma), and gross (sthūla). || 22 ||
One day, three days, five days, seven days, nine days, and another is recorded as twelve days;
then half a month and twenty-one days. || 23 ||
The subtle [day], the gross [day], the month of twenty-seven days, as well as the season, the six months, and the year—thus indeed are there thirteen festivals. (24)
Furthermore, O twice-born one, that [rite] is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished by the primary and other types;
it should be performed on the day previously mentioned, prior to the series of festival days.
Know that whatever is performed after having raised the banner is the primary ritual (mukhyakalpa), whether it arises from divine or human causes. || 26 ||
O Brahmin, for some reason, on the day previously mentioned,
the raising of the banner had not been performed on that day which was the commencement of the festival.
Know that whatever is performed after having raised the banner is the secondary rite (anukalpa);
for this is remembered as being threefold.
O bull among sages, it is preceded by the hoisting of the banner, preceded by the invocation of the deities,
and likewise preceded by the offering of the sacred sprouts (aṅkura).
Preceded by the hoisting of the banner, it bestows the happiness of royal sovereignty;
preceded by the invocation of the deities, it bestows the fruit of enjoyment in heaven. || 30 ||
Preceded by the ritual offering of the sprout (aṅkurārpaṇa), this [ceremony] shall grant liberation to all;
having raised the banner during the day on the first day of the festival, one should [perform the rite] at night.
Following the beating of the drum, one should cast sprouts into the offering vessels;
this festival is said to be preceded by the hoisting of the banner.
First, having sounded the kettledrum, the hoisting of the banner follows;
thereafter comes the ritual sowing of seeds, preceded by the invocation of the deities.
O Brahmin, first, at the onset of night, the planting of the sprouts should take place;
thereafter on the following day, the hoisting of the banner, and after that, the beating of the drum.
This festival is said to begin with the planting of the sprouts;
know this supreme festival to be held three times every year. (35)
It is declared that the middling [performance] is twice, while the inferior is once;
however, according to one's means, it may be four, five, or six times. || 36 ||
O Mahāmati, at the very time of the consecration of the mantra-form,
the banner of the king of birds was installed upon the pinnacle of the temple.
O twice-born one, wherever the two are joined with the King of Weapons (the Śakti), one should always celebrate a festival, even without the mounting of another banner. || 38 ||
In that case as well, if he possesses the means, he should perform the hoisting of another banner;
or he may celebrate a festival elsewhere, preceded by the hoisting of a banner.
One should perform the raising of the flag in accordance with the requirements of a pilgrimage;
now hear about the day of pilgrimage for all festivals. (40)
And during the months beginning with Caitra, under the asterism Śravaṇa, during both solstices, during the two equinoxes, or during eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 41 ||
On the twelfth day, on the full moon, on the new moon, and on the ninth lunar day;
likewise on the Rohiṇī asterism and on the Uttaraphalgunī asterism in the month.
Likewise, on a day of consecration during the lunar mansion known as Punarvasu,
or on the day of the commencement of a palace, which coincides with the birth-star of the city, village, or person.
On the birth-day of kings, or likewise on their day of consecration— on any one of these occasions— one should undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā).
Whichever lunar mansion (nakṣatra) among these has been designated for the pilgrimage,
when that occurs during the month of Utsavakalpita, it shall indeed be twofold [in merit].
Then one should undertake a pilgrimage on that day when it falls within the month;
one should arrange it in this manner during all the months beginning with Phālguna.
Starting from the fifth day until the end of the thirty-first day,
prior to the departure for a pilgrimage to sacred sites, on the twenty-first day— || 47 ||
One should diligently perform the hoisting of the banner for the sake of the festival, or on an auspicious day that is three times as many days [from the previous one]. (48)
O best of the twice-born, O Brahmin, the hoisting of the banner should first be performed on the twenty-seventh day from the day the festival begins.
On the day preceding that [thirtieth] day, the wise one should raise the banner;
on the thirtieth day, he should perform the rites on the day prior to it.
Indeed, for the triad beginning with the seasonal festival (ṛtūtsava), one should perform the hoisting of the banner on the nineteenth day from the day the festival begins. || 51 ||
It may take place on the eighteenth day, or on the twelfth, or even on the twenty-first day; thus it occurs within each of the three sets of festivals.
In this very manner, the best of guides should perform the raising of the banner,
after having first offered the auspicious sprouts as previously described.
Thereafter, on an auspicious day, one should raise the banner;
however, on the very day prior to the raising of the banner, [one should perform the preliminary rites]. || 54 ||
O twice-born one, one should perform the planting of sprouts on the twelfth day, the ninth day, the seventh day, the fifth day, or on the third day.
Now listen in detail to the procedure for that, as well as the three types of vessels used for sowing the auspicious sprouts. (56)
They are distinguished as *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvās*.
Now, the height of the *pālikās* should be twenty-five finger-breadths.
The width of its face should indeed be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
