its height eight finger-breadths, and the lip therefrom one finger-breadth.
O Brahmin, the cavity of the throat would then be eight finger-breadths wide,
O twice-born one, starting from the circle of the mouth up to the cavity of the throat.
One should reduce it by proportional calculation; that stalk is twelve finger-breadths in height, and six finger-breadths in width at its middle.
At the bottom, however, it should be four finger-breadths wide;
from there, one should gradually decrease the width down to the opening of the throat.
The height of the footstool should be known as four finger-breadths;
its width should be ten finger-breadths, and its joint should be one finger-breadth.
O twice-born one, the junction of that [part] should be one and a half finger-breadths;
the face should have the shape of an *unmatta* flower, and its interior should be lotus-shaped.
The ghaṭikās are declared to be equal in height to the pālikā, or three finger-breadths less; above that, it takes the shape of a pitcher (kalaśa).
The water-clocks (ghaṭikās) should have five faces; their central face should be six finger-breadths wide, and there should be four such faces in the four directions.
The width of the neck should be four finger-breadths, and the expansion of the belly of the jar should be sixteen finger-breadths in height; the remainder should be executed as previously described.
When it is three finger-breadths less [in width], then its face should be seven finger-breadths high;
its stalk, however, should be ten and a half finger-breadths.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is three and a half finger-breadths high; its width is the same as in all previous cases.
The shallow bowls (śarāva) and the offering vessels (pālikā) are five finger-breadths in height.
Or, Mahāmati, starting from the width of the mouth and proceeding gradually down to the width of the footstool, it may be smaller.
The width everywhere shall be one-quarter less than that previously mentioned;
the width of the footstool, however, shall be three-quarters less.
When the bowls are deficient by five finger-breadths,
then the mouth should have a height of six finger-breadths and its neck ten finger-breadths.
The footstool should be three finger-breadths [in height]; its width everywhere is as previously stated.
O twice-born one, this is declared to be the supreme measurement for vessels.
O best of sages, this same [measurement] minus one quarter is called the middling, while that measurement minus half is proclaimed to be the lowest. || 73 ||
Therefore, those desiring accomplishment should never make [the image] smaller than this; it may be made of gold or other metals, or even of clay, according to one's wealth. (74)
For each of the *pālikā* vessels and the others, a set of twelve would be excellent;
or, if one has the means, one may arrange thirty-six, which is twice eight. || 75 ||
For each *aṣṭaka*, there should be four of medium size, and four of inferior size;
for all purposes, the *pālikās* should be sixteen or eight, as previously described, according to one's capacity.
Or there may be four; among them, one should fashion auspicious sprouts.
In rites for humans, an odd number of *pālikās* should be used, while for rites for the gods, an even number.

During a great festival, at the hoisting of the banner, on the occasion of a celebration, during the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), and likewise at the ceremony of consecration (sthāpanakarma). || 78 ||
Furthermore, in the rite for restoring a dilapidated temple, as well as in the ritual of the thousand pitchers (sahasrakalaśa),
there should be a support for the three vessels (trivargapālikā) according to the highest number.
Or it may be performed with moderate means, O best of the twice-born, and not otherwise;
in all other rites, however, one should act according to one's wealth and according to one's inclination.
One should construct a pavilion for sowing the seeds,
either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure.
In the third enclosure or even in the fourth enclosure, in an auspicious, secluded, and pleasing place, the most excellent of teachers [should act]. (82)
It has four doors on the four sides and four rows of salutations;
it is encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with strings of pearls. || 83 ||
It was covered with spread-out linen cloths, its floor smeared with cow dung,
strewn everywhere with rows of lamps and unbroken grains of rice.
Having thus constructed a pavilion whose interior ground is decorated with white lime powder—or alternatively, in the bathing pavilion—[one should proceed]. (85)
Or one may perform the sowing of sprouts even in the pavilion called the *yāga*;
he who desires the increase of his kingdom should offer the sprouts at night. (86)
O Brahman, Soma, the lord of seeds, the sovereign of herbs, and the essence of nectar,
is never satisfied if the sowing of sprouts is not performed during the day.
Therefore, with every effort and endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, one should perform the planting of the sprouts at night itself, according to the correct ritual procedure. || 88 ||
When that moon, beloved of the world and the life-sustainer of living beings, is pleased, there shall be a great abundance of all crops in that region. (89)
If one should, out of ignorance, perform the offering of sprouts on a day sacred to cows—the mothers of the world—or likewise to men, in every respect; || 90 ||
The kingdom would become unprosperous and filled with people lacking in success,
O Brahmin, even during the Kali age and even by day, if such an act were performed.
Whatever may be required here, all of that he should collect;
having gathered all the necessary materials, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), [should proceed]. 92.
Having bathed and performed his daily rites, wearing an upper garment, well-adorned, clad in new linen clothes, and equipped with a turban and finger-rings; || 93 ||
With all his limbs made fragrant, wearing a garland, with polished earrings, and having properly applied vertical sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) with white clay. || 94 ||
With the sacred grass in hand, self-restrained, devoted to breath control,
having performed the ritual sipping of water and the placement of mantras on the body, he should indeed recite the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having requested that for his purpose, accompanied by the patron (yajamāna), he worshipped the Blessed One, the source of the world, according to the prescribed rite. || 96 ||
Having offered libations in due order into the water-pot, the mandala, the image, and the fire—
whether into the image, the fire, or the image again, depending on whether it is the highest or other [levels]— 97.
Then, in a new vessel made of gold or silver,
[one should place] sesame, mustard, wild rice, śāli rice, mung beans, and millet.
O twice-born one, these twelve seeds— kuluttha, mudga, niṣpāva, yava, godhūma, and veṇu— should be placed individually in separate vessels.

O best of sages, having gathered [the materials] and placed them upon the head of the initiated Brahmin, one should join the palms in añjali, filled with flowers and unbroken grains of rice. || 100 ||
The preceptor, O Brahmin, should enter the interior of the temple together with the practitioners who are absorbed in the Blessed One; there, he should place [the deity] upon the support.
Then, having worshipped the seed-vessel with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, flowers, and incense,
[one should likewise worship] that which resides in the primary image as well as that which pertains to the festive image.
Then, having worshipped the seed-vessel, one should present it to the deity amidst the sounding of conchs, auspicious sounds, and the resonance of songs. (103)
Then, amidst various sounds of trumpets and the resonance of musical notes on all sides, one should announce this mantra with a loud voice: || 104 ||
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, for the purpose of the festival procession, I shall perform the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) for the sake of the banner; be gracious, O Aum! (105)
Having thus informed the Lord and obtained his permission there,
he placed that vessel upon the head of the initiate himself.
O Brahmin, having gone outside accompanied by the practitioners,
the preceptor [should worship] Viṣvaksena, or Tārkṣya, or those headed by Hanumān.
Having especially adorned the Lord of Weapons (Hetīśa) with garments and other ornaments,
and having placed him upon a vehicle or similar conveyance, one should wash the spade with water.
O twice-born one, having clothed him in a new garment and adorned him with garlands,
the preceptor should have him carried by Brahmins or by Śūdras who have been initiated.
Together with umbrellas, banners, and flags, along with vessels containing sprouts, the three kinds of *pālikā* and other containers, and accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and the like. (110)
Together with devotees of the Lord intent on proclaiming the sacred tradition, with singers, courtesans, and other auspicious beings, [they celebrated] the All-pervading One. || 111 ||
Having circumambulated them all in due order, including all the surrounding enclosures,
one should face either the eastern direction, the northern direction, or the intermediate direction between east and north.
Having approached not far from there, in that charming garden, or in a solitary and pure place, one should collect pure earth. (113)
First, the Guru, having sprinkled the earth with the Astra-mantra and touched it while reciting the Mahīsūkta, should meditate with a one-pointed mind.
Having worshipped the earth with flowers after consecrating it with water from the weapon-mantra (astra) and adorning it with blossoms, one should worship the Varāha-form of the Lord.
Facing the east, one should dig the earth with a spade while reciting the mantra of Varāha,
depositing the clay either in a vessel made of iron or one made of bamboo, according to one's preference.
Having taken [the clay] with the root mantra and having wrapped it in a fresh cloth,
one should likewise take sand from a river and cow dung.
Having taken [the vessel] from Gokula as before, covered it with a cloth, and placed it upon a vehicle or the like, or else upon the head of the initiated person; 118.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, he should then enter the pavilion;
having purified the pavilion according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual bathing.
Then, one should stretch the lines in sequence in the middle of the pavilion;
first, one should cast seventeen lines extending toward the east in due order.
One should lay down fourteen threads extending from east to west;
the interval between each thread shall measure sixteen finger-breadths.
There should be exactly thirteen rows from east to west;
likewise, there are sixteen rows counted from south to north. (122)
For the purpose of consecrating the seed-vessels, one should establish three rows in the middle and two for the sake of the aisles, arranged in the eastern and western rows.
Furthermore, one should establish three rows on both sides;
in the middle, between the south and the north, four rows should be established.
One should again erase two by two on each side for the sake of the pathways;
then, one should establish four by four rows according to the sequential method.
In the eight directions and in the middle, twelve arrow-vessels and twelve jar-standards should be placed; thus, there will be one hundred and eight.
The *pālikās* are placed in the south-eastern, southern, and south-western directions;
the *ghaṭikās* in the western, northern, and eastern directions;
and the *śarāvas* according to the rule in the north-western, northern, and north-eastern directions.
One should arrange sixteen vessels for each of the items beginning with the *pālikā*.
One should lay down five threads extending from south to north; one should lay down the threads extending eastward as before. || 129 ||
O Brahmin, one should perform the arrangement of rows from east to west as before;
there, one should place [the vessels] in sequence within four rows to the south.
Having placed sixteen *pālikās* in the four rows in front of the center,
one should then place sixteen *ghaṭikās* in the north.
Then, having prepared twelve vessels of that same number, one should lay down four threads here, running from south to north. || 132 ||
One should lay out the front and back lines as before;
indeed, there will be forty-eight additional squares.
Having established twelve squares in the southern direction, one should then erase them;
one should then set aside six parts from the center for the sake of the pathways.
Thereafter, one should eliminate six parts from the twelve parts;
furthermore, twelve squares situated in the northern direction should be established in sequence.
One should place the *pālikā* vessels and so forth in three sets of twelve parts,
starting from the southern direction and proceeding in order up to the northeast, beginning with the southeast.
When eight measurements are assigned individually for each of the *pālikā* and other vessels, one should strike three lines running from south to north. (137)
Everything else should be as before; then, upon each set of four squares, one should drop three lines running from south to north. (138)
One should indeed lay down eleven threads for the east-west lines,
for the purpose of encompassing all sixteen *pālikās*.
One should likewise cast five southern threads as eastern threads;
and from the five eastern threads, one should cast three southern threads for each of the eight [squares]. || 140 ||
In the arrangement of twenty-four small bowls, one should cast seven and five threads for the east and south [respectively]. (141)
In the fourfold enclosure, one should cast three lines and another three;
the first laying of the lines should be as before, among the five numbers.
Having thus stretched the threads according to one's wealth and desire,
[one should fill] the squares for the *pālikā*s and other vessels with *śāli* rice and *vrīhi* grains.

One should fashion a pedestal, either circular or square, in sequence according to the previous [measurements] of one āḍhaka and so forth, depending on whether it is for the best, middling, or lowest [type]. || 144 ||
One should wash the vessels, such as the *pālikā* and others, with the root mantra, together with *sahadevī*, *dūrvā*, and the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree. (145)
Immediately thereafter, one should tie śirīṣa sprouts as well as niśā leaves around the necks of the women carrying the water-pots.
One should fill the openings of their holes with kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and other blades of grass;
first with earth, and immediately thereafter with sand.
O Brahmin, one should fill the cavity above with a profusion of dried cow-dung powder,
or else one should fill it by mixing all materials such as clay and the like.

O best of the twice-born, one should place those vessels, beginning with the *pālikā*, in order within the enclosures, starting from the southeast and ending in the northeast, for each successive tier.
One should place nine out of the twelve [syllables], totaling one hundred and eight, starting from Brāhmaṇa and ending with Īśāna, according to the sequence of the stated order. || 150 ||
Having thus completed everything, along with the initiated attendants,
they accomplished all those various tasks that had not been previously prepared.
Then the preceptor, facing eastward, should commence the rite upon the footprint;
having sat down on an auspicious seat to the west of the location of the water-jars.
Having indicated the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should prepare the water for sprinkling and the offering (arghya) according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform the worship with the arghya and other offerings for the mantras deposited upon the body.
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers according to one's means and desire,
one should worship the archways, the banners, and the pitchers at the doors.
Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay,
it should be filled with fragrant water and adorned upon the top.
One should place the pitcher, adorned with garlands, sandalwood paste, and unbroken rice grains, upon its support;
then, one's own self in front and the Bahvṛcas and others behind, in their proper order. (156)
Then the preeminent teacher himself should cause the recitation of the *svasti* and *puṇyāha* mantras,
together with the masters and practitioners who have been honored with the *arghya* offering and other rites.
O Brahmin, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited while carrying the auspicious water-pot,
one should afterwards worship the presiding deities of the *pālikās* and other vessels with offerings such as the *arghya*.
O Brahmin, one should worship in sequence upon the three parts of the vessel's rim: Aḍhjanābha, Pajhanābha, and Dhruva.
In the twelve *pālikās*, from fire (southeast) to Īśāna (northeast) and westward, one places the twelve beginning with Ananta; then, in the twelve *ghaṭikās*, likewise.
In the twelfth [section], one should worship in sequence the twelve vessels beginning with Kūrma, as well as the twelve [vessels] beginning with Ekaśṛṅga, making two groups of six. || 161 ||
For each of the vessels and other items, sixteen kalpanās are prescribed;
these begin with Ananta and end with Pātālaśayana, totaling thirty-six.
One should worship the twelve deities of Peace, beginning with Lakṣmī and ending with Mati;
for each of the vessels such as the *pālikā*, there are thirty-six [deities], ending with Pātālaśayana.
The fourfold group of forms is situated in the state called dream;
likewise, the eightfold group is of the nature of waking through the process of origination and dissolution. 164.
There is a group of twelve other forms, a group of thirteen of their Śaktis, and thirty-six [emanations] beginning with Ananta and ending with Pātālaśayana. || 165 ||
And one should worship the thirty-four powers beginning with Svadhā and that which is beyond them,
along with the discus and conch, in sequence with offerings such as arghya and perfumes.
In the group of eight, one should worship Keśava and the others, along with their respective Śaktis;
in the group of four, one should worship Keśava and the others alone; and in the group of twelve, one should likewise worship them alone.
One should worship, in sequence, the sixteen vessels for all purposes:
the four beginning with Vāsudeva and the twelve beginning with Keśava. || 168 ||
In the group of eight, he [worships] Vāsudeva and the others according to the sequence of their manifestation and dissolution;
in the group of four, however, he worships Vāsudeva and the others according to the order of their manifestation.
Having worshipped these in due order, one should then wash the seeds properly with cow's milk while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having worshipped each of the seeds individually with their names in the dative case, using offerings such as *arghya* and the like, and having wrapped them in a cloth; || 171 ||
Taking the clarified butter remaining from the oblation, or another consecrated substance, in a vessel made of metal or clay according to one's preference; 172.
Taking dūrvā grass by its roots with both hands,
one should dip the tips into ghee and sprinkle them over the *pālikā* vessels and other offerings.
By means of the path of reversing the hands, from the southeast (vahni) to the northeast (īśāna) and westward;
for each shoulder-position, the placement of ghee is proclaimed as a distinct type of *dūrvā*.
Having thus performed the offering of ghee, one should again worship the deities of the shoulders and other parts, and consecrate all the seeds with the twelvefold mantra.

Having obtained permission from the preceptor and others, the lord of teachers, facing either north or east, [should place the seeds] in the *pālikā* vessels and so forth during an auspicious moment. (176)
O twice-born one, one should sow all the seeds with the twelve-syllable mantra;
or rather, with that same mantra, or indeed with both.
From the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśa), on each successive tier in sequence, it was accompanied by the sounds of conchs, drums, and cries of victory. || 178 ||
One should sow the twelve seeds in the twelve [sections] in sequence;
or else, having mixed all of them together, one may sow them according to one's desire. || 179 ||
But if even seeds cannot be obtained, one should sow a single mudga bean;
others who are authorized by the preceptor—namely, the teachers and the practitioners—may do so as well. (180)
Those engaged in meditation, or the preceptor alone, should sprinkle [the area] with water scented with flowers and mixed with turmeric powder. || 181 ||
O Brahmin, the preeminent teacher should sprinkle [the disciple] with many [mantras] in due order;
then, above each section (skandha), he should place [the disciple] within the center of the lunar disc.
The deity, resembling that very luster, was incessantly sprinkling the seeds sown everywhere with floods of nectar arising from his own body.
Having meditated upon them and worshipped the vessels with nine auspicious items of similar quality,
one should cover them with cloths, arranging them one by one according to their respective sections.
O best of the twice-born, one should worship Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, above all others; then one should offer the *bhūtakrūra* oblation in the eight directions.
For the beings Kumuda and the others, according to the sequence beginning with the east;
from that time forward, all those [beings] such as Kumuda protect [them].
Then, with abundant betel leaves, flowers, and fruits as prescribed, [he should honor] all the teachers, gurus, practitioners, and Vaiṣṇavas.
The diligent patron should satisfy the preceptor with wealth;
then, having gradually raised all those [images], he should place them in a well-protected location. || 188 ||
Either in the northeast corner of the pavilion or in another place according to one's preference;
there too, [one should place] the *pālikās* and so forth in the eight directions around it. (189)

One should offer the bali-oblation in the pavilion to the spirits, such as the Kumudas and others, according to the sequence beginning with Indra and following the ritual procedure for the cruel spirits. || 190 ||
One should illuminate many lamps all around that have not yet been extinguished;
to pacify deficiencies and excesses, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations.
Or one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra in the presence of the image;
then, one should perform the dismissal of the Lord who resides in the place of the water-pot and other vessels.
One should offer oblations separately every night for the Pālikās and others,
either during the day or at night, or even at both times.
The best of preceptors should offer the bali-oblation every morning on the day of the ritual;
from the time the seeds are sown, this should be done daily.
No one whatsoever should enter there, nor should anyone touch it in any way;
only the teacher or his disciple, being fully concentrated, may enter. || 195 ||
One should avoid all remnants of food and the like from afar;
moreover, one should not perform the rite of the *pālikās* without having first offered the *bali*.
One should sprinkle the sprouts with water infused with turmeric for their growth.
Sprouts that are dark green, red, black, or likewise curved, [are auspicious]. || 197 ||
O best of sages, one should diligently avoid those that have not yet sprouted;
if they are dark-colored, there will be loss of wealth, and if they are red, there will be strife. (198)
If there is mental distress regarding black spots, or if they appear on diseased areas or on animals, death will occur when they have not yet healed; of this there is no doubt. (199)

When the lines are auspicious, yellowish, white, straight, and upward-pointing, there shall be the attainment of all prosperity for both the performer and the one who causes it to be performed. || 200 ||
The preceptor who first establishes the sprouts for the purpose of the ritual—he alone, even if he is wise, shall perform the rite in its entirety, and no other. 201.
Or, with permission, his son or his disciple may complete it;
in this manner, the planting of the sprouts shall take place for all sacrifices. || 202 ||
Having understood the place, the time, the available wealth, and likewise one's own independence,
one should perform the primary action after duly considering everything that has been said.
Having thus performed the sowing of the seed, one should procure a cloth for the banner—either purchased according to one's means or a new, auspicious one. (204)
It may be made of dukūla cloth, divine silk (devāṅga), or even variegated linen;
or it may be made of cotton, provided it is free from blue fibers and the like. || 205 ||
A cubit that is well-defined, firm, and smooth is said here to be the standard measure;
one should determine the measurement using the cubits of the disciple, the preceptor, or the artisan. (206)
The first [type] should be twelve cubits, the middle ten cubits, and the lowest eight cubits; the width, moreover, should be four cubits. || 207 ||
It should be excellent; the middling should be three cubits, and the inferior should be one and a half [cubits]. Know these, O best of the twice-born, as the first [category]. (208)
The best of instructors should fashion the pinnacle to be two cubits in height;
likewise, he should construct the tail-feather at the lower part of the banner.
One should have the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa) drawn with a height of seven cubits from the waist;
half a cubit is prescribed for the purpose of accommodating the head and the neck. || 210 ||
O twice-born one, the measurement for the placement of the foot-staff should be the same as that;
now I shall describe the measurement of the middle [section] in brief—understand it. 211.
O Brahmin, one should fashion the hand and the half-measure and so forth, joined with three finger-breadths, for the sake of the pinnacle; likewise, the tail is proclaimed.
One should draw Garuḍa in the center with a span of six cubits;
the remainder should be arranged for the purpose of inserting two staffs. || 213 ||
Now, O bull among sages, I shall describe the lowest [grade] of the cloth-painting:
its pinnacle should be one cubit and a quarter. (214)
With the tail at the bottom for the purpose of the hands, and the placement of two staffs [for the wings], one should paint Vainateya with a five-cubit body in the middle. || 215 ||
I shall further describe another method according to one's wealth and desire:
the first [type] should be fifteen cubits, while the middle [type] is thirteen.
Eleven cubits in length is proclaimed as the lowest;
the width should be four cubits plus half a cubit for the highest [grade]. || 217 ||
The middle [size] should be one-quarter larger, and the lowest one-quarter smaller;
however, for the best [type], it should be two cubits larger for the sake of the pinnacle.
In that same manner, one should draw the tail with a hand's breadth, the placement of the two staffs [the wings] with eight hands from the waist, and thus depict Garuḍa.
In the middle [section], the peak is two cubits;
likewise, the tail below is reduced by one-eighth of a cubit for the purpose of inserting the two staffs.
One should depict Garuḍa with seven and a half cubits increased by three finger-breadths;
now I shall describe the inferior [form], which is two cubits less a quarter.
The pinnacle (śikhara) and likewise the tail (puccha) should be made with three-quarters of a cubit;
the placement of the two staffs (daṇḍa) should be at seven cubits less a quarter.
The wise man should likewise depict Garuḍa; now hear further of another method:
the best [image] is nine cubits, while the middling is seven cubits. || 223 ||
Now, the fifth [type] is five cubits; it is said to be of three kinds.
Its width should be half of that, and its pinnacle should be half of that [width]. || 224 ||
The tail is said to be equal to that, and the ear-tail likewise;
it may also be equal in length to the root-disk or to the width of the door.
It is as wide as half its length, with a crest formed by one-fourth;
the tail is equal to the crest, and the ear-tail is half of that.
In both of the previously mentioned cases, one should fashion the ear and the tail;
the cloth for the banner called "hair" (bāla) should be equal in measure to the "banner-cloth" (paṭa). || 227 ||
Its width should be equal to that of a cloth, and its peak should be as described previously; it must be well-washed, free from defects, dried, and endowed with the proper characteristics. || 228 ||
The wise one should have the cloth decorated by a truly skilled artisan;
he should place a parasol at the top and two white chowries on the two sides.
Below that, one should draw a lotus with many petals, and beneath that, a full water-pot;
on the sides of the pot, one should depict a series of flowerpots with sprouts.
O best of men, one should place two very beautiful lamps on either side of the *pālikās*;
for the single-formed [deity], however, there should be a banner in the shape of Garuḍa.
Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya are the four forms of the fourfold self; together with the Lord of Birds, they constitute the four [forms] of the fivefold embodiment. || 232 ||
For the fourfold self, there may be the forms of Suparṇa, Tāla, Makara, or Ṛśya;
however, above all these arrays, Garuḍa is the banner.
In the center of the cloth, however, one should depict Garuḍa with two arms, his hands joined in the añjali gesture, or else holding a handful of flowers, resembling a mountain of gold. || 234 ||
In the sky, accompanied by the flapping of wings at the start of flight, the left foot is bent while the right stands behind. || 235 ||
With slightly elongated and rounded eyes, a blue nose with a long tip,
his appearance was exceedingly peaceful, and his face was smiling.
Adorned with two fangs resembling the young moon, his face was graced by the knitting of curved eyebrows and beautified by curling locks of hair. || 237 ||
With a neck like a conch shell, long arms, broad shoulders, and a firm chest;
with a large abdomen, a deep navel, and adorned by a line of body hair. || 238 ||
His two thighs were as stout as well-rounded golden pillars,
and his two feet rested upon shanks that possessed the appearance of golden plantain trees.
Adorned with a flower-cluster crown resting upon his head, his eyes are as broad and round as lotus petals in their measurement. (240)
The pair of eyebrows is described as being like those of Narasimha; the tip of the nose is like the beak of a parrot;
the middle region is like that of a lion; and its backbone is like the back of an elephant.
Thus, with its divine length, it is spread out like the wing of a swan;
its tail, which has a hundred branches, is twice the measure of its own wingspan.
Know that this is common to all; now the specific [description] is being stated:
[the deity] is adorned with various jewels from the crown down to the soles of the feet. (243)
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and sacred threads, and with beautiful earrings resting against the ends of his long, pendulous ears. (244)
Adorned with a tilaka on his forehead and flower-earrings,
he wore jeweled rings and had his feet marked by the bowstring.
Adorned with other divine ornaments, yet decorated with serpents as his jewelry; wearing blue garments and resplendent with a blue waist-cloth. || 246 ||
His neck was adorned with garlands of full-blown red utpala lotuses,
and he was radiant with other variously colored flower garlands.
Ananta is his left armlet, while Vāsuki is his sacred thread;
Takṣaka is his waistband, and Kārkoṭaka is likewise his necklace. (248)
Pajha is on the right ear, while Mahāpajha is on the left;
Śaṅkha is in the region of the head, and Gulika is between the arms.
He is adorned by these eight primordial and supreme serpents:
Ananta has the luster of white, while Vāsuki is red in color. (250)
Takṣaka has the luster of yellow, Kārkoṭaka is smoky-colored, Śaṅkha has the appearance of snow, and Gulika resembles a bee. || 251 ||
Pajha, Pajhasamānābha, and Mahāpajha who is piṅgala—
one should thus draw the god with five colors and likewise with five weapons.
One should draw, according to the prescribed rule, the discus, sword, arrow, conch, Śārṅga bow, and mace, respectively, above the cloth and on both sides.
Below that, on the right side, one should draw a circle of fire;
likewise, on the left side, one should draw a svastika endowed with its characteristic marks.
One should paint the remainder of the cloth with dark green or black [pigment], provided with various flowers and accompanied by leafy creepers. || 255 ||
In this manner, O best of the twice-born, the supreme instructor should have it constructed by a preeminent artisan, or by a Śūdra who has been initiated according to the prescribed rule.
Or else, O best of the twice-born, the minister should have it made by a skilled potter; for this is declared to be the general characteristic [of the vessel]. (257)
Determine the specific measurement by means of divisions such as finger-breadths (aṅgula):
that which is declared as the finger-breadth in the image is one part out of one hundred and eight. || 258 ||
In that very place, one should determine the measurements using the finger-breadths (aṅgula) arising from the root-image; now, ascertain the proportions for its vehicle. || 259 ||
The orb of his face is marked by a *tāla* arising from its reflection;
two finger-breadths above the forehead is the binding of matted locks, and there are two eyes.
The neck is known to be two finger-breadths in height; the chest is five finger-breadths;
that belly is eight finger-breadths; and the waist is five finger-breadths in height. || 261 ||
The thighs are nine finger-breadths in height; the knees are recorded as being two finger-breadths [in thickness];
the calves are eight finger-breadths in height; and the two ankle-bumps are two finger-breadths [in height].
One śama minus one kalā is the measurement for the encircling of her neck;
the expansion of all her limbs should always be understood as equal to a bimba fruit. || 263 ||
Know that the circumference of the abdomen is indeed two-sixteenths [of the total height] and so forth;
however, the girth of the waist region is certainly four eyes (four times the face) greater.
Know that the girth at the base of her thighs is like that of a *biṃba* fruit;
indeed, the same applies to the middle of her calves and the calves themselves. (265)
The foot is five kalās in length and four aṅgulas in width;
from the region of the heel, the two big toes are three aṅgulas long and equal to one kalā.
The toes should be known to be progressively shorter than the feet;
the navel cavity is very extensive, measuring two and a half eyes in width.
Know that his head and arms, in height, possess two eyes;
and that pair consisting of the upper and lower arms is recorded as being equal to two tālas. || 268 ||
From the wrist to the tips of the middle fingers, the span is nine finger-breadths;
the width of the hand consists of three kalās, and its nails are sharp and prominent. || 269 ||
The arm is one and a half kalās longer than that; the armlet is half of that.
The region of the breasts is measured by two of the portions mentioned for the bimba, while the eyes are [measured] by one.
The eyes should be as broad and rounded in measure as lotus petals;
the pair of eyebrows is described by Nārasiṃha [as being like those of a lion]; and the tip of the nose should be like the beak of a parrot.
The bamboo [of the flute] should be half a *kalā* in length and shaped like the back of an elephant;
its pair of side-projections (*pakṣa*) reaching the region of the belly should be as long as its own [total] length. (272)
That very [tail] is half as wide as its length, like the wing of a swan;
the tail of the hundred-branched [tree] is twice the measure of its own wings.
Know that the "similar class" (sapakṣa) is likewise characterized by extension, truth, and possession of parts;
it is the commonality of all things, and what follows is called the "particular" (viśeṣa). || 274 ||
One should reduce the thighs by two finger-breadths, and likewise the height of the shank-sections by three fingers;
one should also provide a binding with the shanks here.
O Mahāmati, from the root of the wrist-joint known as the *bimba*, it measures half [the height] up to the region of the shank, plus an additional half-finger-breadth. || 276 ||
The web on the foot should be understood to be six finger-breadths in width;
know that everything else has been declared according to truth for all [beings] at all times. || 277 ||
However, when the wings are raised from the feet, their length and breadth are equal to those of the petals;
and for these birds as they fly upward, the span of their wings is equal to their body length. || 278 ||
And for the five [deities] who abide as having half-lakṣaṇas, they are to be fully known;
however, when being drawn upon a cloth, the length of the wings is on both sides. || 279 ||
O Brahmin, until the completion of the cloth, the feathers— provided with their tips and down— should be counted by the number seven, five, and so on, in odd numbers.
Alternatively, according to the path taught by Bimba, the limbs and sub-limbs of the five [faces] beginning with Satya are to be fashioned using one hundred and eight finger-breadths.
Alternatively, it may be made with eight gentle finger-breadths (aṅgulas) arising from the length of the middle joints of the middle fingers of the preceptor.
The preceptor should perform the measurement of the five [deities] beginning with Satya;
the height of the primary image (mūlabimba) shall extend either to the end of the arms or to the end of the navel. || 283 ||
This measurement has been declared; now understand the unmāna (counter-measurement) for Garuḍa when situated on the cloth, as well as for Satya and the others. || 284 ||
One should determine the length by means of the long joint of the middle finger;
however, the measurement for the pedestal (deśikīya) is one hundred and eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The measurement from the head down to the feet is now described:
there are three finger-breadths for the head, and the face should be six golakas. || 286 ||
The neck should be three finger-breadths in measure, and the portion below it twelve finger-breadths;
starting from the space between the breasts and extending to the navel, it should be six kalās. || 287 ||
From there down to the waist should be five finger-breadths;
from there down to the vulva should be seven finger-breadths. || 288 ||
The portion ending at the knees consists of twelve digits (kala), and the knee-caps are three digits (aṅgula) each;
from below that down to the ankles, there should be twelve globes (golaka). || 289 ||
The measurement of the ankle should be three finger-breadths; now hear the measurements in their proper order:
from the end of the plumb-line at the mouth-part, there are two globes (golaka) above.
Likewise, the distance from the end of the nostrils to the chin is also six kalās; the width of the face at its center extends to the end of the ear-line.
The lower portion [of the forehead] should be nine finger-breadths, and the portion at the forehead itself ten finger-breadths;
between the hairline and the brow-line, this [remaining space] shall be one finger-breadth.
The space between the eye and the eyebrow should be one and a quarter finger-breadths in width;
the length of the eye should be two and three-quarter finger-breadths. || 293 ||
Its width, however, should be one and three-quarter finger-breadths;
the width at the base of the nose should be one finger-breadth. || 294 ||
Two finger-breadths with a fraction at the middle, and three finger-breadths below; its length at the tip should be one [unit], and its width half of that. || 295 ||
The length of the mouth should be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and its width should be one finger-breadth;
the lower lip together with the upper lip should be two finger-breadths in extent. || 296 ||
O Brahmin, the length between the two fangs is said to be one and a quarter finger-breadths;
the width, moreover, shall be one finger-breadth.
At the base of those two, their tips are sharp like the edge of a crescent moon;
the length of the neck is five finger-breadths, and its width should be that of a sphere. || 298 ||
The height of the feet should be six finger-breadths; the support for the ears (the neck-base) should be four kalās;
and below that, from the upper part of the pedestal, the chest should be one and a half finger-breadths.
O twice-born one, the *tāra* [mantra] extending from the armpits to the end of the outstretched arms consists of eighteen *kalās*;
below that, reaching down to the waist, the *tāra* consists of twelve *golakas*.
The width of its lower part consists of nine spheres (golakas) plus one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
the width of the belly, however, should be twenty-one finger-breadths. || 301 ||
There, the girdle, beautiful and well-fashioned, measures one finger-breadth [in width];
the width of the hip region is nine *gola*s plus one finger-breadth. || 302 ||
The width at the base of the thigh should be thirteen finger-breadths;
O Brahmin, the width in its middle is measured at twelve finger-breadths. (303)
The generative organ should be seven finger-breadths [in length], the width of the knee three kalās;
below that, it should be five finger-breadths, and the length of the foot one and a half [times] seven golakas.
From the tips of the big toes down to the heels, the measurements there are as follows:
the big toe is three and a half finger-breadths, and the other fingers [toes] are progressively shorter by one finger-breadth each. (305)
The width of the thumb shall be one-eighth of an aṅgula less [than its length];
for the others, it is one and a half aṅgulas, decreasing in sequence as before.
The space between the nails of the thumbs should be one finger-breadth with its fractional parts;
its width should be three-quarters of that, and the others should be decreased in sequence.
When the nail-length is less, it should be half a finger-breadth;
its width at the base of the fingers should be half of that. || 308 ||
The width of the foot should be five and a half finger-breadths;
at the middle of the heel, it should be four and a half finger-breadths. || 309 ||
The height at the side of the branches is proclaimed to be three finger-breadths; in the middle it should be one and a half [finger-breadths]. Now hear concerning those two arms. || 310 ||
From the top of the shoulder to the end of the elbow, it should be twenty-four finger-breadths;
the width at the base of this arm should be six finger-breadths.

Below that, the five [fingers] together with the half [of the palm] and the nine spheres from the elbows to the ends of the wrists constitute the length; this is the measurement for the width of the elbows. || 312 ||
O Brahmin, from the wrist upwards it should be six finger-breadths;
the tip of the hand should have a width of three fingers and a length of six kalās.
The width is said to be two *kalās*, while on the left side it should be two *aṅgulas*; the other two, namely the visible and the concealed, are indeed on the right hand.
The length of the middle finger is fixed at five fingers;
then, for the uncurved index finger and the remaining fingers, it is respectively [less]. || 315 ||
The middle finger shall be half an aṅgula less [than the index], and the width (tāra) between the middle and the thumb shall be one and a half aṅgulas.

The length of the nail on the index and ring fingers should be one [unit], and that of the little finger should be three-quarters; the length of the nail should be one and a half finger-breadths, and its width should be half of that.
O Brahmin, the height of the crown should be eighteen finger-breadths;
its width at the base, O Brahmin, should be measured at sixteen finger-breadths.
Six kalās should be known for the middle part, and three kalās should be at the front;
one should fashion the height of the crest-jewel as one and a half aṅgulas.
The width should be one and a quarter times that [length], with three tālas for the wings;
or else, it may extend to the edge of the cloth, according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Each individual wing-tip should extend three finger-breadths;
the length of the mouths of the nāgas, however, should be one and a half finger-breadths. || 321 ||
O Brahmin, its width is one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and the width of that lake is likewise one finger-breadth;
below that it should be two finger-breadths, and the hair-like fringe (vāla) is half a finger-breadth.
Just as the extent of the coils of the nāgas gradually decreases,
the length of Ananta, the foremost among them, is measured at two finger-breadths.
The *tattāra* (the *tāra* with its *tat*) should be one and a half [units], while the width of its neck (*galavistara*) should be two.
Below that, the two [sections] should be one and a half; the heads (*śīrṣa*) are like those of other *nāgas*.
One should arrange it so that its width is equal to a single hair-tip; as for the length of the coils of the serpents, one may determine it according to one's preference.
The length of the lotus-seat (viṣṭara-padma) is fifty-four finger-breadths;
its width is six globes, which is equal to the extent of the pericarp (karṇikā). || 326 ||
Twenty-one digits are prescribed for its width, and its thickness is three globes;
furthermore, whatever other measurement has been devised for Vainateya [is as follows].
Having made that hundred and eight finger-breadths— which must be divided very evenly— into finger-units as before, one should determine the measurement and so forth.
One should also fashion the nāga and other figures according to those finger-measures;
however, in the first alternative, one should fashion the nāga and others in accordance with the first [measurement].
Adorned with the five-fold ornaments and perfumed with garments, garlands, and scents— having thus prepared everything, the preceptor, being well-composed, [proceeds].
On the night preceding the constellation for hoisting the banner,
he should proceed to the workshop at the onset of night, accompanied by the image-bearers.
Having gazed upon the painted cloth and having thoroughly examined its characteristics,
amidst the sounds of conchs and drums as well as the blare of trumpets, (332)
Accompanied by various delightful songs and diverse sounds from the Vedas,
one should bring it from there to the front pavilion along with the banner-cloth.

Having entered the interior and saluted the Supreme Lord residing within the root-image, one should worship Him with offerings of water for the feet (arghya), perfumes, and so forth, as well as with flowers and incense. || 334 ||

After dismissing the artisan, he should subsequently sprinkle the cloth with the water of the arghya offering and strike it with flowers accompanied by white mustard seeds, consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
The best of practitioners should show [the offering] before the God of gods;
he should perform the rites of burning and nourishing according to the procedure seen in the ritual rules. || 326 ||
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord further with incense, flowers, and other offerings, one should recite this mantra with palms joined in reverence while ascending the mountain peak. || 337 ||
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed Lord of All, who pervades the universe!
It is not possible to act exactly as you have described.

Because of a lack of autonomy, a lack of capacity, and the absence of faith and other [virtuous qualities], therefore, for the sake of pacifying the deficiency or excess of all [mental factors] such as pride and the rest, [one should practice]. (339)
Behold with your two cool eyes the son of Vinatā depicted upon the cloth;
he who removes all defects, be gracious, Om! 340.
Then, O Brahmin, having placed that cloth in the hands of the initiated ones and having performed four circumambulations with them, the preceptor— || 341 ||
Either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure,
the sacrificer should enter the pavilion situated at the top of the temple.
Having placed the *bhadrapīṭha* there, one should construct an altar (*vedi*) above it with rice grains,
and upon its surface, one should draw the mandala called *Bhadra*.
When wealth is available, having spread out a cloth and scattered a heap of sesame seeds upon it,
one should draw a svastika in the middle of that.
Having placed the cloth painting facing the temple above it,
the preceptor, being well-composed, should then sit upon his seat.

One should perform everything previously mentioned, beginning with the purification of the hands and ending with the worship of one's own body, using the Khageśa mantra together with its ancillaries (aṅgas). || 346 ||
One should perform the worship of the door-keepers, the arches, the water-pots, and so forth, as previously described;
then, O twice-born one, one should cause the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) to be made as before.
In front of Garuḍa, as before,
one should place a water-pot together with a small pitcher upon a seat of grain prepared to support the weight.
Then, having placed a vessel such as a wooden water-tub, well-filled with fragrant water, there to the right of the water-pot (karakas), || 349 ||
O twice-born one, in the first group of nine previously mentioned ablutions, one should employ the immediate shadow-garment of Garuḍa.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing by means of the lowest-of-the-low path,
while [the image] is situated upon the altar in front of Vainateya.
Then, after a moment, at an auspicious hour, the Guru should perform the opening of the eyes by the very same method previously described. (352)
One should perform the opening of the eyes for all the serpents as well;
then the artisan, whose body has been purified as before, should bring them to manifestation. (353)
One should perform everything as before, including the filling of the eyes and so forth,
having prepared a seat for both the water-pot (kumbha) and the small vessel (karaka).
Having invoked Garuḍa into the pitcher (kumbha) and the weapon-mantra (astramantra) into the water-vessel (karaka),
and having worshipped them with offerings such as arghya and perfumes, [one should then proceed] with the eight pitchers of the directions.
Having worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the world in clockwise order,
and having performed the sprinkling of the walls, one should then once again establish [the deity] there.
Then, having conceived the seat upon the banner-cloth as before,
one should [visualize] the mantra of Garuḍa, radiant like a thousand suns.
It pacifies all diseases, destroys all calamities, bestows all accomplishments upon men, and eliminates all poverty. || 358 ||
O best of Brahmins, having drawn [the deity] from the heart, one should place it upon Garuḍa depicted on the cloth;
then, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should effect the presence [of the deity].
O best of the twice-born, [explain] the complete cessation, the manifestation, as well as the binding of the mudrās, the sacrifice of dissolution, and the sacrifice of enjoyment, exactly as they are.
One should perform everything with the Garuḍa mantra, together with its ancillary parts, according to the sequential method upon the water-pot, the small vessel, and the cloth. || 361 ||
One should perform the worship with great magnificence,
following the prescribed sequence up to the ornaments and the seat.
O Brahmin, having performed the worship of Garuḍa,
thereafter, within the temple, with the permission of the preceptor, O Brahmin— || 363 ||
Or else, one should cause the worship to be performed properly by another preceptor or a distinguished practitioner for the sake of the primary image. || 364 ||

Even for the Lord who has entered the form for a procession, the ceremonial bath— preceded by special worship— is likewise to be performed until the conclusion of the gift-giving ceremony, while He is seated upon Garuḍa.
Then, for the sake of Vainateya, [the meal] was served, beginning with food and seats and ending with various delightful *madhuparka* offerings and all kinds of roots. (366)
Having worshipped with abundant food offerings as well as various other desired enjoyments, he should perform the recitation (japa) at the end, following the sequence as before.
One should perform the formal gift (saṃpradāna) separately for the artisans according to the rules;
then, one should give to the teachers that which was offered to the mantra, the weapon, and the water-pot.

The preceptor himself should take some of the food offering (naivedya) from the vessel belonging even to the deity depicted on the cloth-painting, and he should indeed offer it to the Guru and others as well.
Whether the deity is situated in the root-liṅga or in the portable liṅga, the food offering (naivedya), beginning with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other items, is presented to Him. || 370 ||
One should cause [the fees] to be given to the preceptor and others, and then perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the proper characteristics in the eastern part of Garuḍa’s [temple], one should proceed.
There, having consecrated the fire and invoked the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa),
he offered seven fuel-sticks and then oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter for the sake of pacification.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, the preceptor should present the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
or rather, the preceptor should perform the fire sacrifice in the occasional sacrificial pit (naimittika-kuṇḍa).
Then, for the patron who was self-restrained through bathing and other rites, the food offering (naivedya) which had been presented to Garuḍa depicted on the cloth was [offered]. || 374 ||
In that regard, having taken some [of it] and given it himself, the preceptor should then make the remaining portions into separate mouthfuls of food as an offering (naivedya). || 375 ||
One should bestow the mantra of Garuḍa upon women who are childless and also upon men who are afflicted by disease, while remaining composed and meditating.

Having caused him to eat food while facing the east, he should then cause him to drink from that sacred water (tīrtha). Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), he should pass the night in a vigil.
Then, at dawn, the most excellent preceptor, having bathed well and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
performed the daily worship of the Lord as well as the special sacrifice.
Then, having worshipped Vainateya preceded by the water-pot according to the prescribed rite,
and having offered the great oblation, he should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) as before.
Then, in the fourth enclosure, within the gateway,
there should be a pedestal for the banner four cubits or two cubits in size on all sides.
O Brahmin, it should be one and a half cubits high, or even just one cubit high,
constructed with stones, bricks, or baked tiles according to one's preference.
O twice-born one, one should make a pit in the center of that [altar] reaching down to the surface of the earth;
or else, O twice-born one, it may be at the third enclosure outside the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Or it may be in the second enclosure, according to the requirements of the time;
O twice-born one, it should be either to the north of the flag-pedestal or in the eastern direction.
One should then lay down the flagstaff together with the flagpole,
its tip pointing either eastward or northward, endowed with auspicious marks and very beautiful.
There are three kinds [of trees]: those with internal sap, those with external sap, and those without sap;
namely, the Campaka, the Devadāru, the Candana, and likewise the Khadira. || 385 ||
The sāla tree, the bimba, the kakubha, and the alaka—these and other such trees are cited as having internal pith. (386)
The *kramuka*, the coconut palm, the *hintāla*, the *tāla*, and the bamboo—these trees with pith on the outside are recommended for the construction of banners. (387)
O Brahmin, those trees such as the *kiṃśuka* which are declared to be pithless—
one should always avoid pithless wood for the work of making a banner.
O twice-born one, [the sacrificial wood] should be moist, fresh, straight, smooth, free from cracks or splits, having an odd number of joints, pure, with its bark intact, and very firm. (389)
Having caused the flagstaff to be erected, one should examine it according to the perspective of the technical treatises:
the best [flagstaff] should be eighty *tālas* in height, and the middling one sixty *tālas*.
The lowest [height] is fifty tālas; that which is five tālas greater than that is indeed declared the middle;
and the highest is measured at fifty tālas. || 391 ||
That [measurement] reduced by five tālas becomes "middling-middling";
that which measures twenty-two tālas is designated as "middling-low. (392)
And thirty-seven tālas, likewise thirty-five, and thirty-two—these three, O Brahmin, are categorized as inferior, superior, and so forth. (393)
O best of Brahmins, when it is possible, one should calculate the measurement here according to the *mātrā* finger-breadth, determining it to be one hundred *tālas*.
Furthermore, the ninefold division of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is now being stated;
likewise, there are twenty-five and also twenty-three [varieties] of the instruments (karaṇas).
Twenty-one, twenty, and nineteen, O seventh one;
eighteen, and another sixteen likewise, O twice-born one. (396)
And fifteen [units] in sequence are proclaimed as the ninefold [measurement];
the measurement shall be according to the standard finger (mānāṅgula) in three ways, according to one's capacity. || 397 ||
In the absence of that, however, the measurement here may be by finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula), or it may be the height of the pinnacle of the temple, or even the height of the temple itself. || 398 ||
The height of the flagstaff should reach the neck or the top of the gate, according to one's wealth;
at the base of the flagstaff, its circumference should be divided into nine parts.
At the base it should be twelve tālas, then nine, then seven;
in the middle of that, it should be six tālas, and likewise five tālas.
Its tip should be five tālas, four tālas, or two tālas;
according to the measurement of twelve aṅgulas, its circumference (nāha) should be eight aṅgulas. || 401 ||
The pillar, which is twenty-four times tenfold and very firm, should be divided into three parts;
having thus divided that pillar into three, one should make the third part [the base]. || 402 ||
Indeed, it should be made from sacrificial wood, placed at the lower part below, in the middle part in the center,
and at the front in the upper part.
O twice-born one, having fashioned three rings joined with three perforations,
they should be perfectly circular on both sides for the purpose of inserting the staff-rod.
Measuring one *phalakāhasta* [in length], they are nine finger-breadths wide at the base and four finger-breadths wide at the tip. || 405 ||
O twice-born one, O Brahmin, having left aside two tālas, one and a half tālas, or even one tāla from the top of the pillar, one should install the *asūraka* at the very tip.
Having properly placed another pair in the joined position,
or otherwise, one should install the *asūraka* above the top of the pillar as previously described.
Having set aside two and a half cubits below, one should place the central *asūraka*;
then, having likewise set aside [the same distance] below that, one should place another *asūraka*.
Having thus released three claps of the hands, he should then place upon it a firm,
straight flagstaff equipped with an iron mechanism.
One should wrap the flagpole with garlands of darbha grass, moving clockwise;
having done this, one should sprinkle the flagstaff with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra).
The preceptor should place jewels and grains into the pit situated at the base of the flagpole,
while the most excellent Brahmins recite the Tārkṣya mantra.

Or by Śūdras who have been initiated, O Brahmin, or even by temple-servants (devadāsas), accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and the like, together with song and instrumental music. || 412 ||
One should place the flagstaff upright in that pit,
fixing it facing the temple, and then fill it with sand.
Having made it very firm with elephant footprints and the like, or else, having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the pillars on the previous night; || 414 ||
Having first established [the image] today, he should afterwards go into the presence of Garuḍa,
having carefully mounted the banner upon a chariot, an elephant, or some other vehicle.
One should adorn the banner with a halo made of variegated flowers;
one should worship it with garments, ornaments, and diverse garlands. || 416 ||
Then, with parasols and chowries preceded by peacock-feather fans, and with various beautiful palm-leaf fans and charming umbrellas; || 417 ||
With various banner-staffs adorned with fine silk cloths, accompanied by the chanting of the four Vedas and the sound of hymns of praise; 418.
With various songs and musical instruments, with the sounds of conchs and trumpets,
with the booming of kettledrums, clay drums, and other auspicious instruments.
Together with groups of Brahmins carrying clusters of seed-pots containing sprouts,
with throngs of well-attired courtesans, and likewise with his devotees.
Accompanied by shouts of "kṣvelita" and "āsphoṭita," and joined with cries of "Victory!",
beginning from the first circuit and ending at the western enclosure of the chariot path.
Having rotated all the enclosures in due order and having led [the deity] clockwise around the village, he stands with the banner in the middle of the village.
One should cause the four Vedas, along with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, to be recited;
furthermore, one should display there the Sūkta known as Sauparṇam.
Having offered vocal music, dance, instrumental music, and the four kinds of musical instruments, as well as offerings such as garlands and betel leaves. || 424 ||
Then, O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, one should cause [the deity] whose banner is Garuḍa to enter the temple during the festival preceded by the rite of sowing the sprouts.
Behind the image of Garuḍa situated on the cloth, according to the prescribed rite,
one should carry the procession image accompanied by offerings during that night.
Because the means and so forth are not fully accomplished and cannot be separated [from the subject], even in that case, if there is capacity, it would wander separately. (427)
O Brahmin, in other circumstances, he should always lead only the banner, accompanied by the procession of offerings, whether in a town or a city. || 428 ||
Wherever a festival is ordained, there one should indeed cause the Garuḍa-bannered Lord to be paraded on those two occasions, accompanied by the processional image.
For the sake of making the subtle elements (tanmātras) fit and for their purification,
he should cause the festive image (bimba) to be paraded through the village together with that [deity].
Having thus performed the circumambulation of the temple and likewise the village and so forth,
one should then install the banner in the pavilion, provided it was not already established previously.
Having then established the flagstaff,
he entered the temple and proceeded with the procession image according to the prescribed rules.
Then, having adorned [him] with various beautiful garments, diverse ornaments, and many lovely garlands; || 433 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, equipped with all the necessary implements,
one should lead it to the assembly pavilion and place it facing the base of the victory banner.
Upon a beautiful golden seat, adorned with couches and other furnishings,
and decorated above by a variegated canopy.
Then, having established [the image] there, the preceptor, being well-composed and surrounded by the practitioners and others, should take up the banner of Garuḍa.
Accompanied by the sounding of conchs and other instruments, having brought [the pillar] around the sacrificial ground clockwise according to the yoga,
one should wash the pillar with pure water at the base of the banner.
When there is the means, having wrapped the flagstaff with cloth and worshipped Garuḍa preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers, || 438 ||
He offered water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), as well as water for rinsing the mouth (ācāma), perfume, garlands, and incense;
furthermore, cakes, flattened rice (pṛthuka), refreshing drinks, and likewise satiating offerings.
Immediately after that, having offered water for rinsing the mouth mixed with coconut water, he should present excellent betel-leaf prepared with camphor and other ingredients. || 440 ||
Having displayed that mudrā, one should indeed take up a firm cord,
made from very strong triple-stranded cotton threads.
O Brahmin, having fixed the machine so that it rests upon the tip of the sacrificial post, one should then fasten the pinnacle of the banner to it in such a way that it is very firm.
Accompanied by the banner of Bāla and provided with a bell,
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and then sprinkle [the image] with water consecrated by mantras.
Then, having sprinkled Garuḍa with water from the great jar,
one should place the Garuḍa residing in the great jar onto the one situated on the cloth-painting.
Then, having carved out the base of the pillar, one should pour the water from the vessel containing the weapons [into it],
and likewise pour the water from the eight jars at the base of the pillar.

O Teacher, preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), as well as the invocation of presence (sannidhi), the firm fixation (sannirodha), and the facing toward [the deity] (sāmmukhya). || 446 ||
"O Lord of Birds, from this day until the final day of the pilgrimage, remain present here for the sake of the king and his kingdom. (447)
For the satisfaction and nourishment of the village, of the sacrificer, and especially of the Vaiṣṇavas, and for the conquest of all enemies. || 448 ||
"O Lord of Birds, be gracious for the sake of victory over premature death! Om.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Birds, he scattered a handful of flowers.
In the forenoon or at midday, during an auspicious moment,
the preceptor should cause the Vīśa to ascend the rope while meditating upon the one who resides in the banner.
One should tie the rope to the pillar in a clockwise direction;
one should then place the Garuḍa-banner facing toward the temple at the pillar.
One may or may not place the image of Vihageśvara at the top of the pillar;
having gone into the presence of the God of gods, one should offer a handful of flowers.
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, whatever has not been performed by me as prescribed—may all that become complete; may you always be perfectly satisfied.
O Lord of the world whose eyes do not wane, O Janārdana whose form is mantra!
Protect me, O lotus-eyed one; forgive me, O Āja, be gracious—Om! 454.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, the omnipresent one who had assumed the form for the procession,
he led him to another pavilion preceded by special worship.
Then, having offered abundant food and performed everything concluding with the fire-oblation (havana) in the proper sequence, one should cause [the image] to enter the temple. || 456 ||
Above the pedestal of the banner,
one should fashion at the base of the pillar an eight-petaled lotus endowed with four enclosures.
It should be provided with a pericarp (karṇikā), just as a pillar shines when situated upon a pericarp;
these [petals] should have a width of four finger-breadths and be raised to that same measurement. || 458 ||
O best of the twice-born, all the girdles should be made square;
except for the pillar-measure, the lotus should be provided with six finger-breadths.
One should place [the vessel] upon the girdle-band with its full width;
then, above the pedestal, one should construct a water-shed provided with four pillars.
Alternatively, it should be provided with eight pillars, joined by sixteen pillars, equipped with four archways, and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass. || 461 ||
Adorned with banners and the like, and provided with a curtain on the outside,
one should light lamps there that remain unextinguished on all sides.

Starting from that day, one should perform worship at the three junctions of the day— concluding with the recitation of mantras— with special care, including the offering of flowers and other rites until the end.
One should perform [the rites] for twenty-one days starting from the day the festival begins;
the worship must not be omitted, but rather performed with double diligence.
At the time of the ritual offering (bali), one should present an oblation to this Lord every day as well,
once the evening has arrived, until the cavity of the image is filled.
Having adorned him according to the rule, he should lead him to the assembly pavilion;
having seated him upon the auspicious throne, he should honor him with his full splendor as before.
Having completed the conclusion of the fire oblation (homa), one should perform the beating of the drum;
indeed, having placed the drum upon a seat of grain in front of the Lord.
To the east of that, a collection of conch shells; in the southeast, a multitude of kāhala trumpets;
in the south, a maddala drum; and in the southwest, a lute together with a flute.
In the western direction (Vāruṇī), one should place a mṛdaṅga drum together with a ḍuḍukka;
and in the northwestern direction (Vāyavyā), having set down a jhallarī cymbal accompanied by a bronze tāla.
In the northeast, one should place the drum (paṭaha), the small drum (hrasvapaṭaha), together with the ḍuḍḍuka;
and the ḍuḍḍuka and the cymbal (jhallī), provided with hand-staffs (hastadyaṇṭā). || 470 ||
Outside of them, O best of Brahmins,
one should place the courtesans on the south for the purpose of auspicious singing, and beside them, the chanters of mantras.
Having stationed the dancers in front, the groups of panegyrists to the north,
and having settled the others who are skilled in instrumental music in their respective places.
Having thus established it in due order according to his capacity, O twice-born one, he should wrap the drum with cloth, or even cover it with a cloth according to his wealth. (473)
Having recollected the ether, which is the structural basis of sound, one should worship it;
having placed the mallet to its south, one should worship the wind there with great devotion. || 474 ||

Then, having placed before him one of mixed caste (pāraśava) who has bathed, whose hands hold darbha grass, who is adorned, and who is equipped with the sacred thread and other ornaments, he should have him look [at the image]. || 475 ||
Thereafter, one should sprinkle [the enemy] with water from the *arghya* vessel using the Astra-mantra;
then, preceded by song and dance, one should strike that enemy with that very [water]. (476)
Accompanied by the sounding of conch shells and other instruments, or else the preceptor himself, having struck the *berikā* when an auspicious moment has arrived, [he should proceed]. (477)
First, meditating on Hayagrīva Janārdana from the corner, one should strike the deities in the three locations and so forth in three ways. || 478 ||
Then, one should strike it as desired with an axe made of iron,
reciting either a consecrated verse for invoking the deity in Sanskrit or in Prakrit.
At that time, he should cause the Lord to hear either a Drāmiḍī song according to his desire, accompanied by the dancing of the deities and various songs and other performances. (480)
One should show [the deity] to the God of gods for the complete satisfaction of the deities;
thereafter, one should cause the Lord of the God of gods to enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). || 481 ||
Then, having taken a vessel of milk-rice measuring one droṇa, as well as water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, garlands, and so forth, incense, and betel-leaf. || 482 ||
Starting from the door of the palace and ending at the outer gate,
[this applies] to all the enclosures as well, up to the western path-enclosure.
Having offered the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by song, dance, and other performances, he then enters the village and stands facing the eastern direction. || 484 ||
The preceptor himself, facing eastward, should perform the invocation of the deities;
or his son, or his disciple, with a loud voice. (485)
O hosts of immortals who dwell in the eastern quarter, both those who are deformed and those who are beautiful, come to this prepared worship! 486.
Having taken [this offering], may you, being satisfied, protect us; may you, the followers of Kumuda, approach this assembly with joy. Homage be to you! 487.
Having invoked Kumuda along with his retinue by means of this mantra,
one should then offer the guest-water (arghya), unguents, garlands, and so forth, as well as incense and water, in their proper order.
Furthermore, one should cause milk-rice, water, and betel-leaf to be offered;
thereafter, one should gratify [the recipient] with beautiful and great sounds produced by conch shells.
Furthermore, through his rhythmic music and dance,
the hosts of gods who dwell in the southern quarter (the direction of Agni) arrived thereafter.
May these fierce ones, whose faces are both terrifying and not terrifying, having accepted this prepared worship and being fully satisfied, protect us as they follow Kumudākṣa.
"May they come to this great [assembly] with joy; salutations be to you!
Having thus invoked Kumudākṣa, the lord of the Gaṇas," || 492 ||
Having gratified them as before, he then proceeds toward the southern direction and says: "Come, O hosts of ancestors, you who dwell in the southern quarter! (493)
May those followers of Puṇḍarīka—whose conduct may be both fierce and gentle—accept this prepared worship and protect us with satisfaction. (494)
"May they approach this great [assembly] with joy; salutations be to you!
By means of this [mantra], having invoked the Lord of the Gaṇas named Puṇḍarīka... (495)
Having worshipped them in due order, one should go toward the direction of the Yātudhānas;
"O hosts of Yātus, come hither! Come to that quarter where you lie in wait! (596).
May those flesh-eaters of cruel intellect, having accepted this offered worship, protect us—being satisfied, they shall follow after Vāmana. 497.
"May they come to this great [assembly] with joy; salutations be to you!
Having thus invoked Gaṇeśa, one should worship Vāmana in due order. || 498 ||
Then, having gone toward the quarter of Varuṇa, [he saw] Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas; those who lie toward the west were the foremost among the serpents as he approached.
May the great serpents, the biters, having accepted this offered worship, protect us—being satisfied and followed by Śaṅkukarṇa. || 500 ||
"May they come to this great [assembly] with joy; salutations be to you!
Having thus invoked them, one should worship as before, and afterwards, having reached the direction of Vāyu (the northwest).
May the hosts of Gandharvas, who dwell in the quarter of Vāyu, beautiful to behold and of terrible speed, come to this prepared worship. 502.
Having taken [these offerings], may you, being satisfied and following all our eyes, protect us;
may you approach this great sacrifice with pleasure—homage be to you! 503.
Having invoked him with this, one should satisfy Sarvanetra along with his retinue;
then, having gone toward the direction of Soma, [one should worship] Sumukha, the lord of the Gaṇas.
"Come, O hosts of Yakṣas who dwell in the northern quarter!
You who are deformed and carry staffs in your hands, [accept] this prepared worship. (505)
Having taken [these offerings], may you, being satisfied, protect us; may you, the followers of Sumukha, approach this great sacrifice with joy. Homage be to you! 506.
Having invoked [the deity] with this mantra, one should satisfy them according to the previous method.
Then, having gone toward the direction of Īśa (the northeast), one should approach Gaṇeśa, who is well-established there.
May the hosts of Piśācas who dwell in the northeastern quarter, holding tridents in their hands, come to this prepared worship. 508.
Having accepted [this], may you, being satisfied and following after a firm foundation, protect us;
may you approach this great sacrifice with pleasure—salutations be unto you! 509.
Having invoked with mantra and performed worship, one should go into the middle of the village and there invoke the Lord of the Gaṇas, Pṛśnigarbha, above [the fire].
Come, O hosts of Siddhas who dwell in the sky;
you who are pure in mind and pure, accept this prepared worship.
Having accepted [this offering], may you, being satisfied and followers of Pṛśnigarbha, protect us;
may you approach this great sacrifice with pleasure—salutations be to you! || 512 ||
Having invoked and gratified [the deities], one should then [invoke] the human [beings] below;
let those hosts of lower beings who dwell upon the earth come here.
May those of many forms and great knowledge, having accepted this prepared worship, protect us with satisfaction as followers of Manu. 514.
"May they come to this great [sacrifice] with joy; salutations be to you! Having thus invoked them, one should satisfy them as before, in due order, until the conclusion of the dance. || 515 ||
Then, for the satisfaction of all beings, one should cast the remainder of the bali offering;
in the rite of bali-offering, however, it begins from the east and ends in the direction of Vaivasvata (the south).
The preceptor, standing facing the east, should perform the invocation and other rites;
facing the north, he should perform the rites for the three directions beginning with the east as previously described.
In the two directions beginning with the northeast, or even in the middle of the village, one should face the east;
likewise, the *samatāla* and the *tālabaddha* are indeed the *bhṛṅgiṇī*.
The *mallatāla* is auspicious (*maṅgala*), while the *jayatāla* is *bhadraka*;
the *tāla* known as *ḍhakkarī*, and likewise the *brahmatāla*. (519)
Anantatāla— these ten tālas are proclaimed,
O twice-born one, for the ten lords of the Gaṇas, Kumuda and the others, in their respective order.
Ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, and likewise pañcama; dhaivata and niṣāda, as well as dhaivata and madhyama. || 521 ||
And the fifth [note]—thus, in due order, the ten notes (svaras) have been described.
[The rāgas are] Gāndhāra-rāga, that called Kaulaya, Kaiśika, and Naṭṭabhāṣika. || 522 ||
Śrīkāmada, Tatkeśī, and likewise Dakṣarāga;
the rāgas named Colāpaṇi and Medharāga as the last. || 523 ||
Thus, these ten *rāgas* of the *kumuda* and others have been proclaimed:
*vilāsa*, *sarvatobhadra*, *kheṭaka*, and *cakramaṇḍala*. (524)
