The *kāntārakuṭṭima*, the *pṛṣṭhakuṭṭima*, the *kaṭibandhana*, the *vāmajānūdhvanatta*, and again the first two. || 525 ||
These are remembered as the specific dances of the Kumudas in their proper order;
indeed, these—beginning with tāla—are recorded as the deities of the cycles in succession. || 526 ||
For all other gods, the Bhadra tāla is recommended;
however, for the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the Madhyama gārūḍa tāla should be used.
The melody should be Goḍa, the dance is indeed Viṣṇukrāntaka;
for the conqueror of obstacles (Gaṇeśa), the rhythm should be Jayatāla, and the dance is called Svastika. || 528 ||
The musical note (svara) is declared to be Ṛṣabha, and the rāga is Varāṭī;
one should perform the invocation of the deities preceded by the beating of a drum.
At that time, the preeminent teacher himself should cause the *Garuḍa-tāla* to be proclaimed in the intermediate directions with refined verses.
Others, headed by the four-faced Brahmā, are to be known as the qualities of the Maruts;
likewise, other hosts of the Blessed One exist for the purpose of serving the festival of the God.
Likewise, other devotees of the Blessed One who dwell at His feet,
or those approved by their guru and strengthened by devotion to the Blessed One— 532.
O twice-born one, those brahmins should then be summoned by means of that divine, firm verse;
having thus wandered through the village and entered the palace, they should proceed.
Having reached the station of Garuḍa and having gratified the one whose banner is the bird,
one should then gratify Viṣvaksena with the *tāla* and other measures.
Those who are here desirous of beholding the invocation of the deities with concentrated minds, as well as those people who hear the sound of the beating of the kettledrums; || 535 ||
They should not depart from that place until the end of the day of the holy site;
if they should depart out of delusion, they will become afflicted with disease.
They should not make one cross a river, nor should they provide a vehicle for a distance beyond a yojana;
if they have traveled such a distance, they must return after having duly worshipped Garuḍa.
"By undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), they shall indeed become free from disease.
Having thus raised the banner, the Guru, being composed, afterwards—
One should observe the vow for twelve days, beginning from the day of the expedition's commencement, using the twelve mantras of the gods Keśava and the others in their proper sequence.
Having performed his ablutions, worship, and other rites, and having drunk the water from His feet mixed with kuśa-water, he should indeed recite the twelve-syllable mantra.
O twice-born one, first one should partake of the food offering (naivedya), then observe the practice of eating only at night (naktāśana);
one should recite the twelve names in sequence while keeping the meaning of what is spoken in mind.
O best of Brahmins, from the day of planting the seedlings until the day of the flag-hoisting,
one should perform the vow every day for a period of six days.
On the day of the sprouting [of the seed], one should perform [the rite] with the twelve-syllable mantra;
on the second day, with the fourth mantra; and on the following day, with those mantras that denote deep sleep.
In the fourth [day], however, with the mantras of sleep; in the fifth, with the mantras of waking;
and with the supreme designators of the wombs or the forms beginning with Keśava. || 544 ||
From the day the festival begins until the final day of the pilgrimage,
the reciters should observe the vow of the nine forms for nine days.
Alternatively, one should observe the vow everywhere with the twelve-syllable mantra,
from the time of the flag, the ritual seed-syllables, and the constellations, until the final day of the pilgrimage.
Thus, the preceptor, endowed with the observances, should perform the ritual duties;
having first made a formal resolve for the festival, preceded by the resolve for the vow.

The best of preceptors who performs the ritual of sowing the sprouts for the sake of the banner shall indeed perform everything up to the lowering of the banner in accordance with the sacred tradition. || 548 ||
Even a wise man, and no other, should perform it; for if he does, the performer perishes.
Or, if that person has died or is afflicted by disease, one may act only after obtaining his permission. || 549 ||
And when [the practice] has been impaired by the neglect of daily observances and other such deficiencies,
one should obtain the permission of that guru according to the prescribed ritual.
His son, his disciple, or another person, such as a brother, being composed in mind, should perform the remainder of the rite after first undertaking the expiation.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure Ending with the Invocation of the Deity," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ.
Chapter Seventeen: Śāṇḍilya said: Now I shall describe the procedure for the festival; listen, O best of beings!
On the fifth day prior to the day of the festival's commencement. || 1 ||
Then, one should perform the sowing of the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having prepared the sacrificial hall as before, one should decorate it.
The preceptor, the lord of teachers, should choose four instructors, or eight, or twelve—those who are disciplined, self-controlled, and pure. (3)
Those skilled in the performance of various rites and learned in the scriptures, provided with turbans, upper garments, and fragrant substances; || 4 ||
All of them must be honored with great effort by the sacrificer;
some, appointed by the preceptor, shall perform the worship of the pitcher and the mandala.

Some should perform [the rites], others should offer the bali-oblation in the forest, and others should worship the Lord as present in the image; or one may perform it oneself according to the proper method. || 6 ||
Or he may choose practitioners adorned with turbans and other ornaments,
who are endowed with virtues such as discipline, skilled, and proficient in policy.
On the eve of the day the festival begins, at the onset of night,
the preeminent teacher, having performed his daily rites, enters the temple.
Having fully worshipped the deity residing in the primary image with arghya and other offerings, and placing his hands at the deity's feet, he should address the Lord as follows: || 9 ||
O Blessed One, O lotus-eyed one, Lord of Gods, I shall perform a festive rite for the sake of a great celebration; therefore, be gracious to me.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and having invoked him for the festival and the rite of wonder,
he worshipped him with offerings of water, fragrance, and the like, and with various auspicious garments.
Having especially adorned him with ornaments and divine fragrances, and having placed him upon a golden vehicle accompanied by conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments; || 12 ||
Adorned with the parasol and other regalia, he should be led in a clockwise direction to the pavilion of the assembly and seated upon an auspicious golden throne.
There, having placed [the image] according to the prescribed rite upon a pedestal adorned above with canopies of pearls and other ornaments, and provided with all necessary implements; || 14 ||
Having worshipped the Lord of the World and offered abundant food, and having performed the rites ending with the satiation (saṃtarpaṇa), one should cause him to enter the temple. || 15 ||
Then, O Brahmin, one should bring a vessel made of gold or silver, well-adorned, and filled with a full measure (bhāra) of Śāli rice grains. || 16 ||
Or else, with half of that, or a quarter, or a sixth, or an eighth part;
above that, the cord should be made of gold, or of linen, or even of cotton.
Having placed a silken cloth made from five, four, or seven threads,
he should then set down that vessel containing betel for the virtuous.
In the inner pavilion of the womb-chamber, upon a pedestal fashioned from rice—
measured by one *bhāra* or half of that— the [deity] is thus established.
One should place another vessel upon the pedestal together with the apūpika;
having worshipped it thoroughly with the arghya and other offerings, one should properly cover it with a cloth.

O twice-born one, having placed two vessels upon the heads of the two initiated disciples, or having established them in a vehicle or similar conveyance according to his means, the preceptor [should proceed]. (21)
Accompanied by those two vessels and joined with dance, song, and other arts,
he performed circumambulations around all the enclosures.
O Brahmin, having circumambulated [the deity] four times in one place, or having performed the circumambulation once around the village and so forth, he should then enter the root temple all at once.
Or else, O twice-born one, [one may worship] Viṣvaksena accompanied by Sudarśana,
or Khageśa accompanied by Hanumān and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle or similar conveyance, one should carry it according to one's preference;
then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into the presence of the God of Gods. || 25 ||
Having placed two vessels upon the support, one should worship them with the twelve-syllable mantra, as well as with the water for honor (arghya), perfumes, and other offerings. || 26 ||
Having made the proclamation of an auspicious day and having worshipped the deity with offerings such as the arghya,
first [one worships] the primary form of the God of gods who resides in the root-image.
One should bind the protective thread (kautuka) with threads made of gold or those made of silk;
having taken a golden thread and anointed it with perfume, one should bind it.

Then, with the mantra known as "Jitaṃte," accompanied by the sounding of conch shells and songs, [the deity] who has assumed the form for the procession is placed in the right hand of the Lord. || 29 ||
Having touched it with the right hand, one should recite the hundred-verse weapon-mantra (astraśata).
One should place the goddess Śrī upon the left hand and perform the protective knot (kautuka) on the silk thread.
Or, O best of the twice-born, while reciting the Śrīsūkta or its mantra,
one should bind it to the left hand with a linen thread for the sake of nourishment.
The preeminent teacher should perform the tying of the protective cord (kautuka) around the bathing image with a silk thread; he himself should tie the cord made of cotton on his own right [hand].
Then, one should perform the binding with the twelve-syllable mantra;
thereafter, having honored the deity with arghya and other offerings, one should present cakes (apūpa).
For the sake of pacifying all defects, one should show a mirror and other such objects;
whatever has not been mentioned here, all that should be performed as previously described.
Having thus performed the tying of the auspicious thread for the God of gods,
one should then bring the deity to the pavilion situated in front.
Then, having worshipped the deity with the offering of self-surrender according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should proceed to the bathing seat.
Having worshipped with all the enjoyments arising from the bath and the seat as before, one should lead [the deity] to the ornamented seat and worship according to the sequential method. || 37 ||
Then, having worshipped as before with various heart-pleasing offerings such as *naivedya* and *madhuparka*, one should praise Puruṣottama with hymns of praise.
Then, O twice-born one, with various golden ornaments ending in anklets, as well as those fashioned from excellent gems and pearls, [the earth was adorned].
Having adorned [the image] with a crown and other ornaments, and having performed prostrations along with circumambulations,
the preparation of the bed is to be carried out exactly as prescribed for the ritual of installation.
Having placed the image upon it, one should set it on an auspicious bed;
likewise, one should place lamps and oil-lamps with sprouts in the corners.
Having praised the Slayer of Madhu with the sounds of musical instruments, the Vedas, and hymns,
and having passed the night in vigil, they then experienced the joy of the festival.
Then, at the time of dawn,
the preceptor, having first performed his daily obligatory rites as before, should cause [the image] to enter the inner sanctum after bathing.
Having brought all the ritual materials into the sacrificial pavilion,
the preceptor himself, when only one watch of the day had passed during the forenoon, [should proceed].
Accompanied by the preceptors, the practitioners, and the patron, he entered the temple of the Blessed One when an auspicious moment had arrived. (45)
Standing before the God of gods, one should make this request:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the God of gods; a festival is being performed by me. (46)
O Lord of the World, whatever action I perform for Your pleasure, from this moment until the final day of the Puṣpa sacrifice; || 47 ||
"Having taken all of that unto myself, be gracious to me out of compassion, Om!"—
having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, the omnipresent one who resides in the primary form.

Having worshipped [the deity] with water for the guest, scents, and other offerings, and likewise having worshipped the Lord of the World as he resides within the portable image (yātrāmūrti), one should then offer the two sandals.
With the sounds of Vedic recitations, the proclamations of "Auspicious Day," and the resonance of auspicious hymns;
likewise with shouts of "Victory! Victory! and the blaring of conchs and trumpets.
Accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, and musical instruments, along with dancing and singing,
together with showers of parched grain mixed with heaps of flowers.
Therefore, having had the Lord of the gods brought out from there by the image-bearers,
and having turned the deity to face the east, they showed him to those who had assembled.
Men went to see the festival, bringing with them various processional requisites, especially umbrellas, chowries, and other such items. || 53 ||
Having placed the Lord of Gods upon the vehicle, which was endowed with a golden luster,
and having worshipped him with offerings such as the arghya, he presented him with flattened rice (pṛthuka).
The Brahmins, meditating upon the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), should carry the palanquin, starting from the first circuit up to the western end of the street enclosure. || 55 ||
One should perform the circumambulation precisely in a clockwise direction, accompanied by Brahmins wearing tunics and turbans. || 56 ||
With original parasols and beautiful peacock-feather fans,
as well as with palm-leaf fans provided with golden handles of that same kind.
With various silk fans and white and black chowries, and with diverse flagstaffs adorned with Vaijayantī banners; || 58 ||
With pure jeweled staffs and other auspicious objects,
as well as with various throngs of bards and the sounds of lutes and flutes.
With the sounds of golden horns and other auspicious noises, as well as with courtesans, temple-servants, and the people of the city; || 60 ||
[He was surrounded] by Brahmins holding cane-staves in their hands, adorned with tunics and turbans, and by other devotees of the Blessed One, including Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and others. || 61 ||
Accompanied by royal retinues and various other attendants,
having performed this, one should lead the Lord of Gods to the assembly pavilion.
And having seated the Lord of the worlds upon a golden seat,
he offered him water for the feet, water for the face, water for sipping, as well as perfumes, garlands, and incense.
Then [he offered] clear water for the guest-offering, as well as cakes and parched rice-flakes;
likewise, there was the water for satiation and the water for sipping made from coconut juice.
Having offered betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume in due order to the God of gods, one should then present the various offerings.
Then, one should bring [the deity] from that pavilion to the sacrificial pavilion;
having placed the Lord of Gods there upon a golden auspicious seat (bhadraviṣṭara).
At that time, one should remove all ornaments and such;
then, having placed the Lord upon the bathing throne covered with a new cloth.
Then, for the purpose of the consecration of the procession, one should begin the worship of the *mūla* [deity], having sat upon an auspicious seat near the location of the water-pot (*kumbha*). (68)
Having first performed everything according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi) and so forth,
one should worship the Lord together with the Weapon-mantra in the water-pot (kumbha) accompanied by the ritual vessel (karaka), as before.
One should perform the installation of the archways and so forth, and the worship as before;
with a concentrated mind, one should perform the worship of Kumuda and the other deities.
Then one should worship Garuḍa between the two [deities] beginning with Kumuda;
and having established the Discus (Cakra) between those beginning with Puṇḍarīka, one should worship it. || 71 ||
The conch, the discus, likewise Lakṣmī, the water-pot, the Śrīvatsa, the mirror, the svastika, and the pair of fish—these indeed constitute the eight auspicious symbols (maṅgalāṣṭaka). || 72 ||
One should place them in order near the white water-lilies and other flowers,
upon a seat made of cloth and grain, according to one's means.
Each [vessel] should be prepared with one or two loads of *śāli* rice,
filled with individual grains of rice and sesame seeds, and provided with a cloth.
One should likewise arrange this everywhere, even in the case of the eight auspicious items;
having invoked the Lord of Mantras upon the ground as before, one should then worship him.
O twice-born one, regarding the previously mentioned types of ablutions in the first group of nine,
one should determine the distinction between the inferior and the superior according to their respective names.
O twice-born one, having gone to the vicinity of the image in the eastern direction of the mandala and behind it,
one should commence the worship according to the prescribed rule.

Having performed everything in due order up to the self-surrender, and having made the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), he should perform the binding of the protective thread (kautuka). || 78 ||

Having worshipped the one of stainless luster with enjoyments such as baths and seats, and having performed the ritual bathing according to the rules, as well as the head-washing, the removal of wet cloth, and so forth; || 79 ||
Having offered [the oblation], one should bring the deity to the eastern part of the mandala;
there, upon a golden seat, one should worship the all-pervading Lord of All.
Having offered ornaments, seats, and other most purifying enjoyments, as well as abundant food offerings (naivedya) in due order; || 81 ||
Having performed everything up to the gift to the twice-born, he should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and,
having undergone the purificatory rites, perform everything there.
Having reached the vicinity of the image at the conclusion of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
and having completed the offering of the oblations, he should then worship [the deity] with clarified butter and other offerings.
Having performed the distribution among the ancestors and having offered the bali oblation in due order,
one should then lead Viṣvaksena, together with his retinue, from there to the Lord of the Universe.
O twice-born one, having led him to the assembly pavilion and seated him upon a cushion,
he performed the formal reception at the time of afternoon arrival.
Having performed the circumambulation of the village with clay and other materials as before,
one should carry out the sowing of sprouts according to the procedure previously described.
At that time, having performed the worship according to the rules in accordance with the majesty of the God of gods, one should offer abundant food.
If one worships on dry ground that resembles ashes in the east, it will be fruitless;
rather, having prepared [the site], one should draw the maṇḍala within a water-pot (kumbha). || 88 ||
Then one should offer [the substances] such as white [sandalwood paste] and purifying pigments into the pitcher;
thereafter, one should worship the Lord of the Gods and the mandala according to the prescribed rule.
Having gone into the presence of the image according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship the God there with great magnificence.
Then, one should perform a satiation offering in the fire according to the prescribed rite;
having gone near the sun, one should perform the offering and the formal announcement.
But having performed everything in due order, ending with the distribution [of food], one should thereafter,
if one possesses the means, perform once more the worship of the Lord.
Having performed everything up to the end of the fire sacrifice (homa),
one should then lead the Lord of the gods from the assembly pavilion to the front pavilion of the temple.
Having placed [the image] facing east upon a golden auspicious seat,
one should perform the binding of the protective thread for the sake of the god of gods' procession.
Having taken the sacrificial materials for the offerings, beginning with the *caru*,
one should perform the oblation (*homa*) twenty-two times for each, using the root mantra.
Having meditated again and again, one should offer oblations to each respective presiding deity of the night;
for the first night, Vāsudeva is the presiding deity.
Know that the second has Saṃkarṣaṇa as its deity, while the third has Pradyumna as its deity, and another has Aniruddha as its presiding deity. || 97 ||
That which occurs on the fifth night has Nārāyaṇa as its presiding deity;
the sixth night is declared to have Hayagrīva as its presiding deity. || 98 ||
The seventh is another Vaiṣṇava one, with Narasiṃha as its presiding deity;
the ninth, O best of the twice-born, has Varāha as its presiding deity.
Know that for one day the festival has Vāsudeva as its presiding deity;
but for three days, it has the deities beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Pradyumna.
For five days, he is the presiding deity of the five forms beginning with Vāsudeva;
for seven days, he is the presiding deity of the seven forms beginning with Vāsudeva. || 101 ||
O Brahmin, the twelve-day festival has Keśava and others as its presiding deities;
everything from the fifteenth day onwards has Vāsudeva as its presiding deity.
On the first night, however, one should offer the bali-oblation according to the rules for bali-offerings,
consisting of meat, powders of turmeric, parched grain, curd, and barley flour.
On all days as well, one should offer the bali-oblation with these materials;
or else, on the second night, one should offer it with sesame seeds and rice.
On the third night, however, one should offer parched grains with water and unhusked rice;
on the fourth night, the best of preceptors should present the bali offering.
On the fifth day, one should offer an oblation mixed with coconut milk, parched grain flour, and rice flour, along with lotus seeds and unbroken grains (akṣata).
On the sixth night, one should offer an oblation together with cakes and sacrificial porridge;
or alternatively, one may offer it on all nights together with the sacrificial porridge.
O best of the twice-born, one should offer the bali-oblation with substances produced on each respective day;
however, on the seventh day it is with rice mixed with molasses (gulānna), and on the eighth with milk-rice (pāyasa).
On the ninth day, the wise man should offer a bali-oblation with kṛsarā rice;
O Brahmin, on the twelfth day of the festival, he should offer masha-rice on the tenth day.
Or, O Brahmin, on the following day, pure food or mung-bean rice;
on the twelfth day, all the offerings consist of pure food or rice grown from paddy.
Milk mixed with curd and ghee, along with jaggery and sugar-candy;
hereafter, however, in all cases, pure food or milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered. || 111 ||
O best of the twice-born, for the four-day period beginning with Ekāha, the sacrificial materials for the offering should be one āḍhaka each, as prescribed for that specific day.
Or half of that, or even a quarter, according to the extent of one's wealth; having thus offered the materials and having especially adorned [the image], || 113 ||
The deity situated within the portable image (yātrābimba) [should be adorned] with various garments, as well as with diverse ornaments and many kinds of garlands. || 114 ||
When an auspicious moment arrived, endowed with every blessing,
he mounted either a chariot, or an elephant, or even a vehicle of Garuda.
Endowed with the golden luster of flowers, adorned with flowers and other ornaments,
he is joined by a golden celestial chariot or one made of peacock feathers.

Having brought [the vehicle] near, sprinkled it with water, and meditated upon it in the form of Garuḍa, one should then worship it with its own mantra, using the vehicle-offering (yāna-arghya) and other rites. || 117 ||
Having made a proclamation of an auspicious day accompanied by the sound of the Vedas,
and joined with conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, he should proceed in a clockwise direction.
Having placed the Lord there upon the vehicle in his processional form,
one should likewise offer arghya and pādya to the God for the sake of the procession.
Rice-water, perfumes, garlands, as well as lamps and incense;
likewise, the respectful offering, the honey-mixture, and various kinds of food offerings.

Having offered the pṛthukā mixture and other drinks, as well as the satiation and water for rinsing the mouth, and having presented betel-leaf, one should then perform the recitation (japa) according to the prescribed rule.
One should perform a satiation offering in the fire, or otherwise offer oblations at that very time;
all the materials for the bali-offering should be presented according to the appropriate season.
Now listen to the specific details regarding the chariot-vehicle, adorned with clusters of golden māñjarī flowers purified by pearls. (123)
With various flower garlands accompanied by strings of pearls, and with a golden canopy, it was distinguished especially by its radiance. || 124 ||
In the center, with a golden auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) likewise, and with various beautiful banners and flags on all sides. || 125 ||
One should indeed adorn the chariot with the emblem of Garuḍa;
having placed the Lord upon it, one should worship Him according to the previous procedure.
The preceptors and the practitioners should stand upon the upper surface of the chariot;
beneath that, on the ground, the umbrella-bearers should be stationed in the west.
There, two bearers of peacock-feather umbrellas should be stationed at his sides;
two bearers of chowries should stand at his right and left sides, and in front.
The charioteer should be stationed there in front, in the middle part;
then, by means of Garuḍa and others, or by the discus, or by Garuḍa himself.
And with eight auspicious items held by initiated Brahmins, together with offerings of water for honor, perfumes, and the like, as well as the sounding of bells. || 130 ||
With conch shells, kettledrums, and the like, as well as with an umbrella and those holding lamps,
the preceptor or the practitioner should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Starting from the gate of the palace and extending even to the center of the village, and starting from the first enclosure, throughout all the enclosures as well. || 132 ||
Having circumambulated the Devayāna path in a clockwise direction,
the twice-born should then cause it to revolve as far as the edge of the street enclosure.
Whether in a village, a city, or even a town, O Mahāmati, or in a large chariot, a vehicle, or by some other means of transport in between. (134)
Having caused it to be whirled, he should thereafter place the Lord of Gods upon a large chariot or similar vehicle and cause him to be paraded through the streets of the village.
The offerers of oblations should go from afar in front of the deity;
behind them should follow those carrying the flagstaffs and those holding conchs and kettledrums. || 136 ||
Intent on sounding the drums, kettledrums, and other musical instruments,
there were likewise singers and throngs of bards following behind them.
The devotees of the Lord were well-attired, as were the courtesans;
behind them followed groups of female servants and men carrying red staffs. || 138 ||
Likewise, bearing various playful ornaments and carrying sandals and other items, they [stood] by the side of the God. || 139 ||
In front and behind him were people holding chowries,
as well as various types of parasols and palm-leaf fans.
Then, while the twice-born and the horse hold [the vessel], one should place the Brahmins who recite the Ekāyana texts, beginning with the commencement of the ritual, on the right side of the deity.
One should have those who are foremost in the Rigveda and Samaveda follow either to the left or behind;
likewise, others should follow behind carrying well-polished incense burners.
Recalling the weapon-mantra, he should proceed in front himself, destroying the obstacles, [carrying] lamps numbering many hundreds that are exceedingly brilliant. || 143 ||
O inspired sage, as many as there are bearers of the sacrificial offerings, let them proceed in the form of a row on both sides of the god, supporting him.
Bearing all the royal insignia in the presence of the deity, other devotees—both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas—should likewise proceed. || 145 ||
The Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as well as those established in the four stages of life (āśramas), were all skilled in every scripture and devoted to the Blessed One. || 146 ||
Looking in every direction for the supreme Lord,
they searched throughout the villages and in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, according to the arrangement beginning with Indra.
And in the midst [of the mandala], one should offer oblations (bali) to Kumuda and the others, along with their retinues, in due order upon the pedestals that were previously constructed.
Now listen to the names of the groups beginning with *kumuda*, in their proper order:
Utkaṭa, Prakaṭa, Unmukha, and likewise Vimukha. (149)
Aśvagrīva, Aśvavaktra, and likewise Aśvajiha; Hastivaktra, Kumuda, Hastipāda, and Keśava. || 150 ||
Vāmana, Naraka, Nara, Mardana, Mandadṛṣṭi, Kantu, and likewise Kantukalocana; || 151 ||
Paṭahākṣa, Viśālākṣa, Kṣāmaka, Kṣamaka, Pāṇḍara, Pāṇḍupṛṣṭha, Durdina, and likewise Sudina. || 152 ||
Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Mahāgni, Madhusūdana, Kanaka, Kālaka, Bhāvana, and likewise Bhavana. || 153 ||
Bhānumān, Bānuvega, Bhāskara, and also Abhāskara; Viśvasena, Visena, Viṣvaksena, and Visāraṇa. || 154 ||
Vistāra, Nistara, Vidaṇḍin, Daṇḍa, Kāmada, Kāmuka, Kāmabhṛt, and Kāmanāśana. || 155 ||
Indeed, these fifty hosts have taken refuge in the eastern direction;
they are declared to be the attendants who follow the command of Kumuda.
Each one of these, beginning with Kumuda, has a hundred groups of houses as his followers; one should offer oblations to them in their respective order.
In this manner, one should offer the bali from the houses into the circles situated at the sides;
these deities and the houses themselves are the sharers of the bali in the eastern quarter.
Āgneya, Nidhana, Agnijihva, Hutāśana, Agnirūpa, Agnivarṇa, and also Agnivarṇa-hi. || 159 ||
Agnivaktra, Mahāvaktre, Mahāsena, Mahodara, Karāla, Kākajihva, Kākavaktra, and Agnivaktraka. || 160 ||
Maṇḍu, Maṇḍūkavaktra, Deva, Devalaka, Śarvaka, Śamaka, Śaṅku, and Śaṅkuśravas; || 161 ||
Mārīca, Droṇamārīca, Mahiṣa, and likewise Māhiṣa;
Kumbhanāsa, Vināsa, Kumbhakarṇa, and Vikarṇaka. || 162 ||
Vidārī and Vikrama, Maskarī and likewise Maskara;
Sūkara and Sūkarāsya, Śaśa and Śaśamukhasa. || 163 ||
Siṃha, Siṃhamukha, Narasiṃha, and likewise Nara; Kāladhṛk, Kālasūtra, Sūtraka, and Sūtra as well. (164)
Vinālī and Nālakaṇṭha, residing in the southeastern quarter,
are indeed these hosts of Kumudākṣa who are joined with the hosts of Asuras.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Kumudākṣa on the pedestal in the southeast;
he is Dharma, the upholder of Dharma, Dharma, Dharmarāja, and the wielder of the bow. || 166 ||
Vinaya, Praśraya, Niśreyas, Nirguṇa, as well as Alasa, Kuṇapa, Krūrabāhu, and Kuñjara. || 167 ||
Tall, self-controlled, free from anger, devoid of compassion, and without a sense of "mine";
possessing power and yet lacking power; the consumer of oblations, and indeed manifold. (168)
And Ūrdhvarakṣaṇasaṃjña, Ekala, Pākala, Kaṅkaṭa, Kaṭaka, Avaṭa, Śaṅkhin, and Cakrin. || 169 ||
O Sage, Gadī, Khaḍgī, Śārṅgī, and likewise Śārṅgadharo;
Vāsudeva, Bhadra, Ketumān, and Ketuka as well. || 170 ||
Kṣamī, Jvalana, Kinnara, Aśvattha, Supta, Sujapana, Japa, and Paścima. || 171 ||
Kaikṣika, as well as Svaja, Bāḍava, and Akṣamī—these fifty groups have taken refuge in the southern direction. || 172 ||
O Puṇḍarīka, these are indeed the Vaśā houses, provided with the Pitṛ houses;
thus, fifty Śaktika houses are ordained everywhere in this manner. || 173 ||
One should indeed offer an oblation to Puṇḍarīka, who is joined with these:
Niṣkṛti, Prakṛti, Sukṛti, and likewise Vikṛti. || 174 ||
Dāruṇa, Damaka, Rakṣaka, and likewise Lakṣaka; Mādhava, Māṃsaka, Niṣṭhura, and Kharabhāṣaṇa. || 175 ||
Pralamba and Lambaka, Prāṇana and Praṇaya, Vīrasena and Aṅgada, Vibhāṣa and Vibhīṣaṇa. || 176 ||
Raktākṣa, Lohitākṣa, Raktajihva, Vijihvaka, Vidyutkeśa, Viśālākṣa, Vikṣara, and likewise Vīrahā. || 177 ||
He is the Imperishable and the Primordial Imperishable, the one who assumes forms at will and the one of diverse forms;
he is all-pervading, all-knowing, the radiant white one, the source of being, and likewise the origin.
Vāruṇa, Vasu, Vimarda, Damana, Vaikartana, Vikartā, Kapardin, and Prabhu. || 179 ||
Kandakī, Kandaka, Nākī, Varuṇa, and Aruṇa—these fifty groups have taken refuge in the direction of Nirṛti. || 180 ||
These followers of Vāmana are associated with the Yātu-dwellings;
one should offer an oblation to Vāmana according to the prescribed rite when he is joined with these.
Varuṇa, Vāruṇa, Pāśī, Pāśadhara, Guru, Kṣepaṇa, Kṣobhaṇa, Nārada, Sarvada, and Ravi. || 182 ||
The swan named Sumanas, Vaikuṇṭha, Parama, Para, Hanumān, Vasumān, Bhadra, Bhadrava, and likewise Prabhava. || 183 ||
Mahākarṇa, Vikarṇa, Śaśaka, Śalaka, Pika, Vānara, Naraka, Kārṣṇi, Karṇadhara, and Aṃśumān. || 184 ||
Cakra, Agra, Vajrin, Vajranābha, Vinābhaka, Karabha, Kurabha, Dākṣiṇa, Dakṣiṇa, and Suhṛt. || 185 ||
Durgandha, Pūtigandha, Tārkṣya, Garuḍa, Virodha, Rodhaka, Rodha, Kaṅkaṇa, and Vṛkodara. || 186 ||
These fifty hosts, belonging to the lineage of Śaṅkukarṇa, have taken refuge in the western direction, accompanied by groups of those who hold nooses.
Together with these, one should offer an oblation (bali) upon the pedestal to Śaṅkukarṇa.
Maru, Mārutaga, Rurū, Ākhu, Vāyusuta, and Anila [are the attendants]. || 188 ||
Galarta, Vartaka, Kaṅka, Mārgaṇa, Prāṅkaṇa, Acala, Bala, Balanidhi, Vīra, Virodha, Rodhaka, and Vidhi. || 189 ||
Siddhava, Suyava, Śaṅkara, Dhīraka, Mālī, Mālāvidhi, Vastu, Samartha, and Sumahotsava. || 190 ||
Karkaṭa, Kaṭaka, Gandha, Gandhavaha, Para, Siktaka, Siktarogin, Sevaka, Sevana, and Sava. || 191 ||
He is the medicine, the healer, as well as the sick man and the origin of disease;
he is the cause, the instrument, the agent, the hero among heroes, and likewise the one who is free from evil.
Vala, Vākuvāha, and Sucāra—these fifty groups likewise take refuge in the northwestern direction. || 193 ||
One should always offer an oblation to Sarvanetra, who is accompanied by his followers and joined with the Gandharvas' abode, together with these [mantras].
Soma, Somakala, Somya, Sāmavit, Sāmanāyaka, Sudhā, Sudhātā, Dhātā, Surāṣṭra, Kāṣṭhaka, and Kali. || 195 ||
Kāladhṛk, Kālacakra, Kālakūṭaviṣa, Bala, Amṛta, Amṛtanātha, Keyūrī, Kevalī, and Balī. || 196 ||
Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇapiśaṅgāṅga, Rekhālekha, Pika, Śuka, Lūbaka, Śuka, Śyena, and likewise Śyenamukha. (197)
Mārjāra, marubhṛdvāla, gulma, kaṇavaka, and kaṇa; śeṣa, viśeṣa, uccheṣa, kardama, and pūtivigraha. || 198 ||
Sāmba, Saṃvatsara, Vegī, and Vegadhara Marut—these fifty hosts have taken refuge in the direction of Soma. || 199 ||
For these, accompanied by Yakṣa-grahas, are indeed under the control of Sumukha;
one should offer an oblation to Sumukha along with them according to the prescribed rite.
Īśāna, Īśvara, Vyāpin, Vyasana, Vinaśa, Budha, Dhara, Baka, Viśa, Vāda, Śakuni, Śakaṭa, and Ghaṭa. || 201 ||

He is the tree, the thicket, the patient one, forbearance, he whose hair is his mother, the kapiñjala bird, the one devoted to Brahman, the knower of Brahman, the female Brahman, the self that is Brahman, and the means to attain Brahman. || 202 ||
Vedī, Vedavidudvanda, Śaṅkara, and likewise Śāṅkara;
Dhīmān, Visṛṣṭi, iṣṭātmā, Duṣṭātmā, and Duṣṭakarmakṛt. || 203 ||
The conqueror, the one with disheveled hair, the disputant, the non-disputant, the one who has passed beyond the three poisons, the eater of but one meal;
the eater of all, the all-pervading, the all, the destroyer of all, the eternal. || 204 ||
Govinda, Gopati, Goptṛ, and Maheśvara—
these fifty hosts indeed take refuge in the northeastern quarter.
For these, joined with the Piśācas and the Gṛhas, are indeed under the control of Supratiṣṭha;
one should offer an oblation together with them, addressing them by the name Supratiṣṭhita.
He is the perfected one, the sustainer, and the ordainer; he is indeed the creator and the lord of creatures.
He is the ruler of the world, the maker of the world, the agent, the progenitor, Brahmā, and likewise the self-born.
Sutāpa, Tula, and likewise Rītivardhana;
Avyakta, Guṇavān, Gauṇa, and indeed Guṇabhuk as well. || 208 ||
Udgīta, Praṇava, and also he who is named Hiraṇyagarbha; Viriñca, Puṣkara, Bhāsana, and Bhāsa as well. || 209 ||
Vikarṇa, Vijaya, and likewise Rathantara;
Chandas, Yajus, and likewise Ṛk, and after that Atharvan. || 210 ||
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pracetas, Śalabha, and Bhīṣma. || 211 ||
Hemanta, Śiśira, and the one known as Kusumā kara;
Kalaha, Virāgin, Amarṣa, and likewise Roṣaṇa. || 212 ||
Śoṣaṇa, Gati, Harṣaṇa, and likewise Vardhana—these fifty groups are accompanied by the dwellings of the Vyoma-siddhas. || 213 ||
O twice-born one, one should offer a bali-oblation together with these to Pṛśnigarbha:
Manuṣya, Mānava, Maṇḍaka, and likewise Mānava. || 214 ||
Makara, Cora, Kampa, Prakaṃpana, Alaṃpaṭa, Paṭadyojaka, Bhajaka, and Grahi. || 215 ||
Recaka, Rocaka, Māya, Dhāra, Vāra, Rasa, Cala;
Cāpālika, Kapi, Bāṇa, Grajana, Garjana, and Guḍa. || 216 ||
Tittira, Caṭaka, Dhvāṅkṣa, Balīvarda, Mahānaṭa, Harṣa, Dharmapraśāstṛ, Śamaka, Dundubhi, and Śaṭha. || 217 ||
Kukṣi, Kumāra, Kāyastha, Lāvaka, Apraśuna, Śuna, Lavaṇa, Ravaṇa, Ṛddha, Rājasas, Tāmasa, and Acala. || 218 ||
Kalyāṇa and Bhagadatta, stationed upon the surface of the earth—these fifty groups are indeed accompanied by the planets of the earth. || 219 ||
Possessing great strength and invincible, they are obedient to the will of Manava;
the practitioner should offer oblations to Manava when he is joined with these [mantras]. || 220 ||
O twice-born one, these fifty lords of the hosts have been declared;
for each one of them, there shall be another hundred hosts.
In this way, there were fifty thousand attendants for them,
at the crossroads, at the junctions, in the assembly hall, and in the center of the village.
At all the village gates, men bearing various weapons stand;
they harass those who are unfit for [their] company, as well as the heretics.
O best of the twice-born, they wander at their pleasure through regions such as rivers and other places; these are the lords of the ten groups beginning with Kumuda. (224)
Then, for the groups beginning with Utkaṭa who have arisen,
[the offerings] should be made in sequence with their respective names, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
One should offer the water for honor (arghya), scents, as well as garlands, incense, and fragrant water; then again, the sacrificial offering (bali), water, and betel leaf, in due order.
O twice-born one, one should arrange all the singing, dancing, and so forth as before,
in groups of fifty thousand each.
Having said, "Homage to the attendants," one should offer an extensive circle of oblations (vali) upon the ground in every direction; this is auspicious and brings about all peace.
For each of the fifty thousand [deities], there is a retinue of one hundred each; these are remembered as the hosts of planets. || 229 ||
The retinues of these hosts of planets, however, are thousands in number; moving about in countless ways, they traverse this entire earth in every direction.
The hosts of planets, as well as gods, daityas, ancestors, rākṣasas, and the leaders of the nāgas, are said to traverse the earth in ten ways. || 231 ||
Gandharvas, yakṣas, piśācas, and siddhas, as well as the hosts of the earth—
these ten classes, O Brahman, are always stationed in the ten directions.
Thus have been described the leaders and the hosts of these fifteen;
by worshipping them, all undoubtedly attain happiness. || 233 ||
The wise practitioner should offer the bali-oblation to Kumuda and the others above the pedestal,
either on the ground smeared with cow dung and such, or wherever he pleases.
One should offer an oblation to the Gaṇas, such as Utkaṭa and others, all around that; one should also scatter oblations for all other [deities] outside of that.

And for all those who have not been released, one should offer an oblation (bali) in the village today, according to the rule for the secondary ritual (anukalpa), for the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśas) beginning with Kumuda. || 236 ||

O twice-born one, having offered the bali-oblation, one should separately offer it to all those who remain, saying: "Salutation to the attendants (pāriṣada). Thus, O brahmin, the bali should be given from that [remainder]. || 237 ||
One should cast the remaining sacrificial materials into the middle of the village for the purpose of satisfying the spirits (bhūtas) dwelling in all lands. || 238 ||
O Brahman, on the day of raising the banner, the invocation of Kumuda and the others, along with their hosts, was not performed during the night; therefore, it shall be done today.
One should perform their invocation and offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) according to the prescribed rules;
this is done on the day prior to the hoisting of the flag, once their invocation has been performed.
O twice-born one, beginning from that day until the day of the festival,
one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) or pure food.
Whether by day or by night, at either of these two times, a great fault accrues to the performer for failing to honor those who have been invited. (242)
If, for any reason, it is not possible to offer the bali-oblation on the day the journey begins, one should perform their invocation (āvāhana) at that time.
O twice-born one, one should thus cause the Lord of Gods, joined with the *balisa*, to be carried around by the right-hand path, whether in a village, a city, or even a town. (244)
While the pilgrimage is underway, one should repeatedly offer mouth-fresheners along with betel-leaf with devotion to the God of gods. || 245 ||
One should offer sandalwood, well-perfumed with camphor and other substances for the sake of pacifying fatigue, as well as various kinds of garlands to the God of gods. (246)
One should offer cool, refreshing water mixed with coconut water, as well as other items intended for the alleviation of fatigue. || 247 ||
In the eight directions of the village and especially in its center, [one should worship] with various songs and dances accompanied by stringed instruments. || 248 ||

One should gratify the Lord of Gods with conch shells, kettledrums, clay drums, and other instruments; having thus circumambulated the God, one should proceed to the village or other locations accompanied by the sacrificial offering (bali). || 249 ||
Having again performed circumambulation around the enclosures of the temple,
he did so with devotion at the gateway of the temple of the God of gods.

Having offered the water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), fragrance, garlands, and incense to the Lord of the gods, one should establish him in his own place. || 251 ||
Then, having gone to the sacrificial hall, the preceptor, being well-composed, should complete the journey-offering (yātrā-homa) with sesame seeds and clarified butter until its conclusion. || 252 ||
In this manner, accompanied by offerings, one should begin the circumambulation of the deity on other days as well, both by day and by night. || 253 ||
On the day of a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā), one should indeed perform circumambulation during the day;
one should perform the bathing of the image, however, both by day and by night.
From the day of commencement until the final day,
one should perform the planting of the sprouts on either the fifth or the seventh day.
On that day, one should perform the binding of the auspicious thread (kautuka) as before;
when the second day has arrived, [one should place] the deity in the assembly pavilion.
Having brought [the fire] either to the sacrificial hall or onto a seat and having enkindled it,
the preceptor should then go to the sacrificial chamber and perform the sacrifice according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having gone to the pavilion after [worshipping] both the water-pot and the mandala,
one should worship the Lord of the Gods with great magnificence.
Then, having properly gratified the fire in the sacrificial hall as before,
he should bring [the deity] from there to the great assembly pavilion.

There, having duly and equitably worshipped the deity, ending with the rite of lustration (nīrājanā), one should then present the great sacrificial offering (mahāhavis) accompanied by cakes and other such items. || 260 ||
Therefore, having invited the deity to the pavilion constructed for the sacrifice,
one should then worship the deity there with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya).

Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rules, concluding with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then adorn the Lord of Gods as before with garments and other offerings. || 262 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon a vehicle and so forth according to the sequence of application previously described,
and having caused [the image] to be circumambulated, one should cause the Lord to enter within the village.
Having brought the Lord of the gods into the pavilion and placed him upon the bathing seat,
one should offer the Arghya, Pādya, and Ācamana to the All-pervading Lord.
With perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and finally the waving of lights (nīrājana), preceded by the chanting of the Vedas, songs, and other offerings of worship. || 265 ||
Cakes combined with plantain fruit and mixed with jaggery, refreshing drinks, thirst-quenching water, and coconut juice. || 266 ||
Then, having discarded his garments and other items intended for the journey, and having offered the bathing cloth along with betel-leaf mixed with camphor, [he should proceed].
Having performed an oil massage and a ritual scrubbing according to the rules, having applied āmalaka fruit to the head, and having bathed him with abundant water; || 268 ||
Having first smeared it with color and then washed it with water,
one should again smear it with devotion using fragrant substances such as sandalwood paste.
O sage, having performed the bath with the thousand-streamed [mantra],
and thereafter having offered salutations, one should then place the head-cloth, the bathing-garment, and other cloths [upon oneself].

Having offered [the oblation] and placed the deity upon another seat, one should perform everything beginning with the purification of the hands (kara-śuddhi) up to the final internal sacrifice (antaryāga). || 271 ||
Then, O twice-born one, one should worship the deity in due order;
or else, when the festival day has concluded, having brought the deity to the pavilion.
Then, having placed [the image] upon a broad auspicious seat as before,
O Brahmin, one should present all the offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the *tāmbūla*.
Having gradually relinquished everything previously prepared, such as clothing and so forth, one should offer a garment for the purpose of removing fatigue. || 274 ||
Having first anointed the Lord of Gods with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like,
one should then worship him according to the prescribed rite until the offering of self-surrender.

Having requested permission for the bathing of the God of gods and having offered [the materials], [he placed] the two sandals before the Lord of the God of gods, accompanied by the umbrella and other [regalia]. || 276 ||
Therefore, having brought [the deity] to the seat prepared for bathing,
one should place [him] there and worship him with all the primary enjoyments as before.
Having performed the sacrifice ending with the offering of betel leaves, one should present a shoulder-cloth (skandhaśāṭī).
Then, taking oil that has been well-consecrated with camphor and other substances, || 278 ||
Having loosened the hair of the deity with both hands and a comb,
and having perfumed it with fragrant substances, one should then anoint it with incense.
Then, having pressed the head of the deity in many ways,
he bound the hair with garlands and a fine cloth.
O twice-born one, by binding [the seal] upon the forehead and likewise upon the lotus-face of the deity, the streams of oil do not flow down.
Then, from the region of the shoulders down to the ends of the feet, he should anoint him with oil and massage all his limbs. || 282 ||
At that time, for the purpose of alleviating his heat, they should fan him from all sides with various kinds of palm-leaf fans and yak-tail whisks. || 283 ||
Then, having rubbed [the body] with cloth and with the powders previously mentioned,
and having applied a paste and a medicinal bolus (khali), one should thereafter give warm water.
Sandalwood ground for the purpose of anointing the face and infused with camphor;
then, a paste of *āmalaka* well-prepared with fragrant substances. || 285 ||
Having placed [the vessel] upon the head of the deity and washed it with abundant water,
one should stir it gently and then offer the *arghya*.
Having offered lodhra and kāleyaka along with water for washing and the arghya offering,
he should bind the hair of the deity with a cloth for wiping.
Then, having offered the fragrant grass (śaṭī) below, one should place the cosmetic paste (varṇaka) in a vessel,
mixed with camphor powder and properly perfumed with incense.
With that [ointment], one should slowly and gradually anoint the limbs of the deity from the neck down to the feet, and then wash them with water.
Then, having removed the head-wrap, one should offer the *arghya* upon the head,
beginning with water from a knotted leaf (*granthipallava*) and ending with water containing all kinds of gems.
Having bathed him with seven kinds of water, the twice-born should offer a head-cloth and a lower garment, and anoint him with fragrant sandalwood paste. || 291 ||
Having especially anointed [the image] with fragrant ice-cold water mixed with powdered moon-plant (śaśicūrṇa) and perfumed with incense; || 292 ||
Likewise, having smeared the limbs of the God of gods with saffron,
and having offered him a sacred thread along with an upper garment, one should remove his bathing cloth.
Then, having bound to his head hair that has been perfumed with fragrant incense, and having offered various garlands and strings of flowers; 294.
Then, O Lord, the officiating priest should perform the bathing of the All-pervading One with many waters consecrated with sandalwood and other substances, using a thousandfold stream.
With a one-pointed mind, he should recite the four all-pervading mantras;
at that time, the twice-born, such as those learned in the Rigveda, should stand in the directions starting from the east.
With concentrated minds, they should recite the *puruṣasūkta* and other hymns;
they should cause conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments to sound properly on all sides.
And let the singers then sing auspicious songs;
thus, after the bath has been performed, the preeminent teacher, composed in mind, [should proceed]. (298)
Taking a full water-pot, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the Lord while reciting the purifying mantra as well as its etymological explanation. || 299 ||
Having thus completed the ritual bath, one should offer the lustration (nīrājana) to the Lord;
thereafter, having presented that which is called the "salutation" (vandana), one should offer a garment.
Another [vessel] filled with water for the purpose of removing the sweat from the body,
and two garments— one lower and one upper— scented with perfumes and incense.
Then, having offered a braid of flowers for the [deity's] trunk, and having offered a bath for the head, and having presented fragrant substances such as sandalwood along with garlands. || 302 ||
Then, having offered the two sandals, one should bring them from that place;
and having offered a third seat inlaid with jewels, || 303 ||
There, one should worship the Lord of the gods of gods, who resides therein, with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings in due order;
and having completed everything up to the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should worship him once again.
Then, having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), one should perform everything as previously described;
thus, every day until the final day of the pilgrimage site.
One should perform the bathing and worship of the Lord without weariness;
indeed, one should carry out the bathing of the deity at the beginning of the daily festival and other such occasions. (306)
One should not perform the ceremonial bathing of the Lord at the commencement of a daily festival;
or, if both [the daily and the occasional festivals] are commenced, one may do so according to one's desire. || 307 ||
One should perform worship properly once every day, according to the prescribed rule, both at the water-pot and at the mandala, during the day and at night. || 308 ||
One should worship the Lord of the Gods, who resides within the image, once, twice, or thrice a day, whether by day or by night, according to one's inclination. || 309 ||
One should always perform the special worship of the principal image situated in the temple;
when the fifth day arrives, one should hold a festival for the day during the forenoon.
Then, having performed the great ablution for the Lord of Gods with great magnificence and accompanied by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi, [he worshipped him]. || 311 ||
When one has the means, one should perform worship according to the procedure for the Mahāhavis sacrifice;
and when the sixth day arrives, preceded by the worship of the water-pot (kumbha).
And having worshipped according to the prescribed rite up to the satiation of the fire,
[he should worship] the Lord of the gods as before, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.

Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle or similar conveyance, one should go somewhere outside the palace, to a very beautiful and delightful garden filled with *vakula* and other such trees. || 314 ||
It was adorned on all sides by various lofty trees and embellished everywhere with flowering creepers.
Having led the deity forward and seated him upon a suitable seat, one should worship him, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi, as before, up to the conclusion of the oblation (homa). || 316 ||
Fine garments of silk, as well as jeweled ornaments, together with lime, musk, camphor, and divine fragrances. || 317 ||
One should smear the Lord of the gods with all his limbs with deer-fat, especially those who are adorned with gathered flowers, garlands, and the like. (318)
Or [one may worship] her who is adorned for the sake of sport with the other Śaktis, while remembering the one who, mounted upon Garuḍa, carried away the Pārijāta tree. || 319 ||
The preceptor himself should present even the flowers used as offerings to the God of gods, saying,
"This has come from such-and-such a person."
Having performed this for the purpose of gathering flowers and having offered them, one may remain either there or in another place, according to the desire of the performer. || 321 ||
Then, one should cause the Lord of the Gods of gods, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi, to be paraded through the village as before; the remainder should be performed as previously described.
When the seventh day had arrived, the preceptor, having entered the palace together with the practitioners, prostrated before the Teacher of the World.
He should inform the Lord with words that are perfectly clear and loud:
"O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge! (324)
"O Lord, on this day you must engage in water-sports for the purification of all the worlds and also for the pleasure of the gods. (325)
"A journey should be undertaken for that purpose out of a desire for my favor";
having thus informed the God and bowing down again and again, || 326 ||
Having placed the deity, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi, upon a vehicle and led him to the bathing hall equipped with all the requisites for bathing; || 327 ||
Then, having displayed all the ritual requisites pertaining to that Lord, one should anoint the deity with sandalwood and other substances and adorn him with garlands.
And having offered betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume, he summoned the attendants present there and gave them his orders. || 329 ||
When the time of afternoon has arrived, there will be water-sports;
therefore, all the necessary materials for that purpose should be placed in the pavilion.
Having thus given the command, he then entered the granary and,
for the prosperity of those lords, displayed the grains to them.
Having brought [the deities] from the garden and other such places and having presented the offerings situated there according to the rules, [he should then proceed] to the assembly pavilion.
One should worship the Lord of the gods of gods together with Śrī and Puṣṭi;
thereafter, one should specially cause Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi to enter within.
Having properly performed, as before, the rites appropriate for the day, he should then bring the God of gods into the pavilion and place him upon the seat.
Having offered everything from the *arghya* up to the betel leaf as before, he should also offer a cloth for the bathing of the Lord of the World. (335)
In one part of the pavilion, upon a seat made of śāli rice grains,
[he should place] a water-vessel made of gold or silver.
Or made of copper, as available, measuring four, three, or two cubits in length; with a width at the top half of that, and at the base one-fourth of that.
O twice-born one, it should be round and elongated at its lower part, provided with a channel,
and resembling the shape of an unmatta flower.
Having installed that [image], which corresponds in size to the original model and is endowed with all the auspicious marks, and having filled it with filtered water; || 339 ||
With sandalwood paste mixed with saffron powder, combined with camphor powder, and scented with flowers. || 340 ||

Having brought the deity to its side and worshipped it with water for the hands (arghya) and other offerings, accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, and conchs; || 341 ||
Having performed the ritual immersion of the Lord with the Puruṣasūkta, accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas and the resonant chanting of hymns and auspicious songs; || 342 ||
Having placed the deity upon the vehicle, together with one whose garment is still damp from bathing, and having anointed [the deity] with saffron from the feet up to the head; 343.
One should sprinkle the courtyard and the street for the pleasure of Varuṇa and for the purification of all people. || 344 ||
Those people who at that time behold the Lord of the Gods with devotion, they all become cleansed of sin and free from affliction. || 345 ||
Then, having seated the deity upon a seat within the pavilion,
the preceptor himself shall personally bring all the requisites for the bath, such as the garments and other items.
Then, one should perform everything until the end of the night festival as previously described;
when the eighth day arrives, one should conduct the hunt for the Lord.
Having worshipped the deity as before in the forenoon, beginning from dawn,
he brought forth the jewel of a horse, adorned with every ornament.
Having mounted the Lord of the World upon such an elephant, or likewise upon a horse, together with many steeds—whether of natural or artificial breed—he [should proceed]. || 349 ||
Having placed both Śrī and Dharaṇī upon a golden vehicle, adorned with all ornaments and other items suitable for the hunt, [he set out]. (350)
Having wandered together with those two through villages and other places as before,
he [honored] the Lord with various armies and likewise with offerings of food and so forth.
Then, O twice-born one, at a distance of exactly one krośa outside the village, in a vast and delightful garden filled with various kinds of trees— 352.
Having brought the Lord and established him in the midst of that place adorned with various lotus ponds and clusters of flowering creepers, [he worshipped him]. || 353 ||
In the pavilion, which was adorned on all sides with canopies and other decorations,
he placed the Lord of the Universe upon a beautiful golden seat.
Thereafter, together with Śrībhūmi, he was fanned with cool breezes from fans,
and treated with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and other cooling waters.
Having brought about the cessation of the sweating, especially like a king of kings,
and having honored him with the arghya and other offerings, one should then present curd-rice.
Mixed with powdered marīca, combined with cumin and other spices, along with sugar balls and candied sugar, these pure preparations include many varieties of syrups (pānaka).
Having also offered sweet fruits beginning with the plantain fruit,
and having performed everything up to the offering of betel leaf in due order, thereafter—
Having first performed the ritual bath, one should worship the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi, with great magnificence according to the prescribed order.
Having offered abundant food and having especially adorned [the horse],
and having mounted it at the head of the procession when the sun had set, || 360 ||

Having led the deity around the village, which is provided with many hundreds of lamps, in a clockwise direction, and having then brought the deity back into the temple, one should perform the night festival as before.
On that night, the preceptor, accompanied by the patron and the practitioners, should perform the tying of the protective thread (kautuka) for the image at the sacred site.
Then, having entered the temple and bowed down again and again,
one should utter this mantra while prostrating like a staff.
"O God, O Lord of the Suras, you must undertake a pilgrimage tomorrow;
it behoves you to grant permission for the commencement of the *pratisarā* ceremony there. (364)
Having thus informed the Lord, one should bring the sacred image from the holy site;
O best of sages, in its absence, one should bring the image used for the daily bathing ceremony.
O twice-born one, if that image is unavailable,
however, one should place an image of Bali before an image of Mūli, invoke him, and worship him.
Within the interior of the palace, one should construct an auspicious altar (vedikā) made of rice grains,
one cubit in height and width, and shaped like a lotus.
Then, having wrapped that [altar] which is square and long with cloths,
one should place the *pālikās* containing sprouts on the eight directions on the outside.
Outside of that, one should likewise place water-clocks (ghaṭikās), and outside of those, water-jars (śarāvas);
then, having placed the deity upon that, one should perform the offering of clarified butter (ghṛtāropaṇa).
Having placed a vessel made of iron before the deity and having filled that vessel with ghee, the preceptor consecrates it as previously described.
Taking dūrvā grass by its roots with both hands,
one should dip the tips into ghee and sprinkle them at the feet of the deity.
Then, at the side of the neck and then upon the head of the deity,
one should perform the washing of the hands at intervals through the application of yoga.
Likewise, the "dūrvā-bheda" (separation of dūrvā grass) is prescribed for the rite of offering ghee;
one should perform the offering of ghee by means of crossing the hands. || 373 ||
"O twice-born one, the mantra is established in sequence: 'sumaṅgalam' at the feet, 'bhadram' on the neck, and 'suśobhanam' on the head. (374)
Alternatively, having performed the offering of the entire mantra known as the twelve-syllabled one while it remains unbroken, one should perform the binding of the protective amulet (kautuka).
With a thread made of wool and with that linen thread,
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should thereafter fan [the deity] with chowries and other such items.
One should show a mirror, an umbrella, and other auspicious objects;
thereafter, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) according to one's means.
Having laid the Lord of Gods upon the bed with his head [toward the north],
one should fumigate him on all sides with incense of guggulu and agaru.
One should complete the remainder of the night with lamps that do not go out;
then, having risen in the morning, the preceptor should perform his bath and other preliminary rites.
Having worshipped the deity residing in the festival image according to the prescribed rules as before,
one should first perform the chariot festival either in the forenoon or at midday.
One should perform the rites at the sacred ford in the forenoon, and then, as before, at midday;
having brought the deity into the house, one should install him in his own place. || 381 ||
O twice-born one, one should also offer to the supreme preceptor the garlands, sandalwood paste, and other items used by the deity; adorned with these, he [the preceptor] shall be honored. (382)

And one should cause a pilgrimage to sacred sites for the Lord of Gods to be performed according to the prescribed rites, having awakened the God residing in the sacred image from His sleep. || 383 ||
Having worshipped [the image] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, and other articles, and having brought it to the pavilion of the assembly hall,
one should worship it again with arghya, water for washing the feet (pādya), and so forth, while performing the imposition of the sacred thread as before.
Having performed the aforementioned ablutions, one should establish the ninth ablution as the fourth among them,
which is designated as "not intoxicating" (amadya).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front, one should place a mortar there;
and having placed mortars upon the mortar, one should arrange pestles in the four directions.
Having taken pieces of dūrvā grass in a mortar made of musāragalva, one should bind them;
having wrapped them with a new cloth, one should pour the powder into it. || 387 ||
O twice-born one, [the mixture] should be combined with gold and powdered turmeric, infused with fragrance,
by four Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas or indeed by Vaiṣṇava women.
One should have the threshing performed even while auspicious hymns are being sung;
O Brahmin, having prepared a pedestal with rice grains and placed the water-pot there—either to the east or to the north of the installed [deity] for the ritual bathing. || 389 ||
Having placed the powder there along with the sūtra, and having wrapped it in a cloth; || 390 ||
Alternatively, having worshipped five or nine jars filled with powder using the root mantra, one should then bathe the Lord.
Having anointed the Lord of Gods with oil and performed the preliminary rubbing as before,
he should then bathe Him according to the prescribed rite, beginning with ghee and ending with auspicious substances.
Having performed the ritual bath with a thousand streams of pure water, and having clothed him in two new garments, one upper and one lower; || 393 ||

Then, having worshipped the deity with fine incense and with offerings such as water for the feet (arghya), unguents, and garlands, [the vessel] filled with gold dust and other substances [is offered]. || 394 ||
Taking the water-pot, one should sprinkle [the image] with those very powders;
having worshipped it with the arghya and other offerings, one should then thoroughly wipe the image.
One should cause that powder remaining after consumption to be placed upon the heads of those who have eaten;
this powder grants the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā and destroys all sins. (396)
Or even if a man wears that powder on his head as a mere plaything,
the sin residing in his body perishes at that very moment.
Then, having worshipped the deity and offered supreme rice-pudding (paramānna), as well as mung-bean rice (mudgānna) and pure food (śuddhānna), according to the prescribed rule elsewhere. || 398 ||
Having completed everything up to the gift to the twice-born,
the best of preceptors should perform all that has been prescribed even before the conclusion of the pilgrimage.
Then, having offered a large ball of rice mixed with saffron to the God of gods, the best of preceptors should indeed present it. (400)
To the teachers, the practitioners, and likewise to others who are appointed to their respective duties, they [the deceased] are indeed offered that very funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Having touched all their limbs, with hearts thus filled with joy,
let them attend upon the Lord of Gods with prostrations and circumambulations.
Having brought a vehicle for the procession— any one such as a chariot or the like— one should place the deity therein, and [the attendants] in another vehicle.
Having mounted Cakra, Tārkṣya, Hanumān, or Vibhīṣaṇa,
he should be equipped with all the necessary implements, such as the parasol, chowries, conch, and so forth.
Having performed circumambulation even around all the enclosures, and having reached the side of the holy site (tīrtha), he should place the image upon its pedestal. || 405 ||

In that place adorned with canopies and the like, as well as with the *prabhā* and *puṣpa* [mantras], he performed a prostration like a staff, preceded by an offering of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). || 406 ||

Then, having established the Lord of Gods upon the head of the practitioner himself—who has been adorned with garments and other ornaments—and having reached a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) there, [he should proceed]. || 407 ||
Standing in water reaching up to his navel, the preeminent teacher, composed in mind,
O best of the twice-born, invoked all sacred fords into that particular holy site.
Having proclaimed the auspicious day and having worshipped [the deity] with offerings such as *arghya*,
when a favorable moment has arrived and the sun has reached midday.
Taking the deity accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
the preceptor should place him as if upon the palm of his left hand, situated within the circle of the earth.
Holding it at the middle portion with his right hand,
he should indeed immerse himself along with it while reciting the root mantra.
Together with the forms of Tārkṣya and others, the preceptor, along with the practitioners,
[should perform the rite] at midday or in the afternoon in a self-manifested or similar sacred site.
One should perform the avabhṛtha bath for the Lord either during the first part of the night;
in that case, no fault arises from the lapse of the auspicious moment (muhūrta).
In a vessel such as a wooden tub or similar container, well-filled with fragrant water,
one should bathe the deity for a moment after having worshipped him thoroughly with arghya and other offerings.
Those men of pure intent who perform their ablutions at that time shall indeed be liberated from all taint and attain the supreme goal. || 415 ||
Then, having placed him upon a seat made of gold on the bank, and having offered two garments and discarded his bathing clothes, [he performed the rites]. || 416 ||
The preceptor himself should take those two garments and place them upon [the disciple's] head,
having honored him with the arghya and other offerings, and having especially adorned him.
Then, having placed the deity upon a vehicle, one should enter the palace;
at that time, the courtesans shall have bathed well and be dressed in clean garments.
O Brahmin, for the sake of auspiciousness, women should walk ahead carrying a vessel filled with water, a lamp-vessel, and a mirror.
Or else, O twice-born one, having reached the door of the second enclosure by following the sequence of circumambulation according to the very same path of the stream, || 420 ||
Having enclosed the first enclosure-gate within it, one should make the mandala perfectly circular,
adorned with cow dung and lime powder.
Having established lamps in the cardinal directions and oil-lamps in the intermediate directions,
[he should place] a jar completely filled with water and adorned with garlands and other ornaments.
Having placed it upon the support and worshipped it in the center with a flower,
one should then [sprinkle] that water over it, having recited the *praṇava* once.
One should worship the Lord of the gods of gods with a handful of flowers,
having first performed the full worship with water for the guest (arghya) and other offerings at the entrance of the temple.
Having established the deity in its own place, one should dismiss it from the primary image;
thereafter, the festival image should be treated according to the prescribed rites, beginning with the ritual bath.
O Brahmin, as before, one should perform the worship without circumambulation;
when the tenth day has arrived, the preeminent teacher, being composed in mind, [should proceed].
Having performed the morning bath and other rites, and being adorned with garments and ornaments, he [should proceed] together with the preceptors, the practitioners, and indeed the patron.
Then, having entered the palace and bowed down again and again, he stood before the Lord of Gods and made this petition: || 428 ||
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge,
[you have performed] this festival beginning from the sprout of the banner’s purpose and ending with the final purificatory bath.
O Lord, whatever action has been performed by me for your pleasure, as well as that which has been done by others and by preceptors authorized by me; || 430 ||
And by practitioners as well as various other attendants, for the sake of completing those respective parts and for the pacification of deficiencies or excesses. (431)
O Lord, grant permission to me today, on this day, to worship you as you abide in your fourfold stations,
out of a desire for my grace.
Having thus informed the Lord and obtained his permission there,
the preceptor placed the Lord, who was situated within the festival image, upon the vehicle.
Having led him to the assembly pavilion and placed the Lord there upon a seat of darbha grass, he then [brought] those devoted to the study of the Vedas.
He likewise appointed those learned in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
as well as auspicious singers and dancers, as appropriate for the amusement of the Lord of the World.
Having placed [the deities] in their respective positions, the most excellent of teachers should then install them within that pavilion (maṇṭapa), in accordance with its dimensions.
In a place adorned with all the canopy and other decorations prescribed for the sacrifice,
one should establish a maṇḍala of a lotus-wheel by occupying its central region.
It is adorned with twelve spokes shaped like mātuluṅga fruits,
provided with a pedestal, gates, and pathways, and surrounded by cities of five colors.
Alternatively, O Brahmin, it should be adorned with a pedestal together with a city, or indeed with a city alone, made radiant by five flowers. (439)

The detailed account of this was proclaimed by the Blessed One himself in the Pauṣkara [Purāṇa], consisting of beautiful [descriptions] arising in their proper seasons and endowed with their respective colors.
Having thus completed everything, including the circle of lotuses,
the preceptor, together with the practitioners, attains the presence of the deity.
Having informed [the king] and brought him there, he should seat him on a golden auspicious throne (bhadrāsana) provided with an excellent cushion in the western pavilion. || 442 ||
Having seated him facing east upon a seat provided with an auspicious covering,
one should [place him] in the lotus of the wheel within the pitcher according to the previously described procedure for the sacrifice.
The preceptor, being well-composed, should perform the worship of the image while song, dance, and instrumental music resound throughout the four quarters.
One should indeed perform the honoring of the preceptor with special distinction at that time, according to the rules, concluding with gifts to the twice-born. || 445 ||

And with garments such as fine silk (dukūla) and other cloths previously offered to the Lord, as well as with various excellent garlands and fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like. || 446 ||
The preceptor as well, O best of the twice-born, having taken an unsurpassed garment such as fine linen and having bound it like a turban upon his own head, [proceeds].
Wearing garlands and other ornaments as appropriate,
and having prostrated himself again and again before the God of gods, he then [proceeded] to the sacrificial hall.
Having arrived there in Vaikuṇṭha and performed the fire-oblation as before, he went into the presence of the God and offered the dedication of the oblation. || 449 ||
Having duly performed the distribution of shares for the ancestors,
he [appointed] Kumuda and the others, Cakra, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), and Gaṇanāyaka.
Having caused the offerings (bali) to be presented in due order to Indra and the other guardians of the world,
he then [studied] the Ekāyanī branch together with the Trayī and the Atharva Veda.
The Itihāsa and Purāṇa, the wonderful Vaiṣṇava hymn, as well as song, dance, instrumental music, and the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments; || 452 ||
Then, having caused the sounds of auspicious salutations as well as auspicious songs to be heard, and having appropriately presented [these] to the Lord, they then— || 453 ||
Having dismissed the deity residing in the pitcher and the one residing in the mandala into his own heart, and having worshipped Viṣvaksena as before from the center of the mandala; || 454 ||
Then, having placed the Lord upon a vehicle made of gold and adorned with every auspicious object, as well as all protective coverings; || 455 ||
Having circumambulated from the outermost [enclosure] inward until reaching the innermost enclosure, whether in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure; || 456 ||
One should seat the Lord of the God of Gods upon the pedestal within the pavilion;
