at that time, the patron, having adorned the preceptor, [should honor him]. (457)
Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle adorned with garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kāhala trumpets, cymbals, kettledrums, and drums.
Having honored the preceptor like a deity, accompanied by an umbrella and lamps, and attended by singers and others, one should cause him to enter one's own home. || 459 ||
Then, when the sun has set, the preceptor, accompanied by his kinsmen, should perform the concluding sacrifice (anuyāga) after duly worshipping the deity in the prescribed order.
One should offer green gram rice mixed with sugar-candy and other sweets;
thereafter, the devotees of the Lord residing in other lands [should be invited]. || 461 ||
For those men who had previously arrived for the purpose of attending the festival of the God,
[the king acted] with the permission of the God to enable them to return to their own country.
After performing the dismissal, one should lead the deity back to the sacrificial hall,
seat him there upon a throne with an auspicious covering, and cause him to enter into that place.
Having duly worshipped the omnipresent Lord, who is stationed in four places in sequence beginning with the pitcher (kumbha), and having provided him with abundant food, || 464 ||
O best of the twice-born, having performed the concluding rite of the festival, one should also arrange for the ceremonial bath (snapana),
whether it be for the processional image (yātrābimba) or for the [primary] image, for the purpose of bathing.
Having thus worshipped in due order and having offered the bali-oblation according to the rite,
the best of those who know mantras [should worship] the Lords of Mantras residing in the pitcher, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit.
Then, one should dismiss [the deity] according to the rule as prescribed;
thereafter, one should worship Viṣvaksena and cause the deity to enter within.

Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (arghya), scents, and other articles, O Brahmin, one should dismiss the deities from the primary image, as well as the groups beginning with Kumuda who were invoked in the village along with their attendants.
Having gratified [the deity] with the offering of oblations, one should dismiss [the deity] with special care;
then, having reached the location of the banner and established the water-pot as before, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped Patatriśa, and especially him who resides upon the banner,
one should then offer a great oblation to Vihageśvara, who is stationed on the banner.
Having dismissed [the deity] into one's own heart or into the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) residing within the water-pot,
O Brahmin, one should then lower the banner according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should dismiss the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), who resides in the water-pot, into one's own heart;
or else, having gone to the abode of Garuḍa, [one should do so] with the water contained in the pot.
Having sprinkled Garuḍa there, one should dismiss him who resides in the pitcher,
as well as the flagstaff, the cloth of the banner, its pole, and the water-shed.
The preceptor himself should take up even the ritual implements;
otherwise, there will be great fault for both the performer and the ruler of the land. (474)
The performed rite would be fruitless, and even the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) becomes angry,
whether on the night when the sacrificial rite was completed or on the following day.

The patron, having adorned and worshipped the preceptor with golden ornaments such as bracelets and the like, as well as with garments, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, [should proceed]. || 476 ||
One should give the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), consisting of a hundred gold niṣkas, or even more than that, according to one's means. || 477 ||
Know that half of that is middling, and a quarter of that would indeed be inferior;
one should give according to the extent of one's wealth or according to one's faith. || 478 ||

One should give half of that to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and half of that to the attendants; to others, beginning with the singers, one should give according to the extent of one's wealth. || 479 ||
A sacrifice devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a fee, however small, should be given in accordance with one's wealth. (480)
Thus has the detailed account of the festival known as Yātrā been correctly related;
now listen to whatever particulars there may be therein. 481.
Whether it be the teacher or the practitioner who is alone appointed [for the task], he alone shall perform the entire ritual action in the sequence previously described. || 482 ||
When many of these have been prepared, one person should perform them in due order:
the planting of the flag-sprout, the hoisting of the flag, and the offering of the sprout for the sake of the festival. || 483 ||
On the day preceding the commencement of the festival, the rite of tying the auspicious thread (kautuka) is performed;
on the day of the festival's commencement, it is prescribed for the purpose of consecration (adhivāsa).
O Brahmin, there is the worship of the four sites as well as the offering of the sacred water-sprouts;
even during that night, one should perform the rite of worshipping the four sites for the sake of the procession.
One should perform the binding of the *pratisarā* for the journey, as well as the *avabhṛtha* rite,
or likewise the worship of the four locations on the day of the flower-sacrifice (*puṣpayāga*).
One who is firm in their vows should, with great effort, perform the dismissal of the mantras residing in the pitcher, the mandala, and the fire-pit, as well as the lowering of the banner.
Other instructors or practitioners should perform those [other rites] in due order;
one should carry out all other activities as appropriate. || 488 ||
Some [advocate] the worship of the pitcher, some the adoration of the image, some the satiation in the fire, and some the ritual of bathing. (489)

O twice-born one, some perform the worship beginning with the ritual bathing at the appropriate times and according to the rules; however, if it is possible for a single person to perform the worship of all four locations, [that is preferred]. (490)
O Brahmin, there should be no distinction between the performers when performing the rite of worship at the four locations,
even if one worship is occurring in the midst of another.
If, due to some disease, the agent's incapacity should arise regarding the undertaking of one part after another part, or indeed from one posture to another posture; || 492 ||
The remainder should be performed by another after reciting the root mantra one hundred times,
provided that it is otherwise impossible for her [the patroness] to do so and there is another person to perform the worship.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, one should perform the worship again starting from the beginning; if one acts otherwise, one should do so according to the path prescribed for each day.
The performer would suffer mental distress, and even the worship would be fruitless;
for when the permanent bathing and the festive rite are assigned to a festival, [the daily rites are neglected]. (495)
One should perform that festival at one and the same time, whether by night or by day, whenever the image of the deity is employed in the ritual of a great festival. (496)
One should perform [the rites] at both times according to the desire of the performer;
however, when the image for the journey has been consecrated, one should always perform them at both times.

O high-minded one, in the primary ritual procedure (mukhyakalpa) or the secondary procedure (anukalpa), a twice-born man should perform the festival procession (yātrotsava) either by day or at night. 498.
When one performs a great festival for the jar, the pedestal, or the wheel, then the procession for the root image and the rites prescribed for the [processional] image should be performed. || 499 ||
Having performed everything in due order, excluding the circumambulation,
[one should place it] either in the water-pot (kumbha) or upon an auspicious seat made of a cluster of darbha grass.
Or, having invoked the deity into the discus and worshipped him with offerings such as the *arghya*,
he placed him upon a vehicle or similar conveyance, equipped with all the necessary implements.
One should cause [the deity] to wander through the village and other places as before, accompanied by the offering of the *bali*.
One should always offer the *bali* in the village and other locations at the time prescribed for the offering of the *bali*.
During festivals, one should always worship the Lord of the Gods everywhere, even in the dwellings of the Pālikās and in the temples of Kumuda and the other lords of the Gaṇas.

The practitioner, seated or standing as he pleases, facing whichever direction he desires, [should worship] with enjoyments such as vast quantities of flowers and other offerings, according to his preference. (504)
In this manner, one should perform the circumambulation even during festivals lasting a single day or more.
On a single-day festival, the procession and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the image should take place either in the preceding night or during the night itself.
Then, on the day of the ritual (karmadina), one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) of the sacred image at the holy site (tīrtha);
then, having wandered through the village in the morning, the procession image (yātrābimba) should be treated as before.
Thereafter, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the sacred site and the image as before;
on the following day, O twice-born, one should perform the flower-sacrifice (puṣpayāga), or alternatively, not.
O twice-born one, whether the festival lasts for three days, five days, or seven days,
the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the image and the procession should take place on the day before the commencement.
On the day prior to the pilgrimage day, during the first part of the night, one should perform the consecration of the sacred image and other items;
indeed, on the following day of the pilgrimage, one should perform the flower-sacrifice (puṣpayāga).
For four days, from one day until the end of seven nights,
one should not engage in the sport of gathering flowers nor even in hunting.

During all the periods beginning with the ten days, one should perform everything according to the method prescribed for the nine-day rite, as appropriate and in accordance with the performer's desire. || 511 ||
However, one should not perform the fourfold festival, lasting from one day up to seven nights, in a place such as a self-manifested celestial chariot (*vimāna*). || 512 ||
Likewise, one should not perform the festival prescribed for that occasion there;
at a self-manifested site, there may be water-sports, but one should not arrange them elsewhere.
O best of the twice-born, all festivals beginning with those of a single day and ending with the annual one should be performed according to the many rules prescribed for them.
Those lasting one, three, five, seven, nine, or twelve days must be performed according to the rite for a single image; it should not be otherwise.
Whether in a village or even in a city, or in a populous town inhabited by those of low caste, one should practice [the recitation] well upon the streets. || 516 ||

O best of the twice-born, if all [the rites] beginning with the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) were otherwise, one should perform the great festival within the inner enclosures of the Lord. || 517 ||
For the purpose of the deity’s processional rites, the entry and exit should take place through that front door, even across all the enclosures.
The entry and exit should be made facing toward the village and so forth;
the entering and departing should be performed through the principal gates and not through others.
It should never be adorned with upadvāras, śaubhas, or upaśaubhas;
if one should do so through negligence, that would belong to the king of that country. || 520 ||
O best of Brahmins, there is likewise a displacement of the primary element from its own place,
even in a village or similar location adorned with walls and other structures.
During the ritual of the deity's procession, neither the entry nor the exit should be made through side doors; if this is done, the procession and other rites become fruitless.
There may even be the destruction of the village, and then of the ruler of the country;
therefore, discern the distinction among these four principal [factors]. (523)
If a village or similar settlement lies to the east of a temple and its gate faces the west, then both [the aforementioned] conditions apply there.
When the village and so forth lie to the west of the temple,
then both the entrance and the exit should be made through the eastern door.
When the village and so forth have been established to the south of the temple,
then the previously mentioned northern or eastern gate [should be used].
When the water for the temple has been prepared from the village and so forth, at that time it should enter through either the southern door or the western door. || 527 ||

Alternatively, O best of Brahmins, the first two [mandalas] are for entry, situated in the southern and northern directions even in a village or similar place, according to the positions of the eastern and western gates.
O twice-born one, entry and exit are prescribed in the primary ritual;
however, in the secondary ritual, they are declared to be through the other two doors.
But when the temple of the God of Gods is situated at a great distance from the village or other such places, there shall be entry and exit during its festival procession. || 530 ||
These two have been described; now, listen to the procedure for when [the site] is nearby:
in a village situated to the east of the palace, on ground where the plow-lines run toward the east. || 531 ||
The entry and exit of the Lord should take place through the foremost part of the central path situated in the west; this applies when [the temple] is oriented toward the west.
One should perform the ritual as appropriate, using the foremost point of the central path situated in the eastern direction, while remaining positioned in the south and north.
Where a village or similar settlement had not been established, one should then construct a street enclosure;
having first offered an oblation to the deities of the street enclosures.
Afterwards, one should offer an oblation (bali) right there to the deities mentioned for the village;
in this manner, one should perform the procession of the deities twice for all of them in due order.
One should establish [the temple] in the center of the village, according to the location of the main gate and the site;
this applies when the village was established at a time when it was not surrounded by a road. || 536 ||
One should not offer bali to the deities mentioned in the Yathāvṛtti [text] there;
for that purpose, O high-minded one, even a procession of the gods (devayātrā) should not be performed.
But when neither the enclosure of the street nor even the village has been conceived,
then one should offer the bali to the deities mentioned for the village in the outer enclosure.
At the conclusion of the offering to the deity as prescribed, one should present it day after day;
likewise, one should perform the village-ordained procession of the deity there. (539)
O twice-born one, whatever rite is prescribed for the middle of the village, all that should then be performed on the *bali-ṣīṭha* according to the stated injunctions.
At that time, one should not perform it during the outer enclosure and so forth; rather, it should be performed during the first enclosure.
In the absence of that [first enclosure], however, all of it should be done to the east of the temple door. || 541 ||
When a festival or procession for the gods has been arranged in a village or similar location, but it cannot be performed due to obstacles such as disturbances in the kingdom; || 542 ||
In this very way, the sequence for the festival of the procession of the gods shall take place even then;
when the time for the offering of the bali-oblation has arrived, one should perform the bali-offering.
And also for the lords of the Kumuda and other gaṇas in the first enclosure,
as well as in the dwelling of the *pālikās* and in the sacrificial pavilion constructed for the rite.
O best of Brahmins, even in a village or similar place, one should always offer the bali-oblation at the four locations,
even if a street enclosure has been constructed there.
One should offer the bali-oblation every day at the entrance of the village for those accompanied by their retinues,
but at other crossroads, one should offer the bali-oblation to them alone.
Except for the dwelling of a *pālikā* (a small vessel), one should perform [the rites] elsewhere, beginning with the village;
and one should offer the *bali* at the three locations according to the sequence starting from the east of the deity.

One should not hold a festival within a village or similar settlement if it is situated more than one *yojana* away; this remains true even if there is an intervening river or other obstacle, provided the distance does not exceed the established limit of one *yojana*.
One should hold a festival in a village or similar place, or in one's own independent temple; or, for the purpose of a procession for another deity, one may construct a city or other such structure.

One should not perform the rites for a procession or festival of the omnipresent God of gods within a city or similar place that has been prepared for the purpose of the omnipresent one's procession and festival.
O high-minded one, one should never undertake a journey for the sake of debate; however, it may be done in a temple constructed as an integral part of a village or similar settlement. (551)
One should not perform the offering of bali elsewhere except at the village and other such sites that are its constituent parts; likewise, one should not undertake a procession for the gods.
Once, while the auspicious festival of another deity was taking place, archways were also constructed for the sake of a procession for yet another deity. (553)
One should never refuse for the sake of a sacrifice to the God of gods;
indeed, during a single festival, one may offer the sacrificial oblation in two villages.
One should not undertake a procession for the deity, for if it is performed, it will be fruitless;
likewise, there should not be two banners, as they would be defiled by such flaws as splitting or holes.
If the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is depicted on the cloth, one should indeed perform the joining [of the image];
but if that is impossible, having set that aside, one should proceed with another as before.
Otherwise, there would be harm to both the king and the kingdom if he were to abandon it;
however, whoever should thus arrange a festival for the God of gods— || 557 ||
Having enjoyed happiness in this world for a long time, along with all desired pleasures,
he attains the state of the Blessed One at the time of casting off the body.
Those best of men who follow the Lord while he is on his journey obtain, at every step, the fruit of a sacrifice. || 559 ||
Those who, at the proper time, gratify the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, with various services beginning with the royal umbrella and the chowrie; || 560 ||
"One always obtains abundant enjoyments both in this world and the next.
Thus, O best of sages, the annual festival has been correctly described.
In this manner, one should perform another occasional festival for a single day,
excluding the previously mentioned components of the procession such as the hoisting of the banner and so forth.
O Brahmin, according to one's means, it should be accompanied by special ablutions and provided with a great oblation, in accordance with one's faith.
On that lunar mansion of giving, provided with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
one should place twenty-five water-jars and perform the consecration.
In the month of Caitra, during the asterism of Punarvasu, one should celebrate the Spring Festival;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of that month, one should perform the Damanaka festival.
One should perform the worship of the four locations and so forth, just as in the Pavitrārohaṇa rite;
likewise, one should adorn [the deity] with excellent ornaments and with *damanaka* flowers.
That [consecration], however, is devoid of a fixed number; having established twenty-five jars according to what is aesthetically appropriate, one should perform the consecration.
With the first water-pot, one recites "Eko ha vai nārāyaṇaḥ"; with the second water-pot, one recites "Tasya dhyānāntasthasya. (568)
Then again, with the third jar, [he recites] "Nārāyaṇa";
then again, with the fourth, [he recites] "Nārāyaṇa. || 569 ||
From the fifth pitcher [he recites] "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads," and from the sixth pitcher [he recites] "The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self. (570)
With the seventh [verse], "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," and with the eighth pitcher, "Whatever there is in this world... (571).
With the ninth [verse], "anantam avyayaṃ kavim," one should perform the consecration;
then, with the tenth, "ato niṣṭyā vitastyām tu. || 572 ||
The continuous [mantra] is indeed with the *siras* (head-verse), while the eleventh is "lam";
in its middle is "mahānagni," which is indeed the twelfth.
By the thirteenth [verse], "He torments his own body," and by the fourteenth, "The clouds are dark with rain. (574)
"In the middle of that crest" is indeed the fifteenth [verse], while "the god who is the controller of all" is the sixteenth. || 575 ||
One should consecrate with the vases situated in the outer enclosure;
however, since there is no [deity] in the outer enclosure, one should do so with those previously stationed [therein].

That which arose from the navel-lotus, by means of the fire [element] situated there, one attains the Supreme while bearing the upright *puṇḍra*; and by means of that situated in the southern direction, one likewise attains it.
On his right arm, O Brahmin, Viṣṇu, who follows the path of the wind, has indeed inscribed:
"I am the one who never tires," while he stands facing the direction of Varuṇa.
"Viṣṇu is the Lord whose primary nature is that of the Person," [this was said] by one who had attained the state of Vāyu;
but "He who [knows] this Great Upaniṣad," [was said] by one who had attained the state of Soma. || 579 ||
One should first utter the name "Oṃ" with the [mantra] directed toward Īśāna,
and then "I am indeed Puruṣa, Vāsudeva" with the one situated in the middle.
Or else, having consecrated [the deity] with the sixteen mantras from the Puruṣasūkta in their proper sequence by means of the water-pots situated in the outer enclosure; || 581 ||
Having performed the ritual ablution in sequence with the jars situated in the inner enclosure, using pairs of the previously mentioned mantras residing in the Brahma-sūkta.
At the end, with the remaining three, one should sprinkle using the central pitcher;
having placed nine pitchers filled with the powder of turmeric.

Having worshipped them with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should visualize heaps of powdered saffron possessing a radiance equal to the rays of the [divine] wheel, and sprinkle [the disciple] with them.
O Brahmin, for the sake of dispelling all obstacles and for the fulfillment of all [desires],
one should [place it] on the right arm with the [mantra] "iti" facing eastward.
With the mantra "nicikidvā suṣaṇam," one should proceed toward the southeast;
with "prate viṣṇo abja cakre," one should proceed toward the south. || 586 ||

With the mantra "ebhirvayam urukramasya," one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) while facing the direction of the setting sun; with the mantra "kṛtacakra," one should do so while facing the western quarter. || 587 ||

With the verse beginning "pavitram" [RV IX.1.6], one should worship Agni; with the verse beginning "vāyugatena" [RV IX.2.10], Vāyu; and with the verse beginning "caraṇaṃ pavitraṃ vitatam" [RV IX.3.1], Soma. || 588 ||
With these eight mantras, beginning with "The radiant gate of the world," which belong to Rudra, as well as other Sudarśana mantras, [one should perform the rite]. || 589 ||
Having bathed him with the central jar and sprinkled him with pure waters, using the Brahma-sūktas previously mentioned which are contained within the Mahopaniṣads; || 590 ||
With the four mantras of the Puruṣasūkta, likewise with the sixteen mantras,
and with the two Brāhmaṇas of the six-syllabled Vāsudeva mantra.
With the four pervasive mantras beginning with Oṃ and ending with pavitra,
one should bathe the deity according to the prescribed ritual with a thousandfold stream.
Or else, one should perform the entire ablution with the mantra of twelve syllables;
then, having worshipped [the deity] in sequence with all other enjoyments as before.

O twice-born one, having performed the oblation especially with the mantras previously mentioned, or with the twelve-syllable mantra, using sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu).
Then one should perform the ritual of the *damanaka* offering according to the prescribed rules;
however, everything not mentioned here is to be understood as being like the procedure for the consecration of the *pavitra*.
In the month of Māgha under the asterism Punarvasu, or in Caitra under both [Punarvasu and Puṣya], or in Vaiśākha under the asterism Śravaṇa, as well as under Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa; || 596 ||
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa under the asterism Ārdrā, in Āṣāḍha under the asterism Hasta, in the month of Kārttika under Rohiṇī, and likewise in other such [asterisms]. || 597 ||
On the days of the incarnations, one should thus hold a festival for a single day,
whether in a village, a city, or the like, or in all the surrounding regions.
One should perform the wandering [of the deity] endowed with auspicious play,
on every twelfth day of each fortnight, and likewise month after month.
On the new moon day, on the full moon day, on the Śravaṇa day, and on the following day; or on other auspicious days, according to one's means and desire. || 600 ||
On the birth asterisms of the sacrificer and others, in the months of Caitra and so forth, during the two equinoxes,
and likewise during the two solstices— both specifically in their subtle and gross aspects.
Likewise, there are two [offerings] called Āgrayaṇa performed year after year, specifically in the month of Āṣāḍha under the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī, and under the asterism Puṣya. || 602 ||
O twice-born one, on the fifth or the seventh day of the month of Māgha,
one should perform a special sacrifice according to one's means and desire.
Especially on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should perform a special sacrifice and cause the Lord to hear [the sacred texts].
All the Vedas, beginning with the Sāmaveda, as well as the proclamation of the Vedas, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and likewise that which pertains to the divine and the human; || 605 ||
But the expansion of the Veda may be another [work], composed either in Sanskrit or in Prākṛt, or even in another language, according to one's faith and inclination. (606)
In this manner, one should perform the special worship on the twelfth day;
one should offer an abundance of milk-rice or rice mixed with jaggery.
When the recitation of the Bhagavadgītā is completed, one should perform the breaking of the fast;
this excellent vow is said to be joined with these two lunar days.
Beyond this, the expansion may be according to one's wealth and desire;
O twice-born one, it should last until the first full moon or until the fifth day.
Either from the tenth day until the new moon, or from the fifth to the tenth;
thus it may last for thirty days, according to one's means. (610)
And in the month of Vaiśākha, under the Viśākhā constellation, there should be a special sacrifice with ripe mango fruits cooked in cow's milk and other ingredients.
In the month of Kārtika, on the full moon day of Kārtika, one should perform special worship;
one should present many great lamps of ghee and oil to the Lord.
One should worship with other auspicious items, beginning with parched grain (lāja), along with pure foods and the like,
such as fruits and flowers, at their respective appropriate times.
In the month of Pauṣa, under the Puṣya asterism, one should perform a special ritual bathing;
and in the month of Kārttika, O best of Brahmins, that which falls on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight—614.
Having fasted during that night, one should satisfy the Lord of the World with vigils and with songs arising from the passion appropriate for that occasion. (615)
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, one should especially worship the Lord;
one should cause him to hear songs, hymns, and various sacred narratives.
One should perform everything at the conclusion of the oblation with particular care;
and those people who sing at that time, as well as those who listen to it—|| 617 ||
Who is able to fully describe the attainment of the fruit of merit for those [who perform it]?
Teachers or practitioners alike should indeed celebrate such a festival. (518)
Among them, the teachers should wear turbans and upper garments;
O Brahmin, the practitioners should always be without bodices, while the [other] adepts should wear bodices.
If the preceptors are wearing their bodices, that worship shall be fruitless.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Festival and Other Rites," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
Śrīḥ!
The Eighteenth Chapter: Sanaka said, "O best among speakers, regarding the daily, occasional, and other sacrifices..."
I wish to hear, however, about the pride of Prāpaṇa and the others; please speak of that.

O Brahmin, Śāṇḍilya [taught] regarding the obligatory, the occasional, the optional, and likewise the expiatory rites; hear now of the ninefold measure according to the primary and secondary alternatives. (2)
In due order, he presented the best and other types of articles;
here, to the One-Formed Lord, at one time, with two handfuls (bhāra).
One should arrange this attainment, which is designated as the "most excellent of the excellent";
one should perform a reduction of each [portion] by the measure of one *droṇa*.
That which consists of four *droṇas* is known as the lowest of the low; know this to be the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*). Now hear from me the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*).
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, that which is designated as the "most excellent" (uttamottama) Prāpaṇa is prepared with a large quantity of food for a single sacrifice to the principal deity.
If that [measurement] is deficient by two āḍhakas, it becomes superior-middle;
one should continue to apply such reductions down to the lowest-of-the-low.
O Brahmin, just as two *droṇas* are designated as the lowest of the low,
so too two *āḍhakas* are declared to be designated as the lowest of the low.
O twice-born one, starting from that point, he should gradually increase it by half a droṇa;
then, O brahmin, the highest of the high is four and a half droṇas.
In times of distress, one may prepare a meal of only one āḍhaka measure, or it may be just enough for a man's meal, according to the availability of resources. || 10 ||
O twice-born one, it is prescribed that [the substances] be placed in separate vessels, measuring either two āḍhakas or half of that, up to a limit of two bhāras.
This same rule applies equally to the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, as well as to those called optional (kāmya) and expiatory (prāyaścitta); hereafter follows the Mahāhavis.
However, ten and one *bhāras* is designated as the highest of the high;
in the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), one should practice a reduction by one *bhāra*, starting from the great meal (*mahodana*).
In this regard, there are two measures: the lowest of the low, which is twenty bhāras, or the highest of the high, which is likewise designated as twenty bhāras. (14)
There is a reduction of two bhāras each at every stage down to the lowest-lowest;
however, hear the rule for the primary kalpa, which measures four bhāras. || 15 ||
Three groups of three bhāras each, calculated as thirty bhāras minus one bhāra, are designated as the "highest of the high" (uttamottama).
One should decrease it by a gradual process until it reaches the lowest of the low;
or one may determine it to be exactly five bhāras. || 17 ||
A load of exactly fifty [palas] is designated as the highest of the high;
by omitting five [palas] at a time, there are thus nine varieties. || 18 ||
O twice-born one, in the rite for Mahodana, one should take a measure of ten bhāras at the very lowest level; however, one may take more than this.
Up to a thousand bhāras, according to one's desire for wealth,
one should provide three āḍhakas of the finest rice for the sake of the mother.
One should decrease it by one *prastha* at each step down to the lowest of the low;
in the primary ritual (*mukhyakalpa*), the best [measure] shall consist of one and a half *droṇas*.
One should perform the reduction by two *prasthas* at each step in due order;
thus, the lowest-of-the-lowest measure would be that which is prepared as half a *droṇa*.
When the primary ritual procedure is followed for an oblation measured by one *adhamāḍhaka*, one *prastha* of rice is required for the purpose of the measure;
when the secondary procedure is followed, half of that amount is required.
One should increase the quantity of the oblation in proportion to the increase in prosperity;
however, for the lowest [grade], one should calculate half a *droṇa* according to the single ritual procedure.
In the alternative procedure for the purpose of measuring the quantity, one should calculate an āḍhaka;
the measure of rice (mātrā) should be double that of the grain, and this constitutes the highest of the high (uttamottamā).
The middle [measure] is said to be equal [to that], and the inferior is declared to be half of that;
it should be fashioned like a grain of rice, existing in three ways according to its seed-measure.
In the absence of seeds, however, even a single mudga bean is recommended;
or else, one of the various seeds may be used according to the requirements of the specific time. || 27 ||

The primary [needle] is proclaimed to be equal in size to a grain of rice; the middling is said to be the measure of a sesame seed; the small is said to be half of that, and the smallest is the measure of a quarter. || 28 ||

Just as there may be pride regarding one's wealth or pride regarding being rich despite having empty coffers, so too, in a sacrifice that lacks the ritual bathing, the measure of rice should not be made [excessive]. 29.
In every procedure for worship, other measurements may be devised;
however, one should not construct [the image] with a measurement exceeding that which is appropriate for the principal form.
All the oblations and other offerings for the limbs and images should be prepared according to the prescribed measure;
however, one should not prepare the oblations and so forth for a duration longer than that. || 31 ||
From the measure of one āḍhaka of food, which is sufficient for the meal of a man,
one should never perform a reduction when conducting a temple festival.
O best of sages, one should not reduce the measure of the grain—whether it be a *taṇḍula* or a *śāli*—from the standard measure of an *āḍhaka*. (33)

One should perform the sacrifice in one's own home according to one's wealth and desire; now I shall describe the measurements for the clarified butter and other materials—pay close attention to that. || 34 ||
With one āḍhaka measure of food, there should be three kuḍuba measures of ghee;
this is known as the "best of the best" according to the sequence of the primary ritual procedure.
This is proclaimed as being of nine kinds by decreasing one handful at a time;
O Brahmin, in the secondary rite (anukalpa), the clarified butter should be one and a half kuḍubas.
By reducing that [measure] by half a handful at a time, it is likewise remembered as being ninefold;
however, when preparing mung-bean porridge, the measure of ghee should be double.
One should increase the quantity of ghee in accordance with the sequence of increasing the food; furthermore, one should provide roots and fruits for the purpose of seasoning the dishes. (38)
Twenty palas are declared by the designation "most excellent," according to the primary ritual procedure for a measure of cooked food amounting to one āḍhaka.
By reducing it by one pala at a time, this [weight] becomes ninefold;
however, in the secondary ritual (anukalpa), the highest [measure] is twelve palas in sequence.
There should be a reduction of one pala at each stage down to the lowest of the low;
however, for the *āḍhaka* measure, the addition of a split mung bean is like the measurement of clarified butter.
In the case of mudga-rice, the quantity of mudga beans should be equal to the rice;
the primary [measure] is when it is reduced by one-quarter, which is proclaimed as the middling [measure]. || 42 ||
One who is diminished is said to be "adhama" (low); therefore, one should not practice diminution.
A single coconut fruit is proclaimed to be equal to one āḍhaka. || 43 ||
Half of that is declared to be the middling [measure], and half of that again would be the lowest.
One should employ salt, black pepper, and so forth, according to what is appropriate.
For milk-rice (pāyasa) and boiled rice, there should be eight times as much milk as the quantity of rice;
the middling portion should be one-quarter less than that, and the lowest should be half of that.
In the absence of milk, one should provide coconut water;
or else, there may be an equal mixture of both types of milk.
Then, for one āḍhaka of guḍābrā, there should be thirty palas of gulā; this is the best quality. For the middling quality, it should be twenty palas, and for the lowest, ten palas. || 47 ||
It may be half the size of a grain of rice, or half the size of a split mung bean,
or else it may be equal in size to a ball of milk-rice or molasses-cake.
One āpūpa measure should consist of two kuḍuba;
that is the primary size, half of that is the middle, and half of that again is the lowest. || 49 ||
One should take half a portion of rice, or a quarter of that, according to one's preference;
for a single measure of cake, there should be six palas of jaggery.
Alternatively, in times of distress, one may prepare even a single pala;
or one coconut-pala, or half of that, or even a quarter.
Just as there would be ghee for the baking of a single cake, so too should salt, black pepper, and other spices be prepared according to the requirements, as previously described. (52)
Three hundred and sixty cakes is the highest [number];
then, as they decrease by forty at each step, there are likewise forty in the last [category]. (53)
Eighty betel nuts and eighty betel leaves—O Brahman, when prepared in this manner, it is called a single *tāmbūla*. (54)
Therefore, one should never make the temples smaller than this;
in the primary rite, two thousand betel nuts are prescribed.
Therefore, the measure for betel leaf is said to be double that;
this is the "best of the best," consisting of eighty, forty, and twenty [leaves] respectively.
O Brahmin, one should diminish both [the number of fruits and petals] such that it becomes the lowest of the low;
there should be seven hundred and twenty fruits and petals. (57)
One thousand four hundred and forty-four;
O best of men, this is said to be the measure of the ingredients for a single preparation of betel.
One-quarter of a niṣka each of cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, and jasmine;
the same measure applies to sandalwood and likewise to the powder. (59)
Eight mānas of camphor, half a coconut fruit, half a mātuluṅga fruit, and one-eighth of a handful of oil. || 60 ||
In this very manner, one should perform the increase of the ritual components step by step;
in the highest form of worship, two palas of sandalwood should be used.
In the primary ritual procedure, it is with one-quarter added;
however, in the secondary procedure, listen to me as it decreases by two niṣkas at each step down to the lowest of the low.
One pala together with one niṣka should be used; then one should gradually decrease by one niṣka at each step, until the sandalwood reaches the measure of one niṣka for the lowest-of-the-low.
In the primary ritual procedure (mukhyakalpa), determine the measure of sandalwood for the bathing ceremony:
eighteen palas is designated as the "most excellent of the excellent" (uttamottama).
The reduction shall be by two palas at a time until it reaches the lowest of the low;
in the secondary rite (anukalpa), there should be nine palas of sandalwood for the bath.

In the home [temple], however, the measurement for the sandalwood [image] should be half of what was stated for worship, or half of that again, according to suitability; such is the measurement prescribed for Bāhlīka.
O best of the twice-born, the measure for sandalwood used in worship according to the primary and secondary rites is as follows; likewise, the measure for camphor is half of that.
One should take one āḍhaka of gold-water combined with two kuḍubas,
and practice a reduction by two kuḍubas at a time until the end.
Know this to be the primary rite; in the secondary rite, it is half of that.
In the primary rite, there is black unguent for the body costing four and a half niṣkas. (69)
It is proclaimed as ninefold by decreasing the step by half a niṣka;
in the secondary rite (anukalpa), the measurement is said to be ninefold by half of that [measure].
The measurement for black body-unguents and for musk should be like that;
likewise, the measurement for kastūrikā (musk) shall be of nine kinds. || 71 ||
Regarding the substances prescribed for the ritual bathing, there may be eighteen, or nine;
thus, from the highest of the high down to the lowest of the low, the excellence or inferiority is determined accordingly.
It may be two niṣkas or even one; one should arrange it accordingly.
Having thus understood the measurement and so forth, and having consecrated the sacrificial oblation (havis) and other materials... || 73 ||
The preeminent guide, whether he be the teacher or the practitioner, should always cause the food to be cooked by cooks according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures. (74)
Or even by oneself, as appropriate, in the absence of those who know the mantras; the rule regarding the number of those [mantras], beginning with the preceptor, is now stated. (75)
O high-minded one, [this applies] to the temple known as Śrīraṅga and others which are self-manifested,
as well as to temples consecrated by Siddhas and gods.
One should appoint four teachers as prescribed by the scriptures;
or, O Sage, eight, twelve, six, or even five may be appointed.
O great sage, they should be arranged together with the principal preceptor, either increasing by one,
or according to the prescribed number, along with him.
In this very same way, one should act even in a place created by humans and fashioned by sages, as if it were a number [of such places] imagined by them. (79)
O Mahāmati, even in the absence of the aforementioned qualified teachers,
three, two, or one teacher may be appointed.

For the purpose of worshiping the primary image and so forth, the teachers (ācāryas) should be appointed according to the primary ritual manual; or, according to the intermediate or secondary manuals, the practitioners (sādhakas) may be included as well. (81)
The practitioners should be appointed as solitary ones according to the prescribed number:
four practitioners should be appointed, or six, eight, or twelve.
Furthermore, one should not otherwise imagine [the deities] in the case of the sixteen-fold manifestation;
likewise, they should be imagined in all five types of self-manifested [shrines] and so forth. 83.
Today, among human stations, a distinction is proclaimed;
yet, by those of mixed castes who perform sacrifices, it is conceived as a station.
In this manner, the number of preceptors (ācāryas) and practitioners (sādhakas) should be established;
however, in the primary rite (mukhyakalpa), there should be ten exclusive worshippers (ārādhakas) in the secondary rite (anukalpa).
One should imagine them together with the teachers of the number previously mentioned;
such is their number for the purpose of worshipping the primary image.
In the conceptualization of the number five, fifteen [deities] are likewise remembered;
however, in the conceptualization of those lords of teachers as being one, two, or three, [the count differs].
Eleven, twelve, and thirteen respectively;
therefore, for those who propitiate [the deity], there is only the number ten.

Therefore, one should not engage in mental construction regarding anything; instead, O twice-born one, one should act according to what is declared in the scriptures concerning those beings who transcend the human state, such as the self-manifested ones. 89.
Just as the number of preceptors and practitioners prescribed is for the obligatory,
occasional, optional, and even expiatory rites, so it should always be.

The number ten should not be postulated; rather, one should postulate it according to the stated principle for the purpose of worshipping the primary image and so forth, as well as in the case of external images. || 91 ||
If it were performed, there would be great harm for the king and the kingdom;
there would be great danger for the site, the one who performs the act, and likewise the one who causes it to be done. || 92 ||
Therefore, one should determine those respective numbers according to the path already described;
the sacrifice among the retinues may be performed with four, six, or eight [deities].
By twelve or sixteen practitioners who have been prepared,
[the site]— whether at a city gate, in a pavilion, in a hall, in a courtyard, or in a garden and so forth— [should be consecrated].
O twice-born one, whether it be the established manifest glory, or an appearance,
or even another primary manifestation that has been installed in a physical form— 95.
O Brahmin, for each respective sacrifice, four, six, eight, or twelve practitioners should be appointed; or, O twice-born one, sixteen may be appointed.

Or rather, O twice-born one, those very same [deities] may be conceived as the retinue for the sake of the entourage, even when images are installed at the gate-towers (gopura) and so forth for perpetual worship. (97)
O twice-born one, when those worthy of that role are not present, only those who are qualified as spiritual guides (deśikas) should be envisioned;
those Brahmins who are suitable for the position of attendants (parivāra) must be devoted to no other. 98.
Or else, initiated Brahmins who are knowledgeable in ritual action and skilled in its performance shall serve as attendants at self-manifested sites such as Śrīraṅga and others. || 99 ||
Indeed, those very ones who are reckoned as eighty in number are the Pācakas;
they are recorded as being exactly seventy in the established abode of the Siddhas.
In a place established by the gods, there are sixty; in one fashioned by twenty-two sages, thirty; and in a site constructed by humans, twenty. || 101 ||
Alternatively, in tasks such as carrying loads or cooking food,
there may be one person, or four, or even three, who are either dedicated to the path or initiated.
In this manner, one should gradually increase the weight according to one's capacity, O twice-born one, so that it may reach twelve or eighteen *ṛtu*-weights. (103)
One person should be appointed for the preparation of betel and cakes;
one person should be appointed within for the work of service. || 104 ||
Thus, forty attendants have been described;
however, for the accomplishment of the offerings of cooked rice (odana) for the fortnights, they are four times that number. || 105 ||
Two were for the preparation of cakes, two for the preparation of betel,
and likewise four were for the duties of internal service.
Thus, there may be eighty in number for the accomplishment of the wing-loads;
beyond that, one should increase them according to each respective load.
The reduction should always be performed by inferring according to that [proportion];
thus it would be when calculating the weight of the three [substances]. (108)
Or, even when conceiving of four [mandalas], one should increase them according to that sequence;
for the practitioners (sādhakas) and the preparers (pācakas) are indeed subject to the authority of the teacher (ācārya). || 109 ||
Always ready to uphold the commands of the teachers and practitioners, all should be cooks and attendants at all times. || 110 ||
In the scriptures, attendants are described as being of two kinds: those who cook and those who serve; these attendants are further divided into two types, the internal and the external. || 111 ||

Those who prepare the food and those who serve as attendants are declared to be the internal [limbs], while those who are intent upon fetching flowers and other offerings are declared to be the external [limbs]. || 112 ||
Furthermore, those others who are bound according to their respective karmas—
all of them likewise remain under the control of the teacher, as is appropriate for each.
Carriers, singers, and cooks should be increased according to their respective roles;
likewise, other laborers should be increased as appropriate. || 114 ||
There were four teachers, sixteen practitioners (sādhakas), and eighty counted as cooks and attendants. || 115 ||
Thus, O Mahāmati, know that this arrangement of the number four for those who follow the single path is the primary ritual procedure; in its absence, there is an alternative.
O twice-born one, know that among those initiated ones, the middle calculation is for those mixed with the initiated; the lowest calculation applies to other numbers as well.
Having thus inferred the distinction between the primary [initiation] and the others, one should conceive of them;
therein, one should conceive of those who have been consecrated by the initiation and consecration of a son.
O twice-born one, they may be consecrated by the teachers during the time of initiation and empowerment, or otherwise; likewise, there may be practitioners alone.
Regarding all those who are external, they should be considered as having received the initiatory consecration (samayadīkṣita),
whether they have been initiated by some method or not at all.
Furthermore, this specific detail is being told; listen to it.
O Indra among sages, the measurement of the number of Prāṇapas and so forth has been declared by Sanaka. || 121 ||
Now, the specific characteristics of their measurement, the varieties such as rice and mung beans, and the ritual procedure preceded by mantras [will be explained]. (122)
Reveal to me, who asks, all of this exactly as it is: the manner of the announcement and the recipient for those who perform the rites.
Śāṇḍilya said: Listen attentively, O sage, for I shall explain exactly as you have asked;
by the mere accomplishment of which the worship becomes complete.
The sacrificial oblation (havis) is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
First, listen to the characteristics of the oblation used in the daily sacrifice (nityayāga). || 125 ||
He who is eight tālas tall measured by his own hand is the middle person (madhyamapūruṣa);
[the measurement] originates from the middle finger of that preeminent teacher. || 126 ||
A drop consists of two joints; thirty-two drops constitute a *truṭi*.
Two *truṭis* likewise form a *śukti*, and two of those become a *prasṛta*. (127)
Two *prasṛtas* make one *prakuñja*, and two of those make one *kuḍuba*.
Two *kuḍubas* make one *mānikā*, and two *mānikās* make one *prastha*.
Two *para*s are declared to be one *śama*; those two [śamas] constitute one *āḍhaka*.
Two *āḍhakas* of Śiva (i.e., two āḍhakas) are one *droṇa*, and double that amount becomes [one khārī]. || 129 ||
Two *droṇas* shall be a *ravārī*, and three of those are called a *bhāra*.
[This applies to] rice grains, mung beans, and so forth, as well as curd, milk, and the like. (130)
By this which has been declared, four *vrīhi* grains are measured as one *kuñja* in rites such as the cooking of oblations; eight of those are called a *māñjiṣṭha*.
Sixty and eight niṣkas constitute one pala;
this applies to fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like, as well as to sugar balls and candied sugar. || 132 ||
Plantains, jackfruits, mangoes, and varieties such as the pumpkin, should be weighed on a scale according to the prescribed measure of palas. || 133 ||
Having thus ascertained the fixed measure for the preparation of the oblations, [he should take] rice, mung beans, barley, black gram, wheat, and priṅga-barley. || 134 ||
These seven grains are indeed suitable for the ritual of cooked rice (caru):
bamboo seeds, śyāmāka, nīvāra, wild sesame, and gavīdhuka. || 135 ||
Seven types of wild rice (*markaṭaka*) growing in the forest should be known;
among them, *śāli* is the foremost, while the others are secondary due to its absence. (136)
Red rice, great rice, *kalamā*, fragrant rice, white rice, awned rice, golden-hued rice, and embryo rice. || 137 ||
These ten types of śāli rice are known to be delicate and subtle;
furthermore, there are many internal subdivisions, and seven varieties of mudga beans have been described.
The Mudgās, Kṛṣṇas, Hemas, Śvetas, Pītas, Mahattaras, and Añjanābhas—these seven are declared to be the internal subdivisions. || 139 ||
White, black, yellow, wild, and large sesame seeds—these five varieties of sesame seeds are proclaimed as those that should be accepted. || 140 ||
O Lord, varieties of rice, mung beans, and other grains, brought from the fields and divine harvests by the farmers, are fit for use in the worship of the All-pervading One.
And free from the eight defects, such as being damaged by falling and so forth,
one should first bring them to the threshing house for the purpose of threshing.
Having smeared it with cow dung, adorned it with lime and other materials, and purified it with water filtered through a hundred-holed strainer and with kusha grass water; || 143 ||

Having uttered the syllable *praṇava* on dry land, [the rite should be performed] by disciplined Brahmins who have been initiated, who bear the marks such as the discus, and who face either the east or the north. || 144 ||
Having thoroughly bathed and having placed mortars made of iron, wood, stone, or clay on all sides, they were washed with strong sticks of Khadira wood.
They threshed them with pestles using the twelve-syllable mantra,
making the rice grains free from husks and chaff by means of winnowing baskets.
They should be pounded until they possess the luster of pearls—unbroken, not too small, and free from black spots. (147)
Likewise, varieties of mung beans—substantial and free from husks—should be prepared by virtuous Brahmin women, in the absence of consecrated [wives]. (148)
Or, for the purpose of performing tasks such as cooking the sacrificial oblation, the act of threshing should be carried out by initiated Śūdras or by temple-servant women in the temple kitchen.
The preceptor should take rice grains that have been husked according to the prescribed rite from the house of Vaiṣṇavas or from the house of those who have received initiation (dīkṣita). || 150 ||
[The rice] should be free from broken grains, husks, and worms, respectively;
likewise, it should be devoid of hair and stones, as well as parts of living beings. || 151 ||
If they are devoid of ash and charcoal, yet unbroken, light, and possessed of grains, there will be disease;
if they have husks, poverty shall arise.
By worms, there shall be the loss of sons; by hair, the destruction of one's wife;
know that death comes through stones, lightning, fire, or water. 153.
With the limbs of living beings, diseases are foretold; with ashes, quarrel is certain;
with charcoal, suffering from fire; and if [the stick] is broken during the struggle, there is defeat. (154)
Since travel is indeed light [in its consequences], one should therefore avoid all those ritual requisites that were previously prepared and approved. 155.
Having gathered together with the preceptors, the practitioners, and the cooks,
they reached the threshing house and took the rice and other grains situated there.
Having said, "It is like the semen of Brahmā," one should look with the eye;
as before, one should purify those [elements] by means of burning, nourishing, and so forth. || 157 ||
Having carefully removed all that rice and other grains for the purpose of cooking, even when they are spread out in clean vessels such as those made of leaves; || 158 ||
By attendants who were skilled in lifting those various vessels, who were well-bathed, well-dressed, and whose faces were covered with cloths. || 159 ||
One should bring her to the kitchen accompanied by auspicious sounds such as conch shells and trumpets;
she should then be placed on the northern side of the door, which has been smeared with cow dung.
One should place those vessels in their proper order in the designated area,
beginning with the jujube-based side dishes and followed by those containing flavors such as salt.
One should place curd, milk, and ghee in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest),
and one should also set down the implements for the fire-oblation in the region of Nairṛta (the southwest).
Having washed it four times with water filtered through a cloth using the four pervasive mantras, so that it may be [pure] as in the case of rice and other grains. || 163 ||
It was as free from husks and debris as rice freed from fragments of stone,
prepared with grains of unhusked rice that had been pounded.
That which is mixed with cow’s milk and clarified butter, combined with jaggery and sugar-candy,
and provided with non-alkaline salt, is called the sacrificial oblation for the gods.
That very same food becomes "paramānna" when cooked with milk, ghee, and jaggery;
however, pure rice sprinkled with ghee is called "havir" in the absence of those ingredients.

This excellent sacrificial oblation (havis), prepared without alkaline salt and combined with jaggery, milk, and fruit, should be accomplished for rites of pacification (śāntika) and for the vow-sacrifice (vratayajña). || 167 ||
Milk-rice, rice with jaggery, rice with mung beans, plain boiled rice, rice with curd, rice with sesame seeds, rice served at night, and all mixed together. || 168 ||
Thus, the eightfold oblation approved for the God has been described;
having sprinkled everything with clarified butter, one should present it along with side dishes.
To accomplish their preparation, however, vessels made of metal or clay,
along with shallow bowls, should be arranged beforehand.
The cooking vessels for the act of preparation should measure sixteen finger-breadths in height, measured by the fingers arising from the palm of the preeminent teacher.
There, the height of the belly is measured at twelve finger-breadths;
in the abdomen, the width at the base should be equal to one kalā. || 172 ||
Four strings should be made on the neck with a space of one finger-breadth between them;
thus should it be endowed with these characteristics regarding its width, height, and measurement. (173)
Or it may be one and a half times, or double that size, according to the desire for a middling or superior result;
such is the prescribed form of cooking-pots for the act of cooking. 174.
Now hear, O best of beings, the characteristics of other vessels such as the *śarāva*:
having fixed an eight-finger-long cord on the ground, one should trace around it. (175)
In its center, the belly is sixteen angulas in width;
it is eight angulas in height at the base and shaped like a half-moon. || 176 ||
The neck should be three finger-breadths high, and the upper rim of the ring should be two finger-breadths;
the width of the mouth, together with the ring, should be ten finger-breadths.
One should draw two straight lines from the neck down to the navel,
and likewise, as before, one should draw four lines to establish the *gula* measures.
There were many cooking pots and others according to the number of oblations, as well as all the vessels for side-dishes, each with a mouth as wide as [the sacrificer's] face. (179)
There should also be additional covers made of various materials;
they should be well-rounded, fitted with lids, and shaped like the crescent moon at their base.
Likewise, O best of beings, one should provide other vessels suitable for cooking, having devised them as before in view of the requirements for wine and so forth. (181)
Then there were iron frying pans for the purpose of eating with ghee heated [in them],
as well as many water-tubs and cauldrons for boiling milk.
Having prepared the collection of vessels for the cooking of ghee as well as for the making of cakes, and having produced other materials and such according to the prescribed rule. || 183 ||
One should begin the cooking of the oblation by the method to be described hereafter,
having taken the fire for cooking the rice from the sacrificial pit or from the domestic (aupāsana) fire.
Having placed [the vessel] on the hearth, uttering "O Tārā, sevenfold flame," he cast in pieces of sacrificial wood.
Having extinguished the insects, worms, and other such creatures from the copper vessels with the *jyotirātrītimantra* while fanning them, he should then [proceed]. 186.
Then, having washed the earthen vessels with pure tamarind water,
the knower of mantras should wash them with the twelve-syllable Vīryamantra.
One should smear the spaces between them with ghee using the Vyūha-vidyā mantra;
then one should pour rice grains into them while reciting the Gāyatrī preceded by Viṣṇu.
With the mantra "aṃbhasyapāre" and again with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya),
he should fill the water up to the top, placing rice grains in each vessel.
For a measure of one āḍhaka of rice, there should be six prasthas of water;
then, at the commencement of the rite, one should place those cooking pots upon the hearth.
Having covered them with lids using the Cakra-mantra in the proper sequence,
one should open them at the time of cooking while reciting the Vīrya-mantra.
Having gazed [at it] with the Netra-mantra while extracting the "root" with a ladle,
one should divide it into four parts and then cover it again with the Cakra-mantra.
Without allowing the water to drain from the cooked rice, while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra,
he should sprinkle it with melted cow's butter and offer the oblation.
On ground purified by the mantra beginning with "śucīn satkriyata" (O pure ones, be honored), or on ground spread with rice grains, [one should place] behind the support. || 194 ||
Having thus set down the prepared oblations with both hands,
one should wash them outside with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Then, one should rub [the body] with that pure mantra using a clean cloth,
with churned ashes and water, while reciting the names of Vāsudeva and the other [deities].

One should then apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) on the various directions using the fingers beginning with the index finger, after covering [the area] with washed garments for concealment. || 197 ||
Thus has the proper preparation of pure food been fully described; now I shall describe the preparation of other foods, beginning with *paramānna*. (198)
One-fourth part of the rice should be the essence of mung beans in the milk-rice (pāyasa);
the quantity of ghee is prescribed as that same measure, while the milk has already been described previously.
One should prepare four times as much sugar-candy powder as rice, combined with the aforementioned mantras, according to the prescribed method, using only boiled rice.
In the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," cow's milk is to be employed;
in its absence, coconut water should be used. || 201 ||
In the phrase "abjāgoje," there is an omission [of the vowel] when joining with the word *gavya*;
likewise, when cooking rice with molasses, one should omit milk and use sugarcane juice instead. (202)
One should offer jaggery or sugar-candy according to the measure of the milk;
one should employ the jaggery and other substances while reciting the mantra for adding milk. || 203 ||
In a dish of mung beans, one should properly add rice and the essence of mung beans; however, in a dish of pure rice, it should be as previously described, especially when drenched in ghee.
In the dish of curd-rice, the addition of curd should be equal to half the amount of milk;
it should be combined with plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and the like, along with jaggery and sugar-candy.
In the case of *kṛsarā* rice, one should add mung beans along with powdered sugar;
in the case of turmeric rice, there should be one *pala* of ground turmeric for every *āḍhaka*.
One should add a small amount of mixed food—accompanied by mung beans and śāli rice, combined with jaggery, sugar-candy, and so forth—and saturated with milk, ghee, and clarified butter. || 207 ||
For the purpose of pacification, it should be mixed with milk; for nourishment, mixed with jaggery;
for subjugation, made from the essence of mung beans; and for attraction, mixed with curd. || 208 ||
Kṛsarā rice is for rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛ), as well as for killing and driving away;
turmeric rice is for paralyzing, and mixed rice is for bewildering.
Plain boiled rice is common for journeys, hunting expeditions, and the like;
however, curd-rice served in vessels of gold or silver is especially recommended.
One should season it with the juices of *marīca*, *śuṇṭhī*, *likuca*, and *tintriṇī*, along with the powder made from *jīraka* and flavorful ingredients. || 211 ||

Those arising from various types of *rasaba* fruits, those produced from the two kinds of *panasa*, and those arising from various types of mangoes that have not yet fully ripened due to the passage of time—[these should be avoided]. (212)
And those originating from the *bṛhatī*, *urvāru*, *vārtāka*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa* plants, as well as those arising from the *kāravallī* creeper and the *kārkoṭa* plant. (213)
Likewise, those arising from the two types of *paṭola*, as well as those produced from *kośātakī*;
and that which arises from the varieties of *alābu*, *karkārī*, and *nimba*, as well as the fruit of *tintriṇī*. (214)
And likewise the small tuber together with the two vine tubers, the two sūraṇa tubers, and the two piṇḍāraka tubers. || 215 ||
And especially that which arises from red and blue lotuses is fit for the sacrificial oblation;
likewise, that which is leftover, bitten by insects, or stung by jackals and the like [is unfit].
That which has been smelled, touched by saliva, produced from an impure place, touched by a foot, grown out of season, or brought from an unclean spot; 217.

The minister of mantras, having examined it in many ways, should avoid in the act of cooking that which is the remains of a meal, that which has been touched by the untouchable, and that which is leftover from what has already been given.
Jīvantī, vāstuka greens, the leaves of kāravallī, as well as tumbī leaves, piṇḍī, camū, and mung bean leaves; || 219 ||
One should cook the Śākinī vegetable with a hundred joints, as well as that which is afflicted by worms, and the Āgastya vegetable; these are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa.
If there is no prohibition, one may take other plants that have a single root,
having cleared them away with a sickle while reciting the Vīrya-mantra.
Having inspected the worms, insects, and so forth, as well as the various vegetables,
he washed them and placed them in those vessels with plenty of water.
Having placed [the substances] in pots as before, either individually or mixed together, along with rock salt, black pepper, mustard seeds, and cumin; 223.
With milky juices mixed with the leaves of *śrīparṇī*, or with its tender fruits rubbed smooth and blended with ghee; || 224 ||
He should provide soups made from various types of mung beans, such as lentils, black gram, neem,
and others, along with vegetable juices (yūṣa) and bean-based broths seasoned with salt and other spices.
Immediately thereafter, one should prepare them together with various flavorings,
having removed the skins and cooked them with the essences derived from mung beans and milk.
One should prepare the gulmaṣa so that it is juicy, by rubbing together long pepper, cumin, and salt mixed with clarified butter,
and seasoning it with a ladle and other such implements.
Bananas, jackfruits, coconuts, and other such fruits had already been cooked in pots and bowls that were filled to the brim.
The fruits of the kūśmāṇḍa, bṛhatī, pūga, and kāravallī, along with small tubers and the piṇḍāraka creeper. || 229 ||
Having placed [the offerings] upon vessels such as those of Ambarīṣa, which are spread out on all sides, smeared with ghee, and heated, and having extended them; || 230 ||
With powdered black pepper, cumin, ghee, and clarified butter,
the moist ingredients are repeatedly stirred with a ladle while being heated.
Items such as salt and the like, as well as fruits—both dry and fresh—should be placed in containers and covered with cloths and other materials. (232)
Mixed with tintriṇī and jaggery, along with black pepper and cumin, and also ground with mustard seeds and coconut milk. || 233 ||
One should place the essence of mango mixed with salt, as well as fresh ginger, either crushed or left whole. (234)
It should be infused with salt and the juice extracted from the *likuca* fruit, as well as the fruits of the *kadalī*, *panasa*, and *āmra* trees taken individually. (235)
With flour made from wheat and śāli rice, moistened with a preparation of jaggery, cooked with the essence of mung beans, and with pieces of coconut; || 236 ||
One should cook cakes in ghee with cumin and black pepper,
making them perfectly round, equal in size to mangoes or emblic myrobalans.
They are shaped like the fruits of the banyan tree, or like those of the *likuca* and other such trees;
they have mung beans placed inside and are flavorful on all sides. (238)
One should prepare cakes of various kinds, shaped like coconuts and bound with molasses-flour paste, by frying them in ghee.
And those derived from śāli rice, as well as those burst forth from śāli grains—light, heated by fire, and mixed with the cooking of molasses (guḍa). || 240 ||
One should prepare *pṛthuka* grains with powdered black pepper, split cumin seeds, and dried coconut fruits. || 241 ||
With roasted flour of śāli rice mixed with cumin and other spices,
stirred and formed into separate balls by means of molasses syrup.
In the same manner, a ball made from well-roasted sesame seeds prepared as flour (saktu) is known as a "sesame-ball" (tilapiṇḍa), which is always approved by the Lord.
Well-cooked and thickened, combined with powdered sugar, milk mixed with honey and clarified butter, and very thick curd. (244)
There was curd mixed with parched mustard seeds and black pepper, along with pieces of young cucumbers and mangoes.
Pure, strained honey from the *mākṣika* bee, contained in a separate vessel, [should be mixed] with the juices extracted and crushed from grapes, jackfruit, *raṃbhā* plantains, and mangoes. || 246 ||
This *rasāla* is to be known as *lolita* when it is mixed with sugar-candy and endowed with cumin and other spices; however, when mixed with curd, it is called *pānaka*. || 247 ||
It should consist solely of curd mixed with an equal amount of water,
churned together with black pepper and seasoned with salts. || 248 ||
A drink mixed with powdered ginger relieves fatigue;
furthermore, mantras were proclaimed of old for the consecration of foods as well. (249)

But for others, the consecration should be performed with the twelve-syllable mantra, or with the heart-mantra together with its limbs, or one should accomplish everything with the root-mantra. || 250 ||
Or else, having consecrated the supreme food along with its side-dishes in due order by means of the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī or the Pañcopaniṣad mantra; || 251 ||

Having placed [the image] upon a wooden plank or similar support and adorned it with vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and other ornaments, [one should bring it] from the ground of the kitchen door to the west of the temple door. || 252 ||
Along a path smeared with cow dung and beautified by white lime powder,
preceded by a stream of water consecrated with weapon-mantras.
With the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, as well as with auspicious songs,
accompanied by lamps and umbrellas, and by those intent on protecting the sacrificial oblation.
[They were accompanied] by others with canes in their hands, intent on clearing away the atheists;
[the brahmins] had bathed, were dressed in white garments, were skillful, and had performed the ritual washing of the feet. || 255 ||

Having sipped water for purification, holding kuśa grass in their hands, and having applied a vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with clay or sandalwood paste, they remained self-controlled in their actions of mind, speech, and body. || 256 ||
Wearing white tunics and with their mouths and noses covered, the attendants should carry the vessels while reciting the *valamantra*. || 257 ||
Either in a spacious pavilion situated at the upper level of the root-abode, or in the garden of Mālikā to the south of the primary shrine within the first enclosure; || 258 ||
In a well-concealed place, richly provided with excellent coverings, adorned with rows of lamps and the like,
and draped with cloth, they should be placed upon a wooden plank or similar surface.
The sacrificial ladles (sthālikās), equal in measure to the oblation and made of gold, silver, or copper,
should be smeared as appropriate and then washed with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Having touched them with his right hand, he should pour streams of clarified butter all around them using that [ladle] while reciting the *tāra* (the syllable Om). || 261 ||
Having drawn [the offerings] from the vessels with a ladle fashioned of gold or other materials,
he, remaining silent, should pour them into that [fire] above in due order, beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having sprinkled sweet side-dishes all around with ghee, one should place goblets filled with curd, milk, and other such items above them. || 263 ||
There were various kinds of prepared cakes, such as *pṛthuka* and others,
as well as diverse beverages served in separate vessels.
Water that has been infused with camphor, sandalwood powder, and flowers, kept cool, covered with cloth, and placed in jars and other vessels. 265.
It should be provided with cloves, *takkola*, nutmeg, and betel nuts, mixed with camphor oil, and cut with razors and other such tools. || 266 ||
Having placed betel leaves together with powdered aromatics and camphor, as well as the betel-roll, in vessels shaped like lotuses; 267.
Having placed the fragrant substances such as sandalwood and likewise various kinds of garlands in their proper places through the mouth of the worshipper, || 268 ||
The officials in charge of those respective duties should inform the Lord while he is seated upon his dining throne; the worshipper himself [should do so] for the Lord. (269)
Having worshipped as before with the *arghya* and other offerings, ending with the seed-syllable of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
[one should worship] in the space in front of the deity located inside the door.
Having purified [the area] with water for the arghya offering and adorned it with sandalwood paste and other substances,
one should scatter rice grains upon the mandala according to one's preference.
Having washed the cloth-wick and spread it out above that,
one should place the food-receptacle upon it, and above that, a vessel made of iron.
Above that, the garments are bound; above that, in the overflowing stream, one should serve the final food and so forth, and the vessels one by one in sequence.
Having established the libation (tarpaṇa) with water for washing the hands,
one should perform the preliminary under-layering and honoring (upastaraṇārhaṇa) with the right hand in the rite for the gods.
Then one should present the sacrificial offerings for the forms of the gods and others:
first milk-rice (pāyasa), followed by rice mixed with jaggery and split mung beans. || 275 ||
One should offer pure food mixed with sesame at night, then food mixed with curd,
and then mixed food in sequence, and finally cakes at the end.
And flattened rice and parched grain mixed with sesame balls, as well as various fruits such as plantains, jackfruit, and others. (277)
Then there were various drinks mixed with different flavors for refreshing,
as well as coconut water and water for washing the hands.
Having offered water for sipping and betel leaf, one should perform what was previously prescribed;
this is especially so when kings have always prepared an abundance of sacrificial offerings (havir). || 279 ||
Having established [the deities] upon their bases within the spacious inner sanctum,
one should present the offerings as appropriate, or else on the ground in a narrow space.
Having placed it in due order upon a single firm support covered with cloth, and having presented it to the deity, one should likewise remove it. || 281 ||
Once sprinkled with the Astra-mantra, another oblation should be deposited;
one should offer it as before, for this specific distinction has been proclaimed here.
That which is devoid of mantra-rites, foul-smelling, discolored, over-ripe, waterless, and likewise from which the water has been drained; || 283 ||

That which is looked upon by those who are uninitiated, by outcasts, or by those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), as well as that which is excessively hot, excessively cold, or lacking the proper proportions; || 284 ||

That which has been removed entirely, that which is defiled by the breath from the mouth and so forth, that which is devoid of condiments and the like, and that which is placed in an unworthy vessel or not consecrated; || 285 ||
Likewise, [food] containing uncooked rice within, or placed in a broken vessel, or that which is without a support, or touched by another, or scorched by the heat of the sun. || 286 ||
It is mixed with charcoal and chaff, joined with hair and stones, infested by worms, clods of earth, and the like, and provided with the limbs of living beings and so forth. || 287 ||
It was not yet fully ripened, lacked a supporting base, was devoid of grain, and was free from cow's ghee, butter, and curds; yet it was desired by other people. (288)
Having recognized that the sacrificial oblation (havis) is thus defiled— being devoid of its cover and intended for another deity— one should cast it into the midst of water.
If one should offer the oblation to Viṣṇu that was abandoned through delusion, or perform his worship, it would be useless for the performers and their destruction would certainly occur. || 290 ||
