Therefore, at that very time, one should perform a thousand recitations of the root mantra; thereafter, one should likewise perform it for those deities who have been installed there according to the prescribed ritual.

Of the forms composed of the aggregate of the powers of manifestation, as well as of those forms established in pavilions, gate-towers, and the like, and even of those whose nature is spontaneous manifestation; || 292 ||
Having worshipped, according to the rule, Satya and the others whose nature is that of birds,
as well as the lords of the Kumuda and other groups, and even the door-keepers in their respective dwellings.

For the devotees who have been established according to the previously mentioned injunctions, [the offerings] should be consecrated separately for each with their respective mantras, in accordance with the prescribed rule. (294)
One should offer the oblations, such as milk-rice and the like, in their proper sequence;
one should prepare the sacrificial food for the offering using the Gāruḍa mantra itself. || 295 ||

One should offer food already prepared to others using the *praṇava* alone, just as the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is accomplished with the oblation (*havis*) according to the form of the root-abode (*mūlālaya*). || 296 ||
Indeed, all varieties of cakes are not suitable for the fire-rite (agnikārya);
other items such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like are used in the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and other rites. || 297 ||
Various kinds of fruits should especially be offered as oblations to the spirits, and milk-rice and other such foods should be offered constantly.
Cakes, barley-meal, flattened grains, and fruits—either combined with balls of sesame or mixed together, or kept separate. (299)
O Brahmin, because they must be satisfied according to the rule, one should therefore offer them curd and other such items during festive rites and similar ceremonies.
In each respective case, one should procure the materials for the bali offering according to the prescribed rule;
in the absence of all such things, however, there should be boiled rice alone with water.
Rice should be offered with water alone by those most skilled in mantras;
thus has the preparation and other details for the oblations been correctly explained. (302)
The manner of offering in the daily rite is performed before the primary deity and the other images;
likewise, it may be performed before the supports, in the hall, or outside in the courtyard and so forth.
And when the palaces had been constructed and the dwellings and other structures established,
[he inspected] the walls, gate-towers, gates, and pavilions on all sides.
Just as in the worship of deities residing within palaces, so too in the images of the arrays of emanations and in the forms of the limbs and abodes.
One should not take what is placed outside the door for the purpose of offering; that which is forbidden food offered as an oblation is defiled by Rākṣasas and other such beings.
It was previously authorized by the god for the sake of the Rākṣasas born of Diti, as well as for other flesh-eating beings who are to be supported. || 307 ||
Therefore, the powers of strength, heroism, and so forth, which reside within it, are not to be grasped—
whether through manifestation or non-manifestation— as distinct from the attainment of the oblation itself.
The prepared food, placed in separate vessels and set down at the entrance,
should be offered in due order, beginning with the supreme rice-milk (paramānna).

Likewise, during rites performed for specific desires or occasional rites, as well as in the worship of the great oblation, for one situated within the temple and engaged in ritual acts such as worship; 310.
The wealthy, including brahmins, kings, and others, should respectfully offer whatever single item is available in a vessel, out of devotion to Mūla. (311)
Having established the Annapūrṇa [liṅga] in the pavilion atop the palace,
one should worship the primary image (mūlamūrti) along with the ritual images (karmārcā) and their respective powers (śaktis).
One should bathe the ritual image situated [there] with the jars previously described;
then, having offered the sacrificial oblation (havis) into a separate vessel at the base as before.
Having brought the deity residing in the ritual image into the pavilion situated at the front,
the mantra-practitioner should present it there, as beheld by the primary form (mūlamūrti).

And there, while the great offerings consisting of excellent food and other delicacies were being presented in due order, preceded by the festive rites of the sacrifice, [the Lord] was worshipped. (315)
And having offered them individually as appropriate into the vessels,
during the festivals at the end of the year and on various other special occasions, (316)
Having brought forth the mobile image from wherever it may be, even from childhood, and having worshipped it extensively, one should offer abundant food. || 317 ||
For that purpose, one should perform the ceremonial bathing according to the rules during the festival of bathing,
or when a hunt or other festive excursion has taken place in the grounds of the gardens outside.
For the purpose of performing the great offering of food, the mantra-master should bathe that image according to the rules in the bathing pavilion located within the inner sanctum.
On the twelfth lunar day and other such times, as well as during the months beginning with Āśvina, on the occasions of annual festivals, and on various other special days; || 320 ||
This procedure for the oblations has been declared as common [to all];
now, for the worship during a festival, one should bring [the deity] somewhere, such as into a pavilion.
Having propitiated him in many ways according to the prescribed rules with milk-rice and other offerings,
one should satisfy him with whatever food is obtained, preceded by devotion.
Now I shall explain the distinction regarding the offering of the great oblation:
those who desire their own welfare should not perform the daily sacrifice of the great oblation. || 323 ||
Either in an expansive inner sanctum, or on a pavilion situated atop a temple, which has been prepared for the purpose of bathing [the deity] and so forth, or for the purpose of sacrifice; || 324 ||
That which has been offered into a single vessel by the previously mentioned means is declared to be the "Great Oblation" (mahāhavis), which always brings delight to Hari.
Within the temple, the sacrificial offering (havis) should be prepared free from any secondary vessels;
elsewhere, however, one should arrange it extensively with particular care.
Having first worshipped the primary image,
the best of mantra-knowers should then worship it with offerings such as arghya and other mantras, ending with incense, just as before.
Therefore, one should descend into the interior of the heart-lotus of the bathing image,
and likewise into the festive rite of the festival.
Having worshipped him as before, he should lead him to the bathing pavilion,
provide the ceremonial bathing attire, and consecrate him with the ritual jars.
After offering the oblation, one should subsequently lead [the deity] to the inner sanctum;
having placed [the deity] there, one should join that mantra with the primary image (mūlamūrti). || 330 ||
Having placed the consecrated image, adorned for the festival, upon a vehicle and so forth,
one should lead it either to the sacrificial pavilion or to the assembly hall.
Having placed the Lord of Gods upon a wide and auspicious seat made of gold and other materials there, he should honor him with a great abundance of offerings. || 332 ||
The preceptor, having propitiated [the deity] with the root mantra through circumambulations and prostrations,
preceded by the offering of water and including arghya, flowers, and other articles.
One should give those enjoyments to the recipient and offer the various portions that have been presented;
for the purpose of offering the oblations, a spacious pavilion has been constructed.
And it was adorned in the central area with canopies and banners, as well as with curtain-pieces, according to the proportions of the full measure of the sacrificial oblation.
One should construct an altar (vedi) with a height equal to that of the pillar, shaped like the base of the pedestal;
it should be square, firm, level, and auspicious, constructed from bricks and other materials. || 336 ||
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and decorated it all around with colors such as lime and with powdered flour, [he should do so] in the western direction.
Having established a seat for eating, covered with fine cloth and cotton and provided with a cushion, neither too high nor too low. (338)
The cooks prepared the vessels for the oblation as before, filled with excellent rice and other foods, along with side dishes and fruits. (339)
Accompanied by various kinds of food and edibles, as well as flavors such as sweet and others, and provided with umbrellas and lamps, amidst the sounds of kettledrums and tabors; || 340 ||
Just as in former times, the area was purified by those intent on clearing away the wicked with the sounding of conchs, horns, and other instruments, using cow-dung and similar substances.

Then, from that great kitchen, [the food] was sprinkled on both sides with water consecrated by mantras and with lime powder, according to the scriptural injunctions, by those who were experts in purificatory rites.
The "anudhārā" position is prescribed;
one should lead [the water] to the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) either between the Yātu and Vāruṇa [points], or between Soma and Sāmīraṇa. || 343 ||
Having established it upon a wooden board produced from a sacrificial tree on ground strewn with śāli rice,
covered with cloth and consecrated with weapon-mantras (astramantra).
Then, having spread [grass] around the sacrificial altar, one should place rice grains produced from the śāli paddy;
metals such as bronze and others are not desired for the offering of the great meal.
Or leaves of the plantain tree and other such plants, uncut and well-purified, washed many times, with their tips pointing either eastward or northward. 346.
Having placed it as before and having spread clarified butter [as an under-layer],
he then takes that sacrificial offering with the root-mantra using a ladle into other vessels.
Having placed it in a wide vessel that is level, one should then pour [the liquid] over it with a ladle, according to the sequence, whether the vessel is perfectly round or four-cornered.
Having recited the root mantra once more, he should again sprinkle it with consecrated ghee-filled oblations that have been cooled by the wind. || 349 ||
He offered mudga beans all around, with the ankle-bone [region] and the heart; and he offered pieces of molasses along with powdered sugar by means of the head. || 350 ||
Various side dishes cooked on the fire according to the prescribed rules, as well as plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and diverse other fruits. || 351 ||
Uttering the *kavaca* mantra, he offered heart-pleasing items that were well-cooked;
then, reciting the *netra* mantra, he offered those along with side-dishes fried in ghee. (352)
Having placed it inside a folded leaf and prepared it above with the Vīrya-mantra, it is then combined with powdered black pepper, cumin, and molasses. || 353 ||
Having filled the vessel with curd mixed with powdered sugar, and having thus first established the great sacrificial offering (mahāhavi) in a single bowl; || 354 ||
One should place around the vessels, which have been filled with milk-rice and other foods as before, various side-dishes such as ghee within their respective containers. || 355 ||
Furthermore, for the Mahānna offering, the eight items beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa) should be deposited in pairs even in the western and other directions. || 356 ||
Alternatively, one may decrease each of the four items beginning with milk-rice by one portion;
in those respective places, one should place pure food, cakes, and so forth.
Either milk-rice, jaggery-rice, mung-bean rice, or plain boiled rice should be placed; however, in the intermediate rite, they are to be arranged in sequence starting from the western direction.
One should offer either sweet mung-bean rice, or the triad beginning with milk-rice (kṣīrānna),
or one of the two— gulapāyasa— or pure food.
Alternatively, by means of a secondary rite, one may offer pure food according to one's devotion and faith;
or, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the prescribed rule, one may offer milk-rice and other such foods as desired.
It was filled with fragrant śāli rice, produced from the absence of [other] rice,
and in its center it was provided with a golden goblet filled with clarified butter.
The bowl, containing seasoned side dishes and other foods, should be placed upon a high stand in the western direction for the purpose of serving. (362)
In the center, having established a trough for the milk-rice (pāyasa) filled with gulānna,
one should then arrange other vessels around it.
Water scented with perfumes, flowers, and other fragrances should be placed in jars and similar vessels;
meanwhile, coverings such as cloths and the like should be arranged for the pavilion on its southern side.

In the west, there should be honey-mixture (madhuparka), the measure of a cow, the seeds of the sādhya-mantras, betel-leaf, sesame, jewels, the measure of wealth, perfumes, garlands, and so forth. || 365 ||
Having placed the other sacrificial materials, such as the rosary and the sacred thread, in the northern direction, and then by those performing that rite: || 366 ||
Having been especially honored, the preeminent teacher, standing before the God, should, with a prostration, make his request to Puruṣottama. || 367 ||
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, whose nature is being, consciousness, and bliss,
you are the imperishable one, eternally satisfied by enjoyments consisting of strength and vigor.
Nevertheless, for the sake of my own accomplishment, I shall now satisfy you with a great oblation; that which has been prepared is complete.
O Lord, for the sake of favoring your devotees and for the consumption of food, [the priest] should thus address the Master;
thereafter, he should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) as previously described.
Having placed the deity upon a vehicle fashioned from gold or other materials, the image-bearers (mūrtipās),
together with all ornaments, should lead [the deity] to the dining hall.
Having first placed [the image] facing east upon the dining seat situated there,
one should offer water for the guest (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamana), together with their respective vessels.

Then, having given a concealing cloth, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) according to the rule, a cow, sesame seeds, and the seeds of the sādhya, with the water for sipping (ācamana), [he should perform the rite].
Having washed his hands with the arghya water for the deity,
and having established [the vessel], he sits down on a seat to the right of the deity.
Then, having looked [at the vessel] with the Netra-mantra, one should present the water for the arghya-offering, drawn from the arghya-vessel and accompanied by a set of separate bowls.

Having sprinkled with the purifying *śatadhārā* water as before, the sacrificial offering (*havis*) consisting of excellent rice and other foods, along with condiments and side dishes, [should be prepared]. (376)
Having performed the burning and nourishing [of all things] with the Surabhi-mudrā,
one should meditate, recite that mantra, and thereby transform what is contained therein into nectar (amṛta).
One should cast up the strength, vigor, and splendor as a worthy flower, and then consecrate it with the armor-mantra, the weapon-mantra, and the eye-mantra. || 378 ||
Then, on one's own right hand, the powers of cognition, sovereignty, and action—the enjoyers who consist of the instruments—should be remembered with their respective mantras. (379)

Then, with that hand of Viṣṇu, having repeatedly touched [the offerings] preceded by the supreme food (paramānna) as was appropriate, and having formed the mudrā of the mouthful (grāsamudrā). || 380 ||
Indeed, those [offerings] which exist within the food-form of Viṣṇu are to be presented;
they arise from the distinctions of taste, form, and so forth, and consist of splendor, vigor, and strength. || 381 ||
For even the Lord, who possesses the sixfold policy and identifies with his own image, is supremely gratified by this well-prepared oblation accompanied by mantras. (382)
Having understood this, [he should proceed] with the sounds of conchs, horns, kettledrums, and tabors, accompanied by the ringing of bells and auspicious songs. || 383 ||
With the sounds of the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Itihāsas that proclaim the qualities of the Blessed One, as well as with the resonances of hymns and Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas; || 384 ||
Following the sequence of circumambulation, there should first be vessels containing milk-rice and other offerings;
thereafter, abundant food, preceded by the *prāpaṇa* meal.
There were various kinds of foods, beginning with cakes (apūpa), as well as soft foods and fruits;
there were also items to be licked, beginning with honey, and items to be sucked, such as mangoes and the like.
Having offered the drinks, beginning with milk and accompanied by appropriate after-drinks, to the deity, they were placed upon the cooked rice.
The mantra-practitioner should then withdraw the mantras of power, heroism, and so forth, along with those devoid of power, heroism, and the like,
by means of the *saṃhṛti-mudrā* while uttering "Oṃ."
Having recited the mantra "From the full, the full," the wise one, being composed in meditation,
should contemplate the God as fully satisfied while uttering the words, "He is fully satisfied."
Cool, refreshing water, filled in vessels shaped like conch shells and mother-of-pearl, was offered for the libation, as well as powder for the sprinkling. || 390 ||
For that purpose, there was a cloth, and then water for washing the hands, as well as water for sipping (ācamana) infused with ground camphor. || 391 ||
Having offered sandalwood for the purification of the hands in a quantity produced from the hand, along with gems, and then betel-leaf infused with camphor; || 392 ||
Then, having offered [the oblation], one should display the root-mudrā while reciting the root-mantra;
and having performed the recitation as before, [one should worship] with the arghya and other offerings, ending with incense.
Having worshipped them and summoned the practitioners who preceded the Guru—
those devoted to the Siddhānta and dedicated to the five-fold ritual cycle (pañcakāla)— [he spoke].
And those who have been initiated according to the rule, as well as those learned in the three Vedas in their absence,
[should be honored] with offerings of water for the feet, unguents, garlands, and incense.
Then, having worshipped them thoroughly, he should place the water for the arghya offering into their hands;
around them, he should arrange various items such as milk-rice (pāyasa) in separate vessels.
Having divided the great rice-offering into four equal portions,
one should then bestow one part upon the artisans for their welfare.
Thereafter, one should offer the second portion of cooked rice to the Lord of the Army (Seneśa), and the third portion of food should be given to all the attendants. || 398 ||
For the fourth [offering], one should provide food to be distributed for the purpose of honoring and consuming by the Vaiṣṇavas and those who dwell in the temple of the deity. || 399 ||
One should offer a cow, the seed-syllables of the deity to be accomplished, grains such as rice and mung beans,
a measure of sesame and gems, and likewise a garment for covering.
Furthermore, at the moment of the appointed worship, one should present a cloth for the removal of impotence and especially betel-leaf to the preeminent preceptor.
The Lord of Gods possesses great majesty and is the bestower of the fulfillment of all intentions;
for from him one should first appropriate the imperishable power of enjoyment as one's own.
Immediately thereafter, one partakes of it made manifest through the mouth of the Guru and others;
therefore, everything indeed becomes an offering to the all-pervading Vāsudeva. (403)
One should always bestow [the offerings] upon those who have served their gurus and are self-restrained during worship;
that gift must be protected from non-devotees by those who perform sacrifices for Viṣṇu.
The donor becomes liable for penance due to the presentation [of offerings] to an unworthy recipient;
however, that which was offered to Viṣvaksena should be cast into the midst of the water.
Or else, for the satisfaction of aquatic creatures or those dwelling on the banks, one should cast a small portion into the water and place the remainder of the food before them. (406)
Then, having thus gratified the Lord of Gods with a great oblation, for those twice-born ones who had spoken thus and were devoted to their own duties— || 407 ||
Afterwards, he should be seated on a seat for eating, or elsewhere in a place for reclining, which is enriched with well-placed banners and adorned with flower garlands and the like. || 408 ||
One should lead [the image] upward from the couch, which is provided with all necessary utensils,
after having removed the garlands, perfumes, and garments.
Then, having personally taken a small portion for Viṣvaksena,
one should offer the remainder to the Lord seated upon his couch.

The water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), a garment, as well as foot-ointment, a gift-vessel (pratigraha), water for sipping (ācamana), water for wiping the hands, and a cloth; 411.
Then, having offered [these], one should anoint [the image] with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like;
and, for the sake of allaying fatigue, one should fan it from all sides with fans.
Then, having massaged the heated deer-fat scented with moon-powder onto the god’s outstretched mass of hair, [he applied it]. (413)
Then, one should wind the hair with various kinds of fragrant flowers and with various types of garlands, filling the interior [of the head] with them.
One should offer cakes, flattened rice, and fruits;
as well as a cooling drink, water for satiation, and coconut juice.
Having informed the Lord that the betel-roll accompanied by the moon and all its constituent parts is ready,
he should proceed to the kitchen bearing the water-offering (arghya) along with an umbrella and a lamp.
There, in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) prepared either for a specific occasion or as a regular rite, and likewise in a consecrated fire that has been previously gratified as before; || 417 ||
Then, having descended into that [fire] which bears matted locks of flames, one should satisfy the Lord of Mantras residing in the heart with seven fuel-sticks.
Especially with all varieties of cooked milk-rice and other foods, accompanied by the sounding of conchs and kettledrums and the ringing of bells. (419)
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with an uninterrupted stream of clarified butter;
having completed the remainder of the ritual, one should give the leftover sacrificial porridge (caru) to the Guru.
Then, having approached the deity, one should offer the oblation;
having first distributed it among the ancestors as before, accompanied by the formal gift.
Having worshipped [the deity] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, and so forth as before, one should perform a circumambulation;
then, having informed [the deity] and placed him upon a vehicle, one should cause the Lord to enter within.
One should offer the triad beginning with the *arghya* to the deity established in his own place;
there, one should apply the previously restrained mantra to the root [mantra] as before. (423)
There too, one should worship with enjoyments such as the *arghya* offering, ending with incense;
then, preceded by a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should address the deity.
O Lord of the World, O All-pervading One, you have been worshipped with this great oblation;
out of your affection for me, who am yours, you ought to be satisfied. 425.
Having thus made this petition at the two lotus-feet of the Lord,
and having uttered the root mantra, one should cast a handful of flowers.
When the occasion for a great feast or similar event has arrived, such as during rites for specific purposes,
it may be performed either before or after the worship and the festive ritual.

The primary image together with its power (śakti), the secondary image together with its limbs (aṅgas), and [the deity] together with his support, accompanied by the lords of the birds, the enclosures, and the gatekeepers, along with their respective portions. || 428 ||
In the outer celestial chariots, in the pavilions, and in the gate-towers and so forth,
the forms of the manifestations of the Vibhava-vyūha were installed according to the prescribed rites.
Having performed the worship as before, one should present the great food offering;
this is declared to be the primary ritual procedure, while in the intermediate procedure it is according to one's capacity.
One should prepare food for each [deity] according to a measure such as an āḍhaka;
or one may worship the deity residing in the root-abode alone. || 431 ||

For one who resides permanently in a temple, the great sacrificial offering (mahāhavi) need not be formally resolved upon; likewise, one who desires his own welfare should not perform the Bali sacrifice for that purpose. 432.
In the primary ritual procedure, both the Mahodana offering and the bathing rite must be performed together; these two are inseparable.
In the case of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), when one [ingredient] is lacking,
it may be prepared with another, either for the purpose of a large quantity of boiled rice or for the purpose of another sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, when the images had been invoked into some [receptacle] and worshipped according to the rules, and while this sacrifice was being commenced and completed, suddenly— 435.

When other occasional rites such as the great oblation-sacrifice (mahāhavi-yāga) have arrived, those who know the mantras should offer [the oblation] there; elsewhere, the ritual of dismissal (udvāsana) and so forth should be performed.
Then one should perform the ritual of dismissal (udvāsana) here; for it is exactly the same even in the case of the ceremonial bath (snapana).
Just as the great oblation (mahāhavis) is to be offered by the mantra-practitioners into the primary image (mūlabimba), so too should it be done here.
One should offer a great oblation (mahāhavir) either outside the third enclosure, or likewise inside, or at some other location during the performance of the great festival.
He who worships Hari with devotion by means of this great oblation shall enjoy vast pleasures for a long time in this world. || 439 ||
When the end of the allotted time has arrived, one who has attained [this state] goes to the imperishable station,
especially by kings who have been consecrated and are devoted to the welfare of all beings.
The worship with great quantities of rice must be performed according to this rite;
and they shall eternally obtain the circle of all rival kings. 441.
The elephant, the excellent horse, and his collection of treasuries—
thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Manner of Presenting the Means such as the Measurement of the Offering," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the glorious Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the Śrī-Pāñcarātra.
Śrīḥ!
The nineteenth chapter:
O Sage, [this concerns] Sanaka, who was steadfast in the Siddhānta and desirous of performing worship.
Declare the expiation for a deficiency in the conduct of the observance (samayācāra). || 1 ||
Śāṇḍilya said:
Listen attentively, O sage; I shall explain the beneficial expiation which, when performed, brings auspiciousness to the four [classes of teachers], beginning with the preceptor.
If the practitioner, without having bathed according to the rule, should worship [the deity] at a river or similar site,
he must bathe, recite the root mantra one thousand times, and then worship the Lord.
If he should honor [the deity] while wearing worn or stale garments,
he should likewise bathe, put on clean clothes, and then recite the root mantra.

One who lacks meditative concentration, one who has not sipped water for purification, and one whose fingers are devoid of purificatory grass (pavitra), as well as one who touches hair, bones, clods of earth, sinews, blood, or other impure things; || 5 ||
Having bathed and performed worship as before, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times;
[this applies even to] one who has been in the company of a woman in her courses, a woman recently delivered, those whose food is forbidden, or a caṇḍāla.
If one should touch the image of the Blessed One, one must first bathe oneself;
then, having consecrated the Lord of Gods with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship him.
If one has been touched by a woman in her courses, a woman recently delivered, or others of that sort, or if one has touched an auspicious thread (kautuka),
one should bathe, and then, for the sake of peace, perform an ablution with the supreme [mantra] upon the Lord of Gods.
Having performed the oblation, one should then recite the root mantra ten thousand times;
even during birth-impurity or death-impurity, if one touches the image or worships it, [there is no fault]. || 9 ||
Having bathed [the image] with the *adhamottama* [mantra] and having performed the preliminary rites as before, one should recite the mantra.
[This applies even if] one has been touched by those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*), or by those who have consumed excrement, urine, or forbidden drinks.

If one should worship the Lord of Gods again after bathing according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the ceremonial bath as before and carry out the propitiatory fire-oblation and other rites. || 11 ||
If one should touch the Lord while covered with spittle, blood, or sweat,
one should bathe the All-pervading Lord especially with water infused with *kuśa* grass and perform worship.

If, having gone during the day, one should touch the Lord while still unwashed after approaching his own wife, he should fast and bathe the Lord with the five products of the cow and water infused with kuśa grass. || 13 ||

One who is addicted to another's wife or has committed evil deeds should worship the Lord; likewise, having touched [the image], one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) upon the physical form. || 14 ||

Having offered oblations by way of the middling or lowest path, one should recite the mantra a hundred times [if the fire is defiled] by worms, insects, bones, hair, moths, nails, and the like. || 15 ||
[One should avoid] leaves, fruits, and so forth that are defiled by animal parts, husks, ashes, and the like;
as well as flowers, water, and other such items, including sandalwood and ornaments. || 16 ||
Likewise, even with other things devoid of ritual preparations, and similarly with leaves, flowers, sprouts, fruits, and so forth that have been kept overnight. || 17 ||
When touched by untouchable living beings, or likewise by untouchable objects, such as Caṇḍālas, women who have recently given birth, Niṣādas, outcasts (patitas), and so forth; || 18 ||
If one should worship with flowers that have been touched, are withered, or covered in dust, one should,
with undistracted mind, recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one should worship the deity with these impure garments and other such items,
having first bathed the deity and then worshipped according to the prescribed rule using only the lowest quality [materials], [the following occurs].

One should perform a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) with one thousand offerings in sequence [for those defiled by contact with] Caṇḍālas, women who have recently given birth, menstruating women, Śabaras, and those who drink from forbidden vessels. || 21 ||
When the food, drink, and other offerings have been touched and presented to the Lord of Gods,
one should discard those made of clay and wash the others.
Having bathed and drunk water mixed with kuśa grass, one should bathe [the deity] with the lowest [mantra];
then, having worshipped again, one should offer oblations a hundred times with the root mantra.
When food and other such items have been touched by village pigs, jackals, crows, hawks, donkeys, and so forth, or by others of this kind, they must be reported.
As before, there should be peace alone; thereafter, one should offer the pure [oblation].
[This applies] to those addicted to approaching the wives of others and those who lack discrimination between what is fit and unfit to be eaten. || 25 ||
Touched by those born of non-Vaiṣṇava lineages who are intent on acting according to their own whims, or seen by them, it becomes defiled by pus, blood, and the like. (26)

If the ministers have offered the oblation, one should perform the pacification rite as previously described; likewise in the case of presenting cooked food that has been defiled by a corpse or similar impurity. || 27 ||
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods as before, one should perform the peace-offering (śānti-homa).
If the food and other offerings have been discarded, one should worship again and offer sesame seeds.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with clarified butter in a number of one hundred thousand;
likewise, he should perform a rite of pacification when giving stale food.
One who is free from greed should discard the offered oblation, fruit, flower, purifying food, juices, and so forth,
either in a body of water, in fire, on the ground, or among cows.

Food consisting of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, that has been defiled by flies, woodworms, bees, or similar creatures moving within the excrement, must be discarded if they have settled upon it. (31)
Having sprinkled [the offering] with astrological water (astrodaka), one should present it to the deity with devotion;
however, listen now to the specific rule regarding the preparation of the great oblation (mahāhavis).
Food cooked elsewhere in a kitchen by those other than initiated ones, food not consecrated with mantras, food that has not been shared, and food lacking auspicious marks— [these are forbidden].

Having sprinkled with water from the weapon-mantra that which has been inspected by those unfit [to look] or touched by flies and the like, one should offer the food for presentation with great care and reverence.
One should not give [the offerings] to the Senāśās; one may perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to one's inclination.
One should not cause the presentation of gifts or the offering of oblations (bali) to be made to artisans. || 35 ||

To guests who have arrived, to those who are destitute, and even to the wretched and the helpless, one should give; otherwise, with an undistracted mind, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
And by creatures such as cats, mongooses, snakes, and frogs;
and by worms, insects, moths, and the like; and by birds and other sky-dwellers. || 37 ||
A defiled or touched great oblation must not be offered to the God of gods.
Once it has been offered, sacrificed, and recited over, one should offer the great oblation again.

The enjoyment, mantras, ritual actions, and meditations of the mudrās who possess bodily forms, as well as those belonging to the gates and enclosures, and those forming the images, pedestals, and so forth; || 39 ||
And when there is a reversal of other times as well—those characterized as constant, occasional, and so forth—it occurs through the five pervasive divine [powers]. (40)
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations one hundred times each with sesame seeds and other materials,
as well as with sacrificial fuel sticks, enclosing twigs, *darbha* grass, ritual brooms (*kūrca*), and clarified butter.

In the absence of vessels such as the *ājyasthālī*, of the fire, of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and the pit (*kuṇḍa*), of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, or of the *praṇītā* water-vessel, one should avoid those that lack the proper characteristics.
For the sake of pacification, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations as before with the five pervasive substances;
in the absence of wooden fuel-sticks, he should offer oblations with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru).
In the absence of clarified butter, one should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks or with sesame seeds;
if other sacrificial offerings are unavailable, the wise man should offer with clarified butter alone. 44.
For the purpose of all fire-offering rituals, one must not omit sesame seeds and clarified butter;
for in the absence of sesame and clarified butter, the oblation would be fruitless.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) during the consecration as prescribed,
whether in the fire, in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), on the ground, or in a hearth that has been consecrated and has reached its proper state.
Having re-established the fires and performed the consecration,
one should offer oblations such as the *śānti-homa* when the fire has been touched by those who are untouchable, or even by hair, bones, and nails.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred times with the root mantra as prescribed;
however, if one has been in close proximity to a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, or others such as these, one should offer ten thousand oblations.
If [the fire] is touched by another, one should compose oneself and offer oblations while reciting ten thousand [mantras].
If oblations are offered into a fire that lacks fuel, one should perform the homa again.
On occasions requiring specific signs, during rites for desired objects, and especially on festivals,
one should perform the sacrifice to the fire— which is a limb of that [rite]— in this very pit.
One should perform the Śānti-homa if the opposite occurs;
[one should worship] the attendants, both the formless and the formed, in their proper order.
Without having performed worship, one should recite those mantras eight hundred times each in front of the deity for a full day and night, beginning with the rites of adoration.

In the event of the falling of sacrificial offerings, or upon touching something untouchable, as well as when a vessel not approved by one's teacher is defiled by hair, a clod of earth, or similar impurities; || 53 ||
Having abandoned that [defective vessel] and prepared another, one should perform the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma).
If the vessel is defective, one should not offer the sacrificial food (bali) unless it is preceded by the propitiatory oblation.
Having offered the bali-oblation especially, one who possesses the mantra should recite the previously mentioned [mantra].
When the image intended for the daily festival falls from its vehicle, [the following should be done]. || 55 ||

Having extracted that very image and bathed it with unbroken grains, the knower of mantras should subsequently perform oblations according to the lowest-of-the-low method for the sake of pacification.
In that same manner, having restored the damaged image to its former state and having performed the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should subsequently install it in its proper place.
For as long as the time of the meditative absorption lasts,
one should perform the daily festival of Hari either with another image, or with a broom (kūrca), or with another form.

If the sacrificial image (balibimba) has been touched by those who are untouchable, one should perform an ablution according to the lowest-of-the-low method, preceded by a propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa).
If the image is situated in a vehicle or if it has been handled by unworthy persons,
one should sprinkle it with water infused with kuśa grass and perform a propitiatory fire sacrifice (śāntihoma).
If the carrier of the image of the Lord has been touched by those who are untouchable,
he should be sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then made to carry [the image] again by another pure person.
If there is a deficiency in the mudrās, mantras, ritual actions, meditations, and substances that constitute the objects of enjoyment—especially at the time of the bali offering—[the rite fails]. 62.
The practitioner of mantra, endowed with meditative concentration, should recite the root mantra one thousand times;
however, if nothing has been offered, fruits, flowers, cooked rice, and so forth must be given.
One should recite the root mantra ten thousand times for the sake of one who is fit;
having consumed the remnants of the oblation and the remnants of the sacrificial offering, provided that no other persons worthy of it have eaten. (64)

The mantra-reciter should mutter ten thousand recitations of the root-mantra for the sake of pacifying his sins, together with the Sātvatas—who are devoted to goodness and are always dear to the Blessed One. (65)
Whatever truth was spoken to the Blessed One was a purifier of purifiers,
even for one who has slain a Brahmin, one who has drunk liquor, or one who has committed the theft of gold.
Even for one who has violated the teacher’s bed or is associated with such [sinners], the consumption [of this] destroys all sins; how much more so, then, for others?
Therefore, that should be bestowed upon those who are foremost among the wise;
it should be given to the initiated members of the three higher castes in the intermediate manner.
However, for those twice-born devotees who possess only the three Vedas, the offering of the principal portion may serve as a substitute;
otherwise, he himself should consume it.
O Lord, that which is offered to Viṣvaksena by the mantra-practitioners at the conclusion of the worship must not be eaten;
it should especially be discarded upon the earth, in water, or elsewhere.
Or, for the sake of the satisfaction of cows who have become Viṣṇu, and for those desiring their welfare,
the eater [of the meat] should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow for the purpose of pacifying his sin.
If, after resolving upon the sacrifice, the oblation is not performed up to the end of the homa,
the best of those who know the mantras should perform double the oblation until the conclusion with the full vessel (pūrṇāhuti).
In the times of one, two, three, four, five, and six [years], respectively;
and likewise in one year, half a year, a month, a season, and a year. || 73 ||
When the fire-rites, both daily and occasional, have been omitted,
one should perform the inferior ablution (snapana) with double the number of mixed oblations (homa).
O Sage, listen as I declare the expiation for the omission of worship regarding those [offerings] that are formal, tactile, and heart-pleasing in form. (75)

And upon the exhaustion of the three types of enjoyments in due order, O Sage, at the conclusion of the worship, one should offer all seeds, wealth measured by the *mātrā* unit, and rice cooked with ghee.
The offering should be presented to the Lord preceded by a special sacrifice;
and on the first day of the fortnight, there should be a special worship at that same time.
One should perform the rites ending with the bali offering and homa using materials doubled for each successive stage,
from the worship of one month up to that of twelve months.
Even when worshipping for a number of months with materials doubled from that amount,
the bathing ritual is likewise ninefold, beginning with the lowest of the low.

One should perform, in due order, the sprinkling with a thousand jars— which concludes with the primary and supreme [consecration]— as well as the ritual sprinkling and the installation as prescribed by the rules.
Beginning with the monthly worship up until the twelfth month,
one should perform the sacrifice with great oblations, increasing the offering by one at each stage.
Having first offered seven fuel-sticks (samidhs) soaked in ghee,
the practitioner of mantras should subsequently offer oblations of ghee, from one thousand times up to his full capacity.
In that very manner, one should perform the recitation of the root mantra with devotion;
however, if the offering of oblations (bali) has been omitted, one should then offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra.
One should offer oblations one hundred times each with ghee mixed with sesame seeds, using the respective names of the deities of the various doors of the enclosure.
I shall proclaim to you the expiation for the daily and other ritual ablutions;
a wise person should perform the daily and other ablutions during the worship at home. (85)
There, one should consecrate [the deity] with water for bathing for the sake of worship.
In the case of multiple images, however, one should bathe the ritual image (karmārcā) in the front maṇḍapa.
In the palace, situated in the eastern quarter and provided with an extensive auspicious seat,
one should perform the ritual bathing with consecrated jars in the front pavilion.
At midday and also in the evening, one should sprinkle [the deity] in due order with waters drawn from bathing jars, either combined with bathing substances or used alone.
Or one should perform the presentation of the primary image and the other images;
in the case of many images, having taken that [offering] from the front pavilion, one should perform the consecration and worship.
If the practitioner of mantra goes outside for the purpose of bathing while [the deity] has gone out,
he should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of that fault.
Once, in the form of Bṛhadrūpa, one should consecrate the ritual image with many large jars, such as those containing a thousand pitchers and so forth. || 91 ||
When the external consecration takes place in the pavilion,
the mantra-master, having bathed the candidate with the auspicious bathing rite according to the rules and with great magnificence, [proceeds].

Having performed worship during the festive procession and having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), if one does not perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) for the purpose of the ceremonial bath with the water-pot (kalaśasnāna), [one incurs a fault]. || 93 ||
Likewise, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times while binding the *pratisarā* cord;
having first offered the sprouts, one should also bind the protective amulet (*kautuka*) upon the image.
Whether by the ministers or the assembly, if one does not perform the ceremonial bath,
one should first perform a propitiatory fire-oblation and then recite the mantra ten thousand and eight times.
One should again perform the consecration preceded by the rite of the sprouts of curiosity;
however, if one has not performed the sacrifice of the sprouts as well as the tying of the marriage-thread, [the following applies]. 96.
If the Lord of Gods is bathed [without these], that bathing shall be fruitless;
likewise, the sowing of sprouts and the binding of the protective thread must be performed according to the prescribed rite. || 97 ||

The mantra-practitioner should perform the ritual bath according to the rules, preceded by a peace-offering (śāntihoma). However, if the intended bath has not been performed, he should perform double the rite.
Even if [the image] has been bathed with substances that have not been procured or are deficient, one should act in this same manner;
however, [this applies] only after first [using] the water contained in the consecrated jar.

There shall be no loss due to the lapse of time through the placement of mantras and likewise through worship; however, if the jars have been set out and then become deficient, they should be established again as before.
One should recite the mantra dedicated to the deity of the pitcher one hundred and eight times while the jars have been lifted up and are empty due to a hole or similar defect.
Having installed another [liṅga] as before, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
likewise, when it has been touched by those who are untouchable, or bitten by cats and the like.
If the collection of water jars is defiled by dogs and the like, or by cocks and the like, or by low-caste people such as Śabaras, or by hair, bones, and clods of earth; || 103 ||
Having established the six substances as before, one should recite the mantra dedicated to that deity a hundred times;
if the deity has been bathed by wicked persons, one should consecrate it once again.
One should offer one hundred oblations for each of the five pervasive mantras.
As before, one should recite the mantra dedicated to the deity of the water-pot while endowed with meditative concentration.
If mantras are extracted out of order, established incorrectly, joined with wrong substances,
or not worshipped, one should recite them one hundred and eight times.
The knower of mantras, having performed the ritual bathing of the God of gods with curd, milk, ghee, and other products derived from buffalo, goat, and camel, using the root mantra; 107.
One should perform the oblation with seven kinds of fuel sticks, one hundred and eight times, without the accompaniment of songs, auspicious musical instruments, hymns, dances, and the like. 108.
Accompanied by the sounds of lutes and flutes, as well as auspicious recitations, one should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times when consecrating without [the full ritual]. || 109 ||
But when the image is being consecrated, if it falls from the bathing seat,
or especially if it moves, one should perform the installation-consecration and the ceremonial bath again.
Having offered oblations with ghee and *caru*, as well as the previously mentioned five roots,
one hundred and eight times, one should then recite [the mantra] that same number of times.
In an image defiled by [defects such as] the radiance, the pedestal, the weapons, the garments, the limbs, or by fractures and the like,
one should join the respective power residing in that image to the permanent liṅga (dhruvakautuka).
Having had the joints joined by artisans and having well-prepared it at that very time,
once the remaining work is completed, one should bathe it according to the supreme procedure.
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds, sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter, each a thousand times, with the root mantra; by that, peace shall be attained. || 114 ||
If, due to the great effort required, one is unable to construct it at that time,
one should perform the remainder of the rite using images placed before oneself for the sake of beauty.

Likewise, in the case of images intended for festivals, pilgrimages, purposes, or as bed-decorations, there is again the installation (*sthāpana*) consisting of the joining of their respective limbs and so forth. || 116 ||

When the substances for the ablution are more or less than the prescribed measure—in the case of a shallow bowl, a pitcher, a grass mat, a cloth, a chest, or even the assembly hall— [the following applies]. (117)
Likewise, [one should worship] upon the sacrificial ladles and other vessels, on the pedestal, the archway, and the eight auspicious symbols;
on the auspicious jars at the entrance, and on all other implements used for the ritual. || 118 ||
The wise practitioner of mantra should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
one who seeks liberation should bathe the deity at all times according to the prescribed rite.
One should always perform [the rite] during the day for the purpose of subduing enemies;
however, one who desires heaven should do so in the forenoon, and one who seeks dharma in the middle of the day.
One who desires all enjoyments at the end of the vow, or one who always seeks expiation,
should bathe the Lord during an eclipse of the moon or sun at that very time.
During the solar transits, both before and after [the moment of transition],
sixteen nāḍīs each are known through the understanding of the time of the transit, just as previously described.

At that time, one should bathe the deity; once the ritual sequence has proceeded, one should offer oblations with the mantra a thousand times, and thereafter perform an equal number of recitations (japa). || 123 ||
Previously, for the sake of all ritual actions, when [the seeds] have been offered as sprouts—[seeds] that are reddish, dark-colored, and likewise curved. || 124 ||
When the sacrificial pits are crooked, not properly dug, or facing south;
when the rites are performed without the prescribed rules, or when they are touched by those who are untouchable, or when they are devoid of the authorized officiants. (125)
If the *pālikā* and other vessels are broken, lost, or fallen,
or if they have been bitten by mice and the like, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times.
When the sprouts had been offered for the sake of a single sacrifice previously, and while that [sacrifice] was not yet completed, another special [occasion] arrived. (127)
For that purpose, one should perform the rite of depositing sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) in small pots at the beginning and end of the festival, excluding the protective thread (rakṣāsūtra). || 128 ||

When the consecration of an image for which the protective thread has been tied is about to be performed by the mantra-practitioner, and another consecration arrives on account of an urgent ritual requirement; || 129 ||
For that purpose, having tied the auspicious thread (kautuka) and completed the rite of bathing,
one should perform the previously commenced task immediately after the expiation (prāyaścitta).
One may perform other rites according to one's desire only after completing what was previously begun;
otherwise, O twice-born one, this ritual becomes fruitless. (131)
To avoid those defects, the knower of mantras should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma) and recitation (japa),
employing the root mantra one thousand times.
When this *snapana* has been completed, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times;
[this protects against] creatures such as mice, snakes, frogs, and *cucuṃdarī* rodents. || 133 ||
If the pitcher is touched, stepped over, or otherwise disturbed once it has been established, one should abandon it;
having established another in the same manner, the Guru should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
When penances have not been specifically mentioned, and in cases such as these,
the Guru should recite the root mantra ten thousand and eight times.
O Sage, I shall now declare the expiation regarding the procedure for the great festival:
one should not perform the great festival once the image has been installed in the house. (136)
The independent and the dependent [forms] are twofold, such as the divine sense-bases and so forth;
[they are located] on mountain peaks, on riverbanks, near sacred fords, and in the presence of the Lord. (137)
O best of beings, know that which is established as a separate residence (ālaya) to be independent;
that which is arranged as a subordinate part of a village or the like is said to be dependent. (138)
O Sage, one should perform for those two a great festival of thirteen kinds,
having made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) regarding whichever one among them occurs during the course of the year.
But one should not make the festival of the day deficient for the sake of personal splendor;
if one should do so unintentionally, one must perform the festival again once it has passed.

However, it should be performed first for the sake of pacification; otherwise, there would be the destruction of the king, even if [the banner] is on a cloth from a lineage lacking authority, or if the banner-staff is small. (141)
In cases involving caste, ornaments, honor, and so forth, as well as punishment, a staff, a Daitya, a comb, a pit, a seat, a water-shed, and the rope of a banner; 142.

One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) according to the rules, ending with the recitation (japa), as previously described, in the event that [the vessel] is cut, broken, scorched by fire, lost, or bitten by a mouse. || 143 ||
Having discarded the banner defiled by feces, urine, blood, undrinkable liquids, semen, spittle, and so forth, one should procure another as previously described.
Then, having established the tip of the staff and measured it with the lowest unit,
one should bathe it and offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter for the sake of pacifying any defects.

For the purpose of protection, it is not a fault for those initiated—such as the twice-born and others—to climb to the top of the pillar to attach the cloth of the banner; this is permissible because it is for the sake of protection.
Having discarded the well-worn tips of the flagstaffs and so forth, one should prepare other [new ones] there,
and having quickly fastened them, one should raise the banner.
One should perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), ending with the ritual bathing of the central image,
when the banner of the bird [the flagstaff] has lost its color due to contact with rain, wind, and sun.

Nothing at all undesirable would occur, up until the festival at the top of the pillar; for if the banner-cloth is fastened to the pillar, it might be caused to fall by the force of the wind or other such factors. (149)
When its base has been severed and it has fallen along with its banner,
one should immediately stabilize the remaining portion without causing further separation of the banner.
One should perform the supreme snapana rite, including worship at the four locations, and should offer gifts of cows, land, gold, barley, and so forth, according to one's capacity. (151)
By the breaking of the festival banner, the king shall be deprived of his kingdom;
therefore, to avoid that, one should quickly perform a propitiatory rite. 152.
If the banner falls to the ground due to causes such as the force of the wind, it must be quickly raised and tied back; furthermore, the lowest initiation (adhamasnapana) should be performed.
For the sake of pacification, one should offer clarified butter with sesame seeds one hundred times;
when the banner has fallen or been broken, one should perform the supreme ritual bathing.
Furthermore, having produced another [officer], he should likewise bind him to the conditioned;
otherwise, there would be fault for the king, the kingdom, and the ministers. (155)

If the pitcher presided over by the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is lost, or has fallen to the ground, or has been touched by those who are untouchable, or by hair, clods of earth, bones, excrement, and the like; || 156 ||

Having transferred that power residing within the central jar into another jar, the practitioner of mantra, having recited the root mantra ten thousand times, should perform the remaining rites. || 157 ||
But for all those not specifically mentioned, one should likewise recite according to one's ability during the act of beating the drum for the purpose of invoking the deities. 158.
When all types of musical instruments, such as the mṛdaṅga and paṇava drums, have been placed in their proper positions during this performance of worship, there shall be no interruption. 159.

In the absence of the recitation for an auspicious day, as well as when there is a low-lying or deep path, and when beings are accompanied by their hosts, and when there are fierce planets and so forth; || 160 ||
In their respective directions, according to the rule, over the unoffered [deities], and likewise upon the gates, the enclosures, the streets, and the village sites in due order. || 161 ||
But when the offering of oblations is omitted, as well as in the case of improper tāla rhythms and so forth,
or when the songs and dances are deficient, one should perform a pacifying rite preceded by a fire sacrifice (śānti-homa).
The wise practitioner should repeat the mantra of each deity eight times;
then he should perform everything again, beginning with the invocation of the deities.
One should commence the great festival with the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa);
or, when the day arrives again, one may perform the offering of the germinating seeds immediately.
One should perform the Śānti-homa a hundred times as before;
likewise for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā) or for the attainment of success in the Būtarātra and other rites. || 165 ||

Likewise, if at the time of the descent [of the deity] and during the rite of applying the sprouts to the limbs, the ritual for the limbs and the binding of the *kautuka* amulet have not been performed; 166 ||
The pacification rite (śānti) should be performed as before through fire-oblation (homa) and recitation (japa),
during the preparatory consecrations for festivals, and also during the worship at the four locations.
During the inaugural consecration of the ritual jar, the bathing of the image used for the bath, the great oblation, and the fire sacrifice, as well as on those days and likewise at night; || 168 ||
The offering for the deities of the night, beginning with the Bhūtas, is made with the aforementioned substances during the fire-sacrifice,
as well as in the garden, during play, and at the festival of the hunt.

If a deficiency occurs specifically during the hunt, one should perform the appropriate pacificatory fire-offerings (śānti-homa) and other rites, and then proceed with the remainder of the ritual. || 170 ||
When the vehicles have been occupied by the image, or have fallen, or even when the mounts have been broken somewhere due to negligence; 171.
Having placed it upon another vehicle or on a carrier out of curiosity,
one should first perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and then recite the root mantra a thousand times.
One should give cows, land, gold, and so forth to the Vaiṣṇavas and also to the preceptor when the image has fallen from its vehicle or its mount. (173)

Following the procedure described in the Valibera [Tantra], one should perform the ritual bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), concluding with the recitation of mantras, preceded by meditative absorption (samādhi). || 174 ||
When the long-term meditative absorption (samādhi) has been completed, one should perform the rites for beauty and auspiciousness;
the remaining rites should be performed during the daily worship once the concluding ritual (sandhikarma) has been finished.
Having established the [deity] facing east as before, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) according to the rules;
likewise, one should hold a festival in empty villages, cities, towns, and so forth.
One should not perform the offering of a sacrificial victim (balidāna); even if performed there, it is fruitless.
However, in a village or similar place, one should do so with a great rite of pacification (mahāśānti) preceded by a state of meditative concentration (samāhita).

Furthermore, one may perform the festival again with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, in the event that the village or its vicinity has been burnt by fire or damaged by a whirlwind, torrential rain, or similar calamities. (178)
Having first performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should subsequently carry out the festival;
when the divine images have been installed upon the mountain peaks, a great festival should be held.
One should perform [the rite] right there as space permits, preceded by an offering (bali);
or, if possible, one may perform the festival in a nearby agrahāra or similar location. || 180 ||
One should perform the circumambulation there without offering the bali-oblation,
at the time of the invocation of the deities, before they have been summoned by the Lord.
One should offer the bali for the sake of the festival day and night upon the great seat (mahāpīṭha) in due order to the hosts of gods, asuras, and other beings. || 182 ||
Having offered sprouts for the sake of the banner, or likewise having raised the banner,
and having tied the protective thread (kautuka) for the sake of initiation prior to the ritual purification at the sacred ford (tīrtha-aghamarṣaṇa).

If the preceptor is ill or has died, or if he is occupied with another task, or if there is an obstacle such as birth-impurity (sūtaka), the completion of the remaining rites should be performed [by another]. || 184 ||
Having had another preceptor perform the rite, one should then mutter the root mantra ten thousand times;
this is to be done in the event of obstacles or during a great festival, due to fear of enemies, thieves, fire, rain, and so forth.
The preceptor should offer the bali-oblation on that very day when [the obstacle] has arisen;
even if it has passed, he should offer the overdue bali accompanied by propitiatory fire-offerings (śāntihoma) and recitation (japa).
On the prescribed day, he should perform festivals and processions, and hold a great celebration;
even when the pilgrimage has been interrupted, he should descend from the vehicle bearing the bird-banner.
Having raised the banner as before, one should perform the festival until the end of the pilgrimage site;
every night, with a change of sacrificial materials, one hundred oblations should be made with clarified butter.
Having offered oblations into the fire with the root mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times;
at other times, one should offer the bali-oblation as soon as it becomes available.

If the great festival has not been commenced, preceded by the offering of sprouts and the recitation and fire-oblation for the offering-deities (balidevas) performed in that manner, [the following must be done]. 190.
In the same manner, having performed the sowing of the seedlings, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
especially so when sowing in earthen pots, on the streets, in enclosures, or during festivals.
One should offer oblations to the spirits at village sites and on roads;
however, one should not perform them in a sanctuary for the sake of increasing the king's kingdom.
One should offer a bali-oblation even in that temple for the sake of the prosperity of the village and so forth;
however, if the bali-offering is performed otherwise, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
If the image is touched by fireflies, dust, mist, rain, wind, heat,
or similar elements during the great festival, one should perform a recitation of mantras along with a fire sacrifice (homa).
In the case of the burning by fire of water-stalls, pavilions, or vessels, it is as stated before;
and when lamps have been extinguished, the rite for pacification is declared to be as before. || 195 ||
Likewise, [he saw] garments, ornaments, garlands, and weapons,
as well as great auspicious objects such as the royal umbrella and chowries.
When a fire has broken out, one should likewise rebuild those pedestals that take the form of the limbs of the banner, the archway, and the other [components]. || 197 ||
One should perform the peaceful fire-oblation (śāntihoma) accompanied by recitation (japa), one hundred and eight times;
this applies especially to all the lamps previously mentioned. || 198 ||
When the [image] has fallen to the ground, the knower of mantras, having offered one thousand and eight oblations with the root mantra, should recite it that same number of times. || 199 ||
One should perform the festival day and night, from sunrise until sunset;
if the sequence of the times is reversed, it is considered an inferior ablution.
A pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā) should be undertaken before sunset;
or one may perform it during the first part of the night, when one's own manifestation and the divine are clearly perceived.
One should perform the supreme ablution when the auspicious time for the sacred ford has passed;
it should be done when the lunar mansion of the ford is joined with the second day and conjoined with the moment of Puruhūta.
If both [the teacher and the disciple] were present, that merit would have occurred previously;
however, during the festival procession of the deity, the preceptor was touched by those who are untouchable. (203)

No fault should be recognized there, especially in the presence of a deity; during a festival or when the rite of oblation is omitted, one should perform double the number of oblations or recitations.
Each of the devotees, facing the direction in which the deity was present, recited the root mantra accompanied by the "eye-weapon" (netrāstra) one hundred times. 205.
He should be gratified according to one's ability with garlands, perfumes, garments, milk-rice, food and drink, cakes, excellent fruits, and betel leaves mixed with fragrances.
When the Lord of Gods has been worshipped by well-established teachers or practitioners seated upon their seats, there is no fault due to the weight of their devotion. (207)
When the image has been lost by thieves or others during an ongoing great festival, one should have another image prepared and installed as before. || 208 ||
Having performed the great consecration, the fire sacrifice, and the recitation of mantras according to the prescribed rules,
one should complete the remainder of the festival, or perform the ritual acts such as worship and so forth.
One seeking total peace should perform it at night; one seeking nourishment at midday;
one seeking growth in the forenoon; and one seeking dharma in the middle of the night.
Likewise, one who desires the destruction of enemies should perform a sacrifice with flowers;
however, one should not worship with flowers that are stale or withered.
When those defects have been eliminated, one should perform the bathing; one should carry out the intermediate rite.
One should not perform the supreme bathing if this Flower Sacrifice has not been performed.
Six types of preceptors (deśikas) have been fully described, specifically for the Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga);
however, four are proclaimed for the purpose of worshiping the four locations. || 213 ||
Likewise, one [type of flower] is for bathing and worship, while another is for offerings such as the *bali*;
flowers that have risen from water remain pure even after three nights have passed. || 214 ||
O best of beings, one may employ them in a flower sacrifice; there is no fault in those cases.
Likewise, even white water-lilies (kahlāra) may be used for the purpose of worship with flowers.
Likewise, one should especially offer leaves of the *damanī* plant during a flower sacrifice;
having fasted during the previous night, one should worship the Lord during the day.
One should not worship in that manner during the night after having stayed awake since the forenoon;
rather, one should perform the bathing only after the great festival has concluded and the [initial] bath has been performed. || 217 ||
Then, for the sake of pacification, one should perform the oblation according to the inferior or superior path.
That night, having lowered the bird-banner from the top of the flagpole—
Having offered the bali-oblation to those residing in the village and other dwellings, one should dismiss them;
at the end of the festival, when the banner has perished, [one should perform the rite] prior to its descent.
Having raised the banner as before, one should lower it once again;
this may be performed on a single day with two offerings, or likewise with only a single offering.
Whether devoid of the Bali-tīrtha or lacking the ritual circumambulation,
one who is endowed with the four Balis [attains the goal] in three days or five days.
For those situated above the five [elements], one should perform the bali offering after subtracting twice the number of days from the total count of days, asterisms, and festivals. || 222 ||
If these great festivals are joined with more or fewer folds [of skin], they bring misfortune to the performer and the patron, as well as to the king, the kingdom, and the ministers. (223)
Terrible diseases and miseries will constantly arise;
to pacify those defects, one should perform ablutions, whether inferior or superior.
When the Vaiśeṣika rites have been performed and the great festival is underway,
one should duly worship all of that on the twelfth day and the following days.

A wise practitioner should not, with effort, omit that which has been specifically obtained; furthermore, for the sake of pacifying any omissions, the mantra-reciter should recite the Astra-mantra ten thousand times.
From here, I shall describe for you the expiation for the omission of the *pavitrārohaṇa* rite,
as well as for the absence of the *pavitra* threads and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and mandala.
Having recited the weapon-mantra ten thousand times, one should worship the binding of the weapon,
as well as the filling substances such as leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
However, if the aforementioned time has passed, one should perform the middle ablution in the midst of the four-month period,
or otherwise perform it at another appropriate time.
Likewise, when the proper time has passed or in other such cases,
pacification is performed in this manner with purifying substances such as hair, stones, leather, charcoal, nails, and so forth.
If it has been defiled by fire, burnt, cut, bitten, or eaten by mice and the like, or touched by crows and the like, one should discard that [portion] and [use] it again. || 231 ||
Having fashioned [the image] in such a manner according to the sūtras and performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as before,
one should perform the supreme ablution (snapana) and then install the sacred thread (pavitraka).

For the sake of pacification, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations in sequence with honey, milk, and other substances one hundred and eight times; likewise, he should recite the root mantra and the others that many times.
If [the fire] has been touched by those who are untouchable or has been improperly superposed, one should again superpose another [fire] and perform the pacification rite as before. (234)
If one who is ritually impure should touch the consecrated and worshipped jar,
he should invoke [the deity] into another jar and recite the root mantra a thousand times.
Likewise, having placed [the image] in a broken jar, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times;
in this case, if the image falls, breaks, or is cut, it is as before.
Having performed the rites of concentration and so forth, and having established peace, the preceptor should perform worship with the purificatory materials in their proper sequence. (237)
Having first performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should recite the root mantra one hundred times once the auspicious moment has passed from the commencement of the extensive sacrifice.
Having transferred that [consciousness] into another [image] and performed the supreme consecration by bathing, when many images have been installed in divine temples and other such places; || 239 ||

In the performance of the primary ritual procedure for the rite of ascending the sacred thread (pavitrāroha), many preceptors are prescribed, provided they are endowed with meditation, mantras, and ritual action. || 240 ||
Among them, one was an expert in the worship of the water-pot (kumbha), another in the adoration of the mandala,
another in ritual worship (arcā), and another in the tending of the sacred fire (pāvakārcana).
Likewise, there is one [mantra] for the Mūlālaya, another for the worship of Śobhāśraya, yet another for the worship of Garuḍa, and another supreme one for the worship of Viṣvaksena. || 242 ||
Likewise, one [image] may be for the bathing idol, another for the offering of oblations;
yet another for the daily fire-sacrifice, and another for the ritual of the great meal. || 243 ||
Or, having considered the lightness of the ritual act, it may be performed with eight [mantras];
in each respective case, the supreme *pavitrārohaṇa* must be performed by them.
Having performed a festival for one day on that day as before,
one should undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites on another day during the daytime.
One should perform the *tīrthāghamarṣaṇa* for two nights, or starting from the first day;
then, beginning from the second day, one should observe the three-night festival on the fourth day.
A great festival shall be held for either a week beginning from the principal day, or for those two days;
at the conclusion of these, the pilgrimage to the sacred site (tīrthayātrā) must be performed as before.

In this manner, the rites for the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed at the various holy sites (tīrtha). If a pilgrimage to these sites has not been undertaken, the supreme ritual bath (snapanottama) serves as the expiation.
Having first performed the rite of offering the sprouts (aṅkārpaṇa), one should commence the festival as before;
then, on the night of that sacred day (tīrthadinayāminī), there shall be the dismissal of the sacred threads (pavitravisarjana).
Having performed [the rite], it should be offered to the Guru by those proficient in the meaning of the Pāñcarātra; in his absence, to other Ācāryas in due order. || 250 ||
It should be offered to others after assigning it to those who are unfit;
then, having formally presented it again according to the rules and having bestowed the purificatory items (pavitra), [one should proceed]. || 251 ||
Having performed the intermediate ablution, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma),
either according to the previously established procedure or in accordance with the rules for the Cāturmāsya sacrifice.
On the previously mentioned superior, middling, and inferior days,
and likewise when only one day is designated, [the practice] should be preceded by the Cāndrāyaṇa.
On the day immediately following that, he should begin it;
for the first eight fortnights, he should remain self-restrained according to the prescribed rule.
Having resolved upon the four-month vow while engaged in this most excellent observance,
should it be interrupted in its midst due to reasons such as dependence on others, [one must perform the following].
Having resolved upon it at another time, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances;
and at that [specific] time, one should duly perform the rites of lying down and so forth.
In the event of their transgression or omission, the mantra-practitioner should perform worship at the four locations and so forth;
having recited the root mantra ten thousand times, he should then offer oblations for the sake of pacification.
[This applies] to those who possess forms such as Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, Kroḍa, Hayagrīva, Haṃsa, and others, as well as to those distinguished by their faces, and especially to Śaktīśa. || 258 ||
And likewise [there are the incarnations] of the Lord Jāmadagnya, of Viśvarūpa,
of the one who took away the Pārijāta tree, and likewise of Hari in the form of Kalki.
One should not, however, sleep upon palaces that possess a stable foundation; rather, having approached a pleasant form, one should perform the marriage-thread ceremony according to one's desire.
For that purpose, one should have [the deity] laid down according to the rules during the Cāturmāsya period;
then, when the Lord of Devas has been raised up and worshipped in his fourfold station, [one should proceed]. || 261 ||
