Having adorned the Lord, who has come for the festival worship, with garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth according to what is beautiful, one should install him upon the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).

Having specifically circumambulated the entire multitude of worlds according to the prescribed rite for the pacification of defects, following the procedure described for the great festival; || 263 ||
Then, by means of the practice of one night and so forth, according to the previously mentioned rule,
one should perform the avabhṛtha bath for the Lord on a riverbank or similar location.
In the absence of that [primary rite], the procedure for the secondary option (anukalpa) consists of the Tīrtha-aghamaṛṣaṇa;
this occurs during the transit of the sun at midday, as well as on the two New Moon days. || 265 ||
In the same way, the month devoid of the new moon (darśa) is called the intercalary month (malamāsa);
this Cāturmāsya period is not to be undertaken at its beginning or end. || 266 ||
When the previously mentioned three-day period has commenced during the middle [of the lunar month],
there is sometimes no fault due to the occurrence of an intercalary month (malamāsa).
Likewise, when Jupiter or Venus are in an intercalary month, one who desires his own welfare should not undertake the commencement of any festive rite anywhere. || 268 ||
In self-manifested shrines and the like, at sacred fords on mountain peaks, and in delightful riverbanks, forests, and groves; || 269 ||
Furthermore, having resolved to dwell for a fixed period in the cow-pens of the foremost sages and in the hermitages of Hari for the sake of accomplishing his desired vow, he remained there.
The leaders of the guides should likewise lead [the devotees] for four months;
during this time, crossing rivers, mountains, and the like must never be undertaken.
Even when separated by rivers and the like, those entitled to an auspicious pilgrimage must go toward a divine sanctuary within a distance of one yojana. || 272 ||
Especially for those who are devoted to the constant worship [of the deity] with the five pervaders preceded by the twelve syllables, and whose souls delight in the five times (pañcakāla). || 273 ||
For those of self-restraint, visiting divine sacred fields does not invalidate their observance; in this time, neither birth-impurity nor death-impurity applies to them.
One must not commit violence against living beings, nor cut down trees, nor breach the banks of rivers or fields, nor wither the crops. (275)
The harassment of those residing in temples and other such places, and the filling up of ponds, wells, and tanks with earth, stones, and the like. (276)
The imprisonment of the twice-born, their living together with those of other castes, conversing with them, as well as the acceptance of gifts from them and the taking of a wife from among them; 277.
At that time, a wise man should especially avoid [such actions];
for one who acts in this manner, there is no atonement through penances. || 278 ||
Sometimes it arises through the establishment of various dharmas;
among those, the installation of Vāsudeva is proclaimed as the foremost.
The installation of the foremost among the exclusive devotees (ekāntin) shall be the middle one;
the installation of all others shall be the final one. || 280 ||
I shall explain, in due order, the expiatory rite for the consecration of [shrines] constructed from earth, stone, wood, and metal. (281)
Whenever those respective materials, mantras, rituals, and so forth have been omitted from their respective parts,
one should again perform pacifying oblations, recitations, and other such rites.
One should practice according to the scripture; otherwise, it is fruitless.
This applies even when the entire selection of the site for the dwelling has not been completed. (283)

Once the image has been brought to the site of the temple, the wise man should, without requiring further honorific rites from the artisans, properly carry out the collection of materials for the worship.

One should proceed in this very same manner with clay, wood, cloth, and so forth; likewise, one should treat a well-fashioned image or stone brought for the purpose of another temple in the same way. || 285 ||
Having taken that image, which is complete in all its limbs yet slow in the act of being established, according to the prescribed rule, one should install it in the abode of the Siddhas.
Having entered into union with another [consort] as before, one should quickly place the fashioned image— which has not yet been installed in one's own home— into the previously prepared location.
It would bring misfortune to the king, the kingdom, and its perpetrator;
after twenty-one days have passed, that [state] will certainly become demonic. || 288 ||
Having performed the great consecration and so forth, one should install [the image]; otherwise, one should abandon it.
This applies to an image that lacks the correct proportions, as well as to its pedestal, weapons, radiance, and so on.
Or else, upon a garment or an ornament, [one should offer] together with śamī leaves, and with rice grains and sesame seeds profusely sprinkled with ghee. || 290 ||
One should perform oblations with each of the five mantras one hundred times during the preliminary consecration in water,
the bathing, and likewise during the opening of the eyes.

On the bed and the altar, during the rites such as the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), and during the worship of the pitcher (kumbha), the mandala, the door-arch (toraṇa), and the pitchers. || 292 ||
If it is not done according to the proper method, peace will certainly not be attained, just as before;
for the image has been installed in an improper place, even though it is provided with a stone pedestal. (293)
At that very moment, having lifted it up, he should install it in its own place;
then, having performed the intermediate ablution, he should carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). || 294 ||
One should not remove the image during this moment when it has not been established; once the bathing and fire-offering have been performed as before, peace will prevail. || 295 ||
When the primary preceptor authorized for the installation is ill, or when his body has been consigned [to the funeral pyre], or while the sequence of ritual actions is still in progress; || 296 ||
The instructor of the ritual mantras, established in the rite of consecration, or the son of the preeminent teacher, should perform the remaining tasks during the installation. || 297 ||
Having first consecrated the Lord of the Gods with a thousand jars,
he then [consecrated him] in the discus-lotus pit with honey, milk, and other substances in due order.
For the sake of pacification, one should perform ten thousand oblations and carry out an equal number of recitations;
this may be done by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras who are absorbed in the Blessed One. || 299 ||
Indeed, for the purpose of installing an image of the Lord, practitioners—whether possessing desires or free from them—should always be devoted to the propitiation of mantras. || 300 ||

Formerly, he was a leader among the twice-born who followed the Pāñcarātra system; he was either one to be propitiated through offerings or one who, preceded by prayer, held a position of authority. || 301 ||

He who is the knower of the manifest Supreme Self, which was previously described in its cosmic manifestation, is always authorized to perform the installation of the images of other deities. || 302 ||
Bestowing grace, establishing [the disciple], and defining the office [of the master]—this is said to be the duty toward those devotees who are endowed with no other [refuge]. (303)
They were non-different from Him, knowers of the five times, none of whom were separate from the Lord;
created before all else, they emerged from His mouth, being contemplators of the twelvefold inner self.
Those for whom the origin and dissolution of all things indeed proceed from the state of the fourfold manifestation,
perform the renunciation of even their actions through the presiding authority in due order.
Therefore, these [persons] are even more difficult to find with respect to that which is supreme:
those whose faith is fixed upon the object of knowledge, or who are clearly established in its practice. (306)
Those situated on other paths do not accept the supremacy [of the Lord] among one another;
and for those who do accept it, there is no such status established in their own systems. (307)
He was indeed one who had transcended all formal qualifications, having attained the true mark,
being unartificial, devoted to the five times, a perfected master, and one who had reached the further shore of the Tantric doctrines and conclusions.
By that very [method], the injunction for even the gross mantras heard from scripture should indeed be performed at every ritual action,
according to the characteristics of the appropriate occasion.
Because, in the activities such as the mandalas originating from the lotus, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, there is always the performance of worship; (310)
Even though its form and its supremacy are eternally established, it will come into proximity for that person who possesses the power [to realize them] within their heart at all times. || 311 ||
The Lord of the World, the Supreme Self, the Imperishable Master, who is the embodiment of mantra—
even for your own mental delight, O Brahmin, he does so without excessive eagerness.
O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining desires or for the sake of fame, he has prescribed that installation [of the deity] with meditation, whether in a temple or even in one's own home. (313)
Thus, O Mahāmati, the primary ritual procedure has been correctly explained; now learn in brief that other secondary procedure which exists herein. || 314 ||

By the twice-born who had previously received initiation according to the rules, who were established in the dharma of the three Vedas, and who were devoted to the constant worship of the all-pervading Lord with devotion; 315.

By those who have attained proficiency in the rites preceded by retention and meditation, and who have exerted themselves in the application of mantras, maṇḍalas, mudrās, weapons, sacrificial fire-pits, and so forth; || 316 ||

By those who are established in the pervasion of the six paths, who possess the habit of renunciation, who are free from envy, who do not abandon the proper sequence, who are skillful, and who protect their own duties; || 317 ||

When the installation is performed, the performer gains a firm standing in the world through those [images] that are renowned for their excellence, as well as through those made of clay, even if they are not famous. (318)
Therefore, for those other than the lotus-eyed Lord (Viṣṇu),
the great festival known as Pratiṣṭhā is always forbidden for performers who offer mixed sacrifices.
Furthermore, those who abide in worldly dharmas and remain in a state of equanimity toward all things,
yet are ignorant of the distinctions regarding the Blessed One, do so only constantly under the influence of their duties.
Indeed, they all proclaim their own superiority through mere words—those who, lacking the requisite authority, have been appointed here to the worship of the deities. (321)
Those who perform sacrifices with mixed motives are indeed established in a state of downfall;
acting in this very manner, they will certainly lead [others] to hell.
But for those purified by true devotion, whose souls are devoted to Vāsudeva,
it never inflicts any fault or destruction upon them on that account.
Therefore, O one of great intelligence, this must first be performed with devotion;
for those established in the mantra, devotion indeed [is essential] in the practice of reciting that mantra. || 324 ||
A mantra that has undergone a transposition of syllables, one in which [syllables] are omitted, or one with an extra vowel or other [element], always brings about misfortune.
Nevertheless, O Lotus-born One, it bestows the desired object upon its practitioners before long, through the power of their supreme devotion. || 326 ||

For this reason, the Lord of Mantras quickly bestows his grace upon those who have purified themselves through true devotion, who have surrendered to him, and whose minds are disciplined, even without following the formal sequence of stages.

How much more so, O best of the twice-born, for those who are perfected in both ritual action and knowledge, who are devoted with faith and bhakti, and who have been instructed by their teachers? || 328 ||
Therefore, O Mahāmati, with every effort, all rites such as initiation and the like should be performed for devotees within this teaching, [which is] compassionate toward its devotees. (329)
Even one who lacks correct understanding of me performs [this practice] for the sake of attaining me;
[this applies to] those of dull or middling devotion whose minds are intent upon desires and enjoyments. (330)
If one performs my initiation for living beings, or the installation [of icons] and so forth, out of delusion, his devotion will arise before long along with the seed-syllable (bīja). || 331 ||

O best of Brahmins, the ritual manual along with its mantras, the systems of action, and the supreme accomplishments will be revealed here quickly; and at the end of the body, one’s lineage shall be extinguished.
Having thus experienced the great consequences of his evil deed, he goes to a terrible hell,
O Blessed One, solely through the power of the mantra and by virtue of its application.
The sin arising from association perishes first; however, by the force of past impressions, one who has committed evil deeds may again obtain a human body.
One should perform auspicious effort by which one may attain peace;
yet one who possesses egoism, even if devoted to his own teacher, is not qualified [for such practice]. || 335 ||
One surely attains one's own destination according to one's own desire, even as a denizen of hell;
yet the twice-born, whose essence is the mantra, pervades all and bestows grace upon all.

Even if it is thus beneficial, one should not resort to that [world] nor remain in its vicinity; rather, having immediately invoked [the deity] from within the image up to the center of the body, [one should proceed]. (337)
O Sage, beings such as bhūtas, vetālas, and yakṣas cause the destruction of wealth and other possessions; furthermore, those who abide in wrong views are not to be favored. 338.
Indeed, such a teacher should be attended upon by one who is terrified of the fear of saṃsāra, who is devoted to perfect devotion, and who is free from hypocrisy and attachment. (339)
Therefore, O Great Buddha, the supreme sacrifice known as Pratiṣṭhā must be performed from beginning to end by Vaiṣṇavas for the sake of the Vaiṣṇavas. (340)
Thus, O Lord of Sages, wherever there is a material structure, it constantly brings about the welfare of both [the builder and the recipient], characterized by compassion and devotion. (341)
For that [rite] called Pratiṣṭhā bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and it is for the sake of self-realization for the twice-born who are established in the True Brahman. || 342 ||
O one of pure vision, that [Veda] is indeed eternally established as something to be performed;
and because of its defects, no expansion of it is found. (343)

There is no other way for that [body] to fall than by the falling away of the physical frame; since its falling otherwise causes excessive fault, therefore, those who have perfected their selves should not practice it from the very beginning.
O Sage, those four who have entered upon that practice should always be properly established by them with a mind of benevolence. (345)
O Sage, there is no obstruction by way of intrinsic nature, nor by greed, nor even by name,
when a sudden affliction such as a bodily fracture has occurred.

Out of compassion for his devotees, [he taught] by means of divine mantras beginning with those of twelve syllables, such as the *bala* mantra and others, which have liberation as their sole defining fruit.
When those devotees have performed the worship, he always effects atonement;
by the destruction of all the images, there is the preparation of [the deity] in the form of a mere limb.
Although the specific details regarding each particular duty have been previously mentioned, nevertheless, listen here to the procedure explained in full detail. 349.

When the image has been thus established by gods, perfected beings, lords of sages, and others, and it is subsequently destroyed by thieves or other causes, one should immediately restore it as before.

The practitioner of mantra should install [the deity] according to the rules during the night, the day, or at the two twilights; however, in the case of a specific restoration of what has been lost, no restriction of time need be observed.
O Sage, listen well to me as I declare the expiation for the first instance of a child’s abode, as well as for the final instance of restoring a ruined temple. (352)

When the time for the construction of a temple and its image has been sought in the past by the patron, the supreme consecration bath (snapana) as declared in the scriptures should be performed. || 353 ||
Even later, one may request the desired time for its completion;
however, this is not possible once the twelve-year period has already passed.

Furthermore, one should perform the re-consecration at the root [shrine] or in the original temple, if the image has been lost to thieves and the like, or due to negligence in the original temple. || 355 ||
Having likewise prepared that image and installed it according to the rules, one should perform the low-grade ablution and carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). || 356 ||
When he has been moved from his own place by whatever cause, one should re-establish Puruṣottama as before and bathe him. || 357 ||
All rites pertaining to the house of a child, consisting of both daily and occasional duties,
up to the final consecration of the sacred thread (pavitrāroha), are to be performed according to the procedure for a single image.
Likewise, if the image has been stolen by thieves, one should fashion a new one endowed with the proper characteristics using the same materials as before, and install it in the very same manner.
The mantra-practitioner should always and everywhere worship the image as before;
or the instructor may fashion it from other materials for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice.
O twice-born one, if the image stolen by thieves is recovered again,
one should perform its re-consecration even without the ritual of opening the eyes.
If one is touched by twice-born men who have become thieves, one should perform the lowest ablution;
however, upon entering the inner sanctum of the womb-chamber, one should perform the highest ablution.
If the image has been left for a long time or has been touched, one should begin the consecration anew;
likewise, if dogs, jackals, cats, or similar creatures have entered the inner sanctum where the deity resides.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) by means of the very same bath for the low-caste;
and when these [images] have been consecrated, one should offer a hundred oblations for the sake of peace.
When the image has been touched by these, one should bathe it with the most excellent liquor;
however, if it is touched by certain birds, a defect will arise in the sanctuary.
If the image is touched by crows, cocks, vultures, or the like through negligence,
one should perform a bath as before and carry out a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
If one is touched by a firefly or similar creatures, one should perform the lowest form of bathing;
however, if touched by bees, flies, or the like, no fault whatsoever shall certainly arise.
Likewise, it is especially not [to be done] with ants and the like, nor primarily with substances such as semen, blood, excrement, urine, things unfit for drinking, meat, and so forth. || 368 ||
If the image of the deity has been touched, one should perform the supreme ritual bathing;
however, if it has been touched by these [impurities] on the courtyard or elsewhere, one should immediately remove it from that spot.
Then, having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should sprinkle it with the five ritual substances.
For the sake of pacification, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of sesame and clarified butter, one hundred times each.

If the image is touched by Vaiśyas who are Vaiṣṇavas, or by Śūdras, or especially by women, when it has been placed upon a palanquin, one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 371 ||

One should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) one hundred times with honey, milk, and other substances, when the image has been touched by those who follow the natural order (anuloma) as well as those of censured descent (pratiloma). || 372 ||
One should always perform the ritual bathing (snapana), the peace-offering (śāntihoma), and the giving of gifts;
however, when [the image] has been touched by Vaikhānasas, it is purified by a bath of milk. || 373 ||
Once one's own path has been propitiated, one should again perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the image,
its pedestal, the temple, and the inner sanctum.
This fourfold form of the God of gods is equal;
likewise, meditative absorption and peace should always be maintained there with equanimity.
Likewise, he drew a lotus within a lotus upon the altar,
in a mandala fashioned with colored powders and constructed from materials such as gold.
Concentration, tranquility, and such practice [are found] within the enclosure adorned with gate-towers, main gates, pavilions, and so forth. (377)
There is no fault if Śiva and others are stationed within the precincts;
however, once they have entered the sacrificial site, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 378 ||

In the pavilions, courtyards, halls, and grounds such as those belonging to the garland-makers and others, by the gurus, practitioners, and initiates who have been enjoined as part of the ritual worship; || 379 ||
There is no fault, O tiger among the twice-born, regarding beds, seats, and food, nor even concerning the washing of feet, sipping water, bathing, anointing with oil, and so forth. (380)

And when these have been prepared by others, one should smear them with cow-dung and sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) accompanied by water infused with kuśa grass. || 381 ||
By means of cats, mice, snakes, frogs, lizards, rats, musk-rats, monitor lizards, rājila snakes, and other such creatures; || 382 ||

Once the inner sanctum has been consecrated, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), even if there are swarms of flies, anthills, or accumulations of insects [within it]. || 383 ||
When the images have been produced within the celestial palaces (vimānas), one should then extract them once more and,
having established them as before, perform the worship and other rites for the four locations.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the God of gods, whether it be of the highest or middling kind, either in a pavilion or elsewhere within the temple of Hari. || 385 ||
When the Brahmadaṇḍa and other trees sprout, when parasols arise, and when the world is crowded with hosts of wicked beings and unprecedented flocks of birds; 386.
One should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) at that very moment after removing them;
once those pavilions have been constructed, one should perform the intermediate consecration bath (madhyama-snapanam).
If the images are present, then one should perform the work of building a residence for the journey and so forth;
having completed the ritual according to the previous procedure, it should conclude with the relinquishment by the king's command.
Having renovated the image, the wise man should re-install it as it was before;
the same procedure applies to images produced from red women. (389)
Having composed himself and established [the deity] once again for the sake of peace, he should bathe the Lord of the God of Gods according to the most excellent of methods. (390)

When these [images] are produced within a vimāna, one should perform the intermediate consecration bath (snāpana); when they are produced in pavilions (maṇḍapa) and similar structures, one should likewise perform the consecration bath. || 391 ||
O best of Brahmins, when these [defects] are seen anywhere, such as on the courtyard or elsewhere,
one should immediately remove them and then sprinkle the area with products of the cow.
For the sake of pacification, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations outside with sesame seeds mixed with ghee,
whenever any improper ritual has been performed in temples or elsewhere.
After the intermediate enclosure, the practitioner of mantras should perform the internal ablution followed by the fire sacrifice (homa) as the final rite;
for the sake of pacification, he should offer oblations into the blazing external fire.

If the temple of the deity is defiled by excrement, urine, saliva, and the like, one should immediately remove those impurities from that place and smear it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The practitioner of mantra should recite the Astra-mantra a hundred times and the Hṛdaya-mantra according to the prescribed rule;
I shall now declare the expiation specifically for touching a corpse.
If a divine image has been inadvertently touched by the corpse of a twice-born person,
one should bathe it with eighty-one jars of water and offer ten thousand oblations with the root mantra.
If the marriage-thread (kautuka) is touched by the corpses of those belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes,
it should be purified with the middle or the highest [mantra] and with a thousand jars of water.
One should bathe the deity one by one in sequence according to the prescribed rule;
having performed the fire-oblation for the sake of pacification, one should recite the mantra as before. || 399 ||
If one touches a corpse in a state of natural decay, one should then perform a ritual sprinkling;
likewise when defiled by a Caṇḍāla, an outcaste, a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, or a corpse. (400)
One should perform the consecration of the images with a bath using a thousand jars;
likewise, one should perform ten thousand pacificatory fire-oblations (śāntihoma) and the recitation (japa) in the proper sequence.
In the case of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), for Brahmins and others, as well as for those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and so forth,
upon touching a corpse, one should wash thoroughly with a jar full of abundant water.
Having bathed the Lord of the gods with each [substance] in sequence— beginning with the highest of the high for the best, and the middling and lowest for the middling and lowest— verse 403.
One should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) and thereafter recite the mantra as prescribed;
beginning with the first circuit, this is done on the western side of the enclosure of the carriage-road.

Once the courtyard area has been purified according to the previously mentioned sequence by those initiated and most proficient in mantras, the ground should be thoroughly cleansed according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed the ablution specifically for the principal, the best, the low, and the lowest in due order,
one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
In this very same manner, one should act upon touching the corpse of those of the lowest castes, whether at a *sāla* pavilion, on a pedestal, at a city gate, or even in a temple. (407)
Outside the celestial palace (vimāna), in certain attendants' quarters and similar locations,
there are [images] of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as those born of natural (anuloma) and other types of unions.

Even when deaths occur among those various lower beings—when these animals such as elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, and so forth have died—[the soul departs] just as it did from each respective inferior body. (409)
In all cases, such as deaths and the like, one should first perform the purification of the ground;
likewise when there are dogs, jackals, corpses, and so forth, or creatures such as crows and hawks.
In the case of cats, monkeys, and other such beings, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) after sprinkling [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 411 ||
When a mouse, a snake, or the like has died, one should perform purification of the ground and recite mantras;
in all cases involving death and similar events, one should first perform the purification of the ground.
In every dwelling, on the great seats, and likewise even upon those made of stone,
one should smear the entire area all around with cow dung.
One should sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), preceded by the proclamation of a meritorious day (puṇyāha).
In the case of a domestic image, there is no fault if it is moved outside the worship chamber once it has died. || 414 ||
One should purify it there with an armor [of protection] consisting of washing, anointing, and so forth;
in the vicinity of the domestic image, one should bathe it with milk and worship it. || 415 ||

In a temple of the Blessed One constructed by gods, perfected beings, lords of sages, and others, or in a village and so forth established as a constituent part of such [a temple], which is crowded with a kingdom; 416.

If the image of the Blessed One has been defiled by Caṇḍālas, outcasts, women in their courses, women who have recently given birth, Śabaras, or others, one should perform the rite of sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
Having consecrated the deity with a thousand jars in close proximity, one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) and the worship of the four locations and so forth. || 418 ||
Thereafter, one should perform that same recitation a thousand times in a temple, at the courtyard gate, in a pavilion, or in the kitchen. (419)
In flower-gardens, water-reservoirs, houses of wealth and grain, and so forth;
on flagstaff-bases, great pedestals, and even among groups of street-surroundings. || 420 ||

In villages and other places prepared as part of a festival, due to the crowding of the populace, [one may encounter] Caṇḍālas, outcasts, women in their courses, women who have recently given birth, Śabaras, and others. || 421 ||
Land that is defiled by the bones of the dead belonging to the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, whether in the natural or inverse order of birth, either everywhere or in a single spot; 422.
Having dug up the earth and cast it outside with pure hands, having filled [the pit] and leveled it, and having wiped it clean with kusha grass and water; || 423 ||
Then, having smeared the ground with cow dung and performed the ritual recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*),
and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should settle the herd of cows there.
Having had the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) recited by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
and having fed the twice-born there, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having thus performed the purification of the gross elements, one should perform, in due order,
the meritorious rite consisting of the five sacrifices (pañcayajña) for the removal of all defects.
Thus, until the end of the rainy season, no propitiatory rite has been performed,
even with a thousand jars of consecrated water.
One should bathe the Lord in five ways with the five all-pervading mantras;
having duly raised the banner, one should first perform the festival beginning with the new vehicle.
For the sake of pacifying all defects, one should perform the *tīrthāghamarṣaṇa* rite in sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a discus,
a conch, a mace, a lotus, and a circle, respectively.
One should perform that [rite] with the five principal [mantras] preceded by the twelve-syllable [mantra],
using the five substances such as honey, milk, and so forth, according to the rite known as *niyuta*.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations by number so that the count reaches one hundred thousand;
this procedure in the alternative method is approved for rites of pacification.
The primary ritual procedure will be explained in detail regarding the performance of the fire oblation (homa),
within an auspicious pavilion prepared according to the prescribed rules for installation.
And when the ten [vessels] located in the east of the wheel-lotus have been properly prepared, having been fashioned from materials such as the *brahma-vṛkṣa* tree and others; 433.
With clusters of sacrificial fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, and clarified butter sprinkled as previously described,
and with the five [substances] beginning with honey mixed together in due order.
For the pacification of great faults, those most skilled in mantras should perform recitation ten thousand,
a hundred thousand, a million, or up to ten million times, according to their strength.
One should offer oblations together with the Pūrṇāhuti in the ten most excellent mantras within the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the center and the east; hear now the rule for these mantras.
In the lotus of the wheel, [one should worship] with the twelve-syllable mantra; in the eight-cornered [lotus], with the eight-syllable mantra;
in the six-cornered [lotus], with the six-syllable mantra; and in the conch-like [lotus], with the *praṇava*. || 437 ||
With the *Jitantā* mantra, one should worship in the four squares; with the *Viśvatrātā*, in the triangle;
and with the *Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh*, in the lotus known to have thirty-two petals.

With the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha [mantra], one should worship in the Cakrakuṇḍa within the Akṣara-spoke; with the Varāha [mantra] in the one called Ardhacandra, and with the Sudarśana [mantra] in the circular [Kuṇḍa]. || 439 ||
The two hearths (dhiṣṇya) previously mentioned should be placed to the south and north of the central altar;
the remaining ones one should construct all around it, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Hotṛs who have mastered the mantras should be appointed for rites of pacification;
all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for all the mantras are to be used according to the will of the Guru. || 441 ||
Or rather, the mantras should be mentally conceived, since they bestow all fruits;
having been properly deposited [on the body], they should be recited according to rule with that specific number.
One should especially bring satisfaction to worthy persons through gifts of cows, land, gold, sesame seeds, and food, as well as to divine shrines and the like.
A king who desires his own welfare and is devoted to protecting his subjects should, with the assistance of many experts in the scriptures and abundant wealth, practice peace in this manner. (444)

If, due to the abundance of all defects, the pacifying rite cannot be performed by those who know the Dharma, then the fivefold rite beginning with the great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed. || 445 ||
And at the conclusion of the great gift-offering, work such as the construction of divine temples and other edifices should be performed repeatedly, according to the rules, with pure wealth.

When there is the falling of meteors or lightning from the sky, when stars fall from the heavens, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze with smoke, and when the king is possessed by spirits and the like; (447)
During a famine, when the kingdom is afflicted by disease, or likewise in times of danger from enemies;
when there is an inversion of the sun's rising, or during an earthquake and the splitting of the earth—448.
In the event of excessive rain, drought, the laughing of a deity, weeping, exhaustion, or even the shaking of the image, [one should perform expiation]. || 449 ||
Likewise, when there is wandering, or when the seats and so forth break, or when there is laxity, or when bees and the like arise in many ways within the house; (450)
When such and other ill omens occur,
peace shall be brought about by performing these [rites] in their proper sequence.
When even a minor fault arises, worship at the four locations must be performed;
for those who are poor, however, a mere gift should somehow be given according to their ability. (452)
If a palace, a pavilion, a hall, a gate-tower, a temple, or similar structures are consumed by fire through negligence, those deities should be taken elsewhere. (453)
Having made it new as before and installed it according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the supreme ceremonial bathing for the pacification of that defect.
If a palace is deficient in even one part due to fire, wind, rain, or for some other reason, it must be repaired by artisans. || 455 ||
Having performed the lowest form of ablution, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma);
and when the temple (vimāna) is broken on all sides, one should designate a place for the child. || 456 ||
In exactly the same way, one should perform all rites—from the daily and occasional duties up to the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa)—upon the image of the Child (Bāla). || 457 ||
Furthermore, for the pacification of those defects, a middling ablution (snapana) should be performed;
regarding the restoration of a broken image, the specific procedure has been previously described.
Nevertheless, that procedure is now being proclaimed in detail; listen to it.
If the primary image has been consumed by fire, one should likewise worship in the place of the child [the secondary image]. (458)
Nevertheless, that procedure is now being declared in detail; listen to it.
If the primary image is consumed by fire, one should likewise worship in the place of the child [the secondary image]. || 459 ||
When discoloration appears on the surface of the fire-pan or other vessels due to the heat, one should perform the ritual bath with a thousand pitchers according to the prescribed injunctions.
One should perform the supreme ablution upon each respective image in due order;
[this is necessary] due to the transgressions of the mantra-practitioners caused by the force of fire, wind, and so forth. || 461 ||
If a golden, silver,
copper, or brass image has a broken limb, it must be immediately joined by the most skilled artisans.
That image should not be joined with another metal, even with great effort;
however, one who lacks wealth may join it with copper or brass. || 463 ||
One should then join it with the same material with which it was originally fashioned;
the discarded image should be cast into the ocean according to the path of the scriptures.
That which is made of gold or silver, even if it has a large fracture or a wound, should not be discarded; rather, having removed the power residing therein, it should be repaired. 465.
One should complete the casting of the image with that same material as before, even if the image made of clay, wood, or stone has been broken for some reason. (466)
Having firmly restrained that power within the image situated in the abode of the ignorant,
and having abandoned the defiled icon, one should then fashion another image.
The clay, the trident, the rope, and so forth, fashioned by the gods, must not be abandoned; nor should they be discarded by the lords of gods, yakṣas, and sages, or by others who follow the Purāṇas.
When the image made of gold or other metals has been thus consecrated and has worn out,
one should subsequently join its limbs back together using gold alone, and not otherwise.
When an image made of stone fashioned by gods, sages, and others is broken,
one should fashion that limb out of gold and join it so that it becomes firm once more.
If an image installed by gods and others has a missing limb or is made of clay, it should never be abandoned; rather, it should then be gradually repaired. (471)
One should always join together a limb that has thus become worn out or damaged;
however, one should not have a child, a house, an image, or the like constructed by anyone other than [the prescribed artisan]. 472.
While the Nitya and other rites are being performed here, all tasks should be carried out by those who are unwearied;
in this very manner, the most skilled knower of the Tantras should cause them to be performed in a self-manifested [shrine].

Or even in the case of a shrine that has been worshipped by gods and others, or one that is self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta), or one made of clay or wood that has become decayed due to worms, fire, water, and so forth; || 474 ||
Having constructed each respective child-house and performing worship as before,
one should gradually perform another rite of worship and install [the deity] according to the prescribed rule.
If the image made of hair becomes worn out here, one should perform this [rite] again and again;
likewise, if an image fashioned by humans ever becomes worn out, destroyed, or defiled.
And when the image is made of stone and lacks the beauty of color and so forth, or even when it is made of clay, or [represented] in paintings, reflections, cloths, and the like; || 477 ||
Having summoned [the deity] into the image of a child and painted it as before,
the best of mantra-knowers should again perform the consecration according to the rules.
When an image intended for desired results (kāmyabimba) or similar object has been fashioned from silver, copper, or even brass, and is being consecrated and worshipped; 479.
When this superior state has been attained and, over time, has decayed, the wise man should abandon the inferior; no fault is found in that.
When the primary image (mūlakautuka) has been established using iron, stone, clay, or wood,
it must never be replaced by any other principal object.

Formerly, when it had reached a state of decay, the primary rite was performed for the two installed [images] within the house—one with many faces and one with a single face—out of devotion to the Mūla-mantra. 482.

Even in the case of restoring a dilapidated temple, the wise have established that it should be performed as before, provided that many images previously installed remain, even if they are devoid of their consorts such as Lakṣmī and others. (483)
Once [the previous] has been digested, one may subsequently arrange [the rite] together with the two goddesses;
in every way, there shall be no loss of great merit, for the opposite would lead to failure.

When the image, the celestial chariot, the enclosure wall, the gate-tower, the gateway, and the pavilion have been established by gods, yakṣas, lords of sages, and others, yet remain devoid of auspicious marks; || 485 ||

In a temple seat, a kitchen, a dwelling, or in objects such as treasuries and the like, when these have become dilapidated, one should repair them as before; one should not alter their original characteristics.

When this [image] established by the gods and others has been utterly ruined by the most wicked, and when the Vaiṣṇava symbols such as the image and so forth are devoid of their characteristic marks; || 487 ||
Or, as before, one should perform [the rite] when the time is appropriate, in accordance with the preceding signs;
otherwise, if it is performed at an improper time, there will be the destruction of the king and the kingdom. (488)
Established and worshipped in ancient times by the lords of gods, siddhas, and munis,
it was later severely defiled by faults such as lightning strikes and collapses.
Having raised her from that faultless seat and dismissed her, he should then,
according to the prescribed rite, establish the previously fashioned [image] upon a pedestal as before.
Likewise, when the pedestal is broken or otherwise damaged, one should firmly join it again;
or, if the temple has fallen due to the breaking of the ground, the force of water, and so forth. || 491 ||
Therefore, one should imagine [the deity] together with its image in another location;
when the abode, including the image, has perished, one should perform the preliminary rites as before for the divine [mandala] and so forth. || 492 ||
But when a human image has been destroyed by the force of a river, fire, and so forth, one should subsequently fashion another image as before, or otherwise. || 493 ||

Because it is the fundamental image whose root is emptiness, the master of adepts should not perform the invocation of the worship of the ignorant and so forth; having established [the deity] as before, he should worship it.
For in this way, [he is the source] of all the gods who possess forms such as Paravyūha and others,
as well as the host of attendants beginning with Viṣvaksena and Gaṇeśa.
Because of the excellence of their presence day after day in the gopuras and other structures, which have been fashioned in the form of magnificent manifestations for those who are worshipped there.
And the specific procedure for the restoration of dilapidated [shrines] has been described by me, as well as by various mantra-adepts, sages, and men. (497)

However, due to the passage of a long time, even well-established houses may suffer destruction through collapse, cracking, splitting, and so forth; such [destruction] does not occur in the temple of the Blessed One. (498)

By the permission of the administrators, devotees, and those learned in the scriptures, [the temple] was constructed with stone and other materials for their protection, both externally and internally. || 499 ||
Skilled artisans should construct a wall-enclosure on all sides,
whether in a palace, a preeminent pavilion, a rampart, or a gate-tower.
In the courtyard, in the kitchen, in the treasury, in the storehouse for garments, in the hall for flowers and water, in the slaughter-house, and so forth— 501.
Either in a pavilion for bathing, or likewise in a sacrificial pavilion,
or in a spacious house that has become dilapidated over the course of time, [one should perform the rite] with abundance.
For the sake of protection and for the sake of application, one should increase it on the outside;
however, starting from the interior, one should never decrease it anywhere.
One should tie all the materials either in front or all around;
however, there would be no prosperity if they were placed to the east or north, or behind [the fire], or in the western or southern directions.
One should perform the rite for prosperity in the north or the west of the kitchen;
likewise, one should establish a hall for Purāṇas, a seat (pīṭha), a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), and a lake.
One should not, even with great effort, move a monastery, a pavilion, or any other structure, nor any emblem such as that of the Sudarśana [discus], when constructing temples and similar edifices.
One should visualize those [lines] externally, having bypassed the ancient [boundary];
when that which was previously situated has increased or decreased both externally and internally. (507)
But there would be no fault in the western [direction] regarding its length, height, and width;
for it was thus fashioned of old by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Yakṣas, and others. || 508 ||
One who desires long life and the increase of wealth should not move [the earth] anywhere;
likewise, one should not fill up a lake or a well with mud and other such materials.
If one causes smaller shrines to be built out of abundance or faith,
and later causes them to be made large, no fault arises.
Regarding the pedestals of the Śāla-gopura, which take the form of ancillary structures such as the maṇḍapa,
this applies specifically to the first design and particularly to the restoration of what has been lost.

When there is no capacity due to a spatial constraint regarding a single object already situated [there], its apprehension would not be a fault; for that which is secondary [is accepted] because of the weight of the primary. || 512 ||

Whatever exists for the foundation of the feet of the Lord of the World in the temple—be it the foundational stone for the feet or the Brahma-stone and so forth—[all that should be offered]. || 513 ||
Even without an installed image, one should perform the supreme consecration bath with honey,
milk, curd, ghee, and sacrificial porridge.
One should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) in the number of one hundred thousand;
and the temple as well as the image should be constructed according to the same scripture.
Having installed [the deity] with that very [mantra], one should worship Hari daily and so forth;
yet he who worships by another method, or likewise causes another to worship, [is at fault]. || 516 ||
Both of those evil-minded men swiftly brought about the ruin, suffering, and affliction of the king, the kingdom, and indeed the family of their preceptor.
They would especially cause the loss of wealth and the ruin of the temple;
therefore, one devoted to the Pañcarātra should not cause a confusion of the Tantras.
Furthermore, if a confusion of tantras has occurred, the re-consecration must be performed;
however, for the sake of the temple, it should have been done previously according to the Vaikhānasa and other tantras.
Even if the placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) has been performed here, if one desires the Pañcarātra system,
one should extract that very embryo at that time and perform the rites as prescribed in the Pañcarātra.
The scripture known as the Pañcarātra is divided into four distinct parts;
its characteristics have been described previously, yet they are also set forth here once more.
The first is established as the Āgama-siddhānta; the second is designated as Mantra; the third is called Tantra, while any other would be a different Tantra (tantrāntara). || 522 ||
The first [Veda] is non-human (apauruṣeya), illuminating the eternally manifest array (nityoditavyūha) and other matters; it belongs to those who sacrifice to the True Brahman known as Vāsudeva.
It is the object of focus for the best of the twice-born, residing in the hearts of those who are qualified;
it is known as the Brahma Upaniṣad and is endowed with divine mantras and ritual actions.
This supreme scripture bestows discernment and grants liberation even to those who do not seek it;
such is the nature of the Lord known as Nityodita, whose form is eternal. || 525 ||
Know that the first definition of the one named Vāsudeva—who is a great ocean of the sixfold qualities and so forth—is like the term "heart" and other such [general] designations for limbs. 526.
Know this to be the established doctrine of the Āgamas, which is indeed of the nature of Śruti;
this is remembered as the Kṛtayuga dharma, the highest of all dharmas.
Then, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
there emerged from that established doctrine of the Āgama a system with many divisions.
That [image], known as Mantrasiddhānta, was carved by the second great-souled Sāttvata, who manifested in the form of the Jāgrat-vyūha and other emanations. || 529 ||
By that [power], there is the one known as Pradyumna; by that, the pervasive Lord who is the Fourth Self (turyātman);
by that, the one called Vāgīśvara; and from that, the body known as Vidya.
Thereafter, it was transmitted to Rudra, Āditya, Indra, and Agni,
and likewise to Nārada and the other hosts of divine sages.
The established doctrine of mantra has been transmitted, divided into many different branches;
therein lies the most peaceful array, which is both quiescent and emergent, and without interval.

The state known as deep sleep, that called dream, and the waking array as it has been described; likewise, the manifestation of other forms such as Keśava and others, each with its distinct internal nature. || 533 ||
On the lotus-throne of the heart and other locations, [he is worshipped] with the powers such as Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi,
with emblems such as the conch and discus, and also with [deities] headed by Garuḍa.
Worship of Viśvatrātṛ Nṛsiṃha, preceded by initiation, is beneficial; it extends from the Bhūtas and Siddhas up to the Sāstras, and likewise beyond that.
The chapter titled "The Subtle Array of Birds" follows in due order;
it concerns the consecration of the four [classes of initiates], beginning with the Samayin and the Putraka.

Likewise, [he taught] the sequence for the installation of the forms of the Samaya-observance, as well as the characteristics of the mantras, mandalas, mudrās, sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), and so forth. || 537 ||
That in which the detailed prescription of such actions as these is found, known by the name Mantrasiddhānta, is endowed with many divisions. || 538 ||
Whether by means of the various arrays of others and so forth, or by a single form alone—whether with its limbs, or as solitary, or as a beautiful array adorned with ornaments. (539)
Likewise, that which is known as Tantra is surrounded by weapons endowed with bodies;
[these include] Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, Kroḍa, Haṃsa, Vāgīśvara, and others.
They are either solitary or joined with limbs, distinguished by the various modes of primary and other functions,
and further adorned with excellent weapons such as the discus and others, as well as ornaments like crowns and the like.
Where she is worshipped according to the prescribed rite by hosts of beloved ones such as Lakṣmī and others, and by her retinues such as the birds and so forth— that is described in another tantra.
For those who have attained perfection through ten million births, their end occurs in this very life;
therefore, this is truly called the "Siddhānta" (the established conclusion) in accordance with its actual meaning.
The acceptance, as before, of the scriptures, mantras, rituals, and so forth, as well as the images, the temple, and a noble preceptor. || 544 ||
In this very manner, it must not be performed otherwise for as long as time lasts;
for if it is done contrarily, it brings about misfortune for the king, the kingdom, and others.
Therefore, one should first perform the installation with diligent effort;
thereafter, those of perfected self should not allow a confusion of the established doctrines.
Whatever is most desired in the world that does not contradict established tradition—this should be accepted;
a wise person should abandon whatever is mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, what need is there to mention those things prescribed in the Vaikhānasa tantras and the Śaiva-Pāśupata systems, which are born of ignorance and are contradictory? (548)
When [the deity] has been installed and is being worshipped according to the ritual procedure of the Pañcarātra,
no other form of worship should ever be performed, even by one who is learned.
It should be especially worshipped by the foremost ones who are devoted to the True Brahman, dedicated to the Pañcarātra, and authorized for the primary ritual procedure.
By Brahmins devoted to the Dharma of the three Vedas, initiated into the established doctrines, and intent on virtuous conduct; or, in the absence of such, by those following a secondary alternative.
A deity installed in a palace must especially be worshipped by more than one person; how much more so in a wealthy house provided with offerings, oblations, and the like? (552)

By the foremost practitioners devoted to the Five Times (Pañcakāla), who were knowers of the established tenets of mantra, wise in the seven categories of reality, and experts in the twelve internal sciences; || 553 ||

In the thirteenfold ritual action, those who are always intent upon their underlying intention, who have renounced worldly action, who are authoritative, and who are qualified for the primary rite—[should perform it]. || 554 ||
Likewise, it should be worshipped incessantly by others who are devoted to the three Vedas and are experts in the meaning of the established doctrines, using two, four, six, or eight [articles]. 555.
Among those [groups], one person should worship inside [the mandala] by rotation day after day, using twelve, sixteen, twenty, or twenty-four [offerings].
Two, three, or four [disciples] should perform this again and again;
other excellent instructors should likewise honor their retinues. || 557 ||
One person should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya), and another should offer the oblation (bali) in due order;
other supreme devotees (bhāgavatottama) should assist them in these matters.
Other practitioners should perform [the rites] according to the procedure instructed by the guru;
or else, everything may be performed by a single person, or by many who have restrained their minds.
In the absence of those who are proficient, knowledgeable, and initiated, when many foreigners have arrived for the worship at the sanctuary. (560)
Having invoked [the deity] from the root-mantra and so forth into the images, they should perform for each rite the festival,
the ceremonial bathing, the procession, and the offering of abundant food.
If there are many practitioners, they should perform these rites upon each respective image;
indeed, even in the daily ritual, they should likewise perform the worship and the libation into the fire.
If all [the rites] beginning with the *bali* offering are performed by the minister simultaneously, no fault is to be recognized here, as it is caused by the influence of time and karma. || 563 ||
Many people should not perform daily, occasional, and other such rites at home;
rather, the sacrifice should be performed by a single person alone, for otherwise it would result in fault.
To pacify those defects, one should perform a propitiatory rite accompanied by fire-oblations;
the practitioner of mantras should respectfully recite the root mantra according to his capacity. (565)
Thus installed in the temple by the devotees, the followers of the Bhagavat, he should be worshipped daily and at other times for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom. (566)
When worshipped by others, the god is never pleased;
he constantly bestows misfortune, especially upon the king and the kingdom.
To pacify those defects, the most excellent of all supreme ablutions (snapana) should be performed when the Lord of the World has been invoked and established within the images.
One should not perform the dismissal (udvāsana) after having invoked [the deity] for worship before it;
this applies even when there are three daily sessions of worship, including the worship of the limbs (aṅga-bimba), ritual acts (karma), and the formal image (arcā). || 569 ||
Having invoked [the deity], one should worship from the root mantra, especially when required by the specific ritual;
however, at the conclusion of each respective rite, one should again unite [the deity] with the root mantra.

If, during the worship rituals such as the invocation (āvāhana) and others, the root [mantra] is performed otherwise, one should perform a purificatory bath (snapana) for the sake of pacification; this is designated as the lowest of the low.
In all expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), having carefully considered the gravity or lightness of the fault and having offered the ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
one should proceed preceded by the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
The worship at the four locations, the worship with a great oblation, the ceremonial bathing accompanied by recitation, and the sacrificial fee for the preceptors.

One should also perform, according to one's capacity, the giving of cows, land, gold, and so forth, as well as the feeding of those who know the five times (pañcakāla), especially during the primary ritual cycle.
One should perform worship, bathing, and fire-offerings according to the secondary rule (anukalpa) when the earth is defiled by extremely cruel and unspeakable faults. || 575 ||
Having thoroughly purified it with the ten methods prescribed by rule, such as digging and so forth,
one should properly extract the dust consisting of jewels and gold.
Having scattered [the materials] in all directions, one should perform oblations there for the sake of pacification;
in empty temples, one should perform the great ablution and other rites. || 577 ||
In independent and dependent [structures], in dwellings such as empty villages, by means of sweeping and smearing, and by sprinkling with products of the cow; || 578 ||
Having purified each of those [sites], one should sow the five products of the cow (gavyapañcaka) in their midst,
and one should perform the offering of oblations (balidāna) to the host of Vāstu deities.
A king who is devoted to truth and intent on protecting his subjects should, according to his capacity, give gifts such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth to the preceptors and others. || 580 ||
The best of the twice-born, knowing the five periods of time, should perform the rite of pacification with diligence;
otherwise, O lord of men, if the king should neglect the work of pacification, [evil would prevail].
He undoubtedly destroys his own self, his kingdom, his treasury, his vehicles and the like, as well as his wife, sons, and grandsons. || 582 ||
Therefore, a king intent on his own welfare should protect these [ministers], whether by his own intelligence or that of others, especially when faced with a perilous crisis. (583)
Through the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa, one is pacified by gold;
likewise, being established in Hiraṇyagarbha, one who is free from greed should perform the gift.
From time to time, especially with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, he constructed a palace together with an agrahāra village. || 585 ||
The God is composed of all the gods; Hari is composed of all the Vedas;
Viṣṇu is composed of all sacrifices; and the All-pervading Lord is composed of all the worlds.
Consisting of all phenomena, infinite; consisting of all beings, eternal;
the yogi who consists of all sacred fords should be installed according to the prescribed rite.
Otherwise, in a wide sacrificial pit with a rim as desired, one should perform [the rite] with purifying Vaiṣṇava mantras that destroy all defects and are enjoined by the Vedas. || 588 ||
The most excellent Brahmins, skilled in the application of mantras,
should perform oblations even when great portents occur in the heavens, the atmosphere, or on the earth.
One who desires prosperity should perform pacification (śānti) according to this procedure;
O Sage, what need is there for much speaking here? It is the destroyer of all sins. (590)
Know that the installation of the great Sudarśana yantra in one's own territory is a supreme ordinance that increases the king and the kingdom. (591)
Having fashioned Sudarśana out of copper or solid stone in the center of the excellent Yantra,
one should place Nṛhari on its rear side.
With four lotus-like hands bearing the discus. || 592 ||
Having installed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite within a palace provided with windows at the entrance to the inner chamber,
he who worships it becomes victorious and enjoys all pleasures right here in this world.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Prescription of Expiatory Rites," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the illustrious Pañcarātra.
Śrī.
The twentieth chapter: Sanaka,
[you have] previously explained to me the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa and other such acts.
O Sage, tell me in detail that procedure for kings.
Śāṇḍilya said:
Listen attentively, O twice-born one; I shall fully describe that which destroys all sins, beginning with the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa, which bestows the fruits of all desires. || 2 ||
For a ruler who is habituated to protecting his subjects and devoted to the virtuous,
divine wrath may sometimes arise due to the omission of ritual duties.
In that same way, turmoil in the kingdom and the oppression of the subjects increase;
likewise, the country becomes defiled by the improper conduct of the social classes and stages of life. || 4 ||
The Vedas and Vedic duties fall away due to the upheavals of time;
one king is oppressed by another king after another in succession.
"May the country become empty; may the people perish at that very moment.
With the realization that this suffering was produced by his own fault, the lord of the earth [spoke thus]. (6)
Together with his family priest, his ministers, and the subjects,
he respectfully [approached] one who was devoted to the welfare of all beings and was an expert in the ritual procedures of the Pañcarātra.

One should take refuge in a preeminent teacher who is free from greed, devoid of anger, upright, a devotee of the Lord, a twice-born brahmin, and one who knows how to perform the two types of ritual actions.
The lord of the earth reported everything exactly as it had happened to his preceptor, recounting the entire past event born of his own transgression. || 9 ||
Crying out "Protect me! Protect me! while prostrating at his feet, he spoke;
and he, who bestows grace upon all, having heard those words—
Having brought wealth acquired through lawful means and righteousness from the king,
that ritual then proceeds with the officiating priests who follow the Pañcarātra tradition.
Even by those learned in the three Vedas, skilled in ritual action, and devoted to the Blessed One,
[this was performed] during the months beginning with Caitra, at the equinoxes, and during the two solstices.
O Sage, [one should perform this] during Vyatīpāta, at one's birth-star, during lunar or solar eclipses, or under the asterisms of Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Aśvinī, or Kṛttikā.
Under Rohiṇī, the lunar mansion of Soma, and especially under Punarvasu,
or under Puṣya, the lunar mansion of Hasta, and likewise under the Uttaras.
Likewise on Citrā, Svātī, Anurādhā, and Mūla;
and also during bad dreams, afflictions of the home, and when great portents occur. (15)
When the kingdom is likewise afflicted by disease, one should perform [the rite] with the consent of the performer;
if it is to be performed for the sake of this specific cause, it must be done at that very time.
One should begin [the rite] in a place such as Svayamvyakta, which is endowed with all auspicious qualities, so that no disturbance from defects may arise. || 17 ||
In front of the temple of the Blessed One, facing whichever direction is desired, one should construct a square pavilion for the three goals of life (trivarga) on all sides. || 18 ||
Having divided the twenty-seven-cubit sacrificial ground into seven parts,
he constructed a great altar (mahāvedī) one cubit high, adorned with every ornament.
One should arrange three [circles] in the middle, joined with ascents in the directions;
above that, in the center and in the directions, one should place five earthen seats (pīṭhas).
It should be three cubits high and one tāla in width for the purpose of worship in the three locations,
and for the consecration of the king as well as of objects made of gold and other materials.
In the center of the circle, upon the middle throne, one should place the scales, the preeminent sword, ornaments, and garments; it stands facing east and resembles a wheel or a lotus.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is the seat of the southern direction and the place for the king's vigil;
the pot-sacrifice (kumbhayāga) is performed when [the moon] is in the west, while the accumulation of gold occurs when it is in the north.
The consecration of the scales and other implements should be performed externally;
having left a space of one cubit, one should fashion the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the various directions. || 24 ||

One should construct a group of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the intermediate directions, starting from Agni and ending with Īśāna, in sequence, having the shapes of a square, a wheel, a conch, and a lotus.
Above the pedestal, one should visualize a triangular shape in the form of a womb (yoni), characterized by eight petals and a half-moon, and marked with the wheels and other symbols.
On all sides, it is provided with three parts and endowed with four gates; its corners are enriched with beautiful walls, and it is adorned with the *mukha-bhadra* projections.
Equipped with various staircases and adorned with all ornaments,
a water-shed (prapā) should be constructed in the front part, resembling a temple of Māna and other deities.
In the center, it is joined with colors; having extended toward the western direction, it is firmly covered with two divisions in the eastern, southern, and northern directions. (29)

During great festivals, consecrations, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), and so forth—just as it has been described in many ways in the past—if only one of those [rites] is performed; || 30 ||
Or one should perform the two rites, such as the weighing on the scales, in a pavilion;
having first prepared the pavilion facing east in this manner.
Thereafter, the ascending balance (paścādārohaṇatulā) should be prepared as prescribed by the rules:
it should be one finger-breadth thick, equal [in weight], circular like a sacrificial ladle (sruva), and one cubit in length. || 32 ||
In a crucible made of gold or other such materials, possessing a brilliance like the rising sun,
one should run [the mold] around, leaving a space of one finger-breadth, and fix it with rings at the cardinal directions.
Upon a balance-beam of equal length, joined with chains and nooses, a rod made of black iron should be fashioned, three cubits in length. || 34 ||
In the middle, it should be three *tālas* high, while on both sides it should be two *tālas*;
leaving aside a space of one *tāla*, it should be made of flexible black iron.
Having formed two fangs from the mouth, which has the appearance of the young moon,
for the purpose of joining them with a chain-noose, one should place [the other elements] above that in the middle.
One should place the tongue, sharp at its tip and motionless, sixteen finger-breadths in length, indicating the equality or inequality [of the breath]; above that, the movable arch.
One should attach a face, eighteen finger-breadths in length and resting on both sides,
with a beak like that of a crane, upon the archway.
Having thus prepared the balance, which is characterized by its specific marks, [he should take] two pieces of wood from a well-known sacrificial tree—substantial, straight, and firm. (39)
They were two cubits in circumference and six cubits in height;
they were square at the base and marked by eight facets in the middle.
Above, two circular forms were fashioned by the most skilled artisan,
located between the eastern door and the square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
They should be placed in the south and north, separated by a distance of two cubits;
they should be five cubits in height and buried one cubit deep.
One should join the northern [pillar] made from a tree of the same species as those two;
it should be as firm as the top of the pillar, with a width equal to its height.
Adorned with eight auspicious symbols (maṅgala) and accompanied by the goddess Śrī on both sides,
one should firmly fix the ring in the middle and below that.
And for the purpose of balancing the scale, a striking rod made of copper or iron should be fashioned,
sixteen finger-breadths in length.
The iron pillar or the one made of heartwood should have a circumference equal to the forearm;
here also are the implements for sacrifice and the implements for the fire-oblation.
All the sacrificial ladles such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, the jars, the water-pots and so forth,
as well as the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) and others, should be made according to one's capacity, or else fashioned from gold and other precious materials.
Then, on one of the previously mentioned days, the knower of the ritual application, for the sake of auspiciousness, should offer sprouts into vessels such as *pālikās* and the like.
And all the necessary materials must be collected with reverence for the purpose of decorating the pavilion and for performing sacrifices at the three sacred sites.
Sandalwood and other fragrant substances, leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as various garments endowed with colors such as white and others. || 50 ||
In all the sacrificial pits, seven large fuel-sticks are for the purpose of the fire-oblation;
and in the directional pits, white mustard seeds are to be offered for rites performed for specific desires.
There are also trees originating from the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, and Udumbara species, as well as varieties of Pippala, Plakṣa, Vaṭa, and Kāśmarya in the intermediate directions. || 52 ||
In all the sacrificial pits, the fuel-sticks should be made of Palāśa wood;
in its absence, they may be made of gold, silver, or copper, or the water-pots may be made of clay.
Rice and other grains, especially seeds, as well as jars of curd, milk, and clarified butter, and the six kinds of flavors. (54)
Pure rice grains ready for cooking at every moment, various edible side-dishes, and numerous cooking vessels. || 55 ||
There were vessels for the purpose of preparing food, bowls for the arghya and other offerings,
and excellent, wondrous lamps and incense burners.
The water for washing the feet, the vessels for receiving offerings, and other implements for the sacrifice, as well as the substances for incense, beginning with guggulu and agaru; || 57 ||
All the medicinal herbs suitable for the bathing jars, as well as wealth, grain, and garments for the purpose of giving to the Brāhmaṇas and others; (58)
Precious ornaments for the lord of preceptors and the officiating priests, as well as gold and other items for the purpose of sacrificial fees, should be procured according to one's means. (59)
One should decorate the sacrificial hall for the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) with canopies,
banners, turrets, and curtain-fabrics.
With various kinds of linen garments, bells, chowries, and mirrors; with hanging garlands of darbha grass, and plantains, jackfruit, and other fruits. || 61 ||
With garlands of fragrant flowers, clusters of golden blossoms, and fruit-bearing trees such as plantains, betel-nut palms, and coconuts; || 62 ||
With rows of lamps, flowers such as white ones, and colored pigments;
with archways, water-pots at the doors, and herds of fragrant cows accompanied by their calves.
Having thus decorated the pavilion as it appears most beautiful, with ornaments such as linen garlands and other finery upon its peaks and so forth; || 64 ||
On the third day, at the end of the day following the previous ritual day,
the preeminent guide, together with the officiating priests, performed the sequence of the sandhyā rites.
Having entered the pavilion as before, and having first completed the worship of Vāsudeva along with the burnt offerings (homa) preceded by the proclamation of the auspicious day (puṇyāha), || 66 ||
Having sprinkled the sacrificial hall everywhere with the five products of the cow,
one should place the materials suitable for sacrifice in their respective locations.
When the night had turned to dawn, in the forenoon, for the sake of purifying his body, the king—having had his hair, nails, and beard shaved, being self-restrained and pure—[prepared himself]. (68)
Having cleansed his teeth, well-bathed, and clad in pure garments, adorned with white unguents, flowers, and the like, he should remain mindful of Hari. (69)
Having fasted and consumed clarified butter, he should sit together with the family priest and Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, listening to the complete recitation of the Ṛgveda hymns.
When the onset of night has begun, the wise and most excellent officiating priest and preceptor,
having performed the worship of the door-keepers, should enter the sacrificial hall.

Having first proclaimed an auspicious day, one should worship the Lord of the World residing in the three places according to the ritual of initiation, while the officiating priests carry forth the water-pot.
Having completed the worship of the pitcher and the maṇḍala in detail,
one should first perform the oblation in one's own fire-pit with seven pieces of sacrificial fuel.

Thereafter, one should perform the pacification oblation (śāntihoma) in sequence with honey, milk, and other substances, reciting the root mantra for each substance one hundred times, ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Then, having consecrated the group of fire-pits according to his own tradition, the Guru should assign them to the directions for the purpose of the fire-oblation, in accordance with their respective powers.
The four [priests], known by names such as Vāsudeva and others, being of the Ekāyana lineage,
shall offer oblations in due order with the mantras prescribed in their own Vedic branches.
One should place the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, in the kuṇḍas of the intermediate directions,
using the purifying mantras arising from one's own Śākhā with which the liṅgas have been worshipped.
O twice-born one, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as appropriate, either with the Puṃsūkta alone,
or likewise with the mantras "Bhūḥ Svāhā," "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā," and "Svaḥ Svāhā."
Or, one may offer according to the sequence of the directions starting from the southeast with the mantras "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ Svāhā," or "Bhūḥ Puruṣāya Svāhā" and "Bhuvaḥ Puruṣāya Svāhā. || 79 ||
"Oblation to the Puruṣa of the sky, svāhā! Oblation to the Puruṣa of bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, svāhā!"—one may offer oblations with these four mantras, following the sequence of the directions.
The installation and other rites for the scriptures, the world-protectors, the host beginning with Kumuda, and the eight auspicious objects should be performed as previously described.
The varieties of sacrificial fuel-sticks, such as those of the *pālāśa* tree, and the varieties of cooked rice offerings (*caru*) are as before;
furthermore, for each fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the placement of the water-jars (*kumbha*) and so forth is likewise as before.

The establishment and other rites for the four [Vedic traditions], beginning with the Ṛgveda, as well as for those who are exclusively devoted [to a single Veda], should be performed according to the procedure previously described. || 83 ||
Having thus performed [the rites] in sequence, at the conclusion, the preceptor should cause the king to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water infused with kuśa grass.
One should consume the auspicious water from the feet of the Blessed One, which removes all sins,
and also eat the remains of the sacrificial oblation (caru) for the purification of the stomach.
Having prepared a seat on the southern pedestal with heaps of śāli rice,
one should place a skin upon it, numbering nine, above that.
Or, having spread tiger-skin above that, or darbha grass together with grains of rice—
with their tips pointing either eastward or northward— he should place the king upon it.
Having placed four water-pots filled to the brim in the four directions as before, adorned with cloths and other ornaments, one should worship the forms [of the deities] within them in due order.
One should then give them four kinds of food in due order;
thereafter, the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed in the sacrificial pits according to the previously mentioned sequence.
Then, having sat upon his seat before the king, the Guru shall perform the purification of the principles (tattvas) residing within that body according to the prescribed ritual.
Having first caused their dissolution, one should then perform the creation;
and one should perform the binding of the sacred thread for them as well as for oneself, just as before.
