Having brought a collection of gold and purified it with water mixed with *tintriṇī* juice,
he should then sprinkle it again with the *vīryamantra*.

On a seat situated in the northern direction, made from three loads of śāli rice, having placed [the image] upon the seat and performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), preceded by the offering of garments and ornaments; || 93 ||
Furthermore, having established everything else, one should envelop it with the armor-mantra (varman).
Then, having drawn a discus and lotus, or some other auspicious mandala; || 94 ||
One should fill [the vessel] with substances made of jewels or minerals, or with pigments;
and with songs, dances, and the like, with hymns of praise, and with the sounds of conchs, musical instruments, and so forth. || 95 ||
One should pass the night with various other auspicious rites and by keeping vigil;
a special worship of the Lord should be performed in a divine temple or similar sacred place. || 96 ||
Then, on the day of the ritual, during the Brāhma-muhūrta, the preceptor himself,
having performed all the rites such as bathing according to the rules for daily obligatory duties, [proceeded].
Then one should especially worship the Lord of the World residing in the pitcher, and likewise the one situated in the mandala, in due order, with various collections of offerings. || 98 ||
There, with abundant accumulations of food such as the finest rice and other delicacies, which were both metaphorically and literally heart-pleasing through their sensory contact. 99.
Having worshipped in this manner, he should then satisfy the All-pervading Lord residing in the fire in due order,
first with seven pieces of fuel, and then with sesame seeds mixed with ghee while reciting the root mantra.
One should perform a hundred or even a thousand oblations;
likewise, one should perform them with the Astra-mantra for the purpose of destroying all obstacles.
And the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) should offer oblations into their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in the prescribed order as before;
and when the pits have been filled to the brim, they should do so in all the pits in due sequence.
Having bathed him with the root mantra as well as the Puṃsūkta,
and having had his hands and feet thoroughly washed, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and be adorned.
With all garments, garlands, and ointments having been kept overnight,
and with all kinds of highly precious ornaments as well.
Taking a sword and a shield in his own hands, the preceptor himself, when an auspicious moment arrived, [seized] the lord of the earth with his hand. (105)

Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day accompanied by all manner of blessings, [he should perform the rites] situated within the jars, the pedestals, the directional pitchers, and all the sacrificial pits. || 106 ||
Having circumambulated the Lord and performed a salutation,
and having obtained permission from the foremost of the Brahmins, he led the scale around in a circumambulation.
Then, while standing in the western direction,
the Guru should place the balance facing eastward again, reciting the root mantra along with its ancillaries.
One should place divine mantras such as those beginning with "balā," as well as the Puruṣasūkta,
and a heap of gold into the first vessel, which is equal to that of the king.
This load on the scale, having been kept overnight, shall be equal [to the suspect];
or likewise, the king should first place himself upon the scale before the load.
One should deposit a hoard of gold facing westward;
one exceeding a hundred *niṣkas* is excellent, while that which exceeds half of that is middling. (111)
That lowest *tulābhāra* would consist of one hundred and more pādas;
at that time, the four [beings] beginning with Ṛk-bhayā were stationed in the cardinal directions. (112)
They studied their own respective branches of the Veda, established in various directions;
those knowers of the True Brahman diligently mastered the most purifying branches.
And those skilled in various musical instruments should play conchs, trumpets, drums, and other diverse instruments on all sides. || 114 ||
Those skilled in the science of song should perform various songs, and they should perform diverse dances in every direction. || 115 ||
Furthermore, one should perform every auspicious rite that exists;
thereafter, one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). || 116 ||
With many sesame seeds and clarified butter, the king should perform one hundred and eight oblations in sequence,
while meditating in his mind upon the Lord Janārdana.
The king should sit upon the balance for one nāḍī or half of that;
then, having descended from it, he should prostrate himself like a staff before Hari.
Then the king should honor the preceptor with ornaments and garments, and he should give a gift of gold consisting of one hundred *niṣkas* or an amount equal to that. || 119 ||
Or half of that [fee] should be given to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and to those others who were appointed there to assist in the ritual, according to their respective roles in the work. 120.
The king should bestow wealth, various garments, heaps of gold, and ornaments as well. || 121 ||
One should offer [the image] of the all-pervading Lord in a self-manifested or similar sacred place;
now listen to the specific fruits resulting from such an offering.
The king who makes an offering at the self-manifested abode of the Lord Hari shall be liberated from all sins and freed from all diseases. || 123 ||
He shall become the sovereign of all lands, enriched with every prosperity,
and he shall enjoy various pleasures both in this world and in the next.
A gift [given elsewhere] would have a fruit of ten million times ten millionfold;
likewise, a gift given at a divine sanctuary would possess infinite merit. || 125 ||
A gift given at a sacred site of the Ṛṣis yields a hundredfold merit; a gift given at a site prepared by virtuous Brahmins yields a thousandfold merit. (126)
A gift given at a place established by a virtuous Kṣatriya becomes a hundredfold;
at a place established by a virtuous Vaiśya, it becomes half that amount. || 127 ||
What is given at a place established by a true Śūdra becomes twelvefold; however, when the place is established by castes who have no other refuge, it becomes twenty-fourfold. || 128 ||
Giving by those of mixed castes who perform sacrifices is said to yield tenfold merit;
that which is given in a temple constructed [by others] becomes fivefold.
The primary rule for giving has been declared; now hear the secondary rule (anukalpa).
In that regard, those who have arrived—Vaiṣṇavas who are learned in the Vedas and the best among Brāhmaṇas—[should be honored]. || 130 ||
And he should give them the collection of gold and other items in due order;
he should cause all the implements for the sacrifice to be presented to the preceptor.
Any king or any other wealthy person who performs this rite called the Tulābhāra even once is liberated from all sins. (132)
And he shall undoubtedly be free from diseases, provided that he performs this rite according to the rule every year. (133)
Who is able to fully describe the attainment of the fruit of his merit, when he performs the sacrifice to the Blessed One at that time, accompanied by worship at the four sacred sites? (134)
The lord of the earth should cause [the image] to be properly installed in a divine shrine and other such places;
on another day, O Brahmin, he should bathe Puruṣottama.
One should perform the ritual properly with a thousand jars according to the procedure previously described,
or indeed by means of another ablution appropriate for that specific occasion.
There, the king should especially cause the worship of the four locations to be performed;
and he should especially cause a great sacrificial offering to be presented. || 137 ||
There too, one should indeed give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in due order to the guide and others,
as well as to the poor, the blind, the wretched, the helpless, children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick.
One should feed [the recipients] according to the prescribed rite and cause various materials and other requisites to be given;
one should also cause various seeds, such as rice and so forth, to be bestowed. || 139 ||
And one should release those who have been made captives and those confined in prisons.
O Brahmin, this procedure for the Tulā and Bhāra weights has thus been described to you in due order.
One should perform the rite in this very same manner for others as well, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha.
Thus should one who performs the Tulābhāra rite, whether once or many times.
There is no doubt that he shall be liberated from all sins—whether it be for the sake of the Blessed One, or for the sake of his mother, father, or teacher. (142)
O high-minded one, for Brahmins and others who sacrifice their own lives out of devotion,
he becomes the instrumental cause through such means as the Tulābhāra and other rites.

O Brahmin, it is indeed through the proper performance of ritual action many times over, or through other very difficult expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) prescribed by others, [that one attains purification]. || 144 ||
Whether purification occurs for the sin of killing a Brahmin who ate [the food] or not, that high-souled one has surrendered his life for the sake of Viśvaratha. (145)
Therefore, O Brahmin, there can be no atonement for that perpetrator;
whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or even Maudgalyas, if they act for the sake of Viṣṇu. || 146 ||
Endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, they may even renounce their own lives through the five methods beginning with Bhrigu, or by means of poison and the like. (147)
For others, there would immediately be for them the fruit arising from the Vājapeya and other sacrifices;
but for one who possesses desire, the desireless one shall attain the supreme goal.
Know those great-souled ones to have sacrificed their lives for the sake of Viṣṇu;
they are never tainted by the faults arising from suicide. 149.
O twice-born one, the faults arising from suicide would always accrue to others;
however, this is not so when one is intent on sacrificing one's life for the sake of the Blessed One. 150.
One should know that he for whose sake another would give up his life is a slayer of a Brahmin;
if that principal Brahmin dies, the fault of the former shall be fourfold. || 151 ||
In the case of a Kṣatriya, the fault arising from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa shall be triple;
that same fault for the one who incited the act shall be double when a Vaiśya has been killed.
If a Śūdra who served as the occasion for the act dies, the fault shall be of a single degree;
likewise, the increase of the fault shall be proportional when a Brāhmaṇa is the one who provided the occasion.

In the case of a woman who possesses the signs [of royalty] among the Kṣatriyas and other castes, due to the increase of each successive quality, the previously mentioned defect would arise; however, there is no doubt that this does not apply when the object is not attained. || 154 ||
Thus, the fault of the one who provides the cause is said to apply even when an ordinary Brahmin dies;
however, when a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) has passed away, the primary fault is fivefold greater.
If a householder who performs sacrifices dies, that fault becomes sixfold;
if a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) dies, the primary fault becomes sevenfold. || 156 ||
O Sage, if one established in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) passes away, the person who caused that circumstance incurs the primary fault multiplied eightfold; thus it has been declared.
When death occurs for the sake of Viṣṇu, there is an increase in merit for those who provided the cause;
thus, for the twice-born and others who acted as the instrumental cause, there is no expiation required. || 158 ||

In this matter, one should follow without hesitation that which has been spoken by Brahmins who are ever devoted to discernment and who know the true essence of the meaning of all the scriptures. || 159 ||
Otherwise, however, there would be great fault for the ruler of the land.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Weighing Scale and the Burden of Expiation," in the section on Ritual Action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) of the *Pārameśvara-saṃhitā* within the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
Śrī.
O Sage, this twenty-first [chapter] concerning Śāṇḍilya will now describe the specific details regarding Hiraṇyagarbha and others.
First, I shall describe the procedure for the interior of gold.
O Sanaka,
whatever action is mentioned here, even if it has not been specifically enjoined in the *Tulābhāra*,
shall be common to all the lineages (*kramaṇas*). || 2 ||

For those [offerings] such as the balance-scale (tulā) and the weight (bhāra), the construction of the pavilion and the arrangement of the pedestal and so forth should be performed according to one's wealth and means, as previously described. || 3 ||
Or one may construct a pavilion and so forth according to the established path,
with a width of eight, seven, six, five, four, three, or two cubits.

The height of the central pedestal (madhyapīṭha) should be thirty finger-breadths (aṅgula), with each successive [pedestal] decreasing by one golaka, according to the respective dimensions of the site.
Starting from four cubits and decreasing by six globules at each step,
one should fashion two pedestals, each with a width of two cubits on its sides.
Starting from a measurement of twenty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and decreasing by two finger-breadths at each step,
its height is such that it reaches ten finger-breadths at the end, when the width is one and a half cubits.
Or the height may be half of what was stated for the two [types of] measures; in all cases, there should be a projection.
One should arrange the space between the pedestals to be equal to one cubit.
One may increase the half-cubit by increments until it reaches four cubits; the intervening space should be such that it is not too cramped.
According to the measurements stated and according to one's desired dimensions,
one should also construct the group of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), characterized by their defining features.
In the pavilion for the installation and other rites, one should arrange things accordingly;
the ritual prescribed for the central pedestal shall then take place there upon the divine seat.
To the south of that water, one should construct two pedestals according to the stated measurements;
specifically, one should make an auspicious pedestal to the east of the eastern fire-pit.
It may be seven, six, or five cubits in height, or four, three, or two cubits;
it may also be one cubit high, or even half a cubit high. || 13 ||
Above that, one should construct a chamber containing gold;
or else, one may perform the rite prescribed for the "weighing of the load" upon a pedestal.

Alternatively, having arranged the worship of the pitcher and other vessels, as well as the rite of consecration (adhivāsana), in the pavilion, one should perform them in the water-shed (prapā). || 15 ||
One should perform the installation within a golden interior or at a water-shed (prapā),
and the form of the ritual, such as the pot-sacrifice (kumbhayāga) and so forth, should be according to the desire of the performer.
On another day, such as the Tulābhāra festival, one should perform the rite in this same manner;
thereafter, one should fashion a solid golden vessel, one finger-breadth in thickness.
With the lower vessel and the upper vessel joined together as they naturally fit,
one should likewise prepare a wide and comfortable seat for the king.
The lower vessel should be made of one thousand palas of gold, or even half of that;
the upper vessel should be made with one thousand niṣkas, or half of that.
In this manner, one should prepare two bowls adorned with all ornaments;
or, according to one's means, one may have all the vessels made of gold.
One should perform the rite of consecration (adhivāsa) as described for the day of consecration, like the weighing on the scales;
indeed, one should perform the consecration upon the pedestal with water from the two vessels.

Then, O Sage, having performed in due order what was prescribed for the day of the rite as before, [one should proceed] with twelve loads upon the pedestal (pīṭha) established in the direction of Indra.
Having prepared a seat of śāli rice, one should place rice grains upon it;
half that measure of those [grains] should be placed above it, and half that amount of sesame seeds should be placed above that.

Or one should place equal quantities of rice grains, husked rice, and sesame seeds; in the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as well, it should be done in this very same way according to one's means.
In the same way, it may also be used in tasks such as weighing on a scale or carrying loads;
or a tiger skin may be placed here and there along the path for rice and other grains.
One should spread out a new cloth, or three cloths if one has the means;
furthermore, one should perform other auspicious rites preceded by the wrapping of the cloth.

Then, when an auspicious moment has arrived, the Guru, having taken hold of the king who has been previously consecrated (adhivāsita), should place the vessel that was below upon that which was above.
Well-bathed and adorned as before with garments, garlands, and various other costly ornaments, yet excluding the sword and shield. || 28 ||
Having performed the withdrawal of the principles as before, leaving only the individual soul (jīva) remaining,
one should cause it to enter [the body] here accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and so forth.
One should place [the vessel] below, facing east or facing west;
one should place the upper vessel above with its opening downward, protected by the armor-mantra (varman).
When he has sat down within that egg, the Guru,
having sat upon a seat before him as previously described, should perform the emanation of the principles (tattva).
Then, remembering that he was born from an egg, the king was seated upon the bathing throne, which was perfumed with auspicious substances. || 32 ||
One should perform the consecration of a non-king using nine or five jars filled with water and wrapped in cloths and other such materials.
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should perform the ritual sprinkling;
then, having had him rinse his mouth and adorned him with ornaments and the like, [he should proceed].
One should repeatedly cause prostrations to be made to the all-pervading Blessed One;
for the sake of the newborn, one should perform the birth-rite and other consecratory rites, making oblations in due order.
Then, for the sake of filling everything completely with abundant sesame seeds and clarified butter,
and for the destruction of all defects, one should pour out the full vessel.
The king should place those ornaments in the vessel for the Lord Hari;
by such an offering at the temple of the Lord, one always obtains the fruit previously described.
In the case of a self-manifested [liṅga] and others, one may perform rites such as weighing on a scale or offering a load;
even then, the fruit for the king shall arise from the gift in due order.
In the case of a substitute rite, one should give half of that to the all-pervading Lord;
likewise, in the case of a Tulābhāra sacrifice, one should give half to the Brāhmaṇas.
The rite known as Tulābhāra and that called Hemagarbha—these two indeed are the foremost among all ritual acts. (40)

One should perform all other rites in their proper sequence, beginning with the mountain of sesame seeds as will be described hereafter, just as one would perform the rite of the balance and the load (tulābhāra).
One should indeed give a thousand gold niṣkas as a teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā),
or half of that, or a hundred niṣkas, or half of that, according to one's wealth.
One should indeed give ten niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that, as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher; one should never [perform a rite] without a sacrificial fee.
The ritual work, such as weighing on scales and so forth, belongs to all the officiating priests (ṛtvij);
however, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for them shall be half of that, and for the attendants, half of that again.
But for others, according to their capacity, on another day thereafter,
he should perform the dismissal (visarjana) of the Lord who resides within the pitcher, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit.
Or on another day, one should perform it joined with a special worship;
O twice-born one, one should indeed perform the ritual of dismissal (visarjana) in this manner in all cases.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for Atonement and Hiraṇyagarbha," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the glorious Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
|| Śrīḥ ||
The Twenty-second Chapter: Sanaka said,
"O best of sages, please explain to me the procedure for ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa)."
In all matters concerning expiatory rites, he who completes [the ritual] is highly praised. || 1 ||
Śāṇḍilya states that when the pedestal of a temple or an image has been defiled through negligence,
it must be purified as before; this is especially necessary when there has been an omission in worship.

[The ground becomes impure] through Caṇḍālas, outcasts, menstruating women, women who have recently given birth, corpses, and the like; or through those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), death-impurity (mṛtaka), or those who are perpetually impure and censured. || 3 ||
When it has been defiled by artisans who follow paths outside the Vedas, by fools whose caste is unknown, and by excrement, urine, blood, undrinkable water, and semen; || 4 ||
In the birth and death of men, within the house crowded with the kingdom,
there were dogs, jackals, donkeys, and the like, as well as crows, hawks, and other species of birds.
But when an image has been touched, or when there is a mixing of tantras upon its being seen,
or in all such cases as these, the procedure for sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) shall take place.
Knowing that a palace, an image, or similar objects have been defiled by poisons,
one who performs worship without first sprinkling them with consecrated water will swiftly bring ruin upon the king and the kingdom.
It would destroy the village along with its temple; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) must be performed for the temple, the images, and so forth.
Having previously determined the day for the consecration— which bestows prosperity upon the king and the kingdom—
the experts in time, on the day announced beforehand, [proceeded].
Having offered the sprouts according to the rules, he should then, after the house has been thoroughly cleansed,
sprinkle it everywhere with cow-dung and water, preceded by the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha).

Having sprinkled [the images] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water from kuśa grass, and [having performed the rite] for the primary image and the other icons with the six [substances] beginning with white mustard seeds; || 11 ||

When the washing has been performed many times with waters consecrated by the *pavitra* mantras, on the night preceding the principal day, in the sacrificial pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for the sacrifice and other rites; || 12 ||

Having performed the consecration and preliminary rites for the water-pot situated on the platform of the pavilion—which was adorned with archways, gates, jars, canopies, and banners—just as in the case of the initiation ceremony; || 13 ||
One should perform the worship according to one's means, ending with the recitation of mantras, in the root shrine;
then, one should bathe the fixed image and the movable image with milk and the other twenty-five substances.
In front of [the deity] residing on a plastered wall or a cloth painting, one should place the ritual image upon an auspicious seat,
or else a tuft of grass reflected in a mirror.
Having duly bathed the images used for festivals and other purposes—the constituent parts that serve as the substratum of the soul—with water from the jars established in the front pavilion; || 16 ||
Worship and bathing should be performed in the western sacrificial pavilion;
there, the oblation should be offered into the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) which bears the marks of the conch, the discus, and other symbols.

The ritual should be performed with honey, milk, and other substances a hundred thousand times, except for the action-image (karmabimba) and the other images representing the limbs [of the deity]. || 18 ||
Then, to the south of the pavilion, one should prepare a great bed with loads of sesame, rice, and śāli grain, along with garments and other such items. (19)
Above that, one should cause the image to lie down according to the rules, with its *kautuka* (sacred thread) tied;
having worshipped it, one should cover it with blankets and the like, using white and other colors.
One should prepare a mandala with pigments, adorned with a wheel and a lotus, remaining near the image until the time of dawn. || 21 ||
The guide should pass the night by the mere recitation of the root mantra;
when the night has turned to dawn, the Guru, having performed the rite of the twilight devotions, [should proceed].
Having performed the worship of the four locations as before, accompanied by the ritual bathing,
when an auspicious moment has arrived, [the image] is adorned with new garments.
Having performed the binding of the protective thread (kautuka), one should worship the upper garment and the sacred thread (upavīta),
upon which all the principles (tattvas) have been arranged, with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites in due order.
From the lotus of one's own heart within them, preceded by a handful of flowers,
[one should offer] that which is ungraspable, indefinable, formless, stainless, and great.
It is eternally pure, incomparable, extremely subtle, immovable, and manifest; it is of the nature of existence and consciousness, universal, luminous, very firm, and great. || 26 ||
Then, having transferred his vital energy and prostrated like a staff, he reported all the deeds performed to the Lord, O best of the twice-born. (27)
Having raised the festival image and other objects as before along with auspicious items, one should have the great water-pot carried in front by the image-bearers and others. (28)
Taking up the hailstone-weapon (karakāstra), the Preceptor should walk in front,
sprinkling the ground with a continuous stream of water as thin as a needle.
Having led [the deity] clockwise into the interior of the temple, O best of sages,
one should perform the sprinkling with the water-pot according to the procedure described for the great festival.
And [he worshipped] the deities of the door-panels who reside in their respective abodes,
as well as all the attendants, beginning with Khageśa and Viṣvaksena.
One should sprinkle with the water remaining in the pitcher in due order on all sides;
one should then consecrate the remaining water from the pitcher upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Having thus sprinkled [the deity] according to the rule and entered within the temple,
one should then release the protective amulet held in the hand by means of the heart-mantra.
Having given gifts such as cows, land, and gold for the pacification of all defects,
one should especially worship the deity with offerings beginning with arghya and ending with oblations (havir).
Afterwards, one should feed a thousand or even a hundred Brahmins;
or else, one may perform the complete sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) of the Lord immediately. Thus [it is done]. 35.
Preceded by flowers and sprouts for the pacification of those respective defects, there is no need for a specific lunar day, nor a constellation, nor a particular time or hour. (36)
O Brahmins, there should be immediate sprinkling [of water] either at night or even during the day;
however, if there is a delay in performing the expiation, one must observe the proper time.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the entire procedure for sprinkling has been declared,
as well as the installation of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which is the means for accomplishing all prosperity.
It is known as *nāgayoga* when [the moon] is capable of being in conjunction with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or a Karaṇa belonging to the Sarpa (serpent) class;
or, through the conjunction of either one of these two with a lunar mansion, it is designated by the name *nāga*. || 39 ||
Having first resolved that "this must be done," the virtuous ones should offer the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) for that purpose and then collect the necessary materials.
Realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, black lead, saurāṣṭra, gorocana, red chalk, and mercury; || 41 ||
Having taken up the jewels of the elements, foremost among them the ruby (pajharāga), as well as pearls, coral, and that which is known as lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya). || 42 ||
Having gathered these gems— gomeda, puṣyarāga, mahānīla, and gāruḍa— one should collect the seeds.
Then [he ate] the grains of śāli and nīvāra rice, priyaṅgu, sesame, and māṣa beans, as well as mṛdvīka, barley, and bamboo, followed by those known as yavasa.
Gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead;
a golden tortoise-form and a golden wheel and lotus. || 45 ||
Then, having brought together silver and the Pāñcajanya conch, as well as plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, bilva, and āmalaka fruits; 46.
Then, having gathered ripe fruits of the pomegranate, the citron, and the coconut according to the season; || 47 ||
One should procure sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and so forth; as well as costus, spikenard, the two types of turmeric, murā, śaileya, and campaka.
Vacā, kaccora, mustā, hrībera, uśīra,
as well as mallikā, jāti, vakula, nandyāvarta, and campaka.
Then, having brought Pāṭala, Pajha, and Kalhāra flowers, as well as white garments and other such items, and especially garlands; || 50 ||
Grains such as śāli rice and others, as well as kuśa and dūrvā grasses, and also the tender leaves of the bilva, aśvattha, kadamba, and mango trees—whatever [these may be]. (51)
O best of men, grains such as rice suitable for cooking the oblation,
all materials for the fire-offering, and lotus leaves [should be placed] upon an earthen vessel.
For the purpose of worshipping Nṛhari, one should prepare a large, sturdy jar along with a smaller karaka vessel, each twelve finger-breadths in width, and containing both pure and impure water.
Having thus collected these and other such substances according to the prescribed rule,
one should take the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in a new, auspicious earthen vessel.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and whey as the fifth—
these five products of a tawny or aged cow are highly praised as the *pañcagavya*.
In the absence of those two, the milk of other cows is prescribed;
however, it must never be taken from one that is distressed, pregnant, or aged.
One should not take the urine or the two types of dung (urine and feces) from a cow that has no calf;
rather, the cow-dung should be taken while it is still on the ground, warm, and free from contamination by worms and the like.
Having squeezed it thoroughly, one should again take the essence of the cow dung;
likewise, fresh butter when heated is pure, as is curd that has been left to stand for a day and night.
Milk that has not been heated should be taken ten days after birth;
cow urine with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, and cow dung with the mantra "gandhadvāram. (59)
One should mix the substances together with milk while reciting "āpyāyasva," with curd while reciting "dadhikrāvṇe," and with ghee while reciting "śukramasi. || 60 ||
Or else, with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī, or with the five Upaniṣads;
the mantra for cow dung is "Parameṣṭhin," while that for cow urine is "Puruṣa."
For curd, there should be the Viśvamantra; for clarified butter, the Nivṛtti-mantra;
for milk, the Sarvamantra; or for all of these, the eight-syllable mantra.
The mantras for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have been declared for the purpose of sprinkling and bathing,
when the rite of installation has been reached, in order to pacify all defects.

The [six] elements ending with milk are to be assigned from the essence of the excrement by means of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) of the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha, beginning with the heart and ending with the eyes.
Curd is twice the amount of the Āghāra offering; thereafter, cream is three times that;
urine is six times this; and feces and water are four times [the latter].
The measurement stated for the installation [of the deity] is also prescribed for the rite of consecration;
for the purpose of purifying the ground, one should sprinkle that same fivefold [mixture] evenly.
Cow urine should be equal to the cow dung; curd should be twice that amount;
clarified butter should be four times the curd; and milk should be eight times the clarified butter.
This measure is declared for the consumption of the five products of the cow;
indeed, this installation and bathing destroys the entire flood of sins. (68)
Accompanied by the *brahmakūrca* rite, it shall destroy future sin;
listen as I describe its procedure in brief according to the truth. (69)
Kuśa-water mixed with powder and barley and bamboo is known as the *brahmakūrca*, which possesses a splendor equal to the flood of Vaiṣṇava weapons.
Kuśodaka is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being dry or not dry;
one should then extract the juice from the non-dry variety by squeezing it with a cloth. (71)
Having struck [the vessel] and cast it into dry water,
one should fetch water while reciting the purifying mantra, or the root mantra accompanied by the *astra-mantra*.
One should take that water of kuśa grass, measured according to the quantity of cow's urine;
one should then mix the powder there with a measure equal to the essence of the dung.
Having recited the mantra of the discus weapon (cakrāstra) and having meditated upon Viṣṇu by means of the Gāyatrī known as the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
one should then employ the Discus-Nṛhari within those [substances].

Alternatively, having set it aside separately and consecrated it with the five products of the cow and water infused with *kuśa* grass, using the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra and ending with the Weapon-mantra, one should join it [to the image]. || 75 ||
The consumption of these two in the morning is praised as the destroyer of all sins;
thus has the ritual procedure for the five products of the cow been fully explained to you. (76)

Then, in the pavilion previously prepared for the purpose of the sacrificial bath, the preceptor should commence the sacrifice for the sake of perfuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 77 ||
On the day before the ritual day, having fasted and bathed three times,
[he should perform the rite] during the Ahirbudhnya muhūrta, accompanied by officiating priests who follow the Pāñcarātra tradition.
Having uttered "An auspicious day" as before, one should sprinkle the pedestal with products of the cow using the Astra-mantra,
while it is placed upon a layer of grain in the eastern part.
Having drawn a lotus with ten spokes and eight petals within a square enclosure,
one should place [the mantra] in the middle of the pericarp, enclosed within a triangle.

Having installed the great pitcher (mahākumbha), which is wrapped with threads, cloth, and so forth, provided with a small ladle (karaka), and accompanied by the pitchers of the world-protectors (dikpālaka). || 81 ||
It was filled with water mixed with curd, honey, ghee, and milk, provided with leaves such as those of the *pippala*, and adorned with fragrant perfumes and garlands. || 82 ||

It should be provided with a beard [of grass], accompanied by fruit, endowed with all kinds of gems and gold, furnished with all medicinal herbs, and honored even with unbroken grains (akṣatas). || 83 ||
Having lit lamps with ghee from a Kapila cow in a metallic or earthen vessel, one should place them in the four directions, having consecrated the eyes with mantras.
One should place [the deity] in the center of a lotus-wheel situated upon a pedestal of grain;
then, as before, one should sit upon a seat in front of the water-pot.
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the rules,
one should apply the mantra of the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha to the hands and the body.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) along with its limbs upon the heart, one should bring [the deity] down from the space at the end of the resonance (nāda), situated in the center of the lotus-wheel, by means of the supreme mantra (parā).

Having worshipped the embodied mantra with its own specific mantra, using all the auspicious offerings such as the water for honor (arghya) and other enjoyments produced from the nectar of meditation, one should then worship with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having thus gratified [the deity] and offered oblations into the fire located in the navel-pit,
one should worship externally in the pitcher situated in the center, within the lotus of the wheel.
Having invoked [the deities] with their own mantras, one should worship them in sequence with the physical forms, arghya, and other offerings,
according to the rules, until the conclusion of the recitation in the fire-pit characterized by a lotus.

Having offered oblations with seven fuel-sticks upon a wheel, a lotus, a conch, a square diagram, or even on a sacrificial mound, and immediately thereafter performing the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti); || 91 ||
With sandalwood, flowers, guggulu, and agallochum, as well as with milk, curd, honey, and jaggery mixed with sugar-cane juice. || 92 ||

Having likewise offered oblations of rice and other grains, milk-rice and the like, and clarified butter, and having brought [the deity] to satisfaction with the final full oblation, he should then properly present [the offerings]. || 93 ||
Then, on a purified site in front of the one established with the water-pot (kalaśa),
upon a pedestal made of all kinds of grain, a lotus marked with a wheel was drawn.
Having taken the previously described water-pot, measuring twelve finger-breadths, which is well-spread with a new cloth and covered from above with kuśa grass; || 95 ||

Having washed it both inside and out and wrapped it with thread as before, one who is composed should anoint it with sandalwood paste and other substances while reciting the syllable Om (praṇava). || 96 ||
One should place that [liṅga] face-down in the center of the pericarp of the lotus within the wheel;
then, by measurement, one should prepare an unbaked earthen jar of equal size.
Having sprinkled [it] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the weapon-mantra (astra) and water with kuśa grass,
[one should encircle it] with a fourfold thread and with downward-facing lotus petals.
Having bound it very firmly on all sides except for the mouth,
and having placed that [image] upon it with its face turned downwards, one should perform the recitation of the Tāra mantra.
One should spread darbha grass over the two jars with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra;
facing east, one should sprinkle them with arghya water while identifying oneself as the Puruṣa.
One should scatter unbroken rice grains above that with the Viśvamantra;
then, turning back, one should raise the final northern [hand] with both hands using the Nivṛtti mantra.

The knower of mantras, having touched [the disciple] with his whole being, should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, using the residual ghee from the offerings.
One should place the substances in this earthen jar with the heart-mantra:
clay, roots, minerals, seeds, metals, and fruits. (103)
Having filled [the vessels] with sandalwood and other substances, flowers, as well as all medicinal herbs, and *kuśa* shoots and *dūrvā* grass, one should place them above that.
Facing the east, one should mix [the materials] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water containing kuśa grass;
having worshipped [them] with offerings such as arghya and perfumes, while reciting the root mantra along with its ancillaries.
Having covered it with a new cloth, one should then offer the bali-oblation to the spirits in temples,
villages, towns, and cities.
Having reached an auspicious site for the installation,
one should dig a pit there in the center while reciting the root mantra.
Having wrapped the interior of the thumb with thread in three folds,
one should rotate it with that very [thread], place it in the center, and there dig a pit.
Measuring one cubit in height and provided with six finger-breadths at the base,
it should be consecrated with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and therein one should place gems and other such items.
Having meditated on the remainder [of the deity] above that, and having worshipped it in due order with water for the guest (arghya) and other offerings,
one should cover it with a cloth and perform the binding of the directions while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having touched the products of the cow with two jars and meditated, the Guru should mutter the root mantra;
then, when the night has turned to dawn, having performed the ritual acts such as bathing and so forth.
Having worshipped Nṛhari situated in the water-pot according to the previously mentioned procedure until the end of the recitation,
and having performed the Puṇyāhavācana rite, the Guru [should proceed] at an auspicious moment.
One should place a jar covered with lotus leaves into a cavity using a sling;
having filled it all around with every kind of grain so that it is as immovable as a mountain, [one should perform the ritual]. 113.
Having extracted the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and placed them in a jar while reciting the Kavaca mantra,
one should fill the pitcher with that very substance while reciting the root mantra (mūla-mantra) and remaining seated on a dog-skin.
Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and other articles, one should fill [the vessel] with collected earth;
then one should cause [the officiant] to recite the Nṛ-sūkta, the Bhadra-sūkta, and the Svasti-sūkta.
Then one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) with the materials previously mentioned in their proper order;
one should carry it out according to one's capacity, whether a hundred, fifty, or twenty-five times. || 116 ||
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor by one who desires the fruit of the installation.
Thus has the ritual procedure for the placement of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) been fully described to you. || 117 ||
It pacifies all portents, destroys great sins, bestows all happiness, is meritorious, and wards off all calamities. || 118 ||
It constantly bestows freedom from all disease and increases one's sons and grandsons;
whatever the practitioner of mantra desires, he obtains that without doubt. || 119 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Atonement, Sprinkling, and the Installation of the Five Products of the Cow," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
|| Śrīḥ ||
The twenty-third chapter:
O Brahman, Sanaka formerly praised the Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha.
The installation of the great machine in a single form is characterized by stability. || 1 ||
If you are gracious toward me, explain it in detail.
Śāṇḍilya said: In ancient times, it was spoken by Nārāyaṇa at the holy hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
Then, for the sake of pacifying the great sin of severing the head of Brahmā,
[the Lord spoke] to Śaṅkara, who was inquiring about the removal of all sins.
Having heard that in detail, he too, having installed it according to the prescribed rite upon the peak of Kailāsa, placed it within a mechanical device situated on a pedestal.
Resembling the sun at the end of an eon, with two faces, imperishable,
consisting of all the worlds, consisting of all the deities, and marvelous.
The support of all, yet itself without support; consisting of all powers and actions;
utterly consuming with its own splendor the entire multitude of wicked defects.
Having propitiated [her], Bhava became purified in a very short time;
likewise, others such as Puruhūta and the rest attained this same knowledge.
From Śaṅkara, who is known as Pūrṇa, they protected their respective quarters;
this is the mode of worship for kings whose nature is the protection of their subjects. || 8 ||
It must be performed without interruption; otherwise, lack of fortitude arises.
How could this [lack of fortitude] arise even for those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin)? || 9 ||

What need is there to mention kings who, for the sake of maintaining the world, do not even look toward the established order, let alone those who actually violate it and thereby forfeit what is difficult for them to attain? 10.
Likewise, for other twice-born ones, it destroys all sins;
having been installed, it is worthy of worship and bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
Listen specifically to that supreme and most secret injunction:
[it should be performed] in a divine temple or the like, in a painted [mandala], or in some place such as the courtyard. || 12 ||
In a village or similar location, on a riverbank, in a forest, or upon a mountain,
one should construct a temple or a pavilion that is decorated with paintings and faces all directions.
It faces either the east or the west, is provided with windows and doors,
consists of one or more storeys, and is marked with the emblem of the discus.
Having constructed it with a beautiful entrance, provided with stairs for ascent, and enclosed by a wall, he established it within the expanse of the palace.
Upon an auspicious seat situated today within a city-fortress marked by a vajra,
adorned with Śeṣa and others in the cardinal directions and a hexagonal city in the center.
It is adorned with the wind-seed syllable and the wind-maṇḍala;
within it, inside an eight-petalled lotus situated in the center of a ten-spoked wheel. || 17 ||
One should install that great yantra, characterized by its specific marks,
starting from a measurement of twelve finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time.
There are thirteen measurements, ranging from one finger-breadth up to twelve finger-breadths;
having determined one among these according to the desire of the maker.
From the feet up to the uṣṇīṣa, it may be divided into twelve or eight parts;
taking half the measurement of the body as the basis, one should measure all around for the purpose of the limbs.
With a central thread, a circle for the pericarp is drawn;
outside of that, six lotuses are formed, each occupying one part, in their proper sequence.
The first [lotus] should have four petals, and immediately after that, one with eight petals;
one should know the third to have sixteen petals and twice eight filaments.
The fourth [lotus] has thirty-two filaments and is adorned with thirty-two petals;
it is endowed with eight times eight filaments, and the outer [lotus] has an equal number of petals.

That [lotus], freed from its filaments, has eight petals; likewise, outside of that, the outer enclosures beginning with the square (bhūpura) and ending with the casket (sampuṭa) are situated externally along with the intermediate space.
With two syllables each, there are two outer enclosures;
in the eastern one are Keśava and the others, and Viṣṇu and the others outside of that.
From Ṛṣīkeśa and Janārdana, who are intent upon the maintenance of the world,
[he took] the portion of the discus, mace, and other weapons from their exterior, as well as from below and above them.
Then, having set aside two parts for the Varāha and Narasiṃha [mandalas],
one should arrange the mechanical devices (yantras) all around the square enclosure (bhūpura) for the sake of enjoyment.
When the width of the great yantra has been divided into five or seven parts,
one should fashion three stalks using the outer and middle sections.
The stalks are somewhat longer than the height of the seats and pedestals;
they have the shape of a boar's face and are broad at their base on both sides.

Having thus understood the measurement from the base to the top and from front to back by following the southern direction and so forth, one should prepare the material here, whether it be metal, wood, stone, or the like.
One should collect [the materials] according to the scripture, with the correct measure and according to the prescribed rule;
it should be fashioned into the shape of a fruit, solid and firm by means of a single portion.
It may be made of stone, with a thickness of six parts or four parts;
its shape is that of a square city on the exterior of the forest of the pericarp.
From this supreme measurement, one may perform the prescribed primary ritual according to the desire for a medium or inferior result by using one-third or one-half [of the size]. || 33 ||
Having doubled the lower lip, one should fashion it according to that measurement;
having removed the portion of the palate as before, it should hang down as it was previously.
Having divided the remainder sixteenfold, one should draw the enclosure lotuses outside that [mandala] with a radius equal to half the pericarp, as before;
then, the city-walls and so forth are formed by three [parts].
Then, with three [parts] each, two enclosures for the forms (mūrtis) should be made;
and with half [of that], a square, which is the second enclosure for the forms. || 36 ||
One should fashion each one according to its proper measure, arising from three parts;
and one should fashion Keśava and the others, as well as Viṣṇu and the others, in sixteen ways.
Or, having deliberated with the intellect through the yoga of meditation, one should perform it in a single enclosure;
in the center, upon the pericarp, there should be a lunar disc on the circumference.
In the center of that, one should place the Tāraka; in the center of that, the Sudarśana, endowed with sixteen or eight arms, possessing the brilliance of fire.
The Lord had tawny eyes and hair, wore red garments,
and from the cavity of his mouth, terrifying with its fangs, issued forth fire.
With its bee-like curls distorted by the knitting of crooked brows, and with the quarters of the sky set ablaze by the flames vomited from the eye on its forehead; 41.
Adorned with a crown kissed by masses of upward-flaming fire,
his chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he is resplendent with a jeweled neck-ornament.
Wearing a divine foot-ornament like a sacred thread,
he stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, assuming the form of one treading upon the discus.
The measurement from the tip of the line at the right big toe of the feet, as well as from the other [left toe],
from the heel, and from the middle of the sole, is to be taken in finger-breadths (aṅgula) obtained from the body's own proportions.
There should be forty-eight [mudrās] in the pratyālīḍha posture, maintained for a long time, beginning from the primary right hand and ending with the primary left hand. (45)
With sixteen arms, he holds, in clockwise order:
a spear, a sword, fire, a goad, a staff, and a lance.
And the axe, the thousand-spoked discus, the conch with the arrow and the bow, the noose, the plough, then the thunderbolt, the mace, and likewise the pestle. 47.
He carried these tridents and weapons, each one individually powerful,
invincible, destroyers of fear, and slayers of enemies.
Otherwise, with eight arms, he holds in his primary right hands, beginning from the first, a lotus, two blades of kusha grass, a mace, and a wheel of most fierce splendor. (49)
Having fashioned, in sequence, the conch, the bow with arrow, the noose, and the Kaumodakī mace,
the artisan should thus create a half-image measuring nine tālas.
Standing on the ground between his feet upon the pericarp,
[one performs] the rites of pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), subjugation (vaśīkāra), inciting enmity (vidveṣa), attraction (ākarṣa), and killing (māraṇa).
Or, if that best of practitioners should desire to perform the rite of eradication (ucchāṭana),
the mantra-master should write the name of the target object enveloped by the power (śakti) of the Lord.
One should gradually draw a hexagon around the periphery of the lunar disc;
in its six corners, starting from the east, are the Pravartaka and Nivartaka [mantras].
Having first written the mantra-syllables beginning with *sā* and ending with the *bindu*, one should then write these [syllables] facing inward within the *varma* and *astra*.
In the spaces between the outer corners, starting from the south,
these are prescribed as the limbs (aṅgas), beginning with the wheel of speech (ācakra) and ending with the wheel of flames (jvālācakra).

On the tips of the four petals, starting from the east, are the syllables *vaṃ* and *astraṃ* (huṃ) with the nasal drop (*bindu*). In the intermediate spaces between them are the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), also with the nasal drop, their faces turned inward.
On the filaments of the eight-petalled lotus, one should place the vowels and the other [consonants] along with the bindus;
on the petals, the syllables of the eight-syllable mantra, and likewise the elements outside of that.
Upon the mass of filaments of the sixteen petals, according to the previous practice,
one should place the letters from *ka* to *sa*, together with the bindu, as before.
On those petals are the twelve syllables, along with the armor (varma), the weapon (astra), and the head (śiras);
this is called the sixteen-syllable [mantra] on the thirty-two filaments and so forth.
One should place the great Ānuṣṭubh mantra of Nṛvarāha and Nṛsiṃha on the eight petals outside, and the mantra of Pātālanṛhari on the [remaining] eight petals.

Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) syllable by syllable as before, one should then place the eight-syllabled Nārasiṃha mantra upon the eight-petalled lotus; and on the outer city-gate (bhūpura), however—
In [the mandala] enriched by the seven continents and oceans, marked with vajras at the corners,
the supreme earthly seed-syllable is located in the great directions starting from the east.
Combined with their respective name-mantras, the semi-vowels (antasthā) are placed in the corner spaces;
then, the seed-syllable together with the earth-element (la) is placed both inside and outside the corners.
Outside of that, one should place the sixteen vowels in reverse order;
likewise, outside of that, one should place the consonants beginning with 'sa' and ending with 'ka' in their natural order.

Having performed the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) of the name of the one to be accomplished with the *paritoṃtya* couplet itself, [one should do so] by means of the reverse application outside the enclosure of the city (*bhūpura*). 65.
Having encircled [the deity] with two, or with both the noose and the goad, or even with many [weapons],
Keśava and the others are to be placed in their respective positions according to the sequence previously described.
The Viṣṇus situated on the outer enclosure stand in the directions starting from the east;
Hṛṣīkeśa is in their corners, and Janārdanas are in their openings.
And their mantras, beginning with the *praṇava*, should be formulated in due order:
accompanied by the vital breath (*sajīva*), endowed with their respective names, and joined with the word of salutation (*namaskāra*). || 68 ||
At the end [of the mantra], one should say "protect, protect such-and-such," adorned with the name of the person to be protected (sādhya);
then, outside of that, in the directions starting from the east, one should place the semi-vowels (antasthā) together with the eight [vowels].
One should write Ya, Śau, Ra, Ṣau, La, and Sau, and then Va and Hā along with their bindus; one should draw these again from the northeast to the southeast and then to the west.
Having encircled [the deity] with two hands holding a noose and a goad, or likewise with many,
one should place the mantra of the Man-Lion (Nṛhari) above all, and the mantra of the Man-Boar (Nṛvarāha) below.
Listen now in due order to the pure meditation upon Keśava and the others:
Keśava is golden-hued, bearing the lotus, the conch, the discus, and the mace. (72)
Nārāyaṇa has the luster of a water cloud and holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; Mādhava resembles a blue lotus and possesses the lotus, mace, conch, and discus. || 73 ||
Govinda is white in complexion and holds the discus, mace, conch, and lotus;
Viṣṇu has the mace, lotus, conch, and discus and possesses the luster of the Bandhūka flower.
Nadhusūdana holds a red discus, a lotus, and a conch;
Trivikrama, reddish like a hibiscus flower, possesses a discus, mace, lotus, and conch.
Vāmana should be red in complexion and hold a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
Śrīdhara has the radiance of the moon and holds a lotus, a discus, a mace, and a conch. || 76 ||
Vidyutprabha, Hṛṣīkeśa, the bearer of the mace, discus, conch, and lotus; the bearer of the mace, lotus, discus, and knowledge; Pajhanābha, who possesses the luster of the rising sun. || 77 ||
Dāmodara is reddish-brown in complexion and holds a lotus, a conch, a mace, and a discus;
[he is described] from the primary lotus-hand on the right up to the primary hand on the left.
Wearing the fourfold array of weapons beginning with the discus,
they bear the crown and the kaustubha gem, and are adorned with forest garlands.
All of them wore yellow garments, with serene faces and eyes;
their hearts were filled with compassion, and they were intent on uplifting the world.
For the sake of quelling the suffering of those men who cannot endure the splendor of the Yantra,
they are constantly sprinkled from all sides with showers of nectar.
Viṣṇu is in the eastern direction and other quarters, while Hṛṣīkeśas are situated in the intermediate directions;
Janārdanas occupy the gaps, and they are four-armed upon the eight pedestals.
Likewise, those holding the discus and conch on their right and left rear hands grant boons or bestow fearlessness with their primary left hand.
The Viṣṇus, terrifying with their blazing fires, held in their principal right hands the discus,
the mace Kaumodakī, and the Śārṅga bow, along with swords.
The Hṛṣīkeśas, golden-hued, stationed in the regions of the corners beginning with the southeast,
carry a conch, a plow, and a mace, with a trident at the end.
And the Janārdanas situated in the gaps starting from the east and southeast,
possessing the luster of blazing emeralds, were gazing at those standing in the various directions.
A staff, a spear, a javelin, a noose, and likewise a goad;
a thunderbolt, one known as an axe, and a hundred-mouthed fire.
Occupying well-proportioned positions, they may be arranged in the svastika and other formations;
or they may all be seated comfortably, either alone or accompanied by their śaktis. || 88 ||
Below that, one should visualize the Boar-faced Lord, who is the embodiment of all sacrificial limbs;
he has the luster of a dark-brown complexion and eyes resembling lotuses.
With his two western hands he holds the discus and the conch as before;
with his primary right hand, he bestows fearlessness upon those who are afraid.
Beyond that, the god Hari, resembling the snowy mountain, is intent on embracing with his left arm the Earth who is seated upon his own lap. || 91 ||
With eight arms, he is exceedingly fierce; on his back, from right to left, he holds a conch, a discus, a lotus, a mace, a sword, and a bow with an arrow.
With six hands, he held Hiraṇyakaśipu with his two principal arms, and in his rage,
he tore him apart while he lay in his lap with claws like saws.
Having raised his hand together with the lotus, or granting fearlessness with the hand alone,
his auspicious chest is marked by streaks of golden blood flowing like streams.
One should surround all these with the living Śakti-bīja;
externally, in the directions beginning with the East, one should place them in embodied forms, having the nature of weapons.
One should draw these: the discus, the kaumodakī mace, the śārṅga bow, and the nandaka sword;
likewise, there are thirty-four forms beginning with Keśava and ending with the weapons. (96)
The mantra-practitioner should either fashion it independently or upon the ground of the enclosure;
having thus made the yantra face eastward, he should arrange the other limbs.
One should fashion a circle of pericarp in the center according to the previously mentioned measurement;
within that, there is a hexagon consisting of the union of light and bliss.
Having divided that exterior area into three parts and [another] half-field within it,
one should place a twelve-petalled lotus outside the *udumbara* at the triple-eighth [mark].

The wheel has twenty-four spokes and is provided with a hub, a rim, and three naves; it is surrounded on the outside by the principles (tattvas), which are situated upon the rim at its outer edge. 100.
He is surrounded by the eight Śaktis, beginning with Jayā,
within the center of the pericarp of a twelve-petaled lotus previously envisioned.
Within the hexagon, which has the form of a triangle joined with its mirror-image and is characterized by light and bliss, one should perceive the God, radiant like the fire at the end of an aeon.
He wears the garments of a king, a great ocean filled with the virtues of knowledge and other qualities;
he has three eyes, four arms, and holds four discs; he is supreme. (103)
His limbs were bound by a yogic cloth, his two arms rested upon his knees, his chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he was adorned with a crown and other ornaments. || 104 ||
With necklaces, crest-ornaments, armlets, bracelets, and finally with anklets,
[he adorns] his devotees who are deeply attached to him and whose souls are devoted to the established doctrine.
Under the pretext of the shade of an Ashoka branch, he was intent on destroying suffering;
his actions were devoted to protecting the virtuous, and his mind was joyful. (106)
Having drawn the one to be accomplished (sādhya) enclosed within the seed-syllables beneath the lotus-feet,
[one should write] three [syllables] each in the six corners starting from the east.
The mantra-syllables of Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha are to be placed in their proper order, as well as its limbs (aṅgas), on the ground within the corners outside of that [mandala]. || 108 ||
One should write the syllable *kṣā* by means of a circular arrangement among the [other] letters;
outside the wheel, starting from the east, are Jayā, Candraprabhā, and Vinī. (109)
Then there is Mohinī, dark as the sprouts of fresh dūrvā grass; Vijayā, with the luster of a sapphire; Kāntā; and Hlādinī, with the radiance of a pale-red flower. || 110 ||
Ajitā is golden-hued; Māyā has the luster of a blue lotus;
Aparājitā is red; and Siddhi is smoke-colored—each [embraces] her own husband. (111)
And they, with eyes like blue lotuses, constantly gazing [at him], were augmented by the splendor of their fresh youth and beauty. (112)
Adorned with crowns and caskets, decorated with all kinds of ornaments, clothed in variegated silken garments, and endowed with flowers from every season. || 113 ||
They have two arms; they are adorned with flower garlands held in their right hands, and in their left hands they hold chowries and fans that resemble the rays of the moon. || 114 ||
In the *bhūpaccara* [mudrā], Nṛsiṃha has a terrifying and fierce appearance with a fearsome luster;
his face is formidable with bared fangs, and his eyes are like blazing fire. (115)
Resembling dark blue clouds, with two arms holding a staff and a discus, their bodies towering and exceedingly fierce, they gazed at one another. (116)
Having thus prepared the great yantra of Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha, both wearing red garments and adorned with garlands of red flowers; || 117 ||

The mantra-practitioner should install [the deity] according to the rules in the center of the temple pavilion, beginning from the ritual demarcation of the site once all the rites have been completed. (118)

Having placed [the deity] upon the seat and established it upon the yantra according to the prescribed rite, worship should be performed at the three times of day; its characteristics are now described.
Its length should be twelve finger-breadths greater than the width of the machine;
or else, when the width of the machine is divided into seven or five parts [the length should be one part more]. (120)
Then, having omitted one part from each end, the width of the *viṣṭara* (seat-grass) should be made with five or three parts situated in the middle. || 121 ||
Having placed each one in the middle with six finger-breadths on either side,
one should fashion two apertures by means of the two tubes situated at the sides of the instrument.
The practitioner of mantras should erase the remaining lines for the successful accomplishment of the square,
having divided the height of the yantra into three, four, or five parts.
The height of the pedestal (viṣṭara) should be made according to the measurement of one part of that [specific dimension];
having decorated it like a throne, one should surround it on the outside with five limbs.
Above that, one should fashion the *viṣṭara* (seat) and the *yantra* (mechanism); hear now the procedure for that:
[one should fix] the portion situated in the middle of the *pīḍa* by means of a thread placed in the center. || 125 ||
Having circled for the sake of the pericarp, when the remainder is divided sixfold,
there is an eight-petaled lotus at the top, provided with sixteen filaments.
In that same manner, outside of that [circle], one should draw a radiant ten-spoked wheel;
and within the middle of the wind-mandala, one should draw a hexagon with three [lines] on the outside.
The square enclosure (bhūpura) is marked with vajras at its corners and is half a part [in width];
this yantra is for the purpose of establishing the dwelling of the one free from laziness (madhyama-nālasya) in the center.
One should pierce it with that same measure, writing the name of the person to be accomplished all around;
having written this, one should encircle it outside on the sixteen filaments.
The sixteen-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha consists of those [syllables] up to the limit of twelve syllables, joined with "huṃ phaṭ svāhā"; this is the sixteen-syllable mantra of Nṛhari. (130)
First, one should place the supreme Anuṣṭubh mantra of this [deity] upon the eight petals starting from the east,
assigning it to each individual petal in a sequence of four.
On the eastern spokes and so forth of the outer ten-spoked wheel, the mantra of the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha is [placed], conjoined with the word "hana. (132)
One should draw it by means of the dual union on the outer wind-maṇḍala;
one should draw the supreme seed-syllable of the wind in a circular form.
One should draw the armor (varma) together with the weapon (astra) at various intervals;
however, in the six outer corners, one should write the fiery syllable (the letter Ra).
One should fashion [the area] in each corner as being endowed with flames of fire;
within the corners of the square (bhūpura), one should inscribe the earthly seed-syllable (pārthiva-bīja).
Then, in the intermediate directions, one should place the syllable Aṅkāra around [the center] like a throne;
then, resting upon the region of the neck, two by two should be placed in order in the eastern direction.
Gazing at one another, intent on maintaining their posture, they should be imagined as the most excellent of the excellent,
with gaping mouths and fierce eyes.
Ananta and Gulika are in the east; Śaṅkha and Vāsuki are in the south;
Takṣaka and Mahāpadma are in the west; and likewise in the north.
Likewise, Kārkoṭaka and Apajha; a distinction regarding these is stated there:
having divided the ground of the pericarp up to the edge of the outer wall (bhūpura) into another manner. || 139 ||
One should construct the Nṛsiṃha-yantra, with a seat for the yantra on the outside;
in the cardinal directions, there should be the weapons of Nārāyaṇa made of kūrca-grass.

One should paint the principal image and the others with colors derived from minerals such as white [lead] and the like, mixed with saffron and other pigments, according to their beauty on both faces.
The beauty of the colors for Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha has been described:
the pericarp is golden in appearance, while the filaments are reddish.
The petals should be pale red, and the surrounding enclosures on all sides should be made with a golden luster; this for the images has been stated previously. (143)
One should fashion two navel-circles with a golden and reddish luster;
the spokes should resemble the autumnal sky, and the interior should be reddish.
One should fashion the three auspicious rims white with gold,
or one should indeed write the syllables of the mantra with yellow or vermilion.
In the filaments and petals of the lotus, in the earth-fortresses (bhūpuras) on all sides,
within and outside the hexagons, and in the hub, spokes, and rim of the wheel.
The letters of the mantras are separated, turned inward, situated between two *tāras*, and finally joined with the *bindu*. || 147 ||
These [mantras] should be written everywhere, encapsulated by the primary *praṇava* (oṃ), enclosed within a perimeter wall, and accompanied by salutations (*namaskāra*). 148.
One should fashion Nārāyaṇa-missiles and green *kūrca* grasses,
bound with a lotus-cord, and then [fashion] horse-headed [missiles].
It should be written on birch bark with juices derived from saffron and agallochum,
along with yellow sandalwood, camphor, and the five products of the cow.
Having fashioned it into the shape of a pill according to the rule with a golden needle,
and having covered it with a gold plate, one should install it according to the prescribed ritual.

For the increase of the lifespan, health, wealth, grain, and so forth of those who are to be protected; and for the attainment of sons, grandsons, progeny, victory, desired objects, and other such successes. || 152 ||
The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the protection of the virtuous, should bear this yantra upon his head;
it is declared to belong to both Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha. || 153 ||
The installation of all the forms has been duly described previously;
having installed them in that very manner, one should perform the rite three times a day or at a single time. || 154 ||
"If the king is honored, the kingdom prospers in happiness.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Great Discus Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
Śrī.
The twenty-fourth chapter: O Sage Sanaka, the [glory] of Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha has been fully narrated.
The machine faces both east and west, and is filled with the various syllables of mantras.

Beginning from the middle [mantra], please explain in due order the supreme characteristics of the mantras along with their ancillaries, for the purpose of ritual placement (nyāsa) and for the purpose of worship.
Śāṇḍilya said: You have asked well, O Sanaka, concerning that which is characterized by the secret tradition of the wise. Listen here to the collection of mantras as they truly exist.
Formerly, for the welfare of all the worlds, it was granted by Śaṅkara and by me as well, once Saṃkarṣaṇa had been pleased— a form consisting of a yantra, preeminent in its qualities.
On a well-concealed and pure patch of ground, one should spread out the wheel of letters (varṇacakra),
which consists of all phonemes from the letter 'A' to the letter 'Kṣa'.
Adorned with its own hub, naves, spokes,
and rims, one should inscribe the Praṇava upon the axle, which is the cause of all mantras.
The vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga are situated in the limbs starting from the navel;
the consonants beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'bha' are located in the twenty-four spokes.
The letters from *ma* to *ha* are on the rim, while the letter *kṣa* stands in the outer circle;
this wheel consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) and contains the entire collection of phonemes.
Then, having duly placed the Mātṛkā-yantra with its names in sequence, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "Namaḥ," the Guru [installs] his own deity according to the rules.
Having thoroughly worshipped the embodiment of the Mātṛkā-mantras with offerings such as water for the feet (arghya) and flowers,
one should then extract the mantras that bestow the accomplishment of all desired goals.

In the beginning, the power of action (kriyā-śakti), which is capable of conquering itself and is intent upon the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe], was designated as the mother of volition (saṃkalpa). || 11 ||
Presiding over the form of Time, this world was expanded by her;
therefore, the wheel of time (kālacakra) is the wheel of the world (jagaccakra), and thus it is the Sudarśana body.
Presiding over that [Prakṛti], that Power exists as the individual soul (jīva);
deprived of her, this entire world would be as if non-existent. || 13 ||
Therefore, one should draw forth the Śakti, which possesses a radiance equal to Agni and Soma,
the eternal Vaiṣṇavī power that is without beginning or end and has the axle as its support.
First is the pair at the end of the rim (nemi), then that first pair with two fires (analau);
the nave (nābhi) consists of four, and the final pair; this entire mass (piṇḍa) is thus adorned. 15.
The great spear of the Sudarśana is the bestower of all perfections;
it is the living essence of the six-syllable mantra, whose nature is light and bliss.
For the sake of accomplishing the limbs beginning with the heart, one should take this *piṇḍa* (seed-syllable) deprived of its vowel;
one should then differentiate it by means of the first three long vowels and the last two [vowels], ending with the "eye" (*netra*). 17.
One should indeed perform these [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava, together with the Hṛdaya and other [limbs], along with the six Jātis: Namaḥ, Svāhā, Vaṣaṭ, Huṃ, Phaṭ, and Vauṣaṭ. || 18 ||
The [mantras] should be employed together with the qualities such as consciousness and the rest.
Now hear the extraction of the six-syllabled [mantra], which is the form of the power of primordial nature (prakṛti). || 19 ||
Having brought together [the syllables] as before, at the end one should place the final pair;
therein, the eighth [syllable] along with the third should be accompanied by the letter 'sa', and finally, the last [syllable] should be accompanied by the letter 'sa'.
One should make that [mandala] adorned with the five vowels and the [five] consonants beginning with *na*,
and subsequently provided with the letters of the eleven spokes, and then with twice as many spokes.
One should place the final syllable at the end of the fifth and sixth [syllables] as Avimukta.
This six-syllabled mantra of the Sudarśana is thus proclaimed. || 22 ||
The third, fifth, and sixth are each remembered as having three syllables;
the other three letters, being joined with the letter 'a', consist of two syllables each.

This eight-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the designator of Viṣṇu, who is Time itself and whose form is the universe; it is accompanied by the power (Śakti) consisting of the syllable *sat*. || 24 ||

Just as the person (puruṣa) abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti) is to be meditated upon through the union of the field and the knower of the field (kṣetra-kṣetrajña) as consisting of both the gross and the subtle, so too is Hari in his Sudarśana form.
The vision of the supreme reality is the vision of its exposition;
for those established therein, this [exposition] is eternally the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance. (26)
He cuts away their doubt so that they may proceed with the proper means;
this is the other form of Him who effects the severance of doubt. (27)
Surely, by the mere sight of those devoted to the conduct of their caste and stage of life, he destroys wicked beings through the power of his own knowledge. (28)
For those devotees of purified soul who are swiftly marked by this [seal], victory shall be held in their hands both in this world and in the next. (29)
How much more so, O Sage, when the yantra is established in its proper place and worshipped? Such is the power of the mantra, O scorcher of foes, as it has been described.
Listen now to the characteristics of this mantra, beginning with its heart and so forth, in their proper sequence;
first, the syllables of the heart-mantra and the others, in due order. (31)
One should then place the seed-syllables at the end of the *tāra* (om) with the *bindu*;
likewise, at the end of the sequence of the *āviṣūns*, there are two solar syllables (*sūrya*).
And at the end of the words *mahāsudarśana-jvālā*,
one should join the word *cakrāya* six times in sequence, ending with the head-word (*śiraḥ*).
One should write [the syllables] starting from the heart and ending with the fourth [center], endowed with the qualities of consciousness and so forth,
using the suffixes *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so on, according to the previously mentioned rule.
The objects of meditation exist in the forms [of deities] at the seats of awakening like roots, through their colors, ornaments, garments, weapons, arms, postures, and gestures. (35)

The final two syllables of the mantra of the armor-weapon (varmāstra) are traditionally known as "namo nārāyaṇāya"; this consists of eight syllables when accompanied by the *tāraka* (the syllable *oṃ*). || 36 ||
Its limbs and subsidiary limbs [should be worshipped] with the mantra-syllables adorned with bindus;
the remaining [limbs], up to the feet, are likewise worshipped in sequence with the final syllable.

The nature of the sixteen-syllable mantra, together with its qualities such as the heart-mantras and so forth, as well as the fourth state (turya) and the other [states], along with the [seed-]syllables, has been previously described. (38)
The [mantras] beginning with "heart" (hṛdaya) and ending with "feet" (pāda) are to be conceived as before.
Therein, one should utter the twelfth seed-syllable ending in *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Listen to the Anuṣṭubh mantra of the omnipresent Lord who has the face of a boar:
it begins with a vowel and consists of the fifth letter, unified and balanced from of old. (40)
Having thus extracted the first syllable, one should take the first caste-syllable;
that is the third ending in 'ra', and at its end is the fifth, which is the rim (nemi). 41.
Then follows the sixteen vowels together with the eleven [consonants] beginning with 'na';
after that, the word "varāharūpāya" (to the one in the form of a boar), and above that, the three *vyāhṛtis*.

Then, [the words] "at the end of the word *pataye* (to the lord), immediately after this, grant me the status of a king (*bhūpatitvam*)," and thereafter the word "cause [him] to give" (*dāpaya*). || 43 ||
This mantra, including the *śiras*, is proclaimed to consist of thirty-two syllables.
One should assign its limbs (*aṅga*) by dividing the words fivefold.
Successively, with seven, six, seven, and then seven syllables produced from the [five] elements, beginning with the *praṇava* and increasing in qualities. || 45 ||
