O Sulocana, this arrangement of the limbs of this mantra, beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon, together with the [five] castes up to the fourth, has been declared.
One should know that *śakti* is *svāhā*, its *bīja* is *bhūḥ*,
and thereafter one should utter the mantra of the form of Nṛsiṃha according to the previously mentioned number of syllables.
The first part [of the name] begins with *dayā* and ends with *agra*; it is not joined with anything ending in *nābhyarṇa*.
It is the middle one among poets, the first of Ramā, and has *saṃmata* as its end. 48.

Ending with *svāhā*, preceded by the *viṣṭara* and others, and preceded by *uru* ending with *kṛṣṇa*; this is then joined immediately thereafter with the fifteen-syllable [mantra] beginning with *nābhi*. || 49 ||
The end of *pūjā*, the long vowel (*lorghvaka*), the end of *ananta* with the nasal bindu, the beginning of *sahasra*, the end of *apūrva*, and thereafter the end of *sarvata*. (50)
Beginning with the crown (mukuṭa) and ending with the face (mukha), it is joined with the letters beginning with the rim (nemī);
having taken that which is between the Kinnaras, it stands above the letter beginning with Ṛcchaya. || 51 ||
The first [syllable] of Hari joined with the Bindu, then the equal one;
that which has a deep middle, the middle of Dhiṣaṇa, and ending with Karṣaṇa. || 52 ||
The first [syllable] joined with the end of *nābhi*, and then the first of *bhadrā* as well;
ending with *unnidrā* and containing the anusvāra within *amṛta*, it is twofold.
At the end of those two, there should be the word ending in *amṛta*; above that, one should place the letter *vā* (va).
Then, one should extract the letters ending in *anna*, *ramā*, and *ramya*, followed by the letter *ha*.
Thus has been proclaimed the supreme mantra of Nṛhari in the Anuṣṭubh meter;
its fifth seed-syllable (bīja) is said to begin with the letter 'sa' followed by 'ka'.
And likewise, Śakti is to be known as preceded by Indu (the moon) and accompanied by Bindu, with all four feet beginning with the Praṇava in due order. 56.
One should conceive of the five limbs of this mantra, beginning with the heart;
these should be joined at the end of the feet, it is said, by one whose self is infinite.

Then [the mantras] are: "to the one whose self is the beloved," "to the one whose self is light," and in the mantra "to the one whose self is Māyā," the word "to the one whose self is the moon" is the fourth.
The [mantras] beginning with Jñāna and the [mantras] beginning with Hṛdaya, ending with Jāti, are as before;
and the mantra of Pātālanṛhari is said to consist of eight times eight syllables.
One should utter each letter in sequence, joined with the preceding vowel;
thereafter, one should recite the ten syllables beginning with *ara* and ending with *nemi*, followed by the vowels.
The third [syllable] is at the end of the spokes, and at its end is the fifth, the rim;
endowed with the eleventh [syllable] as the hub, it consists of sixteen spokes.
Then, [the mantra] joined with the bindu, followed by the line of the peaceful Hara, ending with "kuśeśaya," then "agni," and at its end preceded by "netra. (62)
Having taken up the first *trātu*, the first *yaśa*, the present *sādya*, and the middle *parvata*,
which consists of eight spokes and is situated upon five rims.

One should utter these two [mantras] in this manner: first the *ravinemi* mantra, followed by the *śāntādya* mantra beginning with the twins (*yamala*), each repeated nine times and ending with the syllable *saṃ*.
Uttering these two pairs—the twenty-first and the sixth—in that manner, || 65 ||
The third [syllable] should be *nemi*, and the two [preceding syllables] should be *akṣa* and *anta*, as before, in two ways.
One should then adorn this [mantra] in sequence with the head-mantras of *varma* and *astra* at the end.
The mantra of Pātālanṛhari is recorded as consisting of sixty-four syllables.
The seed-syllable is said to be the first letter, and the power (śakti) is "svāhā" along with its attendants.
One should assign the limbs with the consonants, as before, adorned with the vowels.
[One should worship] in sequence with [the names] preceded by the Praṇava and ending with the Bindu. || 71 ||
And with [the mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Turya, starting from Jñāna and concluding with Astra. || 72 ||
As before, they are endowed with the seed-syllables *namaḥ* and *svāhā*. || 73 ||
Then there is the eight-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
That which begins with "namaḥ" and "praṇava," followed by the syllable "nara" at the end, and concludes with the word "siṃhāya"—this is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra of Nṛsiṃha. || 75 ||
*Kṣauṃ* is its seed-syllable; the third [syllable] near the navel is said to be the power (*śakti*).
One should fashion the heart and other limbs with the seed-syllable itself, just as before. (76)
Listen now to the characteristics of the mantras of Keśava and the others in their proper order:
the ninth, the eighth, the one beginning with *nemāvara*, and the last of the Mātṛkās. (77)
Having divided each one into three parts in sequence, as in the case of the twelve seed-syllables,
he should repeatedly join the *ya*, *la*, and *va* beneath all of them.
One should mark with a bindu above the place situated above the sixth vowel (Ū),
starting from TĀRA (OM) and ending at the heart, together with the fourth [vowel] (I).
Keśava is to be named first, then the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
likewise Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana. || 80 ||
Trivikrama, he who is called Vāmana, Śrīdhara, the lotus-eyed Hṛṣīkeśa, the lotus-navelled one, and he who is known as Dāmodara. || 81 ||
One should fashion the limbs as before using seed-syllables endowed with long vowels;
hear now the mantras for those [deities] beginning with Śrī and ending with Kāntā, in their proper sequence. 82.
First, the three ending with *m* from the *mātṛkā*, and those beginning with *kṣa*, are to be placed fourfold upon the stone;
then the remaining syllables should be joined on all sides, starting from the bottom portion in their proper sequence.
Fire, water, earth, water, Varuṇa, the Earth, fire, and in sequence, two waters, Soma, and then two [more] earthen [elements]. (84)
One should apply the fire-syllable (RA) at the head of the sixth, seventh, and eighth [vowels], and below the ninth and twelfth; furthermore, it is placed above all of them.
One should adorn [the mantras] beginning with the navel using the power of the vowels;
the seed-syllables (bījas), such as the heart-mantra and others, are endowed with the vowel-classes and so forth. 86.
Outside, the Viṣṇus beginning with Vāsudeva are distinguished in the cardinal directions by the discus, mace, bow, sword, and other weapons; hear now their designations. (87)

Having extracted [the mantra] from the first and last vowels at the navel, together with the *tāraka* (Om), one should offer salutation to Viṣṇu by the name "to the Wielder of the Discus" (*cakradharāya*) in the east. || 88 ||

For the third [mantra], one should employ "to Gadādhara" (O bearer of the mace), and for the end of the fourth, one should employ "to Śārṅgadhāriṇe" (O bearer of the Śārṅga bow) and "to Khaḍgadhāriṇe" (O bearer of the sword). || 89 ||
These twelve syllables are taught as the individual designators of the Viṣṇus;
one should perform the rites for their limbs (Aṅgas) and secondary limbs (Upāṅgas) with the mantras and so forth, as previously described.
Those seed-syllables of the Viṣṇus, ending with the vowels in reverse order, have been declared; they are proclaimed as the arrays of Hṛṣīkeśa.
The mantras of the Janārdanas will be declared from the space between the eastern [direction] and fire;
they consist of four [syllables] beginning with *i* and four beginning with *e*, respectively. (92)
One should perform [the rites] preceded by the syllable *praṇava*, and at their conclusion as before;
first, for all [of them], one should assign [the mantra] with "to the wielder of the staff" (*daṇḍadhārāya*) followed by *namaḥ*.
From the heart to the feet, [the limbs] are to be assigned with the syllables of the mantra as before;
the mantra for Nṛsiṃha and Kroḍa has already been shown previously. || 94 ||

The semi-vowels (antasthā) follow that; thus there are eight syllables. At the end of the letters are the vowels and the consonants (hal), which are well known and fully described. Now, however, learn the other limbs (aṅga).
Having first taken the four syllables situated at the beginning of the six-syllabled Sudarśana mantra,
one should then place them [respectively] in the eyes and so forth, ending with the two feet.
The fifth wound is situated on the rim above the sixteen spokes;
immediately after that, one should separate it from the third [wound] between the rim and the hub.

This is the *piṇḍa* mantra of Nṛsiṃha, beginning with the letter *na*, ending with *ha* along with the fire (*ra*), marked by those two from the center of the *nābhi*, and endowed with the color of lightning. 98.

Having extracted the last [syllable] of Siṃha and the first [syllable] of Hṛdaya twice, and then the two [syllables] of Varma and Astra, this nineteen-syllable [mantra] is joined with the Jāti and Āyus. (99)
The seed-syllable of this very [mantra] is the tenth vowel (AU), and that preceded by HŪM is said to be the Śakti.
Listen now to its six limbs, beginning with TĀRA (OM) and beginning with the Heart (HṚD), in their proper order. 100.
Having divided the seed-syllable, which is devoid of the syllable *oṃ*, into six parts as before,
by means of the initial vowels ending with the visarga and excluding the neuter ones.
Having joined them, one should then place the steps in succession above that:
first the step of the Wheel-King (Cakrarāja), and after that the step of the Blazing Wheel (Jvālācakra). || 102 ||
After that is the station called Jagaccakra; the fifth is known as Asurāntaka; and at the end is the one named Dīptacakra, the Mahāsudarśana.

At the end of the word denoting the person to be enjoined, one should place [the name] ending in the dative case; thereafter, with [mantras] beginning with "knowledge" (jñāna) and so forth, likewise with those ending in the dative such as "heart" (hṛdaya) and so forth, and with the [six] limbs beginning with "svāhā. || 104 ||

O Sage, first hear the seed-syllable (bīja) of Nṛsiṃha consisting of twelve syllables; having taken the seventh letter from the rim (nemisaptama), it is characterized by the first letter of the spokes (arārṇa). 105.
One should join this supreme seed-syllable with the preceding letter and the final vowel;
it contains the *natipraṇava* at its beginning and is the solitary hero of great luster. (106)
Know this to be the life-force of all lion-mantras, which consist of various meditative forms; it is the expressive essence of their true nature and the granter of desires.
Now hear the mantras of the forms, adorned with twelve syllables:
the *praṇava*, the heart-seed-syllable, and the word "Bhagavat" ending with the dative case. (108)
Then one should indeed give the five-syllabled mantra to Nārasiṃha;
this twelve-syllabled mantra belongs to Viśvatrātṛ Nṛsiṃha. || 109 ||
This ten-syllable mantra, ending with *tārā*, will have its heart-mantra and others, up to the eye-mantra, explained in due order. (110)
Its sixfold seed-syllable is preceded by *tāra* (om) and endowed with the vowels beginning with *ā*;
one should perform their conjunction as before, marked with the nasal drop (*bindu*). || 111 ||

One may perform the pervasive ritual pervasion (vyāpti) consisting of the limbs and sub-limbs with the twelve-syllable mantra together with the seed-syllables, the nasal bindu, the qualities (guṇas), and so forth, along with prostrations. || 112 ||

This mantra, together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), is declared to be all-pervasive for Nṛsiṃha and for those who have attained his various forms; it bestows the accomplishment of all desired goals. || 113 ||
The letters situated in the middle of the axle are described as being in the middle of the wheel;
the designations consist of the preceding letters together with the bindu, placed in the middle of the *natipraṇava*. || 114 ||
The syllables ending with the fourth [letter] are the designators (vācaka) of the group of powers (śakti-saṃgha), beginning with Jaya;
likewise, there should be two mantras consisting of the two elements Bhīma and Ugrā. || 115 ||
Listen to the characteristic of the mantras established upon the seat;
furthermore, the pervasive nature of the form of the name of the object to be accomplished shall be explained. (116)
If the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the deity are at the end of the Tārā [mantra], then [it bestows] peace, nourishment, subjugation, victory, and so forth. (117)

Having uttered the word ending in the accusative case followed by the repetition of "kuru," one should then add the words "yañcha yañcha" at the end, preceded by the syllables ending in the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 118 ||
And at the conclusion, one should mark it with the characteristics of the object to be accomplished;
this supreme mantra of Nṛhari consists of sixteen syllables and is in the Anuṣṭubh meter. (119)
The external syllable of Vāyu was previously indicated;
likewise, the syllable of Fire and the syllable of Earth are joined with the class of armor and weapons.
This has been explained in detail previously; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here.
That which is to be described for the holders of the yantras consists of the Nāgas, beginning with Kṣādyama. 121.

The seed-syllable (bīja) accompanied by the nasal drop (bindu) and preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by each individual name ending with the fourth state (turya) and concluding with "namaḥ. || 122 ||
Thus have the mantras of the remaining nāgas, beginning with Śeṣa, been correctly proclaimed;
they are joined with the power (Śakti) and the true Tārā, along with the six-syllabled Sudarśana mantras.
One should separate each letter of the eight-syllable mantra, both above and below;
this is the Nārāyaṇa-astra mantra, possessing the brilliance of the fire at the end of a kalpa.

Having first uttered the syllable [Oṃ], one should then employ the seed-syllable of the group of weapons beginning with the discus, conjoined with the fire-syllable (Ra) and the Visarga, or else accompanied by the Praṇava.
Then, the name ending in the dative case should be joined with "phaṭ" at the end;
these are proclaimed as the mantras for the sixteen weapons, beginning with the discus (cakra). || 126 ||

Having thus understood the greatness of the yantra, one should worship it according to the prescribed rules, performing the binding of the directions (digbandha), the fire-enclosure (vahniprākāra), the recitation of the Gāyatrī, the invocation of the vehicle (vāhana), and so forth. || 127 ||

Through the sacrificial implements and mantras, devoid of attachment to enjoyments and free from [selfish] giving, the attainment of all fruits and the accomplishment of mantra arise in due order. || 128 ||
The characteristics of the mantras for binding the ten directions will be explained first: "Oṃ, to Puruṣa in the east," followed by "svāhā" at the end. (129)
"I bind with the weapon-mantra, svāhā"—this six-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā* is declared to be the mantra for binding the directions, which removes the defects of the wicked. (130)
Having first extracted the Praṇava and the mantra between the Vahni (Svāhā) and Jāyā (Aum),
one should place the approaching wheel known as the Agniprākāra (Fire-Fortress).
Listen to the celebrated Cakragāyatrī, which brings grace to the Discus: having placed the [specific] caste name at the beginning, one should utter the word "cakrāya" (to the Discus). 132.

The second [mantra] consists of the three syllables from the beginning of the *Nṛsūkta* and the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*; having taken the word from those two, it is joined with the end of the *nemi-pūr*. (133)
The word "dhīmahi" should be placed at the end of that [Gāyatrī] without restriction;
having extracted the Gāyatrī up to its end, the four-syllable [mantra] is then placed at its conclusion.
The Gāyatrī of the Sudarśana is declared to consist of the syllables of the Tāraka;
with the Tāraka added, this [Gāyatrī] from of old becomes one syllable more. || 135 ||

Having first extracted two *tāra*s (oṃ), one should extract the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*). Then, having placed "dhāma," one should take the first [syllable] of the rim (*nemi*) and so forth, consisting of eighteen [units]. 136.
One should extract the syllable located on the twelfth spoke, with the navel as the fifth from the head;
then one should extract the five-syllable mantra beginning with "gṛhakāmyayoḥ. (137)
Then, one should join [the letter] situated on the second spoke with that which is situated on the ninth spoke of the two naves,
and then with the syllable situated on the sixteenth spoke, conjoined with the second vowel.
Furthermore, the fifth syllable is on the rim and situated upon the sixteen spokes;
it is conjoined with the second [syllable] at the hub, ending at the rim, and is the final *tāra*.
The third [syllable] from the circle of the rim is joined with the third vowel;
it extends to the end of the rim, endowed with a vowel, and reaches to the end of the spokes, which are separated by vowels. || 140 ||
Having joined the third vowel, and then [the letter] consisting of two nines (eighteen);
above the twenty-first [letter], that [vowel] is upon the head of the eighteen-syllable [mantra].
Having joined the third vowel, and then the letter that goes twice and nine times;
again, [the mantra] is the body of the mantra, ending with the *praṇava*, and then *namaḥ*.
Furthermore, the mantra joined with "namas" is suitable for invocation;
that mantra is now revealed for the bestowing of all enjoyments. (143)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, which is the sole cause of all enjoyments, one should then likewise utter this threefold word ending with the rim (nemī) and joined with the Bindu. 144.
"Take [it]" (gṛhāṇa), ending with "the head" (śiraḥ), is the expression for the granting of enjoyment;
it is likewise used in the invocation, the worship, and the rite of dismissal. || 145 ||
Having first extracted the Praṇava and addressed [the deity] as "O Blessed One" (bhagavan), one should provide the word "mantramūrti" and one's own name in the accusative case. || 146 ||
One intent on neutralizing the power of mantras employed by others should utter [the mantra] ending with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), preceded by "āsādaya" and "kṣamasva. || 147 ||
O Sage, listen to this supreme mantra, rich with all heroic mantras:
having first extracted the Praṇava, it begins with the Praṇava and is accompanied by the bindu. (148)
The six-syllable weapon-mantra (astramantra) preceded by the six syllables [of the root mantra], excluding the Praṇava;
first the two previously mentioned syllables, and after that the word "Cakrarāja. (149)
First, burn the word "sarva" with the seed-syllable *duṃ*; then follow it with "duṣṭabhayaṃkara.
After that, the word "cintāmūla," and then "bhindi bhindi. Thus [it is]. 150.
Split in two the word *pada*, then *mantraṃ hrāsaya hrāsaya*;
then the pair of words *bhakṣaya*, and after that *bhūtāni*. (151)
At the end of "trāsaya trāsaya," followed by "varma" and "astra" at the conclusion of the head [of the mantra], this seventy-first mantra is declared to be named Śaktihrāsa. || 152 ||
I shall declare the Anuṣṭubh mantra which bestows fearlessness upon all: having addressed [the deity] with the word "O Blessed One" (bhagavan), one should utter the word "all" (sarva). (153)
After that, the word "vijaye" (O Victorious One), followed by "sahasrākṣī" (O Thousand-eyed One);
then the word "aparājitā" (O Unconquered One), and immediately after that, the word "śaraṇam" (refuge) followed by "tvām" (thee). || 154 ||
After that, one should say "I have taken refuge" (prapanno'smi) with the word ending in the accusative case;
then, following the word beginning with "Śrī," one should say "Sudarśana" in due order. (155)
Known as *prapatti*, it brings about the destruction of all sins;
I shall now declare the *Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī* for the worship of the secondary limb. (156)
First is the two-syllable word "vajre," followed by "śṛṅkhalāyai"; then the word "āyāntam," then "tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭre," and from that, the word "vijṛmbhaya. (157)
At the end of the two syllables "vajra," one should recite "dhīmahi" followed by "nakha.
One should extract the first foot of the Gāyatrī and the first foot of the last [verse]. (158)
One should place the syllable *siṃha* with the *visarga*, ending with the *gāyatrī*;
then, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*) using the two aforementioned mantras.
One should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) together with the previously mentioned weapon-mantra (astra), and the application of the other limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) as before. 160.
Thus has this network of mantras been correctly described as it is situated within the king of yantras, joined with the pair of faces. || 161 ||
Whatever things are to be joined with enjoyments, both internally and externally, may they at some time be revealed to another person of dull intellect. 162.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Extracting the Mantra of the King of Yantras," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrīpāñcarātra Pārameśvarasaṃhitā.
|| Śrīḥ ||
Chapter Twenty-five. Sanaka said:
"O Blessed One, the [mantras] of Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha have been correctly explained."
One should worship this great yantra in the form of mantra, which bestows all desired objects. || 1 ||
Therefore, being gracious toward me, tell me that which is of the nature of worship;
for the benefit of all the worlds, this yantra has been proclaimed by Śāṇḍilya. || 2 ||
By whomsoever [this sacrifice] is performed according to the prescribed rule, everything is thereby accomplished.
I shall describe the sequence of the sacrifice to you, who are desirous of hearing it.
Having performed the ritual bathing and other preliminaries as before, and having entered the sacrificial hall,
he should wash his feet, perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana), and be well-adorned with an upper garment.
Having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and worshipped the two doorposts with flowers as before,
he should open the door-panel and enter within to the Lord.
Having prostrated with the Gāyatrī mantra and performed the washing of the hands and other preliminary rites,
one should then establish the three paths upon the image, the seat, or the yantra.

Having purified the temple, one should place [the image] upon a plank or similar support before it; having sprinkled it with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, [one should seat it] facing forward on a beautiful throne.
Seated comfortably, having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the sacrificial materials kept at his side,
he should perform the purification of his hands and the purification of the site with the Astra-mantra as before.
With both hands joined in the Astra-mudrā while reciting the mantra,
[one should ward off] the obstacles residing at the place of worship, whose forms are invisible from the outside.
Having performed the purgation (virecana), one should perform the binding in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
then, having enveloped [the self] with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before.
Then, having withdrawn the principles (tattvas) residing in the body along with the self,
one [perceives] the solitary form entirely liberated from all principles.
One should purify [the self] by means of dhāraṇās, such as drying and so forth, from above;
then, one should meditate upon the Lord in the form of Sudarśana within the state that begins with the fourth [turiya].
Having dried his own body with the armor of the wind whose essence is strength, he should burn the body starting from the big toe of the right foot. || 13 ||
Having meditated upon the crest-mantra as having the brilliance of tens of thousands of flames from the fire at the end of an aeon, one should contemplate [the body] as being consumed by it.
Having meditated on the heart-mantra, which resembles the full moon and showers a stream of nectar, one should contemplate [the disciple] as being sprinkled by it from the tip of the left thumb. 15.

Then, one should contemplate and meditate upon the mantras assigned for tasks such as drying up, beginning with the Armor-mantra (varma), as having gone to dissolution within the Lord of Mantras (mantreśvara). || 16 ||
One should meditate upon the body as being augmented by streams of nectar from its edges, possessing the luster of a hundred cool-rayed moons filled with the nectar of bliss.

Therefore, having dissolved the principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence, and having presided over that [state] by means of one's own self, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa). || 18 ||

First, one should dissolve the Mātṛkā, the mother of mantras, which begins with the letter 'a' and ends with the letter 'kṣa', into the two hands; then, while reciting, one should dissolve it according to the sequence of the wheel of the body.
Having thus performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa), which possesses a luster like the heat of the sun,
[he should perform it] in the sequence starting from the right, on the branches and also on the two palms.
Having thus placed four [syllables] on each finger from the thumb to the little finger—
making twenty-two in total— one should then place ten on the two palms.
Having likewise placed five and five [syllables] in the middle and in the three and four [sections], situated between two *praṇavas*, thus upon both hands.
Having first performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa), one should then perform the placement upon one's own body,
from the head down to the soles of the feet, with both hands like the rays of the sun.
Having thus pervaded [the body], one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) separately:
at the hairline, around the face, in the two eyes, and in the pair of ears. || 24 ||
In the two nostrils, in the two cheeks, in sequence from right to left, by means of the union of the upper and lower [teeth], and in the two lips; || 25 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should place the other vowels, along with the visarga, upon the head;
then, the ka-group (kavarga) should be placed in due order across the five joints of the right arm.
Likewise, the *ca*-group is on the left;
the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups, located at the joints, are on the right and left sides of the belly respectively, as before.

One should place the *pa*-group [of consonants] on the back, the navel, and the heart; the letters from *ya* to *sa* in the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and the letter *ha* within the heart. (28)
Having first thus placed the letter *kṣa* in the space of the heart along with the Mātṛkā, one should then place the six-syllable mantra, together with the Śakti, upon the hands and the body.
O Lord of Sages, first understand the ritual placement upon the hands (karanyāsa); listen to that, performed with the mantra of the syllable Om (Tārā) joined with the two Puṭīs and the Śakti.
One should wash both hands from the wrists to the tips of the nails as before,
reciting the six syllables with the nasal bindu, preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and the *śakti* (hrīṃ), at the beginning and the end.
Having placed [the letters] from the thumb to the little finger upon the middle joints,
one should place the final letter itself upon the tips of the fingernails.
Having thus assigned the vowels, one should assign the heart and the other limbs upon the root,
middle, and tip joints, according to the sequence of the assignment of the letters.
One should touch the body with both hands, from the head down to the feet;
having thus performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa), one should then perform the limb placement (aṅga-nyāsa).
On the head, the mouth, the heart, the navel, the secret place, and the two feet—this is the nyāsa of emanation; its persistence should be like that of the primary and secondary limbs. || 35 ||
In the two feet, the secret place, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the head—
from the feet up to the head— this is called the *saṃhṛtinyāsa*.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the two shoulders,
the middle of the hands, and the two eyes, in sequence with their respective mantras as they have been declared.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other [limbs], one should afterwards place the collection of weapons upon the two palms— either eight or sixteen [in number].
He [should visualize] the crown, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark as they were before;
he should place the power of will (icchā-śakti) on his right and left shoulders and on his two sides.

Having placed the principle of mind (manas-tattva), consisting of his own mantra, at the base of the thighs, one should meditate within as Lord Hari in the form of Sudarśana, ending with the thought "I am [He]. (40)
O Brahmin, the best of those who know mantras should rotate his own self externally with the Gāyatrī using the Cakramudrā, [visualizing] a garland of wheel-flames all around.
One should perform the sacrifice produced by meditative cultivation as enjoined from the beginning,
having restrained the collection of the senses within the sphere of knowledge, just as before.
One should arrange the seat of mantra from the base (ādhāra) up to the heart,
beginning with the power of the support (ādhāra-śakti) and ending with the seat of the state of consciousness (cidbhāva).
One should cause the previously mentioned sovereignty of the mantra, which is the triple heaven, to expand upward;
this is to be known as common to both Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha. (44)

Offered by means of visualization for the purpose of preparing the seat and the throne, [the offering] is presented either by those who have descended onto the back part [of the body] or externally into the space of the heart. 45.
Formerly, she resided above the pericarp of the heart-lotus, consisting of the Śabdabrahman,
resonating with the Nāda situated within the eye-pupils and pregnant with mantra.
The power of Viṣṇu, whose nature is peaceful, has been brought under control by practitioners;
that power of sound is proclaimed as being situated in the midst of the sky, the Viṣṭarārkas, and the void. 47.
The continuum, which has the nature of sound, has attained the state of phonemes, from the letter 'a' up to the letter 'kṣa', reaching the very limit of the phonemes. || 48 ||
In the supreme, waveless sky, auspicious and free from conceptualization, in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), the Lord is magnified by light and bliss. || 49 ||
He is known as Sat-Brahman and Vāsudeva, the embodiment of the six perfections in their fullness;
the Lord who is replete with great majesty and consists of all powers.
His nature is that of supreme bliss, perfectly tranquil and eternally manifest;
his body is marked with the conch and discus, and his hands grant boons and fearlessness.
Resplendent like a thousand suns and possessing the radiance of a thousand moons,
he was adorned with self-luminous ornaments beginning with a crown and ending with anklets.
Endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, adorned with a forest garland,
wearing yellow silk garments, and possessing a serene face and eyes.
The quarters of space were illuminated by the moonlight of his rows of teeth,
and he was attended on all sides by Śrī and Puṣṭi in their most excellent forms.

He is to be meditated upon through the cultivation of higher knowledge by those who perform actions free from desire, [using] the divine weapons such as the conch and the discus, which are eternally identical with all principles (tattvas). || 55 ||

For the sake of achieving perfection in the yoga of practice, one should [perform it] constantly both externally and internally, in those locations of the vital breath (vṛtti) arranged as the image, the pedestal, and so forth. || 56 ||
Worshipped in the form of the external array (paravyūha) and so forth, he attains everything;
because he is eternally manifest through the reality characterized by light and bliss. (57)

Having assumed a form characterized by similarity [to her devotees], out of a desire to bestow grace upon her devotees, she presided over the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and became intent on uplifting the world. || 58 ||
A portion of consciousness manifested, augmented by light and bliss; it was difficult to behold for those who cause distress to the virtuous through their own radiance. 59.
Because it brings delight to his own devotees, it is called Sudarśana;
having become the deity who has ascended above the six paths, he exists in the form of the fire of time (Kālānala).
Lord Hari in the form of Nṛhari destroys the sins of his devotees when merely thought of;
by him these two [forms] have been worshipped with exceedingly intense splendor.
He shall become radiant, the self of all beings, and happy everywhere;
having thus understood the true essence of the mantra, one should begin the rite of sacrifice.
Having mentally recited the mantra, one should bring down the supreme self, whose nature is consciousness, from the state of the Blessed One, and place it above the seat.
The form of Sudarśana is twofold by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier:
the embodied form is the signified, while the form of the mantra is the signifier.
Both of these should be considered praiseworthy according to the distinction between the higher and the lower:
one should know the higher to be the form of the expressible (vācyarūpa), and the lower to be that which is bound by mantras.
Having understood this, one should bring about the meditation on the supreme, subtle, and other [states];
one should know the supreme form of light, characterized by the bliss that culminates in Nāda. || 66 ||

The subtle characteristic of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which contains within it the head, hands, and other limbs, is the mere Linga; it is radiant with light and possesses the nature of future expansion.
That [mantra] is gross and has a manifest form within the nature of the signified and the signifier.
For mantras in the form of sound, there are three states, beginning with the supreme (parā). || 68 ||
The [energies] beginning with Paśyantī are to be fully known as threefold: self (sva), other (para), and not-other (apara).
Among those, the first is the Savior (tāra) and the second is designated as the Seed (bīja).
The third [method] is that which begins with the *padamantra* (word-mantra); it should be contemplated by men.
Its presence (*sānnidhya*), its manifestation before one (*saṃmukhībhāva*), and its complete cessation (*sannirodha*) are also as described previously.
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) and so forth, as well as the worship of dissolution and enjoyment,
[one should do so] even upon lotuses provided with pericarps, filaments, and petals.
Then, in all cases such as the Bhūpura and other diagrams, there follows the worship of the mantras in the form of lingas,
and the worship of the mantras representing the forms of Keśava and the others.
One should perform the rite according to the rules with the mantras previously mentioned, as in the case of the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga).
One should visualize the lunar orb above the head of the God of gods.
With the streams of nectar flowing from that [liṅga], one should perform the ritual preparation of the arghya and other offerings,
using either sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four modes of service (upacāras).

Having performed the propitiation like that of a king, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) fashioned at the navel-center, hexagonal and possessing three circumferential lines (mekhalā). || 75 ||
Having churned the fire-drill of meditation until it blazed forth with the rope of knowledge,
one should kindle the fire of consciousness, which refines all conditioned formations.
Always knowing that the flame-pointed, blazing, pure light, which is of the nature of the Lord and augmented by Śakti, has entered the sacrificial pit of the navel; || 77 ||

One should recite the root mantra situated above the sky of the heart-lotus, accompanied by prolonged meditation; when this has dissolved at the end of the Truth (satya), [the dissolution occurs]. || 78 ||
When the supreme state free from waves has been attained, one who stands in Brahman should draw [the essence] out with the ladle of meditation through the path of the junction,
by way of the path of nectar, using the full waters.
One should pour forth a stream of wealth, as it were, onto the head of the Lord of Mantras, who has descended from the heart and is stationed at the tip of the flame. || 80 ||

Having thus satisfied the fire of consciousness, one should again perform the acts of offering oblations while contemplating the Lord situated at the tip of the flame, dwelling within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.

Having duly completed the worship on the other limb, he should then worship Hari stationed there with his own mantra, up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa) with the nectars of meditative visualization.
At the end of that, having performed the final completion for the collection of mantras located on the two faces of the yantra-form, one should then perform the satiation (santarpaṇa).
One should worship the form on the seat externally at the two faces with the forms [of the deities], using offerings such as arghya and other enjoyments presented according to the rules. (84)

As before, there is the worship and installation of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, as well as the worship of the mantras placed on the body and those situated at the entrance of the womb-chamber. || 85 ||
And Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍapūrvaka [should be placed] respectively at the outer doors of the pavilions in the east and west. || 86 ||
Furthermore, Jaya, Vijaya, Subhadra, and Bhadraka—these four, along with the Sun and the Moon, are to be worshipped in the windows on the right and left sides. (87)
Having thus performed the sacrifice at the door, one should then enter the interior,
beginning from the power of the support (ādhāraśakti) and ending with the seat of the yantra.
Having worshipped the mantra-seat as well as Gaṇanātha and the others,
one should then perform the invocation (āvāhana) of the installed deity.
From the space of the heart-lotus of the Bimba, there arises the supreme, stainless consciousness, whose nature is light and bliss, eternally manifest and incomparable. (90)
One should contemplate it as seated, resting in the center of the pericarp;
then, having uttered the root mantra, it becomes awakened and radiant.

Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon one's own body; just as [they are placed] on the body, so too [should they be placed] on the locations beginning with the heart, and the excellent wheels beginning with the cakra, ending with the weapon (astra).
Then, having placed ornaments and other items upon the head and other parts so that they are level,
one should worship them with that which is called *laya*, shining like a heap of jewels.
Likewise, one should worship those [deities] stationed in the machine (yantra) within the pericarp and other parts, appearing radiant in form,
with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with those that reach the heart through touch.
Having gratified [the deity] according to the prescribed rite along with the assembly of the forms,
and having recited the mantra according to one's ability, he should offer it as before.
Then, one should worship Narahari, situated within the western machine, together with his limbs (aṅgas), his retinue, and the syllables of the machine. || 96 ||
Thus has been briefly declared the supreme worship of the great yantra;
one should gratify the deity residing in the center of the fire with the fuel-sticks previously mentioned. || 97 ||
"Especially for the sake of accomplishing desired fruits, [one should perform worship] even with optional rites.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Outer and Inner Worship of the Great Sudarśana Yantra," in the Kriyā-kāṇḍa of the glorious Pārameśvara-saṃhitā within the Śrī-Pāñcarātra.
|| Śrīḥ ||
The Twenty-sixth Chapter. Sanaka said:
O Blessed One, knower of the essential truth of the Pañcarātra, you who are dear to all living beings!
Out of a desire to show me favor, you have performed worship in the midst of the fire.
"Explain according to the rules that which accomplishes all perfections—
O Śāṇḍilya, lord of sages, you who are wise in every way— the auspicious bestower of both worldly success and liberation. (2)
Listen with a concentrated mind as I describe the sacrifice situated within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
one should construct an extensive pavilion for the purpose of the fire-oblation, facing the southeast.
It should be provided with smoke-pipes and adorned with a series of windows;
in its center, a square altar measuring four cubits should be constructed.
Twelve finger-breadths in height and characterized by the features of a temple seat,
one should fashion an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) above it, marked with the signs of a wheel and a lotus.
One should lay down three threads in the middle—east-west and north-south—measuring two cubits each; and having thus fashioned a square in their center.
Having fixed a thread eleven finger-breadths in length at the center, one should form a circle for the purpose of digging, by means of an external enclosure.
One should omit one finger-breadth from the lip, two finger-breadths from the circle of the pericarp,
one finger-breadth from the filaments, and two finger-breadths from the expanse of the petals.
The tip of that [spoke] should be known as one finger-breadth; it should be raised one finger-breadth above the navel.
The field of the spoke (arākṣetra) should be two finger-breadths, and the rim (nemi) should be one finger-breadth.
The girdle should be two finger-breadths [in width]; thus, by means of this arrangement of enclosures, the measurement extends as far as the excavation, reaching from the girdle to the heart.
Then, having drawn up to the edge of the rim, one should bring the fields to circularity;
the outermost girdle should be such that it becomes quadrangular.
Now hear about the construction of that two-cubit square frame:
for the sake of the excavation, one should dig evenly to the same depth as the inner circle.
One should fashion the pericarp and the other parts, ending with the rim, in sequence— either three-quarters, half, or one-quarter [of the diameter]— extending outward from the lip.
The space between the pericarp petals should be twelve finger-breadths in height;
its height should be equal to its width, and it should be provided with filaments on the outside.
One should prepare lotus petals according to the desired number;
the field equal in number to the lotuses should be on all sides of the great lotus. || 15 ||
From the center of the filaments up to the limit of the whirling of the petal-tips,
one should cast the middle-wing lines toward the east and west directions.

With a thread passing through the middle of the petal and extending upward through the center of the petal, one should mark it like a half-moon for the sake of clarifying the middle of the petal. (17)
The crescent moon, the middle [line], and those joined at the tips of the petals—
by means of the wing-line (pakṣasūtra), one should produce the tip of the petal like the point of a thunderbolt.
One should establish the individual plots together with their respective numerical divisions;
having divided the field like a petal, one should likewise stretch the measuring lines.
Having divided each [section] either eightfold or sixfold in sequence, one should discard the two side portions from the center of the outer line. || 20 ||
From the tips and the middle of the two lines established by the two maces,
one should fashion the fish-shaped mark (matsya-lāñchana) as far as the base-circumference.
Those situated on the ground should be extended outward, or else those above or on the exterior;
one should then construct [the structure] with bricks together with clay, as desired.
One should make the lower limbs as far as the waistband narrow,
equal in their width and height, even, and very firm.
The yoni, situated above the pericarp and filaments like a pipal leaf, should be made resembling a yoni, resting upon [the tongue] while touching the lip with the tongue. 24.
Having traversed the *kesara* ground with the upper finger from behind, the two crescent moons (*bālacandra*) are positioned on both sides of the central line. 25.
The earlobes are elevated at the base by one finger-breadth behind the tragus,
and they are gradually depressed from the root to the tip like the trunk of an elephant.
And in the corners of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), four conch-marks (śaṅkha) should likewise be made;
thus this has been described, which may vary in many ways according to measurement.
Starting from a measurement of twelve finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time, up to two or four cubits, there are one hundred and eighty-one [varieties]. || 28 ||
One of these has been described; indeed, it is the same for the others as well.
Having set aside the means for that [specific one], and having arranged the array of its constituent parts (aṅgavyūha), [one should proceed]. || 29 ||
Then, one should arrange the materials for the oblation in their appropriate places,
having duly consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and likewise generated the fire according to the rules.
One should sprinkle fuel and other materials with drops of consecrated clarified butter;
likewise, one should perform the satiation of the fire and the placement of mantras upon it.
The arrangement of the seat for the machine, the internal oblation,
and the descent from the heart into the seat of the great machine.
Then there is the offering with the constant fuel-sticks (samidh) and likewise with those for specific desires (kāmya),
as well as the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt and even the expiatory oblation (prāyaścittāhuti).
Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the principal rite, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana) of the deity residing in the yantra;
then, entering the pavilion which is the site of sacrifice, one should [dismiss] the deity residing in the heart.
And there was the dedication of the oblation to the ancestors, as well as their libation, and the offering of bali to the spirits with the rice remaining from the sacrifice. || 35 ||
The giving of gifts by those who are devoted to sacrifice, who act with purpose, and whose selves are purified;
as well as the subsequent sacrifice performed according to rule, including the consumption of the sacrificial offering (naivedya) and so forth. || 36 ||
One should perform everything as before for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, by means of this king of yantras in rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others. || 37 ||
By means of meditation, worship, burnt offerings, and recitation, the desires of devoted ones whose souls are purified are fulfilled. (38)
This single form of meditation is described for rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others; in the fire-oblation (homa), the mantra ending in "svāhā" is always superior by its very nature. (39)

In rites for peace (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), as well as in the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), it is likewise; "vaṣaṭ" is prescribed for the rite of satiation (āpyāyana), and "hum" ending [the mantra] is used for the rite of subjugation (vaśya).
The mantra ending in *phaṭ* is always used for the rites of destruction, inciting enmity, and eradication;
that ending in *hum* is for the enmity of enemies; and that ending in *huṃ phaṭ* is for delusion.
For the rite of immobilization, it should end with "vaṣaṭ"; for the rite of liberation, it should end with "svāhā.
This is for the welfare of the worlds, and especially for kings.
Having observed it there according to the prescribed rites, Ahirbudhnya explained this in detail to the inquiring Nārada, exactly as he had been instructed.
It should be employed in many ways; one who desires peace may act according to his wish.
One should construct a single-faced yantra, install it, and worship it. (44)
Indeed, the occasional rites, the optional rites, and the obligatory sacrifices must be performed with special care, except during sleep and great festivals. (45)
In the case of obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites and so forth, one should not worship the ritual images;
rather, the established machine (yantra), installed by the most excellent knowers of mantra, is to be worshipped.
When the divine and other sense-bases have been established somewhere,
one should perform worship up to the final oblation, distinguishing between the mobile and the immobile.
On the twelfth lunar day and other such auspicious times, as well as on various other holy occasions—thus has the supreme worship of the great yantra been correctly described. (48)
This must be guarded with great effort from those who are uninitiated, those who are not disciples according to the rules, the evil-minded, and those who lack devotion to Janārdana. (49)
For those endowed with devotion in essence, regarding the signified and the signifier, the teacher, and the scripture— endowed with knowledge and action, sattvic, and equal to the Vedas— (50)
Reveal this to those in whom faith has arisen.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire-Rite in the Worship of the Great Sudarśana Yantra," in the Kriyākāṇḍa of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pārameśvara Saṃhitā.
